Was world-renowned molecular biologist David Sabatini a manipulative mentor who coerced a younger colleague into sex and cultivated a hostile work culture at his research lab in Cambridge? Or was he the victim of a spurned former lover and a #MeToo movement gone too far?
A dozen jurors in Boston are weighing these starkly opposing interpretations following a bruising, three-week civil trial that exposed the intense power dynamics and permissive sexual norms inside the world-famous Whitehead Institute, where Sabatini ran his own laboratory. Standing between the jury and a verdict are scores of hours of conflicting testimony, bitter recriminations, and a vast trove of unfiltered texts exchanged by two brilliant scientists.
The yearslong feud offers a rare window into the insular world of top-tier science labs, where directors wield outsized authority. It also highlights a broader challenge confronting modern workplaces: How to maintain professional boundaries within close-knit, diverse teams as behavioral standards evolve.

“It definitely makes you wonder truly who is the real monster in the situation.”
Director Yûta Shimotsu is describing events in a new episode of live-action J-horror anthology show Strange: Junji Ito's Tales for Sleepless Nights, but he could be referring to almost any episode.
The award-winning manga artist of the title, whose macabre short works are adapted into disturbing 30-minute bites, has a way of blurring lines between protagonist and antagonist amid his surreal nightmares.
Tales for Sleepless Nights aired its 12-episode first season on TV Tokyo this summer, and now HBO Max is bringing those eerie frights to US audiences. The first two installments “Lovesickness (Part 1 of 3)” and “The Bully” (previously animated for Netflix’s Junji Ito Maniac) are currently available, but New York Comic Con fans were treated to the US premiere of the episode “Face Thief” based on Ito’s story “The Face Burglar.”
“Face Thief,” which was previously turned into a Japanese TV movie in 2000, follows the new girl in school, Machida (Nanami Yamazaki), who encounters a weirdly clingy classmate named Kamei (Anna Hoshino). After she sees an identical-looking girl in class who claims she is not related to Kamei, Machida learns this changeling’s MO: “She befriends cute girls then steals their faces.” Indeed, Kamei’s face begins shifting during close conversations with Machida. This repulses the new girl at first, but when Kamei scares away some bullies by growing a third eyeball on her cheek, the two start to bond.
We will not spoil the outcome, but the filmmaker turns it into a biting critique of the conformity and peer pressure common in Japanese society. As he told the crowd after the premiere, “We have social pressure that we are supposed to not to be too different from others. Individuality is not very respected.”
Despite Shimotsu’s desire to shape-shift the story by “changing the ending so my live-action version was different,” “Face Thief” still manages to capture the slow burn feel of the original comic published in the pages of Monthly Halloween in 1987, the same year Ito’s famous debut Tomie appeared. That shōjo (for girls) manga magazine’s offshoot Nemuki (“Strange Stories of Sleepless Nights") inspired the new TV omnibus’s title.
Junji Ito himself, now a bespectacled 63-year-old, appeared before NYCC in a video message where he described “Face Burglar” as an early tale he came up with after several unsuccessful stories submitted to his publishers: “Not a ghost, just a unique condition inspired by chameleon camouflage.” Ito added that the new adaptation for Tales for Sleepless Nights was “brought to life by a fresh team of upcoming actors and directors. Rather than jump scares, it builds a slow creeping dream perfect for horror.”
Another means through which Shimotsu (Best Wishes to All, Shudder’s New Group) finds the essence of Ito in all the episodes he helmed is through stillness in the performances and camerawork that evokes the comic book pages. He told a fan that he hopes to push fidelity to the material one step further in season 2 by shooting at least one episode in black-and-white, Ito’s preferred mode of illustration.
When asked by a con attendee which of Ito’s works he would most like to adapt next, the director earned applause by answering Uzumaki, the groundbreaking horror manga which has been brought to the screen several times, including a recent 4-part anime series for Adult Swim. The latter version had a famously rocky production, with quality diving after the first episode to the point that the fourth installment had no director credit. A new live-action version would be incredible—and incredibly strange—in Yûta Shimotsu’s hands.
“I would love to keep creating very bizarre, unique aesthetics like Mr. Ito's work. That's my goal,” said Shimotsu. “I'm developing a Hollywood project, so see you soon.”

Scottish teen chases judo dreams through unique Japanese homestay
Two-time Judo Grand Slam gold medalist Takeshi Sasaki (left) and his wife, Mako, have welcomed Lexi Buchanan into their home with their two children during her trip to Japan.
| Courtesy of Lexi Buchanan
Japan has long served as a destination for martial artists seeking to test themselves against the country’s deep pool of judo talent, but few make the trip alone at age 17.
Without corporate sponsors or a national team delegation behind her, Scottish judoka Lexi Buchanan arrived in Japan last month on a self-driven, three-month mission. Her objective was specific: solve the single biggest hurdle stalling her development back home — a lack of female sparring partners.
“Judo Scotland has very few girls,” Buchanan said. “In my last competition, I competed at 48 kilos, and the next girls were around 63 kilos and upwards.”

Why Rwanda's deal for F1 race remains controversial
- Published
Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time in a generation after Rwanda agreed a 10-year contract to stage a race, with the sport's governing body (FIA) keen to create a "lasting legacy".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, with the first edition in the "early 2030s".
For Rwandan President Paul Kagame, the ambition is to "pave the way" for other F1 races on the continent.
However, the announcement has drawn criticism from some quarters amid allegations of sportswashing and questions around the East African country's human rights record.
Why is this big news?
Africa has not hosted an F1 race since 1993, and the clamour to return to the continent has been growing in recent years - with seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton among those leading the calls.
Morocco was the first African nation to host a Grand Prix in 1958 and 23 races were then held in South Africa between 1962 and 1993.
President Kagame said it was "an honour and privilege" for Rwanda to be chosen for its return.
"This partnership is long overdue but it is a success and a milestone for the entire continent - especially for African fans," he added.
South Africa had been keen to secure its own F1 race, and sports minister Gayton McKenzie remains bullish about his country's hopes of emulating Rwanda.
"They have worked on it longer than SA and deserve it," he posted on X.
"Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two [F1 races] a year, and some react like a continent of [54] countries can only get one. SA will get F1, even before 2030."
- Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993 
  - Published1 day ago
- A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1? 
  - Published1 day ago
What is still to be decided?
The year of the first African Grand Prix in the 2030s, and its timing in the calendar, are yet to be announced.
F1 is likely to want to avoid holding the race in Rwanda's main rainy season of March to May, while there is a shorter, less disruptive, rainy season from October to November.
The sport is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Former F1 driver Alex Wurz will be involved in the design of the circuit, which is due to use the undulating Rwandan landscape to produce a track with a natural flow and elevation changes of nearly 200m to challenge drivers.
Could the race boost African participation?
Jody Sheckter remains the only African to win the F1 Drivers' Championship, triumphing in 1979 with Ferrari.
"It's so expensive to get in," the South African told Newsday on the BBC World Service when discussing whether or not the race in Rwanda could open the door to more drivers from the continent.
"I built my own cars at the beginning. You can't do that anymore."
Africans hoping for a career in motorsport have previously had to chase their dream overseas, according to fellow driver Axcil Jefferies, who has previously competed in Formula 2.
But the Zimbabwean believes that could now change.
"F1 coming to Africa will highlight to everyone what a big industry motorsport is," he said.
"All the elements will inspire the youth, whether that's to come in as an engineer, as a mechanic, as drivers, as team coordinators."
South African presenter Kriya Gangiah, who hosts SuperSport's F1 Extra Africa Trackside podcast, is also hopeful of a boost in the number of female fans and drivers in Africa.
"The more you see something and the more that is present in your world, the more you take interest in it," she said.
"Being in paddocks in South Africa, you're seeing the amount of women that are making it into the sport and are actually doing really well. A lot of the girls are giving the guys a proper run for their money."
Why is the deal controversial?
Allegations of sportswashing - hosting sporting events to improve a country's international reputation - have long been levelled against Rwanda.
Securing an F1 race is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment.
The country has hosted the Basketball Africa League finals in all but one year since 2021 and staged cycling's World Road Championships last year, the first time the event had been held in Africa.
Visit Rwanda has either sponsored or had partnerships with Arsenal, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain, although its sleeve sponsorship of the Gunners ended this year after drawing criticism from supporter groups.
However, the tourism brand then became the front-of-shirt sponsor of fellow Premier League club Aston Villa.
Meanwhile, Rwanda's central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
Human Rights Watch previously said that "the space for freedom of expression" and "political autonomy" is shrinking in the country.
"Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record," said Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns Felix Jakens.
"A 10-year Grand Prix 'presented by Visit Rwanda' is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities."
The Rwandan government has dismissed such accusations, with chief tourism officer Irene Murerwa calling them "a distraction' from the "amazing and outstanding achievements the country has made" when previously challenged by BBC Sport Africa.
"The benefits trickle down to every Rwandan," she said in December 2024. "Hosting F1 would be another step in our journey to becoming a world-class destination."
What has F1 said?
F1 is not blind to issues around sportswashing, with several countries on the calendar accused of utilising the strategy - not least Saudi Arabia.
F1's own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders.
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
However, it has still drawn criticism from human rights organisations, with Amnesty International's Jakens believing the organisation's words "ring hollow".
"It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise," he said.
When asked about the sportswashing accusations levelled against Rwanda when it was bidding to host a race, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem told BBC Sport Africa: "When people cannot get what they want, they always blame it on sportswashing.
"I honestly don't care about what they say."

Seventy-three years ago, Washington decided that an elected prime minister was bad for the oil market.
Mohammad Mossadegh had nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, the forerunner of BP. In August 1953, he was overthrown. For decades, the United States played down its part. Then in 2013 the CIA’s internal history, released under freedom of information law, stated that the coup was carried out “under CIA direction as an act of U.S. foreign policy.” The shah it restored ruled until 1979 — and Iranian politics still carries the scar.
On Oct. 10, U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.” His grievance had nothing to do with corruption or battlefield losses. Volodymyr Zelenskyy kept hitting Russian refineries, and Trump says that hurts American farmers and ranchers who need diesel. “He better damn well stop,” Trump added.

For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.
His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.
“Even my mother calls me Shang now,” the 32-year-old, born Tobi Michael Adeyeye, said in an interview near the university’s lagoon waterfront, where he once emceed gatherings.
Since then he has hosted his own rave, released two EPs and run four editions of his School of Hype – a one-day masterclass with online mentoring that has launched several rising stars.
Hypemen neither sing nor rap entirely, but perform high-octane ad-libbed vocals “and onomatopoeic sounds” over fresh beats or popular instrumentals such as Dorime, a made-in-Nigeria version of 1996’s Ameno by the French group Era, a song that has become a continental nightclub classic. In response, nightclub patrons donate or spray money – the Nigerian custom of throwing or placing money on someone to celebrate them.
Hype is now omnipresent at wedding after-parties, raves and corporate parties. On Instagram, one teenage sensation is now known for recording 30-second hypes for birthday celebrants at the request of friends or relatives.
“Hypemen have the gift of the gab and fine mic control,” said the London-based doctor and cultural critic Dami Ajayi, who encountered one at a party in Tirana last month. “He used the spaces between lyrics for hilarious quips, many of which were frontally risque and misogynistic,” he said.
Despite being a male-dominated sub-genre, a few women have made their mark, such as the Yaoundé-based bikutsi artist Lady Ponce, known as the “100,000-volt lady” because of her energy. Other notable female figures in the scene include Deborah ‘Hype Queen Baddy’ Francis – an alumnus of Shang’s school who died in September – and the radio presenter Melody “M.I.A” Adigo, both from Lagos.
The art of hyping as it is known in west and central Africa has its roots in praise-singing and call-and-response music styles ingrained for centuries in Black populations on both sides of the Atlantic. In west Africa, this tradition took the form of oral historians known as griots. In the US, it was sustained by negro spirituals, sacred folk songs created by enslaved African Americans.
These styles laid the foundation for the atalaku (meaning “look here, look at me” in the Kikongo language of the DR Congo) tradition that came alive in 1980s Kinshasa, followed by today’s hype scene.
Exponents of this style include the American gospel singer Kirk Franklin as well as the Congolese rumba bandleader Koffi Olomide and the Congolese singer Awilo Longomba.
The success of Olomide and Longomba at the turn of the 21st century set off a craze in Côte d’Ivoire, where coupé-décalé music embraced the atalaku trend alongside farotement, the act of showing off by throwing cash at performers or guests at parties.
A line encouraging audiences to gallop like a horse in the Ivorian star DJ Arafat’s 2003 viral homage to a late friend – “Tout le monde galope, kirikata kirikata” – influenced later hits from Nigerian Afrobeats musicians Flavour N’abania and Skales.
Côte d’Ivoire’s national television network, RTI, ran an atalaku talent hunt for several years. Lili Djely, an Ivorian woman of Malian origin, won the 2006 edition with a mix of Ivorian nouchi and French, defeating men to take the crown. In recent years, an MC/hypeman of the year category was introduced at the Ghana DJ awards as hype flourished there too.
Thanks to the success of Afrobeats, Afrohype is now widely recognised as a full-time career. As artists became more expensive to book after Covid-19, promoters turned to hypemen – previously criticised for simply doing voiceovers. Some are now reportedly paid as much as 5-8m naira (£2,844–4,550) for a 30-minute or one-hour performance.
Some observers, however, say hype is a nuisance, amping up noise levels at events or encouraging fraudulent lifestyles, and that many performers do not customise language and tempo to fit the event.
Nevertheless, hypemen are now a permanent fixture on the entertainment scene. For Shang, they are helping fun-seekers and club-goers get back on the dancefloor.
“People are facing a lot of challenges … they need somebody to tell them money is coming in the new week,” he said. “Also, everybody wants to press their phones or show Birkin bags in clubs. Nobody wants to dance because dancing is seen as for small kids. You need a hypeman to bring out that childlike part in every person. A 60-year-old woman can start dancing like a young girl if the hype is good enough.”

Classy premium design. Sensational image quality, brightness, and black levels. Google TV makes for a simple setup. Great remote. Superb connectivity and compatibility.
TIRED
Given the competition, it’s too expensive for an all-in-one projector. Audio performance does not match the picture quality. Too much projector for casual use.
Valerion’s VisionMaster Kickstarter campaign raised more than $8 million in 2024, making it the most-funded campaign on the platform that year. After spending the past few weeks with the flagship VisionMaster Max, I’m confident there are plenty of satisfied backers.
At $3,999, it costs far more than excellent point-and-play rivals, such as the Nebula X1 (9/10 WIRED Recommends), but considerably less than native 4K home-theater projectors from brands like Sony and JVC. That leaves the Max straddling two very different camps.
Its compact design, built-in Google TV, and automated setup suggest the classification of a premium lifestyle projector, while optical zoom, vertical lens shift, a mechanical iris, and sophisticated black-level processing point toward something far more capable. It’s easy to use and almost too pretty to ceiling-mount, but arguably too sophisticated to spend its life propped up on a side table. So the question remains: Who is the VisionMaster Max actually for?
Setting Up Shop
Photograph: Chris Haslam
The 16.5-pound VisionMaster Max is simple to get up and running. Google TV grants instant access to many streaming services, while auto-keystone and autofocus make positioning a frictionless process. (However, because keystone correction digitally reshapes the image, when used heavily, it can reduce resolution—but that's true for all devices with the feature.) Optical zoom, with a 0.9 to 1.5:1 throw ratio, lets you resize the picture without moving the projector. There's also vertical lens shift, which moves the image up or down without needing to resort to digital correction. All of this means that if you’ve got a blank wall and five minutes, you can stream Emily in Paris on a 90-inch screen in no time.
It’s clever tech, though not fully unique, with the XGIMI Horizon range and Nebula X1 offering similar optical-image manipulation. Even so, the VisionMaster Max offers considerably more control than most point-and-play designs. Praise is also due for the remote, which looks and feels great. Many brands scrimp on details like accessories, but Valerion maintains its premium feel throughout.
Looks Great, Sounds OK
Photograph: Chris Haslam
The VisionMaster Max produces a seriously bright image. Its 3,500 ISO lumen RGB triple-laser light source easily projected a 75-inch picture I could happily watch during the day in a bright room. Valerion says it’s good for images between 40 and 300 inches. I maxed out at 130 inches but was impressed by how even the detail remained right to the edges at that size.
While I watched during the day, the colors appeared a bit washed out in this environment, but much less so than I expected. Once I watched in the dark, however, I enjoyed punchy high-dynamic-range (HDR) highlights, excellent detail, and smooth motion.
In terms of color, the Max has 110 percent Rec.2020 coverage, meaning the lasers can reproduce an exceptionally wide range of colors, far exceeding the needs for ultra-high-definition (UHD) and HDR video. In my living room, colors looked rich without becoming cartoonish, while the combination of brightness, detail, and contrast gave movies cinematic quality.
Black levels with most home projectors are good, but not brilliant. Here, however, the proprietary six-stage iris self-adjusts the aperture from scene to scene, closing for darker images to deepen blacks, and opening up when a scene calls for more brightness. Enhanced Black Level (EBL) works alongside the iris, electronically reducing laser output in darker scenes, adjusting the image curve to maintain details. Together, these features dramatically reduce the charcoal-gray blacks common with this type of projector. I was astonished by the depth and shadow detail it produced without losing brighter details. Even the film The Dark Knight, with its muted color grading, looked good.
Photograph: Chris Haslam
Though I didn't put the VisionMaster Max through its paces for video-game testing (I’m not much of a gamer, unless you count Mario Kart battles on the Nintendo Switch), the projector's specifications are nonetheless impressive. It supports refresh rates up to 240 Hz at 1080p, with claimed input lag as low as 4 milliseconds (ms); for 4K, 60-Hz gaming, that input lag is rated at 15 ms. Two HDMI 2.1 inputs and auto low-latency mode further strengthen its gaming credentials, although it lacks a variable refresh rate (VRR) to dynamically smooth out delays.
Less impressive than its picture is its sound: The VisionMaster Max has two 12-watt speakers, and audio is clean, detailed, with effects neatly separated from dialog. But it still suffers from its box form factor. To be fair, with the exception of Anker’s removable satellite speaker designs like the Nebula X1, audio fails to keep up with image quality in many lifestyle projectors. I'd contend that at this price, an all-in-one projector should provide audio that matches the pixel-perfect picture. The Max’s speakers are fine, but push it beyond level 25 of 100, and it just sounds loud.
Thankfully, since the projector supports both DTS and Dolby Atmos, you can connect it to a decent 5.1/7.1 home theater audio system. You can also wirelessly link to a Bluetooth speaker, which makes for a clean living-room setup, although latency can be an issue. For reliable synchronization and true surround sound, HDMI eARC remains the better audio option.
Competition and Verdict
Photograph: Chris Haslam
Valerion is not without stiff competition, and that includes against itself. The Nebula X1 offers a similarly simple Google TV setup and 3,500-lumen brightness, with optional wireless surround sound making it better suited to casual living-room or outdoor use. The Leica Cine Play 1 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) combines superb optics with a more lifestyle-friendly design. Valerion’s cheaper VisionMaster Pro 2 ($2,999) retains key features, including Google TV, RGB triple-laser projection, optical zoom, and EBL, but it loses the Max’s iris and vertical lens shift. For casual movie nights, I’d be happy with this compromise that keeps extra money in my pocket.
While not necessarily casual, the Max is great and likely best suited for the viewer who wants to enjoy its capabilities. Its weight, extensive picture controls, and exceptional brightness encourage a proper screen, external sound, and careful setup, where its superb black levels and cinematic image can be fully exploited.
The brand seems to agree, as it's strongly encouraging customers to go all-in with its baffling array of deals. At the time of publication, you can opt to bundle the $3,999 Max with a choice of screens and four stands—including a tripod and ceiling mount—without paying any additional fee.
It may be overkill for occasional big-screen streaming, but as a compact projector at the heart of a home theater, I highly recommend it.

Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.
The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.
Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.
But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.
“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.
“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, must strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.
He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).
The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year. Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.”
Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.
In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.
Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neo-colonialist” and “damaging”.
“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”
It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.
Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”
It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.
“The study has not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.
At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.
The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.
Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “cancelled or suspended.”
Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

Last night, with considerable showmanship, Tesla CEO Elon Musk proudly unveiled the Roadster 2 just nine years after first announcing the car, and made it “fly.” While undeniably impressive, you could also describe the spectacle as Tesla making its long-delayed luxury car “do a big hop” and then, as Buzz Lightyear would say, “fall with style.”
During the reveal in McGregor, Texas, at SpaceX’s rocket development and testing facility, the two-seater Roadster 2 launched itself over the automaker’s entire lineup, shot from 0 to 60 mph in less than a second, and then drove upside down off a high ramp to then flip over mid-air and land back down on the ground, cushioning its rapid descent using on-board thrusters.
All this was pure gold for social clips (though at the time of publication, Tesla’s stock price was down after the event), but how did Tesla make its new EV prototype perform these tricks? Tesla vehicle engineering head Lars Moravy went into detail with auto lifestyle and insurance brand Hagerty before yesterday’s event, explaining how the Roadster 2 works.
Franz von Holzhausen, Tesla’s chief designer since 2008, designed the angular exterior. He also helmed the aesthetic of the Cybertruck, Models S, X, 3 and Y, as well as the Semi. Blacked-out windows obscured any view inside the EV, which carried no human driver anyway because, as Musk said, Tesla wanted “to make sure we don’t kill anyone” during the gravity-defying demonstration.
Powertrain and Battery
The Roadster 2 will be rear-wheel drive only, a departure from Tesla’s track record of all-wheel drive EVs. Two motors will deliver over a megawatt of power (1,341 horsepower) and over 1,400 Newton-meters (Nm) of torque, meaning this car will have more torque and power than a three-motor Plaid. But all of that power goes through just the rear wheels.
The car will be light, at “just under 1,700 kilos” (under 2 tons), according to Moravy, not significantly heavier than the original 1,300 kg (1.4 tons) Roadster, despite a larger size.
Tesla claims a range of over 300 miles for the Roadster and hopes to mitigate this distinctly average range by also giving the EV the fastest-charging battery the automaker has ever produced, supposedly capable of zipping from 15 to 80 percent in 10 minutes.
Sucking Fans
At a 2013 auction, Elon Musk bought the iconic "Wet Nellie" Lotus Esprit S1 submarine car from the 1977 James Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me for just shy of $1 million. Musk is so taken with his Bond memorabilia that it apparently inspired one of the Roadster 2's key abilities.
That submarine Bond car has four propellers at its rear, so Tesla decided to ape this with four 20-kilowatt fans on the Roadster 2. Moravy says these fans break the laws of tire physics and dramatically increase the EV's traction by becoming what Tesla calls the car’s “sucker system.” Four independent replaceable skirts drop down on the sides of the car, allowing the Roadster 2 to stick (or suck) to the road at lower speeds where its aerodynamic wings aren't yet contributing to downforce. Moravy claims the system can produce over two Gs in a corner when accelerating, even below 50 mph.
This type of aerodynamic manipulation also appears on the McMurtry Spéirling Pure, which uses two high-speed electric fans spinning at up to 23,000 revolutions per minute to actively suck air from underneath the chassis, generating up to 2,000 kg (around 4,400 pounds) of downforce.
This extreme suction lets the Roadster 2 drive up the vertical ramp at the Texas demonstration and hold onto the surface even when upside down.
Rocket-Powered Thrust
So how does the Roadster 2 hover, correct itself, and dampen its fall? That's thanks to what Tesla calls the car’s “SpaceX system,” referring to Musk’s aerospace company, which helped with this part of the car’s development.
Originally, the Roadster was meant to have a 2+2 cabin. Now it’s a two-seater because behind the seats sits a 200-liter carbon-overwrapped pressure vessel (COPV) that holds up to 10,000 PSI to supply the car’s cold gas thrusters, which use expansion of pressurized nitrogen gas to generate thrust, a tech predominantly used for spacecraft stabilization. Cold gas thrusters are the simplest manifestation of a rocket engine.
This combination of suction system and thrusters helps the car hit 0 to 60 mph in supposedly under a second. In this launch mode, Moravy says the rear thrusters produce more than 80 kilonewtons of thrust, which, staggeringly, matches the Dassault Falcon 10X jet. Tesla has seemingly cracked the sub-second race, while the aforementioned McMurtry Spéirling Pure can only manage this feat in a bowel-clenching 1.3 seconds. During this astonishing acceleration, the driver will endure up to 5 Gs.
The Roadster 2's Performance model will feature the sucker system and no thrusters, so 0 to 60 will take a touch longer at 1.6 seconds and a top speed of 210 mph. The Thrust model gets the whole package and a top speed of 230 mph.
Moravy says the “flight system,” as he calls it in Hagerty’s walkthrough, requires yet another 400-liter cold gas COPV, occupying the space where the passenger seat is, making the car a single-seater and bringing total thrust fuel up to 600 liters. This “flight system” also requires six extra thrusters: one in each corner, plus two at the front to yaw.
Bursting the Balloon
Unlike in space, where cold gas thrusters provide consistent levels of thrust until the last drop of fuel is used, on Earth the “flight system” will lose thrust as the compressed gas depletes. Moravy likens it to blowing up a balloon then letting the air out: “When I open the end of a balloon, all the gas comes out, and at a certain point, it starts tapering off. That same thing will happen here.”
Apparently, refilling the 600-liter nitrogen tanks takes Tesla six to seven hours, but the company is supposedly working on a system to dramatically reduce this to 30 minutes.
The current Roadster 2 prototypes are being used for further development, and production won’t begin until 2028—but remember that Musk previously said Roadster deliveries would begin in 2020, so take this with a very large pinch of salt. That's without talking about how the Federal Aviation Administration will react to this "flying" car.
Still, for the Tesla faithful, a reservation page is already live where a $5,000 reservation fee secures the Performance variant, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days. The Thrust is available for an initial $5,000 fee, with a whopping $245,000 due within 10 days.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

NEW DELHI: India’s crude import bill surged 46% year-on-year in Sept, while import volumes rose only 7%, as oil prices remained elevated amid concerns over prolonged disruptions to supplies from West Asia.
Provisional data compiled by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) showed that India imported 21.7 million tonnes (MT) of crude in Sept, compared with 20.3 MT a year earlier. The country spent $15.4 billion on crude imports, up from $10.5 billion in Sept 2025.
Global oil prices remained elevated through the month, with the Indian crude basket touching a monthly peak of $130.19 per barrel on Sept 15. It averaged $116.09 per barrel in Sept, compared with $69.61 a year earlier and $90.19 in Aug 2026. Brent crude also averaged $116.77 per barrel during the month, up from $90.84 in Aug and $68.02 in Sept 2025.
During the first half of the 2026-27 financial year (Apr-Sept), India imported 122.7 MT of crude, marginally higher than the 121.8 MT imported during the corresponding period last year. However, the import bill jumped to $90.6 billion from $61.9 billion.
The LNG import bill remained unchanged at $1.2 billion in Sept compared with the same month last year, even as import volumes fell 8.5% to 2,957 million standard cubic metres (MMSCM) from 3,233 MMSCM.
The net oil and gas import bill rose 40% year-on-year to $13.4 billion in Sept from $9.6 billion. During the first half of the financial year, the net bill increased 35% to $81.1 billion from $60.2 billion in the corresponding period of 2025-26.

'Swelling crowd, situation worsened by rain': What we know so far about Kolkata pandal stampede
The stampede took place at Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durgotsab Samity puja pandal, a prominent puja in central Kolkata, during the peak hours on Saturday evening.
Durga Puja festivities in Kolkata turned tragic on Saturday after a stampede-like situation left at least 18 dead, while several others are said to be injured. The incident took place at Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durgotsab Samity puja pandal, a prominent puja in central Kolkata, during the peak hours on Saptami evening, police said.
Track live updates on Kolkata stampede
While the exact cause of the crowd crush is yet to be ascertained, eyewitnesses said that the surging crowd and rainfall worsened the situation.
“The incident took place around 7:30 pm. The crowd at the pandal was already swelling. As it started to rain more people entered the pandal. This resulted in a stampede. Several people were injured,” Dipali Das, a pandal hopper, told the media.
Deep Dive
Another eyewitness alleged mismanagement and said that people pushing each other in absence of organisers, volunteers and police personnel.
“There were no puja organsier, no police and no volunteer. Everyone was pushing each other and shouting. Many fell ill,” said Saikat Banerjee, another pandal hopper.
As leaders expressed grief over the loss of lives in the Kolkata pandal stampede, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced ₹2 lakh ex-gratia to next of kin of each deceased and ₹50,000 for injured. “Stampede in Kolkata extremely distressing; my thoughts with people who have lost loved ones,” PM Modi said.
Meanwhile, Union home minister Amit Shah Union is expected to visit injured in hospitals on Sunday, news agency PTI reported.
What the authorities said
The incident occurred at around 7:40 pm, and the pandal has now been closed to visitors, news agency ANI reported, citing Kolkata Police.
"Today at around 7:40 pm, a stampede occurred at the exit gate of Sarada Park (Chor Bagan) Puja Pandal, under Girish Park Police Station, due to heavy crowds of pandal hoppers amid rainfall. The Puja Pandal has now been closed to visitors. All injured persons were rescued and shifted to MCH for treatment," the police said.
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari and chief secretary Manoj Agarwal visited the hospitalised injured at Calcutta Medical College and Hospital.

Researchers say that mercenary hackers laced ads with zero-click exploits that installed sophisticated malware on the devices of targeted individuals when they did nothing other than load a website or open an installed app.
The finding, published Thursday by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, said the incident is likely to be the first confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The attacks, which worked on iOS and Android devices, are particularly pernicious because they work without requiring any interaction from the target and are invisible unless users run special forensic hardware or software. Citizen Lab said it confirmed that AdFection, as it named the campaign, infected 45 devices at international media organization Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025.
A clear warning signal
“This investigation should … serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat,” Citizen Lab researchers wrote. “This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members.” Their report went on to say: “The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large.”
The ads were provided by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that brands itself as a legitimate advertising company, but Citizen Lab said it operates as a facilitator for multiple mercenary spyware partners. The company acts as a broker between parties that want to display their ads and publishers or app makers that seek revenue in return for showing them. In this capacity, Discover-Tech acts as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem,” a role that appears to be “Discover-Tech’s primary purpose,” Citizen Lab said.
The brokering involves a bidding process in which advertisers offer a fee in exchange for their ads appearing on the devices of individuals in particular demographics. Using users’ unique mobile ID, location, IP address, and other breadcrumbs, the brokers are able to assemble detailed profiles of millions of people. Citizen Lab said it obtained more than 4 billion bidding records handled by Discover-Tech. They revealed that Discover-Tech ads were displayed in over 70,000 mobile apps and more than 120,000 websites between March and June 2026.

An effective response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic requires the understanding and use of social and behavioural data alongside biomedical data. Recognizing this need, the Behavioural Insights and Sciences Unit of the World Health Organization (WHO) and the WHO Regional Office for Africa (AFRO) designed a survey tool tailored to Africa, to make it easier for countries to collect context-specific social and behavioural data. The objective was to inform the COVID-19 response at the country level while also allowing regional comparisons. This case study describes how the tool was adapted and used in a pilot study in Nigeria and Zambia and complements the WHO guidance on how to use the tool.

The Department of Justice has a warning for health care executives: Don’t be another Theranos.
As the Trump administration continues its fight against Medicare and Medicaid fraud, it is also expanding its investigations into corporate wrongdoing, DOJ officials announced this month.
A key part of that plan is making it easier for companies themselves to report potential criminal activity, and encouraging whistleblowing, Jacob Foster, deputy assistant attorney general in the National Fraud Enforcement division, said Thursday at the STAT Summit in Boston. Foster oversees the unit that investigates health care fraud.
“There’s nothing more that we want to know when a compliance failure occurs than to hear about the great efforts to remediate it, and reward that,” he said.
Going forward, companies in the health care sector looking to file voluntary self-disclosures will find a one-stop shop at the DOJ, Foster said. They previously would’ve had to navigate a separate process at the Department of Health and Human Services, but that is now being consolidated under the health care fraud section at the DOJ.
“What do you do? Who do you call? That is a question that industry should not have to ask,” Foster said.
Under the new policy, companies that report potential criminal misconduct can reap the benefits — such as a limited cap on financial damages — from both agencies at once.
The health care fraud section at the DOJ brings a range of expertise under one roof to handle issues like the emerging field of digital health technology, Foster said. DOJ will make use of data analytics and artificial intelligence algorithms to try and suss out instances of corporate wrongdoing, like providers billing for unneeded services, companies fabricating patient records, or health tech companies adding redundant diagnoses.
The department will also design new programs that “appropriately incentivize” whistleblowers to report fraud, according to an Oct. 1 memo from Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald. Health care investigators also look at social media, news reports, and other sources of information to learn about companies possibly breaking the law, Foster said.
Prosecutors will place extra emphasis on schemes involving health care, controlled substances, and violations of the federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the McDonald memo said. They will also place “great weight” on factors like whether corporate executives knew about or tried to conceal fraud, ran a scheme for over three years or across various states, or affected taxpayer-funded programs, new guidance said.
“No one, irrespective of party, likes the government being ripped off by wrongdoers,” Foster said Thursday. “These cases not only involve the theft of all of our tax dollars, [but] involve the theft from a program, a trust fund — Medicare — that could run out.”

Marking the 30th anniversary of software developer KDE on October 14, the company released Plasma 6.8, debuted a movie, and retired Plasma’s native X11 session support. The announcement from KDE dubs the new Plasma 6.8 as the “30th Anniversary Edition” and describes the update as preparing Plasma for the future. Legacy X11 applications will still function via the XWayland compatibility layer, and KDE applications will also continue supporting X11 under other desktop environments.
After 42 years in service, the X11 protocol is losing another major desktop environment. Plasma will fully adopt the Wayland system and put support for starting new X11 sessions in Plasma to bed. Users opting to stay on Plasma 6.7 will keep their existing sessions for now. The move was expected, with GNOME officially dropping X11 sessions by default in 2025.
The new Plasma 6.8 brings many improvements, including increased support for adding window decorations (like shadows and rounded corners) to third-party apps, and a more streamlined Union theming system. Other notable additions include Nvidia triple buffering being enabled by default, Kup backup integration (KDE’s backup utility—now integrated into Plasma), and kscreenctl, a command-line utility that allows power users to adjust display configurations.

Early voting in the U.S. midterm elections is underway. Voters are deciding which party will control Congress, as well as numerous state legislatures and governors' offices. Snopes' fact-checkers are flagging rumors surrounding the election, debunking false statements by candidates and suspicious voter fraud claims with nonpartisan research and expert sources. Join our effort to keep this election fact-focused by becoming a Snopes member.
- Persistent claims of ballots being lost in fires have surfaced during election cycles in recent years.
- For example, in 2020 and 2021, Snopes investigated what turned out to be false rumors of intentional ballot burnings in Virginia and Arizona. In 2024, the FBI said hundreds of midterm election ballots burned overnight in ballot drop boxes in Oregon and Washington. In 2026, a county clerk's office in Los Angeles reported that a small number of mail-in ballots had burned in a ballot drop box.
- Our analysis of claims about ballot fires found that legitimate, verified events in recent years were all fires in ballot drop boxes, suggesting that was the most likely way a ballot could be damaged in a fire. Such fires are rare but difficult to prevent. It can be challenging for elections officials to locate voters whose ballots are damaged beyond recognition.
- However, our analysis also found elections officials are preparing for the challenge as best they can by updating ballot drop box security measures. Voters can also help by tracking the status of their ballots so they can get a replacement if theirs is damaged in a fire.
- Readers should treat reports of ballot burning that are not ballot drop box fires with suspicion. We will attempt to investigate such rumors as they surface during the 2026 election cycle.
In 2024, hundreds of midterm election ballots burned overnight in ballot boxes overnight in Oregon and Washington. According to the FBI, someone placed improvised incendiary devices two ballot drop boxes in Vancouver, Washington, between 3:30 and 4 a.m. Oct. 8 and one drop box in Portland, Oregon, between 2 and 4 a.m. Oct. 28.
The incidents appeared to materialize fears about a form of election tampering that had played on the public consciousness prior to 2024 and even inspired an episode of the TV drama "Succession" in 2023.
During summer 2026, a county clerk's office in Los Angeles also reported that a small number of mail-in ballots had been fire-damaged inside a ballot drop box days before the state's June primary elections.
Though actual, verified instances of ballot burning are rare, voter fears about legitimate votes going uncounted this way will undoubtedly resurface during the 2026 midterm elections. Incidents like the ones in Oregon, Washington and California raise legitimate questions about what happens when criminals attempt to tamper with democratic elections and how both voters and officials can ensure that every vote is counted.
Real instances of ballot burnings can also stoke existing fears of election tampering and encourage the spread of misinformation. For example, in 2020 and 2021, Snopes debunked rumors about ballot-burning in Virginia and Arizona. These incidents were not ballot box fires and turned out to be either refuted or unproven, but spoke to real voter concerns. In our research, Snopes has not encountered a reported and verified incident of ballot burning that was not a ballot box fire, suggesting that ballot drop box fires are the most likely way a ballot can burn.
Drop boxes most-common source of ballot fires
The legitimate incidents of ballot burning that Snopes encountered from previous election cycles all happened in ballot drop boxes. A ballot drop box is a container where voters can drop mail-in or absentee ballots after filling them out.
According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 29 states and Washington, D.C., explicitly allow the use of ballot drop boxes in elections and 11 states explicitly prohibit them. Six states do not have statues explicitly about drop boxes, but some jurisdictions use them. Four states do not have legislation governing ballot drop boxes and do not use them.
While the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency provides guidelines for the use of ballot drop boxes, individual states determine how, when and where to use them. The NCSL wrote that "drop boxes may be supervised or unsupervised with security features, such as cameras, locks and fire suppression systems."
CISA issued special guidelines about ballot drop boxes and incendiary devices after the incidents in Oregon and Washington in 2024. The agency suggested that states consider emptying the boxes more often and installing video surveillance and fire suppression systems.
How officials mitigate drop box fires
Out of the three ballot drop boxes burned in Washington and Oregon in 2024, the one in Portland reportedly already had a fire suppression system installed, meaning only three ballots were damaged.
Elections officials reportedly contacted the voters whose ballots burned to issue replacements.
However, the fires in Vancouver, Washington, destroyed "hundreds" of ballots. At the time, Clark County Auditor Greg Kimsey issued a statement to voters asking them to check whether their ballot had been received if they deposited it at a certain drop box in a certain time frame.
At the time of the fire in the early hours of Oct. 28, it had been more than a day since elections authorities had last emptied one drop box that burned. Because ballots dropped in drop boxes have usually not been processed by elections officials, there is no sure way to know to whom damaged ballots belong (unless identifying details are still legible).
Kimsey told Snopes via email in October 2026 that approximately 500 ballots burned in the 2024 fires in Washington. Of those, Kimsey said, all but 19 voters got replacement ballots and submitted their votes
Kimsey said the elections board duplicated the 19 missing ballots but "due to the damage we were unable to determine the voters' choices for all offices and issues on the ballots."
Ultimately, though the ballot drop box fires in Clark County in 2024 were destructive, officials were able to ensure that the vast majority of the affected votes were counted.
In October 2026, CNN reported that Clark County had upgraded its ballot drop boxes following the 2024 attacks. The new boxes, CNN reported, "include technology that sends a text message to officials if the temperature inside the box rises above a certain temperature, if the box receives a forceful blow or if it's removed from its geo-fenced location." Kimsey confirmed this information to Snopes.
Aside from better fire suppression technology, CNN reported that elections officials in Pennsylvania, Illinois and California had invested in ballot drop boxes that photographed people dropping off ballots and scanned the ballot return envelope, meaning officials would know which ballots were in a given box at a given time.
Along with fire suppressant technology, the data the updated ballot drop boxes collected would make it possible for officials to contact affected voters directly in the event of a ballot box fire.
In sum, while ballot drop box fires do pose a threat to voters, elections officials have multiple ways to prevent or mitigate their effects. Our analysis suggests that readers should treat reports of ballot burning that is not a ballot drop box fire with suspicion. We will attempt to investigate such rumors as they surface during the 2026 election cycle.
For further reading about common election-related claims, Snopes has previously reported on whether poll workers can mark your ballot or how vote spikes affect elections.

Coe aims for African 'legacy' with 2029 World Championships
- Published
World Athletics president Sebastian Coe hopes holding the 2029 World Championships in Nairobi will create a "legacy" for Africa.
The Kenyan capital will become the first city on the continent to stage the event, having been awarded hosting rights last month ahead of London and Rome.
After the East African nation failed with a bid for the 2025 edition, Coe reiterated it was "the right time" for World Athletics to tread new ground.
"All our instincts - and certainly mine - was to have that opportunity to build our sport to an even higher level in the continent," Coe told BBC Focus on Africa.
"The legacy behind it is important because it's a hard legacy of a new facility, but it's also the softer legacy, the human capital that you build up, because it's really important that countries are able to deliver those championships and more championships going forward.
"That's the legacy of experience and expertise."
- How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships 
  - Published15 September
It will be a big few years for Kenya, given the country will also co-host football's Africa Cup of Nations alongside neighbours Tanzania and Uganda in 2027.
The Kasarani Stadium is undergoing renovations ahead of next year's tournament, and will then also act as the venue for the 2029 World Championships.
Coe, who visited Kenya on Wednesday to meet the country's President William Ruto, says "a lot" needs to be done for the nation to be ready to welcome the globe's top athletes.
"I would be saying that at this stage to any host city that has been given the opportunity to deliver our sport," Coe added.
"The World Championships is hugely important to World Athletics. It accounts for over 90% of our revenues and those revenues are critical because it allows us to build our development programmes, our competition programmes, new formats, innovation, certainly to fund as well as we possibly can our member federations.
"A World Championships is complicated. There are 46 different disciplines, it's over nine days, 2,000 athletes, and you want the kind of operational integration that gives every opportunity for the athlete to perform as well as they possibly can.
"All our challenges, whether it's government, whether it's the local organising committee, whether it's the federation, whether it's World Athletics, our overall objective must be to provide the best possible environment for the athletes, and the fans will appreciate it as well."
Catching the 'fish' who dope
One other area Kenya can improve on is its record on doping.
Since 2017 over 140 of its athletes, predominantly distance runners, have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU), the independent body which Coe helped set up when he was first elected World Athletics president in the same year.
Earlier this month Witold Banka, the president of the World Anti-Doping Agency, told the BBC that Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain credibility ahead of hosting the World Championships.
However, Coe is confident that Kenya is beginning to turn the corner.
"I am always worrying about all issues related to integrity in our sport," the former Olympic 1500m champion said.
"It wasn't that long ago that I persuaded [Kenya's] government to put even more [funding] in anti-doping programmes, and that's beginning to work.
"The challenge, of course, is the more tests you do, and the greater levels of funding, and the more sophisticated you become with the technology, the more you're probably going to catch.
"If you want to catch fish, you have to go fishing. And I think over the long haul, we will see that number starting to reduce.
"We've certainly seen it in track. There still remains some challenges in the road events."

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made a ritual masakaki tree stand offering to war-related Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo on Saturday, the start of its autumn festival.
She offered the masakaki in her capacity as prime minister.
Takaichi is expected to skip a visit to the Shinto shrine during the three-day festival, which runs through Monday. She did not visit the shrine during its spring festival in April or on the Aug. 15 anniversary of Japan’s surrender in World War II.
Yasukuni Shrine is regarded by countries such as China and South Korea as a symbol of Japan’s wartime militarism as it honors Class-A war criminals along with the country’s war dead.
Among members of her Cabinet, Minoru Kiuchi, minister in charge of growth strategy, visited the shrine Saturday and made a tamagushi cash offering at his own expense.
“I offered my sincere condolences to the spirits of those who sacrificed their precious lives for their homeland and expressed my deep respect for them,” he told reporters.
Takayuki Kobayashi, policy chief of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, also visited the shrine Saturday.
Lower House Speaker Eisuke Mori, Upper House President Masakazu Sekiguchi and health minister Kenichiro Ueno, meanwhile, also made masakaki offerings.
Takaichi on Saturday attended a memorial ceremony at the Defense Ministry near the shrine, for Self-Defense Forces personnel who died on duty.
Sources close to the prime minister declined to comment on whether she prayed toward the shrine while there, as she did on Aug. 15 from a parking area following a national war anniversary ceremony at the Nippon Budokan, about 500 meters away from the shrine.
She had continued to visit the shrine during its festivals, including when she was serving as a Cabinet minister, but has not done so since the autumn festival in October last year, shortly before taking office as prime minister.
She appears to be prioritizing diplomatic relations with China, which have been strained by her remarks on a possible contingency involving Taiwan, as well as with South Korea, with which relations have been improving.

US Vice-President JD Vance on Sunday clarified his remarks where he had referred to H-1B visa workers as “foreign indentured servants”, while invoking his South Indian wife and in-laws.

The Donald Trump-led administration had, earlier this month, announced suspension of several firms, including Indian IT companies, from Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, which is the first step to getting a green card. PERM allows companies to sponsor a foreigner who has been working in the US under the H-1B and other visa holders to become a legal permanent resident.
Among the companies suspended from the program were Microsoft, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. Announcing the suspension, Vance had urged US companies to hire more American workers and to “stop importing an indentured servant to do a job that an American worker would happily do.”

‘Immigration system has to balance’: Vance's clarification on remark
When asked about what his “indentured servants” remark, Vance spoke about his in-laws, who he said had moved to America from South India.
“You know where my family comes from, and I love my mother-in-law and father-in-law who immigrated from South India, and obviously their daughter, born in the United States of America, is now the second lady, and I'm very proud of her, and I love her very much,” he said.
However, he called for a balance in the “respect and welcome” for foreign workers, while ensuring it doesn't hurt American interests.
“I think that we can have a respect and a welcome to people who want to contribute to the United States of America…but also recognize that if you're a major corporation – let's say you're a trillion dollar company and you bring in somebody, an accountant, and you say that you cannot hire an accountant from your existing labor pool, and when you're doing that, you fire an accountant that was already on the payroll.
