Refineries in India, Turkiye and Brunei shipped oil products worth €1 billion ($1.2 billion) to countries imposing sanctions on Russia in September, marking a 43% increase from August, according to a report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), cited by news agency PTI. Reliance Industries Ltd's Jamnagar refinery in Gujarat accounted for six of the seven cargoes unloaded at European Union ports during the month, despite the bloc's ban on importing oil products refined from Russian crude, the report said. The findings come as India continues to be one of the largest buyers of Russian fossil fuels following Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, even as Western restrictions seek to limit Russia's energy revenues. The European Union received oil products worth €667 million from the refineries covered by the CREA report in September. Australia imported €168 million worth, while the United States received €154 million and New Zealand €19 million. CREA estimated that €295 million worth of the exported products had been refined from Russian crude. Jamnagar also accounted for the largest share of the group's exports to the US, with shipments worth €122 million. Russian crude constituted 32% of the refinery's crude oil imports between July and September, according to the report. Among EU destinations, Italy received three of the seven shipments, Romania received two, while Spain and Cyprus received one each. The value of exports reported as destined for EU ports from refineries processing Russian crude rose 80% month-on-month, the report said. This included a 104,000-tonne cargo of gasoil, or diesel, from Jamnagar that was still en route to Rotterdam. The European Union prohibited imports of oil products refined from Russian crude in January 2026. However, the rules exempt net crude oil exporters, an exception that CREA argues leaves room for Russian-origin crude to enter global supply chains through refining in third countries. According to the report, a country's status as a net crude oil exporter does not prevent its refineries from processing Russian crude and subsequently exporting the resulting products. CREA has recommended extending the restriction to the refinery level by prohibiting imports of products from any refinery that has processed Russian crude in the preceding six months, regardless of the declared origin of the finished product. The proposal is a recommendation by the research organisation and does not represent an adopted EU policy. India's imports of Russian crude declined 13% in September, marking the second consecutive monthly fall and the lowest level since April, CREA said. Intake declined at all three of India's largest importing refineries. As per the report, Reliance Industries' Jamnagar refinery recorded a 27% drop, Indian Oil Corporation's Paradip refinery saw a 21% decline, and Nayara Energy's Vadinar refinery registered an 8% fall. "Despite the decline, Vadinar overtook Jamnagar as India's largest importer of Russian crude," CREA said. Imports at smaller facilities also largely declined. The HMEL Mundra Oil Terminal and the Kochi refinery recorded month-on-month reductions of 74% and 32%, respectively. The IOC Mundra Oil Terminal was an exception, receiving 570,000 tonnes of Russian crude in September after recording no imports in August, according to CREA. Despite the decline in crude imports, India remained the second-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels in September 2026, spending €4.1 billion on Russian hydrocarbons, according to CREA. Crude oil accounted for 88% of India's purchases, worth €3.6 billion. Coal imports amounted to €309 million, while oil products accounted for €161 million. China remained the largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels. Since December 2022, India has accounted for 37% of Russia's crude oil exports, compared with China's 50%, the report said. India was a relatively marginal buyer of Russian oil before Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Its purchases subsequently increased as Western buyers reduced imports and Russia offered crude at substantial discounts to attract alternative customers. Russian Urals crude averaged $90.70 a barrel in September, but continued to trade at a $23-per-barrel discount to Brent, unchanged from August. The decline in India's Russian crude purchases may reflect factors beyond pressure from the United States, including tighter supply and increased competition from Chinese buyers, according to PTI citing analysts at Kpler. The analysts expect India's Russian crude imports to remain at around 1.8 million to 1.9 million barrels per day in October. Priya cannot remember a time when her mother was not busy. Apart from her work, there were always social engagements to attend, friends to visit or new books to read. But something changed after retirement.
“She seemed to lose some of her sparkle. She became a little inward and moody at times, as though an inertia had taken over. Her outings became less frequent. She no longer went shopping, as everything could be home-delivered. The fact that my father preferred to stay at home further reduced her opportunities to socialise. This transition from a busy, active person to a listless and diffident individual was quite shocking and sad,” she says.
When she opened up to her friends about this, Priya discovered that they had similar stories to share. Parents who had once led full, active lives were now confined to the quiet routines of home. They had not lost their zest for life, but age had caught up with them, sapping their energy and enthusiasm to get out and about.
“Then it struck us that, in a few years, this could be our lives too. Why should we allow the years to steal all the colours from our lives?” says Dimple Mohan, who runs a consultancy service in the city.
Five women
And so, Young at Heart (YaH) was born — a dream that took wings when five women entrepreneurs and working professionals in Thiruvananthapuram came together to explore how they could help their parents rediscover the joy of living and embrace ageing with enthusiasm.
Envisioned as a platform for senior citizens and those in their 50s, YaH hopes to bring people together to rediscover life’s little pleasures — new friendships, new learning experiences, evenings out, and a little fun and frolic. Growing older, the founders believe, should never mean compromising on emotional happiness and mental well-being.
“We all have successful careers, active social lives and wide networks of friends. But living with our parents, we have seen how their personalities and attitudes towards life change as they grow older, even when they are financially secure and have no major worries,” says Ms. Mohan, who is one of YaH’s founder.
“It made us think that, regardless of age, we should be able to embrace life with gusto and live it to the fullest in the company of good friends. YaH is an initiative to help senior citizens and people in their 50s connect, forge friendships, share interests and build a community that helps everyone lead more fulfilling lives. Many have the money and time, but are hesitant to venture out on their own,” she adds
On October 16
A formal launch event of YaH, featuring music and entertainment, is planned in the capital on October 16. The event will also offer participants an opportunity to meet and get to know one another.
YaH plans to organise regular entertainment and recreational activities, while creating opportunities for like-minded people to discover, share and nurture their talents. Events will be tailored to the interests, hobbies and leisure preferences of those who have registered with the initiative.
The group has also identified areas such as diet and nutrition, physical fitness, digital literacy and financial planning as important components of healthy, active ageing.
“We had several women register with us and we asked them what has been on their bucket list. One wants to learn to speak English fluently so she can converse with her grandchildren abroad. Another has always wanted to design dresses, while someone else simply wants to travel — something she could never manage while working. We hope to facilitate the fulfilment of some of these dreams,” says actor Manju Pillai, who is spearheading the initiative along with Devi Mohan, Sankari Unnithan and Maya Menon.
Younger volunteers
In time, YaH hopes to involve younger volunteers, building bridges between generations. They could take senior citizens to the beach or the movies, or simply spend an afternoon playing chess.
As age-related frailties set in, many older people find themselves increasingly disconnected from the world around them. The resulting isolation can take a toll on their emotional health and leave them vulnerable to depression.
Young at Heart hopes to address this often-overlooked need for socialisation and companionship first and help them embrace life, wholeheartedly.

Happy Friday from sunny San Diego. This is Jonathan Wosen, West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. We’ve got a strong lineup to help you kick off the weekend, featuring the lively final day of our STAT Summit, a pharmacist’s insights into why patients sometimes stop taking medication, and a recap of the highlights (or, depending on your perspective, lowlights) of STAT’s coverage of Elizabeth Holmes, for those looking to refresh their memory before watching a newly released documentary of the former Silicon Valley wunderkind’s fall from grace.
STAT Summit, Day 2
Thursday marked the second and final day of our annual flagship STAT Summit in Boston, and the event ended on a high note, with timely sessions on vaccine hesitancy, cutting-edge tools to study the brain, and the future of biotech. Here are some highlights:
- A PSA to health care firms. If you’re an executive at a health care company that may have violated the law, the Department of Justice has a message for you: Please report yourself. The justice department, which has announced plans to expand investigations into corporate wrongdoing, is creating new incentives for both companies and whistleblowers to report offenses such as providers billing for unneeded services and the fabrication of patient records. Read more from STAT’s Isabella Cueto.
- Merck and Moderna go exploring. Merck and Moderna made headlines when they announced in August that their cancer vaccine, which uses messenger RNA, significantly delayed cancer recurrence and metastatic disease in melanoma patients. Their next challenge? Proving this approach can transform other tumors. Read more from STAT’s Jason Mast about where the company’s execs think their next best opportunities may lie.
- A Congressional representative’s thoughts on China. The head-spinning rise of China’s biotech sector has some policymakers endorsing protectionist measures. Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.) has a different idea: Be better than China. Auchincloss plans to introduce a bil that would allow early-phase trials to bypass pre-approval evaluation, speeding up clinical development. He also warned that Trump administration moves to politicize science funding decisions could undermine the nation’s biomedical preeminence. Read more from my colleague John Wilkerson.
What to read before you go see that new documentary on Elizabeth Holmes
We’re leaving room for popcorn and intrigue tonight: The new A24 documentary, “You Can See Everything,” hits theaters today. Its subject is fallen Silicon Valley golden child Elizabeth Holmes, who invited a film crew into her home days before she was about to start her years-long prison sentence.
But STAT, of course, has been covering Holmes for years. We documented Theranos’ halcyon unicorn days. We were at the American Chemical Society meeting back in 2016, for instance, when Holmes was finally to reveal the company’s secretive and dubious data (and, turns out, basically didn’t).
“Would you have Al Capone come and talk about his novel accounting practices?” one clinical pathologist at ACS said at the time. “Is it acceptable to allow someone to talk about science if they’ve used that science so horribly inappropriately?”
It’s been a wild ride: Holmes was convicted in 2022 of defrauding investors and sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison. STAT last year published an op-ed from Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz, which notes the suspicious familiarity between Holmes’ original efforts and her partner’s new diagnostic company, Haemanthus.
Over the years, we tracked the company’s layoffs, legal woes, and eventual shutdown — and kept on top of everything in between with regular Readout dispatches. (Sign up here!) Read up if you need a primer before movie night! — Meghana Keshavan
Why do patients stop taking medication? The answers can be complicated
As a clinical pharmacist, Marcela Gottschald thought she understood why patients usually stop taking medication: They forget, grow tired of dealing with side effects, or don’t understand the severity of their condition. But Gottschald has learned that beneath those initial explanations often lie more complicated concerns. In a STAT First Opinion, she writes about meeting patients worried that taking medication meant they were losing control over their own bodies, and how stopping treatment was a way for them to prove they could still function unaided.
One case left an especially strong impression on her: A young man who’d been on immunosuppressants after he received a kidney transplant. After his body’s immune system attacked the donated kidney, he told Gottschald that he’d simply forgotten to take his medication. But he later shared that his girlfriend was pregnant, and that he’d stopped taking immunosuppressants because he felt he needed to “become a man.”
“This conversation changed the way I understood adherence,” she writes. “Medication can become entangled with the way people see themselves, and the kind of people they believe they need to be.”
A possible silver lining in Pope Leo XIV’s cancer diagnosis
This week, surgeons removed the lower lobe of Pope Leo XIV’s right lung to treat his lung cancer. The Vatican said the surgery was successful with no complications, though it didn’t provide details on the cancer’s stage or whether additional treatment is needed. But some experts are inferring that the cancer was likely caught early, noting that surgery is often prescribed when the entire tumor can be removed.
“The decision to proceed with surgery is encouraging because it suggests the treating physicians believed the cancer could be completely removed. However, successful surgery alone does not necessarily mean the cancer has been cured,” Mohamed Abazeed, a lung cancer physician at Northwestern Medicine, said in a statement.
Lung adenocarcinoma, the type of lung cancer that the pope underwent treatment for, is the most common type of lung cancer and a serious illness. That being said, the 5-year survival rate for localized non-small cell lung cancer is 67%, according to the American Cancer Society. At the absolute earliest stages, 5-year survival can rise to more than 90%. In some cases, surgeons might even do surgeries called a segmentectomy, or a wedge resection, which takes less tissue than one of the five lobes of a lung, to preserve more lung function. — Angus Chen
An FDA policy that made getting a hearing aid easier and cheaper has had mixed results
Four years after the Food and Drug Administration legalized over-the-counter hearing aids, it’s easier and cheaper than ever to get one. So why are companies leaving the market?
Many experts heralded the FDA’s decision in 2022, saying it made it possible for adults with mild-to-moderate hearing loss to get hearing aids over-the-counter rather than through a prescription or professional fitting.
The regulation succeeded in making it cheaper. Prescription aids typically run about $3,400, while over-the-counter aids are roughly $500, according to a JAMA article published Thursday. The majority of first-time buyers are choosing these over-the-counter devices.
But there are some caveats. It’s unclear how many people who need the devices are actually buying, clinicians are struggling to figure out how to refer patients to over-the-counter devices, and it’s tough to know you’re buying a sound product. Researchers found that only 25% of the hearing aids listed on Amazon could be verified with the FDA.
These challenges have forced some of the earliest companies who released over-the-counter hearing aids to flee the market after struggling to gain a foothold. Read on for the solutions proposed by the researchers. — O. Rose Broderick

DHAKA, Bangladesh -- A fire gutted a beach resort in southeastern Bangladesh on Saturday, killing 10 people and injuring four, an official said.
The fire broke out at Tuptup Resto and Resort at Inani in Cox’s Bazar district, a popular destination for domestic tourists, Syed Mohammad Morshed Hossain, deputy assistant director of Fire Service and Civil Defense in the district, said. The resort is located near the Bay of Bengal.

It wasn't immediately clear what caused the fire.

Montreal borough tightens rules on e-scooters as youth injuries skyrocket
80 scooter-related injuries in 2025 — 122 so far this year, Montreal Children's trauma director says
The Montreal borough of Saint-Laurent has adopted a new bylaw banning electric scooters and other motorized personal mobility devices in public areas that fall within its jurisdiction.
That includes city parks, trails and sidewalks.
Vana Nazarian, a city councillor for the borough, says the bylaw was adopted after a series of incidents and near misses over the summer, as the popularity of the devices continues to grow.
"We're not banning them, but we want to make sure that with the speeds that these scooters have, they stay more on places where vulnerable populations won't be at risk," she told CBC's Let's Go.
Nazarian added the borough is home to many young families and seniors, and they should be able to use parks and trails without being afraid or at risk of a collision.
She's hopeful the bylaw will force those who ride e-scooters or e-unicycles and other motorized transportation devices to use them more responsibly.
The move comes just a little over two months after Quebec decided to extend its e-scooter pilot project, even as doctors warned the rules leave children at risk.
The original pilot, introduced in 2023, allowed for anyone 14 and older to use the devices on roads where the maximum speed limit is less than 50 km/h, as well as on bike paths. Helmets are required at all times.
Those rules will still apply along with new restrictions that came into effect on July 18, including a 25 km/h speed limit for e-scooters. Exceeding that limit can result in a $200 fine by police.
14 times more injuries than in 2023
Deborah Friedman, the trauma director at the Montreal Children's Hospital, says that since the pilot came into effect, the number of e-scooter injuries have skyrocketed.
"We have seen 14 times the number of traumatic injuries related to e-scooters than we did in 2023 when it was first implemented," Friedman said.
In 2025, there were about 80 cases in total. So far this year, that number is 112.
Friedman, who is also the director of the Canadian Hospitals Injury Reporting and Prevention Program (CHIRPP), said the severity of injuries is also increasing, with close to 20 per cent of the cases requiring hospitalization.
"We're not talking about little cuts and bruises," she said.
The injuries include traumatic brain injuries, multiple fractures to the face, lots of facial dental trauma, complicated fractures of limbs and abdominal trauma.
Of particular concern is the age of the victims. Friedman says close to 60 per cent of the children that present at the trauma centre are under 14 years old.
"That's a problem," she said.
Stronger regulations, better enforcement needed
Friedman commended the borough of Saint-Laurent for its new bylaw and encourages other municipalities to follow suit, but she says more needs to be done at the provincial and federal levels.
Doctors across Canada have been advocating for stronger regulations and better enforcement of the rules.
Friedman said that in Quebec, they'd like to see the minimum age to use an e-scooter increased to 16, as well as a Class 6D licence made mandatory — the same licence needed to operate a vehicle like a moped.
Friedman says younger children don't have the judgment, skill level, height or control to navigate e-scooters on the road, all while following the rules.
The type of helmets used could also make a difference.
"You need to have something that's going to protect the face as well," Friedman said, saying many injuries they see are a result of children "faceplanting and ending up with profound trauma."
Friedman says e-scooter manufacturers also bear some responsibility with the labelling of their products and how they are sometimes marketed as though they are toys.
With the holidays around the corner, this type of issue is of particular concern, Friedman says.
"So we're trying to work at different levels to try to sensitize the public and encourage policymakers to hear our concerns and to base decisions on real data," she said. 
"Each number that I mentioned is attached to a child, which is attached to a family, which is attached to a community."

Back in February, I went to Los Angeles to take in some art and stayed in Koreatown. Down the street from my hotel, there was this little coffee shop — Stagger — that is, I think, best known for its matcha, which is good. But the drink I unexpectedly found myself obsessed with was their cream top, an iced Americano with, yep, vanilla cream on top. When I got back to Oakland, I kept thinking about how badly I wanted one.
The best gadget I bought this year is a milk frother
Let me convince you to change up your coffee game.
Let me convince you to change up your coffee game.
For more than 20 years, I’ve been drinking my coffee — iced or otherwise — black. Originally this was because I knew I could put black coffee that had cooled off in the microwave to reheat it without worrying that the milk in it would curdle. (Gross, I know.) Then, as I started drinking better coffee, it felt like the best way to appreciate the expensive beans I was buying.
So my attachment to the cream top surprised me. And then, when Oakland had a gnarly heat wave in March, I decided there was one way I’d tolerate it: fancy coffee drinks. I splashed out $14 for the Zulay Kitchen frother and I was off.
A handheld foamer looks and works kinda like an immersion blender. I pour milk into a glass, stick the frother in there, and then hold the power button until it reaches my preferred consistency. When the disposable batteries it uses are fresh, this takes about 30 seconds to a minute. As the batteries degrade, it takes longer; if I’m getting impatient about how long it’s taking me to make my frothy treats, it’s time to change the batteries. The frother also works to beat eggs, mix protein powder or creatine into a drink, and make hot chocolate. But by far it’s gotten the most use making my coffee drinks as I set out to make a cream top of my own.
The cream top descended from the Einspänner, an espresso drink that’s named for a one-horse carriage. The original Viennese version used hot espresso, and the whipped cream on top served as a kind of insulation, which kept the drivers’ drinks hot for them when they were out in the cold. (Obviously, its popularity expanded beyond carriage drivers.) It isn’t clear to me how the Einspänner made it to South Korea, but it exploded in popularity there, with all kinds of variations, mostly iced. And then from South Korea, it made its way to the US, where the ground had already been cleared by Starbucks’ “cold foam” drinks.
The notable thing about the cream top, besides the addition of delicious fat and sugar to coffee, was that the cream wasn’t as light as latte foam, but wasn’t as heavy as ordinary whipped cream. It was melty and dripped slowly into the coffee.
My first experiments with my at-home cream top were pretty simple. I don’t have an espresso machine, but I do make concentrated cold brew in hot weather, which has a strong enough flavor to stand up against the foam. (Some recipes suggest powdered espresso if you don’t want to use concentrated cold brew.)
After I mastered the simple cream top, I began making forays into weirder breakfast treats, my favorite of which I… recreated from a Starbucks ad. It’s a cold brew with coconut ube cold foam, the top of which I dust with toasted coconut flakes. It is dank. (This is a recipe for a more sophisticated version than I make.) So when it was 90 degrees in Oakland for about two weeks running recently, this drink was how I consoled myself.
To be honest, I’m just recommending getting a frother. You can spend a lot on a milk frother and some people do. I relied on America’s Test Kitchen to steer me in the right direction — but outlets like Wirecutter and Bon Appétit have their own preferred options. This one is cheap and simple, and it’s been treating me right. I’m sure the Apple HomeView is nice, too, but in pleasure per dollar can it match a $14 cold foamer that takes AA batteries? I have my doubts.

OpenAI is building a humanoid robot, but the body isn't the real challenge
Figuring out how the 'brain' will work will take a lot of time.
While OpenAI is already busy with the development of AI models and new consumer hardware, CEO Sam Altman and his team apparently have time for one more project: a humanoid robot.
On the Sources podcast, Altman explained that the human form is logical because "the world is very much designed for people." Doors, keyboards and tools are all designed around a certain type of body, and a robot that can move around in the same spaces should probably have a similar form factor. As Altman put it, "matching that form factor seems good."
When asked if OpenAI will actually build one, his response was much more succinct: "We will." However, Altman isn't so concerned with the nitty-gritty details of what that robot looks like. Those questions are "less important than really figuring out ... the brain that makes the robot work," he said. Basically, giving a machine two arms and two legs doesn't get you very far if it doesn't know what to do with them.
This is still some distance from becoming a product. Altman told Fortune: "I think we'll have a cool demo in 2027 ... I don't think there will be robots walking the streets for a few years longer." OpenAI hasn't disclosed what that demo will showcase, what its humanoid will look like or when anyone outside the company will get close to one.
The 'brain' has to make the hardware useful
Calling it a robot "brain" almost makes the problem sound neat, but it isn't.
A capable humanoid must be able to understand what its cameras and sensors are seeing, interpret an instruction, decide how to carry it out, coordinate its body and then correct itself when the real world introduces something inconvenient. When picking up a mug, for instance, it needs to identify the mug, find the handle, estimate the grip and exert the correct amount of force to lift it. Otherwise, you're left with a coffee spill and a floor-cleaning job.
OpenAI is already recruiting people to address those issues. Its robotics roles span motion control, state estimation, actuator control and whole-robot behavior, as well as the machine-learning infrastructure to train physical AI systems.
There's a bit of history here as well. OpenAI's Dactyl research project taught a robotic hand how to manipulate real objects, with its training done entirely in simulation. The company later applied the technique to a Rubik's Cube, an early example of the same headache that plagues robotics companies to this day: a model can learn what should happen through its software, but physics has the final say.
OpenAI still has to build the body
Altman's focus on intelligence shouldn't be mistaken for OpenAI treating the hardware as an afterthought. The company's robotics job listings indicate it is working on custom electromechanical actuators that include motors, transmissions, sensing and thermal systems, while other positions cover manufacturing and the supply chain needed to eventually produce hardware at scale. That's quite a bit of work for the "less important" half of the robot.
OpenAI is also not entering uncharted territory. Tesla has been working on Optimus for years, and XPENG recently had its IRON humanoid autonomously walk off the production line after being assembled. Both are good reminders that even smart software has to coax a very complex set of motors and joints into action.
OpenAI's own plans seem to begin at a more down-to-earth level than placing a robotic roommate in every home. One of its robotics job postings states that the company's short-term objective is to create general-purpose robots that can help skilled workers build infrastructure, and its long-term goal is to develop a personal robot that can help with a much wider variety of tasks.
If you're already imagining a physical form of ChatGPT with knees doing the dishes, you may not need to remove your dishwasher just yet. OpenAI hasn't announced an actual robot yet, or a consumer price, subscription model, release date or robot-specific privacy framework. Those questions get a bit more real-world if a future OpenAI machine is equipped with cameras and microphones and allowed to roam around someone's house.
That said, OpenAI's careers page currently lists 27 robotics openings.

You don't have to turn off your phone to switch SIM cards (but you probably should)
A quick step removes the small chance of anything going wrong and requiring more of your time.
If your phone has a SIM tray, it's not something you likely open often, but there are still reasons to. You may be switching to an MVNO to save money, or maybe you're temporarily swapping out your normal SIM for a cheaper local carrier when travelling. In some cases, your carrier will send you a replacement card if yours is damaged.
Most of today's smartphones let you switch SIMs with the phone on, so you don't need to switch your device off for the process. But there are modest benefits if you do, and for something so quick, it's better to be safe if you have a few minutes.
How to replace the SIM
We're talking about physical SIM cards, which you have to remove from your phone by hand. eSIM replacement should be as simple as using a QR code, carrier app or direct transfer between different smartphones. Most eSIM-compatible phones can store many eSIMS, though only a few can be active at once.
Physical SIM card replacement involves these steps:
- Optionally, power down your phone or enable airplane mode.
- Pop the tray out, usually by gently pushing a paperclip or SIM ejector tool into the ejection pinhole on the phone.
- Change the card, ensuring you use the correct card size.
- Pop the tray back into place.
- Enter your PIN or restart if the phone requests it.
If you have a dual-SIM phone that supports two physical cards, check which SIM you intend to swap before you begin.
While many argue eSIM is a superior technology because it requires no moving parts, others still appreciate the convenience and relative privacy true SIM cards provide. They make it easy to install and use over-the-counter pay-as-you-go SIM-based accounts, for example.
The small potential risks of SIM replacement
Most potential dangers of SIM replacement are physical. You might accidentally insert dirt, grime or moisture into the SIM tray, or force a larger card into a smaller slot incorrectly. You could also break the SIM tray so it no longer aligns correctly, or otherwise harm the card. A damaged SIM card or one incorrectly inserted may cause the phone to continue trying (and failing) to create a network connection, draining its battery and causing it to overheat.
Most people never encounter these problems, since slowing down and being careful does the trick. In most cases, your phone will take a moment to read the new SIM and find the network. Then it will be available for service, subject to account setup requirements.
The benefit of turning your phone off before swapping the SIM is minor. It forces your phone to look at the fresh information provided on the new card when it powers on again, helping register your device on its new network more quickly by reading the new carrier settings. This reduces the chance you'll encounter a software-based "network error" message when you swap.
More to think about when swapping SIMs
Before the 2010s, SIM slots were usually located underneath a phone's removable battery, which obviously required powering off the device to access. Over time, as removable batteries became less common, SIM trays were moved to the outside of phones. Early models using this setup would often show a network error if you swapped SIMs while the phone was on, but they quickly became hot-swappable and this was no longer a problem.
You don't even need to switch your device off completely to make the phone refresh its carrier settings from the card. You'll get a similar result if you turn on airplane mode, wait 30 seconds before swapping the SIM and turn airplane mode off again once the new SIM is inserted. This should prevent any carrier hiccups during the process.
A warning on SD cards
Unlike the iPhone, some Android devices still include a microSD card slot. In some cases, this is in the same tray as the SIM, though placement varies. If this is the case for you, as when ejecting an external drive, it's important to unmount the microSD card before removing the SIM to prevent losing data. On Samsung devices: open the My Files app, find the SD Card, tap the three-dot menu next to it and choose Unmount. Search the Settings app or check online documentation if you're not sure how this works for your device.
So while the benefits are slight, switching off your phone when replacing the SIM can prevent software-related glitches. If you don't want to power down, use airplane mode instead. And in case you encounter a network error after swapping, always try restarting your device first.

Amid intense competition in the quick home services market, Snabbit incurred a net loss of ₹167.8 Cr in the financial year ended March 31, 2026 (FY26) as against a loss of ₹5.7 Cr in FY25. Important to note that FY26 was Snabbit’s first full financial year of operations following its service launch in August 2024. Thus, comparability of the two fiscals is limited. Snabbit posted an operating revenue of ₹12.2 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹26.3 Lakh in FY25. Platform services generated ₹10.8 Cr in revenue, while uniform sales to service professionals contributed the remaining ₹1.4 Cr. The startup recognises platform service revenue net of discounts it bears. Including other income of ₹14.8 Cr, the startup’s total income for the fiscal stood at ₹27 Cr. Interest on bank deposits contributed ₹14.1 Cr, with the remainder largely coming from gains on mutual fund sales. Snabbit held ₹292.2 Cr in cash and bank balances and ₹26.6 Cr in mutual fund investments, totalling ₹318.9 Cr. This balance predates its $56 Mn Series D funding round in April. Founded in 2024 by former Zepto executive Aayush Agarwal, Snabbit connects users with trained domestic help for cleaning, dishwashing, and other household chores, promising arrivals within 10-15 minutes. The April funding round took the startup’s total funding to $112 Mn. It is backed by the likes of Susquehanna Venture Capital, Mirae Asset Venture Investments, Bertelsmann India Investments, Nexus Venture Partners, Lightspeed Ventures, among others. Snabbit currently operates in five cities, including Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad. It intends to expand its operations to 10 cities, with Kolkata and Chennai as priorities. The startup is focusing on penetrating deep into a handful of existing markets, rather than aggressive geographical expansion. Even within cities, it is doubling down on ‘micro-markets’, or certain neighbourhoods where it can ensure quick delivery, rather than the whole city. It was present in 140 micromarkets by May this year, and had onboarded 40,000 professionals on its platforms, with an average order value of ₹169-₹199. Where Did Snabbit Spend In FY26? Snabbit’s total expenses rose to ₹194.8 Cr from ₹6.8 Cr in FY25. Employee Benefit Expenses: These rose to ₹46 Cr from ₹3.3 Cr, including salaries and wages, provident fund contributions, employee stock options, and staff welfare expenses. Expert Service Cost: Its largest expense head stood at ₹63.1 Cr, compared with ₹27 Lakh in FY25. Marketing Expenses: Spending on marketing increased to ₹48.7 Cr from ₹82.1 Lakh in the previous year. Service Fulfillment Expenses: Spending under this head stood at ₹23.8 Cr compared with ₹84.5 Lakh in FY25. Snabbit’s Loss Per Job Falls Below ₹200 In a statement issued today, Snabbit’s CEO Agarwal said the startup closed FY26 with a run rate of 35,000 daily jobs, up 70X from around 500 jobs a day at the beginning of the fiscal year. It acquired nearly 10 Lakh customers and onboarded more than 20,000 service professionals during the year. He attributed the growth to investments in customer acquisition, workforce training, technology, infrastructure and geographical expansion. Agarwal said the startup deliberately invested ahead to scale into the competitive quick home services category. The startup said it closed the fiscal with approximately ₹319 Cr in cash and investments, zero borrowings and a net worth of ₹312.4 Cr. He also argued that its annual financial statements do not fully reflect the underlying economics or maturity of the business. In a separate statement, Snabbit claimed that its losses per job declined from approximately ₹1,500 at the beginning of FY26 to below ₹200 in September 2026, indicating an improvement in unit economics as its operations scaled. Its Q2 FY27 metrics show that the platform completed 64.5 Lakh jobs, up 61% QoQ, and recorded a net transaction value (NTV) of ₹73 Cr, up 34%. House help accounted for 64 Lakh jobs, while more recently launched verticals — home cooking and home salon services — accounted for 50,000 and 10,000 jobs, respectively, in the fiscal. The startup reported an EBITDA loss of ₹145 Cr, equivalent to 199% of NTV. Snabbit also claimed to be the largest high-frequency home services platform by jobs completed and NTV, and the most capital-efficient at the job level. Its strategy centres on building density within fewer cities and micromarkets rather than expanding its geographical footprint aggressively. Competition Heats Up In Quick Home Services Snabbit competes with Pronto and listed home services company Urban Company’s InstaHelp in the instant household assistance market. Pronto closed its $45 Mn Series B round in May at a $200 Mn valuation, adding to the capital flowing into the segment. The quick home services segment also faces scrutiny over working conditions. Inc42’s reporting documented workers’ concerns about earnings, strict logged-in hour requirements, and inadequate access to waiting areas and washrooms.

Supreme Court orders autism patients on stem cell therapy to register on Centre’s portal
The Centre must launch a portal for autism patients undergoing stem cell therapy and issue a protocol explaining rules for clinical trials and research, the SC said.
The Supreme Court has directed the Centre to create a dedicated online portal for patients undergoing stem cell therapy for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) within six weeks. The court also made it mandatory for such patients, their parents, guardians, caregivers and also the treating medical practitioners and clinics administering such therapy to maintain an extensive database.
The order, passed on October 13 and uploaded on Friday, comes in the backdrop of the court’s January 30 order prohibiting the use of stem cell therapy as a routine clinical service, directing it only to be undertaken only within an approved and monitored clinical trial or research setting.
A bench of justices JB Pardiwala and R Mahadevan said, “As regards patients who had already commenced stem cell therapy for ASD on or before January 30, 2026, we direct the Union to establish a dedicated online portal…Such online portal is to be created within a period of 6 weeks from the date of this order.”
The particulars to be given on the portal included the medical records of such patients, including the particulars of the treating medical practitioners, the nature and course of the intervention administered, and such other clinical details as specified on the portal. The bench directed the Centre to ensure appropriate safeguards for the confidentiality and security of the patients’ medical information.
Last month, the court had directed the Centre to disclose how many applications for clinical trials were received pursuant to its January 30 order. It further asked the Centre to indicate steps being taken to shift those ASD patients already undergoing stem cell therapy as of January 30 into a regulated research framework.
The Centre filed an affidavit on September 28 which said that pursuant to January 30 no application for a clinical trial had been received. Regarding the other issue, the Centre stated that a multicenter randomised controlled trial (RCT) has been proposed to be set up at two tertiary care sites – one in north India and another in south India, within a period of six months. This will be funded by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR).
After reviewing the response, the court found that the proposed RCT does not lay down any eligibility criteria for patients already undergoing stem cell therapy for ASD. Further, there was no uniform platform for such patients or their caregivers to provide their information.
After registering on the portal, the court said that until the RCT is established, patients who commenced stem cell therapy for ASD on or before January 30 will be permitted to continue therapy, as a “strictly temporary arrangement”.
“This arrangement shall be confined to existing patients and shall not be construed as recognition or approval of stem cell therapy for ASD as a permissible clinical service,” the court added.
The court further noted that the lack of easily accessible information about the use of stem cell therapy for ASD is a prime reason for many patients and their families to pursue such treatment.
It granted the Centre six weeks to issue a comprehensive protocol clearly explaining the regulatory regime governing the use of stem cells in research and clinical trials relating to ASD. “The objective is to ensure that no stakeholder is left to navigate a labyrinth of regulatory instruments without being able to ascertain the precise requirements applicable to them,” the order said.
The court directed the Centre to clearly inform the public that stem cell therapy for ASD is not permissible as a clinical service outside a duly approved and monitored research or clinical trial setting. Such information was ordered to be put out in a dedicated and easily identifiable section of the Ministry of Health’s official website in a clear and accessible language.
“The need of the hour is to clearly explain the existing regulatory framework applicable to research/clinical trial corresponding to different levels of manipulation of stem cells for ASD,” the bench said. It was critical of the Centre and various authorities concerned in this field for failing to curb this malpractice due to a lack of readily accessible information to the public.
“The failure of the authorities to effectively curb the malpractice of illegally administering a prohibited form of medical intervention as a clinical service has led to the proliferation of clinics and doctors offering such services. The lack of readily accessible information, which the public could consult to ascertain the legal position, has tacitly enabled such malpractice to continue,” the court said.
The bench allowed the Parents’ Forum for Stem Cells in Autism and Cerebral Palsy to make their suggestions to the Centre while formulating the proposed design of the RCT. It also asked the Centre what mechanism will be available for those patients excluded from receiving the intervention under RCT as they too are continuing the treatment as per the present arrangement.
The order required the Centre to deliberate upon this issue and place a comprehensive plan for the continued monitoring and medical supervision of such participants, including appropriate follow-up, assessment of their clinical condition and such further measures as may be necessary to safeguard their health and well-being.
The court further clarified its January 30 order to suggest that the prohibition is on the use of stem cell being administered as a “therapy” for ASD based on the availability of scientific evidence and the prevailing regulatory framework in the country. However, “It does not amount to an immutable prohibition against any future development in this field,” it added.
The court sought compliance report from the Centre before the next date of hearing on December 14.

Sixteen years since FirstCry began its journey, what began as a kidswear marketplace has spawned a massive multi-channel ecommerce and retail empire, and a house of brands that’s grown well beyond kids today. Today, FirstCry is not just a listed kidswear retailer, but also the engine dragging the Globalbees house of brands and a budding education business that will become hard to ignore soon. But how exactly do each of these engines work? Before we dive in, here’s a look at where FirstCry stands after the last quarter, ahead of its Q2 FY27 results. The first quarter (Q1) of FY27 saw its consolidated revenue climb 13.1% year-on-year to ₹2,106.2 Cr, while its overall net losses were slashed by nearly 34%, dropping to ₹44 Cr from ₹66.5 Cr in Q1FY26. According to founder Supam Maheshwari, this milestone marks the company's strongest baseline revenue expansion over the last five years on a consolidated level. It builds cleanly on the momentum of the previous financial year, where FirstCry closed its books at ₹8,548 Cr in total sales while narrowing its statutory consolidated net loss down to approx ₹204 Cr. However, beneath those headline numbers, take a closer look at the business structure and a different story will unfold. While its top-line revenue signals absolute category dominance, FirstCry’s true bottom line is being heavily squeezed by a highly rigid corporate framework and expensive side-bets. For starters, GlobalBees, FirstCry's D2C brand aggregation subsidiary, contributed ₹1,894.3 Cr, or roughly 22% of its consolidated operating revenue in FY26 while revenue from international businesses in the UAE and Saudi Arabia grew 10% to ₹947.4 Cr. However, together these two businesses accounted for ₹148.5 Cr in segment losses. Further, in Q1FY27, while India multichannel revenue grew 17.7% and international business rose 12%, GlobalBees remained largely flat. The fastest growth, at 47%, came from the much smaller 'Others' segment, primarily comprising the FirstCry Intellitots preschool business. Notably, the segment growing fastest is contributing hardly 1% to the overall consolidated revenue, underscoring the uneven economics behind FirstCry's expanding revenue base. The Overburdened India Goliath A majority 70% of FirstCry’s consolidated operating revenue comes from its India multi-channel business. In Q1FY27, the segment generated around INR 1456 Cr in revenue, up 17.7% YoY. However, despite operating across 10+ categories for mothers, babies, and kids from conception up to approximately 12 years of age, this revenue channel is continuously losing out on gross margin. In Q1FY27, the gross margin fell to 35.2% from 37.8% in Q1FY26. In other words, FirstCry was selling significantly more but retaining less from every rupee of revenue before accounting for delivery, marketing and other operating expenses. A major pressure point is the diapers business, which although just a 15% contributor to GMV, acts as the primary top-of-funnel customer acquisition gateway. It is a high-volume category hit heavily by quick-commerce and private-label discounting, which temporarily drags down the overall multi-channel gross margins. FirstCry's parent company, Brainbees Solutions Limited, holds a 76.59% stake in Swara Baby Products Limited, which gives it a promoter status in the company, which is about to go for an ₹1,000 Cr IPO separately. This will allow FirstCry to further vertically integrate its supply chain for the diapers category. To combat the short-term pressures on the diapers segment, Firstcry has been pushing on its private labels particularly Babyhug, Pine Kids, Cute Walk and Babyoye, to gain greater control over product pricing, sourcing and margins. At the same time, FirstCry has been actively pushing efforts around three initiatives. First, it is rapidly deploying internal logistics networks. Its in-house logistics platform RocketBees has scaled rapidly to 72 cities and covers around 50% of total online shipment as of June 2026. In Q1FY27 earnings call, Maheshwari also pointed out a 20% improvement in turnaround time from delivery perspective. The under-3-hour delivery pilot, FC Qwik, is also live across 12 cities completing approximately 1.25 Lakh shipments in June 2026 alone. Founder and MD Maheshwari said, “We had an overall ambition of growing to 10% of our overall shipment onto the FC Qwik platform. Now, we will aim to grow to 20% of our volumes.” He also highlighted that the FC Qwik TAT has been reduced from three to two hours in selected cities and the team is working on further reducing it. As its third pillar, the company continues to be bullish on its physical retail network, which had grown to around 1,190 stores by FY26. Its offline business recorded approximately 15% year-on-year GMV growth in Q1FY27, with management targeting another 90-100 net store additions during FY27. This gives FirstCry an advantage in product discovery and customer reach, particularly beyond large metropolitan markets, but also requires it to manage the costs of an extensive physical network alongside faster online fulfillment. The trade-off is becoming increasingly visible. Despite the 17.7% revenue growth in Q1FY27, the India business's adjusted EBITDA declined from approximately ₹107 Cr to ₹84 Cr. Its adjusted operating margin consequently contracted from around 8.6% to 5.8%. This suggests that higher sales volumes have yet to compensate for the combined pressure of product margins and operating costs. The company expects some relief as higher raw material and currency-related costs are gradually passed on through product pricing, with a fuller recovery anticipated from Q3FY27, as per management disclosures after Q1. However, competitive pressure in diapering could take longer to ease. In essence, the India multichannel goliath is growing faster, but whether that growth can translate into stronger profits remains the bigger test. The Q2 results will clear up some questions around which direction this key business is headed in. Globalbees’ Drag Effect If the India multi-channel business is FirstCry’s heavy brick-and-mortar anchor, GlobalBees is its high-stakes venture capital pivot. In FY26, Globalbees registered a solid 20% y-o-y growth in overall revenue, however, the momentum doesn't seem to continue. In Q1FY27, the revenue remained almost flat with marginal reduction, while core categories revenue saw only 2% year on year growth. GlobalBees has been a significant capital allocation bet for FirstCry. Parent Brainbees Solutions earmarked ₹169 Cr from the IPO proceeds for GlobalBees to gain further control of its portfolio under the house of brands model. By March 2026, it had deployed ₹104.81 Cr of this allocation. Separately, in March 2025, Brainbees approved a further infusion of up to ₹146 Cr. Despite this capital backing GlobalBees has not acquired a single new brand since September 2022. During the FY26 earnings call, CEO Anuj Jain acknowledged that the company rationalised its portfolio, cutting off brands struggling with slower growth and persistent losses. Instead, the focus has shifted towards four core categories spanning home improvement, appliances, personal care and lifestyle. Thanks to this, even on flat revenue, the segment delivered a remarkable 308% year-on-year surge in Adjusted EBITDA, jumping from ₹4.1 Cr to ₹16.7 Cr, and operating margins grew from 1% to 3.9%. Jain said the cutbacks are a temporary and planned transition that should be completed in the second quarter and growth should bounce back in the winter months. Globalbees can unlock more growth in these categories, but how profitable will this model remain in the long run? Investors will undoubtedly be looking at the next three quarters keenly. The International & Preschool Hedge The other two parts of FirstCry’s business are part of its vision of targeting customers early and making a global retail giant. The company entered the UAE in 2019 and Saudi Arabia in 2022, betting on far higher spending per child than in India. While average spend per child on its Indian platform is around ₹9,280–₹9,350, the corresponding figures are approximately ₹61,000–₹71,000 in Saudi Arabia and ₹1,60,000–₹1,70,000 in the UAE. But converting that premium opportunity into profits has proved difficult amid aggressive discounting by larger ecommerce rivals. FirstCry has reduced its proposed allocation for the international business after the IPO. The move raises questions about the pace and capital demands of its overseas rollout, even as management maintains that the region remains a long-term opportunity. And to be fair, international revenue growth is in line with the overall topline. International revenue rose 12% year on year to ₹232.1 Cr in Q1FY27, from ₹207.2 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA losses narrowed 22% to ₹16.7 Cr. The adjusted EBITDA loss margin improved from about 10% to 7%. For now, management is prioritising unit economics over a breakneck expansion push and has avoided committing to a break-even quarter. The premium-spending thesis remains attractive, but the international business still has to prove it can turn that opportunity into sustainable profits. Away from the bruising battles of babycare retail and overseas expansion, FirstCry harbors a smaller, highly lucrative engine quietly gathering momentum. Its preschool operations, housed under the 'Others' segment, are emerging as an unlikely margin champion in a sprawling consumer empire historically plagued by cash burn. The numbers present a striking contrast. In Q1 FY27, the Intellitots preschool business saw net revenue surge 47% year-on-year to ₹19 Cr, while its adjusted EBITDA improved 65% to hit ₹5 Cr. Operating at a 26% adjusted EBITDA margin, this division outperforms FirstCry's primary retail segments. With management aiming to scale the network to 1,000 preschools over the next few years, this asset-light education bet offers a clear blueprint for high margin revenue beyond traditional retail operations. But the ₹19 Cr quarterly revenue base is small and the preschool business accounts for less than 1% of FirstCry’s consolidated topline. The profitability offers little immediate relief to the group as a whole. But it could become a bigger lever if and when the core business matures. Is FirstCry Stuck In The Past? When you zoom out, FirstCry's consolidated revenue model reveals a business in a state of transition, which has not really been solved by its IPO and the funds raised through the listing. It is caught between defensive strategies for margin recovery and an aggressive push for growth. It’s not a crisis by any means but it is a time for the company to reassess its strengths once again and push for growth in that direction. FirstCry is increasingly feeling the weight of over 1,000 physical storefronts, which have saddled the company with fixed, unyielding operational overheads like high commercial rent and retail payroll. The ecommerce moat is also rapidly eroding under a fierce, industry-wide quick commerce frenzy led by Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart and Flipkart Minutes as well as specialised players, which we had reported in detail here. Having gone beyond kidswear and babycare, the harder question in front of FirstCry is whether its disparate pieces can start to show an ecosystem effect to generate enough operating leverage to sustain the business without another major funds infusion, as has been the major trend in the public markets this year for new-age listed companies.

Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
- Published
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.

In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."

Five years ago, the union budget announced its most ambitious privatisation programme to date. The government would keep a bare minimum presence in four strategic sectors and exit everything else. Five years later, the privatisation has resulted in the sale of Air India and Neelachal Ispat, and this week's approval of the sale of IDBI Bank.
While the government will present it as proof of its privatisation drive, it should be read as an exception rather than a success. As they say, proof of the pudding lies in the eating; the country has largely failed to carry out its disinvestment policy. Instead, the entities remain the same while the government continues to collect dividends and lease the assets: a self-serving model that doesn't match the government's lofty 2021 announcements.
What's more, the government has adjusted its books to tailor itself to the current position. Disinvestment doesn't even have its own line in the budget. It is part of “miscellaneous capital receipts” alongside asset monetisation.
Turning to the sale of the IDBI Bank itself to Canada-based Fairfax Financial Holdings, which came after five years, two rounds of bidding, and the rejection of bids that fell short of the reserve price, many questions remain unanswered. The deal is also not yet done: the Reserve Bank of India must still clear Fairfax as fit and proper.
While the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved the sale of a 60.72 per cent stake to a Fairfax Financial Holdings-linked entity for ₹52,878 crore, at ₹81 a share, this was below the initial reserve price of ₹94.42. However, the government used two valuation agencies that arrived at a benchmark price of ₹75.99 per share, below Fairfax's ₹81 per share, which the government cites in its defence. What we need to know is why it changed its valuation method between the two rounds, and why the change lowered the bar for the buyer.
What is also open to criticism is that over the past five years, the bank has improved its financial health considerably. Its net profit for 2025-26 was ₹9,513 crore, compared with around ₹1,359 crore in 2020-21, a year before it was put up for sale. So, the reserve price should have actually been higher than even the initial one.
Another thing to consider is that post-sale, the LIC will continue to hold a stake in the bank. So, could LIC possibly face competition from Go Digit Life, Fairfax's own insurer, which Fairfax plans to fold into IDBI through the same banking channel it has relied on?
These issues tell us that while the government can push ahead with disinvestment when it wants to, delays can undo whatever it set out to achieve.

Stampede at a popular Hindu festival in eastern India kills 19
A stampede during a major Hindu festival in eastern India’s West Bengal state has killed at least 19 people
NEW DELHI -- A stampede during a major Hindu festival in eastern India’s West Bengal state has left at least 19 people dead, officials said Sunday.
The stampede in the state capital of Kolkata happened Saturday night when a crowd near a pavilion ran for cover as it began raining during Durga Puja, an annual Hindu festival celebrating the goddess Durga. According to police, some worshippers fell on the road, triggering the stampede.
Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, who visited Kolkata Medical College and Hospital where victims were taken, said 19 people had died and 25 were receiving treatment. He announced an investigation by a Special Investigation Team to be headed by a judge of the state’s High Court.
Police detained some pavilion organizers, private security personnel and on-duty staff, and launched a probe into any crowd-control and safety lapses.
Around 3,500 Durga Puja pavilions, known locally as pandals, have been set up across Kolkata for the festival. Following the stampede, authorities advised several of Kolkata’s most heavily attended venues to temporarily close to visitors.
Crowd crushes are relatively common in India during religious festivals, as large crowds, sometimes in the millions, gather in confined areas with few safety or crowd control measures. In January of 2025, at least 30 people were killed as tens of thousands of Hindus rushed to bathe in a sacred river during the Maha Kumbh festival, the world’s largest religious gathering.
In 2013, pilgrims attending a Hindu festival at a temple in the central state of Madhya Pradesh panicked amid fears that a bridge would collapse. At least 115 people were crushed to death or drowned in the river below.

Imran Khan challenges ‘leave India’ notice: ‘No reasons disclosed, no chance to respond’
Actor Imran Khan received a 'leave India' notice by the Mumbai office of the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) on Thursday.
Actor Imran Khan has challenged in Bombay High Court a notice asking him to leave India before October 28. His plea alleges that the notice issued to him didn't disclose any reasons or give him an opportunity to respond to the alleged violations.
Days after his participation in a Mumbai protest seeking chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, actor Imran Khan received a 'leave India' notice by the Mumbai office of the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) on Thursday.
The notice referred to the 43-year-old actor as a US national and warned that he will be liable for prosecution if he fails to leave India before the mentioned date.
What Imran Khan's plea says
Imran Khan's petition in Bombay High Court called the notice issued to him as “illegal, perverse, drastic and bad in law”, according to a PTI report.
"The notice has been issued without disclosing any reasons, supporting material, or specific statutory contravention. It was issued without inquiry, a show-cause notice, or any opportunity for the Petitioner (Khan) to respond to the alleged violations," the plea said, according to the news agency.
Also Read: Why FRRO asked Imran Khan to leave India: The law, the notice, and the actor's options
The notice issued to Khan had said that he “contravened” the provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025. However, Imran Khan's plea states that there is no provision under the current law or statutory rules that prohibits an OCI (Overseas Citizen of India) cardholder from participating in a peaceful protest.
Imran Khan had participated in a protest seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan on October 10. He was briefly detained during the stir and the FRRO notice followed days later.
What are the rules for OCI cardholders?
The Citizenship Act, 1955 lays out separate rules for holders of an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card. According to an earlier PTI report, Khan holds this card, which is is open to foreign citizens of Indian origin and to foreign spouses of Indian citizens or cardholders.
OCI cardholders are not Indian citizens, cannot vote or hold constitutional positions, the Bureau of Immigration clarified on Friday. The bureau is an Indian government agency responsible for administering immigration related functions.
In a detailed post, it listed the benefits and restrictions related to OCI cardholders.
Also Read: Imran Khan told to leave India: The immigration law and the rules for OCI cardholders
OCI cardholders are not entitled to vote in India, become members of the Legislative Assembly, Legislative Council, or Parliament, or hold constitutional positions such as President, Vice President, or Judge of the Supreme Court or High Court, the bureau said in a post on X.
They are also not eligible for appointment to posts or public services connected with the affairs of the Union or any State in India. Furthermore, OCI cardholders are not permitted to acquire agricultural land, farmhouses, or plantation properties in India, it said.
The actor's plea is expected to be mentioned for an urgent hearing before a division bench comprising Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna.

McLaren is putting five fully operational Formula One cars from its racing history up for sale, including cars associated with Ayrton Senna, Lewis Hamilton and Lando Norris, with one of the models also driven by Hollywood actor Brad Pitt.
The cars, spanning 1991 to 2023, will be sold individually through specialist dealer Tom Hartley Jnr. McLaren will prepare them for their new owners, with the collection expected to fetch tens of millions of pounds.
McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown said the decision was motivated by a desire to see the historic cars driven rather than kept in storage.
“These cars were built to be driven and raced, and we want to see them being used and enjoyed,” Brown said in a statement on Sunday.

The collection includes two Honda V12-powered MP4/6A cars raced by Gerhard Berger and tested by Senna during McLaren’s championship-winning 1991 season. The cars finished second at the San Marino and British Grands Prix, respectively.
Also available is a 2012 MP4/27A driven by former world champion Jenson Button and tested by seven-time champion Hamilton.
Two cars raced by Norris complete the collection. The 2021 MCL35M secured podium finishes at Imola, Monaco and Monza, while the 2023 MCL60 featured in McLaren’s resurgence, with Norris finishing second in consecutive races in Singapore and Japan.
Pitt drove a 2023 McLaren MCL60 during a private test at the Circuit of the Americas in Austin in June 2025, following filming for F1: The Movie. The actor reached a top speed of 197mph (317kph).
Although no official prices have been announced, the cars are estimated to fetch between 5 million and 10 million pounds each.
Hartley, who previously handled the sale of Bernie Ecclestone’s F1 collection and Mansour Ojjeh’s McLaren road cars, said there was no deadline for the sales, with the priority being to find suitable buyers.

Some Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses were recording people’s conversations without the wearer knowing. The recordings occurred without users saying the prompt phrase (“Hey, Meta”), in a bug that Meta says has been fixed.
This week, some users reported online that their Ray-Ban Metas were recording without their consent. A person going by Kindly-Audience-137 on Reddit, for example, said this happened to them across three Meta Ray-Bans and that they had the “Respond without Hey Meta” setting turned off. The person said the Meta AI app “saves audio recordings and text transcripts of these conversations in my conversation history.”
“I believe this deserves a serious technical investigation. Customers should not have to wonder whether their private conversations are being captured when they have not intentionally activated their glasses’ AI assistant,” the Reddit user said.
Android Authority reported the discussions on Tuesday. Later that day it published a response from Meta that read:
“This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review, and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.”
Although Meta’s brief message suggests that the bug is fixed, the broader privacy problem remains.
Unanswered questions
Meta hasn’t said what caused the Ray-Ban Metas to record people without user consent. Reddit user Kindly-Audience-137 said they “first noticed this behavior after a recent firmware update,” but Meta hasn’t confirmed if a faulty update caused the bug.
We also don’t know how many Meta smart glasses were affected. There are a few reports online, but Android Authority said it was unable to replicate the problem before Meta said it fixed it.
Ars Technica sent Meta a message asking what it’s doing to prevent future bugs like this from happening again and how many devices were affected. We’ll update this article if we hear back.
Even a handful of affected devices is cause for concern, though.
Before reports of this bug, privacy advocates had already expressed widespread concerns about Meta’s smart glasses, as well as those from other vendors. Beyond the fear that naturally accompanies the release of new technology that features a microphone and camera, Meta’s glasses pushed the boundaries of privacy further with their more inconspicuous look, prompting concern about how easy it could be for someone to secretly record another person.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has asked all medical colleges and medical institutions across the country to constitute patient safety committees/cells and designate nodal officers to strengthen patient safety practices and reduce avoidable harm in healthcare settings.
In a recent communication to the heads of medical institutions, NMC has asked institutions to share the composition and details of their patient safety committees, along with the particulars of the designated patient safety nodal officer, with the National Patient Safety Secretariat (NPSS) at the Directorate-General of Health Services (DGHS).
As per the direction, the proposed committee is to be chaired by the director, head of the institution or medical superintendent, with representation from relevant specialties and patient safety domains.
Patient safety framework
According to the NMC, the patient safety framework covers 11 domains, including medication and surgical safety, blood and medical device safety, laboratory and diagnostic safety, and infection prevention and control. Other areas include patient and family engagement, vaccine and injection safety, operational research in patient safety, facility safety covering biomedical waste management, fire safety, structural safety and environmental safety, along with safety in AYUSH services.
The Commission notes that the move places responsibility on medical institutions to establish an institutional mechanism for monitoring safety practices rather than treating patient safety as an isolated clinical responsibility.
According to the latest order, institutions should comply with the directions and communicate the required details to the NPSS.
