Journalist to be crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
- Published
Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country.
For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster.
But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country.
Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.
Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34.
The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned.
A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast.
He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king.
But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward.
According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne.
But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma.
The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son.
Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected.
However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions.
The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome.
Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family".
"As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay".
The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute".
"No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X.
But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind".
While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan".
A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources.
Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965.
Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs.
According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.
After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development.
"I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said.
Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead.
The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala.
The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s.
The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty.
Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him.
The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend.
The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X.
Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage.
His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum".
The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer.
Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300 km (186 miles) from Kampala.
He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999.
He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation.
The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader.
After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people".
His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition.
"I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC.
She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it."
She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man".

During her Oct. 13 debut, new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia answered three questions from outlets typically friendly to U.S. President Donald Trump, stumbling over parts of those answers, and ended the press conference after just 14 minutes.
Many social media users mocked Zacharia's performance afterward. Some posts included a video of a young beauty pageant contestant (archived), supposedly Zacharia, struggling to answer a question.
The video, along with the claim that it showed Zacharia, was shared in several popular X posts (archived) and on Instagram (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and sent emails wondering if the video really was of Zacharia.
The woman in the video was not Zacharia, but instead a 2007 Miss Teen USA contestant, Caitlin Upton. Therefore, we've rated this claim miscaptioned.
The video has gone viral before, as the internet culture website Know Your Meme has documented, and many of those who shared it with a caption identifying the woman as Zacharia appeared to have done so jokingly. However, responses to the posts indicated that at least some people unfamiliar with the video believed the captions were serious.
The question Upton, who was Miss South Carolina Teen USA that year, struggled to answer was about a large number of Americans being unable to identify the U.S. on a world map. She didn't really answer the question; Upton stumbled over her words while referencing people in the U.S. who didn't have maps, education, South Africa, Asian countries and building up the future.
Video of Upton's attempt to answer the question has been available on YouTube (archived) since Aug. 24, 2007, the date of the competition.
A few days later, Upton appeared on the "Today" show and said she was overwhelmed when she was asked the question and made a mistake. While on the show, she gave a more focused answer to the question she was originally asked during the contest:
Personally, my friends and I, we know exactly where the United States is on a map. I don't know anyone else who doesn't. If the statistics are correct, I believe there should be more emphasis on geography in our education so people will learn how to read maps better.
Several years later, Upton spoke publicly about how Upton struggled following the viral fame of her appearance in the Miss Teen USA contest. In 2015, she told Teen Vogue that she suffered from depression and even suicidal thoughts due to bullying, harassment and hate directed her way both online and offline.
In 2024, Vice President JD Vance, then a candidate for the office, posted the clip again to X to mock then-Vice President Kamala Harris for her performance in a CNN interview. At that time, Vance was criticized for bringing attention back to a moment that had Upton contemplating suicide for a time, according to Vanity Fair.
At the time Upton competed in the pageant, she was 18 years old.
In 2007, Zacharia was graduating from Pepperdine University, putting her outside the age range of the Miss Teen USA contest for that year.

Ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party-led protest in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, and on the day of the protest on October 10, Hindu Rakhsha Dal (HRD) chief Pinky Chaudhary and its members posted a series of videos on social media platforms inciting violence against the demonstrators. Strikingly, several such videos were made in the presence of police.
In the clips, Chaudhary and other HRD members urged “Hindutva supporters” to “set the protesters’ minds right” while using communal and inflammatory rhetoric. He described those planning to demonstrate as “anti-national” and “anti-Hindu”.
Despite reports claiming that Chaudhary was placed under house arrest, he continued to issue calls for HRD members and other “kattar Sanatanis” to reach Jantar Mantar and confront the protesters ahead of Saturday’s protest and on the very day.
Moreover, a video posted by News Capsule on October 10, the day of the protest, showed a group of men dragging, beating and physically assaulting young protesters near Kamla Market. Alt News identified one of the alleged assailants as Ravindra Govinda, a member of Hindu Raksha Dal.
Govinda shatred a clip on his Facebook account in which he declared “support for the Delhi police in treating the protesters” while identifying himself as a member of HRD. “…As we, the Hindu Raksha Dal, had declared, we will stand with Delhi police in treating these cockroaches…,” he says, while continue to issue threats against the agitators.
Govinda was also seen in a video posted by Pinky Chaudhary, claiming that HRD members were fighting against CJP protesters to “protect Sanatanis”.
One of the goon seen beating the kid is Ravindra Govinda. Member of Hindu Raksha Dal. He was detained in the morning. Look how Police is handling the goons. https://t.co/nONEQVhY4f
— Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear) October 10, 2026
‘We Will Beat Them With Sticks’
On October 9, Chaudhary posted a video in which he stood alongside a group of men carrying batons and openly threatened physical violence against protesters expected to assemble at Jantar Mantar the following day.
Chaudhary declared in the video: “Laath bajake inke pichwade thik karne, dimag thik karne jayenge” (We will beat them with sticks and set their minds right). He added: “Jo log iss desh ko Islam meh le jane ki galat fehmi rakhte hai” (Those who are under the misconception that they can turn this country into an Islamic nation.) He said HRD members and staunch Sanatani believers will “handle” all those who have the “insect of secularism” in their head.

Threats Continued Despite Police Intervention
A few hours later on October 9, Chaudhary uploaded another video claiming that police had arrived at his residence and placed him under house arrest. However, even as he stood in front of several police personnel, he continued to issue threats.
In this video, he declared that several members of HRD had already reached Delhi and were prepared to confront the demonstrators. Referring to Jantar Mantar as an “adda of terrorists”, he reiterated that HRD members would use their batons against those he described as opponents of Sanatan Dharma. “Jitne Sanatani virodhi hai, unke pichwade laal karke hi wapas ayenge” (We will return only after making the backsides of all those who oppose Sanatanis red), he said. He further described HRD members as warriors who are “neither afraid to die nor to kill.”
Chaudhary portrayed the outfit as pro-police and pro-nationalist, claiming that its members wanted to teach the protesters a lesson for allegedly misbehaving with police personnel. He also accused CJP supporters of insulting Hindu deities, attempting to establish an Islamic state, and acting against the nation. “India is safe till date, only because Sanatani warriors are here,” he said.
View this post on Instagram
Chaudhary’s Son Joins Calls For Violence
In another video, Harsh Chaudhary, son of Pinki Chaudhary, posted a video appearing alongside several HRD members, including Lalit Sharma. The video was accompanied by the caption: “Hindu raksha dal puri takat k saath cockroach-o ki gaand pitne pohunch raha hai” (Hindu Raksha Dal is arriving in full force to beat the asses of cockroaches).
Dismissing the need for batons, he claimed that he was physically strong enough to pick people up and pin them down himself. “We don’t need lathis; I am tough enough to pick them up and pin them down,” Harsh said.
View this post on Instagram
Threats From Inside Police Station
On October 10, Harsh and his team were detained by the Ghaziabad police. They went on to post a video after recording it while sitting inside the police station and in front of police personnel, where they urged Hindu warriors to “set the mind right” of the protesters. Even as the continued to issue these threats while in police detainment, no cops were seen preventing them from recording the videos or issuing violent threats.

Ravindra Govinda, Other Assailants Held
Prior to his Instagram account becoming unavailable, Govinda had also uploaded several videos in which he expressed support for the Delhi police and BJP government. In these videos, he said HRD members would stand along with the police and participate in “treating” the cockroaches.
Independent journalist Pranav Pradhi, posting a video on X, questioned Delhi police officials regarding the apparent disparity in treatment of protestors and “Sanatani warriors” of HRD.
He pointed out that Govinda and other members of HRD, who had been making inflammatory statements and issuing violent threats, were not detained on October 10, while several other protesters faced prompt detention. Pradhi highlighted that there were at least six people gathered together, which violated Section 163.
Delhi Police is stopping ordinary citizens from gathering or protesting, citing Section 163 of the BNSS. But Hindutva groups are gathering openly and threatening protesters.
They claim the protesters are raising anti-India slogans. I have covered these protests and haven’t witnessed this. And frankly, this is an old tactic. Nothing new here.
So I asked Delhi Police a simple question: if ordinary citizens aren’t allowed to gather, how are these groups allowed to assemble and openly threaten protesters?
They had no answer.

Govinda later uploaded a video indicating that he and his associates had been detained by the police.
On October 11, Sunday, Delhi police arrested the four men seen allegedly assaulting protesters in the video. “Taking suo motu cognizance of a video circulating on social media showing four men allegedly assaulting a male protester, Delhi Police, PS Kamla Market, acted promptly and initiated legal proceedings,” Delhi police said in a statement. The four held include Govinda (35), Raman Saini (50), Vivekanand (32), and Kapil Kumar (27).
‘We Won’t Let India Become Bangladesh’
Ahead of the protest on October 8, Sharma released a video in which he issued threats while brandishing a baton. In the video, he stated that the HRD team would go to Jantar Mantar to “treat” the “anti-nationals.” He also declared, “We won’t let this country become Bangladesh.”
On October 9, Sharma uploaded a video showcasing a baton that resembles a baseball bat. He specifically threatened Dipke and Rathee, saying, “Do not confront HRD members, or this baton will enter through your mouth and come out from your ass.”
He stated that in places where Sanatan Dharma is insulted, where Sita Mata is disrespected, and where slogans against Brahmanwad and Thakurwad are raised, they will wreak havoc at Jantar Mantar on those individuals so that seven generations of theirs will remember it. He further claimed that HRD will take revenge for the mistreatment suffered by the Delhi police.
On live video, he used inflammatory language and expletives, urging Sanatanis to gather at Jantar Mantar in large numbers to confront the protesters. Sharma also uploaded several videos issuing threats of violence at Jantar Mantar against the protesters. Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Doing the dishes and riding the subway? Why the royals keep trying to look relatable
Relatability has become a longstanding priority and challenge for monarchies
It all seemed a bit prosaic, really, chatting about doing the dishes with her husband or riding on the subway with her daughter.
But there was Catherine, Princess of Wales, telling seniors how she and Prince William share the washing-up duties, and a few days later, taking a trip on the London Underground with Princess Charlotte.
Beyond that glimpse into their everyday lives, though, these recent moments reflect an attempt to deal with a longstanding and more fundamental challenge that is a priority for the monarchy: how to appear relatable to a public that lives far beyond royal walls.
"The monarchy isn't trying to convince us that William and Catherine are ordinary people," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.
"It's about trying to convince us that despite extraordinary circumstances, they experience the same human concerns as everybody else."
Efforts to do that convincing have long been a priority for monarchies throughout Europe.
Catherine, Princess of Wales, right, sits with residents onboard a West Sussex Minibus, a volunteer-led community transport group, during a visit to Pulborough, southern England, on Sept. 30. (Arthur Edwards/AFP/Getty Images)
"Since … the political upheavals of the 19th century, which saw various monarchs … losing their thrones … there was a real consciousness that you no longer needed just the support of the elite, you needed to be relatable," said Judith Rowbotham, a social and cultural scholar and visiting research professor at the University of Plymouth in southwestern England, in an interview.
"Queen Victoria writes her highland journal — suitably sanitized — but that's an attempt to make herself relatable."
What's thought of as relatable nearly 200 years ago differs from what William and Catherine and other working royals may try to do or show today. But the overall significance is the same, Rowbotham suggests.
"Relatability is something that modern monarchies, certainly modern European monarchies, see as genuinely important," she said.
"Particularly at a time when people are worried about money, when people are questioning government actions over taxes … the fact that yes, they live in a lavish house, but they live ordinary lives in a lavish house … that's the impression they want to give, that they don't have live-in staff, they're not surrounded by flunkies and footmen."
As much as there is that desire to appear relatable, there is little to suggest it can ultimately eliminate the actual separation between the monarchy and the public.
This 1969 photo is one of a series taken to show the informal life of Prince Charles, centre, as he sits with Queen Elizabeth, background centre, Prince Philip, second from left, Prince Edward, left, Princess Anne, background, and then Prince Andrew, right, at Sandringham House, in Sandringham, England. (The Associated Press)
"There will always be distance between the monarchy and the people," said Vovk.
"But all of [it], stretching from Queen Victoria up to William and Catherine is about trying to close as much of the distance as they can that is within their control."
And there's a basic reason behind that, Vovk suggests.
"The monarchy's relevance, its viability, is now predicated on its perceived relatability and accessibility," he said.
"People don't want a Royal Family that is distant and isolated and feels unfamiliar. They want a Royal Family that they feel they can connect with, that they feel like if they were to bump into them on the street, they could just go up to them and talk to them."
That, however, creates something of a paradox.
"If you strip away all of the pomp and the pageantry and some of the mystique around royalty, it raises the question of what makes it so special, anyway? Why have it at all?" Vovk said. "So it is a balancing act."
Pomp and pageantry are on full display as King Charles, left, and Queen Camilla, right, make their way along the Mall following their coronation on May 6, 2023, in London, England. (Charles McQuillan/The Associated Press)
Other factors can play into the monarchy's focus on relatability at any given time.
Queen Victoria's seclusion, particularly after the death of her husband, Prince Albert, drove concerns about relatability during her reign. Rowbotham sees another circumstance closely connected to the monarch at play right now.
"We don't know how long Charles is going to be around, given that he's in his 70s, given that he is still being treated for cancer," she said.
"This time, it's a question of assuring the monarchy's survival by making it clear that there is an heir who is well-prepared and ready to take over the duty.
"That's why I think … they're paying so much attention to the whole issue" of relatability, Rowbotham said.
Vovk sees a greater level of transparency from the current royals compared to previous generations when it comes to relatability.
"We're seeing the curtain being pulled back on the aspects of royal life that are no different or at least have minimal difference from the average person — so, you know, siblings bickering, not liking doing chores, spouses sharing domestic responsibilities."
On the constitutional or political side of the monarchy, however, he sees less revelation.
"There's still some degree of gatekeeping going on here with what amount of royal life is being disclosed and what isn't. That will always be the case with something that is connected with the political life of the nation."
Passing a robot controller to a prince
Benjamin Santiago, left, teaches Prince Edward, right, how to drive a robot using a controller at Queen's Park in Toronto on Oct. 2. (Grant and Martin Curtis/Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada)
Benjamin Santiago had never had an experience like it.
"It's not every day that you get to give a robot controller to royalty and teach them how to drive it," the Grade 12 student at St. Joseph's Catholic High School in London, Ont., said in an interview.
Benjamin, a 17-year-old member of the school robotics team, had that opportunity earlier this month when he passed the controller to Prince Edward, the Duke of Edinburgh, at an event in Toronto.
The gathering that drew education leaders, school board representatives, industry partners and students to Queen's Park highlighted the recent announcement by the provincial Ministry of Education to expand access to the Duke of Edinburgh Award program to schools across Ontario. That comes as the award, founded by Edward's late father, Prince Philip, is evolving and working to blend trades and skills-based experiences into public education to boost opportunities for young Canadians.
"It was amazing. I'm super grateful," Benjamin said of his opportunity to meet Edward. "The prince was super enthusiastic and really just interested about who we are and what our goals were as Ontario students."
In the royal encounter, Benjamin saw the potential to boost support for an area of education close to his heart.
Benjamin says Prince Edward was 'super enthusiastic and really just interested about who we are and what our goals were as Ontario students.' (Grant and Martin Curtis/Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada)
"If someone like the prince can feel the controller and feel how it is to be an engineer in high school and then later on become an engineer in post-secondary … the funding towards programs like robotics may increase."
Edward has had a longstanding interest in youth and promoting opportunities for them, something that has been a frequent focus on his visits to Canada.
"He really took the time to really focus his attention on the students, which is something that I really personally admired about this, but also to make sure that every student felt seen and heard," Laura Briscoe, senior director for business development, communications and experiential education for the Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada, said in an interview.
"He wants to know the realities of youth in Canada and how the award can support their lifelong learning and development, and I found him to be very responsive and open to hearing feedback, whether it's constructive feedback, what are the barriers, where are the gaps, what are we missing?"

The Queen's Park gathering was a "wonderful experience" for everyone there, said Kathy Cepo, Benjamin's chemistry teacher and one of his robotics coaches.
"The prince was so engaged with these students and they felt like they were the only people in the room," she said in an interview.
"He was praising them the entire time and so proud of them."
They meet again
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, speaks with King Charles, right, during an audience at Buckingham Palace in London on Wednesday. (Aaron Chown/Getty Images)
Few world leaders have shaken hands with King Charles as often as the president of Ukraine.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy was back in the U.K. this week, meeting Charles at Buckingham Palace on Wednesday.
"I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience," Zelenskyy posted afterward on X.
"It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine. We appreciate all the assistance provided by the United Kingdom."
It was his third meeting with the King this year, and came as the U.K. doubled down on support for Ukraine and called for its international partners to increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin to respect the U.S. call for an energy ceasefire.
The King meeting with Zelenskyy "on a bit of a consistent basis is a way of … reaffirming Britain's overall support for Ukraine, even though governments are changing," said Vovk.
"It's a way to reassure President Zelenskyy that the United Kingdom stands with Ukraine."
While a monarch is meant to be above politics, meeting with Zelenskyy would also come at the request of the U.K. government.
"The King isn't being party political, taking sides. He's doing his constitutional duty," said Rowbotham.
Prince Harry and Meghan step out in Nottingham
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, left, and Prince Harry, right, greet well-wishers as they arrive at the Community Recording Studio, a youth and community charity that offers a wide range of creative activities, sports, mentoring and youth development programs, in Nottingham, England, on Thursday. (Christopher Furlong/Getty Images)
They aren't official working members of the Royal Family anymore.
But the casual passerby could be forgiven for being a bit confused Thursday as Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, carried out events connected with their private charitable interests in the city where they did their first public outing as an engaged couple nearly a decade ago. It was their first joint appearance in public since they returned to the U.K. from California in late August.
"It's great to be back," Harry said. "Wonderful and great to be back in Nottingham, too."
They began by visiting a recording studio run by a youth and community charity that has received support from a 1.1-million-pound ($2.1-million Cdn) donation announced by Harry last year.
At their next stop at the Himmah charity, which tackles food poverty, Meghan was reunited with four contributors to a charity cookbook released to raise funds in the wake of London's 2017 Grenfell Tower fire disaster. She had donated 10,000 pounds ($18,800 Cdn) from the book's proceeds to help the Himmah hub.
Thursday's visit was the first pre-arranged and advertised occasion since their return, Rowbotham said, but it was not an official royal event.
"However, it was carefully arranged to ensure media reportage and a suitable turnout of sympathetic public by choosing a location — Nottingham — which was … where they were for their first post engagement royal visit."
But it was on a much different scale, she said.
"No local dignitaries were there in official capacity."
Vovk saw the visit as their first outing as part of "the new Sussex court."
He also sees the potential of a "problem of optics" for the monarchy where "Harry and Meghan are engaging in activities that to the average observer look really more or less the same [as] what the monarchy does."
Prince Harry and Meghan, Duke and Duchess of Sussex, visit the Himmah Hub in Nottingham, England, on Thursday. (Annabel Lee-Ellis/The Associated Press)
Vovk expects to see an escalation in public appearances and informal events from the senior working royals.
"I think the monarchy is now going to have to pick up the pace in terms of the kinds of engagements and public accessibility they're doing just in order to keep that clear distinction between Harry and Meghan [having] titles but they are technically private individuals from a legal, constitutional perspective," he said.

Rowbotham doesn't see a threat to the institution itself, although she expects it will be discussed as such.

Freeland believes her resignation led to better outcome for Trudeau, allowing him to exit before likely defeat
In CBC interview, former finance minister defends her record and says history will look kindly on Trudeau
Former finance minister and deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland believes her resignation — which spurred Justin Trudeau to step down — was ultimately a good outcome for the former prime minister given his plummeting popularity.
While her book, Unreliable Boyfriend, is meant to be a guide for dealing with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, it also outlines how her political relationship with Trudeau declined in the final months of his government.
Freeland writes that the prime minister informed her in a Zoom call that he would be replacing her as finance minister just days before she was set to deliver the government's fall economic statement in late 2024.
She abruptly stepped down the same day the statement was to be tabled in Parliament. Trudeau resigned a few weeks later.
Her book outlines how a conversation with former Liberal prime minister Jean Chrétien a month earlier helped her make the ultimate decision to leave.
Speaking to CBC's The Sunday Magazine, Freeland detailed another conversation she had with Chrétien in the wake of the blow-up.
"Prime minister Chrétien said … in resigning, it was ultimately a better outcome for Canada, for the Liberal Party — and also ultimately for prime minister Trudeau because it allowed him not to lead our party to defeat," Freeland told host Piya Chattopadhyay.
"I think that is a very wise observation."
The Conservatives held a huge lead in the polls over Trudeau's Liberals during the final year of his tenure. Mark Carney won the Liberal leadership race to replace Trudeau and led the party to another election win in 2025.
Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Chrystia Freeland rises to present the federal budget in the House of Commons in Ottawa as Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, lower right, listens on April 16, 2024. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
Freeland defends record as finance minister
Freeland had been a cabinet minister in Trudeau's government since it was first elected in 2015 and served as finance minister from the summer of 2020 until her resignation.
When asked if she felt she bore any responsibility for the fading popularity of the Trudeau government — given that the Conservative surge was driven by their focus on the economy and cost of living — she touted her record as finance minister.
"I am very glad that as finance minister, I got us through COVID and I preserved our AAA credit rating while doing that," she said.
"We were able to return to a sustainable fiscal path. Now, that was politically hard to do, but it was absolutely the right thing to do."
Despite their political fallout, Freeland spoke kindly of her early political relationship with Trudeau. And, as she notes in her book, she argued that history will look kindly on Trudeau — but added that she wished he had stepped down earlier.
She insisted multiple times in the interview that Unreliable Boyfriend is "not a book about Justin Trudeau." But she didn't directly answer if she had reached out to her former boss during the writing process.
"I chose what I wrote really carefully. It was important for me to be authentic and to be open. But this really is a book about me and a book about my ideas and my view of where we should go," she said.
"It's not a salacious story."

Elon Musk has quietly financed a major canvassing operation to help Republican candidates in the midterm elections that rivals his effort in the 2024 presidential election, according to federal filings posted Thursday night. To monitor the trillionaire’s overall influence on November’s elections, WIRED created a live-updating tracker that pulls federal filings daily.
The Musk-aligned America PAC has spent $76.7 million in the third quarter of 2026, $35.8 million of which has been spent on a field operation to drive turnout among President Donald Trump's core base across all seven Senate battleground states and a number of House races, the filings show.
That compares with the roughly $45 million America PAC had spent on putting together a field operation at the same point in the 2024 cycle, when the super PAC effectively ran the vast majority of canvassing for Trump's presidential campaign.
In short, Musk has assembled a presidential-level field operation this midterm cycle, underscoring the extent to which he has taken over the get-out-the-vote effort for the party and created something of a shadow Republican National Committee. With three weeks until Election Day, the total contributions are only set to rise even higher.
Canvassing has been America PAC’s largest expense, ahead of the $23.7 million it spent on a combination of digital ads mostly attacking Democrats, campaign literature, and phone bank efforts.
But in an effort to save Republicans' Senate majority, Musk also gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting the GOP's candidates in that chamber. The same amount appears to have been funneled into Texas PAC, which was registered with the FEC in August 2026 and is backing embattled Republican candidate and Texas attorney general Ken Paxton.
Musk has been particularly focused on the Senate race in Texas this midterm cycle, where he has extensive personal and business interests. Musk lives near Austin and his businesses SpaceX and Tesla are based in the state. Musk accounted for nearly 60 percent of the $273 million that the Senate Leadership Fund raised for Texas PAC.
The stunning war chest that Musk has unleashed into all seven battleground Senate races and, to a lesser degree, a number of competitive House races, makes him the largest known donor in the midterms among both Republicans and Democrats.
Since its inception, America PAC has relied primarily on outside firms to conduct paid canvassing, in which people are hired to knock on the doors of likely Trump or Republican voters to remind them to register to vote and vote early.
The super PAC has used mostly the same contractors as in the 2024 cycle, the filings show. The biggest canvassing contract went to Blitz Canvassing, a subsidiary of the political affairs firm GP3 Partners, which helped stand up America PAC.
The other vendors listed in America PAC’s filings were the firms Patriot Grassroots LLC, The Synapse Group, In Field Strategies, Echo Canyon Group, Threshold Strategies, and GEG Strategies LLC. All but the last two also worked for America PAC in 2024.
Going into the final stretch of campaigning, America PAC has more than $12 million remaining, though Musk, the richest man in the world, may contribute more to his PAC as required.
America PAC has spent in 40 races in 17 states since July. The Texas Senate race drew the largest share, in which Musk’s team has spent $15.3 million attacking Democrat James Talarico and $3.5 million supporting Paxton.
The super PAC has also spent about $5.3 million attacking Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio’s Senate race against Republican Jon Husted and $3.5 million attacking Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running against Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, according to the WIRED tracker.

On Oct. 8, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth confirmed (archived) reports that the U.S. military was planning to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, which is currently set for Dec. 3.
A military jury sentenced Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, to death in 2013 after it found him guilty of killing 13 people and injuring 30 more during a shooting rampage at the Army's Fort Hood post in Texas in 2009. U.S. President Donald Trump approved (archived) Hasan's death sentence on Oct. 2, clearing the path for his execution.
On Oct. 8, Hegseth shared an X post by CBS News that read:
The U.S. military plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, when he faces a firing squad on Dec. 3, a Pentagon official said.
Hegseth wrote, "Correct."
One day later, on Oct. 9, the Associated Press reported that Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on whether the Pentagon would actually livestream the execution. "I don't know that that's actually going to happen," he reportedly said. About a week after Hegseth's initial confirmation, on Oct. 15, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that Hasan's execution would go ahead "but this event will not be streamed."
Following Hegseth's confirmation, discussion abounded online about whether executing Hasan in such a public manner was legal (archived, archived, archived). Snopes readers also contacted us about the legality of the planned livestream.
The military justice system, which is separate from the civilian justice systems in the U.S., carried out Hasan's trial and sentencing in 2013. On Oct. 5, Hegseth's assistant secretary for public affairs Sean Parnell wrote on X (archived) that the Army's firing squad would execute Hasan, meaning his execution would be governed by Army regulations.
At the time of this writing, the U.S. Army did not have regulations explicitly allowing it to livestream an execution. Rather, Army Regulation 190–55, which covers procedures for military executions, included requirements that would likely hinder the Army's ability to provide a public livestream.
Trump wrote on Truth Social on Oct. 15 that the "immediate families" of Hasan's victims could still view the execution in person in accordance with current Army regulations.
Gary Barthel, a former U.S. Marine Corps officer and managing partner at the Military Law Center, told Snopes on Oct. 9 that if the Army wanted to legally livestream Hasan's execution, officials would have to either seek an exemption to regulation 190-55 from the Office of the Provost Marshal General as laid out in the regulation itself or amend the existing regulation to allow livestreaming. 
We contacted the Department of the Defense to ask if it was planning to do either of these things and await a reply.
Because the legality of livestreaming Hasan's execution was potentially subject to change, we leave this claim unrated.
What Army regulation says
Chapter 2-5 of regulation 190-55 lists who may and may not witness a military execution. According to the chapter, no person younger than 18 years old may witness an execution and the Army must approve the list of witnesses beforehand.
Those two stipulations could make it difficult for the Army to provide a public livestream without violating its own regulations because it would have to vet the audience's age. Hosting a truly public livestream would make it impossible to approve a list of "witnesses" ahead of the execution because people might log in to watch on the day without registering beforehand.
Barthel told Snopes via phone on Oct. 9:
The Army is required to follow its regulations. If the Army wants to stream this execution they need to change the regulations to allow it. And, either way, I would anticipate that there is going to be some efforts to stop it.
Barthel said that Hasan's defense team could still ask a civilian court to stop the execution and live stream by filing a habeas corpus petition. Such a petition allows a detainee to challenge their detention in court.
Would public execution be 'cruel and unusual punishment'?
Daniel Maurer, an associate professor at the Claude W. Pettit College of Law at Ohio Northern University, told Snopes that livestreaming Hasan's execution could raise constitutional concerns that would ultimately play out in court.
Hasan's defense could bring up such constitutional concerns as part of a habeas petition. Maurer said via email on Oct. 9 that Hasan's defense could argue that being executed on livestream amounted to "cruel and unusual punishment," which is banned by the U.S. Constitution's 8th Amendment. Maurer wrote (links ours):
The remaining legal issue is maybe more complicated and would need courts to resolve it: does such a practice violate Hasan's 8th Amendment protection from "cruel and unusual punishments?" - this protection is also stated in the UCMJ, article 55, and Army Regulation 190-47 ("The Army Corrections System") so it applies to prisoners already confined, not just defendants at court-martial sentencing.
In order to establish whether livestreaming Hasan's execution amounted to cruel and unusual punishment, the courts might apply the "Evolving Standard" test, according to Maurer. The test allows courts to consider whether a punishment is cruel and unusual under current societal standards, rather than according to standards at the time the Constitution was written.
Cornell Law School's Legal Information Library wrote that "in the context of capital punishment, the Court has generally viewed the Eighth Amendment to prohibit punishments that 'involve the unnecessary and wanton infliction of pain.'"
Though livestreaming may not inflict "unnecessary and wanton" pain, Maurer said there are other factors at play:
Given that federal law prohibits photographic or other visual or audio recording of an execution of any other civilian federal prisoner, this is strong evidence that our own federal government (of which the DoD is of course a part) would consider it to be "cruel and unusual," and thus would be an 8th Amendment violation.
Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law, called the decision to livestream Hasan's execution "sick-making" when speaking to Snopes on Oct. 9. He previously told DRM News that a habeas petition could postpone Hasan's execution past the end of the Trump administration as it progressed through the civilian court system. That means Hasan's execution and any potential livestream could be halted by an administration without "the same penchant for executions," Fidell reportedly told the Associated Press.
It was unclear whether Hasan would file a habeas petition. The Associated Press reported that Hasan had begun his 2013 trial by firing his lawyers and telling jurors that he was the gunman in the 2009 shooting. The outlet reported that this move "convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan's only goal was to get a death sentence." It remained unclear whether Hasan's goal remained the same in 2026.
The nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center wrote that Hasan's execution would be the first military execution in the U.S. since 1961.
The Washington Post, citing the center, reported that the last high-profile public execution of any type in the U.S. took place in 1936. Another public execution took place the year after.
For further reading, Snopes compiled 17 claims about the death penalty that we've investigated over the years.

Ratlam (Madhya Pradesh): Six people, including three women, have been arrested for allegedly duping a businessman by selling fake gold as genuine, police said.
According to police, the gang allegedly cheated utensils trader Mustafa Tambawala on Oct 16 by selling him fake gold pieces. Manakchowk police arrested three men and three women during the investigation.
Police seized 11.80 kg of fake gold jewellery and idols, 2.20 kg of fake silver jewellery, nine silver coins weighing 400 grams, Rs 30,000 cash and an electric weighing scale.
Police said information was received that some men and women from Faridabad, Haryana, were roaming in Ratlam selling counterfeit gold and silver jewellery.
Preliminary questioning indicated possible involvement in similar offences in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, which police are verifying.
Police said the arrested suspects include two Faridabad residents and one Lucknow resident. Names and addresses of the three women were not provided in the police statement.
A case has been registered at Manakchowk police station under Crime No. 566/2026. Further investigation is underway.

Durga Puja pandal committee members in south Delhi’s C.R. Park have accused the police of forcing them to shut by 10 p.m., two hours earlier than usual. They say the early deadline is disrupting celebrations and worsening crowd-control problems, even as large numbers of police and paramilitary personnel remain deployed around the venues.
The office of DCP (South) Anant Mittal denied the allegations, saying the intervention was aimed at ensuring compliance with court-mandated noise pollution rules.
The development comes on the day the toll in the stampede at a Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata on Saturday climbed to 19, with four children and 11 women among the deceased.
“Since day one [October 16], the police and paramilitary forces have been coming in large numbers, with batons and whistles, forcing committee members to close the pandals at 10 p.m. Usually, the pandals remain open until 12.30 a.m. or 1 a.m.,” said Kali Mandir Puja Committee secretary Prodip Ganguly. “We just want to enjoy our festival. However, police are scaring our devotees away,” he added.
‘Unrealistic deadline’
A member of the Mela Ground Puja Committee said the 10 p.m. deadline is unrealistic. “The police entering and forcing pandals to close is stopping devotees from enjoying the festival,” he said.
Aam Aadmi Party’s Delhi unit chief Saurabh Bhardawaj criticised the police. “Squeezing the evening window by two hours will cause crowd swell and chaos. This could lead to a West Bengal-type situation, and the government will prosecute Puja committees to hide its own shortcomings,” he wrote on X.
‘Playing loud music’
Mr. Mittal said the police had intervened in cases where the organisers continued playing loud music beyond the permitted time despite agreeing to follow the rules at earlier meetings. “Our regular crowd-control measures include barricading and the deployment of additional forces, with some personnel kept in reserve if necessary. The pandal samitis have also been asked to add more gates to facilitate the entry and exit of people,” he added.
Deputy Commissioner of Police (Central) Rohit Rajbir Singh said similar measures had been introduced at Ramlila grounds in central and north Delhi this year.
“All necessary arrangements are in place, and so far, we have not felt the need for additional measures or a review of security arrangements at Ramlila Maidan based on the inflow,” he added.

The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”
Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.
Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.
She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”
Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.
“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”
Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.
Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.
The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”
Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.
Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.
“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”
Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.
In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”
Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

Hong Kong excels at medical research. So what is holding it back?
Hong Kong’s biomedical ambitions face hurdles beyond research funding, experts say, pointing to limited industry investment, production capacity and specialist talent.
In the first of a four-part Health Matters wellness series on frontier medicine in Hong Kong, Elizabeth Cheung looks into how the city can turn world-class research into real-world treatments and what it needs to become a global biomedical innovation hub.
Raymond Tong Kai-yu spent a decade overcoming challenges in cost and production to develop a device that could change lives: a robotic hand that helps stroke patients regain mobility and relearn everyday movements.
The Hong Kong biomedical engineer is best known for “Hand of Hope”, which he developed 15 years ago at the age of 39. The device is now used in hospitals across 15 countries, but getting there was far from smooth.
“It is challenging to turn scientific research products into real-life applications for others to use … breakthroughs in research and market access cannot happen at the same time,” said Tong, a professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s department of biomedical engineering.

Mauritius reels from worst riots in decades after woman shot by police
- Published
Police in Mauritius imposed an overnight curfew overnight to quell the worst riots to break out on the Indian Ocean island in decades.
Peaceful protests over water shortages and the high cost of living that started a week ago erupted into violence on Friday when a woman was shot and wounded by police at a roadblock.
The circumstances of the shooting are not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody.
Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam ordered the curfew on Tuesday, warning against those "acting against the interests of the country", which is a tourism and financial services hub.
"Those who have carried out these actions will have to face the very heavy consequences warranted by their anti-patriotic acts," he said in an address to the nation.
Protesters burned tyres and blocked roads as the unrest escalated over the weekend, with police stations and other public infrastructure properties being vandalised.
The mayhem prompted the closure of schools and public transport, with foreign embassies issuing alerts warning its nationals to be cautious.
Despite the curfew, police said there had been several incidents overnight and some arrests.
But the police assured people that by Wednesday morning traffic was again moving throughout the island and said people should resume their normal activities.
When protests over the shortage of water initially started, the government had responded proactively by providing more water to households, according to Zoë McCathie, an analyst at South Africa-based Signal Risk.
The escalation had presented a more "unusual situation for the country's security situation", with the government resorting to closing schools and imposing a curfew, she told the BBC's Newsday programme.
"Protests to this scale and to this extent haven't been seen… since around 1999. So the government's response to this in that case is logical and is necessary," she said.
While the government had managed to "curtail the worst of the unrest" there was still a possibility that protests could return in some areas, with water shortages expected to persist until the rainy season in December, she said.
The cabinet is due to meet on Wednesday afternoon to reassess the situation and decide on the next steps.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. this week launched an agency-wide effort to study and document any health problems reported after vaccination, the Department of Health and Human Services said on Thursday.
The initiative is the latest step by Kennedy, who spent years questioning vaccine safety and founded an anti-vaccine group before taking office, to reshape federal immunization policy. The American Academy of Pediatrics says childhood vaccines are studied in placebo-controlled and comparison-group trials and monitored for safety after approval.
The federal Vaccine Injury Table lists 14 compensable injuries across 16 vaccine types under the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, a no-fault system in which claimants file against the government, not vaccine makers. Since 1988, it has awarded roughly $5 billion across about 12,300 injury and death claims.
The new moves, which appear to be part of Kennedy’s decades-long efforts to sow skepticism about vaccines, come as he faces legal challenges to his attempts to alter US childhood vaccination schedules and growing concern among public health experts about falling immunisation rates, particularly against measles, which has seen a resurgence in the US since last year. The effort centers on a National Institutes of Health clinic
opened on Monday to treat and study patients reporting health problems after receiving vaccines, HHS said in a statement. Other measures include a proposal by the Centers for
Medicare & Medicaid Services to reimburse physicians for reporting suspected injuries to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS; a CDC effort to update VAERS; and HHS requiring electronic health records to capture vaccine-related adverse events.
Kennedy has said U.S. children receive too many vaccines, falsely claiming repeatedly that kids get up to 90 doses before age 18, which has been echoed by President Donald Trump. Kennedy has long argued that chemicals in vaccines are dangerous, though experts say there is no evidence of harm.
In his first year heading HHS, he fired all 17 independent expert members of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee and selected new panelists, many of whom shared his anti-vaccine views.
In January, the CDC announced a revamped childhood vaccine schedule that reduced recommended vaccines, dropping universal recommendations for flu, rotavirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B at birth, some forms of meningitis and respiratory syncytial virus.
A federal court issued a preliminary injunction in March blocking key parts of the proposed changes, finding that Kennedy and HHS had violated federal law in reshaping the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunisation Practices. The injunction has prevented ACIP from holding meetings to make recommendations on immunisations often needed for insurance coverage.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on Saturday launched action into the Ankita Bhandari case, a day after her parents met senior CBI officials. According to news agency ANI, a CBI team are questioning ex-BJP MLA Suresh Rathore at a guest house in Haridwar.

“Ankita’s parents also gave a letter demanding narco-tests on both Rathore and Sanawar saying their audio recording recently went viral and it had allegations of involvement of a senior BJP leader in the case,” an officer requesting anonymity had said.
Ankita Bhandari was a 19-year-old resort receptionist whose body was found in Uttarakhand's Pauri Garhwal in 2022.

Pope Leo pledges return to duties following lung cancer surgery
The first US pope had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung
Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter’s Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.
The 71-year-old pontiff had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fuelling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.
Smiling from a window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice on Sunday, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule.
“Having overcome this delicate phase ... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers,” Leo said.

A cluster of Shigella infections linked to a temple festival has put health authorities in Thrissur on alert, with 10 cases reported in the district in the first nine days of October. Seven of the cases, including that of a seven-month-old child, were reported from Tholur among people who had attended a festival at a temple there.
The suspected source of the infection has been traced to a well at the temple, from which water was drawn for rituals. The well has since been chlorinated, District Medical Officer M. Sujatha said.
“The seven Shigella cases reported from Tholur were among people who attended a festival at a temple in Tholur. The source of infection has been identified as the temple well from which water was taken for rituals. The well has been chlorinated,” Dr. Sujatha said.
Health teams are closely monitoring the situation, while hospitals have been instructed to respond immediately if any further cases are detected. Awareness campaigns have also been conducted in the area, with people advised to seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms, she said.
All those who tested positive for Shigella have sought treatment, and most have recovered. The remaining patients are also recovering, according to the DMO.
The other three Shigella cases reported during the nine-day period were from Wadakkanchery, Arimbur and Adat.
The Shigella cluster comes amid a wider surge in fever cases in the district. As many as 4,914 people sought treatment for fever between October 1 and 9. During the period, 39 dengue cases and four cases of leptospirosis were also confirmed.
Dengue cases have been reported from several parts of the district, including Kodakara, Mattathur, Meloor, Thrissur Corporation, Avinissery, Chalakudy municipality, Kaiparamba, Kodassery, Pananchery, Puthukkad, Adat, Alur, Puthur, Mullurkara, Pariyaram, Tholur, Orumanayur, Thalikulam and Choondal.
Leptospirosis cases were reported from Pananchery, Pazhayannur, Porkulam and Kuzhur.
Dengue cases
The DMO said a significant number of dengue cases had been detected in migrant labour camps and among their contacts. “Most of the dengue cases have been reported from migrant labour camps and their contacts. We are keeping a close watch on them and monitoring the situation,” she said.
Health authorities have stepped up surveillance and preventive measures across the district. The DMO urged people with fever to take adequate rest, drink sufficient water and consume nutritious food, while vulnerable people, particularly those with compromised immunity, should take extra precautions and seek medical care when necessary.
With Shigella cases emerging in connection with a common gathering and dengue continuing to surface across multiple locations, health officials are keeping a close watch on possible further transmission and urging the public to maintain strict hygiene and food and water safety.
