India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
- Published
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August.
But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention.
Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said.
A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage.
"The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said.
Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment.
But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes?
India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control.
But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat.
Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods.
Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important.
A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period.
Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online.
Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau.
The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily.
And the dangers extend beyond flooding.
A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms.
While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau.
The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress.
The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations.
Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas.
In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet.
Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project.
But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort.
"One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute.
"What happened after that no one knows," he added.
Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet.
But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022.
China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said.
Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes.
"These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group.
But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved.
One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value.
"What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank.
Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders.
The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow.
"There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD.
He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks.
Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay.
"Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says.
Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain.
For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat.

You can’t really talk about smart glasses without bringing up Meta. HTC, the company behind 2010-era virtual reality headsets and a failed smartphone business, seems quite eager to tackle that comparison directly.
In September, HTC started selling its $499 Vive Eagle smart glasses in the US. The Eagles have lots of the same features as other glasses on the market—cameras for capturing photos and video, speakers in the frames for music playback and calls, an embedded AI agent you can ask questions of and even get recipes from by taking pictures of stuff in your fridge.
But HTC also wants to steer clear of the ongoing debate about privacy in camera-equipped smart glasses. Meta has been dogged by controversy for its smart glasses, with people worried about the company’s interest in enabling face-recognition features, and calling the people who wear them creepy. HTC is aware of that discourse and thinks it is completely possible to make smart glasses that aren’t a privacy nightmare.
“It's not just about protecting the consumer, but it's also about protecting people around the consumer,” Dan McDowell, HTC Vive’s head of enterprise sales, tells WIRED. “People can usher in, I think, what are really tremendous experiences with a new layer of confidence and protection.”
I’ve been wandering around with the glasses for a couple of weeks, and so far they meet my expectations for what smart glasses have become. They protect my eyes from the sun. They snap good photos and videos. You can record and transcribe voice notes. The music playback has decent sound quality. (I’ll always prefer a solid pair of headphones if I’m actually trying to listen to music, but the speakers work just fine.) They come in two styles—one with square Wayfarer-esque lenses and the other more rounded.
The Vive Eagle glasses can get 4.5 hours of battery life on continuous music playback. They can last 36 hours on standby. HTC also sells a companion clip-on battery pack called Power Boost that costs $49. It clips right onto the frame and is noticeable but not as obnoxious as you might think.
Don’t forget the AI assistant, Vive AI, which can utilize OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini. It doesn’t require a login, so users are “de-identified” in a way that keeps the services from retaining personal information. (That also means, by default, you won’t be able to enjoy many of the personalization features these chatbots offer by gleaning information from your emails and messages.) The glasses come with Vive’s AI Plus, free for the first two years. After that, users must pay a monthly $2.50 subscription fee.
Right by the cameras is a bright indicator light. If you cover the light, it won’t record. If someone around you says stop recording, that will stop the recording. Video footage you capture is encrypted and stored on the glasses—it’s not automatically sent to the phone or cloud. If you want to import photos or videos, you have to do it manually in the app.
Meta has faced scrutiny over the indicator light before, as some users have blocked the LED with stickers or broken into the hardware to turn it off. Meta has responded with software updates that disable the camera if someone tampers with the indicator light, along with other privacy-focused measures.
I ask McDowell how HTC, and really any smart glasses maker, can get past the “trust me, bro”–style privacy promises companies tend to make.
“We're not a social media company,” McDowell says. “There's no benefit to me to have any of your info. We don't train our AI model or any third-party AI models with any of the information that is used on the glasses.”
The real problem may be that with cameras on the frames, smart glasses are hard to distinguish between brands. The Vive Eagles look a lot like Meta glasses, and people worried about those privacy issues may not know that the Eagles are different and not tied to Mark Zuckerberg’s company. I’ve had friends see me wearing them and ask if they’re smart glasses. Yeah, I replied, but not the ones they’re thinking of. That didn’t seem to dispel any of their suspicions.
The hope, at least how HTC frames it, is that more players with better privacy practices will help shift cultural disdain for smart glasses. A bunch of other companies are going cameraless, like Even Realities, Viture, and Halliday. Others are building theirs with privacy shields or focusing on virtual displays instead of capturing the world around you. That said, no one has captured the market quite like Meta.
“We'd like to make sure that our technology adapts to society's expectations, not the other way around,” McDowell says. “I hope that everybody that's making products like these takes steps in the right direction.”

Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music
If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
Writer Yiyun Li does not talk about "grief" or the "grieving process." To her, those words make it sound that at some point you emerge from grief. Instead, Li prefers to use the word "abyss," which, she says, is where she expects to be for the remainder of her life.
Li's teenage sons both died by suicide six years apart, Vincent in 2017 at age 16, and James in 2024 at age 19. Her Pulitzer Prize-winning 2025 memoir, Things in Nature Merely Grow, chronicled the loss of her sons and her effort to go on.
"James' death taught me to suffer better," she says. "To say, 'I can do it, and I can live with my pain and sorrow without ever wanting to stop feeling.'"
Li's new novel, Music Against the Night, is set in the late 1700s and early 1800s and centers on two prodigies who are brought together by music, and drawn apart because of their aspirations. The novel focuses on music, which sits outside of words.
"I think I've had the feeling both times after my children's death that words often fall short, and falling short doesn't mean not succeeding, falling short doesn't mean failing," she says. "But when I start a new project, I would like a subject [where] words naturally fall short. So music is that choice."
Li grew up in China and served a year in the Chinese military before coming to the U.S. to study immunology. She eventually left her Ph.D. program to become a writer. Li is now a professor in the creative writing program at Princeton University.
Interview highlights
On the decision to set Music Against the Night in a different time period
I was in the middle of the novel when James died. This is a novel far from my usual interests or concerns, and the reason I think I went back to history is I would like to live again through history, through historical figures, through my characters living in the late 18th and early 19th century. ... I'm making the past into a new now for myself and possibly for my readers.
On how playing piano connects to her grief
I began my piano lessons at the end of 2023, purely to get to know how to play the piano. And James died in February 2024, so two months into my piano lessons he died, and it occurred to me that piano or music is a good way for me to count time — because music is about time. It's about counting the measure, counting the rhythm. And also music is about ... be[ing] engaged with something else. You can sit in your sadness all day long, do nothing, or crying. Or, like me, I could just sit there and just play the same drill again, and again, as a way to know I was, in a way, staying in touch with the world. ...
I'm not a concert pianist, but somehow I find it liberating and healthy to do something that you absolutely love but cannot do well. Every time I go to my piano lesson, I'm so intimidated. I'm sweating because I just can't do it. I can hear other people do it, I cannot do it myself. But I think that's, again, acknowledging the limit of my capacity.
On raising two gifted children
Both my children could be called prodigies, but James, my younger son, especially was extraordinarily odd and brilliant. ... We were greatly baffled. I remember he was 5 or 6, he said, "Mommy, you will never see the world. I see it full of dots and squiggly lines." And that again was a strange perception of the world [that] we adults did not have access to. …
What is the responsibility or the difficulty of bringing up a child [who is] very brilliant? … Some people would say, well, you really have to train him to be the next Einstein, but we did not want him to be the next Einstein, we want him to be a normal, happy boy living in an ordinary life.
On her son Vincent
He was a brilliant painter and we still have all his paintings around the house. He was an oboist and when he wanted to learn the oboe, the oboe teacher said he was a bit young, because he was 8 when he want to learn oboe, but he was certain. ... [He had] started on the piano and he could articulate that piano was not his instrument. He wanted to play the oboe. But mostly, he wrote beautiful poetry. He was a great poet. And he was a greater reader. I wouldn't call him an outlier, as James was, but he was brilliant and fun and interesting.
On struggling with suicidal ideation
Sometimes I think people have all sort of thoughts about or against people who have chosen suicide, and people who've chosen or attempted suicide are often called selfish. But my experience is oftentimes people [are] in great pain, whether it's great mental pain or great physical pain. And sometimes people in deep depression cannot tell the difference between mental pain and physical pain, because everything together is a great kind of suffering. I think it's not that people who experience that kind of suicidal urge, it's not that they want to die or they want [to] use this to hurt other people.
On becoming a writer
I was born with innate curiosity and also sensitivity to things that did not quite make sense. So I grew up in China. And for instance, when I was little, all the adults would say, since you're a child, you have no right to decide who you want to be or what you want to do. And my mother even had a saying, something along the [lines] that an adult decides and the child follows. I was quite young, you know, 4 or 5. I just couldn't make sense of all of these teachings because I thought I was as capable of thinking as the adults, and why did I have to follow them? So I think that sort of sensitivity to things that are very, very nonsensical, I think maybe that's one thing that made me into a writer.

అక్టోబర్ 10న ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద భారీ నిరసన చేపట్టనున్నట్లు కాక్రొచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ప్రకటించింది. ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర ఓటర్ల జాబితా సవరణ (SIR) ప్రక్రియను వెంటనే నిలిపివేయాలని, 2025 జూన్ 25 నుంచి ఓటర్ల జాబితా నుంచి తొలగించిన పేర్లన్నింటినీ తిరిగి చేర్చాలని కూడా CJP డిమాండ్ చేస్తోంది. లెఫ్ట్ వింగ్ విద్యార్థి సంఘాలు కూడా ఈ నిరసనలో పెద్ద సంఖ్యలో పాల్గొంటామని ప్రకటన విడుదల చేశాయి. జంతర్ మంతర్లోకి ప్రవేశించేందుకు ప్రయత్నించిన సీజేపీ (CJP) నేతలను పోలీసులు అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు.

ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలో జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ జరిగిన నిరసనలకు సంబంధించింది కాదు. ఈ వీడియోను ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో చిత్రీకరించారు. అయితే, ఈ వీడియోను ఖచ్చితంగా ఎప్పుడు, ఏ సందర్భంలో చిత్రీకరించారో తెలియదు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేస్తున్న వాదన తప్పుదారి పట్టిస్తుంది.
వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, ఒక ఫుట్ ఓవర్బ్రిడ్జిపై “Diyandi Festival” అనే పదాలతో ఉన్న హోర్డింగ్ కనిపించింది. దీని గురించి వెతికితే, ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో ప్రతి సంవత్సరం సెప్టెంబర్లో దియాండి పండుగను జరుపుకుంటారని తెలిసింది. నగర సంరక్షకుడైన సెయింట్ మైఖేల్ ఆర్చ్ఏంజెల్ గౌరవార్థం నిర్వహించే ఈ పండుగ సెప్టెంబర్ 29న ముగుస్తుంది.
వైరల్ వీడియోలో “Shann Gadget” అనే పేరుతో ఉన్న బోర్డులను కూడా గమనించాం. గూగుల్ మ్యాప్స్లో వెతకగా, ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో రోక్సాస్ అవెన్యూలో, గైసానో సిటీ సూపర్మాల్కు ఎదురుగా ఈ దుకాణం ఉన్నట్లు తెలిసింది.
గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూలో పరిశీలించగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపించే ప్రదేశానికి, స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ చిత్రాల్లోని ప్రదేశానికి మధ్య పలు పోలికలు కనిపించాయి. దీంతో ఈ వీడియోను ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలోనే చిత్రీకరించినట్లు నిర్ధారించాం.
అయితే, ఈ వీడియోను ఖచ్చితంగా ఎప్పుడు చిత్రీకరించారు, ఏ సందర్భంలో చిత్రీకరించారు అనే విషయాలను మేము గుర్తించలేకపోయాం. అందుబాటులో ఉన్న ఆధారాల ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియోను ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో చిత్రీకరించారు. దీనికి ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన నిరసనలకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు.
చివరిగా, ఫిలిప్పీన్స్కు చెందిన ఒక సంబంధం లేని వీడియోను, ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన CJP నిరసనల వీడియోగా తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు

Former Sale Sharks lock Andrews dies at team hotel in La Rochelle
- Published
Former Sale second row Hyron Andrews has died at his Johannesburg Lions' team hotel before their Champions Cup match at La Rochelle on Saturday.
A statement from SA Rugby stated that his death had been an "accident" and that the 31-year-old had "died after a fall".
"We are heartbroken by the passing of Hyron," said Lions chief executive Rudolf Straeuli.
"He was not only a gifted rugby player, but also a cherished member of our Lions family having recently joined us this season.
"On behalf of our chairman, Mr Altmann Allers, the board and everyone at the Lions, I extend our deepest sympathies to [Andrews' wife] Maighlin, their young sons Hendrix and Emerson and the entire Andrews family.
"We stand with them in their sorrow and will remember Hyron with great affection and respect."
The Lions will fulfil their fixture against La Rochelle, which kicks off at 17:30 BST, in Andrews' honour, while a moment's silence will be observed at all the opening round's fixtures.
"This is terrible and distressing news; our hearts go out to Hyron's family and the whole Lions rugby community," said Mark Alexander, president of the South African Rugby Union.
"There are no words to adequately convey our shock and the depth of sympathy we feel for his wife Maighlin, and for his extended family, friends, team-mates and loved ones during this time of immense sorrow.
"His untimely passing is a devastating loss, and we share in the grief of all who knew and loved him."
Andrews left Sale in the summer to return to his native South Africa. He made 45 appearances for the club after arriving in February 2024 from the Durban-based Sharks as injury cover for England international lock Jonny Hill.
"Hyron was just a brilliant guy and a brilliant team-mate," said Sale director of rugby Alex Sanderson.
"He was so skilled on the field but off it, he was always someone you would want to have a beer with.
"He was funny and charismatic in his own unique, dry way and the lads, to a man, loved playing with him and being around him.
"It was a big move for Hyron and his wife Maighlin to come to England, but he truly made a second home in Manchester. It was incredible to see how he and his family embraced the club and area.
"Most importantly, he was a loving husband to Maighlin and a doting father to his two gorgeous boys. It was an absolute privilege to get to know him and it's just absolutely devastating for everyone."
While he was yet to earn senior international honours, Andrews had represented the Junior Springboks in 2015.
Andrews' death comes 10 years on from the sudden death of Munster coach Anthony Foley in Paris before a Champions Cup fixture.
Foley, 42, died in his sleep on the eve of a match against Racing 92 after a heart condition caused fluid to build up in his lungs.
Munster's present-day players will wear commemorative tops, featuring the Munster club crest and Foley's shirt number eight as part of their pre-match routine at their match against Racing on Saturday.
The Lions, who play their home matches at Ellis Park, are making their first appearance in Europe's premier club competition, with South African sides introduced into the continental competition in the 2022-23 season.
They have won two of their first three matches in the United Rugby Championship so far this season, including beating defending champions Leinster in their first game of their campaign.

During my 10+ years of clinical experience in various States and with numerous patient populations, I have seen that dental anxiety is a constant challenge. I have seen this phenomenon in children clutching their parents’ hands before their first cleaning and in accomplished professionals quietly cancelling appointment after appointment in the hope that the problem will somehow resolve itself.
It doesn’t.
In my experience, the longer you leave a fear unchecked, the greater the clinical and human cost becomes. Dental anxiety is not a moral failing. This is a well-documented psychological response—and one with important, measurable public health consequences.
How severe is it?
Roughly a third of people have significant dental anxiety, and roughly a tenth have a clinical phobia. That’s not a little footnote. That means a lot of the population is actively avoiding or delaying care that could prevent serious disease. The downstream consequences of this avoidance are visible daily in my clinical work: infections tolerated for months, decay advanced far beyond what early intervention would have required, and patients presenting with pain that could have been prevented years ago.
Knowing where it starts
Dental anxiety typically has a definite source. A painful or poorly done procedure in childhood can be a source of dental anxiety. A provider who was in a hurry or didn’t tell the patient what was happening. The specific sensory environment of a dental office—the sounds, the smells, and the physical vulnerability of lying back with your mouth open—can leave powerful imprints, especially in young patients. That memory is not just wiped out; it impacts behaviour for decades. For some, it’s not just one event but an accumulation. Years of avoidance layered on top of embarrassment about how their teeth look now, and a fear of judgment prevents them from asking for help. This cycle of shame avoidance is one of the hardest patterns I see clinically. When these patients do come in, they need much more intervention than if they had come in sooner, and this becomes an instance of the very fear that kept them away.
The health price of avoidance
Research literature teaches us, that oral health is not an island. Untreated dental disease is a chronic inflammatory load on the body. It has been linked to cardiovascular risk, dysregulated blood sugar, and impaired immune function. When a patient avoids dental care for years, it is not just their smile that is at risk; they are carrying a preventable health load that will rise elsewhere in time.
In addition to the system effects, the impact on quality of life is immediate and real. A toothache interferes with sleep. It impacts nutrition, concentration, and the ability to speak with confidence. These are not trivial consequences; they affect how people show up in their professional and personal lives every day.
What works in practice
The most significant change I’ve made in my practice is making communication a priority before any procedure begins. When patients feel informed and in control, it greatly reduces their dental anxiety. A stop signal—a raised hand that stops everything instantly—can alter the psychological dynamic in the room. It shifts the patient from passive recipient to active participant, and that shift matters enormously. I also allow extra time for anxious patients. The problem is not that procedures take longer, but that rushing them increases anxiety. I explain everything before it happens, check in frequently, and never minimise what a patient is feeling. These should not be luxury accommodations; they should be routine parts of effective care.
For patients with more severe anxiety, pharmacological support is appropriate. Nitrous oxide is safe, effective, and rapidly reversible. There are also oral sedation choices if needed. These are clinical tools, not last resorts, and patients should feel comfortable asking about them.
A message to patients
If fear has kept you from the dentist, remember you are not alone, and you are not too far gone to be helped. What I ask of patients in this situation is one small step—not a treatment plan, not a procedure, simply a conversation. Come in and tell us about your nervousness. A good provider is a good listener and will start there. There is no need to be afraid of the dental chair. With the right approach, it can be a place where you take difficult things and make them manageable—and where the relief on the other side is worth it.
(Dr. Sowjanya Gunukula is a U.S.-licensed dentist with international training who focuses on preventive and evidence-based oral healthcare and contributes to advancing community and public health dentistry. sowji.gunukula@gmail.com)

Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest
The BBC has witnessed Israeli settlers attack Palestinians and set fire to olive trees in the occupied West Bank.
Several dozens of settlers dressed in black charged down a hill near an outpost – illegal under international law - to a field where Palestinians and activists were harvesting olives. They torched about a dozen trees and hurled stones from slingshots.
Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was at the scene, was taken to hospital where she told reporters she "got jumped" and described being kicked on the ground.
The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year. It says this year levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high.
The BBC's Middle East Correspondent Lucy Williamson reports.

In a major shift in the theatrical tides, Netflix has reported box office grosses for the first time ever.
The streamer’s awards hopeful “La Bola Negra” scored $277,500 from just four theaters, averaging $69,375 per location. Those ticket sales are notable as the second-highest screen average ever for a non-English language film behind 2019’s “Parasite,” which opened to $393,216 from three theaters, averaging $131,072 per location. It’s also the highest-ever PSA — the key metric for arthouse releases — for a Spanish language film. By comparison, Neon’s multilingual legal thriller “Fjord,” another Oscar contender, debuted last weekend to $124,000 from four theaters, translating to $31,000 per location.
Now the test is whether “La Bola Negra” can sustain momentum as Netflix slowly expands the movie’s footprint in the weeks to come. The streamer plans to keep the film in theaters for 45 days, a traditional window in post-pandemic times and the company’s longest theatrical rollout to date, before its Netflix release on Dec. 2. Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known as Los Javis, “La Bola Negra” is a generation-spanning queer epic that chronicles the interconnected story of three men. After the drama was embraced at Cannes Film Festival with a 16-minute standing ovation, Netflix acquired the movie for around $5 million. “La Bola Negra” tied for the Cannes best director prize and won Toronto Film Festival’s People’s Choice Award, which has historically been a reliable indicator of Academy Awards attention.
Popular on Variety
Netflix has long been viewed as a major big-screen adversary, probably because the company’s co-CEO Ted Sarandos has frequently dismissed movie theaters as an “outmoded idea.” And while the streamer has been warming to theaters beyond just Oscar-qualifying runs, with token releases for 2022’s “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Story” and last year’s”Kpop Demon Hunters” re-release and the “Stranger Things” series finale, Netflix has never disclosed how much those movies made in cinemas.
In the past, Netflix has viewed multiplexes, not as a financial strategy, but rather as a marketing stunt to drive interest pack to the platform. But there are other benefits to box office reporting for Netflix, which has never won the coveted best picture Oscar. Unlike streaming metrics, which can be twisted and touted in any which way, box office dollars are uniformly reported — meaning there’s no denying a hit (or a miss). Netflix’s change in strategy comes as the streamer’s stock has been languishing. Last week, the company laid off 1,000 employees and replaced chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Disney veteran Peter Rice.
Moving forward, Netflix plans to disclose grosses for upcoming releases such as David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” around Thanksgiving and Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” and Taika Waititi’s animated “Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory” in 2027. Whether those buzzy projects achieve breakout status, Netflix’s new attention toward theatrical is a win for exhibitors, who are already celebrating the biggest post-COVID year at the box office.

Yokohama – In a stretch of green in Yokohama spanning some 100 hectares, at a site that once housed a U.S. military communication facility, industrious teams of workers are busy planting trees and flowers as organizers strain to get the word out about the Green Expo, which begins in just five months.
Ten million plants will blanket the grounds, including 600 cherry trees that should bloom around the time of the six-month event’s opening on March 19.
The international horticulture expo, which will run until Sept. 26, aims to highlight the human relationship with the natural environment, while also stressing the need for global collaboration in solving environmental issues.
The organizers are hopeful they will attract an international crowd as they strive to offer a uniquely Japanese perspective under the theme of “The Blooming Field of Planetary Citizens.”
As with any major event in Japan, a mascot has been tasked with providing a marketing boost. The brightly colored Tunku Tunku, who is described as an extraterrestrial creature mesmerized by Earth’s natural beauty, can count a photo opportunity with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi as among its recent efforts.
The mascot may be whimsical, but the expo has a serious aim: to shift perceptions and relationships with the environment, and showcase the possibilities offered by cutting-edge technology. It will also put forward a “Japanese model” aimed at “achieving sustainable development,” ahead of 2030, the target year for the realization of the U.N.’s Sustainable Development Goals.
But while much of the focus will be on technology of the future, organizers of the expo are also taking a long look at the past in order to highlight sustainable practices.
Lessons from the past
Thematically, part of the event will highlight the Edo Period (1603-1867) — a time in Japan’s history during which a circular economy flourished.
Back then, with Japan largely cut off from international trade, the country turned inward. Pre-industrialization, experts describe it as a time when little household waste was generated and when reusing and repairing items was essential.
As a result, the concept of mottainai — a phrase that expresses regret around waste — became ingrained. Fearing deforestation amid rapid development, authorities also put in place strict restrictions around timber via the establishment of a forestry office. Rules were so stringent during that period that there was an adage connected to the severity of the punishment for stealing timber: “one cypress tree, one human head.”
Yuko Tanaka, an academic and expert on the Edo Period, describes a society in which the thinking around materials and objects was focused on circularity and recycling and reuse across everyday objects.
“Repairing and reusing things was an integral part of everyday urban life,” she says, citing clothes as one example. “A kimono is made by sewing together rectangular pieces of cloth. Traditionally, it was taken apart for washing, the individual pieces were washed, and then the garment was sewn together again. This meant that it could easily be repaired or remade,” Tanaka explains.
Long before modern recycling, people of that time also made use of discarded paper.
“There were dealers known as kamikuzu-kai, literally ‘waste-paper buyers,’ who bought paper that people no longer needed. The collected paper was pulped and made into recycled paper for use again,” she says. Tanaka also noted that, in addition to this culture of reusing and repurposing waste, there was a great emphasis placed on repairing, and repair specialists flourished.
Kazuko Ishigaki, executive director of the Green Expo’s public relations department, describes the Edo Period as a “golden period” for the circular economy, while also hailing the people’s connections with nature.
“One of the major pavilions — a horticulture pavilion — will be focused on the Edo Period to showcase or highlight how the people of the Edo Period lived in harmony with nature,” says Ishigaki, who has served as U.N.-Habitat’s regional director for Asia and the Pacific.
Ishigaki suggested it was time to “revive the spirit” of that time period, including when it comes to disaster mitigation, citing the period’s natural approach to mitigating calamities such as flooding.
“Now we are mostly preventing floods by constructing high walls or dikes,” she says. During the Edo Period, she notes, hanami (cherry blossom-viewing) was purportedly promoted at a government-level in key areas on top of the dike. The idea was that people would sit on the area and their weight would compact the soil and make it stronger.
“So they enjoy nature, but at the same time they are contributing to disaster risk reduction. There are so many interesting ideas in the Edo Period, some of them maybe we can still utilize” in modern society, she said.
Roman Krznaric, a social philosopher and author of several books including History for Tomorrow, in which he wrote about the Edo Period’s circular economy, said in a modern context such attention could be turned to the latest tech.
“Today, if you take a standard smartphone, it uses half the elements of the periodic table and is thrown away after less than three years. Now, if you think of that with an Edo mindset, you would never permit the sale of standard smartphones, you would regulate the hell out of them,” he says, suggesting that with this mentality, such devices should use recycled materials and include modular designs so that parts could be replaced rather than the whole device being scrapped.
Krznaric says there were many ways in which society could be “looking at the world with an … Edo mindset.” He also rejects the notion that such thinking is utopian, instead describing it as something with a historical precedence that could be applied at scale.
One example the organizers are keen to highlight is their reuse of timber from the Sou Fujimoto-designed Grand Ring that formed the temporary centerpiece of the Osaka Expo. The structure was built using traditional Japanese joinery and fashioned from cedar and cypress.
Ishigaki says this is practical and sends a sustainable message.
“The wood from the Osaka Expo ring will be recycled and reutilized here … this is not just to keep the legacy from Osaka, but also to symbolize the concept of circular society, or zero-waste society,” she says.
Inspiration from Osaka
The Osaka Expo is an obvious point of comparison, but the idea to host the Green Expo originated separately in Yokohama, when in 2015, the U.S. military communications facility was returned to the city. The obvious question was — how should the city utilize the site now that it belonged to Japan once more?
From there, discussions snowballed. A horticulture event quickly became the starting point before a bigger more ambitious conversation developed and academics, nongovernmental organizations and then eventually the national government weighed in.
Now, more than 500 organizations are involved in the Green Expo and the event is aiming to follow on the legacy of Osaka’s World Expo, which attracted around 25.58 million visitors across six months and generated an “economic ripple effect” of around ¥3.6 trillion, according to the economy ministry.
Ishigaki says with the Green Expo, the aim is to utilize the momentum from the Osaka Expo, while avoiding some of what critics labeled its missteps.
“(The) Osaka Expo was very successful but at the same time there were some challenges,” she says, suggesting that these should be lessons that inform the Green Expo’s approach.
One such example is the extreme heat, which was a much publicized issue for the Osaka Expo during Japan’s scorching summer. The expo responded by adding mist fans, cooling stations and more shaded rest areas, while also enhancing its medical emergency systems.
To avoid similar issues, the Green Expo team is planning countermeasures in advance given the event will run throughout the summer.
“Many people suffered from extreme heat (in Osaka) so we have special anti-heat measures,” she says, noting tree cover, cooling mist and cooling areas specifically designed for children as among the measures.
Looking ahead
While organizers are keen to avoid some of the criticism that was directed at the Osaka Expo, that may be a double-edged sword. A lack of criticism has also meant the Green Expo has suffered from a lack of awareness.
Overall, organizers are aiming to attract 10 million visitors, with a goal of selling 5 million advance tickets.
“Maybe some people misunderstand, (thinking) this is just an event to enjoy flowers. This is a national event — this is a formally authorized expo,” Ishigaki says.
For many people, environmental issues may appear to be somewhat abstract or not as relevant to their lives.
While awareness of climate change remains high in Japan, the sense of urgency about the crisis appears to be on a downward trend in recent years.
In a January 2025 survey by Ipsos, only 40% of respondents agreed with the statement, “If individuals like me do not act now to combat climate change, we will be failing future generations” — a drop of 19 percentage points since 2021 and the lowest among the 32 countries surveyed.
“They might think this is not related to their life, but that’s not true,” Ishigaki says. “We want people to rethink the relationship between their life and nature.”

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent has accused European countries of refusing Washington's request to impose secondary tariffs on 
India and China
 for purchasing Russian oil, questioning why the United States should bear the burden of pressuring Moscow alone.
Speaking to NBC News' Meet the Press on Sunday, Bessent said the Trump administration had approached European allies in the spring to seek coordinated action against countries buying Russian energy.
“So we have asked—in the spring, I asked our European allies to join us in putting secondary tariffs on China, on India. They refused. So why should the US bear the burden?” Bessent said.
He added that Washington could re-engage with its European partners, reiterating that President Donald Trump wanted to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
“President Trump has made it clear he wants the killing to stop. And the so-called Graham bill gives the president the flexibility, gives him 60 days to assess the situation,” Bessent said.
US defends 60-day pause on sanctions legislation
Bessent's remarks came after Trump temporarily waived certain provisions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, giving his administration 60 days to assess the potential consequences of imposing sanctions and tariffs.
Defending the decision, Bessent insisted that the administration had not lifted sanctions on Russia.
“No sanctions were lifted on Friday,” he told NBC's Meet the Press, referring to Trump's executive order granting the waiver.
The legislation, which received strong bipartisan support in Congress, provides for tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported into the United States from countries that are among the largest buyers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas, including India and China.
Bessent said the pause would allow the administration to evaluate the situation before deciding on further measures. He also defended Trump's record on Russia, citing sanctions imposed on Russian energy companies Rosneft and Lukoil.
“President Trump sanctioned the two largest Russian energy companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, which dealt a catastrophic blow to the Russian energy industry,” he said. “So no one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than President Trump.”
US secretary of state 
Marco Rubio
 also defended the pause, saying the administration needed time to assess the consequences of imposing sanctions and tariffs on the global and American economies.
“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy, and even to the US economy,” Rubio told reporters on Saturday.
Rubio said the administration was also considering pressures on global energy supplies arising from the Iran war, attacks by Houthi militants in Saudi Arabia and the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
Bessent accuses Europe of financing Russia's war effort
Bessent also criticised European countries for continuing to purchase Russian oil and gas while supporting Ukraine.
Citing shipments from Russia's Yamal facility, he said 140 cargoes had left during the first six months of the year, with 136 going to European countries, including Belgium, Spain, France and the Netherlands.
Those shipments were worth more than $8 billion, he said.
“The Europeans have given Russia and Vladimir Putin more money than they've given the Ukrainians. They continue to gorge on Russian energy,” Bessent said.
He added that the United States imported $4 billion worth of Russian products, including $1.8 billion in fertilisers, while European countries imported more than 10 times as much.
Bessent also pointed to the UK's decision in May to waive its embargo on diesel and jet fuel made using Russian crude, questioning why similar criticism had not been directed at other countries.
Rubio calls India an important ally
Rubio said Washington needed to consider the energy requirements of countries such as India before deciding whether to impose tariffs or sanctions.
“These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries—India, for example, and others,” Rubio said.
He added that countries such as India had diversified their energy supplies but could not immediately stop importing Russian energy.
The comments came amid criticism of Trump's decision to pause enforcement of the sanctions legislation. Indian-American lawmakers Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam criticised the move, arguing that it weakened pressure on Russia and undermined Congress' authority.
Bessent questioned over whether Ukraine is a US ally
During the same NBC programme, Bessent was asked three times whether the United States considered Ukraine an ally. He did not give a direct yes-or-no answer.
“We provide the three different things ... to Ukraine, so that’s what you do for an ally. We’re not providing those to Russia,” he said on the second occasion.
Bessent said Washington supported Ukraine by providing intelligence, Starlink support and allowing Nato countries to purchase American weapons for transfer to Kyiv.
He also questioned why European members of Nato had not supplied Ukraine with more Patriot missile systems, arguing that they had the capability to do so.
His comments followed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's appearance on the programme, during which he warned that it would be a “historic mistake” for the United States to side with Russia.
“We want to trust him, and I hope that he will change his decisions because I think that it's all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help the United States,” Zelensky said of Trump.
Bessent criticised the Ukrainian president for publicly accusing Washington and Elon Musk of restricting resources used by Ukrainian forces. He called the allegations “very reckless”, according to NBC News.
Bessent maintained that Trump wanted to end the war through a negotiated settlement, saying the conflict had to stop and that the president was working towards that outcome.

Ukraine and the U.S. are at odds over Starshield. Here's what to know
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and U.S. officials remain at odds over disruptions to a key satellite communications service used by the Ukrainian military.
Zelenskyy told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday he believes the U.S. government is behind his military's loss of normal access to the Starshield and Starlink services, claiming tech firm SpaceX imposed the restrictions in response to a "message from [the] American government."
Warning that the U.S. siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake," the Ukrainian leader claimed that the Starshield system has not been fully restored, despite what U.S. government officials have said publicly.
In a post on X over the weekend, Zelenskyy said the restrictions on the system have hindered Ukraine's ability to intercept weapons launched by Russia, calling the consequences "very painful and unpleasant."
The dispute comes after days of back and forth between Ukraine and the United States over the Starshield system.
What are Starlink and Starshield?
Starlink is a satellite internet network operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX to provide internet service to the U.S. and other counties. Since 2024, the U.S. Defense Department has shared a high-powered military version of the network called Starshield with Ukraine, which has cost the Pentagon billions of dollars.
Ukraine relies on the network in its defenses against Russia's nearly five-year full-scale war.
"We use Starlink to intercept the jet fighters that are hitting our civilians and killing families," said Zelenskyy online. "We also use Starlink for middle strikes on enemy military targets in our temporarily occupied territories. We were unable to do this when there were restrictions. And the third, most important thing is people. Our soldiers, who have been on the front line for weeks and months, are being delivered food and water using appropriate drones with Starlink."
Starshield controversy
Zelenskyy said the disruptions to Starshield came without warning last week. He told NPR in an interview that losing normal access to the critical defense network had left his military's frontlines vulnerable. On X over the weekend, he said the network's speed hasn't been fully restored.
It's unclear why Ukraine has experienced restricted access to Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that the U.S. government is responsible for the system, and that "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
A bipartisan group of senators is calling on the Defense Department's inspector general to investigate how the system was disrupted.
State Department reaction
Speaking to reporters on Friday, President Trump denied interfering with Starshield. "I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon. And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been," he said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also rejected Zelenskyy's claims that the disruptions to the system were deliberate.
"It's just categorically false. No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn't use it," Rubio told reporters on Saturday, adding that Ukraine requested access to the system to carry out strikes deep inside Russia.
"That's under conversation. It's under discussion right now of how they would want to use it," he said.
America's faltering support for Ukraine
The Starshield disruptions have renewed questions over the United States' commitment to supporting Ukraine against Russia's war, with tensions between President Trump and Zelenskyy growing over the past few days.
Earlier this month, Trump moved to ease U.S. sanctions against Russia that had been passed by Congress. After Zelenskyy pushed back on the move, calling it a "weak decision by strong partners," Trump lashed out, criticizing Ukraine for striking Russian refineries, which he said was affecting U.S. diesel prices. "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump said.
The war of words has continued in the past few days, with the Ukrainian president outlining further areas of disagreement. On Sunday's Meet the Press, Zelenskyy also said that U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine concerning Russia ballistic missile attacks was blocked for three days, but has resumed.
Ret. Navy Adm. Mark Montgomery told Here & Now's Scott Tong he believes the Starshield disruptions are a response by the White House to Zelenskyy's efforts to strike Russian oil refineries.
"This is really a signal. It's a signal to stop attacking oil refineries and President Zelenskyy has properly pushed back on that," Montgomery said. He added it's an extremely vulnerable moment for Ukraine, as more Russian drones are able to get through.
The war continues
Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Russia has launched more than 4,000 strike drones, bombs and missiles against his country over the past week. Russian attacks on Saturday night targeted energy substations leaving tens of thousands of people without electricity, according to Zelenskyy.
Ukraine has responded to Moscow's strikes with its own attacks on Russian oil refineries. Ukrainian forces hit a major refinery southeast of Moscow last Thursday after Zelenskyy had said he was "done" following Trump's calls for an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine.
On Sunday, Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot on fire in the Russian city of St. Petersburg, as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia.

As France burns, Macron looks like a man who has lost control
The French national debt is too big, its economy too sluggish and its parliament and president jointly unable to get state spending down to sustainable levels - the mirror image of the complaint of the protesters, who want more spending on subsidies and schools. And so it’s in gridlock

In his last few months as president of the French Republic, Emmanuel Macron looks more than ever a man who lost control of events, lost touch with the nation he leads, and lost the confidence of international investors with it. This is not a comfortable, confident position for any leader to be, but with a hung parliament hardly able to pass a budget and the very fabric of of the nation unravelling, this lame duck - who once promised so much with his unifying project of a radical centre - has been, and is, reacting in all the wrong ways to the malaise now enveloping his country.
Rather than through, say, a television interview or a speech delivered in person, President Macron, so inappropriately aloof, chose initially to react to the protests that have broken out across France over the weekend, sparking disorder, violence and hundreds of arrests in a rather terse statement on X: “Those who took part in the vandalism, attacked prefectures and stores, and engaged in looting, including in city hall buildings, will be brought to justice and will be punished.”
In his later, key, presidential address to the nation the president struck a more conciliatory tone, and acknowledged that there were “legitimate concerns”. Oddly, he told the angry citizens in effect to wait because he’s only got six months left until the election of his successor, who will try clear up the mess. This is not the leadership France needs or deserves.
Unarguably, those who choose violence should take the consequences, but the government always had the choice between meeting the representatives of the protesters, the classic French mix of students and workers, now bolstered by the resurgent gilets jaunes, listening to their grievances and offering some sympathy and change. Instead, the Macron administration ordered the riot police to do their worst.
Originating in a secondary school protest in the Paris suburb of school in Creteil, southeast of Paris, over a lack of teachers, and culminating in well over half a million people on the streets, many suffering life-changing injuries from police weapons, the authorities have reacted with a counter-productive brutality. A police tear gas grenade shattered a 14-year-old’s jaw and many of his teeth. A 15-year-old lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade. Other adolescents have also suffered life-changing injuries blamed on police weaponry during protests.
No wonder trade unionists and others have joined the protest movement, adding the cost of living, fuel prices (as in other western countries a triggering issue) and a general sense of national pessimism and insecurity. In this way, these disturbances combine some of the themes that caused such comparable disorder in 1958, 1968 and 2005, all of which similarly drained the governments of the day of authority. More than in most democracies, direct action has always been an informal clause of the French constitution, proof that sovereignty lies with the people, rather than any essentially ephemeral institutions or haughty ruler.
This time around, there is an additional issue facing M Macron. Just as ominous as this unrest, and potentially much more far-reaching, has been the other, simultaneous challenge, to the stability of the French state - an incipient sovereign debt crisis reminiscent of the one that spread across the Eurozone fifteen years ago. Of all the major advanced economies, it is France that has suffered the most, and see the largest rise in its bond yields, and the more precipitous fall in the value of French government bonds, known as OATs (Obligations assimilables du Tresor.
As things stand the markets think that the debt issued by the likes of LVMH is more likely to hold its bake and be repaid than the paper offered by the French state. This is because the French national debt is too onerous, its economy too sluggish and its parliament and president jointly unable to get state spending down to sustainable levels - the mirror image of the complaint of the protesters, who want more spending on subsidies and schools. Hence the gridlock in policy making.
As in the earlier Eurozone crisis as it hit Greece, Italy and Spain, the eventual consequence of this devaluation of OATs will be a shrinkage in the balance sheets of the big banks, who own vast quantities of OATs. That would lead to a credit crunch and, most likely, a recession and similar “contagion” across the Eurozone, but this time with the second largest European economy at risk of default. A rescue by the European Central Bank (in practice Germany) would again demand some austerity.
The origins of these multiple crises are long and complex. However, prime among them stands President Macron’s capricious decision to call premature elections to the French parliament in 2024, at a time when he still enjoyed a comfortable majority. It was designed to renew his mandate after his party had been snubbed in the European elections. Instead, it left France with an entirely dysfunctional domestic government, and contributed to more intense political polarisation - the rise of the far right and of the hard left.
France was left rudderless. This kind of “immobilisme” is not uncommon in French history, but it rarely ends well. Apres Macron, le deluge?

Kipchoge, 41, breaks course record at Melbourne Marathon
- Published
Two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge says "his body is still peaking" after winning the Melbourne Marathon in a course record time at the age of 41.
The Kenyan crossed the line in two hours nine minutes 10 seconds for his 17th career win over the distance and first since the Berlin Marathon in 2023.
"I believe that my body is still peaking - still able to compete with the next generation," Kipchoge said.
"The oldest athlete is still competing but I am happy to run with the Gen Zs."
The course was partly raced along the Australian Formula One track at Albert Park and finished inside the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).
"On the course, it was really wonderful, I enjoyed seeing people standing, cheering, and shouting my name," added Kipchoge, who slowed down inside the MCG to wave to the fans.
"It was actually different - running on a beautiful course, but also running on the Formula One track, and above all else, finishing on a cricket ground.
"It makes me proud to run with the younger generation and inspire the running community in Melbourne."
Australian Thomas do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35, with compatriot Reece Edwards third.
New Zealand's Camille French won the women's race in 2:28:25, followed by Australian Sinead Diver and Nichola Sheridan of Ireland.
The Melbourne Marathon was the third leg on Kipchoge's world tour, on which he hopes to complete a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica, over two years.
Each marathon will raise funds for the Eliud Kipchoge Foundation, which focuses on education, environmental sustainability and health.
Kipchoge is considered one of the greatest long-distance runners of all time, winning two Olympic marathon golds, plus a silver and bronze over 5000m.
His honours also include a world title, 12 World Marathon Major victories and two official world records.
In 2019 he became the first person to break the two-hour marathon barrier under special conditions in Vienna, clocking an unofficial time of one hour 59 minutes 40 seconds.

Hit a midlife wall? This test identifies your strengths and what matters to you
When's the last time you asked yourself: What do I love to do? What makes me feel alive?
Earlier this year, as Ailsa Chang planned her 50th birthday party, I welcomed her to this side of life. Ailsa and I pick up that conversation on All Things Considered as I launch a new podcast, Your Turn with Allison Aubrey, aimed at navigating the twists and turns of midlife.
If you've been focused on work deadlines and family obligations, without much time to focus on yourself, you're in good company. And in midlife, a lot can shift: Kids launch. Careers and relationships change. These transitions can be tough, but they also open the door to what's next.
So, I went in search of tools to help me find my way. I invite you to join the Your Turn newsletter journey - starting with this survey that ranks your character strengths.
Start with a strengths survey
The VIA Character Strengths Survey is a free online questionnaire developed by researchers in positive psychology, the scientific study of what helps people flourish. The question behind it: How do we go from feeling just OK to thriving?
"Character Strengths are the positive parts of your personality that impact how you think, feel and behave," explains the VIA Institute on Character. After you answer a series of questions, the survey rank-orders 24 strengths, from creativity, humor and teamwork to curiosity, bravery and spirituality.
Research suggests that applying your strengths in daily life can help boost wellbeing and reduce stress. And a study of women 50 and older, found those who used a signature strength in a new way, had increased levels of happiness and less depression.
The survey takes about 15 to 20 minutes to complete. You can take it on your own or with a facilitator. I took it at a retreat at the Modern Elder Academy with Christine Carter, Ph.D., a wellness and lifestyle coach, and a senior fellow at UC Berkeley's Greater Good Science Center.
Your strengths are a compass
Carter says there's value in reflecting on the results.
"What I really like people to do is take it and then look at their top strengths and remember how you feel when you're engaging that strength," she told me. "I think that it can be a real compass for the types of intrinsic motivation that we're looking for in finding our purpose."
Carter has an art degree and used to be a painter. Appreciation of beauty and excellence ranks near the top of her list, along with gratitude and zest. When she's absorbed in a work of art or a great piece of writing, she says, she feels part of something bigger than herself.
One of my top strengths is a love of learning, a good match for a career in journalism. I get to learn something new every day.
What if your results don't resonate?
This happens a lot. Your top strengths can reflect where you've been and how you've been spending your time. The good news: They aren't fixed. "Your character strengths can evolve," Carter says. Shift your focus, or how you spend your time, and your results can shift too.
3 questions to ask as you review your strengths
- Which strengths do I want to cultivate? Look for a strength you value but haven't made time for. If creativity ranks lower than you'd expect, that's a sign of where to invest a little time. "Humans are meaning makers," Carter says. As your roles shift, so can your sense of purpose. A new project or hobby doesn't need to be big. It just needs to be true to you.
- What brought me joy as a kid? Think back to what absorbed you before life got busy, whether it was exploring the woods, drawing or singing in a choir. Then look for the strengths behind it. If appreciation of beauty ranks high, more time in nature or at a concert may be what feeds you.
- What do I want to leave behind? Notice the habits and expectations that no longer serve you. Change takes courage, especially when it means letting go of something to make room for what's next. But many people who've made big midlife changes describe it as freeing.
If you have a half hour this week, take the survey. Then pick one strength you'd like to make more room for, and invite it into your life. You don't need to overhaul your life to start; one small step can set you on a new course.

Even as the Centre informed the Supreme Court on Monday (October 12, 2026) that it had decided to cap trade margins at 30% for non-scheduled cancer drugs, the court questioned why the benefit of such price regulation should be confined to cancer drugs and not extended to other essential medicines and medical products.
The development comes after a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta expressed concern over stark disparities between the price to retailer (PTR) and the maximum retail price (MRP) of certain medicines, particularly cancer drugs, with mark-ups in some instances soaring to 1,000%. The Bench had flagged that such exorbitant mark-ups constituted “broad daylight dacoity” and placed an enormous financial burden on patients.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, informed the Bench that the proposed 30% trade-margin cap would cover both patented and non-patented cancer medicines, with an expert committee headed by the Director General of Health Services tasked with identifying the drugs to be brought within its ambit. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) will examine the committee’s recommendations before issuing a price notification to implement the cap.
The Bench, however, said that while the intervention was commendable, it was inadequate, and questioned why other medicines and medical devices could not also be brought within the 16% retailer margin prescribed under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013.
“This is just the tip of the iceberg... this has come around only because of the unduly hard observations we made during earlier hearings. What about other drugs,” the Bench asked.
The top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha seeking stricter enforcement of price controls under the DPCO to curb disproportionate margins across the pharmaceutical supply chain.
Justice Mehta drew attention to steep markups on medical devices and consumables, pointing out that an India-made cardiac stent costing around ₹5,000 was being sold by hospitals for more than ₹25,000. He cited the example of a saline drip line carrying an MRP of ₹11 being sold for ₹270.
“We understand that there are transportation costs, raw material costs, R&D costs and other ancillary costs, but all these are included in the MRP. What is the logic behind allowing them to sell at 400 times the actual cost? How can you allow this? What is the benefit for the patients?” the Bench observed.
‘Balance in pricing’
Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, also appearing for the Centre, cautioned against a uniform cap across medicines, arguing that low-value products often required higher margins to remain commercially viable for retailers. Excessive regulation, she said, could discourage retailers from stocking such medicines and affect their availability, particularly in rural areas.
Ms. Bhati stressed the need to preserve some room for market forces rather than subject the entire pharmaceutical sector to price controls.
“Higher margins in such cases are important for ensuring the availability of such medicines to consumers… Our concern is that there has to be a balance in pricing. There has to be some level of market play available for drugs. We do not want to control the entire ecosystem of drugs. The policy was framed with the outlook that there should be intervention only when necessary,” she submitted.
The Bench, however, was not persuaded, observing that ensuring the availability of price-controlled medicines was the government’s responsibility.
“If the DPCO -approved medicines do not reach customers, then it is the duty of the government to ensure it reaches [sic] the patient. The actual dispute is over which medicines should be on the DPCO-controlled list and which should not,” Justice Mehta observed.
Accordingly, the Bench gave the Centre until October 27 to work out the modalities for capping medicine prices, when the matter will be heard next.
Centre’s affidavit
The Centre, in its 551-page affidavit, said the proposed trade-margin rationalisation (TMR) was expected to reduce the MRP of anti-cancer drugs by 20% to 70%, translating into estimated annual savings of around ₹2,500 crore. It said the measure would reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure and improve the affordability and accessibility of cancer medicines, while retaining a 30% trade margin for the distribution chain.
The Centre cited a similar intervention by the NPPA in 2019, when a 30% trade-margin cap was imposed at the first point of sale on 42 select non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines. The margin was based on an industry-practice assumption of 10% for distributors and 20% for retailers.
The measure, it said, led to a substantial reduction in the MRP of 526 brands and annual savings of around ₹984 crore for patients, based on information furnished by pharmaceutical companies. The Centre said the 2019 exercise provided a policy and operational precedent for extending trade-margin rationalisation to a wider range of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines.
Detailing the existing price-control mechanism, the Centre said the ceiling price of medicines listed in Schedule I of the DPCO is determined by taking the simple average of the price to retailer of brands and generic versions with a market share of at least 1%, and adding a 16% margin.
“The ceiling price so fixed becomes the MRP, i.e., the price above which the drug cannot be sold in the market. However, the manufacturer is at liberty to give an appropriate margin to the wholesaler and the retailer within the ceiling price,” it said, adding that ceiling prices had so far been fixed for 935 formulations.
For non-scheduled formulations, manufacturers are free to determine the initial launch price, subject to the NPPA’s regulation of subsequent price increases. The Centre said competition in the pharmaceutical market generally acted as a restraint against arbitrary pricing.
