Welcome to Friendly Argument, a new STAT First Opinion series in which two experts who disagree but respect each other’s point of view engage in a debate about medicine and health policy. In this installment, John E. McDonough, author of the new book “America’s Wrong Turn: U.S. Healthcare in the Neoliberal Era,” discusses the roots of U.S. health care dysfunction with Stuart Butler, a scholar in residence in economic studies at the Brookings Institution. Their discussion was held on Zoom.
Below is a lightly edited, AI-generated transcript.
Torie Bosch: You two have been disagreeing on health care policy for about two decades now, is that right?
Stuart Butler: Not always disagreeing. I think perhaps disagreeing more on methods and what I’ll call engineering issues than on principles of where we want to end up. So we’ll see how it comes out.
Bosch: Even better.
John McDonough: I got to know Stuart from a distance when I was in the Massachusetts legislature and he was a prominent national voice on health policy as one of the early employees at the Heritage Foundation in Washington, D.C. I heard about him, saw his work on many, many levels, not just on health policy. And when I went to D.C. in 2008 to work on what became the Affordable Care Act, working inside the U.S. Senate, I quickly reached out to Stuart, and we started conversations. And he brought me into the inner sanctum of the Heritage Foundation and we started this exchange.
Part of it was because I was involved in Massachusetts since the 1980s. And we started a big effort in 2003 to create some kind of universal coverage vehicle. It was done during the term of Gov. Mitt Romney. And Mitt Romney either got contacted or reached out to the Heritage Foundation, and they acted as his principal national advisers and were quite important in his agreeing to put into the law an individual mandate for people to buy health insurance. And so even though I was from the Democratic side and he was from the Republican side, there had been this cross relationship going back several years around Massachusetts health reform where we both agreed on an individual mandate. And so, you know, what else might there be that could flow from that?
Butler: And I might add that it wasn’t just an agreement on a mandate, it was an agreement that everybody should be able to get access to affordable health care. And we argue to some extent about the methodology of that, but not in Massachusetts, not greatly. I would also just add something to what John said. Yes, he came to work in Washington and came to work for Ted Kennedy. And just as I’ve always thought there were two Ted Kennedys, I think there are two John McDonoughs. And they very much reflect his experience with Ted Kennedy. There was the sort of chest-thumping John McDonough, you know, because Ted Kennedy would denounce people and say they really were totally opposed to doing what was good for the world. And there was the other Ted Kennedy and the other John McDonough, which meeting quietly at the Heritage Foundation or somewhere else and saying, “Let’s figure out a way forward.” And I would just put forward the premise that John’s book is really the first kind of John McDonough: the tough, no-nonsense, exaggerate differences, which I think to some extent misrepresent the people that he attacks.
But when I went to the end of the book and read the way forward, I couldn’t disagree with much of it. And so I felt at the end that there is a lot of opportunity for moving forward. I wouldn’t like this debate or John’s book to overshadow that, because it’s gotta happen. It’s not gonna be with people who think Trump is the most fantastic president there’s ever been, but it’s also gonna be with people who think of themselves as conservatives or neoliberals, in John’s phrasing.
Bosch: I love that as a setup for this conversation because I do think it’s really important to bring together people who respect each other and agree on certain values and disagree about how to do it. I think that’s where we’re more likely to get actual productive conversation instead of just the shouting that we seem to see so much.
So John, so what is, in as few sentences as possible, the ultimate argument that you’re making in the book?
McDonough: So the ultimate argument is that Americans are deeply distressed these days about so many aspects of our health and medical care system. The requirements for approvals before you can get services, the large and harmful cost sharing, deductibles, copays, coinsurance, the mountain of consumer medical debt and medical bankruptcy, the fast-rising premiums on the commercial side, what many people see as the invasion of private equity financing into the medical system, taking over hospitals, nursing homes, medical practices, veterinarian services, plus the extraordinary amount of consolidation and monopolization we’ve seen in so many parts of the economy and so much in in medical care as well.
Most people have heard about one, two, three, or all of these things. And I think for the most part, people look at them as discrete phenomena. And what has occurred to me in writing my book is that they are actually all interconnected.
And the thread that interconnects them is the term neoliberalism, which was a political economic movement that has roots in the ’30s and in the 1940s. It was kind of a fringe movement for a long time, with leaders such as Milton Friedman.
In the ’70s, when the New Deal era came to an exhausted end with the election of President Reagan, we entered a new economic political era that Ronald Reagan exemplified and he was the prime seller of in the United States, along with many others around the world. This was an international movement: Maggie Thatcher in Great Britain, Gerhard Schröder in Germany, Deng Xiaoping in China, all connected to it in various ways.
Neoliberalism wasn’t aimed at trying to change health and medical care so much in the United States. But because health and medical care are so vast and big, it’s preposterous to imagine that we could have all that societal change and medical care would just go unscathed. So my conclusion is that if you want to understand how we got to where we are now, you have to understand the neoliberal movement of that era.
I dislike a lot of their ideas, and I respect the commitment, the power, and the guts that these people had to go out into the hailstorm and shout their ideas to the rafters and then see many, many of them implemented. It was a revolution. The premise of my book is if you want to understand why we are in the sorry state we are now, you have to go back to the roots, understand this, and see how it unfolded over what I call the four decades of U.S. neoliberalism between 1980 and 2020.
Bosch: Stuart, on a scale of one to 10, how much do you agree with that premise? Let’s say one is not at all, ten is we’re in sync.
Butler: I agree with John’s opening points about the kinds of concerns that we have. The patient confusion, debt. No question about it. In a country like this, a country as advanced and as rich as we are, the fact that there are millions of people who cannot get access to adequate health care is first of all ludicrous and outrageous.
The question, and John of course posits an answer to this question, is: Who’s the cause of this? and that’s where I think we’re going to fundamentally disagree. First of all, I have to plead guilty to being what John would call a neoliberal and a fan of Milton Friedman. I was really brought up in my formative years at university and thereafter on Milton Friedman, and met him several times actually, and remain a great fan of his. And I think what John does in this book, unfortunately, is to exaggerate and often misrepresent the core underlying values and objectives of the so-called neoliberals. “Neoliberalism” is a term that I would be comfortable with, because I think of liberalism in the European sense of freedom and respect for people as the core of it.
Just to give you one example, I think John does misrepresent very much the idea of monopoly and laissez-faire capitalism. Neoliberals have always been concerned about monopoly, about the producer having control over the customer. Neoliberalism is very much a kind of “trust the people,” or a people-first approach. It challenges government provision when it’s monopolistic, as when I was brought up in the U.K. and had lived for 30 years under a monopolistic government-organized system. And now I’ve lived under a rather different system, but still the concern with monopoly, of decisions being made in backrooms, whether for profit or to cut budgets or for whatever — these are not unique to private provision.
When we think about the way forward, and as I said, when I look at John’s book, I’m drawn to many of the recommendations at the end, because I do think that whether it be private monopolies or public monopolies, these actions are needed.
But I think it’s really important that we don’t let John convince the public that people who call themselves neoliberals are perfectly fine with people profiteering out of the illness of others and ganging up on the public and patients. This is very much an argument about tools and techniques, what I call engineering issues, rather than a deep philosophical difference.
McDonough: I accept that monopoly/antitrust is a great place to start. It’s so important, and urgent. We see it playing out every day in American society with Disney and Paramount and Live Nation and all the rest. It’s all around us. It started in the U.S. around 1890 with the Sherman Antitrust Act in terms of government involvement. The purpose of antitrust was to prevent companies from getting too large by taking over companies and swallowing them up and thwarting competition. And that, with fits and starts, ups and downs, changed little over roughly 90 years.
Butler: Right.
McDonough: That was the direction and the consensus in the U.S. Dwight Eisenhower took credit for all the antitrust cases he brought when he was president and running for re-election in ’56. It was a bipartisan thing. Even in the early days of neoliberalism, Milton Friedman said, the one area I believe that government has to step in and control, like it or not, is to thwart monopoly and antitrust.
But there was a switch that happened in the ’50s at the University of Chicago, where Friedman was based. Aaron Director and other folks adopted a shift on antitrust. And one of their students by the name of Robert Bork, took on the mantle that we need to reorient antitrust in the United States. He put his thoughts into a book that became quite popular, particularly on the conservative side, called “The Antitrust Paradox.” His premise was: We’ve got antitrust all wrong. The notion that big is always bad is not true. If somebody gets big, that’s because they deserve it because they won in the marketplace. Leave them alone and let the market take care of them.
That idea spread substantially, and Friedman bought into it as well. He switched at some point. With Reagan’s election, they used Bork’s consumer welfare hypothesis: As long as two companies wanting to merge can prove that it will result in lower prices for some consumers, it should get a green light. They should be able to do pretty much what they want if they can show that. So in 1981 and ’82, the new Reagan administration completely rewrote the antitrust guidelines, the federal guidelines that instruct federal judges and prosecutors, state attorneys generals, everybody. Here’s how we see the world. And this was the most dramatic rewrite of those guidelines ever and embodied the consumer welfare hypothesis.
That led to a significant drop in antitrust activity and a significant going to sleep on many levels, including in medical care where we’ve seen a massive amount of mergers and acquisitions since then. Many economists today look at the health care sector, and their conclusion is if you want to understand why health care is so expensive in the United States right now, it is because of the extraordinary amount of monopolization and antitrust.
Today, in over 90% of counties across the U.S., the hospital sector is rated as highly concentrated, the highest rating you can get from the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, the HHI. That’s my reading of it. There was a revolution and the neoliberals won.
What did I miss in my reading of history here, Stuart?
Butler: Well, let me try to fill in the gaps that you have in your understanding and knowledge. I think the antitrust issue really is a perfect example of what I was saying earlier, which is that on the principles and objectives maybe we completely have a broad agreement. And there becomes debate about the engineering of how you get there.
I think the antitrust evolution of neoliberals is a good example of that. The bottom line of Milton Friedman and other supporters of neoliberalism was that there has to be effective competition, there has to be open entry. In other words, there shouldn’t be barriers to people coming in to try to do a better job to deliver for the consumer or the patient in this particular case. As John well knows and says in his book, in the early Friedman years the feeling was that antitrust was the most effective tool and was the critical tool to do that. And on that was there was board agreement.
Then what you see is Friedman and others saying, wait a minute, we might have been ignoring the political game that goes on around this, because what was happening, he said, was that you see the people who are currently providing start to manipulate the Antitrust Act to favor their position and in fact use their good relations with government, close relations with government, to get government to come down on their side of these debates.
Friedman’s position was not that that monopoly was suddenly OK. It was that the antitrust system had basically been corrupted. And that’s why he opposed it, not because he wanted to see more monopoly. And in fact, if you look at the people today who would be called Friedmanites, think of, you know, people like Jim Capretta, the Milton Friedman chair at the American Enterprise Institute. You can’t get more Friedmanite than that. They say, yes, the arguments against, or the weaknesses of, antitrust that Friedman and others and Bork identified were valid. And we’ve got to look at other tools, better tools to achieve the objective of open entry, and real competition, and so on.
You’re very familiar with this Certificate of Need requirement that in many communities says, “well, if we’ve got enough hospital beds, we’re not gonna let anybody else come in and compete or build.” That is so antithetical to open entry and leads to monopoly. So they attack things like that. Or licensing, which yes, to some extent will preserve the quality of services, but on the other hand, we all know is used to shut out people who can deliver services to people at lower cost. And so we see this in so many areas of the industry. So I think it is in fact a good example of how people’s position can change and mine has changed. I know John has changed. When you see the engineering that you thought would lead to a good result doesn’t, and you’ve got to change it. And that’s what we see in this case.
But there remains agreement on the principle. I am totally in favor of universal access — not only a mandate because I think that’s only one element and there’s certain reasons for that. But I support subsidies. Milton Friedman was a big supporter of subsidizing people to enable them to get an adequate level as determined by society, by the political process, whether it be welfare or education or health care. So there was agreement on this. What happened over time were debates about how you get there.
And that’s why I think again, I was heartened by the last chapter of the book. We can argue about some elements of that, but broadly I agree. And so let’s get together and start looking for tools and techniques to get us there. And I know John wants to do this and has always done it. And that’s what we tried to do in Massachusetts and to a large extent with the Affordable Care Act.
McDonough: So let’s switch to another topic of equal urgency and importance. And this was Friedman’s hypothesis laid out in a New York Times op-ed on Sept. 13, 1970, where he said it in his inimitable all-or-nothing fashion: The sole duty of the for-profit corporation is return on equity to shareholders and nothing else. Any sense of obligation to customers, to patients, to communities, to workers is simply a myth. The CEO should look in the mirror every day and say, “What can I do today to make more money for my shareholders?”
I call it the most influential op-ed there’s ever been in American history. And my evidence is that 50 years later, the New York Times had in its Sunday edition an eight-page pullout special section that was simply a reprint of Friedman’s op-ed with commentary from about 25 economists, Nobel Prize winners, political people, others commenting on it, and I’d say overwhelmingly most of them commenting on what they found wrong and objectionable.
That idea became known as MSV, or maximizing shareholder value. It became enormously influential in corporate America, in business schools, in changing people’s mind about how they think the corporation fits into American society. Through one of Friedman’s acolytes, Michael Jensen, it led to the notion that we should stop paying salaries to CEOs and we should pay them in stock options instead so that they would look in the mirror and say, “What can I do for the shareholders?” And they’re looking at and for themselves as well.
Today, about 80% of compensation in large corporations is not in salary, it’s in stock options. And it’s led to all kinds of manipulation with stock buybacks and other kinds of things.
But it was a place where Friedman was particularly influential. I would argue, and I argue in the book, that his thinking became the intellectual foundation of what we know today as private equity, where now we have organizations, a large part of the American economy, totally dedicated to the proposition that “we are out to make as much money as we can,” uniting shareholders and managers together as quickly as possible, five to seven years, and then moving on to our next conquest. It was a powerful idea, and he was incredibly effective at promoting it and I would argue in a way that has been quite damaging to American society.
Butler: Well, let me try to respond to that without having all this in front of me. I know John has a photographic memory, so he can probably immediately spot these things. But I think that’s another interesting example of where you’ve got to look at first of all at the context of that op-ed and that debate, which was whether corporations should have a public purpose, and should the managers of corporations pursue those purposes, whether or not the shareholders approve of it or if it is in the interests of shareholders. That’s the origin of that debate.
Now first of all, we don’t need to spend time on that. I think that there are areas where Friedman and others went too far. And we can talk about private equity and I don’t think John and I are going to be disagreeing too much about that.
But let’s just recall that that was the context. And then when you dig in to Friedman’s and others’ views, including Friedrich Hayek, who is the kind of intellectual grandfather in a way, or father of Friedman, the view was that corporations, and business people generally, that seeking profits at the expense of anybody else was not and should not be their public purpose. Their view was that corporations certainly did have other objectives and Milton Friedman and Hayek and others all felt that profits cannot or should not be used to evade the law. So all corporations should be subject to laws. Also, they should be subject to what one might call the common values and culture of the society, just like anybody should within a community. A community has values and notions of rights and obligations. And as shareholders and as managers of corporations, those individuals have the same.
So I think John is, in a sense, technically correct that the argument was made that rewarding the shareholders should be the one and only objective, and that’s to a large extent what Friedman said. What that really included, however, was the obligations and values of the community that the shareholders had or should have, should be guiding those decisions as well. So the idea that that Friedman and others were saying just, “let’s profit, and grind down everybody, ignore everybody’s rights and so on” — that’s nonsense, to be frank about it. That’s not where neoliberals are and never really have been.
But I would agree that the impact of that debate and that language led to many people taking the view that all that matters is profits. And there are many of them around today, and we know many of the names of those people.
Bosch: This history is so fascinating, especially the way that you two agree on many parts of it and disagree sort of on the effects and what it means. So I’m curious how your different understandings of this history connect to what you think needs to happen to the US health care system now. So, John, what does the way you understand this history mean for how you recommend health care move forward?
McDonough: I react by putting together both of the prior things that we talked about, monopoly and antitrust, and maximizing shareholder value and private equity. Look at what we’ve gotten today with the financialization of U.S. medical care and the corporatization of it in ways that shifted its focus away from communities. So we see that hospitals are increasingly less local. They are local because they’re in communities, but chances are they’re owned by somebody far away in New York or some other part of the country where they own dozens or hundreds of hospitals.
The local control is missing and the local responsibility diminishes significantly. And the people who run the institutions see themselves more as business people who are out for financial returns for themselves and others. You can see this disconnection that erodes the essential trust that people used to feel in medical care. In my book’s last chapter, I refer to Gallup polls looking at trust across American society. If you go back to 1975, 79% of Americans said they trusted American medical care “a great deal or quite a lot” to do the right thing. Today, that same number is around 28%. It’s not just medical care, it’s across society. People just don’t have the same degree of trust that they used to. And it’s not irrational fear. Changes in the American body politic about the role and responsibility of business, there is a diminishment in feeling that “they really are for us.” We saw in this election in Kansas a sitting U.S. senator did so much aggressive bill collecting from former patients, his OB-GYN patients and so forth. We see those stories all the time about the impact of medical debt on people unable to pay their bills getting their cars seized, getting their wages attached. We see this erosion of a sense of brotherhood and sisterhood in the sense of “we’re a nation together.”
We have to figure this out: What can we do to restore trust in U.S. medical care? With regards to private equity, I don’t propose to chase private equity out of U.S. medical care because it’s not realistic. But I don’t think they have any business being involved in organizations that provide direct care to patients if they’re patient-facing. We should move toward a withdrawal of that. It would clearly take time and have lots of repercussions. But there’s gotta be a better way to do this than leave people to the mercies of the market when the market has no mercy.
Butler: Well, other than the last sentence or two, I probably agree 98% with what John just said. I get to that position based on what I said earlier, and what I attribute to the views of neoliberals, including people like Milton Friedman, which is that community values and the idea of rights and the patient comes first, the customer comes first, and that has got to be the test we apply to something like private equity. I feel, and I know John feels the same way, that health care, and particularly public health in a community, is a community venture. It should reflect the community, both the challenges of the community and the desires to a large extent of people within that community. So we totally agree on that. And we totally agree that when you’re in Tennessee, if the decisions about what goes on in your health care are made by a bunch of people in New York who are seeking to maximize their return, it’s probably not going to turn out well. I totally agree that we’ve got to make investments in health care shaped and controlled by local values and objectives. I totally agree. And John knows this. And I’ve been very interested in social determinants of health, on how do you build community institutions to shape health, to recognize that health is not only medical care, but a lot of other things, such as housing.
McDonough: I would second that. Stuart left the Heritage Foundation, I think in 2014, and is now at Brookings and has done incredibly important writing in the Journal of the American Medical Association, diving deeply into social determinants of health, and in particular, how to understand it from a conservative perspective, that it makes sense. It’s such important work.
Butler: I know you agree with that in part. I think it overlaps. I think we may use different words and so forth, but the intent is the same. That’s why I talk about “engineering arguments” so much. Now, that said, let’s look a little bit more at private equity. One of the interesting things about investors in high risk areas willing to put capital into risky ventures is that they have been and can be very effective at enabling ideas, new ways of doing things, to have a chance to succeed when more traditional investment, including local investment, would not tend to do that. Think about the patron of the arts from the Renaissance onwards. You know, we would have much poorer art to go and look at in our national galleries if there weren’t really rich people who just wanted to see certain kinds of art supported. And I think the key as we look forward is how can we get people who are willing to take high risks with their capital, which is what to a large extent we’re talking about with private equity — to have that as an important element but not one that is the overriding feature of the capitalization. Are there different kinds of nursing homes that could be much more effective and efficient and also provide more satisfaction for people who are growing older? I’d be looking probably more towards private equity for those if we could figure out how to do that as a test venture, like a wildcat oil driller from decades ago, right? You want to try to get people who are open to high-risk, high-return capital. So I think it has a role.
But I’m not naive at all in agreeing with John that when that becomes the overriding nature of capital in health care, we’ve got a big problem. We do. So we’ve got to drive forward in that way.
McDonough: I hate to do it, but I have to another complaint about Milton Friedman. I would have loved to meet him and talk with him. I’m sure we would have had a great time. But so much of his presentation is very much black or white. So he says, you’re either for economic freedom, or you’re for equality, and you have to pick one. You can’t have both. You’ve got to be focused on the shareholder and nothing else. And it was very effective in terms of his advocacy efforts. And it ignores someone like Stuart. I look at Stuart and this is a man of grays. This is not a man of blacks or whites. This is a man who sees the who sees the shades inside.
Butler: Yes, I agree.
McDonough: And private equity is the personification of maximizing shareholder value. You go in there, you’re only in there for five to seven years, and then you get out of Dodge as fast as you can with your bags of cash and hoping to find the next sucker to take it over. And we thought they were taking over really risky hospitals, and it turns out from folks who’ve analyzed this closely, they have not been doing that. They go after middle range organizations that have some money and some value where they can go in there and take their real estate and sell it to a real estate investment trust, get rich really fast, and then skate out of town. And so yeah, I think private equity could have been a lot more productive and helpful if it had had some guardrails around it.
But we accepted this notion, just let the business people run wild because they know what they’re doing. It turned out to be a fatal error in so many, many, many situations.
Butler: I think I’ve acknowledged that consequence. But I’d like to just say a few things about Milton Friedman as a public economist. Because I think I said at the very beginning that I was very much brought up on Milton Friedman when I was at university in Britain. And I can assure you, most people in universities in Britain in the 1960s and early ’70s were not neoliberals. And Milton Friedman, in contrast with, say, Hayek and some of the other economists who shared his view, was very much a public economist. He wrote columns for Newsweek. He was on television and so on. He saw his role as shaking up people’s thinking. And he portrayed things as black and white — I would argue that your book, John, is a black and white book. You don’t have to answer that, but that’s my feeling.
But Milton Friedman was very much a black and white advocate because he wanted to shake things up and get people to think. Monopolies in the public sector are in some ways worse, he would argue. That’s the kind of thing he would say, blunt, to the point. And then you have to kind of argue your way to the right position between those blunt positions. So I think it’s important to appreciate that the language of op-eds, even the language of books, the language of television, is short attention span, it’s hitting people over the head with an idea, rather than saying, “This is a complicated idea.” “So on the one hand, on the other hand.” The New York Times doesn’t want an op-ed like that. It wants you to go straight for the throat or straight for the high ground and stay with it.
So I just think it’s important to put that on the table and say that. And I’ve done the same myself. I’ve written pieces that overstate an argument. And sometimes I’m upset that people have taken my words precisely and used them. And you’ve pointed that out in your book occasionally with things that I’ve written that I probably should have been a little bit more nuanced. I think that is the game of how you change opinion. And Friedman had a very particular role in this. But I do think it’s important not to paint everybody who takes the basic neoliberal positions that Friedman and his earlier supporters took as being unsubtle. It’s making a simplified argument. And I wish people noted that I’ve changed my mind, like Friedman, on antitrust and so on. It’s important to see that as part of the equation.
That’s why that’s why I’m actually relatively optimistic about the future because like I said I think John’s final chapter and my views, I really don’t disagree a lot with this. We might disagree about how to get there or I might fault some of the language, but I’m broadly in agreement.
And I think now, in what I hope will be the post-Trump era, I think people like us have to clear away the misunderstandings and the overstating of positions and say: How can we actually get out of where we are? Because we actually do agree on where we want to end up. There’s not really a lot of disagreement about values and principles. There may be intense disagreement about what tools we think will get there. And that’s a fair debate. And it’s not a personal debate.
McDonough: So that that brings us back in history, but a little closer to today, because in some ways where we are right now feels a lot like 2005 and 2006, when we were looking ahead to a national administration change and a need for significant and substantial health care reform. We went into that in 2005 and 2006 with lots of bipartisan groupings, with multisector groups looking at Massachusetts and other models. And it was quite intensive. I remember Sen. Kennedy, every time I sat with him, the first thing he would say is, “John, this is never gonna happen unless it’s bipartisan.” He said it over and over. And of course, it happened though it was not bipartisan. The Affordable Care Act was a strictly partisan piece at the end, not because people didn’t try, like you and others, to bring folks together.
So the question is: Can we learn anything from that experience to avoid a replay of that same ball game in 2027, ’28, ’29, and ’30?
Butler: I very much hope so and I think it’s possible. In fact, in the last piece I did for JAMA, I reminisced about the good old days where people did actually talk about ideas. Ted Kennedy would bring in Orrin Hatch and others and me and others, and we would have a conversation. I laid out some ideas in that piece that I think we need to think hard about. Should all the health care subsidies that people get be dependent any more on where you work or if you work? And if we think that way, then you come up with a very different system than we have today. So I think now is the time to put forward those kinds of broad ideas to get people back in the room again. They can go out on the campaign trail and argue with each other, but get back in the room afterward. Open a nice bottle of pinot and start to talk about these things.
I think we can do it. That’s what I hope will happen. And I think John’s book will make people like me respond. And I think that can then lead us all to say, “OK, let’s dig in further about where is the agreement? How could we think about this moving forward?” It’s urgent, it’s important work.
Bosch: I think that might be a great note to end on, to be honest. I am so grateful to both of you for this really exciting conversation and hopefully it’ll continue.

Australia has survived a dreadful collapse to claim a tense two-wicket victory over New Zealand in the opening Twenty20 International at North Sydney Oval.
The reigning T20 World Cup champions won with seven balls to spare, scoring 8-165 in reply to New Zealand's 2-162 on Sunday night.
Number 10 Kim Garth faced eight balls without scoring before hitting a boundary to give Australia a 1-0 lead in the three-match Rose Bowl series, with the remaining matches at North Sydney Oval on Tuesday and Thursday.
Australia overcame the early LBW loss of Georgia Voll and were charging towards victory when star veteran Beth Mooney and Ellyse Perry were involved in a dreadful mix-up.
They had taken the score to 86 in just 8.2 overs when Mooney was struck on the pad and charged off for the most ambitious of runs.
Perry sent her back, Mooney was slow to turn, and was run out well short of her ground.
The loss of Mooney for 38 from just 25 balls prompted a collapse.
Perry raced to her equal fastest T20 half century in just 27 balls but on 52 dragged a short ball from Jess Kerr to deep backward square, where she was well caught by Issy Sharp running to her right.
Georgie Wareham (10 from 7 balls) sliced a leg-spinner and Kerr's younger sister Amelia straight to point.
Ash Gardner (23 from 17) gave Jess Kerr her third wicket on review and Annabel Sutherland (9 from 5 balls) became her fourth, pulling a short ball to deep square leg.
Nicole Cary (4 from 3 balls) was run out by the recalled Tahlia McGrath and when captain Sophie Molineux (11 from 5 balls) fell, Australia had lost 7-62.
But the home side hung on for their 11th T20 win in a row, while the White Ferns have now lost six of their past nine matches.
Not even a record partnership and a record-equalling total in Australia could secure New Zealand victory.
After a difficult start by the White Ferns, Georgia Plimmer and Maddy Green combined for an unbeaten 127 in 80 balls.
Plimmer made a career-high 85 off 68 balls and Green 56 from 37 balls.
It was a breakout innings for the 22-year-old Plimmer, her fourth T20 half-century in 54 matches for New Zealand.
Going into the game she had an average of 16 and a strike rate of 104.
She was the beneficiary of two difficult chances, a stumping and catch from wicketkeeper Beth Mooney standing up to seamers Sutherland and Hamilton.

If you have young kids or if you know somebody who does, then you know about YouTube’s AI slop problem.
Videos targeted at children on the platform are often filled with bizarre and hyperstimulating content that’s AI generated. Not all of it is age-appropriate. These videos autoplay on endless, algorithmically curated streams punctuated by ads.
Maka, a new streaming app for kids aged 0 to 6, is positioning itself as an antidote to that concern. The platform has zero ads, doesn’t allow autoplay or endless scrolling, and its algorithms intentionally do not maximize watch time.
The company’s cofounder and chief product officer Tanyella Leta tells WIRED the platform is purposely abandoning the mechanisms that “turn children’s media into an engagement machine.”
Maka’s CEO and cofounder Isabel Sheinman adds that a lot of the streamers were built to serve adults, not children. “Kids were really the afterthought,” she says. Sheinman wants to set a much higher bar for what quality looks like in children’s media, which she says has been warped by harmful incentives. “Maka was built with child development science and children's behavior first and foremost.”
Launching today, Maka’s programming slate is a mix of licensed content from global studios and independent creators. It features 25 shows in its curated catalog, including Franklin, The Wiggles, Pocoyo, Vida the Vet and Sesame Street. The platform runs on a subscription service, with a $15 monthly plan and a $107 annual plan.
It was during the Covid pandemic that Sheinman and Leta became obsessed with thinking about how to redesign kids' media. The solution? Every episode streamed on Maka is evaluated by child development experts through Imprint, a framework created with researchers at the Yale Child Study Center. The evaluation process, which examines everything from scene cuts to how fast-paced content is, maps adolescent development across seven core domains. It looks for things like emotional regulation, kindness, how child-caregiver relationships are modeled in a story, and how a story might support critical thinking or language development.
AI-generated content has only added a new wrinkle to kids’ entertainment: videos are incoherent, have no plot, or contain outright misinformation, but are packaged to look like learning. Some of it, as WIRED has previously reported, is disturbingly sexualized, featuring gore and other fetishes.
Michael Robb, director of research at the media literacy nonprofit Common Sense Media, says that on a platform like YouTube, slop videos that have the veneer of education sit side by side with carefully designed educational shows. Robb says YouTube and other kids’ streaming platforms have not done enough to distinguish educational content from slop, which has only made filtering content harder for parents. “Platforms have taken steps to reduce kids’ exposure to age-inappropriate content, and that matters. But ‘not inappropriate’ is a very low bar. There’s a big gulf between that and media created intentionally with kids in mind.”
A 2020 study by Common Sense Media on YouTube videos watched by young kids found 75 percent had “weak or no educational value.” Kids also frequently ended up watching ads and content intended for older audiences.
According to its policy for YouTube Kids, which lets parents approve specific content themselves, YouTube excludes videos that are “deceptive, sensational, or clickbait,” but acknowledges that not every video has been manually reviewed. YouTube also makes clear that automated filtering cannot guarantee every video will be appropriate. “There’s a chance that your child will find content that you don't want them to watch,” the company notes in its support docs.
Earlier this year, in an effort to encourage better digital literacy among kids, the American Academy of Pediatrics updated its guidance beyond screen time recommendations, urging children to avoid “AI-generated content,” “AI chatbots,” “short-form videos,” and “highly sensationalized content or clickbait.” The guide prioritized quality content and coviewing with parents rather than passive watching.
Tiffany Munzer, a developmental-behavioral pediatrician and digital media researcher at the University of Michigan, was the lead author on AAP’s “Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents” policy statement, and tells WIRED in an email that the proliferation of low-quality content has led kids to “miss out on important, slower learning opportunities that promote critical thinking, generate new ideas, and practice stretching their attention spans.”
In April, child advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter, signed by more than 200 organizations and individual experts, asking YouTube to address the spread of AI videos on its platforms, saying AI slop “harms children’s development by distorting their sense of reality, overwhelming their learning processes and hijacking their attention.”
A YouTube spokesperson tells WIRED that on YouTube Kids, which is meant for kids 12 and under, AI content is limited to a small set of high-quality channels, and parents have the option to block channels entirely. The platform has stricter standards for content made for younger viewers, the company says.
For Maka’s business model to succeed, its shows will need to entertain and educate kids while also establishing confidence in parents. “The value that parents want is relief, knowing that what their child is seeing has been vetted by child development experts and everything on Maka they can trust is good for their kid,” Sheiman says.
Yalda Uhls, a former film executive at Sony and MGM who is now a researcher at UCLA focusing on how media affects the social learning of young children, worries that as AI revolutionizes kids’ streaming content, people who study child development are being left out of the process. “When I was a studio executive, every story meant for children passed through layers of accountable adults,” she says. “But today, algorithms, anonymous creators, and AI tools shape what kids see, and people who study child development are rarely in the room.”
“The gatekeepers have been replaced by a metric, minutes watched,” Uhls says. “Nobody in that chain is required to ask what a child is actually learning.”
One of Maka’s core features is a timer that parents set at the start of every viewing session to help the child wind down off the screen. As the show concludes, a character Maka developed named Scoot appears on the screen to get the child ready to detach from their device. Features like that are the difference between capturing a child’s attention versus earning it, Sheinman says. “So it becomes less of a moment of tension in a family and a moment that the child is prepared for.”
The founders ultimately want Maka to help change the perception of kids' relationship to screens.
“We’re seeing a really big challenge around the judgment of parents,” says Leta, explaining that one problem with screen time is the demonization of parents who rely on it. “We have all judged parents who bring out the screen on the train or at a restaurant. Let's be real, most parents will reach for the screen at some point. We don't think that they should be judged for that choice.”
Whether any of this will work is unclear. One question at the core of Maka’s mission is whether it can build a successful streaming company without adopting the same incentives that created the problems it is trying to solve.
Robb from Common Sense Media calls competing with YouTube a Herculean task. “YouTube is free and already on the devices within their homes. Moving them away can be tricky,” he says. The real test for Maka, Robb says, “will be whether it can grow with kids and stay sustainable without being pulled back toward the engagement metrics that drive the rest of the industry.”
Leta, one of Maka’s cofounders, admits that it’s easy to be cynical when it comes to children and screens. “But TV also gave us Sesame Street. It gave us Fred Rogers who believed that the space between the child and the screen was sacred ground.”
“One of the dads in our beta told us that with other platforms, when his kid is watching, it feels like ‘a race to the bottom of my kid’s brainstem,’” Leta says. “It doesn't have to be like that.”

Essential items to stock in your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Is your household ready if you get hit with a stomach bug tomorrow? Sniffles on Saturday? The flu in a month or two?
Life Kit
How to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season
In the United States, cold and flu season occurs in the fall and winter, starting in October and stretching all the way through May, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The combination of dropping temperatures and drier climates makes us more susceptible to common respiratory viruses like the common cold, the flu, RSV or COVID-19, and "back-to-back illnesses," says pediatrician Mona Amin.
Get ready now by creating a cold and flu prep kit. "Have things readily available so that you're not scrambling or depending on someone else to run to the drugstore for you when you become sick," says pharmacist Alisha Reed. That includes fever and pain relievers, hydration supplements and monitoring tools to help manage symptoms.
Many viruses and fevers can be managed at home, says Amin. And the common cold and the flu are viral infections, so they can't be treated by prescription antibiotics anyway.
Below, you'll find a list of items for the whole family, recommended by Amin and Reed. Put the products in one designated place, like a shelf in your medicine cabinet or a handy "sick day" box.
You'll also want to take preventative measures like disinfecting frequently touched surfaces, getting vaccinated and washing your hands. But remember, says Reed, no prevention strategy is foolproof.
What to include in your cold and flu prep kit
Over-the-counter medications
When you're dealing with cough, congestion, sore throat, fever, fatigue or other common cold and flu symptoms, you may be tempted to reach for a medication that hits multiple symptoms.
But those meds often include extra unnecessary ingredients that can sometimes put you at risk of accidentally overmedicating yourself, says Reed. Instead, opt for medications that target individual symptoms.
These items all come with a price tag, of course. So if you don't have something like a flexible spending account to help cover costs, consider purchasing your personal sick day must-haves to start, then building from there as you're able.
Reed and Amin suggest these medications:
Pain relievers. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen can help relieve pain and discomfort from headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation, says Reed.
- For kids: Don't use children's ibuprofen for children under 6 months old; naproxen is only approved for children 12 years and older.
Fever reducer. Medications like acetaminophen and ibuprofen can safely reduce body temperature, though acetaminophen is usually the better choice for fevers.
- For kids: Look for a children's version for 12 years and under. Be sure to follow this dosing chart when using children's acetaminophen.
- For pregnant people: Acetaminophen is the recommended OTC pain reliever for pregnant people, according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
Antihistamine. Yes, the same thing you take for spring allergies! Colds and allergies have similar symptoms like sneezing, runny noses and watery eyes, which is why they can both be treated by a histamine-blocking medication that can help dry up your sinuses.
- For kids: Some OTC allergy medicines are approved for children as young as 6 months, but not all — and some have more side effects than others, says Amin. Check in with your care provider first if you have questions.
Decongestant. Pseudoephedrine pills or nasal spray can relieve a stuffy nose or sinus pressure by restricting blood vessels and opening airways in your nasal passages.
- For kids: Pills are not recommended for kids under 4 and medicated sprays are not recommended for kids under 6.
Cough suppressant for a dry cough. Dextromethorphan — often referred to as "DM" on the cough syrup box — can temporarily suppress the signal in the brain that triggers your cough reflex, says Reed.
- For kids: Not recommended for children under 4; do not use for children under 2, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Cough expectorant for a congested cough. Guaifenesin may help relieve chest congestion by thinning mucus in your airways, says Reed. But before you buy, try just staying hydrated first. "Water is a natural expectorant," she says.
- For kids: Cough medicine is not recommended for children under 4; do not use for children under 2, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Read the label on the box or bottle of OTC products carefully to make sure that what you're taking isn't expired and will treat the ailment it's intended for. And always stick to the recommended dosage and usage to avoid unnecessary risks or side effects, says Reed.
Honey
Honey is a great sick day remedy for all ages, but is especially helpful for small children not yet old enough for cough medicine, says Amin. "Honey is an anti-inflammatory that also helps with coating the throat, which can help with that cough trigger that children will have."
Note: honey isn't safe for children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.
Thermometer
This is a basic, must-have tool to check your temperature on those days you suspect you or your little one are running a fever, says Amin.
Rectal thermometers are preferred for children 3 and under; oral and digital infrared thermometers are both fine choices for anyone older than that. (But oral thermometers are usually more accurate.)
Nasal saline treatment
The dryness of winter can dehydrate your nasal passages and make it easier for viruses to attach and replicate in your nose and throat.
One easy solution is to irrigate your nose with a saline spray or rinse, says Amin. This can be both preventative by helping to keep the mucous membranes in your nose moist, as well as symptom-relieving by loosening thick mucus if you have a cold.
Research even suggests that using saline drops at the first sign of a cold can reduce symptoms in small children by up to two days.
Other comfort items
Chest rub. Vapor rubs containing combinations of camphor, eucalyptus and menthol oils may provide some relief for nighttime cough and cold symptoms when applied to the chest and neck.
Use with caution, says Amin. Though a lot of families use this homeopathic remedy, there's not a lot of research supporting its effectiveness, and it can be harmful if used improperly. Vicks VapoRub, for example, should be applied only to the chest and throat and never heated up. And be sure to check age restrictions before using any products on children — baby and child chest rubs will be formulated with gentler ingredients.
Disposable vomit bags. These are useful to have, easy to store and a great replacement for sitting by the toilet if the stomach flu should hit your house this year, says Amin.
Humidifier. A humidifier adds moisture to the air, which can help loosen mucus stuck in your sinuses. Reed suggests using a cool-mist humidifier when sick, which can help ease stuffiness during a cold.
Pedialyte, apple juice, water, Gatorade. Diarrhea or vomiting, common symptoms of the flu or COVID-19, can sometimes lead to dehydration. Make sure to have a few favorite drinks handy that can help replace those lost liquids for you or your little one, Amin says.
When to call your doctor
As long as your symptoms are improving — and responding to treatment — many viruses can be dealt with from the comfort of your home.
However, if you're seeing these concerning symptoms, reach out to your doctor.
- A fever in infants younger than 3 months; above 102 F for children; 103 F for adults; or any high fevers that last longer than 1-2 days and/or don't respond to fever-reducing medicine.
- Shortness of breath or erratic breathing
- Extreme thirst, inability to drink liquids, trouble urinating or producing tears, dark urine, severe or persistent vomiting
- Confusion, disorientation, extreme irritability or weakness
These aren't the only signs to look for, so when in doubt, reach out, says Reed. "Don't be afraid to call your doctor or talk to a pharmacist about what's going on. It doesn't hurt to double check," she says.

The Africa Cup of Nations could continue to be held every two years, with discussions under way to reverse its proposed switch to a four-year cycle.
Speaking on Friday at a Confederation of African Football (Caf) strategy conference in Cape Verde, president Patrice Motsepe said: "We've discussed it over the last few days.
"We are looking at everything, including having the Afcon coming back every two years. We are very clear, the matter is being reviewed."
The tournament has taken place every two years since 1968, bar a one-year gap between the 2012 and 2013 editions.
However, in December 2025 CAF announced it would shift to being staged every four years after the 2027 Afcon in East Africa and a 2028 edition.
That planned alteration to the schedule had received widespread criticism across the continent.
National associations had raised concerns about the visibility of their teams, the commercial implications and where Africa's biggest competition would sit in the international football calendar.

The UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, will meet the EU’s home affairs commissioner on Monday for further talks just days after Andy Burnham said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases from which the UK has been locked out of since Brexit.
According to the European Commission, they will discuss “migration, border management, law enforcement cooperation and counter-terrorism”, with the latest Frontex data published on Monday showing a 43% decline in small boats crossing the Channel.
It will be the second time Mahmood has met Magnus Brunner in two months and comes amid an increase in engagement between London and Brussels since Andy Burnham announced he would use an upcoming EU-UK summit to “lay out to the country” what he believes are the “different options for Britain’s long-term relationship” with the EU.
Brunner said “the UK’s contribution is indispensable” to continuing efforts to suppress irregular migration after the EU introduced a suite of new laws aimed at speeding up asylum decisions and deportations.
On the agenda for Monday’s meeting will be talks on the UK rejoining some of the police and security databases it was locked out from after Brexit and rejoining a new database, Eurodac, centring on migration.
Last week Burnham told MPs that “one of the most positive aspects of my meeting with [the European Commission] president [Ursula] von der Leyen in New York, was her openness to the conversation about restoring data sharing on immigration across the UK, across Europe”.
He said it was “control” that the UK “lost” and should get “more attention” in the debate about Brexit. “I will work hard to see if we can get a practical arrangement on that very issue at the summit in November,” Burnham said.
Brunner will also meet the MI5 director general, Ken McCallum, and visit the National Counter Terrorism Security Office, as well as meet senior officials from the UK’s child sexual abuse centre to discuss joint efforts to tackle such crimes.
He has also been chosen to deliver a lecture at King’s College London on migration and asylum, where he will talk about the impact of the EU’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum, a framework of 10 pieces of legislation overhauling how the EU manages its borders, processes asylum applications and shares information among member states.
Brunner will tell those he meets that the new laws have already had a significant impact along with a shift in political priorities around migration in key countries such as Germany, Italy and France.
He said the “reforms are paying” off in the UK too, with illegal crossings down 43%.
“We must stay on this course, including along all relevant migration routes, and the UK’s contribution is indispensable,” he said. “We have put our European house in order. Illegal crossings at our external borders are down 55% over two years, with a further third this year, and asylum applications are at record lows in the countries that used to be main destinations.”
One key database the UK wants access to is Eurodac, a new platform which collects fingerprints and facial images of asylum seekers from the age of six, and security flags for people linked to terrorism or serious crime.
Another is the Schengen Information System (SIS), which contains data on missing persons, stolen goods, vehicles and number plates, and fugitives crossing internal EU borders. About 20m searches are made daily on the SIS, according to EU data, mostly on cars.
The Home Office has not commented.

Zelensky speaks to US envoys amid Trump spat after warning US not to side with Russia
The Ukrainian president said ‘a lot depends on America’ and Ukraine was ready to work ‘constructively’ and ‘honestly’ with the US
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky spoke to US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the midst of his spat with US President Donald Trump on Sunday, saying “a lot depends on America” as he earlier warned Washington not to side with Moscow in Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.
The wartime leader spoke to the US officials as both Russia and Ukraine hit each other’s energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on St Petersburg since the start of the 2022 war.
Trump and Zelensky have clashed as the US leader blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow, fuelling fears in Kyiv and Europe that the White House was steering towards Moscow.
After speaking to Trump’s business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner, Zelensky said “a lot depends” on the US position in the war but that “it is clear that there are many things that matter to all of us and that this war must be brought to an end”.

Trump recycles ‘Dumocrats’ attacks at Kentucky rally but behind the scenes is ‘blaming aides’ for gloomy midterms outlook
‘The Republican Party is starting to look pretty good,’ Trump told supporters as polls suggest a potential midterm blue wave

At a rally in Kentucky on Saturday, President Donald Trump reprised familiar attacks on Democrats and predicted a strong Republican showing in the midterm elections. But privately, he has reportedly blamed his aides as polls signal trouble ahead.
In a roughly 90-minute speech in Highland Heights, Trump launched into familiar territory, deriding Democrats as “lunatics” and communists intent on allowing men to compete in women’s sports and letting immigrants enter the country illegally.
“Who the hell is voting for these people?” Trump asked. “They’re gonna annihilate your borders, decimate Kentucky farms and energies, mutilate your children and give 25 million illegal aliens the right to vote,” he said. Praising a slate of GOP congressional candidates, he added: “The Republican Party is starting to look pretty good.”
Behind closed doors, though, the 80-year-old president has struck a different tone, blaming aides and political operatives for a wobbling midterm strategy and voicing doubts about candidate choices, Reuters reported Saturday.
With the November elections just weeks away, multiple polls suggest Republicans could suffer steep losses, potentially surrendering their congressional majorities amid voter frustration over the cost of living and the war in Iran. This week, Fox News projected for the first time that Democrats appear poised to retake control of the House of Representatives.
Despite publicly projecting confidence in Republicans’ midterm prospects and dismissing Democratic candidates as easy to beat, Trump has privately expressed frustration with aides over the campaign.
He has singled out James Blair, who runs the PAC MAGA Inc., questioning his handling of campaign funds and why that spending has failed to improve polling numbers, Reuters reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has also drawn criticism, with some officials questioning her oversight of the midterm strategy.
“What's really happening is a circular firing squad,” one source said.
But a White House spokesperson dismissed the report, calling the sources “armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation.”
The president has also dismissed reports about Wiles. “Susie Wiles is my loyal and longest serving Chief of Staff — there is a reason for that,” he said this week. “She has been with me since the beginning, is my trusted advisor, and has my COMPLETE confidence.”
Trump devoted much of his speech at Saturday’s rally to attacking Democrats, whom he derisively calls “Dumocrats.”
He singled out several candidates, mocking Texas Senate candidate James Talarico as “Talafreako” and calling Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El Sayed a “jihadist.” He also accused his predecessor, Joe Biden, of ushering in a “dark age” in which “they weaponized our government.”
Elsewhere during his speech, which a protester briefly interrupted, Trump touted his administration’s accomplishments, including what he described as record-setting economic gains.
“It was just announced that under Republican leadership, incomes have soared to the highest level ever,” he said, adding that the “poverty rate has just reached the best number we've ever had.”
Trump suggested the economic figures were so strong that a lengthy speech was unnecessary. “So I can stand up here and bull**** for two hours,” he said. “Sometimes, I really think when I have these numbers, I say, you know, let’s just get the hell out of here.”
Still, he said he was working hard to boost GOP turnout, pointing to recent rallies in several states where he has urged supporters to vote as though he were on the ballot.
“There's never been any president that's campaigned like this for the midterms,” Trump told the crowd. “They'll say he was terrible. He campaigned terribly. If I do make it, if we win, I will get absolutely no credit. They'll say the candidates were spectacular. But what the hell? I have to do it anyway.”

An airman was killed during a college football stunt on Saturday. Hegseth is getting the blame
The fall occurred during pregame ceremonies for the University of Texas at San Antonio’s annual military appreciation game against Navy, an event that traditionally includes rappelling demonstrations

An Air Force service member died Saturday after falling from the rafters of the Alamodome during a pregame stunt in San Antonio, Texas, bringing renewed attention to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the military’s use of promotional spectacles at public events.
The airman died at a local hospital following the rappelling demonstration ahead of the University of Texas at San Antonio’s Salute to Armed Forces & Veterans game against the U.S. Naval Academy.
Footage circulating on social media captured the out-of-control descent, showing spectators inside the arena growing silent as first responders rushed onto the field.
“He died,” Jackie Singh, an aide on Joe Biden’s 2020 campaign, wrote on X. “Thanks @PeteHegseth @SecWar for yet another pointless and tragic recruiting spectacle.”
Democratic strategist Chris D. Jackson described the incident as “absolutely sickening.”
“This ridiculous military showboating at football games needs to STOP,” Jackson wrote on X. “Now a man could lose his life, all because some Hegseth-like official apparently thought putting on a macho spectacle for people who came to watch FOOTBALL was a brilliant idea. These men are human beings, NOT props for someone’s political theater.”
Hegseth has previously emphasized a renewed focus on a “warrior ethos” across the armed services, which has included an increase in high-visibility military displays at public events. Rappelling demonstrations have long been an annual feature of the university’s military appreciation games.
The Air Force confirmed Sunday that the service member was assigned to Detachment 2 of the 6th Combat Training Squadron, a unit operating out of Joint Base San Antonio-Camp Bullis under a parent squadron based at Nellis Air Force Base in Nevada. The unit provides training for tactical air traffic controllers.
According to the San Antonio Express-News, one of four service members participating in the demonstration slipped down a rope from the rafters in “an uncontrolled manner” and hit the ground.
Medical personnel quickly treated the airman on the field before the San Antonio Fire Department transported him to a hospital as a Priority 1 patient, indicating life-threatening injuries. The service member later died from those injuries.
The name of the airman has not been released pending notification of next of kin, and the Air Force said the cause of the fall remains under investigation.
“We are deeply saddened by the incident that occurred at the start of tonight’s football game,” a university spokesperson posted on Instagram Saturday evening. “Our heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with the soldier who was affected, his family and his military colleagues.”
The accident delayed the start of the game by 10 minutes as the head coach, Jeff Traylor, kept his team in the locker room while medical personnel treated the airman.
“The only information I had was there had been an incident, and the game was going to be delayed, and we didn’t expand upon it any further than that,” Traylor said after the game. “I didn’t know if I did the right thing or not. I didn't know anything. I didn't know what to tell them, so that's how I handled it.”
Traylor noted that his players “could just tell the energy was gone” when they returned to the field in what he described as a somber environment. The University of Texas at San Antonio went on to defeat Navy, 38-34, before a crowd of 23,297.
“Just thinking thoughts and prayers with that family,” Owen McCown, the team’s quarterback, told reporters after the game. “I know we said a prayer postgame, but they’ll continue being in our thoughts and prayers, and really thinking about them.”
McCown added that resuming play following the emergency was difficult for the players.
“It’s hard,” he said. “I just think as players too, my thoughts go immediately with the family. It’s obviously bigger than football.
“And then as just the game went on, kind of got the ebbs and flows, and getting back to playing football. And I thought at first, it was hard to get around, and then finally got going again.”

In 2025, the DOE finalizetd a rule change saying that it will no longer require new building or renovation projects to meet the standards of accessibility that comply with the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which requires new buildings and renovations to remove "architectural and transportation barriers."
The final rule has not yet been implemented. On July 1, 2026, the DOE delayed its effective date to Dec. 28, 2026. The rule change would also not affect other federal or local accessibility requirements, only the DOE's rules for funding.
Advocacy organizations that oppose the change have sent the DOE adverse comments, and it's unclear how these will affect the rule's implementation.
In October 2026, a rumor spread that the U.S. Department of Energy was changing federal law to rescind a requirement that buildings should be accessible for people with disabilities.
Posts sharing the claim multiplied on social media, including on Facebook and Instagram. "The Trump administration's Department of Energy has moved to eliminate federal regulations requiring accessibility in certain newly constructed and renovated facilities receiving federal financial assistance," an Oct. 15 Facebook post read (archived):
The rumor was not new. The claim began to circulate in 2025, as one Reddit post indicates.
In 2025, the DOE finalized a rule change saying that it will no longer require new building or renovation projects to meet the standards of accessibility that comply with the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which requires new buildings and renovations to remove "architectural and transportation barriers." However the final rule had not yet been implemented. On July 1, 2026, the DOE delayed its effective date to Dec. 28, 2026. The rule change would also not affect other federal or local accessibility requirements, only the DOE's rules for funding.
For this reason, we rated the claim a mixture of true and false information.
We have reached out to the DOE seeking more information about its delayed implementation. We will update this story should we receive a reply.
In May 2025, the DOE published a direct final rule "rescinding" a rule that new construction projects that sought funding support from the DOE needed to comply with the Uniform Federal Accessibility Standards for accessibility for people with disabilities. The UFAS, in turn, follows requirements from the 1973 Rehabilitation Act.
"Upon further evaluation, and for the reasons explained subsequently, DOE has determined this provision to be unnecessary and unduly burdensome," the May 2025 proposed rule read.
However, in July 2025, the DOE delayed its implementation because it "subsequently received significant adverse comments on that direct final rule." The implementation of that rule was then delayed several more times, most recently in July 2026, and as of this writing it was slated to take effect on Dec. 28, 2026.
In other words, the rule has yet to take effect, and it's unclear how the adverse comments the DOE has received will affect its implementation.
Opposition to the rule change
After the DOE first published the rule change, several organizations representing the rights of people with disability sent adverse comments.
If the requirements are rescinded, "covered entities will be misled into believing they need not make their facilities accessible when, in fact, there is no other way to avoid discriminating against people with disabilities. As a result, they will violate the law and be forced to remediate accessibility barriers after construction is completed, likely at significant cost," said the National Federation of the Blind in a June 6, 2025, letter.
New York Lawyers for the Public Interest also filed an adverse comment that said the rule was "unlawful":
The proposed rules are unlawful. "Direct final rules" must be routine or noncontroversial. Here, the proposed changes are neither. Instead, the proposals would delete foundational provisions implementing Section 504 [of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973] in contradiction of Congress's clear understanding of the law.
The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights said in a June 16, 2025, adverse comment that the direct final rule process was not designed for such changes:
The direct final rule process is intended for noncontroversial rules that are unlikely to raise objections. Erecting new barriers to accessibility, as the direct final rule would do, is clearly controversial.
Snopes found no evidence that this rule change would prevent other agencies, federal, state or local, from imposing such requirements on new constructions or renovations.
For further reading, Snopes confirmed the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development updated its policy to effectively remove untrained "emotional support animals."

'Anyone who works with Salman Khan will be next': After attack on Tiger Shroff, Lawrence Bishnoi gang issues fresh threat
A social media post linked with Lawrence Bishnoi gang's Anil Pandit said he along with Anil Harman Sandhu was behind the attack.
The Lawrence Bishnoi gang, which claimed responsibility for opening fire at actor Tiger Shroff in Mumbai’s Juhu area on Sunday evening, warned that anyone in the Mumbai film industry who refuses to heed its warnings or works with actor Salman Khan would be next. However, Mumbai Police have not confirmed any links between the gang and the attack.
In a purported social media post, Lawrence Bishnoi gang's Anil Pandit claimed that he and Harman Sandhu were behind the attack.
“We, Anil Pandit and Harman Sandhu, take responsibility for what happened to Tiger Shroff today. We had called him and tried to make him understand, but he did not listen. So today, we made sure to teach him a lesson properly,” the post read.
“Anyone in the Mumbai film industry who does not listen to us or works with Salman Khan will be next. Wait and watch.”
“Note: Some dogs from other groups who think they can gain fame by using our name will soon be killed and made famous,” it added.
When the attack unfold
According to preliminary information, Shroff was returning after playing football at a club when the three unidentified assailants opened fire near Pushpa Park in Juhu. Three people have reportedly been injured, including Shroff's driver Firdos who suffered injuries on his hand, police said.
Mumbai police personnel and ambulances rushed to the spot after receiving information about the incident. The area has been cordoned off, and a search is underway to trace the attackers.
Police are also examining CCTV footage from cameras installed in the surrounding area. Ballistics experts were called in at the place where the firing took place to gather the shell casings.
Officials said the motive behind the shooting remains unclear and will be established as the investigation progresses. The incident has caused concern in the film industry and the Juhu locality.
An eye witness told the police that Shroff was about to sit in his BMW car when the firing took place. Ballistics experts were called in at the place where the firing took place to gather the shell casings.
Previous attacks
On February 1, unidentified assailants on a motorcycle opened fire outside filmmaker Rohit Shetty’s residence in Juhu shortly after midnight. The attackers fired multiple rounds at the nine-storey building, with one bullet hitting the glass of a gym on the first floor. No injuries were reported in the incident, which took place around 12.45 am.
On October 12, 2024, veteran politician and Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) leader Baba Siddique, 66, was shot dead outside his son Zeeshan Siddique’s office near the Kherwadi signal junction in Bandra East at around 9.30 pm.
Three masked assailants fired multiple rounds at Siddique as he was entering his car, leaving him with bullet wounds to his chest and abdomen.
