The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) announced a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police denied permission and detained thousands of protesters, including three CJP leaders. With Jantar Mantar barricaded, some protesters gathered elsewhere. On 12 October, opposition leaders also marched to the Supreme Court against the SIR exercise, but police stopped them (here, here, here, here).
In this context, visuals showing crowds are being shared on social media with the claim that they show gatherings at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and outside Parliament House (here, here, here). Let’s verify these videos.
Claim: Visuals showing anti-CEC protestors gathering outside Parliament and Jantar Mantar.
Fact: These videos are AI-generated, not real visuals. No media reports mentioned the viral video or any protest by the public against the CEC inside the Parliament premises. Hence, the claims made in these posts are FALSE.
Video 1: 
Upon closer examination, we noticed a Gemini logo, associated with Google’s AI tool, in the bottom-right corner of the video, suggesting that it may have been AI-generated. We further analysed a keyframe from the viral video using SynthID, which also detected AI-generated content in the clip.
Video 2:
On performing a relevant keyword search, we found that no media reports mentioned the viral video or any protest by the public against the CEC inside the Parliament premises. We analysed the viral video using Hive’s AI-detection tool, which indicated that the video was AI-generated.
Furthermore, PIB Fact Check and Delhi Police also clarified that the viral video was fake and had been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).
To sum up, these videos are AI-generated and do not show a protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar in Delhi.

Frederick G. Banting and John J.R. Macleod were awarded the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of insulin, a hormone that regulates blood glucose levels. Their work helped establish insulin as a treatment for diabetes, a disease that, in its severe forms, had often been fatal before insulin therapy became available.
The prize was shared equally. Banting and Macleod were recognised “for the discovery of insulin”. The award acknowledged research conducted at the University of Toronto in the early 1920s, when investigators developed pancreatic extracts that could lower blood sugar in diabetic animals and subsequently demonstrated their therapeutic potential in humans. Charles Best, who worked with Banting, and biochemist James Collip, who helped purify insulin for clinical use, also made important contributions to this work.
Research on pancreas and blood sugar
Diabetes had been linked to the pancreas decades before insulin was isolated. In 1889, researchers Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering demonstrated that removing the pancreas from dogs produced diabetes. Subsequent research established the importance of the islets of Langerhans, clusters of cells within the pancreas, in regulating blood sugar.
The challenge was to identify and extract the substance responsible for this effect. Several researchers attempted to prepare pancreatic extracts, but obtaining a preparation that could be used safely and consistently in patients remained difficult.
Frederick G. Banting was a Canadian physician and surgeon whose interest in diabetes led him to investigate the role of the pancreas in regulating blood glucose. After serving in the First World War, he returned to Canada and worked in medical practice before pursuing research.
John J.R. Macleod was a Scottish-born physician and physiologist who had built his career around teaching and research in physiology, including carbohydrate metabolism. By 1920, he was a professor of physiology at the University of Toronto.
Banting approached Macleod in 1921 with a proposal to isolate a substance from the pancreas that could regulate blood glucose. Macleod provided laboratory facilities, scientific guidance and access to experimental animals. Banting began the work with Charles Best, a medical student who assisted with the experiments. Their collaboration brought together Banting’s research hypothesis and Macleod’s experience in physiology, setting the stage for the experiments that led to the development of insulin as a treatment for diabetes.
The researchers tied off the pancreatic ducts of dogs, allowing the enzyme-producing tissue to degenerate while attempting to preserve the islets. They prepared extracts from the pancreas and tested them in dogs whose pancreases had been removed. The extracts lowered blood sugar and improved the animals’ clinical condition.
These experiments provided evidence that an extract from the pancreas could help compensate for the loss of its normal blood sugar-regulating function. However, the early preparations were not suitable for prolonged use in humans because they contained impurities that caused adverse reactions.
Purifying insulin for treatment
In 1922, biochemist James Collip joined the research team to improve the purity of the pancreatic extract. His work helped produce a preparation suitable for clinical testing.
In January 1922, insulin was administered to Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old boy with severe diabetes, at Toronto General Hospital. The first injection produced limited results, and an abscess developed at the injection site. After the preparation was further purified, a second course of treatment produced a marked improvement in his condition, with a substantial reduction in blood glucose and urinary glucose.
Thompson’s response demonstrated that insulin could be used to treat diabetes in humans. The development of more reliable preparations and the expansion of production subsequently allowed treatment to reach more patients.
Insulin did not cure diabetes, but it changed the outlook for people living with the disease. Before its introduction, severe diabetes was often managed through restrictive diets that could prolong life only for a limited period. Insulin enabled patients to use glucose more effectively and helped prevent the severe metabolic disturbances associated with insulin deficiency.
The role of Best and Collip
The Nobel decision remains a significant part of the history of insulin research. Although Banting and Macleod received the prize, the work involved a larger research team.
Banting was unhappy that Best had not been included among the laureates. He shared half of his prize money with Best. Macleod, in turn, shared half of his prize money with Collip, recognising his contribution to the purification of insulin.
Later historical assessments of the discovery acknowledged the importance of contributions made by researchers who were not included in the award.
Laboratory discovery,modern diabetes care
The introduction of insulin marked a turning point in the treatment of diabetes. It allowed many people living with severe insulin deficiency to survive and helped establish hormone replacement as a major approach to treating endocrine disorders.
Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy or stored for later use. When the body produces insufficient insulin, or cannot use it effectively, blood glucose levels can rise.
Insulin remains essential for people with type 1 diabetes, in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells that produce the hormone. It is also used by some people with type 2 diabetes when other treatments do not adequately control blood glucose.
The treatment has evolved considerably since the first pancreatic extracts were administered. Modern insulin preparations are manufactured under controlled conditions, with different formulations developed to vary how quickly they begin working and how long their effects last.
The Nobel recognition
Banting and Macleod received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for 1923. Banting delivered his Nobel lecture, titled ‘Diabetes and Insulin’, on September 15, 1925, while Macleod’s lecture, ‘The Physiology of Insulin and Its Source in the Animal Body’, followed on May 26, 1925.
The discovery also has a lasting connection to World Diabetes Day, observed on November 14, the birthday of Banting, who was born in 1891. More than a century later, insulin remains a cornerstone of diabetes treatment, changing a condition that was once often fatal into one that can be managed with sustained treatment.

Cherish peace and stability, John Lee urges Hongkongers during Chung Yeung Festival
City leader and senior officials attend annual tribute to city’s wartime defenders and those who died in service at City Hall Memorial Garden
Hong Kong’s leader has urged residents to cherish peace and stability as senior officials marked Chung Yeung Festival with tributes to the city’s wartime defenders and public servants who died in the line of duty.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu attended the annual ceremony at the Hong Kong City Hall Memorial Garden in Central on Sunday, laying a wreath to honour those who died defending the city between 1941 and 1945.
“As we remember the heroes who sacrificed their lives in war and our compatriots who perished, we should learn lessons from history, jointly cherish and safeguard this hard-won peace and stability, and continue working for Hong Kong’s future,” he wrote on social media earlier in the day.
At the memorial, a flag-raising ceremony was held and then attendees observed a moment of silence with their heads bowed before representatives stepped forward to lay wreaths.

Popular Nigerian gospel singer Toluwanisings dies aged 41
- Published
One of Nigeria's most popular gospel singers, Olayemi Bayonile Bolaji, known as Toluwanisings, has died, his family has announced.
In a statement posted on the deceased's Instagram page, the family said the singer had "said goodbye to the world" in the early hours of Wednesday, 14 October. He was 41.
They also appealed to fans to remember his wife, children and family in prayer during this period of mourning.
The family said burial arrangements would be announced in due course.
Toluwanisings was known for his beautiful voice and energetic praise performances that encouraged audience participation, according to some of the tributes paid by his fans on social media.
Some of his popular songs include Unreserved Praise, A Very Big God, Onibuore, E Lagbara and Owo Re Meji Meji.
There was panic among thousands of his fans on social media after news first emerged of his death on Wednesday before it was later confirmed by the family.
Toluwanisings' death comes months after he was involved in a road accident alongside members of his band.
Tributes have continued to pour in from colleagues and fans following the announcement of his death.
Among those who reacted are prominent lawyer Pelumi Olajengbesi and comedian Woli Agba, who had earlier called for prayers for the singer.

A rumor that legendary comedian and satirist George Carlin once performed a comedy bit that involved jokes about televised public executions circulated online in October.
Carlin, who died in 2008, was known for his scathing political takedowns and clever wordplay.
People on social media shared a clip that appears to be from one of Carlin's standup comedy TV specials, in which the comic allegedly waxed poetic about using public executions to help balance the United States' budget.
The clip circulated as the Pentagon announced its plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was sentenced to death in 2013 for killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 during a shooting at the Army's Fort Hood post in Texas.
Some users suggested Carlin "predicted" the Pentagon's move with his comedy bit from decades earlier.
The video was authentic and clipped from Carlin's 1996 HBO special, "George Carlin: Back in Town," recorded at The Beacon Theater in New York City on March 30 of that year. The special is available to stream for free on Tubi and was also released as an album on Sept. 17, 1996.
The clip in question is part of a segment titled "Capital Punishment," which begins around the 14:30 mark in the full special. The clip was also available to viewon Carlin's official website.
During the special, Carlin joked about performing crucifixions during "Monday Night Football" in a satirical bit about executing white collar criminals facilitating the laundering of drug money.
The joke leads into the moment shown in the viral clip, beginning around the 15:15 mark. Carlin said (emphasis ours):
I don't care about capital punishment one way or another, because I know it doesn't do anything. It doesn't do anything except maybe satisfy a Biblical need for revenge. You know, if you read the Bible, you see that it's full of retribution and revenge. So really, capital punishment is kind of a religious ritual. It's a purification rite. It's a modern sacrament. And as long as that's true, I say, let's liven it up a little!
I honestly believe that if you make the death penalty a little more entertaining, and learn to market it correctly, you just might be able to raise enough money to balance the stupid f***ing budget!
And don't forget, the polls show the American people want capital punishment and they want a balanced budget. And I think even in a fake democracy people ought to get what they want once in a while. Just to feed this illusion that they're really in charge.
Let's use capital punishment the same way we use sports and television in this country, to distract people and take their minds off how bad they're being f***ed by the upper 1 percent. Now, unfortunately, "Monday Night Football" doesn't last long enough. What we really need is year-round capital punishment on TV every night with sponsors! Gotta have sponsors. I'm sure as long as we're killing people, Marlboro cigarettes and Dow Chemical will be proud to participate.
To say Carlin "predicted" the Pentagon's planned livestream of an execution was a stretch, but it's accurate to say he joked about televised capital punishment 30 years earlier.
The special also featured Carlin's takes on other hot-button issues that continue to be part of the national discourse in 2026, including abortion and the prison system.
"Back in Town" was Carlin's ninth HBO comedy special, of which he would do 14 before his death in 2008.

Jammu, Oct 18: Two persons are feared drowned after allegedly jumping into the Chenab in Doda and Ramban districts of Jammu and Kashmir on Sunday, officials said.
Rescue operations are underway to trace the missing persons, they said.
Officials said a 30-year-old woman, identified as Priya -- resident of Balwana village and mother of two minor children -- allegedly jumped into the Chenab from Bug Bridge in Doda district Sunday afternoon.
The woman was swept away by the strong current, following which a search operation was launched to trace her, they said.
In a separate incident, a search operation was launched for a youth, identified as Mohammad Imran, who is suspected to have jumped into the Chenab near his residence in Rajgarh area of Ramban district on Saturday.
Search teams comprising police and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) personnel, and local volunteers, launched efforts to trace the missing youth. During the operation, his mobile phone was recovered from the banks of the river, officials said.
A purported suicide message, allegedly forwarded by Imran to his family from his mobile phone, claimed that he was taking the extreme step due to alleged harassment by some individuals over a financial dispute involving Rs 9 lakh, they added.

Twelve years ago, Vermont Democrats tried to make their state the first in the nation to have a single-payer government-financed healthcare system — a bold experiment to push the limits of American health coverage when Obamacare was just being launched.
Vermont once dreamed of universal healthcare. This Democrat wants to try again — with a twist.
Amanda Janoo has a plan to gradually advance single-payer care if she becomes governor.
Their plan failed, and rebooting it became politically impossible, even in Vermont: The Democrats lost the governorship to Republican Phil Scott for what turned out to be a decade.
This year, that could finally change. A progressive political newcomer named Amanda Janoo is taking on Scott in what polls show is a tight governor’s race.
And if she wins, the state could be poised to try a whole new national experiment: one of Janoo’s central campaign promises is to create a pioneering health system where the state pays the full tab for primary and preventive care, while leaving the rest to the existing system.
Key takeaways
- Amanda Janoo, the Democratic nominee for governor of Vermont, wants to move primary and preventive healthcare to a single-payer system — where the state would pay providers for such care, make it free for patients, and cut insurers out.
- Previous attempts to pass or enact full single-payer systems have failed at the state level, including in Vermont in 2014.
- Janoo is trying to focus first on this one relatively smaller slice of the health system, but hopes it could be a starting point to full single-payer reform eventually.
- Yet even this more limited reform faces difficult political and practical challenges.
Janoo’s candidacy is an example of the policy experiments that are becoming possible nationwide in a projected “blue wave” year, when Democrats could sweep into power in a number of states. But in the healthcare universe, her plan is also an example of how even progressive policy idealists are trying to learn from past failures and focus on what they think can actually be achieved.
Compared to the sweeping ambition of Vermont’s 2014 effort, or Bernie Sanders’s signature “Medicare-for-All” idea, Janoo’s proposal for single-payer has very specific limits. Under Janoo’s proposal for “universal primary and preventive care” (she typically avoids the term “single-payer”), the state government would pay for Vermonters seeing primary care providers such as doctors and nurse practitioners. This government coverage would be universal and free for patients, and insurance companies would be cut out.
However, other parts of the health system – such as hospitals, specialists, and prescription drug companies – would remain under the existing insurance system, for now.
Every effort so far to enact full single-payer at the state level has failed — even in blue states, bills and ballot initiatives have regularly gone down to defeat. Vermont’s previous single-payer experiment made it the furthest — it was signed into law but abandoned before being implemented, when the governor concluded it was unworkable. Wherever it’s gained steam, politicians and voters have blanched at the high costs of moving their health systems onto state budgets, and the high taxes that would be necessary to fund them.
Now, Janoo is making an attempt to refurbish single-payer as something more achievable, by cutting off a smaller slice of it.
“I think it’s clear at this point that a profit-oriented healthcare system is a terrible idea,” Janoo told me in an interview Monday. But after assessing that the state budget made it “unrealistic” to do single-payer immediately, she concluded, “we could do universal primary and preventive care,” financed by a tax on the wealthiest.
Indeed, single-payer for primary care seems more achievable precisely because primary care is a relatively less expensive part of the healthcare system. But Janoo hopes it will pay major dividends — that better preventive care will improve Vermonters’ health, reducing costs elsewhere in the system by, for instance, making some hospital visits unnecessary.
In speaking to health policy experts about this idea, I heard much sympathy for the goal of universal primary care, but many questions about the details. Would Janoo’s plan be sufficient to bring more primary care doctors to Vermont — and, not unrelatedly, would it pay them more? Would her hoped-for cost savings from preventive care actually materialize? Is picking up the tab for a relatively less expensive part of the healthcare system the best use of sparse state funding?
These questions are becoming national ones, as healthcare gains traction as a political issue again. It isn’t just Vermont where primary care reform ideas are gaining steam: Democrats in Minnesota, Washington state, and elsewhere have discussed them. “There is growing interest in a number of states across the country in doing a universal primary care for all program,” Kevin Grumbach, a family physician and a professor of family and community medicine at the University of California San Francisco, told me. Even Gov. Scott, Janoo’s opponent, signed a law calling for a study of universal primary care.
One dividing line emerging, though, is whether to keep insurers involved, or to clear them out with a single-payer system, as Janoo wants. Insurers are unpopular with the public, but they can be a formidable political opponent when they argue that the benefits voters currently enjoy might be lost. Scott has said that the idea of universal primary care is appealing — but that if universal is “just code for single payer, I’m not interested. We’ve already been through that.”
Yet Janoo is hoping that single-payer for primary care will be a stepping stone – a trial run for eventually making the rest of the state’s health system single-payer down the road.
“I think about this often,” Janoo told me. “How do you build the new system as you transition the old — or hospice the old?”
Amanda Janoo is tired of “corporate neoliberal bullshit”
Janoo has long been an unorthodox economic policy thinker. Her rise is part of a broader trend in which progressives and leftists are winning primaries and gaining influence in the Democratic Party – but she doesn’t fit the prototype of the democratic socialist candidates in New York City, Colorado and elsewhere who’ve gotten much attention this year. Instead, she comes from a different strand of the left, a movement based on a dissident strain of economics and openly skeptical of the benefits of economic growth.
Dating back to when she graduated from college in 2010, in the aftermath of the financial crisis, she was part of a younger cohort rebelling against what seemed the glaring failures of the economic establishment. “The one thing coming out of university I was clear on was that neoliberalism was the worst,” Janoo said on a podcast last year. “This whole idea that governments should just take a hands-off approach to the economy and trust in sort of the disciplinary powers of the global free market to lead them to infinite growth seemed highly problematic and very anti-democratic.”
So for graduate school, Janoo attended Cambridge to study development economics under the “heterodox” economist Ha-Joon Chang. She then spent several years working abroad in international development for the United Nations and other organizations, before moving back to Vermont and working as an economic policy consultant.
In recent years, Janoo became deeply involved with the “well-being economy” movement: an international group of advocates, academics, and experts who criticize what they deem modern capitalism’s obsession with economic growth, and say the “well-being” of humans and the environment should be prioritized instead. They overlap with the “degrowth” movement, which outright argues economic growth should be reduced; last year, Janoo led a workshop at a DeGrowth Institute event on “Degrowth Policy Design.”
Trump’s return to power horrified Janoo. “I’m feeling angry about the rise of fascism and the growing threat of world war, because I feel like we don’t have time for this shit,” she said in a speech at an environmental event last year. ”The planet is on fire and ecosystems are collapsing, and that should really be the focus of all of our attention.” But, she said, “I believe I was born in this moment of history for a reason” and vowed “to fight for democracy – for life.”
So Janoo decided to jump in the race for governor of Vermont. While she is not running on a degrowth platform, her campaign is deeply informed by aspects of the movement’s thought: skepticism about growth’s benefits, a sense that untrammeled capitalism is leading the world to disaster, and that localism provides a better way. For instance, candidates for governor typically pledge that they’d help bring business investment in, but Janoo said in a July debate: “A lot of the problems we’re facing is because we focus so much on attracting external business.”
“Our economy is not super-diversified, and it is not really centered in the most essential kinds of goods and services you want to make sure people have access to no matter what happens — because honestly, things are bad now and they’re going to get worse,” Janoo told me. “I feel a little bit like a collective prepper right now. My motto is, protect what we love, produce what we need.”
In the Democratic primary, Janoo’s opponent, Aly Richards, had closer ties to the party establishment and led in fundraising. But Janoo ran as a progressive outsider; she promised to advance a “more economically populist vision” instead of “corporate neoliberal bullshit.” Her health plan became a point of contrast with Richards, who said she wouldn’t run on “magical thinking,” and that she wanted a version of universal primary care that would keep insurance companies involved. Janoo won the primary by 2.5 percentage points.
Now, she’s facing Governor Scott, who’s long been viewed as politically untouchable in the state – in 2024, he won his fifth two-year term by a margin of 52 points. But polls show a much closer race this time around, and Janoo could have a national blue wave at her back. If that wave helps carry her into the governor’s mansion. And if she makes it there, Vermont will have its first Democratic trifecta in a decade – and with it, the opportunity for major progressive policy change.
Amanda Janoo’s plan: single-payer for primary care
Advocates for primary care reform argue that it should be at the top of Democrats’ agenda, in Vermont and elsewhere, because the system is in crisis.
Primary care providers are overwhelmed and underfunded, they say – and, as a result, there aren’t enough. Grumbach, the family physician and UCSF professor, said “the workload, the lack of resources, and the gap in compensation” — as compared to more highly paid specialists — “has made it very hard to recruit people coming out of medical school to want to be family doctors like me.”
Patients, then, are having trouble finding doctors they like, and aren’t getting sufficient access to preventive care that could help them be healthier. “The emergency rooms are functioning and doing a lot of the work that normally primary care would do,” Janoo told me. “People are waiting a really long time to see anyone, and so often health issues that could have been caught sooner become more serious and dangerous.”
Finally, both providers and patients complain that insurance companies make the preceding problems worse, by adding administrative burdens and bureaucratic hassle.
So what would Janoo’s plan do?
First, her plan would guarantee free, government-paid primary and preventive healthcare for all in the state, by cutting insurers out of that part of the system.
Second, she wants to phase out the “fee-for-service” model of care, where primary care providers are paid based on specific services. She’s suggested, instead, either government-paid annual salaries, or per-patient per-month payments.
Third, she wants to try and try and make sure there are more primary care providers in the state, via more spending. “We would need some relocation incentives, so maybe $100 grand if you want to move here, or a student loan repayment program,” she told me. “My hope would also be that we could be a place for foreign-trained medical professionals to come here and be safe and accepted and to bring some cultural diversity,” she added.
As for how it would be paid for, Janoo proposes an income tax increase on the wealthiest Vermonters that, she said, would be comparable to the tax break they got in President Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” last year. Though she hasn’t settled on a final amount, she hopes these new taxes would raise hundreds of millions of dollars.
Would Janoo’s plan work in practice?
In speaking with health policy experts both inside and outside Vermont, though, I heard various questions and doubts about Janoo’s plan.
Some of the problems mix the practical and political. For instance, under this plan, primary care visits would be free, but tests such as MRIs would likely still require the existing insurance system, as would most prescription drugs. Janoo acknowledged to me that deciding how many things the government should pay for would “always be a challenge,” but said her first priority was access to getting people at least some healthcare.
There are also questions about whether this primary spending is really targeted at patients’ most urgent problems. Erasing the copay for your doctor visit might be nice, but those copays weren’t driving people into medical bankruptcy. Janoo’s reform plan leaves the bulk of hefty health spending from hospitals and treatments for very sick people untouched.
Other questions are about whether Janoo’s hoped-for benefits from better preventive care — she’s said the state could save as much as $300 million a year — will materialize.
“There’s no question that better access to primary and preventive care makes people healthier in the end,” Larry Levitt, executive vice president of the health policy nonprofit KFF, told me. “But advocates have long tried to sell prevention as saving money. I think it’s more likely that it costs money, but keeps people healthier.” One reason for this, he said, is that better preventive care could help identify more underlying illnesses and conditions in patients, and spur more spending to try and address them.
The shift to a salaried model for providers could bring other practical challenges. Though Janoo hopes that ditching fee-for-service will free up providers to see more patients, others suspect a guaranteed salary might incentivize them to see fewer, and wonder what role the government would play in trying to hold such providers accountable.
Finally, I also heard some disconnect between what providers said they wanted, and what Janoo thought they wanted. When we talked, she told me her impression was that primary care providers were most eager for changes in their work environment. “I’ve asked them, ‘If you could get paid a good annual salary – like, average for the nation – and you didn’t have to deal with insurance and the fee-for-service structure, would you do that?’ They say, ‘Absolutely.’”
Yet Grumbach told me that, for the primary care system, “Problem number one is not enough money, problem two is not enough money, and problem three is not enough money.” In his telling, it’s more money that’s the real key to incentivize more new doctors to practice primary care, and help pay other staff and health workers who could actually deliver good preventive care.
If so, the core challenge to Janoo’s reform will be the one that has dogged single-payer reform attempts everywhere: money.
If the government takes on the responsibility of paying primary care providers and setting salaries for them, providers will want those salaries to be high. If they aren’t high enough, the shortfall in primary care providers will worsen. But the higher such salaries are, the higher the taxes the state would need to raise to pay them. Essentially, taxpayers would be asked to shore up doctors’ salaries to keep them in the state — turning the healthcare argument from one kind of difficult political issue to another.
Getting the balance right would be a challenge for the government, with much at stake. But Janoo says her background in industrial policy has convinced her that it’s possible. Furthermore, she hopes, it will be just a starting point for the full single-payer system she still thinks is urgently needed.
“My hope is, when I’m governor, that I can start to work with some of our neighboring states. Because if we could create a New England-wide system, we could move to universal healthcare really quickly,” Janoo said. “I think it’s a moment where people recognize we need a universal healthcare system.”
And, she added, “If we had done it previously, it would be much cheaper than it is now.”

Katie Zacharia leaving her White House role less than five days on the job
- Published
Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, the BBC has confirmed, as the fallout from her shaky public debut appears to have reached its climax.
Speaking to reporters moments before news of her exit dropped on Friday, President Donald Trump said he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".
Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing in the role on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.
She spent the days after playing defence, answering tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.
Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during a press gaggle outside Marine One.
"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this," Trump said.
"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media.
The BBC confirmed she was leaving the job a few hours later.
As the country draws closer to the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House.
"The White House Press Secretary is gone. MAGA extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.
Zacharia's tumultuous week began on Tuesday, after she appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing that lasted 14 minutes, where she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions, and referred to her husband as the president.
During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practice law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam.
She replied: "When I was in China."
After intense scrutiny and digging by the press, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.
She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".
Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity from conservative-leaning Fox News lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.
When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"
Zacharia also described for Hannity how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"
When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.
She told the show's hosts she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney, because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one.
Host Lawrence Jones, asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?"
She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."
Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.
In his first term, Anthony Scaramucci, left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days.
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories.
Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform, for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win.
This summer, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates.
Even odder? “Nearly all of it—about $284 million—came from pairs of accounts repeatedly buying and selling with each other,” says former Polymarket trader Chris Park, who now runs the prediction-market forensic analysis firm MSR Decode.
Such a high volume of seemingly pointless back-and-forth transactions has raised eyebrows among experts. “It’s obviously some form of volume manipulation,” says Rajiv Sethi, a Barnard College economics professor who researches prediction markets.
When asked about these markets, Shana Bautista, Polymarket’s head of global intelligence and investigations, told WIRED that the team “immediately flagged this activity, investigated, and blocked the accounts from trading.” Polymarket did not respond to follow-up questions about why the accounts were able to trade such a high amount of volume before it took action.
The timing of these trades made things even weirder. Polymarket’s rules stipulated that the Ethiopia market would be resolved in October after the prime minister was formally appointed and sworn in, which meant that it stayed open for several months after Ahmed’s victory was all but a foregone conclusion. For 123 days after the election, bursts of seemingly irrational trading continued, prompting Polymarket users to leave comments like “THIS NOT RESOLVED?” and “fuckkkk.”
Sethi calls the phenomenon a “zombie market,” where people can buy and trade on events that have already taken place or are no longer happening.
Another market about a 2024 election in Romania facilitated what Sethi described as “even more dramatic” trading anomalies. The initial election was called off due to fears about foreign interference. A new race was held several months later, but instead of closing the original market in the meantime, Polymarket kept it running alongside the new option.
It was during this period that Sethi first noticed something weird appeared to be happening with the older market. An algorithm Sethi and his colleagues created to flag potential wash trading on Polymarket identified nearly all of the volume as suspicious. “99.6 percent of volume in this market for certain weeks has been wash trading,” Sethi says.
Wash trading is a type of market manipulation in which accounts repeatedly buy and sell assets to create the illusion of heavy trading activity, when in reality, money is simply moving back and forth. It’s banned on regulated financial exchanges in the United States and is specifically prohibited in Polymarket’s terms of service. An earlier study conducted by Sethi and colleagues found evidence of widespread wash trading on Polymarket’s offshore platform.
Wash trading could explain what happened with the Ethiopian and Romanian political markets, but because the identities of the traders is unknown, uncertainty remains. “What appears to be wash trading isn’t always wash trading,” says Sethi.
MSR Decode ran an analysis of the Ethiopian market for WIRED, which found that the most likely explanation for the anomalous trading is “activity farming,” which is when people try to artificially inflate their trading volumes. The firm suspects that traders may have been interested in boosting their volume because they believed that they could benefit if Polymarket launched a cryptocurrency token. In 2025, Polymarket chief marketing officer Matthew Modabber told the hosts of a crypto-themed podcast that there “would be a token” but did not provide specifics. Sethi also finds it plausible that traders could be motivated by potential “token allocation” to higher-volume accounts.
This type of behavior has been observed before in the cryptocurrency industry. “These are textbook examples on how market participants farm a potential airdrop,” says Andre Guettler, the director of Ulm University’s Institute of Strategic Management and Finance, who researches the structure of prediction markets.
When MSR Decode analyzed the Ethiopian election market, it found that it was highly unlikely that the trading volume could be attributed to sophisticated traders using algorithms to eke out profits. It analyzed over 38,000 “trade loops” that took place after the election (instances where individual wallets bought and sold to each other in quick succession) and found that over 98 percent resulted in neither side losing or gaining money. The median time that the accounts held onto the contracts they purchased before selling them again was nine seconds.
These types of unusual trading patterns are not a new phenomenon on Polymarket. Earlier this year, Barron’s reported that much of the activity on markets predicting the 2028 US presidential election centered on unlikely candidates such as Elon Musk and New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, neither of whom is eligible to run because they were born outside of the country.
Both Polymarket and its chief rival, Kalshi, have been publicly scrutinized for unusual market activity in recent months. Furor over suspicious activity on its recently launched perpetual futures market for cryptocurrency grew so intense on X that Kalshi published a blog post denying allegations of wash trading on it. (Sethi agrees with Kalshi that the allegations were unfounded. He argues that the unusual volume could instead be explained by Kalshi’s incentives for market makers, which create opportunities for other traders to profit from small price discrepancies.)
Polymarket recently raised an over $1 billion round of funding led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. The company is now valued at an estimated $21 billion, and earlier this summer, it announced that its annualized revenue was now over $1 billion. Polymarket’s explosive growth is often measured in volume traded, since it’s a metric that can point to how active users are.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets in the United States, declined to comment on whether it is looking into these election trades. The CFTC previously investigated a number of suspected instances of market manipulation on Polymarket, including several exclusively reported by WIRED, but they usually involved potential insider trading rather than wash trading or other suspicious activity.
In the past, the agency has issued hefty fines for wash trading in other sectors. “It seems to me that the CFTC would want to know about weird activity in a very large market,” a former CFTC employee tells WIRED.

How to lose a job in five days

Welcome to The Logoff: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is out of a job after only five days.
What happened? Zacharia was fired on Friday after less than a week in her new role, after a rocky start that included a halting performance in the briefing room, a scandal over her legal credentials, and a round of less-than-successful cleanup interviews.
The firing makes her the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in history, outstripping even first-term Trump communications director Anthony Scaramucci, who made it 10 or 11 days (figures vary) before getting the boot.
“Records are made to be broken,” Scaramucci posted on Friday. “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.” (No word yet on whether the “Zacharia” will emerge as a unit of time, as the “Scaramucci” has.)
What’s the context? Zacharia’s remarkably short stint behind the podium unfolded as the White House is engaged in an unprecedented attack on press freedom: The administration is still trying to ban three media outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House, though as of earlier this week, a judge is still blocking the ban from taking effect.
The diminished nature of the press secretary job was on full display in Zacharia’s sole briefing on Tuesday, when she took questions from just three outlets: Breitbart, Fox News, and the Daily Mail.
Why does this matter? Zacharia’s no good, very bad week is not likely to leave much of a lasting mark in its own right — other than, perhaps, as pub trivia — but as NBC’s Garrett Haake points out, it’s a very tangible manifestation of a White House that seems to have no idea how to spin itself out of crisis with just weeks until the midterm elections.
Most recently, Trump has landed on flat-out lying about the state of the economy — but like Zacharia’s time as press secretary, it doesn’t seem like it’s going to go all that well.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Geneva – His Excellency Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, today signed several funding agreements totaling € 25.5 million to support critical health priorities.
The agreements include € 4.5 million of funding for the Core Voluntary Contribution Account (CVCA) of WHO; these are fully flexible funds which allow WHO to allocate resources to key priorities outlined in its General Programme of Work. An additional € 15 million will be used to deliver on specific key priorities, such as One Health, the advancement of universal health coverage, and primary health care, communicable and noncommunicable diseases, the medical countermeasure initiative, and the country readiness strengthening through WHO’s office in Lyon.
A large part of the contribution (€ 6 million) is aimed at covering the humanitarian response on several fronts: € 2 million will go towards enhancing mental health initiatives in Ukraine; € 0.35 million is to support the response to the cholera outbreak in Malawi; € 1 million will support WHO’s humanitarian response in Gaza, with an additional € 2 million dedicated to strengthening the technical and human activities of the WHO Office in the occupied Palestinian territory. Finally, € 0.65 million will go to the Contingency Fund for Emergencies, to be used as needs arise.
“As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health. France's financial contributions and agreements, signed today, provide flexibility and align well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, power and perform for health” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General.
France’s WHO Framework Agreement for the period 2020-2025 ensures sustainable funding for priority health programmes, aligned with WHO priorities.
Some of the joint 2022-2023 collaboration priorities include the work of the WHO Academy, based in Lyon, stronger health systems towards universal health coverage, health emergencies – in particular the International Health Regulations (IHR) and health emergencies preparedness – and reducing health inequalities.
These priorities align with the France Global Health Strategy 2023-2027, published in October 2023.
“Committed to global health, France supports the WHO’s action in crises and for the benefit of the most vulnerable,” said Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations.
In 2020-2021, the Republic of France contributed over US$ 143 million to WHO, (including assessed and voluntary contributions), with 76% of the contributions in flexible and thematic funds. Flexible funds allow WHO to assign resources when and where they are needed most, ensuring that key priorities are funded, and a better flow of funds, enabling a more agile delivery of WHO’s objectives as per the General Programme of Work.

United needed a morale-boosting win, however, like the previous Premier League match, the team squandered the lead under limited pressure. Carrick believes MUFC were tough to break down and that the players stuck to their roles and responsibilities well.
Lisandro Martinez’s post-match comments after Atletico Madrid brought further issues for Carrick to deal with, and he had to focus on reuniting the squad before the game.
“I suppose you’re looking at the togetherness, the spirit, the unit. I don’t doubt that within the group,” he said. “The way that we went about it today gives me a lot of belief in us moving forward.”

Under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Food and Drug Administration is moving forward with plans to ease access to unproven peptide drugs that are popular among members of Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement—despite FDA staff scientists finding that the drugs have not been sufficiently studied to establish safety and efficacy and may cause harms.
The FDA submitted an “Interim Access Policy” on peptides for review by the White House, according to a filing notice posted on an Office of Management and Budget website. The posting does not provide information on the proposed policy. But people familiar with the proposal told The Associated Press that it would give the FDA “enforcement discretion” on certain peptide drugs. This would allow the agency to choose not to enforce current restrictions on peptides and provide an assurance to specialty pharmacies eager to start making them that they will not be targeted by the agency.
The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the FDA, did not respond to a request for comment from Ars Technica.
The proposal comes as the FDA is currently re-reviewing a dozen popular, but unproven, injectable peptide drugs. In 2023, FDA scientists determined that the peptides lacked data on safety and efficacy and posed risks. As such, they were stricken from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies, called compounding pharmacies, which make customized formulas for drugs.
“Charlatans”
Still, the dodgy drugs have grown more popular, with sellers claiming, without evidence, that the drugs can improve appearance, boost energy, and help heal injuries, among other wellness claims. They’re especially popular among the MAHA crowd; many prominent MAHA figures sell peptide products, and Kennedy, a self-proclaimed “big fan” of peptides, vowed to end “FDA’s war” on peptides upon taking office.

Before being fired five days into her stint as White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia spent much of the day attempting to explain her past.
Throughout her brief tenure, Zacharia’s resume was the source of much intrigue. Foremost was the fact that despite claiming to be an attorney for much of her career, she never actually passed the California bar, as she was eventually forced to admit. Another element of her professional history, WIRED reported, was a role as an affiliate marketer for Beachbody, a fitness MLM.
WIRED has now uncovered new details of her relationship to an AI-powered rare earths mining operation called NRED Intelligent Mining, which counts former Department of Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem as a strategic advisor.
On June 24, NRED—then known as NovaRed Mining, a small copper-and-gold exploration company in Vancouver, Canada—issued a release to share that Zacharia, who had left a role as a DHS spokesperson two months before, was joining the advisory board alongside Noem.
In her new role, according to the release, Zacharia would provide “strategic guidance” to NovaRed’s board of directors as it advanced exploration projects as well as “emerging artificial intelligence initiatives.”
It does not appear, though, that she ever worked there. When asked on Friday whether she was still on the board, she said, “That was fake,” and referred WIRED to Sam Amsterdam, a “strategic marketing and media engagement professional” whose clients have included the government of Kazakhstan and political parties in Georgia, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe.
“That release was not approved by Ms. Zacharia and was issued without her consent,” says Amsterdam, whose brother is listed as a member of NRED management on the company’s website and said he was speaking as a friend and colleague of Zacharia, not a representative. “I know all that to be factual.” He quickly added that while there had been discussions of her joining the company, she hadn’t actually done so.
Valentin Saitarli, who was NRED’s chief technology officer and says he is onboarding as CEO, confirmed that there were discussions about a role, but said that it “never materialized,” adding, “It was a bit like signing up for a gym but never actually going for a workout.” Describing NRED, Saitarli says, ”We go full robots and AI.”
Despite Amsterdam’s understanding that it had been withdrawn, the press release claiming Zacharia was joining the company remained on NRED’s website as of Friday. An archived version of their website showed Zacharia listed as management as of at least July.
When WIRED asked Saitarli about this, he said that the site was being updated.
Zacharia, whose NovaRed role was announced eight days after Noem’s appointment was announced, worked under Noem as DHS’s deputy assistant press secretary for public affairs for about a month, and was reported to have close ties with de facto DHS chief of staff Corey Lewandowski. (She denied any such ties to The Daily Mail.)
The announcement that Noem was joining the advisory board of a Canadian mining company triggered an outcry among Canadians, who pointed to past statements she made referring to Canada as the “51st state.” At that time The Globe and Mail described NovaRed as “a copper and gold exploration company that generates no revenue.” The paper noted that in January, NoraRed was holding only $65,689 in cash, which the company said “wouldn’t be enough to cover all of its expected expenses for the next 12 months.”
But around the spring, something changed. NovaRed began stacking its advisory board not with geologists and technical consultants—which would be typical for a junior mining company—but with heavy hitters with ties to the defense sector, MAGA, and other international entities.
Earlier this month, NRED announced that it was pivoting away from its flagship Wilmac Copper-Gold Project, and putting all its resources into developing and commercializing “MetalCore,” its “ AI-assisted mineral exploration platform.”
“I want to build a new generation of robotics and mining,” Saitarli tells WIRED. “Do we want to get stuck in the Stone Age or horses age? No, we want to live on Mars, spend time in hotels in space, have a wedding party on the moon…We will bring robotics and AI to global mining and beyond our planet, hopefully.”
Phil Ehr, a retired US Navy commander who is running for Congress as a Democrat in Florida, was brought into NovaRed earlier this year. “I know nothing about mining. I know nothing about commodities,” Ehr tells WIRED in a phone call. “But I do know that we need more copper. I do know that we need more critical minerals.” He had only been at the company for a couple of months when, he said, he was blindsided by NovaRed’s announcement that Kristi Noem and “another DHS spokesperson”—whom he recalls being Zacharia—had also been brought onto the advisory board.
“To the best of my knowledge, [Zacharia] came at the same time as Kristi Noem did without any consultation to me and was just like, boom, there,” recalls Ehr.
Noem, who did not immediately reply to requests for comment, was fresh off overseeing the disastrous ICE occupation in Minneapolis, and Ehr didn’t want to be associated with her. “So I asked the company, “Why is Kristi Noem here? I just can't work with her because she is so controversial. We are on different sides of what's right and wrong in, in the federal government,” says Ehr.
He thought it was odd that NovaRed seemed to be stacking its ranks with people who, like him, didn’t know very much about the mining industry. He expected some geologists in the mix, or technical consultants. Instead, some of the other people hired included Gregory Fedun, who previously “served as a key advisor to the United Arab Emirates’ Al Mualla Royal Family on a range of international projects,” and media executive Lee Caplin, coproducer of HBO’s True Detective series. Ehr resigned from the advisory board not long after Noem joined.
While she was attempting to clarify the nature of her relationship to NRED, Zacharia was also tending to other matters. On Thursday evening, while she still held her position as White House press secretary, Zacharia reached out to a WIRED reporter to suggest they contact fitness influencer named Jenelle Summers for “clarity” on Beachbody, the MLM she was previously affiliated with and which Summer brought her into.
Summers said she didn’t recall much about Zacharia—whom, she said, she met online—other than that “she was always kind to me and someone that was into fitness and believed in the products and programs.”
“To my recollections,” she added, “she didn't do much with it.” Summers rejected the idea that she had been involved in a “pyramid scheme,” which is how Zacharia had characterized the company to WIRED. ”That's kind of old school thinking,” Summers said. “It was a network marketing business model.”
“I don't have any comment on that other than to say she's always been kind to me,” she said when asked what she made of Zacharia’s rise to prominence.
Zacharia did not respond to requests for comment on her firing. When asked if he had comment on her having been let go, Amsterdam told a WIRED reporter, “Well, that’s news to me!”

Survey suggests one-third of us are burnt out
Amlan Sharma says feeling exhausted, less purposeful, less confident and achieving less at a job he loved became normal in the years after the COVID-19 pandemic.
The 38-year-old occupational therapist says he began to recognise what he was experiencing in some of his patients too.
"That's where I started to realise: 'Hang on, I might be burnt out,'" he says.
According to a new survey, more than one in three Australian workers are experiencing burnout, and for those whose workplaces have "high levels of system friction" it is far more likely.
The State of Workplace Burnout Report, published by think tank Infinite Potential in partnership with Beyond Blue and the University of Technology Sydney Business School, collated the responses of 999 Australian survey respondents.
Study author and managing director of Infinite Potential John Chan says there was a big divide between organisations with very low levels of burnout and those with very high rates and he wanted to "pick out" those differences.
"We're trying to move this conversation away from the individual," he says.
Paula Brough, a professor of organisational psychology and director of the Centre for Work, Organisation and Wellbeing in the Business School at Griffith University, did not contribute to the survey and says it's important to bear in mind the small sample.
Professor Brough says the levels of burnout reported are a little higher than she would expect, but there's "nothing new" in environmental factors being linked to burnout.
"There's key workplace characteristics … which contribute to high levels of mental ill health, which may or may not lead to burnout," she explains.
Professor Brough says the industries people work in are an important consideration, and are not included in the survey findings.
Higher levels of burnout typically occur in public-facing industries and high-risk industries, from bus drivers and customer-service roles to emergency services, she says.
What is burnout?
The survey relied on the World Health Organization (WHO) definition of what it classifies as an "occupational phenomenon" and "not a medical condition".
According to WHO, burnout is characterised by three dimensions:
- Exhaustion
- Increased mental distance or cynicism toward one's job
- Reduced professional efficacy
To have burnout, Dr Chan says, you need to be experiencing all three.
He says burnout has become a buzzword and while that has helped reduce stigma the term is often misunderstood.
"If you're just simply exhausted, that's not burnout," he says.
Professor Brough says stress and burnout are also not interchangeable terms.
"Burnout is the extreme end of the continuum [and] stress is the start of it," she says.
Burnout "red flags", according to Professor Brough, include sleeping changes, anxiety returning to work after the weekend, abandoning usual hobbies and other changes.
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
'I'm not the problem'
Amlan, who is a father and also has a caring role for a family member, says he became very disillusioned with rigid schedules and limited autonomy at his work.
"It was high job demands, excessive workload, time pressure, constant interruptions," he says.
He says issues that were beyond his control felt like they were wearing him down.
While it presented financial challenges, Amlan moved to self-employment and reduced his work hours, which helped with recovery.
"Over time I started to realise that actually I'm not the problem," Amlan says.
Unnecessary meetings, bad systems and red tape
Senior lecturer at the University Technology Sydney (UTS) Business School and researcher at The Ultimo Institute Anna Stephens, who helped design and conduct the survey, says the organisational factors linked to burnout are things "that create unnecessary difficulties in actually completing your work".
Dr Chan says this is the cognitive load or the "friction" involved in doing the job.
According to the survey results, this kind of work friction means you have 84 per cent higher odds of experiencing burnout in Australia.
Dr Stephens lists poorly designed online systems, lengthy bureaucratic processes, unclear instructions and expectations, and pointless meetings as examples.
Professor Brough says workplace stress can be thought about in two ways.
Firstly, "the big stuff" and then there are the small things that happen frequently, known as "minor stresses", "workplace hassles" or "red tape".
"They are also a key predictor of occupational stress, [which is] not necessarily burnout," Professor Brough says.
"It's often the workplace hassles which just eat away at you because they're daily."
Workload is also an established factor, and this can look like long work hours for an extended period, a lack of resources, not enough support and a lack of control, she says.
"You might not be able to control your shifts that you work, or your colleagues … or the [hospital] ward you work on," Professor Brough says.
But ideally, Professor Brough says, employers would offset that workload with extra support or independence.
"You can have a high workload, but if you also have high levels of support and control, it doesn't necessarily equate to levels of stress or burnout," she says.
Job security and 'fragmentation'
Dr Chan says job security and fragmentation are also significant factors.
The survey results found 68 per cent of Australians who don't feel secure in their job are experiencing burnout, compared with a burnout rate of 20 per cent for those who feel very secure in their job.
Job insecurity could be caused by restructures, global politics or AI uncertainty, Dr Chan says.
And fragmentation, he explains, is all the switching you do throughout the day without much control. This might be between meetings, tasks and software.
Dr Stephens describes it as the "constant interruption or multiple competing priorities" that divide our attention.
What individuals can do
Dr Chan wants organisations and employers to really think about the process and systems people work within.
Loading...
"The leaders and organisation have the responsibility to create the right type of environment, but then people also need to speak up when something isn't right or they need certain support," he says.
Dr Stephens recommends paying attention to your workload, communicating with your manager often and avoiding (where possible) normalising the frictions and fragmentations.
"They are a drain on our cognitive and our emotional resources, and they leave us with less fuel in the tank, not just for work, but for the important things in our life as well," she says.
Professor Brough says a worker and an employer "have a joint responsibility to look after your mental health".

The continuing mumps outbreak in Keralam, which began in late 2023 and has persisted into 2026, has renewed demands for including the mumps-measles-rubella (MMR) vaccine in the Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP). Outbreaks have forced the closure of schools and hostels for weeks in Alappuzha, Thrissur and Kottayam.
The demand has gained strength following studies from Keralam documenting immunity gaps among children, complications that can cause long-term disability, and genetic differences between the circulating mumps virus and the strain used in the vaccine, indicating how the continued exclusion of the MMR vaccine from the UIP represented an important gap in disease prevention.
From an annual average of over 2,000 cases, mumps infections began surging in November 2023. Keralam reported 74,907 cases in 2024 and 26,462 in 2025. A further 6,606 cases have been reported so far this year.
Low priority
Despite being vaccine-preventable, mumps has remained a relatively low priority in India’s immunisation policy, largely because of its low mortality. Although a time-tested combined MMR vaccine is available, the UIP provides two doses of the measles-rubella (MR) vaccine, which does not protect against mumps.
The Indian Academy of Paediatrics (IAP) has long recommended MMR in place of MR, a vaccine combination available to children through the private sector since the 1980s. It has argued that mumps’ public health significance is underestimated because clinical cases, complications and long-term outcomes are inadequately documented.
With outbreaks also occurring regularly in other States, several have urged the Centre to include MMR in the UIP.
In a response to the Tamil Nadu government obtained through an RTI application, the Centre said decisions on introducing vaccines under the UIP consider disease prevalence and incidence, mortality, vaccine efficacy and cost-effectiveness, among other factors.
According to the response, the National Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (NTAGI) considers mumps-associated disability not a significant public health concern. Adding the mumps component, it said, would more than double the vaccine’s cost compared with MR, without proportionate additional health benefits.
‘Poorly documented’
Paediatricians contest this assessment, arguing that the disease burden and long-term complications of mumps remain poorly documented.
“The increased cost argument is being made in a setting where the mumps burden and associated long-term complications are poorly documented. Systematic surveillance, documentation of complications and disabilities, transparent vaccine-price comparisons and an economic evaluation factoring in health-care costs, school absenteeism and complications should settle this,” they say.
“Mumps may not cause mortality, but its morbidity is significant, particularly during epidemics among unimmunised children. Complications include acute pancreatitis, encephalitis and aseptic meningitis. The virus can affect the reproductive glands in both sexes, with long-term consequences that may not be immediately apparent. It is also a leading cause of acquired sensorineural hearing loss in children, sometimes resulting in permanent, irreversible deafness due to nerve damage,” says K.K. Purushothaman, former Professor of Paediatrics, Government Medical College, Thrissur.
He also questions whether the Centre has applied consistent standards of evidence and affordability when deciding which vaccines merit public funding, given the subsequent inclusion of relatively expensive vaccines such as the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) in the UIP and later the HPV vaccine (as a special initiative). MMR, he argues, is a time-tested and safe option that has not been assessed against current evidence using comparable cost-effectiveness standards.
Molecular characterisation
A study by the Keralam unit of the National Institute of Virology, published in Infection, Genetics and Evolution in September 2026, adds another dimension to the debate. Molecular characterisation of mumps viruses circulating in Keralam during 2024–25 identified genotype C, genetically different from genotype N (L-Zagreb), the strain used in the mumps vaccine.
The researchers emphasised the need for continued molecular surveillance to track viral evolution and evaluate the current vaccination strategy. However, genetic differences alone do not establish that the vaccine is ineffective.
The study noted that available seroepidemiological evidence and outbreak patterns indicate a considerable mumps burden. The continued exclusion of a mumps vaccine from the UIP, it suggested, leaves an important gap in disease prevention.

Workers in China are teaching robots everyday tasks. Their movements become training data, helping machines learn household chores and respond to real surroundings. The South China Morning Post reported on Liu Yun, who joined the programme after losing her job. The 40-year-old previously worked in the automotive industry. She struggled to find another job because of her age. At a Beijing studio, Liu wore a sensor bracelet and chips on her fingers. Instructions appeared on a computer screen as she moved cups and scrubbed surfaces. She compared the experience to teaching a 2-year-old child. Workers were closely monitored, with large screens displaying their productivity and accuracy rankings. The daily target was 160 samples, while leading workers completed over 260. Liu found the repeated tasks tiring. Washing dishes and wiping tables 200 times daily was already her limit. Sun, a 22-year-old student from Shanxi, joined during his summer break while seeking an internship. He folded clothes, swept floors and recorded standard movements for robot training. Day shifts paid 120 yuan ( ₹1,704), while night shifts paid 135 yuan ( ₹1,915). Sun felt the money did not justify the physical and mental strain. Many workers left after only a few weeks. However, the work suits some people seeking flexible hours. Guo Hongjuan, from Jiangsu, collects data at home for around six hours daily, according to SCMP. Her tasks include arranging books, wiping tables and moving objects. She earns about 4,000 yuan (nearly ₹57,000) monthly while caring for her child. Robot training now extends beyond homes and studios. In August, Shenzhen company Physen AI partnered with a sanitation company. Street cleaners wore devices that recorded their movements while sweeping roads. Their responses to passing electric bicycles helped capture changing conditions in real surroundings. Online reactions have been mixed, with some users calling the work a cyber assembly line. Others compared it to home-based migrant labour. One worker said he had at least learned household chores. “It is deeply ironic. Humans are teaching robots to work, yet those machines will one day replace the very workers who trained them,” wrote one user. Reuters reported in August that human trainers in China used headsets and controllers to guide simple tasks like sorting crates and making coffee. Progress was slow, with beginners sometimes needing 300 attempts to produce a usable movement. Experienced trainers may need 50 attempts, according to Reuters. Such robots could help address worker shortages as China’s population ages and shrinks. However, three staff members said the subsidised project currently lacks a clear route to profits. They cited high costs and low data prices. Government funding and manufacturing investment are advancing faster than robots’ ability to work beyond carefully planned demonstrations, Reuters added.
