Lately, AI data centers are public enemy No. 1. The concerns are legion: how much water and electricity they consume, the noise they generate, the sprawling buildings they bring to communities, and the technology they’re powering that may or may not take all of our jobs and usher in the robot apocalypse.
The case for data centers, explained by a person who wants you to like them
Can data center developers talk their way out of a backlash?
Earlier this year, Gallup found that 71 percent of Americans oppose building data centers that support AI in their communities. And the backlash is bipartisan: Majorities of Democrats, Republicans, and independents opposed local construction.
Even in Texas, where data center development has been booming, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has hit the brakes. In September, he directed state regulators to halt permits for data centers pending audits examining their effects on the power grid and water resources.
But while many data center projects have run aground, others are still getting built — and the companies behind them are employing experts like Nicole Thomas to smooth the way.
Thomas is the senior vice president of media and community engagement at JSA, a marketing and public relations firm that represents data center companies. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about how the industry is responding to public opposition — and why she argues that these facilities can still be good neighbors.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
You’ve been at this for 21 years. Obviously, 21 years ago, data centers were not the hot-button issue they are today. When did you notice the shift?
I’d say about two years ago. I came into this industry myself about four and a half years ago. I come from a state transportation background where community engagement is just paramount. When you’re putting a new traffic intersection up, they expect you to interact with the public.
When I got to this industry, I said, “Oh, what’s your community engagement like?” And they said, “We don’t even have any community engagements in this industry.” And they weren’t wrong. Because 21 years ago, [data centers] were just like infrastructure. It was like building a warehouse for your computers. And so it was very similar to the way that you would build a Costco.
You would just go in, request a zoning permit, the zoning board would say, “Yeah, that works. Stamp, boom.” And you build your data center. And as a matter of fact, it was very secretive before, because data, and having that data in the wrong hands, has a lot of [cybersecurity] implications. About two years ago is when we started noticing the mainstream journalists coming around asking questions about data centers. And that’s, to me, when it started.
It still feels secretive, I think, to a lot of people, and that’s why people are mad. If you read about this data center that was proposed in Utah by Mr. Wonderful, Kevin O’Leary, it caught a lot of people off guard. Seventy percent of Americans, at the moment, do not want them in their backyards. How do you go about trying to change that 70 percent’s minds?
First and foremost, I think education is really important. And so one of the things that we did notice very early on because of the previously secretive nature of data centers, there wasn’t a lot of education out there about what they even are. And so that’s something we need to change. We need to make the connection between [phones] and data centers so that people understand what a data center means to their life on a daily basis.
Every app on your cellphone requires a data center to save your information in there. When you put your password into anything, you are interacting with a data center, which will verify your password and then let you into that app. Not to mention all of the information about you that you store in that app is then stored in a data center so that it can be recalled at any time.
We could not be having this call without digital infrastructure. It doesn’t work that way. We can’t have email without digital infrastructure. And that stat about 70 percent of people not wanting the data center in their backyard — I’d be interested in seeing the stat of how many people actually live near a data center and don’t realize it.
Because there are nondescript data centers doing work quietly in your neighborhood that have been there for decades and you don’t even know it. And so in some ways I feel, and I think the industry does as a whole, but I won’t speak for them, that the pushback on data centers is somewhat related to the pushback on AI, because people can’t control AI.
You even have Sam Altman telling us that AI will destroy society. So you have this concern about AI and you don’t know how to control it, but you can push back on data centers. And so it becomes the physical manifestation of AI are these data centers that people are trying to get overturned or get to not be in their neighborhoods.
It’s understandable. I’m a citizen too. You’re a citizen, and if things come into my neighborhood, I want to know about them. I have questions. There’s a big data center that just came to my community not long ago and their community engagement was horrible, absolutely horrible.
Can I ask where you are?
I’m in Indiana and I won’t say which hyperscaler it is, but a hyperscaler came into — I would say, not my neighborhood, into my city. They’re definitely not in my backyard, but they’re in my city. And so we took them to task because their community engagement was basically non-existent.
Wait, you work in data center PR, but you took a data center in your community to task for not being transparent enough?
Yeah, absolutely.
Which side are you on?
I’m on the side of responsible development.
We’ve all kind of accepted that we need a cloud for X, Y, and Z. And that it’s worth it so I can take lots of photos. I think everyone’s cool with that.
But the issue here is that people aren’t necessarily cool with AI, but we’re barreling forward anyway. How do you separate this essential need we have from AI, which people don’t necessarily feel is essential to their lives?
I think it goes back to education. Educating consumers on the difference between data centers: a small data center, a medium data center, a large data center. Educating them on why data centers exist and how they interact with data centers on a daily basis multiple times.
I hear you. But again, I feel like the issue here is not the data centers my cellphone needs, but instead is the data centers these AI companies need and these AI companies who the public doesn’t necessarily trust because they keep telling us that they’re going to kill us, and who the public is wary of because they don’t want their jobs being replaced by AI.
There’s all sorts of reasons that people are skeptical of new technology. So how do you specifically respond to that fear and to those people?
I think it’s, again, understanding the actual data center that’s being built in your community. Is it a 5-megawatt data center? That’s never going to house AI. That’s not enough power to house AI. Is it a one-gigawatt data center like Mr. Wonderful in Utah? That’s different.
But I think that AI is probably going to be something that is a lightning rod in the American public for a very long time. There are going to be people who are going to be anti-AI and pro-AI, and there’s going to be some people in the middle. I think it’s just, again, for us, it’s education, educating the community.
Have you ever been part of a project that a community rejected and you guys just packed up and said, “Okay, we’ll go find another community?”
Yeah. We have some clients who have had pushback from residents and they have said, “Let’s do a one-on-one community meeting where people can come in and ask us questions.”
And after the questions were answered, the community leaves and says, “Okay, this isn’t as bad as I thought it was.” Or we have a community that says, “No, we now have a moratorium and we’re pushing all data centers away.“
Sometimes they’ll wait for their client — my client is a developer and they’ve got clients that they’re developing for. If that client will wait, then maybe it is something that we’ll try to work out with the community. But oftentimes, they’ll just say, there’s communities who are literally raising their hand saying, “We’ll take a data center. We’ll take one. We’ll take two. Bring it here.”
So there are communities who recognize the benefits of data centers. And there are going to be other communities who say, “No, we don’t want this.” And then in five, six, eight years, they’re going to be like, “Wow, that county has a lot of tax dollars. They have a lot of really cool stuff. Why don’t we have that?” And the answer will be data centers.
I don’t think this ends anytime soon though, right? I counsel my clients that we could still be here in three to five years, really trying to help the American public understand the benefit of data centers. But it’s going to take a lot of education across the industry, and once we get those seeds planted, I’m a firm believer that they grow into educated community members who make educated decisions to bring community-minded data centers to their community.

A video of late actor Nana Patekar is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) amid the Cockroach Janata Party’s protest at Jantar Mantar. In the video, Patekar apologises to a man named Abhijeet before speaking in Marathi. The video is being shared with claims that Patekar was apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending an event and was supposed to accompany him to the protest at Jantar Mantar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending the protest at Jantar Mantar.
Fact: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to Marathi film producer Abhijeet Gholap for missing the NAFA Marathi Film Festival. Gholap, who produced the 2011 Marathi film Deool, shared the video on his Instagram account on 8 October 2026, stating that Patekar was unable to attend the festival. The video is unrelated to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke or the protest at Jantar Mantar. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
After reviewing the video with Google’s NotebookLM tool, we found that Nana Patekar speaks in Marathi, apologises to Abhijeet, and regrets not attending an event. Addressing Abhijeet, he says, “It was great working with you in the film Deool.”
Deool is a 2011 Marathi film in which Nana Patekar acted, and Abhijeet Gholap produced it. This suggests that Patekar was referring to Abhijeet Gholap in the video, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke. Patekar also praises Sonali Kulkarni, who acted in the film.
Further search revealed that Abhijeet Gholap had posted the video of Nana Patekar on his Instagram account (archived) on 08 October 2026. In the caption, he wrote, “Nana was unable to attend the NAFA Marathi Film Festival, and he promised he would definitely come this year. We will miss you very much.” In a Facebook post, he wrote, “Nana, you missed your visit. Now we will just keep waiting.”
Abhijeet Gholap is the founder of the North American Film Association (NAFA), which was established to promote Marathi films in North America. According to the organisation’s website, Gholap founded NAFA to bring together actors, directors, choreographers, singers, cinematographers and editors to create Marathi films, web series and documentaries based on local stories and subjects in North America.
To sum up, this viral video shows Nana Patekar apologising to film producer Abhijeet Gholap, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke.

What we learned from heated US midterm Senate debates
- Published
Candidates running for the US Senate in next month's midterm elections have taken to the debate stage over the past few weeks - with some heated exchanges and stinging personal attacks.
As the 3 November election approaches and parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged, particularly within some of the hotly-contested Senate races.
Here's what you need to know.
1. Not all Republicans are standing behind Trump
Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump?
Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters.
The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices.
While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump, a Reuters analysis indicated, external that two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle.
Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president.
"I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week.
"The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said.
Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead.
Elsewhere, some Republican candidates are choosing to separate themselves from the Trump administration's specific policy decisions, while expressing loyalty to Trump himself.
In Iowa, traditionally a Republican stronghold, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is facing a tougher-than-expected challenge in her Senate race.
She is taking on Democrat Josh Turek, and some polls suggest he has a narrow lead.
Hinson has not gone as far as Maine's Collins in separating herself from Trump, but she has broken with the president on some policy points.
During a 13 October debate with Turek, Hinson was asked about the Trump administration striking a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes to the US, followed by several other shipments.
The Republican candidate did not mince her words: "We need to lower gas prices in this country, we need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it."
2. Personal attacks are a common theme
As they have debated in recent weeks, the candidates haven't held back on deploying pointed personal attacks against their opponents.
The race for the vacant Michigan Senate seat - between rivals Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, a Republican - has seen its fair share.
Rogers, a Trump-backed former congressman, questioned during a debate whether anyone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist".
El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, pushed back strongly.
He called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration" and said he was "weak, cowardly [and] won't stand up until his poll numbers drop".
On Thursday, as a protester interrupted a Maine debate between Jackson and Collins, who suggested that the person interrupting the debate was associated with her opponent.
Jackson then said to Collins: "Oh shut up, I don't even know that kid."
Further south in Georgia, more personal attacks were exchanged between incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Representative Mike Collins, a Trump-backed Republican.
What started as an exchange where Ossoff accused Collins of taking money out of Georgians' hands to give to data centre developers, quickly turned into a hurling of insults that included Ossoff calling Collins a "bigot" who has "hired half the Third Reich".
Incendiary posts on social media from Collins' son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, have become a point of contention in the race.
In one post, Scheer blamed "Israel and Zionist Jews" for policies he said were intended to "undermine the white, Christian nature of America".
Collins defended himself by accusing Ossoff of "spewing" "craziness".
"I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don't care where the source is," the Republican said.
3. Some candidates are skipping debates entirely
There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found.
One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general.
Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win. Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority.
Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton, meanwhile, has not accepted any of those invitations.
In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets that he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign, and Paxton, have said little on the matter. Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has even urged the candidates to debate.
"One thing about not showing up is you lose the opportunity to make the case for yourself, and instead, what you do is you give your opponent the ability and the opportunity to make your case as negative as possible," Peter Trumbore, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the BBC's US partner CBS News last month.

The Delhi Police crackdown on the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protest on October 10 has drawn international scrutiny, with human rights bodies and press-freedom organisations flagging police excesses, and international media outlets reporting on the severity of force used against young protesters.
Police detained over 2,000 protesters and used force to suppress the mobilisation in the national capital. In arguably the most brutal assault on press freedom in India since the Emergency, journalists from both independent and mainstream media outlets were stopped from doing their work and detained in a display of police excess that bordered on madness. Some were dragged by their clothes, pushed and manhandled, some had their phones snatched, and pressured to delete footage of police action.
‘Restrictions Violate India’s Obligations under Int’l Law’
The global human rights non-profit Amnesty International on Friday put out a statement urging Delhi police to ensure that the fundamental right to peacefully protest is guaranteed to Indian citizens. In the statement, titled, ‘Delhi police must facilitate right to peaceful protest amid lockdown-like restrictions in capital’, Amnesty highlighted that “approximately 22,000 armed personnel from across the country have reportedly been brought to Delhi, in addition to more than 10,000 Delhi police officers expected to be deployed.”
Aakar Patel, chair of board, stated: “From denying permission for a peaceful demonstration, halting all Delhi-bound trains, and sealing the city’s borders, to issuing an internet suspension order near the protest site, and pre-emptively arresting activists – India’s authorities are leaving no stone unturned in their bid to prevent this march from happening. The right to protest is protected in India’s constitution. The authorities must immediately lift all these arbitrary restrictions, which violate India’s obligations under international law.”
After reports of rapid mass detentions began to surface on Saturday, the United Nations Human Rights Commission published a press release: ‘Concerns over mass detentions before and during protests’. Spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan called for the unconditional and immediate release of all those arbitrarily detained. “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled. Restrictions on peaceful protests must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality. The Indian authorities should also ensure law enforcement forces exercise utmost restraint in response to peaceful protesters, consistent with the country’s democratic traditions and human rights obligations,” read the statement.
Similarly, the global media watchdog Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) urged Delhi police to “immediately release all detained journalists and media workers, return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests…and the police response without interference.”
CPJ highlighted the detentions of Newslaundry reporters Ashwine Kumar Singh, Astha Savyasachi, and Anmol Pritam, and Scroll reporter Ayush Tiwari. “Newslaundry has also reported that police seized its reporters’ phones, while other reports indicate that journalists were physically manhandled,” the statement read.

Putting out a list of around 20 journalists detained through out the day on October 10, global journalists’ body Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said, “Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police’s actions against the press are unacceptable.”
BBC Focus on Scale of Government Pushback
The BBC published at least five reports specifically focusing on the heavy security deployment, police crackdown and mass detentions. The BBC published first on Saturday, ‘Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest’. The report highlighted the sheer scale of government pushback — it stated that the BBC saw at least five people being detained near the site as “police and paramilitary personnel [were] stationed behind barricades and ropes, preventing people from entering the protest site…and drones could be seen flying overhead.”
The report stated that 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed and that the “restrictions caused major disruption across central Delhi, with traffic diverted from several key roads.” It also mentioned the “dramatic scenes” involving Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi and other Opposition leaders since October 6, as the police vehemently prevented them from agitating.
In a second report, the BBC reported the detention of Dipke, Das, and Ranka and hundreds of other demonstrators. In ‘‘Cockroach’ group leaders among hundreds detained in Delhi protest’, BBC highlighted the way the three were detained before they could even deboard their flight, prominent protest face, All India Students’ Association (AISA) leader Neha Bora’s detention, and how more protesters were jam packed into buses than on the streets. “The large number of protesters expected to descend on Delhi were unable to get anywhere close to Jantar Mantar due to the heavy security presence and road blocks,” the report stated.
In a third report on October 11 — ‘Delhi sees more protests as freed ‘cockroach’ group’s leaders vow to fight on’ — after the detainees were released, the BBC highlighted the 7,000 protesters who were detained and released on Saturday and hundreds were also detained on Sunday. The report led with Dipke’s promise to continue fighting. BBC also posted live updates on the detentions on its website.
The New York Times also published multiple reports on the wrath the Delhi police unleashed on the protesters on Saturday. All their reportage described the scuffle between the state agents and the demonstrators with headlines reading: ‘Indian Police Round Up Protest Leaders and Lock Down Delhi’, ‘From a Sikh Sanctuary to Chaotic Streets, Protesters Brave Police in Delhi’, and ‘Blocked by Police, India’s Youth Voice Their Fury’.
‘Indian Police Round Up Protest Leaders and Lock Down Delhi’ read the headline of a report published by US-based news outlet NPR. The report described at length how “Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India’s youth…sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.”
Highlighting the elaborate measures taken by Delhi police to curtail the movement on Saturday, the report stated: “The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities’ determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilised thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi.”
The British news outlet The Guardian also extensively covered the police action on Saturday. Alongside Dipke’s video from when he was being arrested inside the aircraft, where he can be heard saying, “You can see where the nation is heading…this is dictatorship,” the outlet published a report ‘‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown’, wherein it describes the police lockdown as “severe”.
‘Modi is in Trouble’
Qatar-based Al Jazeera reported on the mass detentions on Saturday, and published a feature headlined ‘Meet the man helping India’s detained protesters get home’ and an opinion piece ‘Modi is in trouble’ on Sunday.
The former video report featured 25-year-old Rajiv Choudhary who built an AI-powered app to help the detainees get home safely after police drop them off at the city’s outskirts; the latter opined that the protests “exposed India’s hollowed-out democracy.” “These acts further erode the tenuous position Modi is in, prompting more rebuke from critics who now question his fitness to occupy the office of the prime minister. On Friday, the opposition parties, led by Rahul Gandhi, met President Draupadi Murmu and submitted to her that the government had subverted India’s democratic framework…Under Modi’s watch, problems have accumulated like barnacles on the side of the ship. Every time he has been challenged, he has gone farther away from the democratic principles on which this nation was founded,” the article read.
British news agency Reuters published at least six reports on the protest since Friday. The first report, ‘Why India’s tens of millions of voter deletions have led to widespread protests’, discussed the contentious SIR deletion which have led to the mass outrage and protests.
“The BJP and the Commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately impacted by the deletions…They say the deletions have affected the outcome of some recent state elections that the BJP won, and have cast a shadow on the electoral process in the world’s biggest democracy,” explains the report.
On the day of the protest, another report details the preemptive measures and subsequent police action. With the headline, ‘India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest’, the report describes the frequent protests as a “new challenge to Modi”. “The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi…The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027,” it states.
While various other articles report on the CJP leaders’ detention and eventual release, the police excesses faced by thousands, a news feature by the agency spotlights Neha Bora’s rise “as one of the most visible faces of a protest movement in India that has mounted the most serious challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government in years.”
Germany-owned international broadcaster DW published four reports on why the protests were taking place, the dramatic detention of CJP leaders ahead of the protest, the police crackdown on Saturday, and the CJP leaders’ vow to continue protesting despite the heavy police action, respectively.
In the report, ‘Indian authorities crack down on ‘Cockroach’ protest’, which was accompanied by a 24-minute-long video carrying footage of the police excess, DW describes the crackdown as “extraordinary”. “Indian authorities launched an extraordinary security operation in Delhi on Saturday to prevent a major demonstration…Roads across India’s capital were sealed, police checkpoints established and public transport heavily disrupted before demonstrators could gather,” the report read.
UK-based Financial Times published two reports on Saturday and Sunday, ‘Police arrest leader of India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement as protesters take to streets’ and ‘India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement plans more protests after release of leaders’, respectively. Both focused on the police crackdown and the protesters’ predicament.
While the global news hub CNN published multiples features on he CJP movement through May-July, on Sunday, it reported the release of the CJP leaders and the excessive police clampdown. In ‘India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement founder and leaders released from detention after Delhi protest crackdown’, CNN stated that the movement’s “target” this time around is the “62-year-old chief of the Election Commission that holds the keys to India’s democracy – the world’s largest – and who the CJP alleges is responsible for disenfranchising tens of millions of citizens.”
CNN witnessed, the report mentioned, that “despite the capital turning into a fortress to keep out protesters and mobile internet blocked, supporters gathered Saturday — as security moved swiftly to crack down on the unrest with many people at the protest site detained by police.”

European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
- Published
A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.
But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".
The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.
The diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.
Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.
The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.
Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice.
"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said.
"As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice.
"Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."
Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.
But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters."
"According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.
But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.
It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".
A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."
It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".
Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

EXCLUSIVE: Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival has announced the third cohort of emerging talents from across the Arab world selected for its Rising Stars program.
They are Egyptian director Abdallah Dnewar, Saudi Arabian writer-director Razan AlSoghayer, Palestinian filmmaker Omar Rammal, Palestinian Jordanian director-producer Asmahan Bkerat and Syrian DoP, editor and director Rama Abdi.
Launched in 2024, the initiative is part of El Gouna’s CineGouna Emerge program aimed at nurturing the next generation of MENA film professionals. CineGouna Emerge in turn is a strand of El Gouna’s CineGouna industry program alongside the Forum talks lineup, Funding project showcase, Market and new Series focus.
“This year’s Rising Stars are already leaving their mark, each in their own corner of the industry,” said Hayat Aljowaily, Director of CineGouna Emerge & International Engagement, who spearheaded the Rising Stars program.
Watch on Deadline
Cairo-based Dnewar produced the critically acclaimed Rotterdam-selected animated short My Brother, My Brother, and Locarno-selected Khufu, and been a script consultant on several short films. He is currently Head of Specials at Egyptian media company Zest. There, he oversaw the Eish Short Film Competition, a joint initiative between the El Gouna Film Festival and United Nations World Food Programme (WFP).
Based between Saudi Arabia and The Netherlands, AlSoghayer’s work explores womanhood, memory, friendship, patriarchy and growing up within a rapidly changing society. Drawing from personal experience and everyday life, she creates intimate, nostalgic stories rooted in Saudi culture and the complexities of change. Her debut short Son Of Badriyah plays in this edition of El Gouna.
West Bank-born Rammal has carving out a unique path between digital storytelling and independent cinema, with his visual style and deeply human storytelling racking up hundreds of millions of views across digital platforms.
He made waves this year with Everyday in Gaza, which won the best short documentary award in the 2026 edition of Italy’s David di Donatello awards. His debut fiction short, Kentucky Gaza makes its MENA premiere at the El Gouna, having premiered in the International Competition at Clermont-Ferrand in France. He is currently developing his first feature film.
Bkerat ,whose work explores themes of displacement, identity, and cultural heritage, is currently on the festival circuit with her debut feature documentary Concrete Land, which premiered at the Locarno Film Festival and won the Insights Audience Award at VIFF (Vancouver).
It recently played to sold-out screenings at the BFI London Film Festival and is now on a major festival tour, including Dok Leipzig, IDFA, and Doha. She is currently producing the feature documentaries If These Stones Could Talk and Landwards, and is in early production on her next directorial feature.
Damascus-based Abdi began her filmmaking journey in 2018, working across commercial, journalistic and cinematic productions as a camerawoman and director. In 2022 she directed her first short Fish Dance, and is now working on her first feature-length documentary House Number 7, which she is presenting in the CineGouna Funding project showcase.
Through the program, this year’s Rising Stars will connect with industry leaders and take part in the festival’s main activities, from panel discussions and media engagements to the red carpet. The experience is curated to give each of them the visibility their work has earned.
“What we offer them is not a beginning, but a moment of recognition: a chance to be seen, to be heard, and to find one another,” said Aljowaily. “Our role is simply to bring them into the same room, and into the light, at a moment when their work is ready to be seen.
Amr Mansi, Co-Founder and Executive Director of El Gouna Film Festival added: “We need to ensure that stories from this region are shared with the rest of the world. We strongly believe that our participants will be the dominant voice in telling these stories.”
Andrew Mohsen, Artistic Director of El Gouna Film Festival, emphasized the fact that the participants are fully integrated into the festival program.
“What makes Rising Stars meaningful is that it does not stand apart from the rest of the festival,” he said. “Many of these filmmakers are here with projects they are pitching at CineGouna Funding, or with films that are competing, or have competed, in our official selection. The program recognizes talent we are already invested in, and whose work we have watched grow from one edition to the next.”

Carney says 4 service members killed and dozens injured in fire at Alberta military base
EDMONTON, Alberta — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that four service members were killed and dozens more seriously injured in a fire at a military base in Alberta, describing it as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's military on domestic soil.
Fire crews scrambled late Saturday as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area. The Canadian military said Sunday there were no indications that the incident was the result of terrorism, but the cause remained under investigation.
Speaking in a televised address, Carney said the families of those killed had been notified and that the situation was still evolving.
Flags would fly at half-staff on federal buildings across the country in honor of those affected by the tragedy, he said.
It was not immediately clear exactly how many people had been injured
Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among the military personnel critically injured. "As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family," she wrote on Facebook, saying she was traveling to Alberta.
A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 kilometers (112 miles) northwest, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were taken to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster."
Hospitals declare emergency
Acute Care Alberta said several hospitals across the province had activated a "Code Orange," an emergency designation used when multiple severely injured patients require coordinated medical care. The agency said emergency medical resources were stretched so thin that extremely few ambulances were available in the Edmonton area. It urged people to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible.
Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town's small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised the response of local medical personnel. He said helicopters and planes had been transporting patients to other facilities for treatment.
At least 10 ambulances were parked in and around the Wainwright health center late Saturday as paramedics and soldiers rushed about. One patient was seen being loaded into an ambulance.
The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.
Military rules out terrorism as cause
Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate." He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.
McGuinty said Sunday he was traveling to Edmonton to be briefed on the latest developments. He said the military was working closely with Alberta's government and local authorities.
The Canadian Armed Forces said it would not release casualty figures until relatives had been notified. "The full extent of the impact remains under assessment," the military said in a statement late Saturday.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.
Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kph (62 mph). The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.
By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.
McGuinty, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, confirmed the casualties but had no other details to share.
"I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," McGuinty said.
"We will have more to say in the coming hours and days," he added.
He said Armed Forces members were at the scene and that RCMP were also involved. "This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation."
Alberta receives offers of support and assistance
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.
"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday's referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
- Published
Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.
Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.
The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.
Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.
Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.
The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.
During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.
Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.
Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.
Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.
Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon.
As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police.
Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.
The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.
George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes.
He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.
In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.
Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too.
"We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution.
"Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."
Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana.
She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights."
She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.
Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades.
The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?
Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".
The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.
In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".
He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030.
He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.
The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity.
Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule.
Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni.
She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest.
Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.
Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups.
Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions.
"Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC.
"He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."
Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

Volodymyr Zelensky has expressed hope that a bill of sanctions against Russia can be revived, calling on Kyiv's allies to "voice support" for the measures.
US president Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday that blocked a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the "national interest". The sanctions were due to come into force today.
In a statement on social media, Zelensky described Trump's move to put the sanctions on hold as unfortunate, without directly criticising the US president.
“This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters,” he wrote.
Members of Congress from both parties have strongly criticised the executive order, with Republican senator Thom Tillis calling it "beyond irresponsible".
Trump's secretary of state Marco Rubio described the order as a 60-day pause to "analyse" the economic impacts of the sanctions bill.
He pointed to concerns about high energy prices in the US and the ongoing Iran war, saying: “We need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is."
Rubio defends US agreement with Russia over diesel supplies
Marco Rubio has defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.
Under the agreement, Donald Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the US, followed by shipments in November and beyond.
"That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get."
Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.
Rubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions
The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US president Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter.
Secretary of state Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.
Rubio said that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier.
"A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.
The waiver comes just weeks before November's midterm elections, with Trump under pressure over high energy prices as war with Iran disrupts global oil supplies.
“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.
Trump’s deal with devil 'keeps getting dirtier'
"Beyond irresponsible," said senator Thom Tillis on social media, outraged about Donald Trump’s decision to pause sanctions on Russia.
"What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisers not understand?" Tillis said.
"It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine.
"Republican senator John Cornyn of Texas said "Lindsey would be appalled," referring to the late senator Lindsey Graham, who worked tirelessly on the bill before he died this summer. The bill is known as the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a statement that "by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump's deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier."
Senator Elizabeth Warren said Trump is "thumbing his nose" at Congress and "enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression." She urged her colleagues to take action to reverse course.
Next steps uncertain with Congress out until after Election Day
Donald Trump's actions come as Ukraine is bracing for a stark winter confronting Russia's ongoing attacks on its energy infrastructure to heat homes and keep the lights on.
The next steps are highly uncertain with the House and Senate on recess until after Election Day. Trump had indicated he was waiving the sanctions indefinitely, citing national security concerns.
Later Saturday, Trump told reporters that they don't know what his decision is yet regarding sanctions in Russia, despite the executive order he signed Friday night.
"We'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out. But it's a very good decision, and it's going to be a decision that's good for the country, and I think good for the world," Trump said at a fundraising dinner at his Florida estate.
Secretary of state Marco Rubio, separately addressing reporters on Saturday before departing for Central Asia, suggested Trump would take 60 days to review the global and US economic impacts of imposing the proposed sanctions on Russia and other countries, in light of tariffs already in place.
Pointing to high energy prices and the Iran war, "we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is," he said.
Poland says it is verifying a possible violation of its airspace
Poland is verifying a possible violation of its airspace by an unidentified object, the army said on Sunday.
So far, there has been no confirmation of a violation of the airspace, the army said in a post on X.
The army said it had deployed a ground search-and-rescue team in the south of Lublin, which is conducting searches for the possible crash site of the object.
Zelensky hopes for revival of Russian sanctions
Ukraine's president expressed hope that sanctions that were supposed to take effect on Sunday targeting Russia's economy could be revived.
Volodymyr Zelensky described Donald Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticise the US leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.
"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelensky wrote in a statement on social media.
“This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”
He separately thanked Democrats and Republicans who supported the legislation, saying that blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing and that limiting Ukraine’s ability to retaliate would not bring peace.
“Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make (Russian president Vladimir) Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war,” he said.
It took almost a year for Lindsey Graham to persuade Trump to agree to the Russian sanctions package.
It was designed to impose steep tariffs on countries that import large amounts of Russian oil and energy products and was promoted as a way to halt the flow of funds fuelling Putin's four-year war against Ukraine.
Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress
President Donald Trump's abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage on Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.
Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late on Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia's Vladimir Putin.
Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the US that are roiling the midterm elections on 3 November.
"I think it's clear Russia is the aggressor, and we've got to do everything we can to put economic pressure on Russia," senator Rick Scott said in an interview with the Associated Press. "So it's not the first thing I would be doing.”
Zelensky says issues persist with Starlink and matter is being discussed with US
Ukraine still cannot use its interceptor systems against Russian drone attacks because of speed restrictions imposed on Starlink, president Volodymyr Zelensky has said, adding that Kyiv was discussing the issue with US officials.
Zelensky told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat that Ukrainian officials had been told the restrictions were linked to technical issues.
He said Ukraine had tested Starlink on European Union territory and encountered no such problems there, with the system operating at higher speeds.
On Friday, Donald Trump said he did not believe either the US government or Elon Musk was to blame for deliberately restricting Ukraine’s Starlink access, and the UK government said it had received assurances from the White House that access had been restored.
At least 1,500 troops to participate in war exercises in Poland
At least 1,500 troops from Britain, France and Germany will take part in the war exercise next month, according to The Times, alongside Polish forces.
The wargames will simulate moving troops and supplies such as food and fuel, and was agreed at a coalition of the willing summit in July.
Russian air strike on Kherson kills ambulance driver and injures almost 20
A Russian air strike on Kherson in southern Ukraine killed one person and injured 19 others, governor Oleksandr Prokudin has said on Saturday.
The person killed was an ambulance driver, and one child was among the injured, Prokudin said on Telegram.

Gordon Ramsay has never let me down when I need a quick recipe, whether it's a 15-minute Bolognese or a 10-minute bacon cheeseburger.
So I was ecstatic when I discovered that the Michelin-starred chef has an entire cookbook dedicated to dishes that can be made in 10 minutes.
The very first recipe I tried from "Ramsay in 10" was a turkey and leek pasta with crispy sage breadcrumbs.
"For a change, skip the Bolognese and make this creamy turkey and leek sauce in a fraction of the time instead," Ramsay writes in the description. "It might just become a regular midweek family meal, as it has at my house."
Ramsay's 10-minute pasta includes turkey, breadcrumbs, and leeks.
To make Ramsay's 10-minute pasta for four, you'll need:
- 17 ounces of fresh penne or fusilli pasta
- 14 ounces of ground turkey
- ¾ cup of heavy cream
- 4 sage leaves
- 4 regular shallots (or 2 banana shallots)
- 3 garlic cloves
- 2 leeks
- 1 lemon
- A handful of flat-leaf parsley leaves
- Freshly grated Parmesan cheese (for serving)
To make the breadcrumbs, you'll need:
- 6 tablespoons of fresh breadcrumbs
- 2 sage leaves
- 2 tablespoons of olive oil
Ramsay notes in his cookbook that the breadcrumbs are optional, but I recommend taking the extra step. It was my first time making fresh breadcrumbs, and it couldn't have been easier.
But feel free to play around with the ingredients depending on your preferences. Ramsay said this dish also works well with ground chicken or sausage; the sage can easily be swapped for thyme, parsley, or tarragon; and any shape of fresh or dried pasta will do.
Before I started cooking, I needed to prep my ingredients.
First, I brought a saucepan of salted water to a boil so it'd be ready for the pasta in a few minutes.
Then, per Ramsay's recipe, I peeled and grated my shallots and garlic. If the handheld grater proves tricky — and risky for your fingers — feel free to use a knife to finish mincing the veggies.
After grating my shallots and garlic, I finely sliced the leeks.
Ramsay recommends prepping your shallots and garlic while the olive oil is heating up in the pan and slicing your leeks right before you add the pasta. I'm still pretty slow at chopping veggies, so I got my prep out of the way so I wouldn't be stressed about burning anything. I also soaked my sliced leeks in a bowl of cold water to ensure they were fully cleaned.
The recipe took me a tad longer than 10 minutes, but you can follow Ramsay's lead if you're confident in your chopping speed!
I also prepped my fresh breadcrumbs.
I simply tore two slices of bread into pieces and threw them into the food processor.
I placed my Dutch oven over medium-high heat and added two tablespoons of olive oil. Then I added my shallots and garlic to the pan.
I allowed the shallots and garlic to cook for two minutes, stirring regularly.
If you don't have a Dutch oven handy, Ramsay says this recipe also works with a heavy-based frying pan or skillet.
After two minutes had passed, I threw in the turkey and sage leaves.
I broke the turkey up with a wooden spoon and allowed it to cook until the meat was lightly browned, which took around three to four minutes.
While the turkey cooked, I added my leeks to the boiling water.
I let the leeks cook for one minute, per Ramsay's instructions.
I threw in the penne and allowed the noodles to cook until they were al dente.
Since I chose penne, my pasta didn't cook in the speedy two minutes Ramsay recommends for fusilli. But just follow the instructions on your box, and the noodles will taste great.
While my pasta was cooking, I added the cream to my turkey.
I stirred everything together and brought the sauce to a boil. Then I reduced the sauce to a simmer until I was ready to serve.
Next up were the crispy sage breadcrumbs.
I placed a frying pan over medium heat and drizzled some olive oil. Then I added two sage leaves, which I had finely chopped.
I cooked the breadcrumbs until they were crisp and golden brown.
This happens very quickly — make sure to watch the pan carefully so they don't burn!
I drained my pasta and leeks and added the penne to the sauce.
Ramsay recommends saving two to three tablespoons of the pasta water and adding it to the sauce.
I added the finely chopped parsley leaves, along with some lemon zest.
I also added some salt and pepper before giving everything a big stir.
I topped everything off with the sage breadcrumbs.
After I added the freshly grated Parmesan cheese and drizzle of olive oil that Ramsay recommends, I stepped back and admired my pasta.
The dish looked bright and inviting, thanks to the pops of color from the parsley and breadcrumbs, and I loved seeing so many different textures meld together. Plus, it smelled absolutely delicious.
Ramsay's 10-minute pasta took me a couple of extra minutes, but the final result was worth it.
I don't usually go for poultry with my pasta, so I was skeptical when making the turkey sauce. But I was pleasantly surprised by how much I loved Ramsay's recipe.
The sauce is light but packed with so much flavor. The leeks add a hint of lovely sweetness, and the lemon brightens each bite. The contrasting textures of the crispy sage breadcrumbs and the creamy sauce also make a fantastic team.
I don't usually crave a big meal on a weeknight, so I love that this pasta makes dinner interesting without being too heavy.
Whether you're longing for a quick weeknight dish or just want a light and bright recipe during the busy season, Ramsay's favorite 10-minute pasta will satisfy all your cravings.
And if you're looking for more recipe inspiration, you can check out my ranking of Gordon Ramsay's pasta dishes.

Drivers across the United States are being warned to watch out for deer entering their annual mating season, which officials say poses a serious collision risk and a possible danger to life on the roads.
National insurance figures show drivers face a 1 in 145 chance of colliding with an animal, according to an analysis by State Farm. The insurer estimated that more than 1.6 million animal collision claims were filed nationwide between July 2025 and June 2026, with deer topping the list of struck wildlife.
Drivers face the highest risk during the peak mating and hunting months of November, October and December.
West Virginia, Montana and Wisconsin rank as the top states for animal crashes, prompting officials across the country to issue regional warnings. In New Jersey, the Department of Environmental Protection noted that the “fall rut” runs from mid-to-late October through mid-December.
“Collisions with deer pose a very serious safety threat and can cause significant damage to vehicles and possible loss of life,” said Dave Golden, assistant commissioner for NJDEP Fish & Wildlife, in an agency release. “It’s especially important that drivers be extra vigilant to this threat and take time to know steps that can be taken to reduce the risk of collision.”
State authorities also said that daily commutes frequently overlapped with peak animal activity around dawn and dusk. During the fall rut, deer are more likely to be present near and on roadways as bucks attempt to court does.
The safety hazard is expected to intensify when daylight saving time ends on November 1, shifting heavy traffic periods into darker hours.
The problem has grown worse as suburban development spreads into natural habitats. In New Jersey, around 100,000 deer now roam the state, according to Gothamist.
Nearby New York sees a similar toll, with state transport officials estimating between 60,000 and 70,000 deer crashes every year.
To reduce risk, officials advise motorists to slow down, watch for crossing signs and use high beams in the dark. If a collision is unavoidable, state guidelines urge drivers not to swerve, as counter-maneuvers make fatal crashes far more likely when vehicles hit oncoming traffic or roadside structures.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

Hurricane Trudy brings heavy rain and strong winds to Mexico’s Pacific coast
Hurricane Trudy brings heavy rain and strong winds to Mexico’s southwestern and west-central Pacific coast, according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center
MIAMI -- Hurricane Trudy lashed parts of Mexico’s Pacific coast with heavy rain and strong winds Sunday as the U.S. National Hurricane Center warned of potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
A hurricane warning remained in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco. The latest NHC data showed the Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 100 mph (155 kph) about 135 miles (215 kilometers) south of Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco state and 115 miles (185 kilometers) west-southwest of Manzanillo, moving northwest at 9 mph (15 kph).
Meanwhile, Typhoon Champi strengthened into a Category 4 super typhoon as it moved past Guam.
Trudy’s center was expected to remain near the Mexican coast through Sunday evening before moving south of the Baja California Peninsula. A tropical storm warning remained in effect for Las Islas Marias. A warning for the coast east of Punta San Telmo to Lazaro Cardenas had been discontinued.
The Mexican navy urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of rising rivers, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.
Colima authorities said the risks remained low, but warned that heavy rainfall could cause damage because the ground was already saturated by successive storms along the Pacific coast.
Trudy was expected to bring 4-8 inches (10-20 centimeters) of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of around 12 inches (30 centimeters) along and near the coast in Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. The hurricane center warned of potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas with steep terrain.
Also in the Pacific, Champi was moving away from Guam on Sunday after passing close to the island’s southern tip, with sustained winds of 150 mph (240 kph). At 1 p.m. Sunday local time it was 130 miles (210 kilometers) west of Guam, moving west at 16 mph (26 kph), according to the U.S. National Weather Service.
The storm could strengthen into a Category 5 super typhoon early Monday local time. Guam and Rota remained under a typhoon warning, while the tropical storm warning and typhoon watch for Tinian and Saipan were canceled.
The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands both requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday.
On Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Guam authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate all federal disaster relief efforts. FEMA announced that federal disaster assistance was available for the territory of Guam to supplement local response efforts following Typhoon Champi.
Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed. Resources were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, according to Saturday updates from FEMA.
The territories are still recovering from super typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July, respectively.

The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has denounced the settler attack that left the Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine badly beaten and needing surgery as a “despicable act of terror” and called for the arrest and prosecution of those responsible.
Levine, an award-winning journalist who lives in Israel, was set upon last Friday by masked Israeli settlers who used clubs and other weapons to attack Palestinian people attempting to harvest their olives in occupied West Bank towns.
The 63-year-old photographer, who is in a hospital in Petah Tikva near Tel Aviv recovering from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack, said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.
“I was attacked, pushed to the ground,” Levine said. “Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me.” She added the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
Huckabee, a rightwing ally of President Donald Trump with a track record of hardline, pro-Israel rhetoric, was notably blunt in his condemnation of what he called the “vicious and cowardly attack” on Levine. In a post on X on Saturday, he noted that she was a US citizen who had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
“We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this,” Huckabee added. “Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence.”
Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been ambiguous in addressing Levine’s assault, condemning “violence against anyone” but referring to the attack as “alleged” and saying its circumstances remain unclear.
The attack on the Palestinian farmers and Levine was followed on Saturday by another outbreak of settler violence directed against European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of the French city of Cambrai, who were visiting the occupied West Bank.
Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground. Violence is surging ahead of bitterly fought elections to be held on 27 October, with Palestinians’ annual olive harvest being repeatedly disrupted by Israeli settlers as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his pro-settlement rightwing base.
France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, has called on Israel to “urgently halt criminal violence” and to arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux. The EU has condemned the attack and urged “full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists”.
The European Commission executive vice-president, Teresa Ribera, went further, posting an interview with Levine in hospital and adding the caption: “They want no witnesses.”
Israel’s foreign ministry has condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
President Isaac Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, called Levine in hospital on Saturday, saying the attack was “outrageous and shocking” and was weighing on his conscience.
Netanyahu’s main rival in the elections, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, criticised the prime minister over the violence, saying it was “burning away the little legitimacy the state of Israel still possesses”. He described the attacks as “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government”.
Trump officially endorsed Netanyahu for re-election in a post on his Truth Social network on Sunday, hailing him as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran”. He added: “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
The Washington Post has reiterated its call for a full and transparent investigation into the attack on Levine, even though Israel rarely investigates settler violence fully.
Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says around 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.
