Tamil Nadu: ‘Thenisai Thendral’ Deva laid to rest amid tears, tributes
Ranipet , Veteran Tamil music composer and singer Deva, popularly known as 'Thenisai Thendral', was laid to rest with full state honours at his family farmland in Sakkaramallur near Arcot, Ranipet district, on Sunday.
He was 75.
Deva died of a heart attack in Chennai on the morning of October 17. His mortal remains were taken from his Chennai residence to the farmland, where the final rites were performed.
Thousands of people gathered at the site to pay their last respects to the celebrated music director.
Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay had visited Deva's residence in Chennai to pay his respects and announced that the funeral would be held with state honours in recognition of the composer's contribution to the music industry.
Revenue and police officials oversaw arrangements for the ceremony at Sakkaramallur.
Relatives and villagers recalled Deva's enduring connection to his roots, saying he regularly visited his native village during festivals such as Pongal and contributed to local initiatives, including funding the construction of a Sri Ranganathar temple.
Born Devanesan Chokkalingam, Deva had a career spanning nearly four decades and composed music for more than 400 films in Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam.
Before turning to films, Deva was an employee of the Tamil Nadu government's Public Works Department .
He made his entry as a composer in 1986 with 'Mattukkara Mannaru', which did not fare well in theatres, though its songs found a loyal audience over time.
'Manasukketha Maharasa' , starring Ramarajan and Seetha, was the film that first drew attention to his work. His real breakthrough, however, came in 1990 with the Prashanth-starrer 'Vaigasi Poranthachu', which won him widespread acclaim.
Deva rose to prominence in the late 1980s and 1990s with his high-energy, folk-rooted tunes, and is widely credited with bringing the 'gaana' genre into mainstream Tamil cinema.
Few composers in Tamil cinema are as closely identified with one genre as Deva is with 'gaana', the urban folk music born in the working-class neighbourhoods of North Chennai.
He worked with nearly every leading star of his time, among them Vijayakanth, Sarathkumar, Vijay and Ajith, and delivered some of the biggest hits of their careers.
Among his chartbusters were the Rajinikanth films 'Annamalai', 'Baashha' and 'Arunachalam', and the Kamal Haasan outings 'Avvai Shanmugi', 'Pammal K Sambandam' and 'Panchathanthiram'.
His death drew tributes from political leaders, members of the film fraternity and fans across Tamil Nadu.

After booting 760K off ACA health plans, the Trump administration adds some people back
Late last month, the Trump administration announced that it had cut 760,000 people from the Affordable Care Act rolls, claiming fraud and improper enrollments and touting billions in potential taxpayer savings.
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
Not all of those kicked off were fraudulently enrolled, KFF Health News has learned. Insurance industry sources said the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has reinstated a small number of people whose coverage should not have been canceled. More could follow in the coming weeks if enrollees discover they are uninsured when they go to use their coverage.
A fix for widespread fraud?
Still, the sweep was long overdue, say supporters such as Brian Blase, whose Paragon Health Institute has supplied many of the sometimes controversial findings cited by those who allege widespread enrollment fraud in the ACA. But other policy experts question how many legitimate consumers were caught in the dragnet, perhaps because they failed to open a letter from their insurer or answer a phone call.
Questions continue to swirl, even as a second phase of the anti-fraud effort is underway. An additional 419,000 sign-ups are being scrutinized. Insurers must let CMS know how many of those enrollees don't respond to outreach efforts by "around mid-to-late November, after the midterm elections," said David Merritt, senior vice president of external affairs at the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association.
He confirmed that some BCBS members are among those who have been reinstated. He also said that CMS has an expedited review process for those who discover they have been improperly disenrolled.
Few details
Overall, however, the administration is providing few details about the cancellations, such as how robust the outreach was to those it targeted, how long it takes for people to get reinstated after discovering their coverage was wrongly canceled, and how many such cancellations have been reversed.
"It may be true that some of those enrollments were not authorized, but it can be equally true that people got lost in the shuffle and have a valid enrollment. Without more information, it's almost impossible to tell," said Katie Keith, a director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown Law. "That they are not being very transparent is telling too," she said of the administration.
The enrollment cut comes as part of a larger Republican strategy to focus on fraud in government programs, including Medicaid and hospice care, which polls show resonates with GOP voters.
At an Oct. 14 press conference, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz touted the removal this year of subsidies for about 189,000 ACA enrollees with duplicate Medicare, Medicaid, or Children's Health Insurance Program coverage, citing not fraud but a failure to look for concurrent enrollments or continued coverage for dead people. They credited an effort begun last year by the Trump administration to restore more frequent data matching checks than were done under the prior administration.
Unauthorized sign-ups by rogue insurance agents seeking commissions and other potential impropriety in the ACA marketplace — applicants' providing incorrect income estimates, for example — has been a concern for several years, with much debate over the magnitude of the problem.
Even so, how the move will play out politically is uncertain. Healthcare costs are tied with gas prices as a top concern for voters. It is likely that many removed from the ACA are in red states, such as Texas, Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi. Those areas saw rapid growth in ACA enrollment from 2020 to 2025, driven in part by now-expired enhanced subsidies put in place during Joe Biden's presidency. Additionally, the cancellations target only states that use Healthcare.gov, the federal ACA marketplace. The 21 states fully running their own marketplaces generally have more robust fraud prevention programs and have reported few or none of the kinds of unauthorized sign-ups plaguing the federal marketplace.
"To the extent there is a reaction depends on whether the government got it wrong, whether people try to get care and then find out their coverage is no longer active," said Adrianna McIntyre, assistant professor of health policy and politics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.
How it played out
According to information the agency provided to KFF Health News, CMS in June selected for further review nearly 1.2 million enrollments that had all of what it deemed four warning signs for fraud:
- The application included no Social Security number or immigration document number.
- A broker was involved in the sign-up process.
- The plan had no monthly premium payment.
- The enrollee had had no contact with their insurer and no claims filed.
Then, as first reported by KFF Health News, CMS sent lists of those ACA accounts to specific insurers, instructing the carriers to review them and use at least two methods of contact — such as a phone call and a letter — to try to reach the enrollees. Policyholders were given 30 days to respond to the insurers' outreach and provide the missing information. CMS disenrolled those who didn't respond.
Johnny Wallin, chief operating officer of Texas-based Marketplace Insurance Exchange, which helps clients in about 35 states enroll in coverage, said insurers reached out to his organization for help contacting people on the CMS lists, prompting "an all-hands-on-deck" effort by agents to reach clients, some of whom were vacationing overseas.
"Getting them to answer the phone isn't easy," he noted, although he suspects his agents had a better chance of getting a reply than an insurer because their clients are familiar with their phone numbers. Still, they could not reach about 60 of them.
Additionally, his team has been asked by insurers to help contact those targeted in the second phase of CMS' review. A recent case involved a client who needed to upload his new green card after his previous one expired, but language barriers meant that he had to take time off work to come in for agents to help with the process.
Information from a financial filing
CMS would not provide a list of the insurers it contacted, but publicly available documents show that New York-based Oscar Health was one.
In an August earnings call with analysts and investors, CEO Mark Bertolini said the company was reviewing the files and that "there are a number of cases where we've actually had contact" with people on the list. In other words, the company reached enrollees CMS had targeted over fraud concerns.
He did not specify how many it had reached. The company declined to comment for this article because it is in a voluntary "quiet period," when publicly traded companies limit disclosing information before the release of an earnings report.
Still, in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Oscar Health estimated that 250,000 to 300,000 of its members might be disenrolled because of the CMS effort. Nationally, the company had about 3 million members in the second quarter and reported strong profits.
Overall ACA enrollment has declined sharply, falling by nearly 3 million in the first few months of the year, due in large part to the expiration at the end of last year of the enhanced subsidies. The Trump administration has also taken some credit, saying its focus on weeding out improper enrollments and other changes, such as eliminating a special year-round low-income enrollment period, led to the decline.
CMS has also suspended some brokers for improper activity and barred new brokers from enrolling clients in ACA insurance on the federal exchange during the upcoming open enrollment period.
CMS did not respond to requests for data on the reasons it canceled enrollments. What percentage of enrollees were deemed ineligible due to incorrect income reporting or because they had other health coverage, such as through their jobs? How many because their ACA applications lacked immigration documents or Social Security numbers?
"Currently, there is no additional data to share," the agency's press office said.
But people outside the administration have been vocal.
"This was clearly phantom enrollees," said Paragon's Blase. He thinks more than 99% of the cancellations are of zero-premium coverage that people were signed up for by rogue call centers without their knowledge, or for people who don't exist at all.
Blase said the carriers had a big incentive to get hold of the enrollees because they would lose the subsidies they were being paid if the plans were canceled.
And for any people unfairly caught up, Blase and Trump administration officials say all they have to do to be reinstated is call the marketplace and provide their Social Security number or other missing information.
"Everyone has the political incentive for that process to be that easy," Blase said. "We're a month before the election."
But, as prior reporting has shown, it isn't always a quick process to get an ACA plan canceled or reinstated following an unauthorized sign-up or switch, even when a consumer discovers it themselves and reaches out to the marketplace.
Brokers and policy analysts note that some of the factors used to question enrollments — such as a plan's having no claims filed in a year — are not that unusual. Many people, for example, don't visit a doctor or hospital in a given year.
Insurers "want those healthy people in the insurance pool to help bring down the rates," said Ronnell Nolan, president and CEO of Health Agents for America, a trade group for health insurance agents. "We're against fraud, and CMS has allowed a lot of fraud to happen. But we don't want people who just didn't go to the doctor to be canceled."
And even with the outreach required by CMS, not everyone answers phone calls from unknown numbers or opens their mail or emails.
A recent marketing report found an average "open rate" on emails of 28.6%.
Policy experts also note that, while lack of a Social Security number on an ACA application could indicate a fake enrollee, it might also be an oversight, or the number might not be required, like for a child if the person applying is an adult who is not seeking coverage for the child.
"There will be legitimate people who don't have a claim or don't respond to an inquiry from an insurer," said Matthew Fiedler, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. "If the goal is to target fraudulent enrollment, what CMS did is better than tossing people at random, but is likely to miss the mark."

At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
- Published
At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.
More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition.
Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC.
The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris.
Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes".
Warning: This article contains distressing details
An English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances.
Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said.
"I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away."
"There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water."
Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels".
The school building had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak.
Earlier reports suggested the destroyed classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down.
There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.
It appears that when the roof of the top-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.
Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.
The school is on a very narrow street, meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals.
Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported the deaths of 32 children and a teacher while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead.
The police chief said the building was still "extremely dangerous" and urged people to move away.
The Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Faisal Karim Kundi, has ordered a safety audit of all schools in the province to "identify potential risks and ensure that immediate corrective measures are taken wherever necessary".
"We cannot allow the safety of our children to be compromised," he said.
Furious family members of deceased pupils accused the school of ignoring safety concerns. "Make an example of them, a lesson for all," Mohammad Zaman, a man who lost two nephews in the disaster, told Reuters news agency.
In June, fourteen children died after the roof of a private tuition centre near Lahore collapsed.
And in August, 14 newborn babies were killed by a fire that ripped through a neonatal unit at a hospital in the capital, Islamabad, which an inquiry found lacked fire alarms and sprinklers.

How to fix scaling and app size issues on your Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
If you have trouble getting apps to scale properly on your foldable, read on.
The extra screen real estate that comes with the design of a foldable phone can be pretty enticing. Whether you're looking to play games, watch videos or read, a foldable offers more room for your favorite activities. But the expanded space can also complicate how apps adapt to a device that changes the aspect ratio of its screen depending on how it's being used.
Samsung unveiled the Galaxy Z Fold 8 at its Unpacked event in July. The phone's App Continuity feature lets you switch between the displays without interruption. But now, some owners are running into issues with apps that may not scale correctly to their phone's internal 4:3 display. They're even convening on various forums to discuss potential fixes in order to get the most out of the foldable screen experience. Here's how to fix scaling and app issues on your Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8.
How to adjust apps' aspect ratios
Though many apps are designed to work across the different screen sizes you might find among phones and tablets, they might not automatically adjust to the Galaxy Z Fold 8's inner screen. Fortunately, there's a way to change an app's aspect ratio on an individual basis, according to SamMobile. Aspect ratio refers to the proportional relationship between the width and height of something like a video or image. For example, a square (which has equal sides) would have a 1:1 aspect ratio.
When you unfold your Galaxy Z Fold 8, go to Settings > Display > Aspect ratio. (Depending on your One UI sub-menu, you might also navigate there through Settings > Apps.) From that screen, you can pick the app you want and then select either full screen, 4:3 or 16:9. That screen also notes that apps you have running in the background might need to restart once you've changed their aspect ratio. Whatever you select will become the default aspect ratio for how the app opens.
Another way to adjust your apps' aspect ratios
An additional way to accomplish this is by pressing and holding the app icon, and tapping the small info button on the top right. Tap on App aspect ratios, and from there you can also pick which aspect ratio you want to set as the default. Even after setting your preferred aspect ratio, an app might not perfectly scale to the screen. Some have reported awkward positioning or cropping on the screen if the app itself hasn't been optimized.
Still, Engadget's review of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 praised the main screen's 4:3 ratio, in part for how it cuts down on the letterboxing around widescreen content compared to the more square internal screen on previous Galaxy Z Fold models. The improved screen may be worth the trade-off of dealing with apps occasionally misbehaving.

For more than a year, a claim has spread that Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its embassies released a message warning about a website called "lionnights," which supposedly seeks to locate and harm Israelis and Jewish people overseas.
On Oct. 7, one social media user posted a version of the alleged message on X (archived), saying it came from Israel's embassy in the Netherlands:
Please share this with your Jewish networks. The Israeli Embassy has asked us to share the following message with the community:
Dear friends,
Right now, a website is circulating that claims to help Jews living abroad:
https://lionnights
This website collects information about Jewish and Israeli families abroad and invites people to "host Jews and Israelis."
There is a serious suspicion that this site is operated by hostile entities seeking to identify and harm Jewish and Israeli families.
Under no circumstances should you provide personal information on this website!
Stay away and spread this message: do not use this site and rely only on official channels of the Israeli government, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and its embassies.
Snopes readers contacted us about the claim as the message also circulated on Facebook and Threads.
It is unclear, as of this writing, where the alleged warning about the "lionnights" website originated from. Such a website does not appear to be online at the time of publication, meaning Snopes could not independently verify claims it is attempting to collect location information from Israelis abroad.
Claims about the website date back to June 2025, meaning the warning could be outdated.
We contacted the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs to ask if it released the alleged warning message and, if so, when. We await a reply.
In the meantime, due to a lack of evidence regarding who sent out the alleged warning, we leave this claim unrated. It is unclear whether the website in question targets Israelis overseas with the intention to cause them harm.
Searches on Google, Yahoo and DuckDuckGo returned no examples of reputable news media outlets reporting on the "lionnights" website (archived, archived, archived).
The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has one archived snapshot for lionnights.com in July 2025. That site contained no information. We also searched Wayback Machine for snapshots for lionnights.net, .il and .org but found no captures. Archive.today has several snapshots for lionnights.net but all lead to archived error pages.
Five examples of social media posts attribute the warning to the Israeli embassies in Germany, the Netherlands, the U.K., South Africa and the U.S. in June and July 2025 and October 2026 (archived, archived, archived, archived, archived).
However, it was not possible to locate the warning message on those embassies' own social media pages or websites. It is unlikely embassies would have asked community groups to share a message the embassies did not share themselves.
Snopes attempted to reach out to the relevant embassies to ask if they shared the messages but we were not able to make contact.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) called for a Tricolour March on 16 October 2026. Police were deployed across Delhi, while CJP member Abhijit Dipke was picked up from his residence in Jhandewalan and Neha Bora was detained at Mandi House, both in Central Delhi (here, here, here).
Against this backdrop, a video showing a crowd marching with Tricolour flags is being shared on social media (here, here), claiming that it shows the Tiranga March organised by the Abhijeet Dipke-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) in Delhi on 16 October 2026. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows the Tiranga march called by the Abhijeet Dipke-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) in Delhi on 16 October 2026.
Fact: The viral video shows a protest march led by RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav near Gandhi Maidan in Patna, Bihar, on 19 August 2026. It is unrelated to the CJP’s Tiranga March in Delhi on 16 October 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to social media posts (here, here) from August 2026 mentioning that the visuals show a march organised by RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav in Patna, Bihar. This confirms that the video predates the CJP’s Tiranga March scheduled for 16 October 2026.
Based on this clue, a keyword search led us to reports stating that RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav led a protest march in Patna on 19 August 2026 towards Raj Bhavan. The protest was held over issues including question paper leaks, unemployment, and the alleged firing on student protesters in Siwan, Bihar.
We also geolocated the viral video and confirmed that the location shown in the clip is near Gandhi Maidan in Patna, Bihar. The comparison between the viral video and geolocation can be seen below.
To sum up, the viral video shows Tejashwi Yadav’s August 2026 protest march in Patna, not CJP’s Tiranga March in Delhi.

Police have filed an FIR against officials of Reliance Consumer Products, Reliance Retail, Blinkit and Hyperpure by Zomato after the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) seized food stock worth ₹48 lakh during a multi-district crackdown on sale of expired food products, an official said on Saturday.
The FIR, registered at the Shanti Nagar police station in Thane, names 10 persons including senior officials and employees associated with Reliance Consumer Products, Reliance Retail, Blinkit and Zomato Hyperpure, along with disposal agency operators and local suppliers.
The FIR was registered under relevant provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
Those named in the FIR include V. Subramaniam, Whole-time Director, Reliance Consumer Products Ltd, Ashok Kumar Singh, Reliance Consumer Products Ltd, Vijay Bhikaji Kharmale, Nominee, Reliance Retail Ltd and Nilesh Ramdasrao Deshmukh, Warehouse Manager, Reliance Retail Ltd.
The others include Arbinder Singh Dhinsa, Director, Blinkit Commerce, Deepak Singh, Blinkit Commerce, Abid Shaikh, Zomato Hyperpure, Babar Miya Ahmed Siddiqui, B K Dispose, Gulzar Abdul Khan, supplier, Chavindra, Bhiwandi and Abdul Mobin Khan, Discount Store, Bhiwandi.
FDA sources said the operation was conducted simultaneously at multiple locations in Thane and Pune districts between October 14 and 15.
The seized stock included products valued at over ₹24 lakh from a Bhiwandi-based disposal yard, around Rs 4.92 lakh from Reliance Consumer Products’ warehouse at Vadpe, and nearly ₹7.81 lakh from Zomato Hyperpure’s facility at Usatane.
The total seizure was valued at ₹48,09,924.
FDA’s preliminary investigation indicated that expired, damaged and customer-rejected food products meant for destruction were allegedly diverted through disposal agencies, unlicensed sorting yards and brokers before reaching retailers for sale to consumers, a source told PTI.

FDA officials also found discrepancies in disposal records, including mismatches in quantities and inconsistencies in consignor-consignee details.

It's probably tucked away in a drawer, stashed in your desk or nightstand, beneath chargers, stray cords, and pieces of paper you don't think you're supposed to throw out but probably will never need again.
You probably haven't thought about it since you put it there.
But Zach Griff's old phone is in his carry-on backpack.
Griff, a travel expert and author of the travel newsletter From the Tray Table, estimates that he flies an average of 150,000 miles a year. And for the past 11 years, he said, he's carried his retired cellphone with him around the world.
Why you should always travel with 2 phones
Your old phone won't take up much space in your carry-on, and if something happens to your current one, it may be the most important item you pack.
"Your phone is the one thing you need to stay connected," Griff told Business Insider. "And the last thing I need when I'm traveling is to try to find a new phone."
Griff said he came to this realization in 2015 while on a safari in the Serengeti with his wife, Jill. They were staying at a remote lodge when Jill cracked her phone and damaged the camera. In the presence of elephants, giraffes, and lions, Jill couldn't snap a single picture.
Right about now, you may be thinking, "Why not just bring a camera?" I say go for it, but it won't fit as easily in your carry-on. And it won't help you if your phone gets lost or breaks.
"That was the time when I was like, 'From now on, I'm bringing a spare phone every single time,'" Griff said about the safari trip.
In over a decade of travel, Griff has only used his backup phone as a replacement once.
"We were in Paris, and I was walking near the Eiffel Tower, taking pictures at one of the overlooks," Griff said. "It was so crowded, I was worried about pickpockets, so I was fumbling things around, and then it happened."
While attempting to slide it back in his pocket, Griff dropped his phone on the ground. A crack ran across the top of the screen, disabling Face ID, but the phone was otherwise functioning just fine, he said. He decided to switch to the backup phone anyway to make the rest of his trip easier.
So far, Griff hasn't needed his backup phone to maintain contact while traveling. But if he ever does, he won't stay disconnected for long.

Online travel aggregator ixigo swung to a consolidated net profit of ₹63.4 Cr in the September quarter of FY27 from a loss of ₹3.5 Cr a year earlier, helped by an exceptional gain linked to the sale of part of its stake in Freshbus.

Police in New Delhi detained scores of protesters on Saturday as thousands of officers and paramilitaries patrolled India’s capital, metro stations were shut and mobile internet suspended to guard against a youth protest demanding India’s chief election officer quit.
The protest, called by the “Cockroach” youth movement, hopes to draw thousands of demonstrators who want the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to quit over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party.
Television images showed police in the city’s central business district chasing down a few dozen young protesters, before they were loaded into vehicles and taken away.
About 200 protesters were detained in the area, a police source told Reuters. Those detained outside Delhi included protest supporter Dhruv Rathee, a popular figure on YouTube, a police spokesperson said.
Touted by organisers as a protest to “save democracy”, it aims to be the biggest of the demonstrations that were launched last week after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s deputies had questioned and disagreed with him over the revision process that saw about 130 million voter names removed.
Opposition parties have long alleged the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage.
Kumar has not commented. The election commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.
The BJP says Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth are some of the reasons for its electoral dominance and that opposition parties are misleading the country because they are unable to win elections.
Near daily protests by opposition groups pose a new political challenge to Modi, just months after similar demonstrations forced his education minister to quit over exam paper leaks.
It also comes months before a series of important state elections starting in early 2027, including in the BJP-ruled most populous state of Uttar Pradesh.
The protesters, led by the self-named Cockroach Janta party, that began as an online satire, said they would gather at Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning – a site designated for protests by authorities in the heart of New Delhi.
Delhi police said on Friday they had not given permission for the protest because the request did not come on time, adding that CJP had violated undertakings given during previous protests, and that authorities had to enforce the law and maintain peace.
Police said protesters would face the force of the law if they violated the ban.
Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders rejected the police decision and said they would go ahead with the protest.
Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi. However, the supreme court on Friday said some trains must still run and there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.
“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” the CJP chief, Abhijeet Dipke, said on X.
“Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.”
Mobile internet services in a radius of 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area were ordered suspended from Friday night to Saturday night, ANI news agency reported citing a government order.
The CJP has said “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.
Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions.

What is the star button for on your Roku remote?
Roku's remote is straightforward, except for its multi-purpose star button.
A Roku system's remote control is one of the most straightforward remote designs you'll find. The function behind nearly every button is clear from its icon, except for one: the mysterious star button that lurks above the fast forward button. Whether you're using the physical remote or the remote in the Roku mobile app, you're going to encounter it — but what is it for?
Its purpose isn't as cut and dry as something like the OK or Netflix button, because its usage is contextual depending on when you press it. It's essentially a mix of an "options" button and accessibility shortcut, with some functionality depending on whether you have a Roku TV or one of the company's streaming boxes. Once you know all the scenarios where you can utilize it, you'll be able to improve several facets of your Roku watching experience.
Everything the Roku star button can do
What the star button does is dependent upon where you are on your Roku device. Let's consider the three major ones.
On the home screen
When you're on the Roku home screen, the star button's functionality depends on whether you're in the Quick Access section or the general app selection screen. In Quick Access, hitting star while an app is highlighted will only give you the option to remove it from the section; in the full apps list you'll have more options.
When you have an app highlighted there, pressing the star will show you the app's version and build number, let you move the channel's positioning or remove it, rate the app, give feedback or check for app updates. On a Roku TV, if you highlight an external device like a video game console, you'll be given the option to rename it.
When watching something
If you're actively streaming video on your Roku TV, the star button opens a host of viewing options in a sidebar. Here, you can improve your Roku's image quality, set a sleep timer, turn on closed captioning, change the volume mode and much more. The specific options will vary slightly from app to app based on their capabilities, but in general, this is the place to precisely tailor your viewing experience. On a Roku streaming box, this menu won't hold as many options as a Roku TV does.
As an accessibility shortcut
Some Roku devices support a text-to-speech screen reader (formerly called Audio Guide), an accessibility feature that helps navigation. This feature is currently only available in the United States. Roku devices that support the screen reader include:
- Roku TV
- Roku Streambar and Streambar Pro
- Roku Smart Soundbar
- Roku Express and Express+
- Roku Express 4K and 4K+
- Roku Streaming Stick and Streaming Stick+
- Roku Streaming Stick 4K and 4K+
- Roku Premiere and Premiere+
- Roku Ultra and Ultra LT
Though the screen reader can be activated via the accessibility settings menu, you can also toggle it by quickly pressing the star button four times in a row. To adjust controls like the precise speech rate and volume of the screen reader, you'll need to go to the Accessibility category of the Settings page, but the star button allows you to activate the feature without venturing into menus.

Islamabad, Oct 18: Pakistan has extended its airspace ban on Indian-registered aircraft and planes owned, operated or leased by Indian airlines for another month, until November 24, according to the country's airports authority.
The restriction, initially imposed on April 23, 2025, has been extended periodically since then amid strained relations between the two neighbouring countries.
The Pakistan Airports Authority (PAA) announced the extension in a post on X on Saturday, saying the restriction also covers military flights.
The latest extension will remain in effect until 4:59 am (local time) on November 24, 2026, according to the authority.
A PAA spokesperson said a fresh Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) had been issued to extend the ban, Geo News reported.
Pakistan’s airspace is divided into two flight information regions (FIRs) -- Karachi and Lahore, according to a Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority (PCAA) document from 2022. The latest NOTAM applies to both the Karachi and Lahore FIRs.
India and Pakistan imposed reciprocal airspace restrictions on each other's aircraft following the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack in the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir.
India accused Pakistan of involvement in the attack, an allegation Islamabad denied. The incident was followed by a sharp escalation in diplomatic and military tensions between the two countries.
India closed its airspace to Pakistani airlines on April 30, 2025, in response to Pakistan's move.
Pakistan has imposed airspace restrictions on Indian aircraft during previous periods of heightened tensions, including the 1999 Kargil conflict and the 2019 Pulwama crisis, according to Geo News.
The continuing airspace restrictions have affected airline operations between the two countries, forcing carriers to take longer routes on some international flights.

Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories.
Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform, for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win.
This summer, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates.
Even odder? “Nearly all of it—about $284 million—came from pairs of accounts repeatedly buying and selling with each other,” says former Polymarket trader Chris Park, who now runs the prediction-market forensic analysis firm MSR Decode.
Such a high volume of seemingly pointless back-and-forth transactions has raised eyebrows among experts. “It's obviously some form of volume manipulation,” says Rajiv Sethi, a Barnard College economics professor who researches prediction markets.
When asked about these markets, Shana Bautista, Polymarket’s head of global intelligence and investigations, told WIRED that the team “immediately flagged this activity, investigated, and blocked the accounts from trading.” Polymarket did not respond to follow-up questions about why the accounts were able to trade such a high amount of volume before it took action.
The timing of these trades made things even weirder. Polymarket’s rules stipulated that the Ethiopia market would be resolved in October after the prime minister was formally appointed and sworn in, which meant that it stayed open for several months after Ahmed’s victory was all but a foregone conclusion. For 123 days after the election, bursts of seemingly irrational trading continued, prompting Polymarket users to leave comments like “THIS NOT RESOLVED?” and “fuckkkk.”
Sethi calls the phenomenon a “zombie market,” where people can buy and trade on events that have already taken place or are no longer happening.
Another market about a 2024 election in Romania facilitated what Sethi described as “even more dramatic” trading anomalies. The initial election was called off due to fears about foreign interference. A new race was held several months later, but instead of closing the original market in the meantime, Polymarket kept it running alongside the new option.
It was during this period that Sethi first noticed something weird appeared to be happening with the older market. An algorithm Sethi and his colleagues created to flag potential wash trading on Polymarket identified nearly all of the volume as suspicious. “99.6 percent of volume in this market for certain weeks has been wash trading,” Sethi says.
Wash trading is a type of market manipulation in which accounts repeatedly buy and sell assets to create the illusion of heavy trading activity, when in reality, money is simply moving back and forth. It’s banned on regulated financial exchanges in the United States and is specifically prohibited in Polymarket’s terms of service. An earlier study conducted by Sethi and colleagues found evidence of widespread wash trading on Polymarket’s offshore platform.
Wash trading could explain what happened with the Ethiopian and Romanian political markets, but because the identities of the traders is unknown, uncertainty remains. “What appears to be wash trading isn't always wash trading,” says Sethi.
MSR Decode ran an analysis of the Ethiopian market for WIRED, which found that the most likely explanation for the anomalous trading is “activity farming,” which is when people try to artificially inflate their trading volumes. The firm suspects that traders may have been interested in boosting their volume because they believed that they could benefit if Polymarket launched a cryptocurrency token. In 2025, Polymarket chief marketing officer Matthew Modabber told the hosts of a crypto-themed podcast that there “would be a token” but did not provide specifics. Sethi also finds it plausible that traders could be motivated by potential “token allocation” to higher-volume accounts.
This type of behavior has been observed before in the cryptocurrency industry. “These are textbook examples on how market participants farm a potential airdrop,” says Andre Guettler, the director of Ulm University’s Institute of Strategic Management and Finance, who researches the structure of prediction markets.
When MSR Decode analyzed the Ethiopian election market, it found that it was highly unlikely that the trading volume could be attributed to sophisticated traders using algorithms to eke out profits. It analyzed over 38,000 “trade loops” that took place after the election (instances where individual wallets bought and sold to each other in quick succession) and found that over 98 percent resulted in neither side losing or gaining money. The median time that the accounts held onto the contracts they purchased before selling them again was nine seconds.
These types of unusual trading patterns are not a new phenomenon on Polymarket. Earlier this year, Barron’s reported that much of the activity on markets predicting the 2028 US presidential election centered on unlikely candidates such as Elon Musk and New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, neither of whom is eligible to run because they were born outside of the country.
Both Polymarket and its chief rival, Kalshi, have been publicly scrutinized for unusual market activity in recent months. Furor over suspicious activity on its recently launched perpetual futures market for cryptocurrency grew so intense on X that Kalshi published a blog post denying allegations of wash trading on it. (Sethi agrees with Kalshi that the allegations were unfounded. He argues that the unusual volume could instead be explained by Kalshi’s incentives for market makers, which create opportunities for other traders to profit from small price discrepancies.)
Polymarket recently raised an over $1 billion round of funding led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. The company is now valued at an estimated $21 billion, and earlier this summer, it announced that its annualized revenue was now over $1 billion. Polymarket’s explosive growth is often measured in volume traded, since it’s a metric that can point to how active users are.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets in the United States, declined to comment on whether it is looking into these election trades. The CFTC previously investigated a number of suspected instances of market manipulation on Polymarket, including several exclusively reported by WIRED, but they usually involved potential insider trading rather than wash trading or other suspicious activity.
In the past, the agency has issued hefty fines for wash trading in other sectors. “It seems to me that the CFTC would want to know about weird activity in a very large market,” a former CFTC employee tells WIRED.

CJI Surya Kant inaugurates permanent Ladakh Bench in Leh
CJI Surya Kant inaugurated the permanent Ladakh Bench at a ceremonial sitting in Leh. The bench will reduce travel costs and improve judicial access across the Union Territory.
A ceremonial bench of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh was held in Leh on Sunday to mark the inauguration of its Ladakh Bench by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
The new bench is aimed at bringing justice closer to the people of the Union Territory. The ceremonial sitting was presided over by Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, an official spokesman told PTI.
The sitting was attended by High Court judges Justice Sanjeev Kumar, Justice Sindhu Sharma, Justice Rajnesh Oswal, Justice Sanjay Dhar, Justice Mohd Akram Chowdhary, Justice Rahul Bharti, Justice Moksha Khajuria Kazmi, Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal, Justice Rajesh Sekhri, Justice Mohd Yousuf Wani, Justice Sanjay Parihar, Justice Shahzad Azeem and Justice Yash Paul Bourney.
Addressing the ceremonial bench, Justice Bhati said the establishment of the Ladakh Bench fulfilled a decades-long aspiration for accessible, inclusive and equitable justice.
He said people in Ladakh had long faced difficult terrain, harsh weather and substantial travel expenses while pursuing cases in Srinagar and Jammu. A permanent bench would ensure that geographical isolation did not result in exclusion from the justice system, he said.
Justice Bhati thanked the Chief Justice of India for his leadership and acknowledged the efforts of the Union government, the Ministry of Law and Justice and the Union Territory administration in establishing the bench within a short period.
He also stressed the responsibility of the bench and the bar to uphold constitutional values, protect the rights of vulnerable sections and preserve Ladakh's fragile environment. He said he hoped the Ladakh Bench would uphold fairness, truth and timely justice for future generations.
Vishal Sharma, Deputy Solicitor General of India for the Jammu Wing, said the establishment of the bench reaffirmed the constitutional promise of accessible justice, strengthened the rule of law and brought constitutional remedies closer to the people.
Tahir Majid Shamsi, Deputy Solicitor General of India for the Srinagar Wing, spoke about the development of judicial institutions in Ladakh since 2019. He said regular judicial sittings, digital facilities and legal aid would considerably reduce the difficulties faced by people pursuing cases.
Leh Bar Association president Gonbo Stobgyal said the occasion fulfilled a long-standing aspiration of Ladakh's people and assured the bar's full cooperation in the administration of justice.
Kargil Bar Association president Reyaz Ahmad Khan called the establishment of the Ladakh Bench a historic milestone and acknowledged the sustained efforts of the judicial leadership to bring justice closer to the people.
The full court also adopted a resolution stressing the need to improve access to education and provide safe, accessible and affordable residential facilities for girl students in Ladakh, particularly those from remote and far-flung areas.
Recognising the challenges posed by geographical remoteness, long travel distances and inadequate accommodation, the court called for greater legal awareness and coordinated efforts by educational institutions, legal services authorities and other stakeholders to ensure equal educational opportunities.
The resolution requested the Regular Bench to take further action in the matter, the spokesman told PTI.
The inauguration of the permanent Ladakh Bench is intended to reduce the travel and financial burden on people pursuing cases while improving access to judicial services across the Union Territory.

This week, Snopes received emails and searches from readers asking if U.S. President Donald Trump's administration chopped down 430 trees last weekend at East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C., the same site where Trump planned to renovate the East Potomac Golf Links property.
Earlier this year, the Trump administration revealed visual plans to overhaul the property into a championship-style golf course. Then, Trump announced on Truth Social that work on the golf course would begin in September. The DC Preservation League filed a lawsuit challenging the project, with District Court Judge Ana Reyes presiding over the case.
One reader asked us via email, "Did the Trump administration order removal of 430 trees from the East Potomac Golf Links?" People shared the claim on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Threads (archived) and other social media platforms.
In sum, the claim that the Trump administration cut down and planned the removal of 430 trees from the same park where planned golf course renovations will take place is true. 
A memorandum opinion that Reyes authored on Tuesday, in which she granted an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order in the DC Preservation League's case against the Interior Department, confirmed the tree cutting was taking place. That order blocked the Trump administration from continuing the work for two weeks, through Oct. 26.
Reyes' opinion, arriving one day after an emergency hearing on Monday, specifically mentioned the suddenness of crews cutting down 430 "healthy, non-invasive" trees, with the government only notifying the court minutes prior to close of business on a holiday weekend. She also noted the Trump administration argued the removals aligned with recommendations in a 2019 National Park Service report, leading Reyes to write she was "skeptical" of the timing. More about that report appears later in this article.
Snopes' email correspondence with the Interior Department, in which a department spokesperson appeared to indirectly acknowledge that crews cut down hundreds of trees with no reasonable notice to the court, also appears later in this article. We emailed the park service, an agency the Interior Department oversees, and the White House, as well as the DC Preservation League to ask for additional documentation and a statement, and will update this article if we receive further information.
430 trees cut down with very little notice
Reyes' opinion, handed down on Tuesday, laid out the timeline of events:
- Tree-cutting plans began internally within the Interior Department at least early last week.
- The government provided unreasonable notice to the court (at 4:55 p.m. last Friday) of its plans to remove "up to 529 trees" to restore the golf course's "historic links-style character."
- Tree-cutting work began 15 hours later at 8 a.m. on Saturday.
- An emergency hearing occurred the following Monday — on Columbus Day, a federal holiday.
During the Monday hearing, Reyes reportedly said she was "furious" that the government told the court they knew of the tree-cutting plans at least days earlier than they notified the court. In May, she told the government she wanted to receive notice if crews planned to remove more than 10 trees, the Associated Press reported.
An NBC4 Washington journalist reported, "In all of my years of covering court proceedings, I have never seen a judge so angry," adding Reyes was "raising her voice" at government attorneys.
Reyes wrote in the opinion:
The Government then did precisely what Plaintiffs feared. Sometime between the September 3 hearing and October 2, plans moved from removing only hazardous, dead, dying, or invasive trees to removing hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees. And then it removed them without providing meaningful notice to Plaintiffs or the Court.
Reyes wrote that Trump administration lawyers said the Interior Department "ordered, considered and approved" a plan for the park service to oversee the cutting down of hundreds of trees, as well as that the government said it knew of no reason for any urgency to complete the work. She said the administration acknowledged in court that crews cut down 430 nonhazardous trees, adding that "about 300 additional trees are on the literal chopping block" but weren't yet fallen thanks to a "rain delay." (A tally of well over 700 targeted trees exceeded the "up to 529 trees" part of the notice Reyes said the government provided.)
Journalists live-posting from Reyes' courtroom on Monday documented the administration's mention of chopping down 430 nonhazardous trees and planning to cut 299 more — out of the park's roughly 3,800 total trees.
We emailed Riverbend Tree Service in Virginia, a company with crews that appeared in a local news video report, to ask if its workers were present and when they first learned of the job, among other questions, and will update this story should we receive details.
Interior Department response, 2019 plans
In an email to Snopes, an Interior Department spokesperson chided Reyes for her involvement with the case and didn't directly respond to our request to confirm the department ordered and approved the removal of hundreds of trees with very little notice. The email appeared to only indirectly confirm the tree-removal work.
The department spokesperson described the current state of the golf course as "riddled with garbage and choked by overgrown trees" and that "the work carries out a plan, seven years in the making, to address tree overgrowth" at the park.
Reyes wrote that the government claimed the tree-cutting work, referenced as a Tree Management Plan (TMP), applied to a Cultural Landscape Report the park service authored during Trump's first term in 2019, and had "nothing to do with" Trump's golf course plans. She continued, "The Court is skeptical," and wrote:
The Government claims that the TMP implements a 2019 Cultural Landscape Report and has nothing to do with the Washington National Plan. It is a coincidence, the Government seems to suggest, that DOI cut down hundreds of trees at the Course weeks after the President asked DOI to cut down trees at the Course, and not, say, any other time in the last seven years.
That 2019 report credited golf course architect Walter J. Travis with designing "the original links-style, eighteen-hole course" in 1917 and emphasized retaining the character and history of the property. One part of the report said the early design of East Potomac Park Golf Course (EPPGC) originally largely lacked trees:
Links–style courses typically have very few trees and shrubs. Too many trees would interfere with the characteristic views and ever–present wind.
At EPPGC there were some trees originally, but overwhelmingly the property was treeless allowing for views across the golf course and to the surrounding water. Many trees have grown up within the course due to lack of maintenance, creation of dumping areas, and aggressive planting without regard to the history or function of the golf course. Trees and understory will have to be managed in order for EPPGC to return to its links character.
The Interior Department's email response to Snopes featured three attached images allegedly showing glimpses of a large garbage problem at the park. We followed up to ask if the images showed debris from Trump's White House East Wing demolition, seeing as crews reportedly began dumping debris from the construction site of Trump's ballroom project on the golf course last October. A department spokesperson denied it with a one-word answer: "No."
For further reading, we previously reported about a similar rumor alleging Trump ordered the removal of cherry trees from the same park, the site of the nation's first cherry blossom planting. Reyes' opinion didn't mention anything about the removal of cherry trees.

Restaurant chain Burma Burma’s parent entity, Hunger Pangs Limited, saw its net loss skyrocket nearly 31X to ₹15.4 Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26) compared to ₹50 Lakh in the previous fiscal year. According to its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP), the restaurant chain’s revenue from operations also zoomed 46.6% to ₹155.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹106.1 Cr in FY25. Including other income of ₹1.5 Cr, Burma Burma’s total income stood at ₹157 Cr in FY26. On the operational front, the restaurant chain’s EBITDA also climbed 20.2% to ₹25.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹21.4 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Besides its FY26 financials, the DRHP also shed light on the company’s Q1 FY27 numbers. Burma Burma’s parent reported a net profit of ₹1.1 Cr in the quarter under review against an operating revenue of ₹53.7 Cr. Given total expenses of ₹55.2 Cr during the quarter, what helped the company mint a profit in Q1 FY27 was ₹1.98 Cr in deferred tax credits. Burma Burma also reported an EBITDA profit of ₹11.4 Cr in the quarter ended June 2026, while the EBITDA margin stood at 21.3%. Founded in 2013 by Ankit Gupta and Chirag Chhajer, Hunger Pangs operates premium casual restaurant chain Burma Burma, which serves vegetarian Burmese cuisine. It competes with the likes of brands such as Mainland China, Mamagoto, Yum Yum Cha, and Berco’s. At the end of July 2026, it operated 22 restaurants across nine cities, including Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kolkata, and Delhi NCR. After raising $4 Mn at a valuation of over $50 Mn earlier this year, the hospitality chain has now filed its DRHP with markets regulator SEBI. Its proposed IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹150 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 2.8 Cr shares. Of the fresh IPO proceeds, Burma Burma plans to use ₹117.3 Cr to open 27 new company-owned outlets by FY29. The remaining capital will be used for general corporate purposes. Notably, Hunger Pangs disclosed in its DRHP that it plans to launch a new brand. “We have conceptualised a premium casual dining chain of Japanese restaurants and noodle shops, with influences of Buddhist traditions,” read the document. Where Did Burma Burma Spend In FY26? In line with its revenue growth, Burma Burma’s spending also saw a major uptick. The company’s total expenses zoomed 61.8% YoY to ₹175.8 Cr in FY26. Let’s dive deeper into the company’s expenditure. Employee Benefits Expenses: Representing the company's largest cost head, Burma Burma’s personnel costs surged 53.3% YoY to ₹50.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹33.1 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Cost Of Materials Consumed: Burma Burma spent ₹30.4 Cr on raw materials and kitchen supplies in the fiscal under review, 51% higher than ₹20.1 Cr in FY25. Finance Cost: The restaurant chain’s interest and borrowing-related expenses grew 70% YoY to ₹6.6 Cr in the year under review. Other Expenses: Spending under this line item also grew 54.6% YoY to ₹48.8 Cr in the fiscal year ended March 2026.

Early 1900s India was a place where your gender determined what you could be in life. That nation could not stomach the thought of, trivial as it was, common as it is today, a woman pursuing the sciences. This antediluvian thought though, this kind of restriction was only the cause of a temporary disruption Mary Poonen Lukose’s path to glory.
It is inescapable irony that India’s first woman Surgeon General Mary Poonen Lukose was not allowed to study science. Born in Ayamanam (incidentally, Arundathi Roy’s backdrop in the God of Small Things) in Kottayam in 1886, Mary was so bright, she topped the matriculation exam. Nevermind how bright she was, her gender was a disqualifier as Maharaja College in Tiruvananthapuram declined her admission to the sciences. Only a temporary detour, Mary went on to get a degree in history, becoming the first woman from Travancore to graduate from Madras University in 1909.
However, her family could afford to send her to London to pursue medicine, and she was the first Indian woman to graduate in Medicine from the University of London, according to an article published by Cambridge University Press (CUP) as part of a compendium of Modern Asian Studies. She earned an MBBS from the University of London in 1915, trained in obstetrics and gynaecology, and studied paediatrics at Great Ormond Street Hospital.
Reports of her life, rendered through an autobiographical account, Trailblazer, released in 2020, record Mary as working hard in Dublin at the Rotunda Hospital, coping with the increasing work load created by the outbreak of World War 1 in 1914. When her mentor and guide, her father passed away in 1916, Mary was shattered; she had to take a call on whether she would continue in England or come back home to serve her people. She, of course, decided to come home and blazed a path of glory, only long forgotten. She returned to Travancore in 1916 as its first woman doctor.
The CUP article further quotes from an autobiographical note penned by Mary herself: “In her autobiographical essay, Mary Poonen Lukose reflects on her decision to become a doctor. She traces it to her early experiences helping out in hospitals where her father worked as a doctor, and to his example and influence on her. ‘As I grew up, he made it a point to instill into me the spirit of service to humanity.’
The article further notes that the style of her 1916 job application, her requests for references, and the correspondence surrounding it suggest that she was aware of the fact that her qualifications were exceptional for an Indian woman of her time.
Mary Poonen Lukose went on to build the scaffolding of modern public health in Travancore, one that can be attributed to the many advances that Kerala has achieved today in health care indicators. Her work helped lay the ground for what we now celebrate as the “Kerala model” of health—fronting strong primary care, institutional childbirth, public health outreach, and unusually good social indicators. Acknowledging her contributions, in the 2018 budget speech, the finance minister of the State said, on record, in the House: ‘Dr. Mary Poonen Lukose is one of the most talented people in the development of Kerala’s health system.’
At the Women and Children Hospital in Thycaud, Mary worked as an obstetrician and superintendent, initiating daughters of local birth attendants into training midwifery, an attempt to subsume traditional midwifery into scientific deliveries and maternal care. Some historic references to her indicate she performed Travancore’s first Caesarean section before 1920, reportedly sometimes working only by the light of a hurricane-lamp light.
As Surgeon General from 1938, she was responsible for 32 government hospitals, 40 dispensaries, and 20 private institutions. In colonial era India, this could be notched up as a mega achievement for a woman, not only in health care, but also an administrator. Mary also founded a tuberculosis sanatorium in Nagercoil, and established the X-Ray and Radium Institute in Tiruvananthapuram.
It was not only for the issue of providing women adequate health facilities that she lent her voice, but was equally vociferous on women’s political rights. She herself, in 1922, was nominated to Travancore’s legislative council, becoming the State’s first woman legislator.
But Mary was a multi-splendored person, capable of achievements across sectors. As the nuns sing in the Sound of Music of Maria the reluctant nun: How do you catch a cloud and pin it down? Mary co-founded the Tiruvananthapuram branch of the Young Women’s Christian Association and served as its president for 50 years. She was also a member of two professional bodies, the Indian Medical Association and the Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India.
Many honours came her way, including the Vaidyaśāstrakuśala by the Maharaja of Travancore in 1935, and the Padma Śhri in 1975, just a year before her death at the age of 90.
Mary is part of a legacy of tall women in Indian health care that helped sculpt systems that are propping the nation up today, including Muthulakshmi Reddy, Kadambini Ganguly, and Anandi Joshi. They are the forebearers who chipped away at the glass ceilings that prevented them from rising, and cleared the ladder for women who came after them, though history has not given them their due space.
But it is now time for reparation, it is time to say their name loud. Say her name: Say Mary Poonen Lukose, so every one can hear, and celebrate.
