The irony was not lost on many. Around the same time as the internet in India’s national capital Delhi was shut down for several hours amid massive security and incessant protests, SpaceXAI chairman and founder Elon Musk waded into one of his quintessential Twitter feuds with the Indian government over Starlink and its satellite internet services. This time, his target was not just the Indian government. Musk took on Reliance Jio — and then Mukesh Ambani too — accusing the conglomerate of strong-arming the government into creating a monopoly when it comes to satellite internet or satcom services. He even called Ambani the Prime Minister of India. “Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license?” Musk posted, asking whether Ambani is the “real boss of India”. Out came the responses from all quarters of India. Reliance Industries rejected suggestions that it fears competition, saying it welcomes satellite broadband players, including Starlink, provided they follow Indian laws and policies. Reliance also pointed out that Jio’s satellite services are awaiting clearances. The Ministry of Communications, meanwhile, has denied allegations of unequal treatment. It said the authorisation framework is fair and non-discriminatory, and that Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb are at “broadly the same regulatory stage.” And then, Starlink responded to Reliance saying, “We have worked closely with regulators, industry and operators in India for 5+ years, and built a network of dedicated systems, gateways, and other infrastructure all in-country to exclusively serve Indian traffic safely and securely - and all with the requisite government approvals.” Everyone’s Waiting In The Queue The immediate question is what Starlink means by having the “requisite government approvals”. Its statement does not explicitly say that its security assessment is complete or that spectrum has been assigned. Those are separate steps from obtaining a satellite communications licence and an IN-SPACe authorisation, and they stand between the operators and commercial launch. The DoT has taken a similar line on the approval process. It said all three operators have received GMPCS licences and that security assessments remain underway. Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) is a satellite-based communication system that provides voice, data, fax, and messaging services directly to portable terminals anywhere on ground. The DoT added that spectrum assignment will follow once the relevant assessments are complete. So a licence does not, by itself, authorise a company to start commercial services. Operators must meet the conditions attached to their services, clear the security process and complete spectrum-related requirements. The dates of approvals have become part of the debate. Eutelsat OneWeb received its GMPCS licence in August 2021 and IN-SPACe authorisation in November 2023. Jio’s satellite communications arm received its GMPCS licence in March 2022. Starlink received its GMPCS licence in June 2025 and IN-SPACe authorisation in July 2025. However, this timeline does not tell the full story. According to a Financial Express report citing DoT records, Jio Satellite Communications Limited (JSCL) completed its security and technical compliance demonstration on March 20, 2025, while Eutelsat OneWeb conducted its demonstration in January 2025. Starlink’s demonstration took place only in early 2026. So if anything, OneWeb should be ahead of Starlink and Jio in the queue after the final assessments. Bharti Enterprises chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said OneWeb had applied for approval five years ago, its ground network had been ready for three years, and its satellites had been positioned over India for around five years. Mittal added OneWeb would be happy to receive approval “at least a few days before him .” The different timelines do not, on their own, establish that one company has been favoured or that others are being held back. They also do not explain what conditions remain outstanding or unfulfilled in each case. Therefore, the relevant questions are which requirements each operator has met, what is still pending and whether the same standard and timelines apply to all three players. This will help us get to the bottom of the questions that Musk has raised. The Regulator Takes Its Time Sohom Banerjee, a public policy and technology strategist and founder of Quantive Advisory LLP, said the delay raises questions about regulator predictability, but is not in itself proof of unequal treatment. A fair process, he argued, requires equivalent security standards, documented criteria, clarity on outstanding requirements and a defined next step for each applicant. Banerjee also cautioned against treating proposed timelines for one regulatory stage as deadlines for the entire process. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s suggested 30-day window for spectrum assignment and objections relates to a stage after prior in-principle network clearance. It should not be interpreted as a deadline for completing security assessments. The criteria for security assessment are not open for public discussion or consultation, but given that internet services are critical not just for civilian use but also defence infrastructure, experts presume that such assessments may not necessarily take the same time for each applicant. The approval process involves four distinct steps: a GMPCS licence, IN-SPACe authorisation, security assessment and spectrum assignment. Conflating them and calling this a single approval is what complicates the narrative. Starlink May Be Ready, But Is That All It Takes? Starlink’s latest statement is a claim about its preparation and infrastructure, but this does not indicate anything about whether the Indian government has completed its diligence when it comes to the security assessment. While Starlink says it has built dedicated systems and gateways in India to serve Indian traffic, and that these have the requisite government approvals, this is not a guarantee of spectrum allocation. The distinction is also relevant to Reliance Jio. In its IPO papers, Jio Platforms identified satellite broadband as a potential competitor to JioFiber and JioAirfiber, particularly in areas where terrestrial networks are expensive or difficult to deploy. It also flagged that administrative allocation of satellite spectrum could give satellite operators a different cost structure from terrestrial telecom players that acquire spectrum through auctions. It’s imperative to understand the structure. Jio Satellite Communications Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of Jio Platforms, was incorporated in October 2021 to provide communications services, including satellite-based connectivity. It reported revenue from operations of ₹34.3 Cr in FY26 up from ₹10.7 Cr in FY25, against no revenue in FY24. The company reported ₹10.5 Cr for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. These figures relate to the subsidiary and should not be read as revenue from a launched retail satellite broadband service. The filings also identify uncertainties around the timing, approvals and competitiveness of Jio’s own satellite plans. The company therefore has a commercial stake in the rules governing satellite broadband, even as its services await clearance. And indeed, that has to be made amply clear: no company has launched satellite internet services in India yet. Banerjee said predictable regulation does not mean relaxing security checks. It means setting out the criteria, identifying the authority responsible for each decision and communicating what remains to be done. Security checks are central to satellite broadband because the operator controls parts of a communications network that may be used in strategically sensitive areas. The assessment needs to establish how India can retain oversight of network operations, access to sensitive information and service continuity. One could also argue that this is a cultural difference, that Musk is used to a different governance approach when it comes to such matters. A security clearance is part of the overall approvals in the US, for example, and not a separate process. Tarun Wig, cofounder and CEO of Innefu Labs, said foreign-controlled satellite networks can create risks around data sovereignty, service continuity and external control over critical communications infrastructure, particularly during conflicts. Starlink’s role in Ukraine has brought those concerns into focus, he said, though the circumstances there do not automatically mean India would face the same risks. Wig said India should have a security framework in place before these services launch. He pointed to data protection and localisation requirements where necessary, network security audits, encryption, lawful interception under Indian law, incident reporting and safeguards against unauthorised access and cyberattacks. Banerjee spoke on the operational control aspects of the security assessment. He believes that relevant checks could examine who can activate terminals, change routing or coverage, access sensitive network information and suspend services. Domestic control over key network functions, auditable access, terminal identification, restrictions in sensitive areas and clear incident-reporting processes likely also form part of the assessment. The commercial case for satellite broadband is clear in places where fibre and mobile networks are difficult or costly to extend. TRAI data for August 2026 recorded 48.63 Mn wired broadband connections and 19.34 Mn fixed wireless connections. Satellite services could help connect remote communities and businesses including mines, energy sites, schools and health centres. Their reach will depend on pricing, network capacity and the conditions attached to spectrum. The government’s position is that all three operators remain subject to the same security process. But to settle questions about delay and unequal treatment, it will need to make the next steps clearer: which requirements remain pending for each operator, who must sign off and what needs to happen before spectrum is assigned. Starlink says it’s ready to launch but is not being allowed to. Reliance says it doesn’t fear competition. OneWeb says it’s also waiting in the queue. Ultimately, no one has launched anything yet, so all of this seems more like a case of Musk’s impatience. Edited By Nikhil Subramaniam Creatives: Abhyam Gusai

Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken her vote for granted. That was, until it was suddenly taken away. She presented officials with her Indian birth certificate and family land documents from the village going back to 1962.
Both her parents had been on the electoral roll going back decades, so she showed proof of that too. But when the final revised voter list came out in April, Fakir was not on it.
The 38-year-old migrant worker, born into a poor Muslim family, was not alone. Since last year, 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – have been removed from India’s electoral roll through a process known as SIR, or special intensive revision. In the nearly eight decades since India’s independence, never have the voter rolls shrunk by such a huge amount over such a short time.
The Narendra Modi government has called SIR a legitimate exercise to clean up the electoral rolls. Overseen by the election commission, tens of millions of dead and duplicate names have been removed. Yet so have the names of millions of living Indian citizens.
Critics allege that the pledge to “purify” India’s voter roll of illegal immigrants has instead been used for more sinister purposes – disenfranchising tens of millions of Muslims, other minorities, and poor and lower caste communities, who are largely not BJP voters.
In a matter of weeks, nationwide anger at SIR has boiled up and spilled out on to the streets of India’s biggest cities, presenting a formidable challenge to the government. Over the weekend, Delhi was transformed into a high-security fortress of barricades, roadblocks and tens of thousands of police and paramilitaries who detained thousands of people, as they attempted to stop youth-led protests calling for the man who oversaw SIR, the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down immediately.
On Monday, opposition parties – who have decried SIR as a “weapon for vote theft” by the Modi government – drew tens of thousands of supporters as they marched through the capital and presented a petition to the supreme court, demanding Kumar’s resignation. The youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, who were behind the call for Saturday’s action, have vowed to “fight on” in their protests against SIR.
Opposition and civil society leaders allege that SIR has already given the BJP an electoral advantage in states such as Bihar and West Bengal, claims the party denied. Others say the exercise has had even more concerning implications: under changes to SIR unilaterally implemented by Kumar, the election commission has become the arbiter of Indian citizenship, a sweeping overreach of its remit.
The consequences are already playing out in West Bengal, where Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) recently came to power and began a crackdown on “illegal” immigrants, complete with several new detention centres. Civil society groups say Muslims excluded by SIR are being targeted.
Fakir was among them. Just three months after the voter list was published – and while her hearing to challenge her exclusion was pending – she was picked up by police and accused of being an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant.
In July she was pushed over the border to Bangladesh, a country she had never been to nor had any connection with, and remains stuck there. “I have all the documents to prove I am an Indian citizen,” she said in a tearful phone call from the Bangladesh border village where she has been sheltering. “I fell on their feet and begged the police not to send me to Bangladesh but they pushed me over the border.”
A Bangladesh border guard officer confirmed Fakir’s account. “We checked all her documents and are convinced that she is an Indian citizen,” they said. In September, her family submitted a petition to the supreme court challenging her deportation. The Indian government was given a month to respond.
“All I want is to return to my family and my home in India. I am waiting desperately for that day,” she said. The backlog of millions of voters in West Bengal challenging their exclusion means it could be years before Fakir’s case is heard.
Those across West Bengal who have been stripped of their votes speak of their terror of being accused of being an alien in their own land. Some have had benefits taken away. Mohammad Hedayet Ullah Siddiqui, 80, from the North 24 Parganas district, said his grandfather had been a freedom fighter for Indian independence and three generations of his family were on the voter rolls. Yet after SIR, Siddiqui described his “humiliation” on finding his name gone.
“With my name erased from the voter list, I am in constant terror. What if they send me to a detention camp?” he said. “I cannot bear to think about being separated from my children and grandchildren at this age, especially when all my ancestors have been buried in India.”
Critics say the problems began in 2023, when the Modi government changed the process for appointing the three-body election commission, giving majority control to the government for the first time. Within a matter of months, the Modi-led panel had appointed Kumar as the election commissioner in spite of opposition objections.
“For decades, the election commission was one of our more credible, independent bodies, but now that has been eroded,” said Ronojoy Sen, a senior fellow at the South Asian Studies Programme, National University of Singapore.
By the following year, the new election commission body had begun SIR, starting in Bihar, where it immediately raised concerns among human rights groups after more than 6 million names were removed. Not long after the revisions, the BJP won a landslide victory in the Bihar state elections.
Despite concerns over SIR rumbling on for months, it did not spark national protests until the Indian Express newspaper last month revealed that two members of the election commission had raised 14 objections to how voters were being excluded from the rolls, but they were unilaterally overruled by Kumar.
“India has always been a flawed democracy but at least citizens felt they had the right to vote and that elections were regular and fair,” said Sen. “SIR has taken away that right. From how it has been conducted, it’s difficult to see how the motive was anything other than to enhance the election prospects of the BJP.”
Three former election commissioners have openly criticised SIR as a “hostile exercise” that has undermined the sanctity of the country’s electoral rolls by focusing on the exclusion – rather than inclusion – of voters. OP Rawat, a former chief election commissioner, described changes to the voter registration form as “wrong and illegal”.
Ashok Lavasa, who was an election commissioner between 2018 and 2020, called for the SIR to be scrapped. “An unfair procedure has been imposed on millions of people in the country, and you have the judiciary which has validated that,” he said last month. “How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?”
None have been more vehement in their opposition than SY Qureshi, who was chief election commissioner between 2010 and 2012. “This is a national harassment exercise designed to throw Muslims off the electoral roll,” he claimed. “The only way to restore the credibility of India’s elections is to restore those deleted voters.”
The BJP has denied any political involvement or motive in the SIR process, accusing the opposition Congress party of “jealousy” over its recent electoral victories and saying any deleted voters can simply re-enrol. The BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the allegations were “disinformation” and part of an opposition campaign “being orchestrated to create an atmosphere of division and anarchy”.
Nonetheless, the election commission has appeared to accept some flaws in the process. Late last week, it belatedly put a cap on the number of voter deletion forms – which allow people to submit objections on behalf of others – after incidents in which people submitted thousands of forms targeting legitimate Muslim voters.
Public anger, meanwhile, has continued to build. In Delhi, where the SIR exercise left millions of people off the draft list, protests are expected to continue this week.
A Delhi resident for 30 years, Prashant Tandon, 60, said he could not believe it when a notice came to his door, questioning his life as a voter. “If someone doubts my citizenship, they should produce evidence against me,” he said furiously, adding that he would be protesting alongside the young people. “I should not have to prove that I am an Indian citizen.”

Hong Kong to review Peak lighting installation after outcry over felled trees
Tourism Board will review light trail project following public outcry over chopped flowers, trees and “eyesore” devices
Hong Kong tourism authorities have pledged to review the roll-out of a lighting project along a trail on The Peak after mounting complaints that flowers and trees were chopped down to make way for the installations.
But the Tourism Board defended the project, saying it had consulted local residents and sought advice from tree experts to minimise the impact on the surrounding environment.
In a statement on Sunday, the board said it valued residents’ views and would now “conduct broader consultation to review the overall arrangements of the project” to “refine its details, with a view to achieving a balance between tourism development, environmental protection and residents’ needs”.
Small light installations were planned for selected points along the walking trail to add new features to The Peak’s attractions.
They were originally intended to form part of a new light show staged alongside the coming Hong Kong WinterFest.

Blazes ignite at St. Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches more than 1,000 drones at Russia
Ukraine targets Russian oil sites, while Russia launches attacks on Zaporizhzhia
Ukrainian attacks set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday, as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments.
The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
One person was killed and five more were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at both the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, said local Gov. Alexander Beglov. A logistics centre belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data centre for local tech giant VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Meanwhile, a woman died and at least two other people were wounded, including a six-year-old girl, after Russia launched two attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia Saturday, local officials said.
A local man carries carries buckets of broken glass in front a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Oct. 17, 2026. (Kateryna Klochko/The Associated Press)
Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution were damaged as a result of the attack, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin said.
Russia continues energy attacks, Kyiv says
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Ukraine confirmed Thursday it had resumed attacks on Russian oil after a three-day hiatus.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia’s continuing aerial bombardment of his country’s energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump’s demand last Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government initially said that it was heeding the ceasefire.

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.
Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.
A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.
Police authorities didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.
The CJP said that among those detained was a group of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being taken away in a bus to an unknown location.
The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.
The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.
The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.
The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.
The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.
Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.
“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture student who attended the Bengaluru protest.
There were also protests over police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.
On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of using “brute force” to briefly detain party leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Vadra, and other lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.
Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.
BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.
Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

China has invited the now-ousted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia to visit the country again after she claimed that the Asian superpower lacked “proper toilets”.
The controversy began last week before Ms Zacharia was sacked by US president Donald Trump less than a week into her job.
Ms Zacharia was speaking in an interview with podcaster Jack Posobiec on Thursday when she took a jab at a country whose president had recently received a grand red-carpet welcome from Mr Trump.
Talking about the perception around 2016 that “the gold days, the glory days of the US were over and China was on the horizon”, she said: “I remember this very distinctly having just come from China, thinking, how is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets.”
On Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning responded to the comments, saying: “[We] welcome her to visit China more often when she has the opportunity.”
Ms Zacharia, a former spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, had started her new job as press secretary less than a week ago, after Karoline Leavitt left the administration earlier this year.
The White House said she was “uniquely qualified and whip-smart”. Before losing her job, she had been expected to travel to China with Mr Trump next month for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.
But those comments about Chinese toilets were by no means the biggest controversy of Ms Zacharia’s brief tenure as press secretary, which was dogged by scrutiny over her credentials as a lawyer. Earlier on Tuesday, she said that she passed the bar exam “when I moved to China” with her husband.
According to her LinkedIn, she worked at Zhong Lun Law Firm – one of the country’s biggest – from 2011 to 2013. But while Chinese law firms can hire foreign nationals, they cannot be licensed as lawyers in the country.
The Campaign for Accountability has filed a complaint with the State Bar of California demanding an investigation into her claims of being a advocate.
Ms Zacharia’s tenure will be remembered for a disastrous first press conference that lasted only 14 minutes and saw her take just three questions from reporters.
During her briefing on Tuesday, she announced that US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to resign. But she also mixed up her husband and President Trump, a gaffe that left even the most ardent MAGA Republicans wincing.
The final nail in Ms Zacharia’s press secretary coffin came during appearances on Fox News, where she told Trump’s pal Sean Hannity that the administration did not adequately prepare her, and then raised questions about the vetting process on Friday’s Fox & Friends.
Mr Trump told reporters on Friday afternoon that he had suggested Zacharia step aside. “I said to her honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider [her position],” he said.
She sets a new record for the shortest time served in the role by a White House press secretary or communications director, more than halving the 11-day record set during Mr Trump’s first term. In 2017, Mr Trump had fired Anthony Scaramucci after he gave an expletive-filled interview to a New Yorker reporter in which he badmouthed other senior White House aides.

The West Bengal government will set up a Special Investigation Team (SIT) headed by a sitting judge of the Calcutta high court to probe the stampede at a Durga Puja in Kolkata that has left 19 people dead so far, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari said, even as seven people were arrested.

The stampede occurred around 7.30pm on Saturday at Chor Bagan, one of the city’s most popular Durga Puja venues, in cramped north Kolkata, as crowds jostled through a narrow bylane on Saptami, the seventh day of the festival, even as rain lashed the city and left the streets slippery.

Kenya must be 'clean' to be credible, says Wada chief
- Published
Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility as it prepares to stage the 2029 World Athletics Championships, according to Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), .
Banka was speaking at the end of a three-day visit to Nairobi where he held talks with President William Ruto, government and sports officials, the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya (Adak), athletes and representatives of law enforcement.
Wada said the visit was intended to build on recent progress in Kenya's anti-doping programme at a critical time following Nairobi's selection to host the 2029 World Championships.
"Kenya calls itself probably 'home of champions', but every home has to have a good host and has to be clean to be credible," Banka told the BBC.
"We absolutely need to instill the culture of clean sport."
Kenya was awarded the 2029 championships in September, making it the first African country selected to host the event.
The decision has increased scrutiny of its efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem.
More than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit since 2017.
The Polish former sports minister said he had received a clear commitment from Ruto's government to a policy of zero tolerance towards doping, but warned promises would have to be matched by results.
"Wada will monitor this situation and observe the dynamic. Action speaks louder than words," he said.
Banka said his discussions with Ruto also focused on strengthening an independent Adak, and ensuring it has sufficient government support.
- How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships 
  - Published15 September
2029 will be the real test
Nairobi 2029 could provide a global test of Kenya's ability to protect its sporting legacy.
For a country whose distance runners have helped define global athletics for generations, the stakes extend beyond staging a successful championship.
"The problem with anti-doping is not with rules and standards," Banka said. "The problem is with implementation."
Another challenge is testing infrastructure.
Africa currently has no Wada-accredited doping control laboratory following the loss of accreditation of the facility in Bloemfontein, South Africa.
Wada initially suspended the laboratory in March 2024 because of multiple failures to comply with its International Standard for Laboratories.
Its accreditation was formally revoked in May 2025 after those problems were not satisfactorily resolved.
Banka said Kenya has shown political interest in establishing its own facility, but cautioned against expecting a laboratory to be accredited in time for the 2029 championships.
The process, he said, takes years because the consequences of laboratory error can be enormous for an athlete.
That leaves Kenya facing a more immediate priority: strengthening the system around testing rather than relying on a new laboratory as a solution.
'Doping has no colours and flags'
Banka also rejected the idea that doping should be viewed as an exclusively Kenyan, or African, problem.
"Doping has no colours and flags," he said, pointing to cases across established sporting nations including the United States, Germany and his native Poland.
"The problem would be to ignore this issue, not to tackle, or to pretend that there is no doping here."
Wada, he added, can investigate sport but cannot dismantle the criminal networks supplying prohibited substances.
"We are not a superpower. We are not law enforcement," he said.
"They have tools to really go after those who are destroying the credibility of the sport and the country."
He said intelligence indicated performance-enhancing drugs were being produced in Kenya and described Africa as a significant market.
According to him, athletes are often the "weakest points in the ecosystem", arguing that anti-doping authorities need to pursue not only competitors who break the rules but also the coaches, doctors, managers and suppliers who enable doping.
Some athletes, he suggested, are being exploited by people "who have money, who have power" and see them as a route to profit.

Trump’s plan to deport a member of Congress
The investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar just became more alarming.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump wants to deport a member of Congress.
What’s happening? On Monday, Homeland Security officers raided the Washington, DC, home of US Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) in an investigation reportedly tied to immigration paperwork filled out by her father when she was a minor.
That was, at the time, more than enough cause for alarm. Trump’s animosity toward Omar, who is Somali-American and an outspoken critic of the administration, is well-known, and the raid is an extraordinary violation of the Justice Department’s usual rule to avoid taking visible action around politically sensitive cases within 60 days of an election.
On Wednesday evening, however, we learned more about the raid from the Wall Street Journal. The Omar investigation, the Journal reported, is explicitly aimed at stripping Omar of her citizenship — and thus her ability to hold office — and deporting her.
How would they do that? Omar came to the US as a refugee when she was 12 and became a US citizen when she was 17. The Trump administration’s investigation is said to focus on whether she or her family misrecorded her age in order to more easily gain citizenship.
The government cannot unilaterally denaturalize a citizen, however; it would have to ask a court to do so.
What’s the context? Historically, it’s rare for the US to strip citizenship from naturalized US citizens. But doing so at volume has been a major, if less visible, priority for the second Trump administration.
As of earlier this year, NBC News reported, DOJ was targeting hundreds of people for possible denaturalization, and has reportedly hoped to put forward hundreds of new cases per month (though successfully stripping them of citizenship is another matter).
Why does this matter? Trump’s campaign to bend the traditionally nonpartisan DOJ into a tool to punish and harass his enemies has been one of the major stories of his second term.
Even if it never advances beyond Monday’s raid, an investigation targeting Omar’s citizenship with the eventual goal of deporting her from the US represents a new and even more dangerous evolution of that effort — and it threatens to move the US to a far darker place, where citizenship and the rights it guarantees are predicated on the president’s goodwill.

Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993
- Published
Rwanda has signed a 10-year deal with Formula 1 to host races in the African country, starting "in the early 2030s".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali and next to the city's new international airport. It will be the first F1 race in Africa since 1993.
A statement from F1 said the project came as a result of "years of collaboration to ensure the right foundations, with the best partner, are in place to deliver a successful, sustainable and world-class grand prix for generations to come".
The circuit, designed by the former F1 driver Alex Wurz, has been "designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans," the statement added.
F1 hopes the race will provide an opportunity for the sport to expand its profile in Africa, a relatively unexplored market compared to Europe, Asia and the Americas.
It has not yet been established where the race may best fit into the schedule during the year.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published7 hours ago
The sport is likely to want to avoid holding the race in the main rain season of March to May. There is a shorter, less disruptive rain season from October to November.
F1 is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: "For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement.
"Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.
"The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."
F1 president Stefano Domenicali said the new contract was "a landmark moment for F1", which would mean the sport was racing "on every inhabited continent".
Domenicali added: "Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."
Sportswashing controversy
The race is likely to lead to opposition from human rights groups accusing Rwanda of sportswashing, as has been the case with its sponsorship of Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa.
Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
A spokesperson for F1 said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."
The track's build process will be overseen by three companies, with long-time F1 track architect Tilke and DAR working alongside WurzDesign as the creator of the circuit.
It is designed to be fast and flowing, with significant elevation change, using the natural contours of Rwanda's hilly landscape.
The first grand prix in Africa was the final round of the World Championship in Morocco in 1958.
South Africa hosted a race during the apartheid era - from 1960-66 in East London, now known as KuGompo City, before the race moved to Kyalami near Johannesburg from 1976-85.
Kyalami returned for two races in 1992 and 1993 as apartheid was coming to an end.
The country has held talks with F1 in recent years about a return at various venues, including Kyalami and Cape Town, but a deal has not proved possible.

Toulouse denied Exeter Chiefs a famous Champions Cup victory in France, fighting back to win a frenetic pool game with 14 men following Rodrigue Neti's first-half red card.

"Who has done it? The police will find out first. Mumbai Police will find out who has taken responsibility and who is behind it," he said.
He added that neither the Mumbai Police nor the Maharashtra government would spare those found responsible.
"Our priority is the safety of the people," Shinde said, promising strong steps to prevent such incidents from continuing.
SHINDE RECALLS MUMBAI'S CRACKDOWN ON GANG WARS
Referring to the gang wars of the 1990s, Shinde said Mumbai Police had acted against criminal gangs during that period to stop them from spreading terror.
He said the police would take similar action now to protect citizens and celebrities.
Shinde also referred to previous incidents in which the Lawrence Bishnoi gang had been named, including the killing of former Maharashtra minister Baba Siddique and the firing outside actor Salman Khan's residence.
He questioned why such incidents continued despite alleged gang members being in custody and said the situation had gone beyond acceptable limits.
However, Shinde maintained that investigators would first establish who was behind the firing at Tiger Shroff's vehicle.
TIGER SHROFF SAFE AFTER FIRING
Three rounds were reportedly fired at Tiger Shroff's BMW in Mumbai's Juhu area on Sunday. The actor was returning home after playing a football match when the incident took place.
Tiger escaped unhurt, while his driver was admitted to Nanavati Hospital. Police cordoned off the area and formed 12 teams to track down those responsible.
A social media post attributed to gangsters Anil Pandit and Harman Sandhu, who are based abroad, claimed responsibility for the firing in the name of the Lawrence Bishnoi group.
Police have not confirmed the authenticity of the post or the group's alleged involvement in the incident. The investigation is underway.

Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging’s ₹852.1 Cr IPO continued to receive healthy investor interest on the second day of bidding. Investors have placed bids for about 5.93 Cr shares against the 85.26 Lakh shares on offer, implying an oversubscription of 6.95X. Demand for the IPO was led by retail individual investors, who have placed bids for 2.70 Cr shares against the 42.6 Lakh shares reserved for them. This translates to a 6.34X oversubscription of their category. Trailing RIIs, non-institutional investors (NIIs) have cumulatively bid for 2.25 Cr shares against 18.24 Lakh shares reserved for them, implying an oversubscription of 12.36X. Within this category, investors have placed 1.18 Cr bids for lots valued over ₹10 Lakh while lots in the range of ₹2-10 Lakh have attracted 1.08 Cr bids till now. Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) have bid for 95.83 Lakh shares against their quota of 24.3 Lakh, implying 3.94X oversubscription. Meanwhile, employees of the company have placed bids for nearly 1.68 Lakhs shares against the 14K shares reserved for them, oversubscribing to their allocation by 12.03X. Prior to the opening of the IPO, Tonbo allotted 36.5 Lakh shares to 43 anchor investors at ₹700 apiece, raising ₹255.4 Cr. Its IPO, which comprises an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 1.2 Cr shares with no fresh issue component, will close on October 19. The company has set a price band of ₹665-₹700 per share for the offer, indicating a valuation of ₹4,009.8 Cr at the upper end of the price band. Tonbo started off as a subsidiary of a research company, Sarnoff Corporation, providing R&D and technology development services. It was bought out by promoters and cofounders Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza in 2012. Since then, the company has pivoted to design and development of advanced imaging and sensor systems used for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting, and other military applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging systems, weapon sights, fire-control systems, missile seekers, etc. In terms of the value chain, Tonbo handles the prototype development, system integration, and qualification testing in-house, while outsourcing manufacturing to partners such as Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technology. On the financial front, Tonbo reported operating revenue of ₹36 Cr and a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr in Q1 FY27. For the fiscal ended in March 2026, its revenue from operations declined 22.7% to ₹362.6 Cr from ₹ 469.1 Cr in FY25. Net profit declined 43% YoY to ₹50.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹72.8 Cr in the previous year.

A video is circulating on social media (here, here) that purportedly shows a young woman criticising the ongoing Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a young woman criticising the ongoing CJP protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
Fact: The video is AI-generated and does not show an authentic recording of a young woman criticising the ongoing CJP protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed a watermark bearing the Instagram handle @sifatsangh. A Google search for the handle led us to the same video (archived), which was uploaded to the account on 07 October 2026. We also observed that the speech patterns throughout the video resemble those commonly found in AI-generated audio.
To further verify the video, we analysed it using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive, SynthID, and Hiya. Hive and SynthID indicated that the video was AI-generated, while Hiya identified the audio as likely to be a deepfake.
We then analysed the photos and videos posted on the profile using Hive’s AI detection tool, which indicated that the content appeared to be AI-generated. This suggests that the profile may be entirely AI-generated and could be fake.
To sum up, this viral video of a young woman criticising the CJP protest demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation is AI-generated.

The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA), led by an Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer and FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, is continuing its crackdown on unhygienic and unsafe food practices, with its latest action targeting a Reliance Retail warehouse for the second consecutive day and a Blinkit-linked facility. Officials found safety violations, including rodent infestations, improper storage and failure to maintain records of the disposal of expired food products, according to news agency PTI. According to the news agency, the licence of Reliance Retail's warehouse in Chakan was cancelled, while the licence of a Blinkit-linked facility in Nighoje was suspended. FDA officials inspected Reliance Retail's warehouse in Chakan, in Khed taluka, on October 14 and found rodent infestations, cockroaches on the floor and employees spitting within the premises. "Rodent infestation was found across the warehouse, while expired and spoiled products were stored together without segregation. Cockroaches were also found in floor crevices, and employees were seen spitting within the premises," the statement said, according to PTI. Although the company produced an agreement with a waste disposal agency, it failed to submit verifiable evidence of the actual disposal of the expired products, the FDA pointed out. The FDA official cancelled the licence on October 15, and a First Information Report (FIR) was registered at North Mahaluge MIDC police station. The inspection of the Blinkit-linked warehouse in Nighoje, in Khed taluka, was conducted on October 14. Officials found leaking packaging and cockroach infestations at the warehouse of M/s Linkit Commerce Pvt Ltd. The FDA also found that the cold room was too warm, and the facility could not provide records showing that the required storage temperature had been maintained. The cold-room temperature exceeded 5 degrees Celsius. "Raw and non-raw food items were stored together, while 50 kg of Tata Salt and 60 kg of semolina were kept directly on the floor. Leaking packets and cockroach infestation were also observed. Of around 600 employees, only five had FoSTaC (Food Safety Training and Certification)," the statement said. The FDA suspended the facility's licence on October 15, and an FIR was also registered at South Mahaluge MIDC police station. On October 17, the FDA acted against several warehouses in Pune and Thane districts over suspicions that expired, damaged and rejected food products meant for destruction were being diverted back into the market. The facilities under scrutiny included warehouses linked to Reliance Consumer Products and Reliance Retail at Wadpe in Bhiwandi, and Zomato Hyperpure at Usatane in Ambernath. The regulator also directed two unlicensed establishments to cease operations. As part of the broader operation, the FDA suspended five warehouse licences and seized 8,392 kg of stock worth ₹48.08 lakh. It’s official: Lena Dunham’s millennial magnum opus Girls is coming back, and it’s in large part thanks to Gen Z giving the show its long overdue redemption arc.
Using their native tongue: the internet, Gen Z proselytized the show through memes, clips, and podcasts, and now, as if by collective manifestation, it’s being rebooted for five episodes, which HBO announced Wednesday.
When Girls first aired in 2012, it was cataclysmic. Rave reviews were usurped by the relentless onslaught of sexism and misogyny, which commented on Dunham’s body, the kind of sex depicted onscreen, and the nepo baby allegations against the show’s stars—as well as the series’ lack of diversity. There was endless backlash and backlash to the backlash; it became everyone’s favorite show to both fairly criticize and willfully misunderstand, and creator Dunham was the one stuck grasping onto the lightning rod of so much ire, as she began to stand for everything wrong with millennial white women.
But then something happened. A decade after it aired, everyone started rewatching Girls. It’s not just that people were talking about it online; the series’ viewership doubled between November 2022 and January 2023, compared with the previous three months, The New York Times reported. On Tiktok and Instagram, memes and supercuts started unfurling: Marnie poised with a microphone in the infamous teal dress; Hannah snapping “I am busy, trying to become who I am,” or Shoshanna saying, “Obvi we’re the ladies!” It finally clicked for viewers, spawning a cultural and critical resurgence. While the reviews aged like milk, the show had aged like wine.
It was a phenomenon largely fueled by Gen Z viewers who had missed the show the first time around. (As well as prominent millennial Girls “truthers” like Hunter Harris, Peyton Dix, and Evan Ross Katz.) Among these Gen Z viewers were Amelia Ritthaler and Evan Lazarus, Brooklyn comedians who launched the Girls Rewatch podcast in 2023.
“I think the rest of society caught up to (Dunham),” says Ritthaler, 28. “Everybody was kind of under the impression that they weren’t allowed to be publicly saying that they loved the show and thought it was great. But me and Evan were like, this show is amazing. Why is everybody mad at her?”
Gen Z especially was able to identify with a style that so many millennials had failed to grasp. “So much of what we were raised on was this post-ironic, emotionally removed, ‘world is burning, but let’s dance through it’ kind of social media,’” she says. “I feel like when it was coming out, millennials were just kind of in their earnest era. The millennial optimism of it all. I feel like Gen Z never got that, so we were always watching it from this satirical lens that Lena wrote it in.”
Ritthaler and Lazarus posted Girls memes on TikTok and Instagram, amassing a following that allowed them to have guests like Dunham, as well as cast members Allison Williams (Marnie), Andrew Rannells (Elijah), and Zosia Mamet (Shoshanna) on the show. “I think this was like 70% cuz of you guys,” Jemima Kirke (Jessa) commented on the podcast’s Instagram account the day the revival was announced. “I feel like I loved my favorite show back to my life,” Lazarus said in a teary-eyed video.
The show’s redemption arc coincided with Dunham’s memoir Famesick, published in April, further fueling the Girls nostalgia. “I feel like reading Famesick felt like getting a director’s cut of girls,” says Dix, who hosts the podcast Lemme Say This with Hunter Harris.
The book was an instant New York Times bestseller with a buzzy tour. More importantly, there was a public reckoning around the way culture mistreated Dunham. It felt like a bow tied neatly around the physical and mental toll making Girls. She had moved to London, gotten sober, written extensively about chronic illness, worked on shows like Industry and Too Much. Last month, she announced she’d welcomed a baby via surrogacy.
There were never explicit fan calls for a reboot, particularly after the universally-panned Sex and the City reboot And Just Like That… But the swell in the show’s popularity undoubtedly caught the attention of HBO execs, thanks to the tenacious Gen Zers who spread the good word online. In a Substack post published Wednesday, Dunham credited the fans for helping her be ready to return to the series. “Maybe there was once a part of me that wanted to outrun Hannah and her ladies,” she writes. “Seeing the love you’ve so generously shared for it helped to turn me around.”
“The fans are just tender queers and sensitive girls who journal and heart their eyes,” says Dix. “The people she’s reaching and nurturing aren’t critics anymore, it feels like, or people who want to make weird comments about her body. It’s just young people, she wants to help inform or entertain.”
Part of the reason for the revival is, of course, that everything has come back: Gossip Girl, Pretty Little Liars, iCarly, and countless others have also seen reboots and sequels in recent years. “It’s nostalgia-core for sure,” Ritthaler says. “But it sucks that we don't have any new IP that has topped it. I walk around Brooklyn every day, thinking ‘how did we make Girls in 2012 and then everything went back to being worse?’”
But Gen Z is also ripe for a millennial optimism they never got to experience. Nostalgia for the mid-2010s has been cropping up online, with people posting photos of themselves in 2016, longing for fixed gear bikes, sepia toned photos, and stomp-clap music.
“I think there’s an energy, particularly in New York right now, that really embodies millennial optimism, and I think that Girls is absolutely a part of that cultural conversation,” says Dix. “It falls neatly into this new world we’re building that is kind of based on ‘Obama first-term joy.’ It’s nice to feel joy again when it’s really difficult to find it.”

Woman murdered at Gurugram home, husband finds body in bathroom with hands tied, mouth taped
The woman, identified as Neetu, was found by her husband, Prashant, a teacher at a private school, when he returned home with their children from school.
A 34-year-old woman was found murdered in the bathroom of her home in Daulah village in Gurugram's Sohna on Friday, with her hands tied and tape covering her mouth and face.
Police are probing a possible theft angle and examining CCTV footage from the surrounding area, though the motive and identity of the suspects remain unknown, Times of India reported.
The woman, identified as Neetu, was found by her husband, Prashant, a teacher at a private school, when he returned home with their children from school around 2 pm. He found household belongings scattered across the house and searched the premises, where he found Neetu lying in the bathroom. Prashant rushed her to a private hospital in Sohna, where doctors declared her dead.
The ransacked house has led police to examine the possibility of theft, although it remains unclear whether any valuables or other items were taken.
Police, forensic teams inspect scene
A police team led by ACP (Sohna) Mukesh Yadav and the SHO of Sohna Sadar police station reached the house after receiving information about the incident and inspected the scene. A forensic science laboratory (FSL) team also examined the premises and collected evidence, the report added.
Police are examining CCTV footage from cameras in the surrounding area to identify those involved and establish the circumstances of the murder.
Police said they were initiating the process of registering a murder case against unidentified persons based on statements from the family.
“We will register a murder case against unidentified persons. The victim’s mouth was taped, and there were some injury marks. The cause of death will be ascertained after autopsy,” the SHO said.
The investigation is continuing, with police working to identify the suspects and establish the motive behind the murder.

On Thursday, researchers from The Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto revealed a worst-case scenario found in the wild: spyware silently infecting targets as they browse past ads in their daily digital lives.
Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads.
Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk.
“AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. “Someone who gets hacked like this would not see anything amiss. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.”
The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well.
“The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher.
During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads. The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru. Infected devices had contact with domains linked to Discover-Tech and then connected to infrastructure associated with Candiru, according to Citizen Lab’s analysis. (Al Jazeera, which participated in the investigation and shared device logs with Citizen Lab researchers, did not respond to a request for comment.)
“The ability to push individualized, arbitrary content at specific users is a hallmark of the modern online ads ecosystem, and is perfectly suited to the mercenary spyware industry,” Marczak says. “Until this architecture changes, or ad companies get serious about customer vetting, we’re going to keep seeing this kind of abuse.”
Emails and messages sent to Discover-Tech and its CEO by WIRED did not receive a response before publication. Integrity Partners, which is believed to own Candiru’s assets, following sanctions by the US government in 2021, also did not respond to requests for comment.
Google, which operates one of the world’s largest advertising businesses, terminated Discover-Tech’s registration after collaborating with Citizen Lab and researchers from the cybersecurity firm Confiant and confirming a spyware link. “Following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant, Google blocked Discover-Tech from our ad platforms for systematically violating our policies,” a Google spokesperson says. “We also set up Safe Browsing warnings to help protect people if they navigate to websites linked to this group.”
The European branch of the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), an ad industry body, confirmed to WIRED that it has suspended Discover-Tech from its global vendor list, known as the GVL. The company was suspended by IAB Europe following an audit of its policies, it says. “Further confirmation of the findings regarding spyware could also justify a definitive expulsion from the GVL,” a spokesperson for IAB Europe says.
A spokesperson for Beeswax, an online advertising industry company owned by Comcast, says in a statement: “Beeswax removed Discovery-Tech from our platform following recent activity and independent validation by a third-party security specialist. We maintain a zero-tolerance policy for malicious advertising.”
Often when you see ads online or in apps, they’re displayed following a complex process known as real-time bidding—essentially an automated auction where advertisers place bids to show you specific ads. The milliseconds-long process can result in advertisers collecting huge volumes of data about your device, your location, and browsing history, plus a whole lot more. The process has been a privacy nightmare for years, with murky data brokers selling people’s personal information, and law enforcement agencies and hostile nations buying it to track or target people.
The Citizen Lab researchers say that Discover-Tech operates an advertising platform, Controlium, that can allow its users to “de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices” once an ad appears. Overall, the researchers estimate that millions of devices were directed to Candiru’s servers, where they could be profiled. By analyzing ad-bidding records that were publicly exposed on the Discover-Tech website, the Citizen Lab researchers say, ads linked to the firm with attacker script tags were shown in more than 70,000 mobile apps and more than 120,000 websites between March and June this year. Multiple apps, the researchers say, displayed more than a million ads linked to Discover-Tech.
The firm’s ads weren’t necessarily all weaponized to potentially distribute spyware, but the researchers say that, in general, they have seen Discover-Tech ad impressions on government and national-security-linked networks around the world. These include NATO and United Nations networks, as well as lawmaking bodies in Europe, critical infrastructure providers in Australia, plus armed forces and government agencies in Norway and Sweden.
Previous zero-click targeted ad campaigns that distribute spyware have rarely surfaced publicly, but the Citizen Lab researchers say this is likely a symptom of ad infrastructure being so extensively trusted and incorporated in all aspects of digital life without specific oversight.
“The network logs from Al Jazeera were key in understanding the ad-based nature of that attack,” Marczak says. “If a user’s personal device were targeted, say, while they were connected to their home Wi-Fi or mobile data, there’s not going to be the same level of network monitoring there. So I think the lack of prior reporting is probably mainly a visibility issue: Defenders have to be in the right place at the right time, looking at the right data.”
Speaking generally about threats that can result from the sheer ubiquity of the digital ad ecosystem, Jason Kint, CEO of the digital media trade organization Digital Content Next (WIRED parent company Condé Nast is a member), says these kinds of attacks are both plausible and damaging.
“Although rare and sophisticated, I wouldn’t be entirely surprised to learn about zero-click attacks through ads,” Kint says. “Anything that goes directly against users’ expectations or lowers the trust in the open web is deeply concerning.”

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Heidi Widmer. It has been edited for length and clarity.
In July, I moved into an apartment in Los Angeles, exhausted from a six-day drive across the country from New York. All I wanted to do was get into the apartment and sleep, and luckily, my bed had been delivered on the same day I arrived.
Trying to fall asleep at 2 a.m., all I could hear was a loud noise coming from the apartment upstairs. It sounded as if someone was bowling. Although I was tempted to shout for them to be quiet, I held my tongue — I was the new neighbor and didn't want to be difficult.
But the noise just didn't seem to stop. Whoever lived up there also never came downstairs. Who lives up there? I thought to myself.
I realized my neighbor had Parkinson's
Two weeks after moving in, I heard someone coming down the stairs and had to get a glimpse of who lived above me.
Peeking out of my door, I saw Carole for the first time, slowly making her way down the stairs, shaking badly from what was clearly Parkinson's, and trying to carry a bunch of bags full of recycling.
Just as I was about to open the door to see if she needed help, she dropped all the bags with only a couple of steps left. I burst out of my apartment to help her.
"Oh my gosh, thank you," she said in her sweet British accent. "Did you just move in? Am I too loud for you?"
In that moment, I felt totally and completely humbled.
Having grown up in the Catholic church, I was taught never to judge a book by its cover, and with Carole, I hadn't even seen the cover. I judged her simply by the noise she produced upstairs. How could I be so judgmental?
It turns out that sound had been Carole rolling a three-wheeled, broken chair across her floor to get to her mini fridge — the mini fridge social services had given her when her refrigerator broke. She had to hoist herself out of her broken chair to get down and access the mini fridge.
That was the noise.
I was determined to figure out what I could do to help
Two days after we met, I knocked on her door. She peeked through and nervously let me in. The conditions inside weren't great.
Although she can live independently, she just needs a little help. I later learned that she doesn't like accepting help from people, especially social services. The fact that she is frightened of the very people meant to help her breaks my heart.
That day, I took all of her trash out for her, reassuring her I wasn't judging her at all.
In the weeks and now months that have followed, I have been up to Carole's to help with the trash, cooking (she'd only been having microwave meals), cleaning, and contacting the landlord to get him to replace and repair items in the apartment. We've decorated her apartment, too.
I raised $80,000 to help her out
Together, we made her an Amazon wish list, and I shared it on social media so that people could order things she needs and have them delivered directly to her. People have been so generous, purchasing things like an expensive Buddhist "butsudan" that Carole didn't expect anyone to buy.
We set up a GoFundMe, which has raised about $80,000, and we plan to use the funds to have a stair lift installed for her. Any leftover money will be spent on in-home care as she continues to age and her Parkinson's Disease progresses.
I know I've been helpful to Carole in these last few months, but she's been the perfect person at the perfect time for me, too. Moving to LA, I had hardly any connections. Lots of Carole's family members are either no longer living or back in the UK (she moved here in her 20s as an au pair).
Carole became the family I haven't had, and I became hers. We text back and forth each day, and I see her most days. She calls me granddaughter, and I see her as my grandmother.
When I've had a hard day at work teaching at a local middle school, Carole is ready to give me a big hug when I get home. She's been my safe space, and I've been hers. The universe knew we needed each other.
It's an unlikely connection, but it shows that when you lead with kindness rather than judgment, the person you were ready to judge can become someone you can't imagine your life without.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Assam Police to move SC against bail for Mahanta, Sandipon in Zubeen Garg death case
Gauhati High Court had granted bail to two of the accused persons, Amritprava Mahanta and Sandipon Garg.
Assam Police will challenge the Gauhati High Court's bail orders for Amritprava Mahanta and Sandipon Garg in the Zubeen Garg death case before the Supreme Court, once the courts reopen.
Special DGP CID and SIT Chief Munna Prasad Gupta said, adding that the trial is progressing on a day-to-day basis, with 134 witnesses examined so far.
Speaking to ANI, Gupta said that the proceedings were underway in a fast-track court.

"As far as bail granted by the Gauhati High Court to two of the accused persons, Amritprava Mahanta and Sandipon Garg, it has been decided that we will move to the Supreme Court challenging the order of bail granted to these two accused persons,” Gupta said.
"The procedure will happen very soon. Nowadays, the court holidays are going on, and the moment the courts reopen, we will file the appeals," he added.
The Gauhati High Court on Friday granted bail to suspended Assam Police DSP Sandipon Garg, who was arrested by the Special Investigation Team (SIT) in connection with the Zubeen Garg death case.
A single bench of Justice Rajesh Mazumdar granted bail to Sandipon, a cousin of late singer Zubeen, after hearing his petition.

An evening of mystery, anticipation and hope ended in misery as the fifth and final T20I between India and the West Indies was abandoned after just 7.4 overs of play and 48 minutes of action because of incessant, but not so heavy, rain.
When the match was called off at 10.03 p.m. at the M. Chinnaswamy Stadium here on Saturday, India, after being put into bat, had reached 118 for five.
The contest started two hours and fifteen minutes late and was reduced to nine overs a side. Even that was largely possible because of the state-of-the-art SubAir drainage system which helped get the ground ready in no time.
Once the pitter-patter stopped and players trudged on to the glazed green turf, the crowd roared in approval. The fact that Bhuvneshwar Kumar, an RCB fan favourite, found a place in the Indian XI, made them rejoice.
The 56 runs India scored in the first three overs gladdened their hearts further. After starting at a washout for long, it felt like they had hit a jackpot.
Ishan Kishan was the stand-out batter (30, 10b, 3x4, 2x6), clubbing Romario Shepherd for two massive sixes in the second over, one of which went out of the ground.
Sanju Samson impressed for a short burst of time (16, 7b, 2x4, 1x6), with the wristy maximum over backward-point off Shamar Joseph his best hit.
ALSO READ: India’s New Zealand Tour: What ODI and Test squad selections reveal about Gautam Gambhir’s plans
But the entry of Shamar Springer in the fifth over put the brakes on. He sent Samson’s stump cartwheeling first ball and conceded just seven runs. Shreyas Iyer and Tilak Varma couldn’t really get going, collectively scoring just 29 runs from 20 balls.
However, Naman Dhir turned the tables on the West Indies, smashing three sixes in his first five balls, two straight down the ground and one square on the leg-side.
Just as he was promising more (25 n.o., 6b, 1x4, 3x6), the heavens opened up again, sending players scurrying back to the pavilion, only for them to never return.
The result ensured that India kept its record of not losing a bilateral T20I series at home since February 2019. It also meant the West Indies has now gone two consecutive T20I series against India without losing. Both sides would have liked to get that record after a full match, but it was not to be.
The 2-2 result, though, can be termed a fair reflection of the sides’ excellence over the last few days. There was little to separate the two, something even the rain gods agreed with.

The Keralam Assembly on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) referred the Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection) Bill, 2026, which aims at ensuring the rights and protection of the elderly, to the Finance Subject Committee for further scrutiny.
The Bill, piloted by Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, aims at promoting healthy and active ageing, registration and regulation of senior citizen care centres, capacity-building for family and care givers, and protection of rights, dignity, and social security of the elderly.
Opposition alleges Constitutional breach
However, the Opposition alleged that the provision that a copy of a Bill to be tabled in the Assembly should be made available to members at least three days before had not been fully complied with. N.K. Akbar, MLA, in a point of order, alleged Constitutional violation, failure to calculate the financial burden correctly, violation of Supreme Court directives on advanced medical directives with regard to the Bill’s provisions on execution of ‘living will.’
The LDF government had brought out a policy for the elderly, set up a commission for them, and prepared an elderly budget. “So, the Opposition is not against the Bill. But, serious legal issues exist,” he said.
The Chief Minister, who holds the portfolio of the Department of Senior Citizens, contended that special Acts could contain penal provisions. Moreover, the finance memorandum in the Bill clearly specified recurring and non-recurring expenditure. The government would not incur any particular expenditure in setting up senior citizen unit and forums as proposed in the Bill. The Supreme Court guidelines would be incorporated when Rules for the Act were framed, he said.
The Speaker ruled that the Bill was published in the Gazette on October 10 and its copies circulated among members the same day.
During the discussion on the Bill, the Chief Minister reiterated that “the measure of a civilised society was how it treated its senior citizens”. If the Bill were to be passed, the Keralam Assembly would become a model for the world, he addded.
Focus also on silver economy
Referring to demographic changes and migration of children and youth outside Keralam, he said the population of the elderly in the State was expected to be double the national average by 2036. However, the government was focussing not only on the welfare of the elderly, but also “silver economy” so as to transform the challenges posed by the rising elderly population into an opportunity.
The United Democratic Front (UDF) government had set up a dedicated department for the elderly. Government interventions were planned to ensure active and healthy ageing, tapping into the skills and knowledge of the elderly, conducting a survey of all elderly in the State and their health status, setting up a volunteer corps, registration and monitoring of care homes, and training and certification of care-givers, he said.
“No one should feel they are alone. They should be protected and their rights ensured,” the Chief Minister said.
He also explained the rights and principles that informed the drafting of the Bill.
