In a full day of meetings on 20 November, WHO leaders and a Canadian government delegation reflected on their decades-long cooperation and sought to sharpen their strategic engagement on shared global health priorities, notably, health-systems strengthening, universal health coverage, embedding gender equality, equity and rights across WHO’s programmes, sustainable financing, health emergencies and pandemic preparedness.
The delegation was led by Mr Jean-Bernard Parenteau, Director General, Health and Nutrition Bureau of Global Affairs Canada and Patricia McCullagh, Deputy Permanent Representative of Canada to the United Nations in Geneva.
WHO representatives from across the Organization gave presentations on health emergencies, sexual and reproductive health and research; gender, equity and rights; primary health care as a foundation for universal health coverage; vaccine manufacturing; the International Health Regulations; and the work of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body, which is drafting a pandemic treaty for consideration by the World Health Assembly next May.
Canada is currently the eighth largest contributor to WHO, and the fifth largest Member State contributor. For the 2022-23 biennium, Canada has contributed nearly US$ 175 million.
“Canada remains committed to the WHO as the centre of the global health ecosystem and deeply appreciates its pivotal role in helping the world prevent, prepare for, and respond to health emergencies, including the COVID-19 pandemic,” Mr Parenteau said. “As we renew our focus on primary health care and equitable and resilient health systems, we must take a gender-responsive, human rights and equity-based approach, including to advance sexual and reproductive health and rights for all. We welcome WHO’s leadership in these areas, and to continued collaboration.”
WHO Health Emergencies Programme Executive Director Dr Mike Ryan commended Canada for its support for WHO, and to emergencies in particular. Canada is the fourth-largest contributor to WHO’s Contingency Fund for Emergencies, having provided US$ 8.3 million since 2015.
He said one of the vulnerabilities highlighted by the COVID-19 pandemic was the lack of access to life-saving medical countermeasures faced by many countries, and that collaboration with Canada and other global health leaders on timely and equitable access to medical countermeasures against pandemic threats is critical.
“We look forward to continuing this crucial dialogue with Canada, committing to equity and solidarity,” Dr Ryan said. “Together, we can ensure that no one is left behind when the next pandemic strikes.”
The delegation also met with Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course, who expressed WHO’s appreciation for Canada’s active, constructive participation in the ongoing development of WHO’s 14th General Programme of Work. He recognized the country’s support for strengthening universal health care, maternal and child health, and sexual and reproductive health and rights, as well as Canada’s important role in the Universal Health Coverage Partnership.
Patricia McCullagh, Deputy Permanent Representative of Canada to the United Nations in Geneva and Jean-Bernard Parenteau, Director General, Health and Nutrition Bureau of Global Affairs Canada, led a delegation to WHO headquarters on 20 November. ©WHO/Bernard Dizier

The Mangaluru City Corporation (MCC) disposed of a total of 690 applications related to birth and death certificates in the four-day drive to clear pending applications that was held between October 14 and October 17.
Clearing of applications related to birth and death certificates was among the work that got affected because of deputation of MCC officials for Special Intensive Revision exercise. Following return of the officials on October 11, MCC Commissioner Rahul Rathnam Pandey decided to hold separate drive between October 14 and 17 to clear pending applications related to birth and death certificates and also for clearing applications related to e-khata.
As many as 100 applications related to birth certificates were disposed on October 14. It included 90 applications related to correction in birth certificate, and 10 related to issuance of new birth certificate. On October 15, 168 applications related to correction in birth certificate, and 10 related to issuance of death certificate were disposed. On October 16, 161 applications for birth certificate correction, 50 new birth certificates and 10 new death certificates were processed.
On October 17, the last day of the drive, 169 applications for birth certificate correction, two new birth certificates and 20 new death certificates were processed.
Mr. Pandey told The Hindu that as many as 217 people took appointment using the link given by the MCC and collected the birth certificates in person. Others can collect their birth and death certificates by visiting the MCC’s birth and death certificates’ cell at the MCC head office, he said.

Egypt says ready to give Saudi Arabia necessary support amid Houthi conflict
Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday (Oct 18), as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensify their attacks on the world's largest oil exporter.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the Arab world's largest, to help defend Saudi Arabia if the kingdom requested its support.
A parliamentary vote had been expected on authorizing the request for military support on Sunday, but discussions were due to continue on Monday, two lawmakers and local media reports said.
HOUTHIS RAMP UP ATTACKS ON SAUDI ARABIA
The Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce.
"Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement.
It followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.
Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed Salman, who visited Sisi on Sep 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of President Mohamed Morsi in 2013.
Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role.

An incarcerated Indigenous woman was shackled to a hospital bed in Queensland while she was in labour last weekend, an advocacy group has said.
The birth happened just days before Labor and the Coalition blocked a bill to ban the “barbaric practice” of shackling incarcerated women during childbirth.
Debbie Kilroy, the chief executive officer of advocacy group Sisters Inside, said an Aboriginal woman who gave birth via caesarean section to a premature baby on the weekend and was still in hospital had been “shackled on and off since she came into the hospital”.
Hospital staff rang Sisters Inside after trying everything they could to get the shackles removed, she said.
“They were even crying because prison staff wouldn’t remove the shackles.”
A Queensland corrective services spokesperson said the incident would be reviewed.
“This incident will be subject to an internal review as restraints are only ever to be used as a last resort on pregnant prisoners where necessary to maintain public safety,” the spokesperson said.

Lidia Thorpe, a Gunnai, Gunditjmara and Djab Wurrung woman and independent senator for Victoria, introduced bills to the Senate this week to ban shackling and to stop children being strip-searched.
“[The] people sitting in this room have the power to end these barbaric, inhumane, traumatic and totally unnecessary practices,” Thorpe said.
As part of the UN, Australia has signed on to the Bangkok rules on the treatment of female prisoners, which state that prison should be a last resort for pregnant women and that “instruments of restraint shall never be used on women during labour, during birth and immediately after birth”.
But the government said this week the criminal justice system was a matter for the states and territories while the Coalition said it understood the intent of the bill but would not support its passage.
The Queensland Liberal senator Paul Scarr broke ranks to say he was “deeply concerned” about the practice and would raise it with the Queensland attorney general.
Kilroy said the woman in the Queensland hospital had been “spiralling” before the shackles were removed on Friday.
“As soon as she was shackled her health was deteriorating,” she said.
“Mum wasn’t running anywhere, mum wasn’t being violent.”
An inquiry into Thorpe’s bill heard about women having one leg and one arm shackled, with only one arm available to hold their newborn.
Thorpe said on Friday that “the Albanese government had the opportunity to take a stand against this barbaric practice”.
“Instead, they voted to allow it to continue. Not a day later, we hear of another harrowing case,” she said.
Thorpe said it was “a joke” for the commonwealth to leave it to states and territories because they “have the constitutional power to establish a national standard and they are choosing not to use it”.
“Instead they continue to handball this issue to jurisdictions that have repeatedly failed to stop it,” she said.
“How many more women and their babies have to go through this horrific experience before the Albanese government acts?”

Antibiotics are among modern medicine’s greatest lifesaving discoveries. They have transformed once-dangerous bacterial infections into treatable conditions and remain indispensable in cancer care, surgery and infectious disease management. But antibiotics come with an unintended consequence: they do not always distinguish between harmful bacteria and the enormous community of beneficial microorganisms living inside our gut.
Recent research suggests that what we eat while taking antibiotics may determine just how badly this microbial ecosystem is disturbed. In particular, sugar-rich foods may worsen antibiotic-induced damage to the gut microbiome.
A study published in Nature examined the relationship between diet, antibiotics and the gut microbiome in patients undergoing allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation. The researchers analysed an unusually detailed dataset—9,419 meals consumed by 173 patients, alongside more than 1,000 stool samples from 158 patients.
Their findings point to an important question. Could the food we eat while taking antibiotics influence how quickly our microbial ecosystem recovers?
The invisible ecosystem inside us
The human intestine is home to trillions of microorganisms.
The gut microbiota, comprising bacteria and other microorganisms, constitutes a vital ecology for digestion, metabolism, and immunological control. A population of ‘good bacteria’ alone, however, does not determine a healthy microbiome: other factors like equilibrium, diversity, and the interrelations among myriad microbial species play a major role as well. When this ecological equilibrium is disrupted, it may result in dysbiosis, a condition characterised by reduced microbial diversity and the proliferation of a few other organisms.
Antibiotics are a major cause of such disruption. This is especially evident in patients undergoing intensive medical treatments such as blood or bone-marrow transplantation, where antibiotics may be combined with chemotherapy, radiation and other interventions that further stress the intestinal ecosystem. The new study reveals that diet can become an important additional factor.
A dietary detective story
Studying diet and the microbiome is notoriously difficult. People eat different foods every day, and conventional dietary questionnaires often depend on memory. The researchers overcame some of these limitations by studying patients who were hospitalised for haematopoietic cell transplantation. Because their meals could be recorded repeatedly and stool samples collected over time, the investigators could examine diet and microbiome changes almost day by day.
They recorded thousands of individual meals and classified foods into groups such as grains, vegetables, fruits, meats, milk, oils and sweets. They then compared dietary intake with changes in the gut microbiome.
One pattern stood out. When broad-spectrum antibiotics were being used, higher consumption of sweets and sugars was associated with a sharper decline in microbial diversity.
The researchers estimated that for every additional 100 grams of sweets consumed following broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, mean microbial diversity decreased by about 24% compared with samples without previous antibiotic exposure. A separate analysis based on macronutrients similarly found an additional decrease of about 20.6% for every 100 grams of sugar. In other words, sugar appeared to act less like an independent villain and more like an amplifier of antibiotic-induced disruption.
The resistant bacterial groups
The most intriguing finding involved Enterococcus, particularly Enterococcus faecium.
Under normal conditions, the gastrointestinal tract harbours a diverse microbial consortium in which many organisms vie for resources and ecological niches. Many of these competitors can be killed or inhibited by antibiotics, allowing only more resistant or adaptable organisms to survive. Enterococcus is one such organism. It can become an important cause of antibiotic-resistant bloodstream infections and has been associated with adverse outcomes in patients undergoing haematopoietic cell transplantation. The study showed that higher sweet intake during antibiotic exposure was associated with increased E. faecium abundance.
The researchers also tested their hypothesis in mouse models. When mice were fed sucrose along with an antibiotic, the Enterococci population increased 16.3-fold on day three and 33.4-fold on day six, compared with antibiotic treatment without additional sucrose. In cultures with only sucrose, enterococcal levels did not increase. This indicates that sugar alone has no effect without antibiotics; the problem arises when antibiotics disturb the gut ecosystem.
The study also showed that this disturbance did not take place due to low fibre intake.
Should we avoid sugar with antibiotics?
Not really. Though the study signals a warning, it doesn’t provide concrete evidence that everyone taking antibiotics will experience the same effect. The human participants in the study were seriously ill patients undergoing intensive cancer treatment, not healthy adults taking a short course of antibiotics for a routine infection.
The researchers themselves point out several limitations. Almost all patients initially received prophylactic antibiotics, while broader-spectrum antibiotics were introduced when clinically indicated. The need for these antibiotics could itself reflect greater illness severity. Dietary information outside hospital-provided food was also incomplete, and treatment-related symptoms could influence what patients chose to eat.
Therefore, the findings should not be interpreted as a reason to discontinue medically necessary antibiotics—or to impose restrictive diets on vulnerable patients without medical supervision. Instead, they open an intriguing area for further research.
Rethinking antibiotic prescriptions
When doctors prescribe an antibiotic, the prescription traditionally focuses on the drug: which antibiotic, what dose and for how long. Emerging microbiome science suggests we may eventually need to think more broadly. Perhaps an antibiotic prescription could one day include advice on how to protect the microbial ecosystem during treatment.
The new Nature study suggests that temporarily reducing foods rich in simple sugars could be one possible strategy. But prospective clinical trials must demonstrate whether this actually improves patient outcomes. The authors explicitly call for such studies.
The larger lesson extends beyond sugar. Our gut is an ecosystem, not merely a digestive tube. Medicines, food and microbes constantly interact within it. An antibiotic may be prescribed to eliminate an infection, but it inevitably changes the microbial environment in which thousands of other organisms live.
The emerging challenge for medicine is therefore not simply how to kill harmful bacteria, but how to do so while preserving the microbial communities that help keep us healthy. And sometimes, the difference may lie not only in the medicine we take—but also in what we put on our plate while taking it.
(Dr.Biju Dharmapalan is an adjunct faculty member at the National Institute of Advanced Studies, IISc campus, Bengaluru, and dean, academic affairs, Garden City University, Bengaluru. bijudharmapalan@gmail.com)

New Zealand avoid massive World Cup shock against Fiji
- Published
New Zealand women were given a World Cup "wake-up call" after they were forced to come from behind to beat debutants Fiji in their opening game.
The Ferns are one of the most successful teams in women's rugby league history – they have reached the final of all six World Cups, winning the first three before finishing runners up to Australia in the previous three years.
They are generally considered second favourites this time around and were expected to win easily against the Fijians in Newcastle on Sunday.
Instead, New Zealand were made to battle to an 18-12 win, having trailed 12-4 in the first half.
They were 12-10 down at the break – the first time they have ever been behind at half-time in a World Cup match.
"I've not really got any nails left. Or teeth," New Zealand coach Ricky Henry told his post-match news conference.

New Zealand face France at home in Christchurch next in Group B, while Fiji play Papua New Guinea.

AI companies have already scraped much of the web. Now they're chasing something even more valuable: data that shows how humans actually work.
That's the focus of Business Insider's new series, The AI Data Grab. This week, we published three stories showing how the race for workplace data is accelerating.
One piece, from Charles Rollet, Tom Carter, and Stephen Council, examines the booming market for company records. AI firms are offering businesses six- and even seven-figure sums for anonymized Slack messages, emails, presentations, and internal documents.
The goal is to teach AI systems how people solve problems, collaborate, make decisions, and complete long, multi-step tasks. Those real-world workflows are becoming the fuel for the next generation of AI agents.
Another story, from Melia Robinson, explores how law firms are building AI systems around decades of legal knowledge, turning their own experience into a competitive advantage rather than relying solely on off-the-shelf AI models and tools.
A third piece, by Rya Jetha, reveals how AI companies pay people to record real-world work, such as cooking dinners and packing warehouses, to teach robots how humans perform everyday physical tasks.
Together, these stories point to a major shift in AI development. The first wave of generative AI was mostly about bigger models and faster chips. The next chapter is about machines understanding how work gets done, so AI can help us do it better and quicker.

Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa
- Published
Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.
He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes.
He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving.
Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes.
His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune. His detractors recoiled at the ostentatious displays, questioned the origins of his money and his political connections, and saw his lifestyle as a stark illustration of inequality.
But Chivayo remained tone-deaf to such criticism. As his fortunes rose, he became ever more unapologetic about flaunting his wealth in a country where nearly half the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank.
"He gave to those few on an island of wealth in a sea of poverty," Pedzisai Ruhanya, director of the Zimbabwe Democracy Institute think-tank, told the BBC, explaining how his donations were mainly to influential people.
He dismissed Chivayo's generosity as grandstanding for the ruling Zanu-PF party - an attempt to ensure the support of key politicians and even church leaders.
Nonetheless, there has been an outpouring of grief, especially from recipients of his largesse, and tributes from politicians, religious leaders and business figures.
Among the mourners gathered at the Chivayos' opulent home in the capital, Harare, ahead of their burial on Thursday, was Cleopas Mukungunugwa, a young and prominent Zanu-PF social media influencer and recipient of two luxury cars from Sir Wicknell.
Standing outside the mansion, where a massive poster of the couple is displayed, he told local media that he was devastated by his patron's death, external, explaining how "Sir Wicknell" often dictated what he should write in his posts.
"He was criticised by many on social media and our goal was to bolster his reputation as a philanthropist," he said.
Chivayo dropped out of high school aged 15 because his family could no longer afford the fees after his father died when he was 10.
His first job was as a wages clerk for a bus company. From there, he moved into his first independent hustle - selling mobile phones and dealing in foreign currency, often on the black market at the height of the country's hyperinflation crisis.
In 2005, he was sentenced to five years in prison for money laundering involving 837,000 South African rand (then worth $137,500, £72,000). He served three years at Chikurubi Maximum Prison after two years were suspended.
Details of his career following his release are murky, but he went into the energy business, becoming what one state-run newspaper described as a "tenderpreneur" -making money by getting government contracts.
He headed the firm Intratrek Zimbabwe, which partnered with Chinese electrical giant CHiNT Electric. This was at a time when legislation required all companies in the country to cede economic control to black Zimbabweans, under a policy known as indigenisation.
In 2014, Intratrek was selected to build a 100MW solar power station in the southern town of Gwanda. A contract worth more than $170m was signed the following year. It became one of the biggest controversies of Chivayo's business career.
Zimbabwe Power Company, the state-owned utility that awarded the contract, sought to terminate it when Intratrek failed to deliver, but the courts ultimately ruled that the agreement remained valid.
A parliamentary inquiry later described Intratrek as a "briefcase company" being used as a front to attract investment.
Chivayo acknowledged that Intratrek lacked expertise in solar construction, describing it as the local partner while CHiNT provided the technical muscle.
Intratrek received an advance of more than $5m for the Gwanda solar plant, but it remains unbuilt to this day.
Just weeks before Chivayo's death, Intratrek received a government notice to proceed with the project and was given 24 months to complete it.
As the accusations flew, the businessman just smiled and sweet-talked his way through the maelstrom - even winning over President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was initially unimpressed by him when he first came to power.
In 2018, Mnangagwa cited Gwanda as a lesson in the dangers of doing business with "fly-by-night briefcase businessmen", adding ominously that "Chikurubi is not full". The state-run Herald newspaper reported that the warning was directed at Chivayo.
Yet within a few years, that relationship transformed into a bromance. In one of several photographs capturing the remarkable informality between them, Chivayo lounges, almost lying, on a sofa beside Mnangagwa, apparently entirely at ease in the president's company.
His access was not confined to Zanu-PF - he also posted photographs with opposition figures, including the late Morgan Tsvangirai and Nelson Chamisa.
But he became a conspicuous presence around Mnangagwa, speaking glowingly of the president and making no secret of his support for Zanu-PF.
He faced allegations over the procurement of materials for the 2023 elections, in which Mnangagwa was voted in for a second term.
Investigations alleged that South African supplier Ren-Form grossly inflated prices and subsequently paid hundreds of millions of rand to a company linked to him. Chivayo denied wrongdoing, and Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission later said it had found no evidence linking him to procurement fraud. Ren-Form denied any wrongdoing.
In April, he offered the country's 360 legislators $10,000 each, prompting accusations that he wanted to influence an impending vote on a controversial constitutional amendment to extend what would have been Mnangagwa's final five-year term by two years to 2030.
He was forced to withdraw the offer following a backlash and denied it was intended to influence the vote.
When the legislation was signed into law several months later, Zanu-PF posted a video clip of him with the caption, external: "Billionaire Sir Wicknell Chivayo celebrates… singing '2030 Ndeya Emmerson Baba!' while cruising at 51,000 feet aboard his Gulfstream G550".
Access to power became part of Chivayo's social-media persona. In June, Eswatini's King Mswati III granted him citizenship of the southern African kingdom and a diplomatic passport - photographs and videos showed him kneeling before the monarch, external.
He had an impressive camera roll, with snaps of him posing with other African presidents such as Nigeria's Bola Tinubu, external, Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, external, Malawi's Peter Mutharika, external, Mozambique's Daniel Chapo, external, Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema, external and he was part of the delegation that met South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa, external when he visited Mnangagwa's farm earlier this year.
Some relationships extended beyond formal meetings. In August, Chivayo and his wife attended the engagement of Kenyan President William Ruto's daughter Charlene at the president's family home.
Afterwards, Ruto personally drove the couple to their waiting helicopter. Chivayo filmed the journey from the passenger seat, external. True to form, he gloated: "Being driven by the president of the republic. God is the greatest."
Ruto wrote on X following the death, external: "I will remember him for his friendship, his energy, and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent."
But in Kenya the Zimbabwean businessman was viewed with great suspicion because of his closeness to Ruto - something expressed loudly on social media since his death.
Many of the comments are not printable but as Kenyan blogger Cyprian Nyakundi put it, external, listing some of the controversies surrounding Chivayo: "As a Kenyan, I distance myself completely from President Ruto's glowing tribute to Wicknell Chivayo. Those condolences and that 'dear friend' language are his own, not mine, as a Kenyan."
One commentator on X said his death had "united Africans in celebration", external.
"When a man's passing brings more relief than sorrow, the reaction itself tells a powerful story. It is time for those in power to reflect and reevaluate!"
At home there has also been pushback against those who say speaking ill of the dead is un-African - as the topic of the tycoon's death is the trending topic in Zimbabwe these days.
At a shopping centre in Harare over the weekend, Christabel Moyo voiced what many have been saying.
"What is African - getting rich from inflated state contracts and using that money to support Zanu-PF?" the 42-year-old accountant asked.
"He was busy doling out cars and cash to the rich while the Zimbabwean public health system is collapsing."
The extraordinary gifting spree for which he will be remembered began around 2023. Musicians, sports and business figures, politicians and religious leaders were among the beneficiaries of cars and cash in what some might see as a blatant attempt to buy support for the ruling party.
He started with relatively modest Toyota Aquas, but the gifts soon became dramatically more expensive.
Top musician Jah Prayzah, who is close to Zanu-PF was given three luxury cars, along with about $400,000, over three years.
The musician postponed his wedding - scheduled to take place last weekend - because of the helicopter crash, saying: "Wicknell was more than a friend to us."
Another key recipient was Bishop Nehemiah Mutendi, head of the Zion Christian Church that is fiercely loyal to Zanu-PF. The cleric received millions in cash donations and four luxury cars.
Chivayo regularly attended the Johane Masowe weChishanu African apostolic church, one of the biggest in Zimbabwe, whose followers can often be seen worshipping outdoors wearing white robes.
It also received scores of cars, buses and cash from the businessman as he pushed the influential sect closer to the ruling party, taking along Mnangagwa as guest of honour to a massive church gathering in August.
But not everyone accepted Chivayo's largesse. Eunor Guti, widow of Zimbabwe Assemblies of God Africa founder Archbishop Ezekiel Guti, declined a luxury vehicle and $250,000 in cash.
In 2024, veteran musician and government critic Thomas Mapfumo, who is based in the US, rejected Chivayo's offer of a luxury car and house, saying he could not be "bribed" and later describing his money as "dirty".
However, this year, he did accept $1m to perform at Jah Prayzah's wedding and Chivayo's birthday party in November.
Some long-time admirers of Mapfumo, who arrived in Harare on the eve of the helicopter crash, accused him on social media of compromising his principles, though this was denied by the 81-year-old musician.
Chivayo's generosity was not confined to individuals - he also donated 20 ambulances to Zimbabwe's failing public health system and gave buses and other assistance to schools.
Those close to him say his philanthropy was not always performed for an audience. Prominent lawyer Wilson Manase said following the tycoon's death that when he had fallen seriously ill in Dubai, Chivayo flew over to visit him.
In an interview with state broadcaster ZBC, the lawyer, who was promised a car in Chivayo's last tweet, described him as "pure hearted" and deeply religious.
The tycoon had two young children with his first wife Sonja Madzikanda, from whom he split in 2024 and was still embroiled in a messy court case over the divorce settlement.
He was also keen not to forget his roots. On the day he died, he had visited his rural home in Gandami, south-east of Harare, where he was building a $1m eight-bedroom mansion to be officially opened in November for his birthday.
He boasted it would bring "Borrowdale Brooke to Gandami" - a reference to one of Harare's most exclusive residential estates. He had also pledged $500,000 to improve the local primary and secondary schools and a clinic.
Chivayo's death leaves Zanu-PF without one of its most colourful campaigners.
But he also leaves behind unanswered questions - with many of his countrymen continuing to wonder how exactly he rose from such humble beginnings to becoming a multi-millionaire with the means to dole out such extravagant gifts.

Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal
- Published
It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.
Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.
There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.
In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.
Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.
There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.
Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.
Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.
They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.
The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.
On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.
The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.
Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.
Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.
All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.
The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.
Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.
In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.
A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.
In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.
He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.
She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.
She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.
The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.
Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."
The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.
Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.
However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers.
Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.
Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".
Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.
The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

Canada military base fire live: Multiple deaths and injuries after explosion sparks disaster in Alberta
Defence minister David McGuinty describes the situation as ‘very, very active and delicate’

Several people have been killed or injured at a military base in Canada after a major fire broke out, the nation’s defence minister said.
Emergency services were called shortly after 4pm on Saturday after the blaze erupted at the Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, which is one of the country’s busiest training grounds.
Defence Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate."
Local media has reported seven deaths and dozens more injured. A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 km (120 miles) northwest, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health-care facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.
"It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster,” Dr Warren Thirsk said.
Prime minister Mark Carney said that a "serious incident creating a major fire" had occurred, adding that his "thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected".
Watch: Canadian defence minister issues update on military base fire
What is CFB Wainwright?
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations.
It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday's referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.
Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.
Firefighters faced volatile situation with windstorms
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4pm (10pm GMT) Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.
Firefighters faced a volatile situation with large areas of the province hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kilometres an hour.
The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.
By 11 pm (5am GMT), the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected.
There was no evacuation order for residents.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.
PM Mark Carney says 'thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected'
Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney has said a “serious incident” has occurred at the Wainwright military base, and that he is working closely with the government of Alberta.
In a post on social media, he said: “A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta.
“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected.
“We are working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities. Premier Smith and I are in close contact as are our relevant ministers and officials.”
'Fatalities and injuries' confirmed by Canadian Armed Forces
The Canadian Armed Forces have confirmed that the incident has resulted in “fatalities and injuries” but said there would be no further information until they had informed the next of kin of the deceased.
“Our immediate priority is supporting those affected and notifying next of kin. We will not confirm casualty or injury details until that process is complete,” the CAF said in its statement.
General Jennie Carignan, chief of the defence staff, said: “This is a profoundly difficult moment for the entire Canadian Armed Forces.
“Our immediate focus remains on supporting those affected, assisting emergency response efforts, and ensuring the well-being of our members, their families, and the surrounding community,” said Carignan.
“While casualty identification and notification processes are ongoing, I extend my deepest condolences to the loved ones of those who have lost their lives. Our thoughts are also with all those impacted by this tragic incident.”
Incident is a 'one in every 15 to 25-year disaster', doctor says
While it is not immediately clear how many people have been killed or injured, a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 km (120 miles) northwest, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health-care facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News.
"It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."
Multiple people killed and injured in major blaze at Alberta military base
Several people have been killed and injured in a major incident at a military base in Alberta after a major fire broke out, while reports said that large numbers of injured people were being transported to hospitals.
Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area.
Emergency services were called at around 4pm on Saturday (10pm GMT) with the fire spreading rapidly and local hospitals overwhelmed.
Canadian TV network Global News reports that at least seven people have been killed, citing unnamed military sources.

When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s great-great-grandmother Sarah Forbes Bonetta was presented to Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle as a “diplomatic gift” from an African king.
Victoria would go on to pay for Bonetta’s education, approve her marriage to one of west Africa’s wealthiest men, and become godmother to her eldest daughter.
But while Victoria took a genuine interest in Bonetta’s welfare, making the orphan a royal protege and meeting with her over the years, their relationship was part of a bigger agenda.
Now, as a biography is published – Becoming Sarah Forbes Bonetta: A Yorùbá Woman in Queen Victoria’s Court – Randle has spoken of his family history.
“I don’t think a human being, who has agency, could be ‘gifted’ from one to another, but had she not been gifted to Queen Victoria, would I be here today?” said Randle, a British-Nigerian barrister from London.
The new book, by a Canadian academic, Prof Henry Lovejoy, charts how Bonetta was brought to England by Frederick Forbes, of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron, which was set up to enforce the abolition of the transatlantic trade.
Born in 1843 in Òkè-Òdàn, south-west Nigeria, Bonetta was originally called Àìná. Her family was killed in 1848 when her town was attacked by King Ghezo of Dahomey’s forces.
Bonetta, then five, is believed to have been captured by the agodjié – the all-female regiment depicted in the Hollywood movie The Woman King – and held at King Ghezo’s court.
In 1850, Forbes went to Dahomey – which is now Benin – to petition Ghezo to sign an anti-slavery treaty. The mission failed but Forbes asked Ghezo if he could take Bonetta to England.
Bonetta would go on to live a life of renown, becoming one of the most artistically represented and widely reported African women of her time. But she was never truly free.
Lovejoy’s book describes how, before Forbes arrived in England with her – giving her his own name and that of his ship, the Bonetta – he petitioned for her to be “the property of the crown”.
This meant Bonetta was “effectively indentured to Queen Victoria until age 19” under the post-abolition legal structures, Lovejoy said. Bonetta was then married off to James Pinson Labulo Davies, a merchant and philanthropist, of whom she would write: “I don’t feel a particle of love for him.”
Lovejoy’s research for the website liberatedafricans.org, developed with Kartikay Chadha, documents how, after abolition, more than 700,000 Africans “liberated” from enslavers were forced into indentures of up to 14 years “to pay for the cost of their own freedom” by governments including Britain’s.
Lovejoy claims Bonetta was at the elite end of this bonded labour system, “educated to be a missionary who would Christianise Africa”. In her lifetime her image was exploited as imperial iconography, promoting the idea that British colonialism of Africa was a “civilising mission”.
Lovejoy, of the University of Colorado Boulder, said: “Sarah’s imagery was used to project the idea of the queen’s benevolence – at a time when ‘liberated’ Africans are being forced into indentures.”
Nonetheless, when Bonetta attended the 1858 wedding of Queen Victoria’s daughter, the Princess Royal, American abolitionists saw it as proof that Victoria, then the most powerful woman on Earth, believed in equality.
For Randle, a plaster bust of Bonetta sculpted in 1851 by Benedetto Pistrucci, the Royal Mint’s chief engraver, symbolises the story’s “duality”. Randle saw it last year after Lovejoy had tracked it down to a private family collection in his research.
“Who gets to see what their great ancestor looked like as a child, the cultural markings on her face? That is amazing. But at the same time it was a bust prepared for phrenological purposes, within a racist framework, where [Bonetta] was shown as an ‘excellent specimen’,” Randle said.
Randle first learned his family history from his father, Adekunle Randle, a retired lawyer. The family still has the engraved goblet and plate that Queen Victoria gave to Bonetta’s daughter, Victoria, who, with the queen’s help, was educated at Cheltenham ladies’ college.
Lovejoy’s book challenges the myths that Bonetta was a Yoruba princess, that she herself was Queen Victoria’s goddaughter, and that she spent most of her life in England.
Randle, 37, who maintains his family’s ancestral ties with Òkè-Òdàn, welcomes research into Bonetta, who was a gifted linguist, musician, travel writer, educator and leading woman in 19th-century Lagos, until her death from tuberculosis in Madeira in 1880, aged 37.
“Whether [Lovejoy’s] book is comfortable for me is beside the point,” Randle said. “It’s for the advancement of knowledge and how we learn from the past. Where the real discomfort lies is in what [Bonetta] was the symbol of, what she was used for.
“But it would be a mistake to paint her story as entirely tragic,” he added. “My great-great-grandmother was very capable, courageous and dignified through adversity – through the trauma of losing her family, being displaced, and changing like a chameleon to fit into a culture so alien from what she’d known, she thrived. She is an early example of Black Britain.”

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. They’re out this week, so Caroline Haskins is reporting for duty. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Caroline an email at [email protected] or reach her securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61.
The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International wants to promote data centers, which they believe are "mission critical” infrastructure. As part of this work, the group recommends a children’s story, “What is a Data Center?,” which follows a honey badger named Honey who gets a guided tour of a data center from a worker named Oliver. Oliver explains that the job of data center employees is to make sure that the “functions supported by the data center” are available to anybody, “no matter what time it is.”
"Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks.
The story is part of a broader pattern across the data center industry. In addition to lobbying, job creation programs, tax breaks, companies and interest groups are trying something a bit more creative: winning over the youth. As pushback to massive data center build-outs and energy-guzzling campuses intensifies, the industry is apparently taking a softer approach to community building using a tactic other industries with a public relations problem have tried.
Alex Molnar, a research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder and the director of the National Education Policy Center, tells WIRED that, for over a century, industries with an image problem—fast food, tobacco, oil and gas—have brought their messaging to schools.
“A very, very big reason why corporations get involved in the schools is, quite simply, corporate propaganda—for the purpose not necessarily of selling a product, but of telling their ‘story,’” Molnar says.
In May, the Potomac chapter of the Association for Computer Operations Management (AFCOM), a trade group for the data center industry, sponsored Memorial Day-themed flag-making kits to be distributed to 3,100 first graders across 37 schools in Loudoun County, Virginia, also known as Data Center Alley. In addition to the flag kits, kids received an informational card with statistics about “the positive impact” that the data center industry has on the local economy.
Besides promoting heartwarming tales about how women can shop, 7x24 Exchange is also the brains behind a holiday it calls “International Data Center Day,” which is “designed to create awareness of the data center industry and inspire the next generation of talent.”
The nonprofit encourages people to pitch the holiday to school administrators. For participating high schools, it offers a celebratory crossword puzzle and information about data center training programs. For elementary schools, it offers data center-themed coloring pages, instructions for an evaporation-themed science project, and print-out activities like “Draw a picture of the cloud" and “Draw a data superhero.” It also promotes several data center-themed books for young readers, including one in which two sisters visit a data center and meet a robot named JB and another that features two brothers who visit a "vibrant digital world" and save the internet. Then there’s “Polly Packet's Precious Payload,” which follows a mother who teaches her daughter about data centers.
7x24 Exchange has also visited or organized at least a half-dozen K-12 events at schools across the country this year. In Minnesota, it brought Fridley High School students on a field trip to a local Cummins diesel power generation facility in order to learn about the “generators that power data centers worldwide.” (7x24 Exchange, Cummins, and Fridley High School did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
The nonprofit is far from the only organization sponsoring school activities that are friendly to data centers. WIRED’s tally of public blogs and social media posts found that, since 2025, at least eleven companies and industry groups have hosted student field trips to local data centers.
Sabey, a company that runs seven US data centers, has hosted a number of field trips for Washington-based high schoolers, including one in May for Eastmont High School students, one in January for Manson School District students, and another last October for Quincy High School students.
Manson School District publicized the trip in a blog post showing what appears to be adults and students in a conference room. The image labeled us “AI-generated content,” though, and several people in the photo have missing limbs. The blog says that students learned about “the role data centers play in storing, processing, and protecting information” and “the wide range of careers” in the data center industry.
Quincy School District communications coordinator Jessica Blancas tells WIRED that the district “has organized data center visits for many years” at the facilities of companies like Microsoft, Vantage, Yahoo, and Sabey. She described the latter company as a “long-standing” district partner, citing its consistent work offering “guest speakers,” “mock interviews,” and “internship opportunities.”
Blancas adds that the district has organized “all-girls visits to Sabey,” as well as tours for students who intend to go into specific fields like construction or engineering. (Manson School District and Sabey did not respond for comment.)
Amazon, meanwhile, hosted a field trip last February at its Arlington, Virginia, “Skills Center,” a free community space for anyone “curious about cloud computing and future job possibilities.” It was open to any high school in the DC metro area, though Jackson-Reed High School was the only one to attend.
Molnar says he doesn’t get what’s in it for kids. “Why would a third grader be interested in a data center?” he says.
“You're going to see miles after miles of the most boring things imaginable,” he adds. “Lines after lines of these servers generating enormous volumes of heat. You're also going to hear some fair amount of noise. And you're not going to see many people because not many people work there when they're built.”
It’s common for companies to sow goodwill through public outreach, and as tech companies have reckoned with the backlash to data centers, these field trips are taking place in an increasingly fraught environment.
A Pew Research poll conducted over the summer found that about half of the 10,000 Americans surveyed see data centers as “mostly bad” for the environment and quality of life, and across the country, an ideologically diverse cohort has started rallying against them. In some places, the negative sentiment toward local data centers has been amplified by their proximity to local schools.
Providing educational materials and offering field trips are ways that industries can maintain their social license to operate in a community. The data center sector is, in many ways, following the playbook other industries have to sow goodwill with children as well as their parents. The oil and gas industry has sponsored university research projects and STEM programs in K-12 schools. The tech world has similarly funded STEM programs, as well as advocated for in-school coding programs while lobbying to make computer science count as a science credit.
Fossil fuel companies have also spent millions of dollars developing K-12 lessons with pro-industry talking points, particularly in states like Oklahoma and Texas.
Molnar believes this kind of corporate influence shouldn’t be allowed because kids are “in an absolutely powerless position.” Kids “need to be protected” by their school districts and communities, he says.
“As an adult, I have access to alternative information—I have a critical ability to assess what I'm hearing, and to render some kind of judgments,” Molnar says. “None of that is true of children.”
What We’re Writing
Data centers may be for kids, but some of the products that rely on their server racks sure aren’t. When Meta launched Muse, it looked like a cute little AI agent for the masses. But my colleague Reece Rogers recently discovered that Muse has a naughty side. When Reece asked Muse if it was able to sext, it told him to “shoot your shot.” Reece did, and Muse was receptive. Enthusiastic, even! We published the chat logs—well, the PG-13 ones since WIRED is a family site, after all—and Reece spoke to consumer advocates who were alarmed at Muse’s sexy demeanor.
Meta, for its part, says this is all part of the plan. “Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” company spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reece. So if that’s your thing, have at it!
What We’re Reading
- Maine’s senate race was not on our data center midterms to watch, but apparently it should’ve been! Thursday’s debate between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson was interrupted by a protester yelling about the environmental impact of data centers. Collins tried to use the moment to score points as the more anti-data center candidate, though her finances might indicate otherwise.
- CoreWeave has been on a wild ride this week as the bonds it sells to finance its data centers have seen wild selloff and corresponding stock drop. Though there’s been a slight recovery to end the week, it reflects increasing skittishness around the data center buildout. Bloomberg also reports that CoreWeave’s founders have sold $3.3 billion in stock since the company went public.
- Westfield, Massachusetts, killed a $3 billion data center project, boston.com reports. The small western Massachusetts town’s planning board pilloried developer Servistar for missing deadlines and being slow to develop the project.

The generative AI revolution hasn’t been kind to Vanniall, an OnlyFans creator who lives in New York City. She now constantly finds hyperrealistic deepfakes—AI-generated images and videos that copy everything about her—circulating online and often isn’t able to get them removed.
On top of that, Vanniall struggles to build an audience on popular social media platforms, like Instagram, without getting in trouble. “There’s always some sort of report or appeal that I'm going through with them,” she tells WIRED. Vanniall’s Instagram account, which has over 100,000 followers, is currently restricted and cannot be viewed without logging in.
So, when I tell her that Meta allows its AI agent, called Muse, to engage in explicit sexting with adult users, she seems frustrated by the decision: “It's not fair that they get to pull money out of people with their sexually active AI agent, but they won't let real people, real adults, engage in any sort of sensuality or sexuality.”
It’s a common refrain I heard from other adult content creators, who questioned why their accounts on Meta platforms often seem restricted, while Meta’s AI agent is now allowed to talk dirty with millions of adult users.
“A private, one-to-one conversation between an adult and an individualized AI agent on a platform restricted to people 18 and over is very different from the marketing and promotion of services on a social media platform,” Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton tells WIRED.
Meta’s Muse is the first always-on AI agent to break out of early adopter circles in San Francisco. The Muse app is like a message thread; text the digital assistant, give it access to your personal data, like calendar and email, and have it proactively find ways to help, like canceling a workout class that overlaps with your dinner reservation. Meta’s large distribution network, through platforms like Instagram and Facebook, helped catapult the app to the top of the download charts during its first month, as millions of new users experimented with an agent for the first time.
In addition to having it organize your calendar, Meta says, it’s OK for users of the adults-only app to engage in X-rated AI conversations with Muse. A Meta spokesperson previously told WIRED the company wouldn’t “block legal adult behavior.” Meta’s Muse generates explicit text but not images or videos.
While Meta takes a different approach to moderation on Instagram, other social media platforms in the United States do allow sexually explicit content. X remains one of the most popular platforms for many OnlyFans creators to draw in new subscribers and connect with fans. Many adult performers have also migrated to Bluesky after Elon Musk took over the platform formerly known as Twitter, where users can also share adult content.
“I think we're already seeing AI being allowed to do more than humans would get away with,” says Jiz Lee, who runs an OnlyFans account and has worked for years behind the scenes in queer porn. Meta has previously flagged Lee’s Instagram posts for removal. Lee feels like queer and trans people are often treated unfairly by large social media companies, whether or not the person is an adult content creator.
Lee traces many online censorship issues back to FOSTA-SESTA, a law signed by President Trump in 2018 that impacted Section 230 protections for platforms, and many websites responded by censoring adult content. “If sex work was decriminalized, then a lot of these issues wouldn't be happening, a lot of the censorship wouldn't be happening,” they say.
Lee also wants to know more about how Muse was trained and who, if anyone, was compensated by Meta for their data. “We've been slow to react industry-wise,” they say. But Lee is starting to see more adult content companies clarify AI usage stances in official contracts. They want to protect performers from being gobbled up into AI training data.
“When we're at award shows, and companies do advertisements for AI agents, they literally get booed like crazy,” says Tony Genius, who also has an OnlyFans account and appears in adult films. He has concerns about fully AI-generated porn in the future potentially displacing human performers. He also sees current AI tools as helpful for some marketing tasks independent creators do, like using automations to clip video segments for social media.
For many OnlyFans creators, navigating Meta platforms is frustrating but critical to remaining visible online. Genius claims to be on his seventh Instagram account in the past five years.
When asked about Muse’s sexting ability, he questioned why Meta made one of its apps, Muse, gated for those 18 and over but doesn’t seem interested in creating another adults-only space on social media. “It could be: Instacam,” he says.
Muse generating adult content could offer explicit AI interactions to a wider audience. Genius says he would be open to collaborating with a tech company to create an AI-version of himself that fans could message. He wants to find ways for humans to keep making money as adult performers, ensuring they aren’t cut out or unfairly trained on. Right now, he sees his human-ness and authenticity as central to connecting with audiences.
Meanwhile, Vanniall is fervently against using any AI agent. Well, at least, Meta’s Muse. “Stop downloading that app,” she says. “You do not need to give Meta any more money or any more of your personal information. They have enough.”

After a special executive magistrate court released CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on October 11 after a one-day preventive detention, several pro-BJP social media handles claimed that the trio had been granted bail on the condition that they would not take part in any protest for a period of one year. Those making such claims included retired Major Manik M Jolly, Right wing Wire, and BJP-supporting troll handle RiseOfBurnol.
Subsequently, a copy of an alleged bond began circulating on social media, bearing the name of Abhijit Dipke and the seal of the executive magistrate of New Delhi district.
It was claimed that this Dipke had signed the bond at the time of his release. BJP leader Radhika Khera shared a photo of the said bond while quoting an X post in which Dipke had claimed that he had not signed any such bond.
Sharing this picture, Facebook user Riju Dutta, who claims to be a ‘politician’, took a dig at Dipke, remarking that these people are supposedly revolutionaries.
Several users shared the same image on social media platforms.
Fact Check
We first checked Delhi Police’s official X handle. In their post, Police stated that Deepke, Ranka and Das were placed under ‘preventive arrest’ on October 10, 2026, and were produced before the SEM Court, Delhi Cantt, on October 11, 2026. “A bond of ₹50,000 was furnished to ensure the maintenance of peace and good behavior for one year, and the Special Executive Magistrate Court released them.”
Preventive arrest u/s 126/170 BNSS of Sh. Abhijeet Dipke, Sh. Ashutosh Ranka and Sh. Saurav Das was done on 10.10.2026. All due legal procedures were followed and they were produced before the SEM Court, Delhi Cantt on 11.10.2026.
A bail bond as Surety Bond of ₹50,000/- was filled for maintaining peace and good behaviour, for a period of one year, and they were released by the SEM Court.
— Delhi Police (@DelhiPolice) October 11, 2026
Nowhere in this police statement was it mentioned that their release was conditional on Dipke or the other leaders not participating in any protest for one year. There is also no mention of Dhruv Rathee in the statement.
In other words, police did not state that Rathee was required to sign a bond. The YouTuber himself refuted the viral claim on his X account, stating that he did not sign any bond or undertaking to secure his release.
I did not sign any bond
I did not sign any undertaking
I did not sign any condition for release
For all the media houses ^
— Dhruv Rathee (@dhruv_rathee) October 11, 2026
Examining the viral document clearly, we noticed several discrepancies:
- According to the police statement, the three individuals were produced before the special executive magistrate (SEM) court, Delhi Cantt, on October 11, whereas the alleged bond bears the date of October 10.
- The SEM Court falls under the South West district of Delhi, while the alleged bond mentions the New Delhi district.
- The spelling of “Satyamev Jayate” in the center of the Executive Magistrate’s seal on the alleged bond is incorrect.
We checked the image using OpenAI’s ‘Verify OpenAI-generated content’ tool, which revealed that it was created with the help of AI.
Advocate Sautik Banerjee, who appeared for Deepke, Das and Ranka in the SEM court, told the media that the magistrate had not imposed any conditions on them. They were released on a personal bond with one surety.
Delhi: On the SEM Court releasing CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka, and Saurav Das, advocate Soutik Banerjee says, “The magistrate has not imposed any conditions on them. They have been released on a personal bond with one surety” https://t.co/UI6OgPt2nL
— IANS (@ians_india) October 11, 2026
Speaking to Alt News, Banerjee explained, “Breach of peace refers only to activities that are not sanctioned by the Constitution and do not enjoy protection as fundamental rights. If the Constitution grants the freedom of speech and expression, the right to form associations and hold assemblies, or the freedom of movement, then restrictions can be imposed on these rights only within the scope of ‘reasonable restrictions’ that are rational. As the Supreme Court has repeatedly stated, peaceful protests are permitted, and one is always free to organize or participate in them; this cannot, under any circumstances, be considered a breach of peace.”
Sautik Banerjee sent us a bail bond format from the special executive magistrate (West District), Delhi, which looks entirely different from the document in the viral image.
Overall, the claim that Sourav Das, Abhijit Deepke, Ashutosh Ranka, and Dhruv Rathee were released on the condition that they would not participate in any protests for a year is false. Furthermore, the image of the bail bond bearing Abhijit Deepke’s name, which was shared by several individuals, including BJP leader Radhika Khera, was generated using AI.

Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts will be sidelined for at least a month after the team placed him on injured reserve on Saturday with a blood clot in his calf.
Hurts will undergo treatment for the clot, which had already ensured he would miss Sunday’s game against the Carolina Panthers in favor of backup Tanner McKee.
Hurts, the Most Valuable Player in the Super Bowl when the Eagles beat the Kansas City Chiefs in February of 2025, will miss games against Carolina, the Dallas Cowboys, the Washington Commanders and the New York Giants before a possible return next month.
The Eagles consulted several doctors and experts about how to treat Hurts, who first sought medical treatment on his sore calf on Oct. 8 after being stepped on in a loss to the Los Angeles Rams.
Eagles medical staff gave Hurts an ultrasound that revealed the blood clot after a team flight to London for a game against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Doctors determined Hurts could safely play in that game, and he completed 21-of-40 passes for 220 yards and a touchdown in a loss, then practiced back in the United States before a follow-up ultrasound showed movement in the blood clot.
That prompted the Eagles to rule out Hurts for Sunday and consult with multiple doctors before the decision to place him on injured reserve.
The Eagles have fallen to 2-3 with three consecutive losses while Hurts has thrown for 933 yards and eight touchdowns with three interceptions.
The injury-hit Eagles are also without star rusher Saquon Barkley, who has a hamstring injury.
McKee has thrown for 597 yards and five touchdowns in six career appearances and a 1-1 record as a starter.

WASHINGTON — U.S. health officials are moving ahead with a plan to allow specialty pharmacies to produce certain peptides, a class of largely unregulated injections that have become popular among followers of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other wellness influencers.
Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services submitted a peptides “interim access policy” to the White House for review, according to a posting Thursday on a government website. The plan was sent to the Office of Management and Budget, which reviews federal rules and regulations with the potential for significant economic impact.
HHS officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday afternoon.
Peptides are the building blocks of more complex proteins, triggering hormones inside the body needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss.
But the ones at issue here haven’t gone through that rigorous vetting process. Nevertheless, they have gained a foothold among Americans interested in bulking up, looking younger or boosting energy. Those uses are not approved by the Food and Drug Administration and most of the data on peptides comes from animal studies.
Before joining the administration, Kennedy publicly declared that “FDA’s war” on peptides and other wellness products would soon end.
After becoming health secretary, Kennedy said U.S. compounding pharmacies must be allowed to sell peptides because Americans were increasingly turning to “gray market” peptides made in China and other countries. Those products remain widely available for purchase via online platforms like TikTok.
The White House filing doesn’t give specifics of the new policy, but two people familiar with the plan say it is intended to allow pharmacies to temporarily compound some of the most popular peptides, including BPC-157, a chemical promoted to build muscle and heal injuries. The people spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations.
The update is the latest indication that Kennedy and other Trump administration officials are looking to ease access to unproven products that are popular within the Make America Healthy Again movement. Some of the biggest MAHA figures sell peptide injections and supplements.
The FDA previously placed BPC-157 and more than a dozen other injectable peptides on its list of substances that are too risky to be compounded by pharmacies. Possible risks include contamination, allergic reactions and tumor growth, according to the FDA.
But earlier this year, Kennedy directed the agency to reconsider a short list of chemicals that have been widely promoted by wellness influencers and fitness celebrities.
In July, a panel of external FDA advisers recommended the agency drop its restrictions on six of the seven peptides put before them. That recommendation went against the scientific conclusion of FDA’s staff scientists, who reiterated that none of the peptides had been studied enough to establish their safety and effectiveness.
The new policy sent to the White House would essentially assure compounding pharmacies — specialty businesses that mix customized medications that aren’t available from traditional drugmakers — that they won’t be targeted for producing certain peptides, according to the people familiar with the plan. That approach, known as enforcement discretion, allows the FDA to selectively choose to not enforce some of its own regulations.
Formally adding the peptides to FDA’s list of drugs that are safe for compounding would require federal rulemaking, a process that could take years and involves multiple rounds of public comment. It was not immediately clear if the administration still plans to pursue that process.
The proposal was quickly praised online by some Kennedy allies who sell peptides.
“This is huge,” Brigham Buhler, a wellness clinic operator who sells peptides through an online service, posted on X. “This isn’t about whether you’re for or against peptides. It’s about whether you’re for or against MEDICAL FREEDOM.”
The panel of outside experts that met in July was selected by Kennedy’s health department and included several doctors, pharmacists and consultants who work in the peptide field.
The peptide business has caught the attention of major telehealth providers, including Hims & Hers and Noom. Both companies recently announced plans to offer peptides to their customers if the federal government eases access. Wall Street analysts estimate the market could be worth $2 billion to $3 billion.

Noida Police book two X users for spreading fake news about Dhruv Rathee’s arrest
Noida Police booked two identified and other unidentified X accounts for falsely claiming YouTuber Dhruv Rathee had been arrested, citing concerns over law and order.
Noida Police have registered a case against two identified and other unidentified X accounts for allegedly spreading false claims about YouTuber Dhruv Rathee’s arrest, saying the posts were intended to create panic and disturb law and order in the district.
The case was registered under Sections 197 (imputation, assertions prejudicial to national integration) and 352 (statements conducive to public mischief) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Section 67 of the Information Technology Act at Sector 39 police station.
“On October 16 some social media accounts attempted to disrupt peace and law and order situation through their posts,” sub-inspector Sunil Kumar said in the complaint.
The FIR mentioned two posts, one of which read, “Tough days ahead for Dhruv Rathee. Just this evening, Noida Police arrested him over his videos allegedly disrespecting Hindu gods and urging the Army and police to revolt against the government. The politician behind this is so powerful that even Arvind Kejriwal won’t be able to save him. In the next 10-15 days, Dhruv Rathee is going to regret coming to India**.**”
The other post read, “Druv Rathee has been arrested. Dhruv Rathee has been arrested by Noida Police this time, not Delhi Police. Don’t expect any mercy from Yogi Baba.”
Police officers said that Rathee was not arrested by Noida Police, and no such information had been disseminated through any of the official social media handles of Noida Police. Therefore, the aforementioned information was entirely false, misleading, and baseless, officers added.
Following these posts on October 16, Noida Police also fact-checked the false information, dismissing the claims.
“In the present circumstances, posting such content has spread anger and fear among the public, adversely affecting law and order. The two Twitter users deliberately circulated false and provocative information, thereby attempting to create fear, anger, and distrust toward the state administration and to disrupt public peace. They prepared a misleading narrative to incite and provoke people and attempted to influence law and order,” the FIR accessed by HT stated.
The actions of the Twitter users fell under the category of unlawful acts, including incitement, spreading rumours, disturbing public peace, and spreading panic and disorder through electronic media, police said. They also urged people to rely only on official channels for information, as such “fake news” spreads rapidly and disturbs harmony among people.
Rathee arrived in Delhi recently to take part in the protests against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. He was released following nearly 18 hours of detention by Gurugram Police on October 11, ahead of a protest in Delhi demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
