There has been no shortage of coverage on Elizabeth Holmes, the Silicon Valley fraudster whose biotech startup Theranos reached a peak valuation of $9 billion in 2014 before its supposedly groundbreaking blood test machine was revealed to be vaporware. Books, magazine articles, documentaries, TV dramatizations—the exposés have piled up high.
So, you might ask yourself, why the hype for the forthcoming You Can See Everything, yet another documentary about Holmes, and one that spans three hours?
The excitement is thanks to Nathan Fielder, one of the film’s directors. (Fielder codirected the documentary with Lance Oppenheim). Fielder is a cult-favorite television auteur whose devotees have awaited his showdown with Holmes ever since rumors about him visiting her in prison surfaced last year.
Now that Fielder appears poised to break the containment of an obsessed fan base and conquer the cineplex, it behooves you to get caught up. This will not be a typical documentary: Fielder has made a career of heightened unreality, sowing confusion wherever he goes. To give you some notion of what to expect from his analysis of Holmes, here’s a rundown of his unusual and captivating style.
Business Bona Fides
One reason Fielder makes sense as an interlocutor for big tech’s most notorious con woman is his own history of corporate chicanery. In his breakout TV series Nathan for You (2013–2017), he contrived and implemented bizarre publicity stunts for struggling small businesses. (While he jokes that he “graduated from one of Canada's top business schools with really good grades,” the fact remains he did graduate, unlike Holmes, a Stanford University dropout.)
Andrew Bricker, an associate professor of English at the University of Ghent and academic coordinator for the research project Democratic Literacy and Humour, writes in an email that it’s important to recognize that, throughout his career, Fielder has always played the same altered version of himself, leaving us unsure just who he really is.
Fielder “has made the borderlands of persona and person so ambiguous, so indeterminable, so indefinable, that none of us is entirely in on the joke,” Bricker says.
Nathan for You and Fielder’s subsequent HBO series The Rehearsal, Bricker explains, cast him as “a kind of outlandish problem-solver, someone possessed of what I sometimes call the engineer’s brain, which sees the world strictly through the radically simplified framework of problems and solutions, even if the solutions themselves, ouroboros-style, always lead to new problems.”
Indeed, in his fixer role on Nathan for You, Fielder seeks out overcomplicated loopholes and goes to great lengths to carry out any particular scheme once he sets his mind to it. To help an international exporter avoid high shipping costs on smoke alarms, for example, he comes up with a plan to market them as musical instruments. Then he creates an instructional DVD on how to play one, forms a band that records an original track that includes the device’s shrill beeping, and gets the song featured on the local news, all to legitimize the tariff dodge.
Fielder’s Nathan for You promotions involved careful readings of pertinent laws in order to skirt liability—he went viral by opening a coffee shop called Dumb Starbucks—as well as clever hoaxes and media manipulation. He staged a video of a pig saving a goat from drowning in a pond at a petting zoo, successfully tricking social media users and news stations into thinking it was real, and founded Summit Ice, a nonprofit winter apparel brand that stands against Holocaust denial, which earned it mainstream exposure.
Holmes, of course, played investors and the press for years with savvy PR, styling herself as the next coming of Steve Jobs in order to hype a bogus advance in medical science. If there’s anyone who can grasp the scope and scale of duplicity it took to make the world believe in a nonexistent product, it’s Fielder.
Awkward, Maybe Neurodivergent … and Mean?
Early in his career, Fielder tackled the business world with a recurring spot on the satirical CBC Television news show This Hour Has 22 Minutes. His segment, “Nathan on Your Side,” was a send-up of local consumer advocacy investigations and an early showcase for Fielder’s deadpan humor, as seen in a 2008 report where he role-plays as a customer at an electronics store and invites a salesman to pitch him on an MP3 player but continually dismisses these efforts because he is “just browsing.”
Throughout Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, Fielder has relied on this discomfiting affect to maximize the awkwardness of his conversations with everyone he encounters. Although polite and unassuming—many of his fellow Canadians relate—he lets heavy silences linger, maintains uncomfortable eye contact, and never quite breaks, no matter how funny a situation may be. Fielder also has a knack for flatly echoing what someone else has told him in a way that underscores its absurdity.
With these tics, Bricker says, Fielder often catches his interview subjects off guard, spurring them to blurt out surprising confessions.
Holmes is an ideal target for this poker-faced approach. Kate Rennebohm, a professor of film at Lawrence University, has written about the ethics and artifice of HBO’s The Rehearsal, which follows Fielder as he constructs elaborate simulations of pivotal life events in order to better understand human behavior. Rennebohm writes in an email that Holmes the fraudster represents something like an ultimate test of Fielder’s methods.
Holmes is, according to Rennebohm, “a woman whose infamy rests solely on her apparent ability to totally disregard reality.” For this reason, Rennebohm expects Fielder’s skills as a performer and instigator “will get perhaps their most strenuous exercise yet in this match.”
Bricker says that “we are about to witness a bizarro-land Frost/Nixon, where both interviewer and subject have almost exclusively inhabited semi-fictional personae in public”—Fielder as a mad social scientist, Holmes as an inventor ahead of her time.
But while Holmes may be deserving of invasive scrutiny, some critics are unable to stomach how Fielder incorporates unwitting, ordinary people into his satirical plots, occasionally allowing them to look somewhat foolish or flustered while he remains unflappable. Just as your appetite for “cringe” comedy will determine whether you laugh at the scenarios Fielder orchestrates, the shows have turned into litmus tests on questions of conscience and empathy. Does he take advantage of the working-class folks and background performers drawn into his elaborate web of control, or is he merely reflecting a dysfunctional society back to us?
This tension, along with Fielder’s preoccupations and overall demeanor, have occasioned plenty of speculation around whether he has ever been diagnosed with a mental condition. The Rehearsal has led to viewers theorizing that Fielder is on the autism spectrum or otherwise neurodivergent. Fielder acknowledged this discourse in the second season of the show and underwent an fMRI brain scan that could have pointed toward such a diagnosis, though he did not divulge the results.
Others have thrown the word “sociopath” around when discussing Fielder’s work, but not always in a negative sense. As one X user recently noted in a post anticipating You Can See Everything: “Nathan Fielder doing a movie about how Elizabeth Holmes is a deceptive sociopath feels exactly like when Dexter takes down a worse serial killer.”
Unpredictable Anthropology
Even starting from the simplest premise, Fielder ventures into strange territory. In a Nathan for You episode in which he counsels a realtor to employ a psychic medium to ensure that the homes she’s selling aren’t haunted, she drops the bombshell that she was once choked by a ghost in Switzerland. In another, Fielder has a gas station owner advertise impossibly cheap prices, attainable only through a hilariously inconvenient rebate process. Yet the memorable part of the segment is when the business owner reveals that he drinks his grandson’s urine when he feels scared.
Fielder often follows up on peculiar discoveries, allowing people’s eccentricities and the unintended consequences of his own meddling to dictate where he goes next. As such, there’s an investigative element to his process that is certainly appropriate when dealing with an enigma like Holmes, a convicted criminal who continues to proclaim her innocence with a cheery warmth that comes off like utter self-delusion.
In 2023, Fielder and Oppenheim, the codirectors of You Can See Everything, moved into the Del Mar, California, house shared by Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans. The group lived together in the house for over a month, right up until the day Holmes reported to prison for her 11-year sentence. They weren’t sure if what they were shooting could be turned into a movie, but as Fielder said at the New York Film Festival last month, a sense of deepening mystery compelled them to move forward.
“Lance and I would talk about what we thought happened there, and we’d completely disagree on … what we thought was happening,” he explained. “And we were like, ‘Oh, this is really interesting, if we can’t agree on what’s happening, there’s something here.’”
Fielder has “a remarkable talent” for using those frictions to twist and expand his narrative, Rennebohm says. She cites The Rehearsal's second season, which is inspired by Fielder’s theory about how the breakdown in communication between airline pilots and copilots can lead to deadly accidents. In order to act out his model of cockpit cooperation, he spends two years earning a commercial license for himself, ultimately flying a Boeing 737 full of actors (all of whom have scripted roles to perform while aboard) from San Bernardino, California, to the Nevada border and back.
When it comes to Fielder following a thread as far as he can, Rennebohm says, “I expect this document of his time with Holmes to be no different.”
The Search for Reality
What has emerged in Fielder’s most recent output might be described as anxiety over the nature of truth.
The Rehearsal (2022–present) is, on its face, a setup to explore the way we conduct ourselves under destabilizing circumstances. In the first season, Fielder concocts a scene where a man can practice confessing to his bar trivia team that he lied about having a master’s degree. For the rest of the season, Fielder is consumed by an elaborate, multi-episode experiment in which a woman evaluates what life would be like as a mother, aided by child actors (and Fielder serving as her platonic coparent).
Yet there are countless moments when Fielder is more concerned with the authenticity of these staged interactions—and their ongoing failure to fully match reality—than their potential outcomes. The actual subject of the show, we learn, is his fanatical mode of observation.
Fielder is often shown walking around with a laptop attached to his torso with a harness so he can take notes on the move. He catches the smallest inaccuracies and oversights, and he tweaks the next reproduction accordingly. He intuits the psychological dissonance of pretending to do something instead of really doing it, and he has frank interviews with his cast and consultants in hopes of closing those gaps.
The Rehearsal, according to Rennebohm, “offers the fictionalized Nathan the chance to substitute manufactured, seemingly controllable realities for the reality of his actual life, though often even these fabricated scenarios ultimately resist Nathan's totalitarian drives.”
Bricker points out that the fundamental “paradox” of Fielder’s “supposed revelations of truth” is that he only arrives at his conclusions through his constructed persona and meticulous simulations. “Even if these are true moments of authentic self-disclosure, how would we even know, given the artificial framework of their disclosure?” he asks.
But that, too, makes You Can See Everything a fascinating proposition. Bricker notes that Fielder and Oppenheim are in a position to play with the “mushy boundaries between reality and fiction” through dramatic reconstruction, stylization, and careful editing.
Rennebohm says that Holmes also serves as an avatar of a tech industry with ambitions of exceeding or dispensing human reality itself. In this and so many other ways, a face-off between Fielder and the disgraced startup founder is the collision of an unstoppable force and an immovable object. All you can do is brace for impact.

For entrepreneur Akhila Vijayaraghavan, whey has always been a convenient way to get 100-120 grams of protein every day. “I train regularly, so it was an easy addition to my routine and helped me consistently hit my protein intake,” she says. This is why she couldn’t help but notice how much whey prices have increased over the last few months “I understand that there are broader supply and import issues behind the increase, particularly because India is so heavily dependent on imported whey. But for a consumer, the result is pretty simple: something that used to be an everyday purchase suddenly feels expensive,” she says.
For instance, a kilogram of True Basics and Whole Truth whey concentrate, which once cost around ₹2500 last year, has gone up to around ₹3500, a clear leap of nearly ₹1000, points out Akhila. Other brands aren’t far behind, either. Optimum Nutrition, the protein brand associated with numerous elite athletes, including Neeraj Chopra, Rishabh Pant, and Priya Punia, is currently pricing 4 kg of its Gold Standard 100% Whey Protein at ₹17,649, while the same amount of MuscleBlaze’s Biozyme Performance Whey is ₹13,999, an over 20% jump from last year, when they were about ₹15,000 and a little over ₹10,000 respectively.
Several forces
According to Vijay P, operations and procurement manager at Chennai-based OMG Labs, a functional nutrition brand offering both whey and plant-based protein products, this sudden hike is not the result of a single event, but of several forces coming together. Though India has a large dairy industry, we still do not produce enough whey for the protein supplement industry because much of our dairy processing focusses on products like milk, curd, paneer, and ghee rather than large-scale cheese production, Vijay explains. “Whey is mainly obtained as a by-product of cheese manufacturing, and because domestic availability is limited, we depend significantly on imports.” This means that when there is a shortage or price increase in the international market, it directly affects the Indian market, says Vijay.
“Freight costs, currency fluctuations and other import-related costs also add to the final prices,” he says. For instance, whey isolate prices, which were ₹2,200 per kilogram exclusive of GST in December last year, now cost around ₹3,400. “Apart from the whey, we also have to account for the flavours, packaging, other raw materials, labour and manufacturing costs, which have pushed the overall finished product cost to ₹4,200-5,000 from ₹3,000-36,000, depending on quantity and customers.”
The price spike also stems from a significant increase in demand for dietary protein that current supply just can’t meet. “We are going through a protein bubble right now where everyone is talking about it, so everyone is aware of and looking for protein,” says Chennai-based fitness and nutrition coach Raj Ganpath.
Given that the Indian diet is notoriously protein-deficient, most of us may need a scoop or two of a protein supplement to get the ideal amount of protein, “about 1.25 to 1.75 grams of protein per kilo per day,” says Raj, pointing out that our meals consist largely of carbohydrates, fat, and some vegetables. Even though most Indians do eat meat — a recent National Family Health Survey (NFHS) found that 70-80% consume meat, fish, poultry, and eggs — for many of us, it does not happen regularly enough to meet daily protein needs. “In India, a non-vegetarian is essentially a vegetarian who eats a little bit of meat, so we still rely on vegetarian protein sources,” says Raj, the co-founder of The Quad and founder of The Slow Burn Method, a sustainable weight-loss coaching programme.
Additionally, while other new protein options exist in the market, for instance, functional dairy products like Greek yoghurt and protein milk, gram for gram, even with the increase in costs, “it roughly costs you the same amount of money as whey (if it is a concentrate or blend, isolate is a little more), around 6-7 rupees per gram of protein,” he says.
That is why people like Santosh Raghavan, an entrepreneur also based in Chennai, prefer whey protein to hit their daily goals. Given that he does not cook meat at home, “whey gives me the best protein-to-calorie ratio, allowing me room to eat other whole foods too. It is also convenient post-workout since I can have it immediately for recovery and absorption, without needing to wait for a meal to be prepared,” he says. And yes, he also likes the supplement’s taste. “It helps me think I have had some dessert, which is great for a guy like me, with a sweet tooth.”
The rise in whey prices, however, has influenced his choices considerably, he says. “I used to be loyal to a couple of brands, but now I have become brand agnostic. I just look at the label and pick up what is affordable,” says Santosh, who has also experimented with vegan protein, “which didn’t work for me,” and fermented yeast protein, “which I found decent.”
Options and opportunities
This trepidation among long-time whey users seems common, as Aditi Mammen Gupta, the co-founder of plant-based protein powder brand Origin Nutrition, points out. Earlier, people who used whey regularly often found the transition difficult, “but the thing is, plant protein was very different. Now, with new technologies and processes, plant protein has become much better in terms of taste, texture, mixability...everything really,” she says, pointing out that skyrocketing whey prices have led to “a lot of people shifting to plant protein. They seem to be quite happy with plant, especially when they discover that when they stick to it for a while, they feel a lot better.” As a business, given this shift, Origin is all set to expand its product range, says Aditi, who believes, “I think it is a really exciting time to be in the plant protein space.”
While rising whey prices will likely push more people to try affordable, equally effective plant- or yeast-based options, the consensus is that whey will continue to have a strong user base. “Whey still has strong demand because it is well established in the fitness and sports nutrition market,” says Vijay, while Sahil Kukreja feels that whey offers distinct advantages that justify the premium. “Whey provides all nine essential amino acids, is highly digestible, and is naturally rich in leucine, which helps stimulate muscle protein synthesis. That makes it an efficient protein source, particularly when someone wants a substantial protein serving in a relatively small volume,” says the co-founder of The Func Lab in Mumbai, a functional nutrition start-up that manufactures whey, plant protein, and electrolytes.
As the whey conversation goes beyond sports nutrition, it is now also being used in everyday beverages, snacks, and foods. “Healthy ageing and weight management are expanding the consumer base, while GLP-1 usage adds to this demand because reduced appetite makes getting adequate protein more challenging,” says Sahil, adding that he would, however, be careful not to attribute the entire price increase to GLP-1s.
But Sahil feels that the whey protein shortage challenge may also be an opportunity for the domestic industry to strengthen whey recovery and processing capacity. “Sustained whey premiums will also encourage innovation in plant proteins and other protein sources. That requires investment in collection, quality systems, and specialised processing — not just higher milk production,” he says.
Vijay, too, agrees that the crisis could prove a “strategic opportunity” for India to build a stronger domestic whey ecosystem. “Indian dairy and nutrition companies are moving in this direction, with major players investing in whey and value-added dairy products. This could reduce our exposure to international supply disruptions and foreign exchange movement.” However, given that capacity-building takes time, for the time being, “whey protein is likely to remain a strategically important and relatively expensive ingredient for the Indian nutrition industry.”
And despite rising costs, whey remains the preferred option for consumers like Akhila because of its familiarity, taste, texture, and convenience. “I know it works well for me as a practical way to get more protein,” she says. What has changed, however, is how often she turns to it, cycling it with other protein sources, including fish, meat, eggs and low-fat paneer, “because the price makes daily use harder to justify. At the current prices, I am much more conscious about when I actually need it, rather than automatically having it every day.”

President Donald Trump is still playing hardball with Russia, according to US Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
Wright defended Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia during a Sunday interview on CNN's "State of the Union with Jake Tapper and Dana Bash."
In September, Trump signed into law a sanctions package targeting Russian officials and parts of its economy in an effort to pressure Russia amid its war on Ukraine. Last week, Trump issued an executive order waiving those new sanctions, other restrictions, and some duties on Russia.
In early October, Trump also announced an agreement with President Vladimir Putin under which Russia would supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to America and the global market.
"President Trump waived sanctions just on diesel exports, and what's the one thing Russia has not been able to export over the last month or so? Diesel, because they're short of diesel," Wright said.
The Energy Secretary said waiving the sanctions solves two problems: the diesel oil shortage and Russia's ongoing war with Ukraine.
"This is pressuring Russia. Russia does not have diesel to export," Wright said. "The only way they can get additional diesel to export is if they turn down the conflict with Ukraine."
Wright said Russia would have to enter into an energy ceasefire or reduce its war efforts to have enough additional diesel to export.
"This is not going soft on Russia. This is an incentive to end the war," Wright added.
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said waiving sanctions on Russia "seems wrong" to him. US lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle also criticized the move, including Republican Sen. Thom Tillis.
"Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day," Tillis wrote on X.
He added, "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin."
Diesel and regular gas prices have skyrocketed globally as the US war on Iran drags on. Following surprise attacks by the US and Israel on Iran in February, Iran effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz, which is a major waterway through which much of the world's diesel and oil is shipped. Last week, the International Energy Agency said the diesel shortage could run into 2027.
That's a problem for Trump, who is hoping voters overlook high gas prices and concerns over the cost of living when they head to the polls this November for the midterm elections. Higher diesel prices mean higher shipping costs, which trickle down to consumers as inflated prices for everyday goods.
Wright also appeared on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday, during which he said Trump was trying to find "innovative" ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
"This is a motivation for Russia to figure out how they can actually export some diesel," he said.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

At Windsor Park in Riverside, just outside Launceston in northern Tasmania, a masked lapwing has claimed prime real estate in the middle of a community sports ground, showing complete indifference to the weekend cricket matches taking place around it.
Warming a nest of eggs, the bird has been affectionately dubbed “Faf Swoop Plessis” by locals – a play on former South African cricket captain Faf du Plessis.
Because the species is protected under state law, carrying fines of up to $21,300 for disturbing nests, ground staff have had to mow around the site, while players steer clear.
During a match early in the season, Great Northern Raiders player Caleb Brewer drew the short straw and was stationed directly beside the nest.
“At the start it was pretty weird, but towards the middle we kind of got used to it and the plover wasn’t too bad at the end,” Brewer told local paper The Examiner.
The following weekend, Riverside first-grade opener Josh Partridge was tasked with fielding near the plover, but reached a peaceful “mutual understanding”, according to The Examiner.
“It was like the plover knew there was a game of cricket going on,” he said. “We weren’t interfering with what was going on in its life, so it didn’t want to interfere with what was going on in ours.”
That kind of sporting truce is common, according to Mark Holdsworth OAM from BirdLife Tasmania.
“Lapwings will often become accustomed to the local patterns of people using a site and in many situations people modify their behaviour to avoid the core nesting area,” Holdsworth said. Everyone has learned to live with each other.”
While masked lapwings – widely known across Australia as plovers – have an intimidating call and reputation for swooping during spring nesting season, choosing a wide-open lawn is actually a calculated survival tactic.
Sports ovals are a “fantastic place” for them to nest, Holdsworth said, because unobstructed views mean parent birds can spot threats early.
Sean Dooley from BirdLife Australia also said that what looks like eccentric behaviour to humans makes sense for plovers.
“The places they choose to nest can seem crazy from our perspective, but there is logic to it,” Dooley said. “They like to nest out in the open so they can see danger coming and they rely on camouflage to hide their eggs and their chicks. So by nesting on an oval, they have a clear view in all directions.”
He said that when people give the bird a wide berth, lapwings generally realise they are not under threat.
“They definitely aren’t out to get us by nature, they really only care about making sure their chicks aren’t being threatened …
“Swooping isn’t their only tactic; they also put on a display that mimics having a broken wing to lure potential threats away. They’re just being good parents and doing all they can to protect their young.”
Lapwing eggs hatch after 28 to 30 days of shared incubation by both parents. If a clutch is infertile, incubation can continue for several weeks, while birds will often nest again at the same site if their eggs are destroyed.
Once hatched, the chicks quickly leave the nest. Dooley said parent birds carry stray egg fragments away to avoid attracting predators, before guiding their offspring across the turf.
“If we can just give them their space, they can move away from the nest area once they are walking,” he said.
The West Tamar mayor, Christina Holmdahl, said council maintenance teams look after dozens of parks and sporting grounds across the municipality, encountering at least 10 nesting sites every year.
“Given the protected listing of the masked lapwings in Tasmania, our staff take their responsibility of looking after these birds very seriously and take extra precautions to protect the birds and any nests they find,” Holmdahl said.
Council workers maintain strict buffer zones around the birds and their nests when conducting maintenance.
“The plovers never act aggressively towards our staff on the ground,” she said.
The standoff coincides with the annual Aussie Bird Count which runs from Monday 19 October.
Now in its 13th year, the national citizen science project invites the public to record bird sightings to help researchers track how native species are coping with urban development and a changing climate. Last year, the Australian magpie was the most commonly spotted species, while the rainbow lorikeet recorded the highest overall tally.
“The count is a great opportunity to discover the birds that share your neighbourhood and understand more about them,” BirdLife Australia’s James Johnson said.” For many of us, that’s likely to include the amazing masked lapwing.”

NFL announcing duo Joe Buck and Troy Aikman, who helped revive Monday Night Football after moving to ESPN in 2022, now find themselves at the center of one of the NFL’s dishiest off-field dramas.
Money, as usual, is seen as the root cause.
Buck last month agreed to a contract renewal with ESPN parent Disney, with the 5-year deal reportedly worth $108 million. He has branched out to non-sports fare, guest-hosting Good Morning America and hosting streaming quiz show Sports Jeopardy!
Aikman, meanwhile, has yet to re-sign, with his current contract set to expire after the Super Bowl, which ESPN will carry for the first time next February. (Sibling broadcast network ABC will have the big game for the first time since 2006.)
Watch on Deadline
The pair, who called games together on Fox for 20 years, are said to have clashed over the differing contract status. Front Office Sports last week detailed a heated exchange between the two witnessed by a number of colleagues prior to last Monday’s L.A. Rams-Buffalo Bills game.
Aikman did not push back on the report when asked about it during an appearance on Dallas-Fort worth radio station KTCK-FM. “Well, I think there’s probably a time and a place for all that to be discussed,” he said with a chuckle. “I don’t know if now is the time. I don’t know that it’s hard to figure out kind of what happened.”
The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback said he plans to continue as MNF analyst through the end of the season. “I’ll be a free agent at the end of the year and kind of see what happens,” he said. “But I’m looking forward to whatever the rest of this year does hold, with the Super Bowl and all that and where my next landing spot may be.”
Meadowlark Media co-founder Dan Le Batard, who had his own stormy relationship with ESPN during a decade as a host there, said on his daily podcast Friday that he was stunned by Aikman’s comments. He said he interpreted them as “‘I’m not coming back.’ And it’s before the Super Bowl! They’ve got to work together!” Le Batard also blamed Buck for the reported sequence of events. “I can understand where Troy would be very upset if Joe Buck just negotiated his own deal.”
Disney put Buck and Aikman onstage last May toward the top of its upfront presentation to advertisers, an event that also featured remarks from Josh D’Amaro, who succeeded Bob Iger as CEO last February. As chief exec, D’Amaro has reaffirmed that ESPN, rumored over the years to be a spinoff candidate, is very much a part of the corporate portfolio.
Prior to the past week’s bumps, Buck and Aikman had been having a smooth ride. The pair’s jump from Fox injected restored energy and credibility to MNF, with many sports media pundits reaffirming their view that the duo is the best in the business. Before 2022, the onetime prime-time pioneer cycled through a succession of announcers and received increasingly middling games on the NFL schedule, which led to stagnating ratings and frustrated ad buyers.
Times have changed at ESPN, however, thanks to a sweeping deal with the NFL that exchanged a 10% stake in the network for control of media assets including NFL Network. The ownership ties open up intriguing possibilities, with speculation centering on numerous candidates to succeed Aikman.
Two of the most intriguing names being bandied about are Peyton Manning and Travis Kelce. The former’s company, Omaha Productions, is part-owned by the NFL and Manning is a ubiquitous media presence on top of his Hall of Fame playing credentials. Kelce is still playing for the Kansas City Chiefs but is of course even better known to the masses as Taylor Swift’s ball and chain.
An ESPN rep declined to comment when contacted by Deadline. After news of Buck’s re-upping surfaced last month, the company issued a statement saying it was determined to focus on its historic Super Bowl broadcast, which Disney is hyping with a year-long promotional blitz. “To that end, we won’t be addressing talent contract specifics publicly before the Super Bowl,” the statement said.
Deadline encountered the same sentiment from multiple sources in the ESPN orbit in recent days, who noted that the big game is nearly four months away, leaving time for some climate change. “A lot can happen between now and then,” one said.
Despite those efforts to calm the waters, a fairly broad consensus has formed that Aikman is a short-timer at ESPN.
“It sure feels like goodbye, doesn’t it?” said Bryan Curtis of the Ringer during an appearance on Jimmy Traina’s Underscore Media podcast Friday. “It sure does,” Traina replied.
	They both went on to marvel at the turn of events for MNF and the tensions in the broadcast booth “spilling out into the public in this weird, weird way,” as Curtis put it. ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro’s “biggest win before he resigned the NFL deal,” he added, was “getting Joe and Troy away from Fox because it solved the problem. It was over. … And for the drama to be located over there now, what a turnaround that is.”

If you have the scratch, they have the scares
The horror biz is booming, as recent Weekend Edition reporting has made clear. But not everyone wants to be up close and personal the with the IRL frights of a haunted house or spooky corn maze. Many would rather experience nightstalkers, goblins and witches that can't escape the theater or TV screen, or zombies and werewolves that won't lunge off the pages of a book.
Chanthal Harris owns Long Dark House in Alexandria, Va. It's a bookstore devoted exclusively to horror and the supernatural. It's been doing business for just over a month and Harris says she already has steady traffic from both genre stalwarts and first-timers.
"You know, I think people are looking for things that they wouldn't normally find in a lot of other places. I've had people comment about the curation and how they're finding something unexpected," Harris says. "And I'm also surprised at how many people are trying to dip their toe into horror."
Harris is no newbie herself: books and horror have been constant companions.
"My love of horror started from an early age. And I joke, but I do truly blame my parents because my dad was a[n] avid reader. He probably takes responsibility more for my fantasy/sci-fi love, but my mother always loved horror," Harris says.
"To me it was completely normal. I didn't think of it as a spooky thing."
So after a career in aviation, Harris decided to follow her passion and open Long Dark House.
"It's exceeded my expectations and, you know, could be the season. But I just am so appreciative that people are as excited about these genres and this experience as I am. And so anytime someone walks through the door, I'm a little surprised and happy and grateful," she says.
The numbers say Chanthal Harris shouldn't be very surprised. Market research by Nielsen says profits from the genre have jumped almost 26-percent year over year.
And the numbers are good for films as well.
Last May, Backrooms — about a horrifying liminal space that exists beyond our own reality — smashed box office records.
With just a $10 million budget, petty cash for Hollywood, it grossed over $400 million worldwide. The feature film started as a short on YouTube. And It's just one title from the newly-merged studio Blumhouse Atomic Monster.
Abhijay Prakash and Michael Clear head up the studio. Prakash is Blumhouse Atomic Monster's president and CEO. Clear is the president of Atomic Monster and leads the studio's emerging directors program.
"We're drawn like moths to a flame to things that are scary," Clear says. "We reached out to Kane Parsons who had created the short and at the time he was 15 or 16; he was still in high school."
Despite the headlines Blumhouse Atomic Monster garnered for hiring Parsons, Clear adds it's not really all that new for them.
"We've always kind of scoured a variety of sources, particularly for filmmakers who have a sense of how to scare people. Going all the way back to one of the first movies we produced, Lights Out, David Sandberg, the director of that film, was actually himself a YouTube creator," Clear says.
"They say it's hard to describe what scary is but I know it when I see it."
A post-COVID reanimation?
Abhijay Prakash says the COVID-19 pandemic had an outsized impact on the horror film industry.
"Horror as a share of the box office…pre-COVID, was never more than 10% of the box office. Then after COVID though, it's occupying a much larger share. It's over 15%, almost 20% last year and this year. And inside of that we are over half of that box office," Prakash says.
"So our market share is over 50% of the horror box office. And that's where we're focused. We live and breathe it."
Our friends over at the Recreational Fear Lab theorize people are flocking to fear more these days because the real world has been just so darn scary.
But Michael Clear thinks it could be a bit more complicated than that.
"I agree it's part of it, but I also think that one of the things that shifted [is] the bar has been rising for what people need or what draws people to the theatres. It's been rising consistently over the last 10, 15 years," Clear says.
"Maybe all the isolation has just driven people towards more social activities," he adds. "People are craving collective experiences. We're finding more now than before the pandemic that people are going to movies in larger groups. And it just so happens that our genre, because it's participatory — if we do our jobs right, we're getting reactions, audible reactions from the audience — and it can be more fun to experience that with your friends."
"Scary stories in the dark," Abhijay Prakash underlines. "[It] has delivered for thousands of years."
It has to be "real"
While Blumhouse Atomic Monster makes its bid to reign supreme in theaters, many scream queens and kings are finding bite-sized horror scrolling social media. And often, those scary shorts are the products of AI.
"Personally, I think that, you know, anything that makes filmmaking more democratic can can be great. You know, people who find tools that can enable them to create it will allow more people, more talented people, to enter the space," Michael Clear says.
He cautions that audiences want things to feel authentic, as though the horror on the screen is genuine.
"When it comes to our movies, I think one of the things that just happens to be a characteristic of our genre is that the things that are scariest are the things that feel the most real. So really, when you get down to the way that AI images or whatever may impact movies, you know, our focus is always on doing things as real as possible. Doing things as practically as possible," Clear says.
The 'Disney of horror'
Abhijay Prakash told The Ankler early this year that his goal for Blumhouse Atomic Monster is to be the Disney of fear.
He breaks down what he means:
"Every place that consumers engage with scary stories is a place that we as a business, as a company obsessed with horror and scary stories will be. And then it's only a question of the business model," Prakash says.
Prakash says the studio is exploring creating an attraction from its Five Nights at Freddy's franchise and he also points to the popularity of the stage version of Paranormal Activity.
"So that really is a guiding principle for our company. We want to be everywhere where horror is relevant and it's taking a bigger and bigger place in the culture," Prakash says.
Michael Clear says the idea isn't just to cater to existing fans of the genre, but to grow the fanbase for all things spooky itself. "We like to think that we can provide a kind of gateway horror," he says.
Next week we get a lesson in horror storytelling from one of the most prolific writers in the genre — Stephen Graham Jones.

Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
- Published
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.
The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.
"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."
Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
[The youth] just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created"
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.
"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.
More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.
Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.
- 'They aimed to kill' - BBC identifies security forces who shot Kenya anti-tax protesters 
  - Published28 April 2025
Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.
He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.
"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.
He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.
I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.
They promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths"
"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.
"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."
"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.
"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.
"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."
He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."
Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.
The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.
"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."
Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

The three accused in the firing incident involving Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff reached Andheri railway station after opening fire at his car in Mumbai’s Juhu area on Sunday, October 18. The investigation has revealed that they abandoned the motorcycle used in the attack at the station before fleeing.
Police have seized the motorcycle and are examining its records to establish the accused persons’ movements. Preliminary findings suggest that the vehicle is registered in Mumbai. Investigators are checking its previous records using the registration number and chassis number, while CCTV footage is being analysed to trace the suspects’ movements after they abandoned the bike.
Meanwhile, videos of the firing incident have surfaced on social media, showing two attackers firing at the actor’s car from different positions. One of them also attempts to open the vehicle’s door before the duo flees on a motorcycle.
In the footage, one attacker is seen firing from the front of the car, while the other shoots from the side, near the passenger seat. The second assailant tries to open the car door but fails. Both are then seen escaping from the scene on their motorcycle.
It remains unclear whether the attackers knew where Shroff was seated inside the vehicle when the shooting took place.
In another video, Shroff is seen taking control of his car and rushing his injured driver to a hospital. The actor is seen moving from the passenger seat to the driver’s seat before driving away to seek medical assistance. Blood is also visible on the car door and on the road.
People at the scene were heard urging the actor to hurry, shouting, “Jaldi Leke Jao, Tiger. Go fast, Go Fast, bhai.”
In another video capturing the moment of the firing, recorded by a bystander, the car is seen approaching the exit gate of a football ground in Juhu as people attempt to catch a glimpse of the actor. As the vehicle leaves the premises, five gunshots can be heard in quick succession, followed by screams from people at the scene.
A social media post linked to the Bishnoi gang has claimed responsibility for the firing on Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff. The post, attributed to gangster Anil Pandit, surfaced after the incident. Police are currently verifying its authenticity and the claims it contains.

A year-long celebration of renowned clinician, teacher, and humanitarian, the late K.V. Thiruvengadam will kick off in his centenary year on Sunday (October 11, 2026). The celebrations, in memory of Prof. Thiruvengadam’s extraordinary impact on medicine both in Chennai and beyond, will focus on restoring the art of listening to the patient, examining at the bedside, thinking before ordering a test, and finally, and dwelling on the fundamental question of what it means to be a good physician in an age of extraordinary technology.
K. Vardachari Thiruvengadam, fondly known as KVT, was born in 1926. He graduated from Government Stanley Medical College in 1950 and taught for 31 years both at his alma mater and at Madras Medical College, and subsequently at private institutions. His core areas of specialty were chest medicine, allergies and infectious diseases. His career coincided with a period when medicine was rapidly expanding, but his students remember that he did not teach bedside examination as a ceremonial ritual — he taught it as a way of thinking, listening to the patient, and asking the right questions.
Prof. KVT was a scientist as well as a clinician. He received formal training in chest diseases in the U.K., under the Colombo Plan. He published nearly 100 papers in national and international journals. Among the many areas of his research were chikungunya fever, neurological complications following influenza and amoebiasis. He also investigated traditional medicines in allergic lung and skin diseases. He worked for decades in the government system, among the poorest in society, and believed that government service could achieve extraordinary things when doctors had the willingness to serve. For him, medicine was a social responsibility.
Enduring legacy
Prof. KVT’s awards and recognitions were numerous, and included the Padma Shri in 1981 and the Dr. B.C. Roy Award for Eminent Medical Teacher, alongside multiple other distinctions. But perhaps the most enduring aspect of his legacy is in the number of students who remember him and his teachings and went on to become teachers and leaders themselves, committing to his principle of what you learn and experience must be passed on to the next generation.
The centenary year celebration’s objective is not merely to celebrate him, but to translate his philosophy into medical education. The commemoration is not an argument against technology, but an argument against technology without context, and for the need for human clinical reasoning to be paramount.
The proposed celebration aims to take to medical students and postgraduate doctors the importance of history-taking, clinical examination, clinical reasoning and their role not only in diagnosis and management, but also in medical research.
On October 31, the third Prof. K.V. Thiruvengadam Memorial Oration will be delivered at Sree Balaji Medical College and Hospital, by S.R. Chandra, on ‘The Patient Speaks, the Doctor Thinks and the Research Begins’, alongside a national conference on movement disorders.

West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari and Chief Secretary Manoj Agarwal visited those injured at Calcutta Medical College and Hospital....Read More
Condolences pour in
Several leaders, including PM Narendra Modi, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari and former chief minister Mamata Banerjee, expressed condolences over the stampede deaths.
“Deeply shocked and saddened to learn about the stampede at the Chore Bagan Puja Pandal. I pray to Maa Durga for the speedy recovery of all those injured and for strength and courage for their families during this difficult time,” she said in a tweet.
Adhikari said families of some victims have reached the hospital while authorities are trying to get in touch with the others.
Bengal governor RN Ravi, union home minister Amit Shah, the Aam Aadmi Party and TMC leader Kunal Ghosh also expressed grief.
What we know so far
The stampede occurred at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durgotsab Samity puja pandal in Kolkata. The pandal was subsequently closed, and so were other such pandals that were seeing a heavy footfall on Durga Puja.
The state government launched a helpline 18003455678. The Kolkata Police launched another helpline 03322141310.
“The incident took place around 7:30 pm. The crowd at the pandal was already swelling. As it started to rain more people entered the pandal. This resulted in a stampede. Several people were injured,” Dipali Das, a pandal hopper, told the media.

Mapped: The fastest-growing cities in the world
Ghaziabad, a city next to Delhi, tops the table of annual growth rates at 5.2 per cent, followed by Surat in the western Indian state of Gujarat

The world's fastest-growing cities are all in Asia and Africa, with Indian cities topping the list in terms of annual growth, according to a global ranking of urban population growth.
Every city in the top 10 lists for the "Fastest Growing Cities in the World 2026" rankings, published by World Population Review, is either in Asia or Africa.
Ghaziabad, a city next to Delhi, tops the table of annual growth rates at 5.2 per cent, followed by Surat in the western Indian state of Gujarat at 4.99 per cent, Kabul in Afghanistan at 4.74 per cent and Lagos in Nigeria at 4.44 per cent.
Delhi itself is growing at 3 per cent a year, and the table also includes capitals like Dhaka at 3.79 per cent, Nairobi at 4 per cent and Kampala in Uganda at 4.03 per cent. Toluca in Mexico is the one city in that group outside Asia and Africa.
The fastest-growing cities, by annual growth rate
- Ghaziabad, India (next to Delhi): 5.2 per cent
- Surat, India (in Gujarat): 4.99 per cent
- Kabul, Afghanistan: 4.74 per cent
- Lagos, Nigeria: 4.44 per cent
- Toluca, Mexico: 4.25 per cent
- Lubumbashi, Democratic Republic of Congo: 4.1 per cent
- Kampala, Uganda: 4.03 per cent
- Joint eighth, all at 4 per cent: Luanda (Angola), Dar es Salaam (Tanzania), Nairobi (Kenya), Bamako (Mali), Patna, Rajkot and Faridabad (India) and Maputo (Mozambique)
The ranking draws on growth rates from the City Mayors Foundation, a research group that studies cities, and on United Nations estimates that cover different periods.
Ranked by total growth in a five-year-period, the top ten list is led by Malappuram in the southern Indian state of Kerala, where the population rose by 44 per cent, followed by Can Tho in Vietnam and Suqian in China at 37 per cent each.
Kozhikode, also in Kerala, grew by 35 per cent, Abuja in Nigeria by 34 per cent and Suzhou in China by 33 per cent, while Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates and Putian in China grew by 32 per cent each and Muscat in Oman and Kollam in Kerala by 31 per cent each.
In terms of most new residents each hour, it puts Delhi first, followed by Shanghai, Dhaka, Kinshasa in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Chongqing, Lahore, Bengaluru, Lagos, Cairo and Beijing.
The list of the world’s most populated cities has also changed in the last decade. Jakarta, the Indonesian capital, has overtaken Tokyo as the world’s biggest city, with 41.9 million people against Tokyo’s 33.4 million. Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh, rose from ninth place to second with 36.6 million people, and the UN projects it will become the biggest city by 2050.
The 20 biggest cities, by total population
- Jakarta, Indonesia: 41.9 million
- Dhaka, Bangladesh: 36.6 million
- Tokyo, Japan: 33.4 million
- Delhi, India: 30.2 million
- Shanghai, China: 29.6 million
- Guangzhou, China: 27.6 million
- Cairo, Egypt: 25.6 million
- Manila, Philippines: 24.7 million
- Kolkata, India: 22.6 million
- Seoul, South Korea: 22.5 million
- Karachi, Pakistan: 21.4 million
- Mumbai, India: 20.2 million
- São Paulo, Brazil: 19.0 million
- Bangkok, Thailand: 18.2 million
- Mexico City, Mexico: 17.7 million
- Beijing, China: 17.0 million
- Lahore, Pakistan: 15.2 million
- Istanbul, Turkey: 15.0 million
- Moscow, Russia: 14.5 million
- Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam: 14.1 million
World Population Review said about 55 per cent of the world's people live in urban areas, a share that is expected to reach 68 per cent by 2050. It attributed the growth to the larger job markets, higher wages and better schools and services that cities offer, and said cities across Asia and Africa were growing fastest.
The United Nations projects that India, China and Nigeria will account for 35 per cent of the growth in the world's urban population between 2018 and 2050, according to the ranking.
Many cities are growing faster than their infrastructure can cope with, World Population Review said. In Lagos, it said, fewer than 10 per cent of people live in homes with sewer connections and fewer than 20 per cent have access to tap water, with many homes in slums and informal settlements on the edge of the city.

Greens senator Jordon Steele-John says he has been falsely accused of inappropriate conduct
In short:
Greens senator Jordan Steele-John has addressed allegations of inappropriate conduct towards women.
In a public statement on social media, he denied any wrongdoing and blamed the public fallout from the allegations against him on party "factionalism".
What's next?
Senator Steele-John says he is not on leave and the matter is now subject to an internal Greens investigation.
Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has denied allegations of inappropriate conduct raised in a letter to the Greens, which he says included false allegations of sexual assault, and blamed the public fallout from the allegations against him on party "factionalism".
The Greens have been in crisis management since the existence of a 47-page dossier surfaced about how the WA Greens would manage media coverage of allegations made about Senator Steele-John.
It was previously reported Senator Steele-John had taken leave from the party room last week after a letter from seven party members was sent to the office of Greens leader David Shoebridge.
According to media reports the letter alleged the writers were aware of "multiple allegations" about his behaviour in the presence of women, although none of the writers was said to have direct knowledge of "the matters involved", according to Senator Shoebridge.
In a public statement on social media, Senator Steele-John said, among the false allegations made against him, was an allegation of sexual assault, which police had investigated and made no adverse findings against him, with a finding of no charges.
He said that, with respect to that complaint, he had faced abuse and threats before the original complaint to police was made.
Senator Steele-John addressed several other allegations which he said were put to him by a journalist, which are now the subject of an internal Greens investigation.
He said a nickname others used to refer to him, "Feels on wheels", had grown from its original meaning to something "more sinister".
"Other parties started using [the name] to refer to me after I became emotional early in my career while giving speeches about the Royal Commission into Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation of Disabled People," he said.
"This phrase, which mocked my disability and my emotions, had taken on a new, more sinister meaning: that I had treated women inappropriately."
The senator said his experience as a victim of abuse had collided with "political games", and denied he had taken leave after the allegations surfaced.
"I had hoped to be able to share all of this when I was ready, but because of a political clique in Greens WA and a leader facing his first serious test of leadership, I feel that the silence of self-protection will be [and has been] perceived as the silence of guilt," he said.
The senator claimed an "unofficial faction" of the Greens WA branch had released a letter detailing the allegations against him.
"This is not accountability. It is factionalism, and it has no place in the Greens," he said.
In a statement, a Greens WA party spokesperson said they were "putting together an independent process to assess the allegations".
"To ensure the integrity of that process, we will not be commenting further at this time," the spokesperson said.
Senator Steele-John said he had asked Senator Shoebridge "not to announce that I had requested leave" as it would appear to validate the allegations against him.
"I had expected him to recognise that absent any specific allegations, there was no procedural need for me to take leave of any kind," Senator Steele-John said.
"It was a bad call from David. We've all made those in politics.
"So, to be clear, I am not on leave and did not agree to the inclusion of that line within David's statement."
Senator Shoebridge's office has been contacted for comment.

Pope Leo pledges gradual return to duties in first event since cancer surgery
Pope Leo's surgeon said the pontiff was in "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition", estimating another ten days before he was fully recovered.
VATICAN CITY: Pope Leo pledged on Sunday (Oct 18) to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.
The 71-year-old pontiff had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fuelling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.
Smiling from a window of the Vatican's Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice on Sunday, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule.
"Having overcome this delicate phase ... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers," Pope Leo said.
The pope, who was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on Saturday, came to the window in the palace unaided and held his weekly midday appointment as usual.
He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God "without compromise".
People in the square welcomed the pope's speedy return.
Christopher Butler, 68, a parish priest from Leeds in northern England called Pope Leo a "great shepherd for the Catholic Church".
"I'm concerned he needs to take time to make a full recovery but he's obviously a very resilient man and keen to return to work, to lead the Church and to be a world leader," Butler said.
Soledad Espinosa, 59, from Ecuador, said she was happy to hear that the pope would be allowed by his doctors to visit Latin America next month.
"We are all hoping for his recovery and that he has gotten through the situation well. We know that he is ok and we're pleased," she said.
Norma Grasso, 76, from Argentina, said: "We are waiting for him."
Following the surgery, there had been doubts about a planned papal voyage scheduled for Nov 6 to Nov 17, to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where Pope Leo spent two decades as a missionary.
But his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News he believed there were "no clinical reasons why the trip should not go ahead".
"ABSOLUTELY SATISFACTORY"
The pope's discharge on Saturday capped days of uncertainty that rattled the Vatican and the world's Catholics, less than two years into the Chicago-born pope's papacy.
Margaritora said Pope Leo was in "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition", estimating another ten days before he is fully recovered.
Margaritora told Vatican News that Pope Leo's tumour had been discovered by chance, during a routine abdominal X-ray that captured the "little spot" at the base of his right lung.
While calling the lung operation "routine", he saluted the pope's commitment to his recovery, saying he "really put his heart and soul into it, like the most motivated patients".
"His determination to achieve a very quick and very effective recovery from every point of view was really commendable," Margaritora said.
The results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending.
Pope Leo has resumed some work, making a call on Friday to Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.
This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.
Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP won state elections in West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.
Mass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. The Cockroach movement was born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.
This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakes impossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.
There is still reason for hope in India. The Indian Express newspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011, corruption scandals became evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.

The Ministry of Health and health authorities  respond to Ebola outbreak in North Kivu in the Democratic Republic of the Congo with WHO support. ©WHO/AFRO
Geneva, 2 February 2022 - Contributors to the WHO's Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE) met today with WHO representatives to reflect on the impact that has been achieved through the Fund, and to discuss how to further strengthen it. The CFE, created in 2015, is one of WHO's most powerful tools for responding immediately to acute health emergencies. During the dialogue, participants acknowledged the agility and rapidness of the Fund, emphasizing that in an emergency "every hour and every dollar count", and highlighting CFE's role in promoting global health security.
Simply put, the CFE has transformed the way in which WHO responds to emergencies. Whereas before we were left to scramble for start-up funding in the face of disease outbreaks or humanitarian crises, the CFE has now turned us very much into first responders, and at times, also providers of the last resort.
- Dr Mike Ryan, Executive Directory of the WHO Health Emergencies Programme
Jane Ellison, WHO Executive Director for External Relations and Governance said that "in many cases the CFE saves us the need to go after additional resources to respond to acute events. The CFE saves us time, and most importantly, it saves lives."
From 2015-2021, donors to the CFE provided more than US$ 200 million. During this period more than 50 countries and territories have received CFE allocations, which have been used to respond to more than 130 emergencies, including disease outbreaks, complex humanitarian crises, natural and other disasters. The donor base of CFE has grown to 24 countries, and during the briefing the US confirmed that it is in discussions with WHO on support to the CFE and looks forward to soon becoming the 25th member of this life-saving group.
Over the last two years alone, the CFE has been critical in stopping five Ebola outbreaks in Africa, providing emergency health supplies in response to the Beirut Port blast, and getting mobile medical teams to remote locations in Vanuatu following Tropical Cyclone Harold. The Fund has also provided a lifeline for hundreds of thousands of people caught up in protracted humanitarian crises such as those in Afghanistan, Ethiopia, occupied Palestinian territory, South Sudan.
"Let me thank you, WHO Member States, for having the foresight to create a Fund back in 2015," Dr Ryan said. "You have followed this up with great generosity. We have seen tremendous growth over the last few years in terms of contributions and the number of donors, and we look forward to welcoming more donors in the near future."
