Recently, Zoho cofounder Sridhar Vembu raised concerns over the economics of building software in an AI-driven market. In a post on X, Vembu said server prices have risen 4-5X in a year, while AI usage and token expenditure are pushing up operating costs. Zoho, however, plans to respond by cutting its marketing budget, freezing headcount for 18 months and pausing its usual salary hikes this year. Vembu’s concern is that while AI has made software easier to build, running a software business is getting more expensive. At the same time, AI coding tools and agents are challenging traditional subscription and per-seat pricing models. Another concern, as per Vembu, is that AI-driven productivity gains in software development currently stand at 25% to 50% when measured across the entire product development process. While developers can build prototypes faster, testing, verification and other stages of taking a product to market continue to require human involvement. When AI Costs Start To Bite As AI eats into SaaS revenue, it is also making software more expensive to run. Every AI query requires computing power, adding to operating costs. At the same time, growing demand for AI infrastructure is driving up hardware prices, making it more expensive for companies to run their software. According to ICONIQ’s 2026 data, AI products have an average gross margin of around 52%, compared with the 80% benchmark for traditional SaaS. For established SaaS companies adding AI features, gross margins can fall by 12-17 percentage points, depending on how efficiently they manage AI computing costs. The pressure is also forcing software companies to reconsider how much profitability they are willing to sacrifice to build AI products. On October 15, 2026, SaaS giant Figma’s CFO, Praveer Melwani, said the design software company might not return to its previous gross margins of over 90% as it invests in AI features. Its margins were in the mid-80% range, with the company prioritising long-term growth and competitiveness over an immediate return to earlier profitability levels, according to Reuters. Meanwhile, rather than treating every decline as a problem to be eliminated, some software companies are accepting higher costs, expecting AI features will attract more users, strengthen their products and create future revenue opportunities. Similarly, some are adding more capabilities without proportionately increasing subscription prices. Krish Ramineni, cofounder and CEO of Fireflies, said that the company has not raised its subscription pricing in the five to six years since launching its meeting note-taking product. It is now expanding beyond meeting notes into tasks such as summarising emails, responding to workplace messages and preparing users for meetings, while aiming to include more tools within a single subscription. The Push To Rein In AI Spending The pressure to manage AI expenditure is also showing up in the financial results of Indian companies. Groww, for example, reported a 28% year-on-year increase in total expenses to ₹556 Cr in Q2 FY27, even as revenue from operations grew 47% to ₹1,501 Cr. In its shareholder letter, the company identified inflation in compute costs due to AI adoption as one factor behind higher serving costs. Cofounder and CFO Ishan Bansal said AI-related costs began rising as the company increased its focus on AI, alongside higher compute usage on trading days and a one-off operational expense. Groww expects inflation-driven costs to remain part of its operational baseline going forward. This is prompting companies to re-evaluate their technology investments. Instead of relying entirely on large, general-purpose models, some are fine-tuning smaller models for specific tasks, optimising infrastructure and using more expensive models only when necessary. Perfios, a financial technology company serving banks and other financial institutions, is taking this approach to manage the cost of deploying AI. Sumit Nigam, chief technology officer at Perfios, said the company is fine-tuning smaller language models and optimising model and GPU architecture to make specific workloads cheaper to run. According to him, GPU utilisation costs for some use cases have become significantly lower than the cost of relying on external models such as Google’s Gemini or Anthropic’s Claude. Companies are also looking to improve visibility into how AI expenditure builds up across teams, applications and workflows. On October 12, US-based software company Freshworks signed an agreement to acquire Torii, a software management platform. The deal is intended to extend Freshworks’ Freshservice product into software management and AI spend governance. Torii tracks software applications, licences and AI consumption and attributes spending to the people and teams driving it. The platform is designed to help IT and finance teams understand what is being used, identify cost spikes, set limits and forecast expenditure. Perfios, meanwhile, is combining cost optimisation with closer scrutiny of business returns. Sridhar Narayan, chief business officer at Perfios, said the company tracks profitability at both the product and customer levels. The focus is on optimising costs and directing spending towards areas where it can deliver better business outcomes, rather than cutting expenditure indiscriminately. These approaches point to two parts of AI cost management: making usage visible and controllable, and reducing the cost of delivering each AI-powered task. While AI is making software cheaper to build, the real value lies in data, workflows, integrations and the ability to run business processes reliably at scale. Adapting To A New AI Reality As Indian technology companies head into 2027, they face a two-sided challenge: customers are demanding more productivity from AI, while companies must figure out how to earn sustainable revenues. For IT services firms, this is changing how clients pay for work. A Reuters report found that AI is pushing clients to link payments to productivity gains rather than the hours billed by IT services companies, forcing the industry to rethink its pricing models. For SaaS companies, the challenge is different. As AI makes software easier and cheaper to build, products with limited differentiation risk becoming easier to replace. According to Prashant Singh, the cofounder and COO of LeadSquared, “If AI makes software cheaper to build, then software that was only ever an interface over a database becomes harder to defend. That pressure is real.” But Singh believes the threat is not uniform across the industry. “What is being commoditised is the ability to build an application, not the ability to run a business process reliably at scale,” he said. Proprietary data, integrations and industry-specific workflows will continue to help companies retain their competitive edge. Going into 2027, the challenge for Indian tech companies will be to adapt to AI-driven changes in pricing and customer expectations while protecting their margins.

An immunization worker gets set up to receive her wages on her mobile wallet in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
Campaigns in Africa to stop polio and other diseases have a more stable, better-motivated workforce thanks to WHO’s collaboration with countries and partners to pay frontline health workers through their mobile phones instead of in cash.
“Over 80 percent of workers are saying they prefer the digital payments,” said Ahmed Hamani Djibo, head of WHO’s Digital Finance Team.
WHO has been leading among international organizations in moving away from the unwieldy, less-secure practice of disbursing salaries in cash. Over the past few years, the Organization launched its Digital Finance Team and joined the Better Than Cash Alliance, an 80-member United Nations partnership with a mandate to develop the digitization of payments and expand financial inclusion – activities that support the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Since it was established in 2020, WHO’s Digital Finance Team has designed and implemented digital payment solutions in 24 countries in Africa, including, last year, in Benin, Botswana, Madagascar, Rwanda, Togo and Zimbabwe.
“WHO has successfully digitized payments for more than two million health workers across Africa,” said Tidhar Wald, Managing Director, a.i., at the Better Than Cash Alliance. “With these inspiring results, WHO is taking a clear leadership role in accelerating the digital transformation in the provision of health outcomes globally.”
A polio immunization team on the job in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
“A really big difference in speed”
Workers surveyed in Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia and Tanzania said they appreciated the security of not carrying cash, the convenience of no longer having to travel to a disbursement site to receive their wages, and above all, the speed of payment – as short as half an hour after finishing work compared to waits of weeks or even months.
The surveys, funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, linked timely compensation to better morale and worker retention.
“There is really a big difference in speed,” said Jean-Luc, a health worker interviewed in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at the end of a polio immunization campaign. “We finished the campaign mop-up yesterday and received a text notification the next evening. I’m going to pay my child’s school fees. Now we can relax.”
Digital payments also save time and money for health campaign organizers, including the burden and expense of transporting large sums of cash and completing documentation.
“When you have 300 to 500 volunteers to pay, doing accounts and signing receipts takes a lot of time,” said Saïdi, a polio team leader in DRC.
WHO first used the new digital payments in polio immunization campaigns in Côte d’Ivoire. Although outbreaks of vaccine-derived polio were on the rise, vaccination campaigns were having trouble getting off the ground. In the first quarter of 2020, almost half the polio campaigns in WHO’s African Region were postponed, saw workers drop out, or suffered other detrimental effects stemming from delays in cash disbursements.
As WHO and partners worked to develop the nuts-and-bolts aspects of a digital payment ecosystem (registering workers into a database, verifying their profiles with the mobile network operator and more) the benefits of a cashless approach became more apparent.
"There is substantial evidence that digitizing payments can support people, especially women, to gain access to financial services and increase control over their earnings,” said Maria May, Senior Program Officer, Inclusive Financial Systems, at the Gates Foundation. “Over the past four years, the World Health Organization has utilized the growing presence of mobile money across Africa to ensure that the courageous frontline vaccinators in polio outbreak campaigns are paid completely, quickly, and securely.”
Alain Labrique, director of WHO’s Department of Digital Health and Innovation, said that “digital payments are one of the key pillars of Digital Health Public Infrastructure currently strongly encouraged within WHO’s guidance to member-states on Digital Transformation.” WHO views digital payments as a foundation for many more digital development activities, together with Data Exchange and Digital ID Infrastructure. He added “we are delighted to work with partners in the digital space and add our voice to this celebration of WHO's joining the Better Than Cash Alliance”.

Listed home services major Urban Company’s board approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr yesterday, seeking to shore up its war chest at a critical juncture. On one hand, Urban Company’s instant home services business, InstaHelp, is facing stiff competition. Fighting rivals Snabbit and Pronto for a slice of the market has turned out to be an expensive affair, with spending on InstaHelp contributing to Urban Company’s widening losses. At the same time, the company is looking to expand its product lineup under the Native brand by entering the residential air conditioner market. Meanwhile, its bread and butter consumer services continue to generate stable results. Urban Company’s financials reflect these pressures. The company reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹144 Cr in Q2 FY27, driven by a ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. Excluding InstaHelp, it reported an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹30 Cr. During the quarter, consolidated revenue from operations grew 41.4% YoY to ₹537.3 Cr, while total expenses increased 61.5% to ₹745.7 Cr. Consequently, the company’s consolidated net loss more than tripled to ₹182.5 Cr from ₹59.3 Cr in the year-ago period. However, the management maintains that Urban Company can meet its profitability targets without the proposed fundraise Yet, the management has rejected the suggestion that the fundraise is necessary to offset InstaHelp’s impact on its financials. How Badly Does Urban Company Need The Cash? Urban Company has positioned the proposed ₹2,500 Cr fundraise as a means to bolster its balance sheet and provide greater flexibility to invest across its businesses. “Our ambition is to go beyond being just a home services company and eventually become the trusted home platform for Indian consumers – almost the operating system for the Indian home. So given that ambition, we want the strategic flexibility over the next few years to invest in all our areas of business,” CEO Abhiraj Singh Bhal told analysts during the company’s Q2 FY27 earnings call. The company also plans to deploy the capital towards growth opportunities, including acquisitions. While no acquisition deals have been finalised till now, the management is evaluating opportunities that could help Urban Company consolidate its position in an existing market or enter a new category. Bhal added that the company would take an opportunistic approach to international markets and Native. However, an acquisition in InstaHelp would be “highly unlikely”. “If at all we do an M&A, it would be to add on categories that we don’t operate in today where we feel that the decision of build versus buy may be tilting in favour of buy,” he noted. Urban Company has guided for adjusted EBITDA breakeven by Q3 FY28 and ₹1,000 Cr in adjusted EBITDA profit by FY31. The management maintained that its current financial position, even without raising additional capital, is sufficient to meet these targets. However, Bhal acknowledged that the company’s existing balance sheet limits its financial flexibility, given InstaHelp’s losses. While the management maintains that the company can meet its profitability targets without additional capital, the proposed fundraise would provide it with greater room to invest in growth and respond to changing market conditions. In particular, Urban Company is facing intense competition in the emerging quick home services segment. For instance, after Urban Company disclosed that InstaHelp completed 6.2 Mn orders in Q2, Snabbit's founder Aayush Agarwal claimed that the startup had served 6.45 Mn orders during the period. Diving Into A New Market While it faces intense competition in the quick home services market, Urban Company is simultaneously looking to expand into a new category. Alongside approving the fundraise proposal, its board proposed exploring residential air conditioners as a new business under its consumer appliances brand Native, whose portfolio currently comprises water purifiers and smart locks. “We’ve now operated in the segment of air conditioning servicing and repair for close to 11-12 years, ever since the inception of the company. And there’s a lot of data and knowledge that we have gathered on what are the consumer pain points and what are some of the unmet needs of the consumers. Based on those data points and our own understanding of the market and the unmet needs, we have been quietly working on creating an innovative cutting-edge product,” Bhal told analysts on the call. The company is yet to disclose further details, including a commercial launch timeline. Notably, Inc42 reported last year about Urban Company’s potential foray into AC business. Bhal said the first one to two years in the new market would focus on learning and gathering customer feedback. He also noted that Urban Company’s app would be the sole distribution channel for its ACs. The CEO emphasised a “calibrated and measured” approach to capital allocation, adding that Native has a clear path to profitability that should not be affected by the new venture. For context, Native’s net transaction value (NTV) grew 35.4% YoY in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue rose 40% to ₹105 Cr. The segment remained loss-making on an adjusted EBITDA basis, reporting a loss of ₹9 Cr. However, loss as a percentage of NTV declined to 6.8% from 9% a year ago. Urban Company’s platform sees 10X as many AC servicing, repair, and installation orders as water purifier orders, giving it a larger existing customer base for AC-related services. This provides a potential channel to market Native’s ACs, although service demand does not necessarily translate into appliance sales. With InstaHelp facing stiff competition and Native preparing to enter a new product category, Urban Company is pursuing multiple growth opportunities even as its losses widen. The proposed fundraise would provide additional capital to support these plans, although the management maintains that the company can achieve its stated profitability targets without it.

A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site
- Published
What is the point of a protest?
To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen?
For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi.
But that may now be coming to an end.
This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site.
The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collective which began as a joke - led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned.
Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief, ended in a police crackdown.
Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day.
Delhi Police says, external it acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford.
Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed.
This week, when the BBC visited, those scenes seemed a distant memory.
Yellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand.
In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions.
Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined.
Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament.
Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament.
"Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote in a 2023 paper, external.
Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years.
Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes.
Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause.
It was also where she formed solidarities with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance.
"It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra.
Dipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmark rural jobs guarantee scheme, the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar.
"It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says.
Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise".
But sustaining a protest for months was not easy.
Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up.
In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests.
A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution.
When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time.
"That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she remembered them saying.
Sinha points out that Jantar Mantar was also near institutions like the Press Club and Constitution Club, making it easier to get media coverage, and for politicians to drop by and meet protesters.
It was a simpler time - sometimes they would ask for permission from police only on the morning of the protest.
Those rules have become much stricter, external now.
In recent years, when Dhingra tried to protest at Jantar Mantar, she was told no-one could stay the night.
"Where do you go with hundreds of people who have travelled all the way to the capital to protest?" she asks.
While Jantar Mantar has its supporters, others share memories of an even more vibrant protest culture.
Mary E John, a gender studies scholar who lived in Delhi both as a student and as an academic, says that before 1993, she attended protests at the Boat Club on issues ranging from workers' rights and women's issues to topics of international significance.
"We lived in a climate where protest was part of life. In fact, we took it for granted," she says.
When the spacious Boat Club lawns made way for Jantar Mantar, it actually felt "claustrophobic", she said.
She pointed out that they, and others before and after them, protested at multiple sites - universities, colleges, streets - instead of just at Jantar Mantar.
She sees signs of that in protests by farmers who camped at Delhi's borders for months, and people who sat at the Shaheen Bagh neighbourhood demanding the repeal of a controversial citizenship law.
Even the 2012 anti-rape protests, she points out, were not restricted to Jantar Mantar but almost reached the Indian president's heavily guarded complex and beyond into other parts of Delhi.
It's not clear what Jantar Mantar's future is - the Supreme Court is hearing pleas challenging its removal as a protest site.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders have said that Jantar Mantar belongs to the people and will be "reclaimed".
As the debate rages on, Jantar Mantar is the quietest it has been in decades - will it hear slogans again?

West Bank settlers brutally attack a Washington Post journalist
Settler violence is growing ahead of Israeli elections this month.
On Friday, Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians living in the West Bank, as well as a Washington Post photographer, who was hospitalized with serious injuries.
Photojournalist Heidi Levine was knocked down, beaten, and robbed of her camera equipment by masked settlers in an attack captured on video by other journalists. Those other members of the press rescued her from the attackers while Israel Defense Forces soldiers reportedly stood by.
Levine had lacerations and a wound to her hand that split her finger to the bone, according to the Post, which condemned the attack in a statement. Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who helped Levine escape the attack, said that Levine also had cracked ribs, and may have been stabbed.
Assaults like this one are becoming more common in the West Bank, where settler violence — which is currently targeting the ongoing olive harvest — has worsened. Last week, another photojournalist for the news wire Agence France-Presse was beaten with rifles by settlers, and Palestinian residents of the West Bank have been shot, beaten, and terrorized while the Israeli settlers targeting them face few consequences.
Why settler violence is growing in the West Bank
As my colleague Zack Beauchamp recently explained, under international law, the settler movement in the West Bank is clearly illegal. Nevertheless, it’s continued to grow, and it has a friend in the current Israeli government led by Benjamin Netanyahu. It’s also becoming increasingly violent.
Two current Israeli officials, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir, are settlers themselves, and both have used their offices — as ministers of finance and national security, respectively — to further the settler cause, including by making it easier for settlers to commit unchecked violence against Palestinians.
The United Nations reported in June that settler attacks had reached “the highest sustained levels ever recorded…with [an average of] six daily attacks that have resulted in casualties, property damage or both,” and in many Palestinians being forced from their homes by settlers. In late September, the International Committee of the Red Cross said that expanding Israeli settlements and violence by settlers was “making everyday life untenable” for Palestinian residents of the West Bank.
As Zack has reported, settlements and settler violence are both intentional tactics, serving to force more Palestinians off their land, isolate the ones who stay, and push any potential two-state solution further out of reach.
That kind of violence is likely only to worsen in the weeks to come: Israel will hold elections on October 27, which could well result in Netanyahu’s settler-friendly government losing power. As a result, the Washington Post reported earlier this month, settlers are “racing to lock down gains” before the election with ever more extreme violence.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) announced a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police denied permission for the protest and detained several protesters, including CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke. A Delhi court ordered their release on 11 October 2026, while the Supreme Court intervened over restrictions on public movement and allegations of unlawful detention. On 15 October 2026, the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation submitted an affidavit to the Supreme Court, stating that police imposed restrictions at 45 Metro stations (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming it shows a lawyer confronting the Chief Justice of India (CJI) over a CJP protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a lawyer confronting the Chief Justice of India (CJI) over the CJP protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
Fact: The viral video dates back to 16 October 2025 and shows a heated exchange between Jharkhand High Court judge Justice Rajesh Kumar and advocate Mahesh Tiwari, not a confrontation with the Chief Justice of India over the CJP protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar. The exchange occurred during court proceedings concerning a widow whose electricity connection had been disconnected over outstanding dues. The Jharkhand High Court initiated criminal contempt proceedings against Tiwari, which were later dropped after the court accepted his unconditional apology. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals from October 2025. According to these reports, a heated exchange took place between Jharkhand High Court judge Justice Rajesh Kumar and Advocate Mahesh Tiwari on 16 October 2025, following which the court initiated criminal contempt proceedings against Tiwari. The proceedings were being streamed live when the incident occurred.
The incident began when a lawyer sought relief for his client, a widow whose electricity connection had been disconnected over outstanding dues of Rs 1.30 lakh. Justice Kumar questioned the manner in which the lawyer was seeking relief and explained how the matter should be argued in accordance with court ethics. He also said that the Bar Council chairman should take note of the lawyer’s conduct. Tiwari, who had been standing at the back of the courtroom, then joined the argument, stepped forward and pointed at the judge.
A report published by NDTV on 23 January 2026 stated that the Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, criticised Advocate Mahesh Tiwari for challenging the criminal contempt proceedings initiated against him by the Jharkhand High Court. The Supreme Court asked the High Court to take a sympathetic view if Tiwari apologised. Subsequently, a report published by The Indian Express on 19 February 2026 stated that the Jharkhand High Court dropped the contempt proceedings after accepting Tiwari’s unconditional apology. The High Court observed that an advocate with more than 40 years of legal practice was expected to exercise greater restraint and was as much an officer of the court as the presiding judge.
To sum up, an unrelated courtroom exchange video is shared, showing a lawyer confronting the CJI over the CJP protest against Gyanesh Kumar.

Instakart Services, the Flipkart-owned logistics company behind Ekart, nearly broke even in the fiscal year ending March 2026 (FY26). Its loss narrowed 98.3% to ₹26 Cr in the fiscal under review, compared to ₹1,508 Cr in FY25. The brand’s revenue from contracts with customers fell 4.2% to ₹13,194 Cr in FY26, from ₹13,779 Cr in the previous fiscal year. In this, Flipkart itself contributed ₹9,112 Cr, or about 69% of the total operating revenue. Operationally, logistics, transportation and shipping contributed the most share, approximately 50% to ₹6,419 Cr in the reported year. Revenue from this vertical plunged 39.5% YoY. Ekart also generates revenue from collection services and warehousing services. Collection services income fell 68% to ₹510 Cr, while warehousing services income rose 44% to ₹2,212 Cr. Including finance and other income of ₹418 Cr, Instakart’s total income fell 3.9% to ₹13,612 Cr in the year under review. Founded in 2009 by Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal as an in-house logistics entity within Flipkart, Ekart was spun off as a separate entity in 2016 to support the fulfillment services not only for Flipkart and Myntra but also for D2C brands, online sellers and retailers. As of last year, the company claimed to be operating more than 7,000 trucks running daily across the length and breadth of the country, 70 fulfilment centres, 80 sortation facilities and 3500 delivery hubs to ensure timely delivery across 14,000 pin codes. Earlier in July, Ekart opened its pan-India logistics network to MSMEs, D2C brands, FMCG companies, and enterprises, allowing external businesses to access the logistics infrastructure used by Flipkart. The logistics arm has already operationalised more than 300 franchise outlets across Surat, Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru, and had plans to expand the network to over 1,000 outlets by the end of 2026. Magnifying Ekart’s Spending Ekart’s total expenses for the fiscal dipped by 13% YoY to ₹13,638 Cr in the year under review, while its costs stood at ₹15,673 Cr in FY25. Here is a closer look at where Ekart spent the highest: Freight, Handling and Servicing Expenses: The spending under this head fell by 17.1% to ₹9,191 Cr in FY25 from ₹11,093 Cr in the previous financial year. Of the overall expenditure, freight costs comprised 67.4%. Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs, which include salaries, provident fund, gratuity, among others, shrunk by 24.9% to ₹958 Cr from ₹1,275 Cr in FY25. Further, it accounted for 7% of the overall expenses in FY26. Depreciation And Amortisation Expense: These costs increased by 5% to ₹1,456 Cr from ₹1,387 Cr in FY25.

Vice President JD Vance addressed concerns about corruption inside the White House — just days after U.S. ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned amid allegations that she pressured a MAGA donor to pay her six-figure credit card bill in exchange for influence in the Trump administration.
During a tough CBS News town hall Saturday night, Vance addressed corruption allegations and criticism that President Donald Trump and his family have profited from the office during his second term.
CBS Evening News anchor Tony Dokoupil noted during the event that corruption is high on the list of voter concerns — ranking even above gas prices. Dokoupil said that a recent poll “found that even half of Republicans believe Donald Trump’s personal business interests are affecting his decisions as president.”
“Have you seen anything inside the White House, when it comes to corruption, that makes you squeamish?” Dokoupil asked the VP.
“You’re asking, has Donald Trump’s decision-making been influenced by his business interests -” Vance began to ask before Dokoupil interjected.
“No, I’m asking if you’ve seen anything from anybody inside the White House,” Dokoupil said.
“I’ve never seen anything like that from the president,” Vance said, claiming that he has personally investigated corruption inside the administration.
“No, Tony, I just don’t. I think that there’s a lot of allegation out there and there’s a lot of stuff where, frankly, I’ve read these articles, and I’ve read the superficial summary, and I say, oh, that doesn’t sound right,” Vance said.
“And then I go and do the investigation myself, and I say, wait a second, what they’re saying the President did or what they’re saying the president’s son did, he actually didn’t do,” he added.
Vance then accused Dokoupil of saying that Trump is at least sanctioning such behavior, to which Dokoupil replied, “The voters are saying that.”
“Donald Trump hates when people make money off him. He hates the idea that somebody would come in and say, I’m gonna give you a meeting with the president and I’m going to get rich because I gave you access to the president. The president would never tolerate that behavior, Tony,” Vance said.
His comments come days after a bombshell report claimed that Guilfoyle asked MAGA donor Eric Deters, a Kentucky attorney and former congressional candidate, to pay her $100,000 American Express bill in exchange for influence in the Trump administration, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host who was once engaged to Donald Trump Jr., resigned from her ambassadorship on Tuesday, following encouragement for her to step down from the White House.
Her lawyers have disputed the authenticity of text messages Deters shared with media outlets. Deters also told CNN that he did not give Guilfoyle the money.
Deters filed a defamation lawsuit against Guilfoyle and her legal team on Thursday in Kentucky state court.
“Kim Guilfoyle and her lawyers claimed my allegations were false and they would defend the allegations vigorously,” Deters wrote in a statement with the lawsuit. “Now they can in Kentucky.”
Guilfoyle has not commented on the lawsuit or her resignation beyond a social media post after it was announced she was asked to resign.
Upon her resignation Tuesday, Guilfoyle thanked Trump for the opportunity to serve and vowed to “vigorously” fight the “false” allegations against her.
“Serving as the United States Ambassador to Greece has been the honor of a lifetime,” she wrote on social media. “From my first day as Ambassador, I have worked tirelessly to advance President Trump’s America First agenda, strengthen our strategic alliance with Greece, and deliver meaningful victories for the American people.”

Zelenskyy urges support for new US sanctions on Russia after Trump puts them on hold
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in defense of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.
The White House decision has further raised fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults with winter approaching.
Russian attacks overnight killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities.
In a statement on social media, Zelenskyy described Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticize the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.
"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote.
Later, in audio clips answering journalists' questions, Zelenskyy thanked Democrats and Republicans who backed the legislation and praised its bipartisan support. He said blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing and do nothing to bring the war to an end.
He also added that limiting Ukraine's ability to retaliate against Russian attacks would not bring peace.
"Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war," he said.
Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin
Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation.
The president told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."
"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said.
Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
The decision has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran.
Kyiv says Moscow carried out a 'massive' energy strike
Zelenskyy also said Saturday that Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.
"The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said.
Ukraine's air force said that Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight. All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.
Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.
Russian attacks killed three people in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, said Saturday. Writing on social media, Liakh said that two apartment blocks were partially destroyed and other homes damaged.
A Russian strike also killed an ambulance driver in Ukraine's Kherson region, head of the local military administration Yaroslav Shanko said. The strike, which used guided bombs, wounded at least 33 others, he said.
Ukrainian drones kill 1, ground hundreds of flights at Moscow airports
Elsewhere, a Russian woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian border region of Belgorod, local officials said.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its forces had shot down 610 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that more than 100 drones were shot down en route to the Russian capital. More than 350 flights were canceled or delayed at Moscow's airports, local media reported, as planes were grounded in response to incoming drones.
The Kremlin announced Saturday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had approved a government program to help restore trade and logistics facilities damaged in drone attacks.

France protests latest: Macron to address nation as Trump says ‘France is burning’ and hits out at protesters
At least 1,800 people have been arrested over the nationwide protests

Emmanuel Macron is set to address France after a day of protest that descended into rioters setting fire to cars and buildings – with at least 1,800 people arrested.
More than 500,000 people took to the streets before violent groups clashed with police officers in demonstrations across the country.
In Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall, causing its roof to collapse, with the lootings of hundreds of businesses in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, and other cities.
The French president is set to hold an emergency meeting with top government officials on Sunday afternoon, before addressing the nation at 8pm.
US president Donald Trump hit out at the protesters, writing on social media: “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country.” French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu attributed some of the violence to "radical far-left groups".
The protests began last month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
Protests over poor living and education standards also take place in Albania
Elsewhere, police in Albania said that 388 people had been charged with criminal offences as widespread protests take place in the capital Tirana.
Prime minister Edi Rama on Sunday rejected calls to step down from growing street protests, and said they were a threat not to his government but to Albania's progress toward joining the European Union.
Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana and spread to other cities in the past week.
Demonstrators demanding Rama's resignation have set fire to government buildings as well as banks and pulled up paving stones to throw at police, who have responded with tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets.
The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful protests in the summer against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, pose the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and last year won a fourth term in office.
"I am not being challenged, the government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged," Rama said in a live address on Facebook.
Parisians blame 'troublemakers' who turned protest into riot
Inspecting the damage, many Parisians took photos of the partially dismantled base of the central monument at Place de la République — a statue of Marianne, a symbol of France.
Jean Foissy, 74, said he wanted to join the protest but found "a wall of riot police and fires everywhere," and went back home.
"I was very scared," he said. "I've been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me."
Margaux Eude, 26, said she supports the protest movement but "didn't think it would escalate like this."
"It's the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimises the movement," she said.
Donald Trump says 'France is burning!' on social media
US president Donald Trump posted "France is burning!" on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to "the immigration of people from an entirely different world."
"Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!" he wrote.
19th century Limoges city hall destroyed and widespread damage in Paris
Authorities said masked groups on Saturday set fires and attacked public buildings, including city halls, in several cities.
In Limoges, a city in central France, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall, causing its roof to collapse. Haute-Vienne prefect Maurice Barate told LCI television that the fire was deliberately set and nearly destroyed the building. The fire was under control Sunday.
Around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday morning, dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass marked the aftermath of the events.
Looting and damage were reported around the square and in some other tourist and shopping areas in the city centre.
1,800 arrested with one dead from a suspected heart attack
Police arrested at least 1,800 people across France after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during nationwide demonstrations that drew hundreds of thousands of people who denounced rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.
Paris police said Sunday that 855 people were arrested in the French capital region alone.
About 550,000 took part in protests across France, according to authorities, while organizers counted about 800,000.
More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured, Nuñez said.
One person died of a heart attack, Paris police said in a statement, without providing details. Paris prosecutors' office said it was investigating.
Emmanuel Macron to address the nation after violent protests
French president Emmanuel Macron is set to address the nation at 8pm, after holding an emergency meeting with top government officials on Sunday afternoon.
On Saturday, he wrote on social media: “No room for violence in our Republic. Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished.”
"The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not," Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X, pointing to the lootings of hundreds of businesses in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, Limoges and other cities.
Around 1,200 protesters arrested across major French cities
French prime minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Saturday evening that some 1,200 people had been arrested as part of the protests, which a union said involved up to 800,000 demonstrators.
Large groups gathered in Paris and Marseille ahead of the official marches and hours later protests erupted across the whole country.
Masked protesters stormed Marseille's town hall after ramming the doors with security barriers in the morning, and were followed by attacks on town halls in Grenoble and Lille.
Protesters later set fire to the tourism office in Lyon in eastern France and attempted to prevent firefighters from tackling the blaze.
French police response under scrutiny
The protests in France began last month at high schools in Paris' working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.
Police tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade.
The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.
Prime minister Sebastien Lecornu said more than 150 police officers had been injured in Saturday's protests, but did not say whether any protesters had been hurt.
Interior minister Laurent Nunez confirmed reports that one person had his hand torn off in clashes with police on Saturday. French media reported he tried to pick up a stun grenade.
The UNSA police union posted a video on X showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point.
"Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes," the union said. "Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go onindefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum."
French PM says government 'will not be intimidated'
French prime minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals just months before a presidential election next year.
"To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X.
Some 1,200 people had been arrested as part of the protests, Lecornu added while visiting the sites in the evening.
Around 550,000 people had participated in the demonstrations across the country, interior minister Laurent Nunez said.
The CGT union told Reuters it estimated the number of protesters at 800,000.
Hundreds arrested as protesters clash with police across France over rising living costs
Clashes have broken out between police and protesters in cities across France as tens of thousands of people angered by rising costs and declining public services took to the streets – in some of the country's most violent protests of recent times.
More than 270 people have been arrested across the country, while in Lyon, protesters torched the tourist office. In Marseille, the mayor said the town hall had been vandalised and that additional police were being sent to the city following talks with the government.
The protesters said most people were protesting peacefully and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. The Interior Ministry said, however, that violence was increasing, and that there had been "confrontations with law enforcement, looting or attempted looting of shops, attacks on and damage to public buildings." It blamed the unrest on what it described as the "ultra-left".

In the 54th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu, Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, discuss the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, experimental approaches to studying human brain development, and incidents from Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya that highlight barriers to healthcare access.
The episode begins with the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The discussion explains how optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins to control the electrical activity of selected nerve cells. By activating or inhibiting specific neurons, researchers can investigate how neural circuits influence movement, memory, emotions and behaviour. The technique has become an important tool in neuroscience research, including studies of neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, it remains largely a research tool and is not a routine treatment for brain disorders.
The next segment examines an experimental approach described as ‘xenocortication’, in which human brain tissue is transplanted into the brains of mice. Researchers have been exploring this approach to study aspects of human brain development that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory-grown cells or animal models alone. The discussion looks at how the transplanted tissue may receive a blood supply, develop connections and interact with its surroundings within a living brain. The approach could help researchers investigate human neuronal development and mechanisms involved in neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders. However, it remains experimental, and findings from such models cannot be assumed to reflect human brain development fully. The work also raises ethical questions about the use of human neural tissue in animal research.
The episode then turns to barriers to healthcare access, examining how social discrimination and inadequate infrastructure can prevent people from receiving medical care. In Uttar Pradesh, a Dalit woman was allegedly denied admission to a government hospital while in labour and was forced to deliver outside the facility. Her family alleged that untouchability was involved. The incident highlights how discrimination can obstruct access to care even when a health facility is physically available.
Another incident in Meghalaya’s West Khasi Hills district, an ill child died in his mother’s arms while his parents were making a three-hour trek to reach the nearest hospital. According to the village headman, the family had tried to arrange a vehicle after the child’s condition deteriorated, but no driver was willing to travel to the village because of the poor road conditions. The incident draws attention to the difficulties faced by people in remote areas, where distance, road connectivity and the availability of transport can delay access to emergency medical care.
The episode ends with a fun-fact segment on why mice are widely used in laboratory experiments. The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

Srinagar, Oct 18: Around 2.7 lakh students are set to appear in the annual Class 10th, 11th and 12th examinations across Kashmir and the winter-zone areas of Jammu, beginning Monday, as Education Minister Sakina Itoo on Sunday extended her best wishes to the candidates.

“Around 2.7 lakh students are scheduled to appear in the examinations across Kashmir and the winter-zone areas of Jammu. The Class 10th examinations will commence on October 19, followed by Class 12th on October 21 and Class 11th on October 29, 2026,” the minister said.
She said JKBOSE had completed all necessary preparations to ensure the smooth and orderly conduct of the examinations. Itoo urged students to approach the examinations with confidence, relying on their hard work, dedication and perseverance. “Stay confident, manage your time wisely and approach every examination with a calm and positive mindset,” she advised.
The minister also appealed to parents to support their children with patience, understanding and encouragement, avoid unnecessary pressure and provide a peaceful environment that safeguards their physical and mental well-being.
She further urged centre superintendents and examination staff to ensure that the examinations are conducted in a fair, transparent, disciplined and impartial manner, while upholding the sanctity and integrity of the examination system.
Itoo also said JKBOSE had constituted a Grievance-cum-Monitoring Cell to ensure transparency and timely redressal of examination-related complaints.
Students, parents and other stakeholders can contact the designated offices for assistance. For the Kashmir Division, they can email [email protected] or call 0194-3186762. For the Jammu Division, they can email [email protected] or call 0191-2585732, the minister said.

Live updates: South Africa vs Australia, second Test, first day from St George's in Gqeberha
Australia looks to build on its spectacular first Test victory over South Africa when the series moves to Gqeberha in the Eastern Cape.
Follow all the action from St George's in our live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our ScoreCentre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
Stop changing the batting order
Australia has chopped and changed the batting order a few times of late, with a rotating cast of middle order batters tried and discarded up top.
Former Australia captain Steve Waugh has led the calls for the team's selectors to stop changing it up and to let the players settle in fixed roles, despite some questionable returns in Durban.
"They've got to pick and stick now," Waugh said.
"Don't mess around with that now. [Renshaw] has been successful, and he's comfortable, so I'd keep him there, for sure."
Makeshift opener Travis Head scored just 9 and 11 at Kingsmead, with the returning Nic Maddinson managing a 50-minute, 33-ball duck before a far improved 48 in the second innings.
Meanwhile, Matt Renshaw, who has opened for Australia and Queensland in the past, totalled match-winning scores of 190 and 82 at number five.
"It's got to be pretty compelling to move him [Renshaw] from there," Pat Cummins said after the first Test.
"We're always working out the six batters, or seven plus [Alex Carey] and how is that going to function as a whole?
"I still think he [Renshaw] can be a great opener … we're pretty certain that we like Marn [Labuschagne] at number 3, Smithy at number 4, and then, the six and seven felt pretty locked up.
"I think bringing in Maddo, we really like the idea of bringing that flexibility, that unlocks a lot [such as] Trav back to number 5, Renners down to number 5, even Maddo himself at five.
"We haven't had that option [in] the last few years where we feel like we've got plenty of options at the top.
"We're very big on that flexibility. I think having the structure that we do now with a few guys that can open, that's really unlocked that."
Matthew Wade said the players were happy to be flexible.
"If the conditions tell us it's time to change the batting order, we'll make that change," he said.
"We've seen over the last little bit that we've been able to adapt really quickly and more importantly the players take it on so easily - and credit to them."
- with Reuters
Scott Boland is marking out his run up...
If you needed further suggestions that Scott Boland is in the line up to play, he is warming up at the moment.
I'd suggest that means Cameron Green is not going to be selected - and I'd guess that Nathan Lyon might miss out too.
Yesterday Pat Cummins said that all the bowlers were available and he would name the side at the toss, in about 8 minutes time.
Pitch looks... spicy
The covers have been on and off this morning, our spies in South Africa tell us - which is no mean feat given how windy it gets in the city formerly known as Port Elizabeth.
But as it happens, you might need directions to where the pitch is when the covers aren't on it, as this photo from Dan Cherny shows.
That looks like a dog of a pitch, damp and with plenty of grass on it.
Spicy.
Our spies have also suggested that Scott Boland is out there warming up for Australia, no surprise given the overcast conditions and state of that pitch.
Rabada return spells danger for Aussie batters
Former Test wicketkeeper Matthew Wade has warned Australia to expect a far more dangerous South African attack in this Test, with pace spearhead Kagiso Rabada set to return.
Rabada missed Australia’s 214-run victory in Durban with a hamstring injury.
"The thing that stands out with him is his competitiveness," Wade told reporters earlier in the week.
"He takes it to the opposition, he'll be in our face, he'll keep coming for the whole Test match, so we really know that."
Wade worked with Rabada in the Indian Premier League and said the bowler's ability to sustain pressure would give the hosts greater versatility after they struggled to contain Australia in the series-opener.
"They went with two spinners last time but ... him and [Anrich] Nortje can basically take one quick spot and [do] short spells and really attack as hard if they want to."
- with Reuters
South Africa make changes
After a pretty comprehensive 214-run defeat last time out, South Africa made a couple of tweaks to their squad, calling up Matthew Breetzke and dropping Tristan Stubbs.
That has meant a batting order reshuffle for today's second Test.
Proteas coach Shukri Conrad said on Wednesday that there was no need for knee-jerk reactions to the defeat and that his team just "need to get bloody better" this week.
However, on Thursday he announced that Ryan Rickelton will be the wicketkeeper, which is likely to mean Kyle Verreynne, who has not scored a Test 50 in his last 13 innings, will be dropped from the team, despite still being in the squad.
Breetzke, who has played two previous Tests for South Africa, in Bangladesh in late 2024 and Zimbabwe last year and has a first-class average of 37, last played a first-class match in February.
He did score a century in the first One Day International against the Aussies last month though.
"Matt has been part of the squad before and the fact that his ODI form is as hot as it is gave him an inside lane and also, more importantly, the attitude and the character Matt brings, and has, will go a long way," Conrad said.

India vice-captain Tilak Varma admitted that dropping down the order from No. 3 was not easy, but he is trusting his skill enhancement and mental preparation to ace the demands of his new role.
Tilak has been batting either at No. 5 or 6 in T20Is for a while now, and, for him, it came down to working on his game constantly to come up trumps.
“It’s not that easy to change the numbers from 3 to 5 and 6. It will be slightly challenging. But I have been working on that. How can I finish the games? I have said that I love finishing the games for the country,” said Tilak after the washed-out fifth and final T20I against the West Indies in Bengaluru on Saturday night.
“So, for me as an individual, if you see, it will be easier batting at 3. But unfortunately, now I should bat at 5 or 6 because we have got that combination at the top right now,” he added.
From nine matches, the left-hander averages 65.66 while batting at number six, at a strike rate of 195. In 26 combined innings at 5 and 6, he averages 46 at a strike rate of 158.
But Ishan Kishan’s arrival, skipper Shreyas Iyer’s presence at No. 4 and the management’s decision to stick with the Abhishek Sharma-Sanju Samson combination at the top meant a mandatory demotion for Tilak.
The Hyderabad batter is aware of the situation. “Kishan is batting at number 3 now, and he is batting really brilliantly there. So, for me now, I think there is no option but to bat at 5 and 6 and do the job for the team. So, I am mentally prepared for that role. And if you see the last few games, I have won from there. So, I am pretty confident to do well there as well,” he said.
The 23-year-old said he has been working tirelessly in the nets to improve his range of shots and skill level to meet the challenges of batting lower down the order.
“Yeah, we should do that; otherwise, it will be slightly tough. When you go in to bat as a finisher, if a slower one comes into your arc, you should go for 6. Otherwise, if you see in T20, most of the time, if you go into that role of 5 or 6, you will get a maximum of 5 to 6 overs to bat,” Tilak said.
“So, I have changed personally. I have been in this role in my childhood as well. I have got the shots going all over the ground. So, I am confident that if I bat at 3 or 5, I have the technique to adapt. So, if I practise for 1 or 2 days, I can do any role for the team. Now, if I come back to No. 3, I can adapt after a day or two of practice. I am confident of batting anywhere,” he noted.

The Indian team has been going through a busy schedule over the last few months, playing across the United Kingdom, Japan and India. The players will now travel to New Zealand soon for an all-format tour.

“It will be slightly challenging. But as professional cricketers, we can’t give any excuse because when we play back-to-back series, there will be different time zones and all those things. We are used to it now. If you see, for any youngster coming into the team, it will be slightly challenging.

The 23-year-old hoped to translate the positives from the series against the West Indies into good performances in New Zealand.
“There have been quite a few good things. Especially in the batting, every game we have scored over 200 plus. So, that’s a big positive, and that too, we haven’t got a proper all-rounder in the team. We have played both Nitish (Reddy) and (Shivam) Dube as well. But both have done decently well,” Tilak said.
“Then Naman (Dhir) bowled well under pressure. As an off-spinner, bowling to right-handers, and that too against a big-gun team like the West Indies. So, hopefully, we will do well in the New Zealand series,” he added..

An analysis of 33,159 cancer journal articles revealed tell-tale patterns of fake citation numbers across 4,000 articles by 'research paper mills', or fraudulent research organisations.
The suspect papers received 50-100 per cent more citations than other articles within one to three years of publication, yet had fewer readers and were accessed less often online, findings published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Researchers said suspect papers tended to cluster in a subset of journals including 'Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research' and 'Molecular Cancer' whereas other journals were only marginally affected.
They said 'research paper mills', the fraudulent organisations that make money by offering to list people's names on fake research papers, may also be manipulating citation counts -- a key measure of academic performance.
Artificially inflated citation counts distort the evidence base to misinform future research and clinical translation, the team said.
"Just as likes and shares indicate social media influencers' audience engagement, citations from other researchers are an important academic measure for evaluating scientists' research impact," author and statistician Adrian Barnett, from Queensland University of Technology's Australian Centre for Health Services Innovation, explained.
"Because citation counts are now a key measure of academic performance, they can incentivise journals and researchers to maximise citations counts," Barnett said.
The author said the researchers documented a pattern that suggested widespread, coordinated manipulation of citation counts by paper mills.
"Artificially high citation rates can inflate journal impact factors, amplify unreliable findings, and slow scientific progress," Barnett said.
The team evaluated the impact of paper mills on citation patterns in 33,159 articles published in 20 journals between 2012 and 2023.
"Applying our previously developed detection model, we flagged a total of 4,085 articles as potentially associated with paper mills, based on their textual similarity to the titles and abstracts of retracted paper mill articles," co-researcher Baptiste Scancar said.
Papers flagged by the model had many more citations, compared to non-flagged papers, but had fewer readers, the researchers said.
"Having more citations but fewer readers makes no sense, as citations come from readers," Scancar said.
"Flagged papers mostly cite and are cited by other flagged papers, measurably inflating the citation metrics of some cancer research journals," the co-researcher said.
"Flagged papers tended to cluster in a subset of journals including Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research and Molecular Cancer whereas other journals were only marginally affected," Scancar said.
Our results support the screening of articles and journals for the patterns of citation manipulation we have described, the researchers said.
"Across leading cancer journals, clusters of interconnected papers bearing the hallmarks of paper mill products accumulate far more citations than other papers despite having fewer readers," the authors wrote.
"This study provides evidence that citation manipulation leaves measurable traces in citation patterns, offering a practical basis for future screening and intervention," they said.

Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
- Published
A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.
The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand Condé" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the Château de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.
The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.
It will once again be on display in the Condé Museum at the Château de Chantilly until 3 January.
The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.
Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.
While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.
The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.
Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.
The exact origins of the Grand Condé remain a mystery.
It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, drawn up following his death, the Château de Chantilly said.
It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-Amélie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of Orléans, the Duke of Aumale.
He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the Château de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the Musée Condé collection.
