As coral reefs have undergone massive bleaching events across the globe, the corals of Egypt’s Red Sea have offered some hope. They’ve been unusually resilient to rising water temperatures, and if the oceans continue getting hotter, some scientists even predict that Egypt’s northern reefs could become the world’s last-remaining corals.
That’s what Mahmoud Hanafy, a professor of marine biology at Suez Canal University and consultant for the Hurghada Environmental Protection and Conservation Association (HEPCA), has previously predicted. But in the summers of 2023 and 2024, heat waves strained Red Sea coral ecosystems. A HEPCA survey led by Hanafy found bleaching throughout the Red Sea corals in 2024. In the northern areas, less than a tenth of coral colonies surveyed were affected, but further south, bleaching took out half the corals.
Scientists are racing to piece together what these events mean for reefs long described as “super coral” for their unparalleled hardiness. But now the question is not just how much heat they can withstand, but what has protected them until recently—and whether that protection will hold.
In overly warm waters, the algae nestled amongst the corals’ polyps begin to produce toxic substances. As a defense mechanism, the corals eject the algae. This is what is referred to as coral bleaching, and because these microscopic organisms are corals’ primary food source, bleaching events leave corals to starve.
That’s among other negative impacts hot seas may be having on corals, which is an issue not just for the corals, but all the other life among the reefs. According to the United Nations Environment Program, reefs cover less than 1 percent of the seafloor yet support at least 25 percent of marine species—some that are only just now being discovered.
For many years, northern Red Sea reefs remained quite stable as temperatures rose, while other coral ecosystems suffered bleaching. Eslam Osman, a marine ecologist at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), points to the Egyptian corals’ evolutionary history as a likely explanation for their heat tolerance.
Corals are believed to have spread into the Red Sea through the Bab al-Mandab Straight, which lies at the southern point of the sea between modern-day Djibouti and Yemen. Crossing through these especially warm waters acted as a natural filter, Osman posits. Heat-tolerant species and genotypes survived, and their offspring spread northwards into cooler waters.
However, resilience varies across the region, which is part of why Hanafy is unconvinced that evolutionary history is the primary explanation for the resilience of Egypt’s reefs. He places greater emphasis on water circulation.
The northern Red Sea experiences changes in current direction. This can create vertical mixing, which brings cooler water from far below toward the surface, he explains. These conditions could be buffering the corals against the heat even when the surrounding air temperatures remain high.
The distinction matters. The survival of these reefs may not have much to do with the biology of the corals or their symbiotic algae, and this might explain why the Red Sea corals began bleaching in 2024.
The sea remained unusually calm for about a month and a half during the 2024 heat wave, weakening the circulation he believes normally helps protect the reefs. HEPCA’s report identifies weak water circulation as a contributing factor in the bleaching. Exceptionally low tides in July 2024 may also have intensified stress on shallow coral communities.
Osman accepts that calm seas could have made bleaching more severe but says the circulation explanation needs further research. “I’m not denying the possibility of that,” he says. “But what I’m saying is, the temperature was the main issue.”
The two explanations are not necessarily mutually exclusive. But understanding their relative importance could help scientists assess how vulnerable these reefs are to future heat waves.
There are signs of recovery. HEPCA’s preliminary estimates a year after the bleaching event put recovery rates at 75 to 88 percent, depending on species and location. That is a far stronger rebound than seen elsewhere across the globe, where many reefs are only beginning to recover—if they show any progress at all.
Work to protect the Red Sea reefs ahead of the next heat wave is also under way, with the Egyptian government designating new protected areas as well as partnering with the United Nations Development Program and the Global Fund for Coral Reefs on conservation and sustainable management.
Osman sees such initiatives as a positive step but stresses that conservation requires sustained support. “We definitely need more stable financial resources, because conservation is not a single-year act.”
For Hanafy, the future of Egypt’s reefs also depends on whether climate change alters the circulation that has perhaps been keeping the corals alive.
Whatever explains their unusual resilience, local conservation cannot halt ocean warming. “Therefore, the key is to reduce carbon dioxide and greenhouse gases. Any other solution will just buy time,” Hanafy adds.

Welcome to Edition 9.15 of the Rocket Report! The launch I’m most looking forward to in the next few weeks is that of Japan’s Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission. MMX is one of the marquee space science missions launching this year, and it’s set to leave Earth as soon as Monday (US time) aboard a Japanese H3 rocket. The spacecraft will visit Phobos and Deimos, the two asteroid-like moons of Mars, deploying a rover and collecting specimens for return to Earth in 2031. Exploration at its finest.
As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Reflect Orbital looks to India for launch capacity. California-based Reflect Orbital, the startup attempting to offer sunlight on-demand with in-space mirrors, announced the purchase of two launches Wednesday from Indian launcher Skyroot Aerospace, Payload Space reports. One of the launches will use Skyroot’s Vikram-1 rocket, which became the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit in July. The other will fly on an upgraded rocket called the Vikram-1U.
Shining a light … Reflect Orbital plans to launch its first satellite on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rideshare next year. The company’s business model involves flying a constellation of some 50,000 mirrors in orbit to beam sunlight to the ground for power generation and illumination. The FCC approved Reflect’s first in-space mirror satellite earlier this year. The company’s selection of India’s Skyroot also shines a light on what satellite operators fear is a coming under-supply of launch capacity in the United States as SpaceX phases out its Falcon 9 rocket in favor of the much larger, but relatively unproven, Starship.
LEAP targets smallsat launch market. A Colorado rocket startup named LEAP is aiming to enter the market for dedicated small-satellite launches in 2028 as growing demand for access to orbit creates new opportunities for smaller rockets, Space News reports. LEAP’s Bighorn rocket is designed for an initial payload capacity of 320 pounds (145 kilograms) to low-Earth orbit, with a first orbital launch slated for 2028. Bighorn is sized for dedicated launch services, with a single-engine booster stage and a kick stage named Cottontail for orbit insertion.

She lies awake at night. The next morning, she struggles to concentrate at work, snaps at loved ones over things that never bothered her before, or wonders why her own body suddenly feels unfamiliar.For some women, menopause arrives quietly; for others, it brings a wave of physical and emotional changes that can leave them exhausted, anxious and searching for answers.And often, the hardest part is not just dealing with the symptoms, but getting someone to take them seriously.Menopause is a natural biological transition, but the symptoms can be disruptive enough to affect everyday life. While some women dismiss them as stress or ageing, others find their concerns brushed aside or are unsure where to turn for help. Despite growing conversations around women's health, gaps in awareness, medical guidance and access to appropriate treatment continue to shape their experiences.A quantitative descriptive survey involving 150 women from urban areas assessed the impact of menopausal symptoms on quality of life. The study, published in the Indian Journal of Preventive & Social Medicine, was authored by Somibala Thokchom and David Ratna Paul Talagathoti.
Participants aged 40 to 55 years completed the 11-item Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) to assess their symptoms and a modified 32-item Menopause-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire (MENQOL) to evaluate how menopause affected their daily lives.The study found that 58.7% of participants were aged 40–45 years, while 75.3% had already experienced menopause. Overall, 92% reported moderate to severe symptoms, 4.7% experienced mild symptoms and 3.3% reported very severe symptoms. Nearly all participants (99.3%) reported changes in their daily routines.
Menopause can bring a range of physical, emotional and urogenital symptoms, affecting women’s sleep, mood and everyday lives.
Although the findings cannot be generalised to all Indian women, given the small, urban sample, they highlight the potential impact of menopause on everyday life.The question is not simply how women experience menopause, but why so many may struggle to recognise their symptoms, seek medical advice or access appropriate care.
When menopause symptoms are dismissed as ‘just ageing’
Many women continue to experience menopause symptoms without seeking medical help, often assuming that fatigue, anxiety, disturbed sleep and mood changes are an inevitable part of ageing.Doctors say this can delay assessment and treatment, particularly when women prioritise family and work responsibilities over their own health.“Menopause is a natural condition, but that does not necessarily imply that symptoms cannot be treated,” said Dr Mitul Gupta, senior consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Cocoon Hospital, Jaipur.Dr Gupta cautioned against attributing symptoms to ageing without proper examination. Fatigue, irritability and poor concentration can also occur with conditions such as thyroid disorders, anaemia, sleep disorders and anxiety, making a detailed medical assessment important.Maya, a Uttar Pradesh native who now lives in Delhi, said, “I started experiencing menopause when I was 51. I did face difficulties, but back then, we didn’t really talk about these things at home. I used to feel hesitant."“I thought it was just a normal part of aging, and no one in my family really knew what I was going through. Even today, many families are unaware of what women experience during menopause, and often, women end up dealing with it on their own,” she adds.Menopause care extends beyond irregular periods and hot flashes. Hormonal changes can affect sleep, mood and sexual health, while the menopausal transition is also an important time to discuss longer-term health concerns, including bone health.
Treatment options for menopause range from hormone therapy and non-hormonal medicines to lifestyle changes
A systematic review titled Menopause Symptoms Experienced by Women in India, examined 23 studies reporting symptoms among menopausal women in India. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and included eligibility criteria, a literature search, screening and data extraction.The review found that somatic symptoms were the most frequently reported category, with an average of 73.66% across the studies. Joint and muscular pain and fatigue were the most commonly reported complaints, followed by hot flashes.Psychological symptoms were reported in an average of 63.03% of women in the studies assessing this category. Eighteen studies reported psychosomatic symptoms, while five did not report psychological symptoms.Urogenital symptoms were reported in 13 studies, with an average prevalence of 51.40%. Ten studies did not report symptoms in this category. Although urogenital symptoms were the least frequently reported, the review noted that women who experienced them reported greater symptom intensity.The findings highlight the range of symptoms associated with menopause and the importance of recognising them rather than dismissing them as an unavoidable consequence of ageing. The percentages are averages reported across the reviewed studies and should not be interpreted as prevalence estimates for all Indian women.
The doctor’s dilemma: recognising symptoms, choosing treatment
Menopause symptoms can vary considerably from one woman to another, making individual assessment essential before deciding on treatment.Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) can help women experiencing troublesome symptoms, including hot flashes and night sweats, but it is not suitable for everyone. Decisions about treatment must take into account an individual's symptoms, medical history, age, time since menopause and potential risks.“HRT is neither universally dangerous nor suitable for everyone. The right treatment is the one that is carefully chosen according to your individual needs, with proper medical guidance and regular follow-up,” said Dr Bharti Soy, consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Fortis O.P. Jindal Hospital & Research Centre.Doctors emphasise that consultations should cover the potential benefits and risks of hormone therapy, as well as non-hormonal alternatives where appropriate. Women should be able to discuss their concerns and make informed decisions with their healthcare providers.Symptoms should not automatically be attributed to menopause, as other medical conditions may require separate investigation and treatment. A thorough consultation can help distinguish between menopause-related changes and other possible causes, allowing care to be tailored to the individual's needs.
Is India’s healthcare system prepared for menopause?
Awareness alone may not be enough if women cannot access appropriate and affordable care. Gaps in menopause-specific knowledge, counselling and healthcare access can leave women without adequate guidance on managing their symptoms.The challenge is not limited to the availability of gynaecologists, but also whether consultations address menopause-related concerns beyond menstrual changes. Symptoms affecting sleep, mood, sexual wellbeing and bone health may require a broader discussion of a woman's physical and emotional health.
Treatments available in India
“Women need a complete evaluation not a consultation for the issues related to menstruation,” said Dr Priyanka Sharma, senior consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Cocoon Hospital, Chandigarh.Barriers such as the cost of travel, time away from work, lack of awareness and limited access to healthcare facilities can make seeking care more difficult. Strengthening primary-level assessment, training healthcare workers and establishing referral pathways could help women receive appropriate support.Education in local languages and more affordable treatment options are also important to ensure that women can understand their symptoms, discuss available choices and access care when needed.Making menopause a routine part of women's healthcare could help shift the focus from simply enduring symptoms to identifying and managing them appropriately.
How social stigma plays a role
Medical care is only part of the picture. Family attitudes and social expectations can influence whether women feel comfortable discussing menopause or seeking help.“In many Indian households, menopause is still not discussed openly because of social stigma, lack of awareness, and the belief that it is simply a natural process. As a result, many women suffer silently rather than seeking medical help,” said Dr Bharti Soy.When symptoms such as disturbed sleep, irritability or discomfort are dismissed as inevitable consequences of growing older, women may begin to question whether their concerns deserve medical attention.
Dr Soy talks to TOI
“If relatives tell her that discomfort, irritability or sleep problems are simply part of growing older, she may question whether her concerns deserve medical attention,” said Dr Swati Sinha, senior consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Rosewalk by Rainbow Hospitals.Families can help by making menopause a subject that can be discussed without embarrassment or judgement. Listening without dismissing symptoms, offering practical support and encouraging medical consultations when problems affect daily life can make the transition easier to navigate.
Partners, children and other family members need not have all the answers. Understanding that menopause affects women differently, and that help is available when symptoms become disruptive, is an important first step.Menopause may be a natural stage of life, but that does not mean women should have to endure its more difficult symptoms without support. Better awareness, informed medical consultations, accessible treatment and understanding families can help ensure that women are heard and their concerns taken seriously.

The group had asked its supporters to come to a park in Connaught Place, one of Delhi's busiest commercial districts, to wave the Indian flag.
The turnout was smaller than at earlier CJP demonstrations though the crowd seemed to be swelling. The BBC saw some young protesters being detained and shoved into a bus which already held some female detainees - there were about 50 female police personnel in the bus, vastly outnumbering the protesters.
Dipke had just left home and was moments away from reaching his vehicle when the BBC saw police officers surround him and force him into a police car. Some CJP supporters tried to block the vehicle from leaving.
Anish Gawande, the opposition politician at whose house Dipke had been staying, questioned why police had detained him. Police have not yet publicly confirmed the grounds for the detention.
"Detaining a lone man walking with the national flag in his hand is a bit of a joke," Gawande said.
It was the second time in less than a week that Dipke was detained. Last Saturday, police boarded his plane shortly after it landed in Delhi and took him away before he could reach a planned demonstration.
Police barricades and mass detentions prevented thousands of other protesters from reaching the venue. Dipke was released the following day, but two other CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were later jailed for five days after entering Jantar Mantar, a protest site recently declared off-limits by police.
Friday's march was partly intended to show solidarity with the two jailed leaders.
Dipke had acknowledged the possibility of being arrested again. In a video message on Thursday, he urged supporters unable to travel to Delhi to raise the Indian flag in their own towns and cities.
"I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said.
Earlier on Friday, police had served Dipke with a notice warning him against holding the march without permission.
Authorities also closed Central Park for two days, citing "administrative reasons". Police offered to let a small group wave the national flag and sing the anthem at another location.
The CJP responded by changing its plans, urging supporters to enter Connaught Place in groups of fewer than five, unfurl the flag, take a photograph and leave.
"Waving the Tiranga is not a crime," the group said in a social media poster, using the Hindi name for India's tricolour flag. It encouraged supporters to share their photographs online.
By the time the protest was due to begin, around 200-300 people had gathered near Central Park. Prevented by police from entering, they moved around the park, waving flags and shouting slogans.
Among those detained was Neha Bora, a prominent leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) who has emerged as one of the faces of the recent protests. She was also detained during last Saturday's crackdown.
Security personnel, meanwhile, continued to arrive. More officers emerged from buses stationed around Connaught Place, joining the thousands of police and paramilitary personnel already deployed. Journalists also crowded the streets, with police and media in much larger numbers than the protesters.
Barely five months old, the CJP began as an online campaign in May after India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches. Dipke embraced the insult and turned it into a rallying cry.
By July, the group had become a formidable force, drawing thousands of young people into protests over leaked examination papers. A march towards Parliament in July descended into clashes with police, bringing the movement wider attention and intensifying pressure on the government. The unrest eventually forced the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.
Police cited earlier demonstrations in their warning against Friday's march. In the notice served to Dipke, they accused the CJP of defying restrictions and said previous attempts to march towards Parliament had led to violence and damage to property.
They also warned that a large gathering in Connaught Place could disrupt traffic, affect businesses and obstruct emergency vehicles.
The CJP wants Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign, accusing the poll panel of favouring Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the commission and the government deny the allegations.
At issue is a sweeping revision of electoral rolls, known as Special Intensive Revision (SIR), that critics say has removed more than 130 million names, putting legitimate voters at risk of losing their right to vote.
Friday's march comes less than a week after police prevented the movement's last mass demonstration from taking place, detaining its leaders - Das, Dipke and Ranka - and putting the city under a sweeping security lockdown.
Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel had fanned out across Delhi, sealing roads, shutting metro stations and intercepting protesters long before they could reach Jantar Mantar, where the CJP had planned its mass demonstration.
The BBC witnessed dozens of people being detained, including journalists and students. In footage from across Delhi, protesters could be seen shouting as police seized them by the arms, dragged them across the pavement and pushed them into waiting buses.
Those who managed to gather elsewhere were swiftly dispersed. There were also reports of protesters being assaulted by police.
The BBC captured footage, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.
The scale of the crackdown drew widespread outrage, with the CJP likening the police action to India's Emergency, when civil liberties were suspended between 1975 and 1977.
Delhi police defended the measures as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings.
Dipke, Das and Ranka were released on Sunday after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour.
Police then took Jantar Mantar off Delhi's list of approved protest sites, designating three alternate venues. Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory sits near parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent. The CJP accused the authorities of pushing protesters away from the seat of power to make their demonstrations less visible and easier to ignore.
On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned with a handful of supporters, unfurling the Indian flag and shouting slogans against Kumar.
Police said they had entered the restricted site without permission, some by climbing over a locked gate, and breached the conditions of their release.
The following day, the two were sent to jail for five days in judicial custody. Another organiser, Ajinkya Shinde, was released on a bond to maintain peace and good behaviour.
The CJP's campaign is unfolding alongside a separate wave of protests by India's opposition parties, which have also accused the Election Commission of manipulating voter rolls to benefit the BJP.
Last week, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other lawmakers attempted to march to the commission's headquarters in Delhi but were stopped by police and detained. Opposition politicians have since taken their grievances to President Droupadi Murmu and marched towards the Supreme Court.
Although the CJP, student organisations and opposition parties have largely protested separately, their demands have increasingly converged. Gandhi has condemned the arrests of CJP organisers and called for Jantar Mantar to be reopened to peaceful demonstrators.
Home minister Amit Shah, meanwhile, has accused opposition parties of spreading falsehoods about the voter-verification exercise and defended the Election Commission's independence.

The Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026, presents an opportunity to strengthen Keralam’s response to population ageing. The Government of Keralam’s initiative to introduce this first-of-its-kind legislation in the country is a welcome step towards protecting the rights and well-being of senior citizens.
By recognising dignity, independence, safety, participation and access to care, the Bill provides a foundation for moving beyond welfare and towards a comprehensive, entitlements-based approach to ageing.
Central principle
A central principle of the Bill is ageing in place, enabling older persons to remain in their homes and communities for as long as possible, with institutional care as a last resort. This requires supporting families through accessible health care, community-based services, trained caregivers, rehabilitation, and social support. Care must be organised as a continuum, responding to changing needs rather than only during crises.
Equally important is the shift from managing dependence to preventing or delaying avoidable functional decline. The Bill’s provision for standardised care assessments, incorporating intrinsic capacity and functional dependency, is particularly relevant. Linking these assessments with primary and community health care could enable earlier identification of changes in mobility, cognition, sensory function and daily activities, followed by timely interventions that help preserve independence.
Addressing critical gaps
The Bill also addresses critical gaps in the care ecosystem through provisions for registration and regulation of care institutions, caregiver training and certification, and minimum standards of service delivery. These measures must be accompanied by appropriate supervision, continuing education, fair working conditions, and support for family caregivers.
The proposed district-level institutional mechanisms offer an opportunity to strengthen accountability, grievance redressal, and coordination. The Bill also introduces penalties, including fines and imprisonment, for specified violations, reinforcing the importance of compliance and protection of senior citizens’ rights.
The effectiveness will depend on clear responsibilities, adequate resources, effective enforcement, and convergence across health, social welfare and local self-government systems.
An age-ready Keralam must be measured not only by the institutions and services established but also by whether older persons can maintain their functional ability, remain connected to their communities and live with dignity, independence, security and purpose.
The next priority is translating legislative provisions into accessible, equitable and quality services, particularly for older persons living alone, those with disabilities or dementia, and those without adequate family support.
Overall, the Bill presents a robust framework for geriatric care. Its efficient implementation can help set an effective precedent that can be replicated nationwide.
(Prof. (Dr.) Sudha Chandrashekar is CEO, Swasti - The Health Catalyst, a not-for-profit global organisation in the field of public health).

Hong Kong authorities have said lifts at 74 more private buildings installed by Taizoom Elevator are missing crucial door frame components, taking the total of affected properties to 152.

Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting
- Published
France awoke to scenes of widespread damage on Sunday after a day of riots and demonstrations, with shopfronts shattered, burnt out cars, charred bikes, and piles of glass and debris on the pavements of Paris.
Police arrested about 1,800 people on Saturday as some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for protests that were largely peaceful.
They were demonstrating against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
In Paris, protesters clashed with riot police, who turned tear gas and water cannon on the crowds. During the day, some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles. At least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.
Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.
Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram. In Lille, a McDonalds was set on fire, police said, and an Apple store in the city was broken into and looted.
More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured in the unrest on Saturday, France's interior ministry said.
Around 1,500 shops and retailers were also damaged in the disturbances, the Retail and Trade Federation said.
On Sunday morning in Paris, residents surveyed the aftermath, which included the smashed glass frontages of designer stores including Ralph Lauren, Gucci and Versace.
Shopkeepers were out early with brooms, picking up large shards of glass as they began the clean-up. Rubbish trucks worked their way down some of the larger streets to clear some of the debris.
Many shops were daubed with graffiti, some reading "tax the rich" and "eat the rich."
The BBC visited a clothes shop close to the Place de la République which had been ransacked, with piles of clothes and furniture scattered across the shop floor.
The shop's distraught owner told the BBC he saw looters on the CCTV who were in the shop for just over an hour and a half, and that during that time he saw no police in the process.
The owner - who asked not to be identified - told the BBC he did not believe any of those who robbed the shop were genuine protesters against school conditions or the cost of living. He said the looters were taking advantage of the demonstrations.
Close to the Place de la République, a BBC reporter visited the Good Vibes bakery, whose glass front was completely shattered, and the Nicolas wine store, where every bottle was either stolen or smashed, leaving smell of alcohol lingering in the street.
CCTV footage shown on France's Channel 2 shows groups of teenagers, mostly wearing masks, in a shop selling mobile phones helping themselves to items from the shelves.
Student protests in France have seen hundreds of thousands take to the streets since they began late last month. Protesters have been demanding additional investment in their schools, criticising the lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.
Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.
In the city of Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling French outlet BFMTV that "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".
Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.
Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost."
"A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department.
Elsewhere, a young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media.
"Such a tragedy should never have happened," he said.
France's interior ministry said Saturday's protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also in Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse, and the western city of Angers.
Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.

Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.) has some advice for fellow lawmakers: unapologetically support the biotech industry, vilify insurance companies, and focus on making America a biotech research haven, instead of relying on protectionism.
Right now in Washington, it’s popular to support protectionist policies against China in industries like tech. China is rapidly gaining on the U.S. biotechnology industry, and there is bipartisan support to extend those protections to the biotech sector.
Auchincloss said that approach hurts America’s competitiveness.
“Washington needs to fix itself and worry less about what China is doing because China is going to be excellent,” he said at the STAT Summit in Boston on Thursday. “But we can be even better.”
That attitude aligns with the views of the biotech industry and its investors. America cannot stop China from becoming a biotech powerhouse, the thinking goes, so Congress should invest in the domestic biotechnology industry and speed research and development.
Auchincloss plans to introduce a bill that would adopt the approach taken by the Australian government, which has sped up the clinical trial regime in part by allowing early-phase trials to bypass pre-approval evaluation by the national regulator. It will never be as cheap to conduct early-stage trials in the U.S. as it is in China, Auchincloss said, but it should be as fast.
He said he’s also interested in cracking down on pharmacy benefit manager business practices, reforming the 340B hospital drug discount program, and creating small business grants.
Although drugmakers have become a popular target of lawmakers, Massachusetts lawmakers should boldly promote the industry, which plays a crucial role in the state’s economy, Auchincloss said.
“Some advice from a six-year veteran of Washington, D.C.: You do need a villain, and the villain is the insurance company,” he said during the conversation with STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo.
Another villain, in his eyes: Russ Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, who Auchincloss said considers science a “blue state subsidy.” The OMB proposed empowering the White House to override the recommendations of peer reviewers, terminate grants at will, and exercise more latitude in the type of research federal agencies support.
Auchincloss also took issue with the Food and Drug Administration’s Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher program. Former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary created the program, and it has come under scrutiny from industry stakeholders and public health advocates.
Auchincloss said it politicizes decisions that should be guided by transparent, well thought-out standards. For example, Makary awarded vouchers to psychedelics after podcaster Joe Rogan texted President Trump about research around ibogaine.
“If Washington behaves that way, there’s nothing that we’re going to do about Beijing that’s going to save our biomedical leadership,” Auchincloss said. “Because ultimately, what makes us great is high, clear, transparent standards paired with the world’s best talent getting funded to pursue curiosity-driven research.”

Leigh Hoffman wins second silver at UCI Track World Championships, Harrie Lavreysen wins 23rd world title
In short:
Leigh Hoffman claimed a silver medal in the men's individual sprint at the UCI track world championships in Shanghai.
Dutch legend Harrie Lavreysen won sprint gold for the eighth year in a row, winning a record-extending 23rd world title.
Australia won just two medals at the track world championships, down from the five won 12 months ago.
Australian cyclist Leigh Hoffman has claimed silver in the individual sprint at the UCI World Championships in Shanghai.
Hoffman, who won the bronze medal at the world championships 12 months ago, was beaten by Dutch legend Harrie Lavreysen in the gold medal race.
"To come away with a silver is still pretty amazing," Hoffman told AusCycling.
"But it is bitter sweet to be so close to getting a world title and having it slip away."
It was Australia and Hoffman's second medal of the world championships, after the men's team sprint squad won silver to the Netherlands on the first night at the spectacular Shanghai Velodrome.
Lavreysen won both sprints in the gold medal match, but there is little doubt that the 29-year-old five-time Olympic champion was still made to work for it.
Hoffman was the fastest qualifier for the sprint, the South Australian laying down a stunning 9.285 for his flying 200m on Saturday, and progressed comfortably through to the final.
Leading off in their first match up, Hoffman appeared to be in control before briefly dipping off the racing line.
That momentary lapse washed the Whyalla man's speed and allowed Lavreysen to power past him in the home straight.
The Dutchman made no mistake in the second race, leading from the front with brutal power to stay away and win a record-extending 23rd world title.
"Obviously wanted to win it but just didn't come away with it," Hoffman said.
"Lavreysen, he's won 23 world titles so he's got a ton of experience whereas for myself, that's my first gold-silver [race] at world champs."
No rider has managed to beat Lavreysen in an individual sprint at a world championships since Australian Matthew Glaetzer won gold in 2018.
But Hoffman showed once again that he is getting closer to becoming the first man to wrest the rainbow jersey from Lavreysen shoulders in almost a decade.
"I had a lot of confidence going through the rounds yesterday and today," Hoffman said.
"Beating [Japan's] Kaiya Ota in straight sets [in the semifinal], someone who has beaten me at the Olympics and beaten me at Copenhagen Worlds as well, it was good to get some runs on the board against him."
Missing from the sprint field at these world championships was former Australian rider and world record holder in the flying 200m, Matt Richardson.
Richardson was withdrawn from the British squad earlier in the week over alleged misconduct, with the 27-year-old writing on social media that he both understood the seriousness of the allegations and would cooperate with any investigation.
"I understand the seriousness of what has been raised in recent reports about my withdrawal from the 2026 UCI Track Cycling World Championships," Richardson wrote.
"British Cycling has said it looks into matters like this through its established procedures. I will cooperate fully with its processes.
"I assure everyone that I will do so properly, and appropriately and with contrition for the feelings of anyone who might be affected.
"Out of fairness to everyone involved, and on advice, like British Cycling, I will not be commenting further until any process is complete."
The UK-born, Perth-raised rider won three Olympic medals for Australia before switching allegiance to Great Britain after the 2024 Paris Games.

I was reporting on the ground near Connaught Place, close to Rajiv Chowk metro station, when Delhi Police detained me and several other journalists at around 11:20 am on October 10, 2026.
Delhi Police and central security forces had cordoned off the area around Jantar Mantar, preventing protesters and journalists from approaching the designated protest site. I was filming the police action and speaking to people present at the scene when officers began pushing and shoving individuals standing at the intersection of Connaught Place and Kharak Singh Marg. Several people were holding placards to express their dissent when police arrived and began detaining them.
While I filmed the detentions, one officer thrust his hand towards me and attempted to grab me. I showed him my press card. He backed off but continued gesturing aggressively. On camera, I asked him what legal guideline or constitutional provision allowed him to detain or attempt to assault a journalist on duty. He became enraged, and a heated exchange followed. The police then detained several journalists, including me.
We were shoved into a bus and driven across the national capital. When we repeatedly asked the officers which legal procedure they were following to detain us, they did not respond. They also refused to tell us where we were being taken.
The journey lasted around two hours. We travelled along Deen Dayal Upadhyay Marg, crossed the Yamuna, passed Shahdara flyover and Burari, and eventually reached the Delhi-Karnal highway. We became increasingly concerned about our destination. At 8 am, when I had begun reporting on the ground, I had noticed several police vehicles bearing HR and UP number plates. Our apprehensions grew as the bus continued along the Karnal expressway for another 20 minutes or so.
During the two-hour journey from Connaught Place towards neighbouring Haryana, we were not provided with sufficient drinking water or other basic necessities in the scorching heat. We managed to get some water only when a truck driver passed his bottle through the bus window. However, packed food, including bananas, biscuits and kachori, were already available on the bus.
Around 2 pm, we arrived at Rajiv Gandhi Stadium in Bawana, Delhi, approximately 65 km from Connaught Place. The stadium had been converted into a detention centre, where around 100 people detained from different parts of Delhi were being held.
I began documenting the situation inside the detention centre, speaking to detainees and trying to understand the circumstances in an area that had been without internet connectivity since the previous night.
A Cockroach Janta Party coordinator, reportedly picked up from his residence in Burari around 3 am on October 10, described his experience to me. “No food, no proper water, and a contingent of police officials who were not cooperating with anything since I was detained,” he said.
The stadium, usually filled with the sounds of athletes and cheering fans, now echoed with protesters’ slogans. “Vote Chor, Gaddi Chor” (The vote thief needs to resign) rang out across the premises.
A few minutes later, another bus brought in a group of protesters. They alleged that the police had shoved them into the bus and assaulted them. Despite this, they continued raising slogans against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the BJP-led Union government. Those detained included supporters and activists of the Muslim Students’ Federation (MSF), the All India Students’ Federation (AISF), the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), and leaders of the Communist Party of India (Marxist).
CPI(M) leaders Sujan Chakraborty and Manik Sarkar, the former chief minister of Tripura, were also at the detention centre, along with several other leaders from across the country. Sudip Dutta, general secretary of the Centre for Indian Trade Unions (CITU), a prominent national trade union affiliated with the CPI(M), had also been detained and brought to the stadium.
I spoke to a student from Delhi about how they intended to pursue their demands. Aman, an AISF member, said voter deletions and irregularities in Form 6 could affect future generations of voters.
“See, this issue of voter deletions is going to impact the upcoming generations who are going to vote tomorrow. As college students, it is our responsibility to make our peers aware about these issues. After today, we would hit the classrooms, reach out to our friends and make them aware of how this issue of ‘vote Chori’ that has come to light is going to impact them and the generations to come,” he said.
Another student, Ali, spoke about police brutality and the use of central security personnel to curb the right to protest.
“We were picked up from Minto Road. The police had barricaded the entire area. Around ten police officers were charging at a single protester, and dragging them to the police van. CRPF, BSP, ITBP, CISF, and even Uttar Pradesh Police are on duty. Why is the government acting like this to curb the voices of the students,” he said.
I spent another hour documenting events at Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, where protesters continued raising slogans despite being detained. Around 3:30 pm, after repeated negotiations with police officers, I was released along with another journalist.
As we left the premises, we were asked to provide our personal details. When we identified ourselves as journalists, several officers appeared astonished and initially thought we were lying. They believed us only after we showed our press cards.
The exchange lasted around ten minutes. It became clear that the officers at the detention centre had received no instructions or communication informing them that journalists were also being detained.
During the four to five hours I spent under detention, the same ort of resentment came up in every conversation: Allegations, an investigation and protests against Gyanesh Kumar had prompted the Union government to take preventive measures in the name of maintaining law and order. These measures were so extensive that people seeking reforms to Indian democracy were being detained. The scale of the restrictions was equally alarming.
Metro services, railway stations, roads and shops in parts of Delhi were directed to be shut down, affecting daily commuters, roadside hawkers and shopkeepers. Internet services were also suspended within a four-kilometre radius of the Janpath-Kartavya Path area and in and around makeshift detention centres across Delhi. Internet connectivity was suspended in the area surrounding Rajiv Gandhi Stadium as well.
A shopkeeper in Bawana, near the stadium, told me that the internet shutdown had caused significant losses because customers could not make online payments. The preventive measures affected not only protesters but also ordinary people, disrupting the lives of commuters, daily-wage labourers, shopkeepers, railway platform-based workers, auto drivers and others going about their daily routines.
Why was Delhi being subjected to what resembled a state of emergency?
Article 19(1) of the Indian Constitution guarantees individuals the right to express their opinions and protest, subject to the applicable constitutional restrictions and the rights of others. The government can also take measures to maintain law and order. But how far can such measures legally and constitutionally extend?
I continued to think about these questions as I travelled to Samaypur Badli metro station, approximately 17 km from the detention centre. The 30-minute journey offered no concrete answers.

One of the reasons plastic has become so ubiquitous is that, generally, it’s very chemically stable, meaning it does not readily react with the substances around it. That’s why this material is so often used for food packaging and water bottles.
The same was thought to be true of microplastics—those tiny pieces of debris that break off from larger plastic objects and which, according to numerous studies, have spread to virtually every ecosystem on the planet. But scientists at Columbia University and UC Berkeley have just discovered that water can make the surfaces of microplastics chemically active and turn them into a potential hazard.
According to the findings of the article published in Nature, this activity can trigger the spontaneous formation of chemicals capable of altering other molecules, like those that are essential for living organisms. The phenomenon, the authors note, occurs even under normal environmental conditions, without the need for sunlight or other agents that cause plastic degradation.
So how can microplastics be so reactive when bigger plastics generally aren’t? The scientists suggest this has to do with the greater available surface area for these reactions to occur.
“As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously,” Wei Min, a professor of chemistry and biomedical engineering at Columbia University, said in a press release. “Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure.”
Among these potentially dangerous chemical products—called reactive oxygen species—a variety known as hydroxyl radicals stands out. They are particularly dangerous because they can snatch electrons from the proteins and fats that make up cell membranes, disrupting their structure and function. These “are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue,” added Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Min’s lab who helped lead the research.
Our body has some defenses against this kind of damage. This is the biological function of the buzzy molecules known as antioxidants. These neutralize the reactive chemicals, but if the reactive compounds greatly outnumber antioxidants, this line of defense can be overwhelmed.
This can develop into a scenario called oxidative stress, leading to the damage of cells. Previous research had already identified oxidative stress among the cellular responses associated with exposure to microplastics, although the mechanisms responsible for this damage are not yet fully understood.
The extent to which microplastics have pervaded our bodies remains an open debate, with some of the more sensational findings having been called into question. But if even a small amount of microplastics are present in our tissues, they could be reacting with the water in our bodies.
The researchers were particularly concerned with the potential effects on blood, which is largely composed of water. If contact with this fluid can chemically activate the surfaces of microplastics, their presence inside the body could pose an additional danger beyond that of the pollutants they carry or release.
When the researchers exposed red blood cells extracted from mice to different types of microplastics, the cells became deformed and ruptured—a phenomenon known as hemolysis. The effects were greater with plastics that were more reactive with water, indicating that this activity was the cause of cellular damage.
Research into the effects of microplastics has long focused on other chemicals leaching from the particles or on their physical effects, often considering the plastic itself chemically inert. The larger pieces generally are, but these findings challenge the assumption that what is true of plastic on a grand scale is also true of the microscopic pieces it breaks down into.

The deputy mayor of Saijo, Ehime Prefecture, died on Saturday after being trapped beneath a festival float during the Saijo Festival, police said.
Akihiro Nabae, 62, was among those carrying the float when the incident occurred on a riverbed in the city at around 5:45 p.m. He was taken to the hospital and was pronounced dead about an hour later. No one else was injured.
According to the police and the municipal government, the float, known as a taikodai, stood about 5.3 meters tall and weighed between 2 and 3 metric tons.
At the time of the accident, 11 floats were lined up side by side for a traditional contest known as kakikurabe, in which teams of carriers compete to demonstrate their strength and skill in maneuvering the floats.
The Saijo Festival is a collective name for the annual festivals held at four shrines in the city. Dating back to the Edo Period (1603-1867), the festival features more than 100 floats and other portable structures, including mikoshi, or portable shrines, and danjiri festival floats.
Nabae had previously served as director of the city’s environmental department and took office as deputy mayor in July this year.
Mayor Mitsuyoshi Ochi expressed shock and sorrow over Nabae’s death.
“Just when we were about to work together to build a new administration for Saijo, this tragedy occurred. I still cannot believe it. I offer my heartfelt condolences,” Ochi said in a statement.
The Saijo Police Station is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.
Nabae’s death comes just a week after two people died in separate incidents at danjiri festivals in Osaka Prefecture.

From the Royole FlexPai to the iPhone Duo: How the modern foldable phone has evolved
Are foldables finally ready to go mainstream?
Technological advances often come with growing pains. This is no less true of phones. The 1984 "brick" phone (DynaTAC 8000X) required users to carry over 1.7 pounds of weight for only half an hour of talk time, at a hefty price tag of $3,995. Foldable phones are not so troublesome, but I still struggled to fit the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 4 in my pocket when I first got it. What's more, the size of it kept prompting friends to ask why I was carrying two phones around. I wish I had been, for at least it would mean one would have a decent camera. Still, the moment when the phone unfolded and the screen adjusted to the larger size was as awe-inspiring back then as it is now.
Today, after having gotten my hands on some newer models, I have become very impressed by the lengths foldable technology has reached. Models including the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 have propelled the technology forward. Even Apple has decided to enter the market, with the iPhone Duo launch that has everyone talking. Suddenly, the future uptake of foldable phones is almost a certainty. Apple might well end up having everything to do with this change, but it would not have been possible without the long list of breakthroughs — and failures — that came before it.
The first stumbles: Royole, Samsung and Huawei
Trend pieces declared 2019 the "year of the foldable." It was not, though those 12 months did provide the first meaningful strides in the technology. The first device of this type to make a splash in the headlines was designed by an unknown Chinese display manufacturer: Royole. The company presented the FlexPai at CES 2019, with all the pomp and circumstance that "the world's first commercially available foldable smartphone" required. It was a feat of technology. It captivated the audience, if only momentarily. For all its charms, Engadget's reporters at the time found the Royole FlexPai to be "rough around the edges," strangely sized and, overall, "janky." Regardless, it demonstrated that flexible OLED could ship in a real product.
Later that year came a second attempt. Samsung's first Galaxy Fold was released in February 2019, kick-starting a series of unfortunate events for the phone manufacturer. If you were there, you might remember the influx of terrible reviews that followed. Despite a high price (just under $2,000), many reviewers complained that their phone screens had broken after little use, and it was revealed that most of them had peeled off a layer of plastic that was acting as a screen protector. The phone's fragility forced Samsung to delay the public launch and recall all units sent to reviewers so it could re-engineer the product. The new version was, however, only "somewhat" more sturdy. Overall, those first Samsung phones showed the importance of perfecting the crease, hinge durability and screen resistance as key to the success of foldable phones.
The next step showed the route not taken. Huawei's Mate X, presented at MWC 2019, folded outward instead of inward. It used a single high-resolution display that wrapped around the outside of the phone. The resulting design was extremely elegant. The problem? The screen could easily be scratched and damaged. On top of that, the phone was never sold in the United States due to the sanctions imposed by then-President Donald Trump on Chinese technologies. Still, for as striking as the Mate X was, the company's next foldable, the Mate X2, used the inward fold introduced by Royole and Samsung, showing that different does not necessarily mean better.
The Android maturity years
The years between 2020 and 2025 gave way to an avalanche of foldable phone models, pushed by Android phone makers. Almost every phone released over these years came with a significant advance. It was all this hard work that has made the foldable phone viable. Still, no specific model achieved what the manufacturers truly wanted: to make the foldable phone mainstream.
At first, foldable phone makers were mainly concerned with protecting the screens against pressure, water and dust. In 2020, Samsung's Galaxy Z Flip introduced ultra-thin glass in the inner screen, making it more robust. The Z Fold 3 and Z Flip 3, released in 2021, came with IPX8 water resistance. Dust was harder to protect against than water, but still the Fold 6 came with partial dust protection (IP48). In 2025, Google's Pixel 10 Pro Fold reached full IP68. The other big battle was how to address the crease. It was Oppo, with its 2021 Find N, that achieved a near-invisible crease. After that, Honor's Magic V series kept cutting thickness until Samsung answered with the slim Galaxy Z Fold 7.
The other element that needed to change for the technology to be widespread was pricing. Over this period, clamshell phones like the rebooted Motorola Razr and the $999 Galaxy Z Flip 3 brought prices down to regular flagship levels, making foldable phones better for everyone's physical and figurative pockets.
Apple comes to town
Can Apple make the final push that will take foldable phones into the mainstream? It has done it before and could, no doubt, do it again if the iPhone Duo is everything that has been promised.
During its history, Apple has mastered the ability to wait until the first hiccups of a technology have passed before entering a market and disrupting it. The company did it with touchscreens, and again with foldable phones, waiting until the crease problem that Samsung struggled with had been resolved before putting out its own model. In 2026, the announcement finally arrived in the form of the iPhone Duo. Folded, the phone is passport-sized. It has a 7.6-inch internal display and a 5.4-inch external display, at a starting price of $1,999. Overall, it has all the ingredients to be a huge success, with reviewers deeming the iPhone Duo Apple's "most exciting device in a decade." Counterpoint even told Bloomberg the phone's sales are expected to reach 6 million units in 2026 alone. Taking Apple's history as a guide, we could be about to witness the exact moment when foldable phones finally become fashionable.

A 49-year-old Brazilian man sold his possessions and travelled nearly 1,200 miles (1,931 km) to meet a woman he believed he would marry, only to find out that she was an artificial intelligence (AI)-generated character.
Edimar Martins, a bricklayer from Maranhão, a state in northeastern Brazil, told local broadcaster TV Mirante that he discovered a social media account featuring a woman named Jessica Oliveira, also known as Jessica Fazendeira, in 2020.
The account, which reportedly had over 300,000 followers, shared videos depicting the woman living a seemingly perfect rural life on a farm. She invited men to live with her, offering them accommodation and financial support.
Martins, who had been dealing with loneliness after his mother's death, believed the woman could help him rebuild his life. In one of the videos posted on the account, she promised financial assistance and offered him a place to stay on her farm.
Convinced that he had found a potential life partner, Martins decided to travel to meet the woman. According to the New York Post, he sold his belongings on October 9 to finance his journey to Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais in southeastern Brazil.
After spending more than a day travelling by bus, he arrived in the city on October 11, hoping to meet the woman he had seen online.
However, the journey ended in disappointment. Armed with photographs of the woman, Martins searched for her around the city and asked passers-by whether they recognised her. When nobody could identify her, he approached a local radio station for help.
It was there that he learnt that the woman did not exist and that the social media account was fake. Martins subsequently discovered that the person he had hoped to marry was an AI-generated persona.
"It only brings sadness, discouragement, and depression. Many people wanted to find a relationship, so I came," he said.
The person operating the social media account later confirmed that the woman was created using AI, while denying having any direct interaction with Martins.
"I came here to state the obvious: I am made of artificial intelligence. have never spoken to anyone with this profile. The intention was to gain engagement for sale. I never spoke directly to anyone, much less took anyone to Belo Horizonte. It was a surprise to me to see what is happening," the made-up woman said.
Having spent his money travelling to Belo Horizonte, Martins found himself stranded in the city and turned to municipal authorities for assistance.
Social workers stepped in to help him, providing food, access to shower facilities and a bus ticket so that he could leave the city.
Despite the setback, Martins has not abandoned his search for a partner. He is currently staying with a family member but still hopes to return to Belo Horizonte to find someone with whom he can build a life.
"I didn't find her, but I'll find another one, and it will be in the same place I went, and I'll go again," Martins said.
According to The Sun, Martins is the third man in less than six months to travel to Belo Horizonte in the hope of meeting a woman who later turned out to be an AI-generated character.

Data centers house computer servers for storing and managing data. The rise in artificial intelligence has led to an increase in the construction of massive data center buildings to support the technology's training and intense data requirements.
The recent boom in their development has been unpopular with many people in the United States, particularly when those structures are being built in their local area.
While data centers did exist prior to the development of AI as it's known today, little attention was paid to them before. With the American public now more widely scrutinizing the structures, Snopes has been researching numerous claims about them, particularly their construction and potential impact on local communities and the environment.
Here are 11 stories we've looked into about data centers over the last two years.

First responders
Many a time, it is the peers who are in the best place to spot early signs of mental distress. That is a reason why the Department of Social Work (Mental Health) at Madras School of Social Work in Egmore trains its second year students to offer peer support in mental health.
Although the programme is offered to all, not all students sign up to become a first responder, the diffidence stemming from the fact that being a first responder requires niche skills.
J. Damen Queen, associate professor, Department of Social Work - Mental Health, says this is a sustainable support service within the system that addresses three As - accessibility, affordability and availability. For students, this is an opportunity to offer care and support while they are still studying, boosting their confidence, knowledge and practical skills to recognise and respond to early signs of mental distress.
The faculty says that they are next working on a pilot programme where they want to reach out to 20 colleges in Chennai to train them as trainers and thus create mental health ambassadors in these institutions.
The gratitude wall
Research says that practising gratitude can reduce stress, improve mood, and strengthen relationships. So once in every two or three months, Gratitude Walls are sure to be spotted on the campus of CTTE College for Women in Perambur. They come in all shapes, sometimes taking the form of a tree with branches, many a time on a specially designed notice board and placed at strategic locations so that a good number of students can take part in this mindfulness activity.
Some are guided on the objective behind the wall — a space to celebrate life’s little and big things one is thankful for.
Alima Zahra, head, Department of Psychology, says the gratitude wall actually does bring in a measurable difference in a short time. “It is easy to execute and is a space to reflect. We have some faculty who have started doing this activity with their students,” says the HOD. She adds that one therapeutic event involving music, sand, movement are among activities they conduct to address mental health issues. The college also has a mental health and wellness club.
Teenagers break the stigma
This year-long volunteer peer support initiative at Chettinad Vidyashram empowers students across classes to speak up, reach out for help, tackle stigma and inspire change. Led by psychology students of Class XII, the “Young Helper Project” was started in 2024.
In Class XI, they are given a primer on mental health and the next year, they start taking mass sessions for students across classes I to XI, spread across the academic year, at least one a month and on a range of topics such as bullying, peer pressure and self-esteem.
What makes these sessions engaging are they are sometimes play-based or involves seniors sharing their respective journeys.
Sometimes a class XII student is sent to engage with a child through a drawing activity and in the process make him/her open up about certain topics disturbing him.
G. Parvathi, head of department, Psychology, says when teachers don an additional role as counsellor there is some hesitation from children to open up or reach out for help. “Young Helper Project was started to bridge that gap. Besides giving students an opportunity to be a trainer, the sessions nudge children to reach out to the counselling department in case of pressing issues bothering them and never hesitate to ask for help,” says Parvathi.
Nature as therapist
Two nature-based outdoor activities at Women’s Christian College on College Road in Chennai are linked to positive mental health outcomes such as improved focus, lower stress and better mood. Community gardening has been in the curriculum at this sprawling green campus for some years and what makes it special is the flexibility quotient that it offers students. The Centre for Environment Studies at the College invites students across disciplines to sign up, allowing them to choose a plot and work on growing vegetables and greens. Seeds and tools for gardening and the necessary guidance are offered.
There are no timelines given or number of hours they have to clock; students choose to work as and when they wish, but they are encouraged to come as a group. A student with a bad day might choose to spend more time at her green patch.
C . Anupama, Dean, Centre for Environmental Studies, WCC, says they have 25 students across departments who have enrolled for this in this academic year and updates on progress of veggies are shared on a WhatsApp group to motivate them.
The Centre also initiated Forest Bathing, a walk on the campus where they encourage participants to slow down, breath deeply and engage their senses while spending time with trees.
Both activities are therapeutic, and in Forest Bathing the strategy changes depending on the group. If there are literature students then they write poetry or if it is an mixed group they hug trees, says Anupama.

The college football rankings are in for a shakeup after a historic weekend for the Associated Press Top 25

After a weekend never before seen for teams in the Associated Press Top 25, a major shakeup is on tap in the college football poll on Sunday.
Five of the top seven teams in the rankings — No. 1 Georgia, No. 2 Notre Dame, No. 5 Indiana, No. 6 Alabama and No. 7 Texas — lost on the same day in the regular season for the first time in the history of the poll that began in 1936. It’s the first time Nos. 1 and 2 lost on the same day in the regular season since 2012 and eight Top 25 teams lost in all.
No. 3 Miami (6-0) was among the survivors — barely. The Hurricanes are set to take over the top poll spot for the first time since 2002 after beating rival Florida State 43-35 in a double-overtime thriller.
If they do, the Hurricanes can only hope to do better than the No. 1 team has the last two weeks; Texas and Georgia lost to unranked teams, the first time that's happened in consecutive weeks since 1990.
Also up for possible promotions are No. 4 Ohio State (6-1), which beat the Hoosiers 19-15, No. 8 BYU (6-0), which knocked off Notre Dame 28-24; No. 9 Mississippi (5-1), which routed No. 13 Missouri 31-3; and No. 10 Texas Tech (6-0), which beat Arizona State 53-25.
It could be quite a day for the Big 12, with No. 11 Utah (6-0) among the unbeaten after holding off Colorado 27-24.
The questions include be how far Georgia, Notre Dame and Indiana might fall after close losses. Alabama and Texas now have two losses each and No. 14 Tennessee (6-1) is in line for a step up after beating the Crimson Tide 26-10.

The surprising afterlife of an elephant in the African savannah
New study finds elephants continue to transform the savannah ecosystem years after death
Across the sun-baked plains of the African savannah, elephants are bringing new meaning to life after death.
At least, that’s according to the findings of a new study by an international team of researchers who examined the sites of elephant carcasses in South Africa’s Kruger National Park.
These gentle grey giants — often referred to as “ecosystem engineers” — are known to shape the savannah when they’re alive, excavating waterholes, knocking down trees and consuming copious amounts of vegetation. That much, researchers knew already.
“What we didn’t know was whether those impacts that are so significant when they’re alive could actually continue after they die,” ecologist Courtney Reed, lead author of the study, told As It Happens guest host Dave Seglins.
“Their bodies contain so many nutrients, tons of carbon and nitrogen and phosphorus, we wanted to understand if the nutrients from those carcasses could actually continue to play a role in the ecosystem.”
The findings were published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. Reed, who now works at Princeton University, conducted the research while she was a post-doctoral researcher at the University of California Santa Barbara.
Cycle of renewal
By studying soil chemistry, biodiversity and animal grazing around the megacarcasses, the researchers found that decomposition released “enormous pools of nutrients” into the earth. This stimulated soil microbial activity and helped nutrient-rich plants grow, attracting herbivores to the site long after any remaining signs of the elephant carcass.
The effects of decomposition last for more than seven years after the elephants die, the researchers found.
But that burst of regrowth and biological activity doesn’t happen right away. In fact, the caracasses’ high concentration of nutrients initially kills off vegetation on the site, leaving large bare patches or “cold spots” in biodiversity, Reed said.
The study found that the high concentration of nutrients in elephant carcasses initially kills off vegetation around the place of decomposition, leaving large bare patches or 'cold spots' in biodiversity. (Submitted by Courtney Reed)
“Too much of a good thing isn’t always a good thing,” she said. “You have this huge pulse of nitrogen, often in the form of ammonium, which at really high concentrations can actually be really toxic to plants.”
Over time, however, Reed says the ecosystem begins to recover as the excess ammonium dissipates and bacteria convert some of it into nitrate, a form of nitrogen that plants can more readily absorb.
Reed says the vegetation that returns is particularly rich in nitrogen, an important source of protein for herbivores.
“Then you have herbivores like zebra and buffalo and rhinos who are all coming in and they’re selectively chewing on these nitrogen rich grasses,” she said. “So you actually get this burst of herbivore activity that continues for years after the elephants died.”
And the benefits don’t stop there. Researchers found that grazing animals continue to visit these burial sites years later, further enriching the soil through their waste.
For Reed, that cycle of renewal is one of the study’s key takeaways: the potential for positive feedback loops to keep influencing the surroundings long after the elephant’s death.
Researchers found that grazing animals and scavengers continue to visit the site of the carcass years later, further enriching the soil through their waste. (Submitted by Courtney Reed)
But the ecological legacy of an elephant carcass isn’t necessarily a positive one in every landscape, suggests one expert unrelated to the study.
Chase LaDue, elephant ecologist and curator of research at the Oklahoma City Zoo, said the paper's findings highlight how delicately balanced an ecosystem must be.
In the African savannah, where biodiversity is shaped in part by natural disturbances, an elephant carcass can help sustain the ecosystem, he said, but if the habitat has shrunk due to humans encroaching on it, those carcasses can instead disrupt the balance.
“If enough elephants die in a very concentrated space, that has an impact on the biodiversity that sort of can’t be spread out as it would in a more undisturbed larger landscape,” LaDue said.
“This area of southern Africa has a lot more elephants than the landscape can support and so this just may be another reason even after the elephants have passed, that the landscape is negatively impacted by being so restricted by human activity.”
