Banking on bricks: entrepreneur builds a business case for recycling plastic waste
Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Shervin Sharghy left banking to build a business turning plastic waste into concrete paving and wall blocks
Former investment banker Shervin Sharghy takes a practical approach to plastic recycling, first asking whether it makes financial sense before tackling the technical challenges.
The founder of Hong Kong-based EcoBricks said the main obstacle to recycling plastic was often economic rather than scientific.
Collecting, sorting, cleaning and processing waste plastic typically costs more than producing new materials from oil and gas, particularly at the small scale at which most recyclers operate.
Sharghy is a finalist for the Spirit of Entrepreneurship Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post.

Permanent outdoor lights are the perfect solution to a holiday season's worth of lights, and will last you for years to come. The name suggests exactly what they are: a type of string light designed to stay up all year instead of coming down after the occasion you hung them for, whether it's the holiday season or a big party that inspired you to deck out your front porch.
Whether these lights are truly “permanent” is up to you, since you can choose to anchor them to your home with either screws or adhesive. Note that they may not be a fit for every home's architecture—you will need eaves, and preferably flat ones, to hide the thick cords. Our favorite options are from Govee ($300, 100 feet) and Eufy ($350, 100 feet); both are great sets you can cut and splice to customize to your home's roofline. My favorite affordable set is from Cync ($117, 100 feet)—it's easy to use and install and has lots of great color options.
No matter which set you choose, these lights are made for year-round enjoyment, though they shine best in the holiday season. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck uses hers in the post-holiday season to display her husband’s favorite sports team colors, while I'm currently using mine to backlight the giant spiderweb spread across my balcony for Halloween. We're both looking forward to switching over to Christmas color schemes soon, and you can too after picking up one of our favorite sets below.
Updated October 2026: I've updated this guide with current pricing as we head into the holiday season, and added a new section about the lights we're testing next.
What Are Permanent Outdoor Lights?
Permanent outdoor lights are exactly what they sound like: outdoor lights meant to be permanently affixed to your home, so you don't have to go up and down a ladder every Halloween and Christmas season. They're similar to smart Christmas lights like those from Twinkly ($125) and Philips Hue ($220), and other smart lighting options like Philips Hue's smart bulbs ($90), in that they connect to an app and have custom color control.
The lights we recommend below are all DIY-friendly, but you can also hire a professional to affix them to your home. Some higher-end brands, like JellyFish and Gemstone, are for professional installation only. Hiring an installer is recommended either way if you have harder-to-reach eaves or a trickier home design, which may add considerably to the overall cost.
What Your Home Will Need
The most important thing to check is if your home is even compatible with permanent outdoor string lights. If your home has any of these features, installation should work for you:
- Accessible roof eaves, often found on one- or two-story homes
- An outdoor ceiling, like a porch roof
- Flat, smooth materials, including glass, cement, wood, or metal, under the eaves (or other spots on your home's exterior that would make sense for lights to live permanently, like a porch covering or pergola)
- Access to an outlet, ideally an outdoor one that's at least partially covered to protect the control box, or the ability to run the cord to one inside a garage or other interior space
Most one- and two-story homes can accommodate permanent outdoor lights, since they typically have roof eaves accessible on both levels. Govee, for example, claims its permanent outdoor lights ($300) will work on everything from cottages and tiny houses to large homes and even mansions. (I'm sad to report that no, I did not have a mansion available for our testing.) Eufy (another set we recommend!) warns that certain paints, including those with texturing, could prevent secure adhesion of its permanent outdoor lights ($350).
Most permanent outdoor lights come with multiple options for attaching them to your home, ranging from sticky tabs to more permanent options with screws, though some brands may require you to buy anchors separately. Some of our testers used sticky options with success, while others chose to use the included screws to ensure the lights wouldn't move. It depends on your home style and personal comfort as to which style you'd like to use. We've tested sticky adhesion for the better part of six months in the Midwestern US with great success, but obviously, tape isn't as permanent as drilled anchors.
Here are the home styles for which installation of permanent lights will be a struggle or may require a professional for installation:
- Homes and properties with a stucco exterior
- Homes with no roof eaves of any kind
- Homes with cross-style eaves that don't allow for flat adhesion
- Three-story homes with no eaves on the lower levels
- Townhomes and condominiums that don't allow for permanent changes, or don't have rooflines to fit these light styles
I live in a three-story, stucco-covered townhouse, which disqualifies me from installing most permanent outdoor lights. The stucco makes it impossible to stick anything to it, and I have an HOA that forbids “permanent changes” to my exterior, so they frown upon me drilling. And, most important, I don't have the right eave design with my townhouse to hide the strip of lights when they're off.
But that doesn't mean I have zero options (more on what I can do instead below). Still, if you want the full-home look, you'll need a home with a more standard roof.
What to Look for in Permanent Outdoor Lights
Most permanent outdoor lights look pretty similar, with puck lights on a string. How different can they be, right? Well, we've found a couple features that really make a set stand out.
Cut-and-splice abilities. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck has tried two different sets of permanent lights on her home, and she finds the ability to cut and splice the lights to be a key feature. Many homes have varied architectural features like peaks, gables, and sections without eaves, so the ability to cut out pucks and splice the cord ends back together creates a much more customized and professional look. Our favorite sets from Govee ($300, 100 feet) and Eufy ($350, 100 feet) both include this ability.
Weatherproofing. Every model needs an IP (weatherproofing) rating to survive outside, so if you don't see one, don't buy those lights. There's usually a lower rating for the control box compared to the rest of the lights, so be sure you can put that somewhere that's a little less exposed to the elements. (As mentioned above, make sure you have an outdoor outlet, and check if there's only one on a certain side of your home in case it limits your installation options.)
A range of installation options. You'll want a set that comes with plenty of options for your own installation, including adhesive and drilled mounting options. What you need will vary based on your home design and materials; e.g., you'll want adhesive for homes you can't drill into. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, who tested a couple of different permanent lights, liked sets with screw-on holders that the puck-style permanent lights can slide onto.
Controls for individual lights. This should be a no-brainer, but some cheaper lights won't offer this ability or have more roadblocks to customized control. Make sure you'll have easy individual controls, or you might find yourself frustrated with the design results of these lights. It's similar to design controls that you'd see on smart bulbs and smart string lights.
A great app. This goes hand in hand with the need for individual light control—a good app determines whether that and other features are accessible. Govee and Eufy, two of our favorite permanent outdoor lights we've tried, both have good apps that are easy to use and come with preloaded light themes. These tech companies make more than just outdoor lights, including other favorite gear of ours, so they're a good brand to trust to make a usable product and app. We also like Lepro's more affordable lights, though the app had some extra hoops to jump through to get to controls, while Lumary's app was a brutal experience for our tester.
What Time of Year Should You Use Permanent Outdoor Lights?
Most people are interested in this style of lights for the fall and winter, and it's the time of year I've found myself using it the most. That's a great time to set them up and use them, since you've got Halloween and Christmas decor that the permanent outdoor lights could complement with colorful holiday scenes. The days are also shorter, so you've got more nighttime hours to take advantage of these lights.
They’re a fun way to deck out your home for a sports game, especially for major games like the Super Bowl (WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, a resident of Washington state, was surprised to discover just how many people in her neighborhood had permanent lights this past February) and the World Cup, or for smaller holidays like St. Patrick's Day or the Fourth of July. They're a fun way to jazz up your home's curb appeal in the evening year-round (though if you have an HOA, you might have to check your rules about displaying lights regularly) or add a little pizzazz for your next outdoor party. No matter what you use it for, there's no wrong way or wrong time of year to use these lights.
Our Favorite Permanent Outdoor Lights
We've tested a handful of permanent lights on different homes and have a few clear favorites. These are all options we recommend, provided your home's exterior meets the constraints mentioned above.
These lights from Govee have been one of our top picks in our smart Christmas lights story for a reason, and they're still our favorite at this price point for everything you'll get with them. WIRED reviewer Simon Hill tested the 100-foot string that came with six sections, plus an extension code. He used adhesive and screw clips to secure the light pucks and cables, and found installation easy. This is a set that you can cut and splice, but he says that isn't a task for the faint of heart. The lights have an IP67 rating, and an IP65 rating for the control box. The busy companion app has everything you could want: color controls, tons of Scenes (Govee's lighting effects), scheduling, and even a music sync option (though that felt a little gimmicky). There's Matter support, and Govee can connect to Alexa and Google's ecosystems for voice control. Simon says he would like these lights to be closer together and the design to be a little more subtle, since you can see the cords pretty easily.
★ New Model Out: There's an updated version of these for 2026, the Govee Permanent Outdoor Lights 2 Pro (100 feet, $280), which I'll be testing this fall. This set has similar weather ratings and sizing options, but promises more than 100 modes and has an AI tool to design custom lighting, called AI Lighting Bot 2.0. Stay tuned for my next update on how these lights turned out.
WIRED reviewer Kat Merck has tested two sets of permanent outdoor lights on her home, and Eufy's S4, which incorporates RGB with both warm and cool whites, is by far her favorite. She's found the app incredibly easy to navigate and find the features she wants, from preset holiday scenes (120!) and colors to schedules and brightness adjustments. There's even an AI feature that lets you create customized light shows based on moods and scenarios. They were relatively easy to install on her home, which has nonstandard architectural features, as this set has extensions and can be cut and spliced. She says the lights aren't quite as bright as the Lumary Max set below, but the brightness is adjustable. There's also a radar motion sensor included, though she was never able to get it to work. The Eufy S4 set also works with the Matter protocol, so it's compatible with Apple, Google, and Alexa's smart home ecosystems. It's got a waterproof rating of IP67 like the Govee set above. They've been on Kat's house for the better part of a year now, and are still working well with no issues.
Cync, from appliance maker GE, makes affordable smart bulbs and other smart lights I like, so it's not a huge surprise that I also appreciate the brand's Smart Eave Lights. They were easy to install with 3M sticky strips already on the individual lights, and since my eaves are out of safe reach on my townhouse, I used the lights on my balcony railing with great success. One piece of the 100-foot set (it comes with four strings, plus an extension) was the perfect length to loop around my 9-foot-long railing. The set quickly connected to the Cync app, and the power cord is nice and long to make it easy to reach wherever your power outlet is. It has a waterproof rating of IP65.
These lights have been on my balcony for about a year now, and have had no issues, even after months of leaving them off. I've been able to easily reconnect to them whenever I want and get the light colors and routines set up for whatever holiday or event I'm celebrating.
If You Can’t Install Permanent Outdoor Lights
Not every home is a good fit for these types of lights. I haven't yet found a permanent light set that can attach to my home, so here's what I've used instead for a similar result.
Twinkly's smart string lights have a weatherproof rating of IP44 for both the lights and the power supply. This means they're splash-proof but not waterproof, so you can use them outside, but make sure they're somewhat protected. I love how much you can customize these lights. You'll use the app to take a photo of how you've set up your lights, whether that's around a Christmas tree, around your balcony's railing, or along the front of your house, and then you'll be able to customize the lights and pattern based on how you arranged them. There are tons of fun light designs already in the app, and you can make your own. It's a good option if you can only do string lights but want smart capabilities. These lights are also compatible with Amazon’s, Google’s, and Apple’s ecosystems. Twinkly also makes an icicle-style smart light string ($110), which I love using outside too; they hung over my garage door for the holiday season. I'm on my third year of using this set and it's still going strong.
More Outdoor Lights We’ve Tested
Cync Outdoor Light Strip for $154: I was really hoping this would be a good solution for outdoor lights for my balcony, but this light strip is heavy and tall and is better designed to line a yard versus sticking onto the side of a railing. It comes with grass stakes.
Lepro’s EE1 AI for $450 (300 feet): These permanent outdoor lights are sold out right now, but they are another more affordable option when the shorter length is available. They aren't as cheap as Cync, however, and you will have to get around the app's AI to really get the most out of it. Right now only the longer set is in stock, too, making it more expensive to invest in.
Lumary Outdoor Permanent Lights Max for $331 (105 feet): Lumary's lights were frustrating and limiting for our tester. The app wasn't intuitive or easy to use, and our tester actually had to have the power box replaced after she tried to connect the lights to a different phone. She liked how bright the lights were and that there’s a physical remote, but the app, power box shutdown, and installation limitations compared with other sets (no splicing ability, installation recommended from the left) make this one we’d skip. Lumary has since released new versions, and is now on its third iteration with the Lumary Permanent Outdoor Lights 3 ($220, 100 feet).
What We’re Testing Next
We're looking at testing a few permanent outdoor lights this fall and winter. Here are the sets on our list to hopefully test: the Govee Permanent Outdoor Lights 2 Pro ($280, 100 feet), the Nanoleaf Permanent Outdoor Lights ($200, 49 feet), and the Hampton Bay Permanent Outdoor String Lights ($89, 50 feet).
FAQs
What Are the Cons of Permanent Outdoor Lights?
The main downside to permanent outdoor lights is the cost. These sets usually cost significantly more than a light string, even the smart ones. That's because they're designed to last longer on your home, and the more expensive sets allow you to cut and splice the cords to perfectly fit your home instead of dangling strings and extra lights. It's an investment, but one you can enjoy year-round.
Are Permanent Outdoor Lights Worth It?
Yes, because you'll install them once and be good to go with every holiday in your future: Christmas! Halloween! Your fave sports team headed to a big championship match! Your kid's graduation (or your own)! Similar to how smart bulbs can give you so many options inside your home, the possibilities are endless and something you'll be able to use and enjoy year-round.
When Should You Buy Permanent Outdoor Lights?
There's no wrong time of year to use these lights, but I often see them on sale during events like Prime Day and Black Friday. I've seen them sporadically on sale throughout the year without special holidays and events attached to the sale, so it's worth checking regularly to see if a set you like gets a surprise discount. But the easiest time to aim for is one of these deal events. I'd recommend aiming for Amazon's summertime Prime Day or early fall deal event (last year it was called Amazon Big Deal Days 2025, but we'll see if it gets the same name this year) so that you can have your permanent outdoor lights in time for Halloween and Christmas.
How Does WIRED Test Permanent Outdoor Lights? What Happens When We’re Done Testing?
WIRED tests permanent outdoor lights on the homes of our reviewers. We've tested these lights on three different homes in separate areas with serious weather: Washington state, Missouri, and Scotland. We've also tested a set in the more mild climate of Southern California. We install these on the homes themselves and leave them up for at least a few weeks, if not months and years (depending on performance), to see how they hold up. Our picks remain on our homes for long-term testing, as these lights are supposed to be permanent, and used sets are safely disposed of.

When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents.
The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7.
Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group, rather than a direct hacking victim.
AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities.
Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties.
When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd, to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.)
Da.gd’s investigation and ongoing efforts to prevent further abuse of its tool have taken “a fair bit of time,” says Joe Needleman, one of the security researchers providing pro bono assistance. But he and the others supporting da.gd view the situation as a valuable learning opportunity.
“This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.”
Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs.
Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.”
Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes.
Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge, whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive.

The Puducherry government has started disbursement of Union Territory’s share of ₹30,000 to the consumers of Electricity department who have installed rooftop solar power plants of capacity 3 kW and above.
During an event held at Kamarajar Manimandam on Saturday, Minister for Home and Electricity A. Namassivayam inaugurated the disbursement of subsidy to around 3,333 consumers who have installed the 3 kW plant in their buildings. Minister for Adi Dravidar Welfare P. Rajavelu was also present.
Besides the Union Territory’s share, the consumers who have opted for 3 kW rooftop solar plants would get a Central subsidy of ₹78,000 under Pradhan Mantri Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana. For the installation of 1 kW and 2 kW rooftop solar plants, consumers would get a subsidy of around ₹40,000 (₹30,000 from Centre and ₹10,000 from U.T.) and ₹80,000 (₹60,000 from Centre and ₹20,000 from U.T.) respectively. Mr. Namassivayam said the government had incurred an expenditure of ₹10 crore towards providing subsidy to 3,333 consumers.
The department has received 8,135 applications of which 6,452 rooftop solar installations have been completed with a total installed capacity of 23.32MW. A subsidy amounting to ₹40.99 crore has been disbursed to 5,295 beneficiaries. At present 80 vendors are registered and actively engaged in rooftop solar installations across the Union Territory, the release said.
A 3 kW rooftop solar power system could generate approximately 4,500 units of electricity annually, depending on solar radiation and the characteristics of the installation site. The installed solar systems are designed to operate for 25 years and more. Eligible beneficiaries under the scheme could obtain a bank loan at an interest rate of 5.75%, the release said.
Power secretary A. Muthamma told The Hindu that around 13,000 residential consumers would be enrolled for installation of solar plants under the subsidy scheme on a first-come-first-served basis. Around 79 government buildings have already been provided with solar power panels and more would be covered in the days to come, she said.
“The government’s decision to provide subsidy has certainly encouraged more people to join the scheme. More than 6,400 consumers have benefitted from the scheme so far and another 6,000 more would be added soon. We have a total installed capacity of 20.85 MW,” she said.

Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
- Published
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder
Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.
Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.
Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.
"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.
"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."
Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.
It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.
The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.
It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.
Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.
But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.
The choice
Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.
Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.
It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.
He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.
"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.
"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."
The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.
Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."
Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.
Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.
Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.
But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.
Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.
Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.
"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.
While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.
"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.
Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.
More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.
The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.
"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.
"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."
- Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, US court hears 
  - Published18 August
- Social media is 'deliberately' addictive 
  - Published4 July 2018
The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".
Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m).
"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.
The challenges
There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.
In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise.
"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.
Right-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.
But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.
The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.
However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.
The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.
Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.
"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.
On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.
The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.
The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.
Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global.
"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."
Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.
Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."
Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.
Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice.
"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."
If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

During anti-Trump protests, No Kings’ Instagram page got pulled. Platform says oops
The outage hit as organizers coordinated nearly 3,000 early-voting events across all 50 states and Washington, DC

Meta disabled the primary Instagram account belonging to the No Kings Coalition on Saturday, briefly shutting down access to the page during nationwide demonstrations against President Donald Trump.
The suspension came as nearly 3,000 events were taking place across all 50 states and Washington, D.C., as part of the group’s early-voting push ahead of the November midterms.
The social media giant attributed the disruption to an automated safety filter.
“When accounts post, share or comment at very high frequencies, it can trigger automated systems,” Meta communications officer Andy Stone wrote on X. “That’s what happened with the No Kings IG account in the lead-up to today’s day of action. Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error. Everything is now working as it should, and we sincerely apologize.”
The temporary outage occurred during the fourth series of No Kings demonstrations held across the United States since President Trump took office in early 2025. The coalition, organized by Indivisible, emerged after the president returned to the White House following a movement focused on ensuring political power remained with the people rather than Washington leadership.
Organizers reported that administrative access was cut off around 1:30 p.m. Eastern Standard Time, leaving leaders unable to update supporters at a critical point during the day's actions. Even after the page became public again, organizers said they remained locked out of the account’s backend for roughly four hours.
“In the middle of that joyful experience at the protest locally, I got word from my team that Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta had suspended the Instagram account for the No Kings Coalition,” organizer Ezra Levin told MeidasTouch. “They suspended it. We didn’t have access to it.
“We couldn’t post to it. Nobody could go to the page. That was for about an hour-and-a-half, during the height of the mobilization while people were still getting their No Kings protests together.”
Levin added: “This is strikingly reminiscent of what we saw in Brazil just this week. A court ruled against Meta for favoring the authoritarians in that country. And we might be seeing something similar from Meta in our country right now, but rest assured, we’re not going to stop organizing against this regime.”
The White House previously responded to the demonstrations through spokeswoman Lauren Bis, who told Newsweek that the group’s focus on early voting proved “they should change their name,” adding that Americans faced a choice between Trump’s policies and ”extreme Democrats’ radical socialist, open-border policies.”

8 killed as vehicle carrying pilgrims to Rajasthan's Khatu Shyam temple plunges into drain
The vehicle, carrying Khatu Shyam pilgrims, broke through the divider, plunged into the drain and crashed into a wall.
At least eight people were killed and 17 others injured after a tempo traveller carrying pilgrims from Madhya Pradesh to Rajasthan's Khatu Shyam temple broke through a road divider and plunged nearly 20 feet into a seasonal drain along the Delhi-Mumbai Expressway in Kota district on Saturday morning, police said.
Police officers said the tempo traveller was carrying around 25 passengers, most of whom were residents of Betul district in Madhya Pradesh. They had left Betul on Friday night to visit the Khatu Shyam temple in Reengus, Sikar district.
Seemliya Station House Officer (SHO) Nand Singh said the vehicle had crossed the Karadiya toll plaza and was heading towards Sultanpur when the driver lost control. The vehicle broke through the divider, plunged into the drain and crashed into a wall.
Seven of the deceased have been identified as Aruna, Vaishnavi, Trisha, Krishna, Anita, Om Suryavanshi and Raju, while the identity of the eighth victim is yet to be established. A total of 17 passengers were reported injured in the accident, although only some have been identified so far. The injured include Hemlata Gaikwad, Ajay, Vanshika, Monisha, Chitresh, Saransh, Chetan, Krishvi, Vaidhi, Neelu, Santosh, Varsha and Kamlesh.
Police said all the deceased and injured are believed to be relatives or family friends. The bodies of the eight victims have been brought to Kota and kept in the mortuary.
The accident occurred between 6 am and 7 am. Four passengers died on the spot, while four others succumbed to their injuries en route to the hospital.
The impact severely damaged the front portion of the vehicle, leaving several passengers trapped inside. Police suspect that the driver may have fallen asleep at the wheel, although the exact cause of the accident is yet to be established, officers said.
Villagers and passersby rushed to the spot and began helping the passengers. Police personnel, National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) rescue teams and emergency ambulance services subsequently joined the operation. An NHAI crane was deployed to retrieve the badly damaged vehicle from the drain, officers said.
“Four ambulances were immediately dispatched to the accident site after authorities received information about the incident,” Sultanpur Block Chief Medical Officer (CMO) Rajesh Samar said.
The injured were taken to the New Hospital attached to Kota Medical College and MBS Hospital for treatment. The condition of several passengers remains critical.
Meanwhile, the NHAI, in a statement posted on its official X handle, attributed the accident to suspected driver fatigue and excessive speed.
“According to preliminary information received from the spot, the tempo traveller was moving at high speed in the overtaking lane when the driver apparently dozed off, causing the vehicle to go out of control and fall off the expressway near Karadia village,” the NHAI said.
The authority further stated that emergency response teams were mobilised immediately after the accident was reported.
“Four NHAI ambulances, a route patrol vehicle (RPV) team, a crane, a JCB, two ambulances from the 108 emergency service and other available emergency vehicles reached the spot and began relief and rescue operations,” it said.
Following the accident, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla visited the hospital and met the injured passengers. Taking serious note of the incident, Birla directed the Kota District Collector and Superintendent of Police to constitute a special investigation committee to examine the circumstances that led to the crash. He said further action would be taken based on the committee's findings.
“Based on the findings of the investigation, comprehensive measures will be taken to prevent such accidents in the future. We are conducting a road safety study on the Delhi-Mumbai Expressway,” Birla said.
He added that a final review meeting would be held in November, following which accident-prone stretches and black spots falling under the jurisdiction of the NHAI or other departments would be rectified.
Chief Minister Bhajan Lal Sharma also expressed grief over the loss of lives. In a post on X, he described the accident as deeply distressing and said he had directed officials to ensure proper treatment for the injured and provide necessary assistance to the affected families. He also extended condolences to the bereaved families and wished the injured a speedy recovery.
Former Rajasthan Chief Minister Ashok Gehlot also expressed grief over the accident. In a post on X, he described the loss of lives as deeply saddening and heartbreaking.
“I extend my heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families. May God give them strength to bear this irreparable loss. I also wish the injured a speedy recovery,” Gehlot wrote.

Your smart TV has one big problem: It's tracking what you watch
LG or Samsung really doesn't need to know what you've been watching lately.
Smart TVs are everywhere, but they hide a big problem in plain sight. Not only do they push constant ads in your direction, but they also monitor what you watch to help advertisers personalize ads — not just on the TV, but everywhere else too.
What is Automatic Content Recognition?
Like most smart devices, smart TVs gather extensive data on your viewing habits using Automatic Content Recognition (ACR). They do this by capturing screenshots every few seconds (or even multiple times per second), which they use to identify what you watch on built-in apps and streaming services, as well as connected devices like gaming consoles and streaming boxes. Just like Shazam, ACR only needs a snippet to identify what's being shown.
Beyond content, TVs capture valuable technical data, such as your IP address, Wi-Fi details, app usage patterns and more. If you use a voice-enabled remote or built-in voice assistant, the TV will capture short audio snippets for processing.
While manufacturers say ACR improves the experience and is disclosed during setup, critics say it's far too complicated to switch off and that none of this is made clear.
What happens to the information your TV collects?
Data is fed through an algorithm to generate a "fingerprint" of what you do, then uploaded to the manufacturer for processing. The processed data may then be sold to data brokers, who combine it with other information to build spookily accurate profiles of you. Vizio's Platform+, which includes FAST TV, ads, sponsorships and similar, made $598 million in 2023.
This is a lucrative business. Analysts predict the ACR market will reach $23.37 billion by 2034. Meanwhile, manufacturers say ACR revenue helps keep TV prices low.
In some cases, state privacy laws mean manufacturers must be more open about this practice. This sofa surveillance system has already led to court cases, including litigation against big TV manufacturers in the state of Texas.
Advertising agencies have existed for decades. Now we also have data brokers, who work with them to identify ad audiences. Brokers grab data across the digital experience, from website ads to loyalty schemes to apps tracking your activity, in order to build profiles.
TV is just another data point in this privatized personal data intelligence complex. The extent of the data they collect can be intrusive, which is why you might see an ad for tennis rackets in your browser after watching a bunch of beginner tennis guides on your TV.
How to switch Automatic Content Recognition off
Manufacturers use different terms for ACR and offer different management tools to disable it, which may impact other TV features. While this can depend on your exact TV, the following guidelines will give you a start:
- Sony: Settings > All Settings, then turn Samba Interactive TV off.
- Samsung: Settings > All Settings > General & Privacy > Terms & Privacy. Turn off Viewing Information Services and Interest-based Advertising.
- LG: Settings > General > System > Additional Settings. Turn off Live Plus, then enable Limit Ad tracking in Advertisement.
- Vizio: Settings > All Settings > Admin and Privacy. Turn Viewing Data off.
- Roku TVs (TCL, Hisense, Philips and Sharp): Settings > Privacy, then turn off Smart TV Experience and Use info from TV inputs. Under Privacy > Advertising, enable Limit ad tracking. Restrict microphone permissions in Privacy > Microphone.
- Amazon Fire TV: Settings > Privacy Settings. Turn off all three.
- Android and Google TVs: Settings > About > Legal Information. Opt out of receiving personalized ads. Open Settings > Privacy > User Agreements to reset these and opt out of what you can.
Check back sometimes, because your TVs could re-enable ACR after software updates. Wirecutter also found some TVs keep capturing ACR data while offline and upload it the next time they connect.
Beyond turning off the primary toggles, there are a few more steps you can take to limit the data your TV grabs:
- Take your TV offline: Disable Wi-Fi access and use a media streaming device like an Apple TV for all your apps and streaming. Your TV's ACR system can still sees what's on-screen, so make sure you've deactivated it. Depending on the streaming device you choose, you may also need to stop your Roku from tracking what you watch, for instance.
- Turn off the microphone: Deactivate voice assistants in your TV's privacy or voice settings. Disable the microphone inside the remote and built into the TV (if present) if you can.
- Advanced network control: Block outbound TV traffic at the router level or use a DNS blocker, though this may break apps or updates.

From left to right: Director-General Development Cooperation & Humanitarian Aid Belgium Dr Rombouts, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros, H.E. Ambassador Mr Marc Pecsteen de Buytswerve, Permanent Representative of Belgium to the United Nations. @WHO
Geneva, 9 November 2022 – In a full day of strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO shared global health priorities of the longstanding partnership and agreed to build their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential health technologies.
The delegation from Belgium – headed by Dr Heidy Rombouts, Director General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid, and HE Mr Marc Pecsteen de Buytswerve, Ambassador, Permanent Representative – discussed issues of strategic importance, including sustainable financing of the Organization, accelerating equitable access to health technology, reaching UN Sustainable Development Goals targets on universal health coverage through resilient and transparent health systems, and joint action on neglected tropical diseases and sexual and reproductive health and rights.
Belgium affirmed that WHO must continue to play its critical role in the global health architecture and repeated the country’s commitment to help sustainably fund WHO through a gradual increase in Member States’ assessed contributions. The delegation underlined Belgium’s support for a recent World Health Assembly resolution calling for the increase.
In the 2020-21 biennium, Belgium was among WHO’s top ten donors of core flexible funding.
“Our partnership with Belgium is very strong and goes far beyond multi-annual financial support,” WHO Chef de Cabinet Dr Catharina Boehme said.
During Wednesday’s sessions, Belgium highlighted its support for WHO’s work on equitable and timely access to quality health products and technologies, along with its continued support for the Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases, and the Special Programme of Research, Development and Research Training in Human Reproduction.
The dialogue also addressed Belgium’s collaboration with WHO on health-systems resilience, while expressing interest in more tightly coordinating the work of Belgium and WHO in priority countries, through Universal Health Coverage Partnership activities.
Integrating sexual and reproductive health and rights and integrating prevention and control of HIV, TB and AIDS in essential health services were flagged as points of attention. Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, Belgium has been a steadfast partner of WHO, providing financial support to the Universal Health Coverage Partnership for fragile health systems.
Belgium hosts the WHO Office to the European Union, and the WHO European Observatory on Health Systems and Policies, and its Public Service for Health maintains a partnership with the WHO Regional office for Europe. Supporting Belgian regions include Flanders and Wallonia. In September 2022, Wallonia signed an agreement with WHO to expand technical cooperation, particularly in African countries.
The strategic dialogue also reflected on the great value of the expertise that Belgium has provided through its collaborating centres and young professional officers to help WHO deliver on its mandate.

I've always been a city mouse, so when we decided to move from Melbourne, Australia, to Bright in country Victoria in 2021, I wasn't sure how long I'd last. Our family ended up falling in love with the slower pace of life and the people, and spent four years in the small alpine town at the foothills of the Victorian Alps.
But in January, we moved from Bright to the Gold Coast, where I grew up. My parents' health was declining, and I wanted to spend quality time with them before it was too late.
Moving from a small regional town of fewer than 3,000 people to a city of almost 700,000 was a profound lifestyle shift for our family of five. We had to make new friends, learn how to navigate a traffic light again (joking!), and get used to the buzzing city life.
Overall, we've gained a lot from moving to the city, and I feel it's been especially beneficial to our kids, as it's helped build resilience. But there are definitely things about country life that I do miss, if I'm being honest.
Life is full of trade-offs, and we've definitely made a few.
We've gained convenience and accessibility
In country Victoria, our nearest major retailer was an hour's drive away. If the kids needed new shoes or I needed new underwear, off we'd drive to the nearest major town. It often felt like a mission just to access simple amenities.
Nowadays, everything we need is at our fingertips. If we want to eat Italian one night and Nepalese the next, we can. The Gold Coast has all the amenities we need, and a good mix of beaches, hinterland hikes, nightlife, festivals, and an up-and-coming food scene.
There are more career and education opportunities
Cities generally offer better career and education opportunities, without a doubt. In our family, my husband has probably benefited the most in that regard.
When we moved here in January, he expanded his Muscle Freedom remedial massage and myotherapy business and started a clinic on the Gold Coast. Since then, the opportunities have been incredible, and he's treated some of Australia's biggest sporting identities. That would likely never have happened in country Victoria (unless they were holidaying there).
Likewise, our kids seem to be thriving at school and in their extra-curricular activities, many of which were unavailable where we used to live.
I enjoy the anonymity, and the diversity here is also a big plus
When I was having a bad mental health day in Bright, there was no escaping friends and family (bless them). Once, at the supermarket, I was weeping in the bread aisle, only to be greeted by my husband's cheerful colleague, who was keen to chat about the weather. I wanted to scream and run away.
In the city, I quite enjoy the anonymity and being a number in the crowd, especially on harder days.
I also love having access to a diverse range of art, music, entertainment, and food on the Gold Coast. After four years living in the country, I began to feel a bit starved of culture.
My kids are also mingling with children from different backgrounds and walks of life, which I am really happy about.
However, we miss having nature at our doorstep, and wide open spaces
Bright is surrounded by mountains, forests, rivers, and cycling trails, with gorgeous national parks a short drive away. It really is a smorgasbord of activities for outdoor enthusiasts.
The Gold Coast has plenty of sunshine and offers some spectacular natural scenery, but you do have to drive to access it. I've actually put on a few kilos living in the city, and I think it's mainly because I'm not walking or cycling as much.
When we recently returned to Bright for a family holiday, I realized how much I've missed those wide open spaces. The air seems to feel fresher there.
Living in suburbia on the Gold Coast, the blocks are tighter, and some areas feel like the properties are on top of each other. Even as I write this, I can overhear the next-door neighbor arguing with her husband about his messy household habits.
I also miss the close-knit community and slower pace
I've been lucky enough to make some wonderful friends on the Gold Coast. The kind who check in on us when we're sick or offer to babysit if my husband and I need a night out. But it also seems that people are busier in the city, and get-togethers happen less often.
In a small town like Bright, it's easier to catch up with people because everyone lives close by. I found that living in the country helped me form deeper connections with friends. That brought a sense of security, knowing that someone always has your back.
Since moving to the city, life has felt frantic. For the first six months, every weekend was jam-packed with catch-ups with family and new and old friends.
In a small country town, the pace of life was much slower. Recently, while we were holidaying in Bright, I felt my shoulders relax, and my stress levels decrease. There's something to be said for a simple life.
What our next chapter holds
We'd intended to give the Gold Coast 12 months and then make a call about where to base ourselves long-term. But now that we're almost at that mark, we've realized it's too soon to make a decision.
And so, we'll be spending 2027 here, then reassessing our options late next year. Part of me craves the open skies, fresh mountain air, and the stillness I took for granted in the country, but I'm also enjoying having Aldi a kilometer away and more choices overall.
I suppose at the end of the day, there's no perfect place to live, just places that suit you at different life stages. For now, the Gold Coast is giving us convenience, variety, and time with my folks, and I intend to enjoy the best of what city life has to offer.

During my years as a clinical pharmacist, I thought I understood why patients stopped taking long-term medications — one of the biggest challenges in medicine. They forgot to take them, became frustrated with side effects, or didn’t fully understand their conditions. But over time, my clinical experience showed me that these explanations only told part of the story.
I first noticed this pattern across very different medical specialties. In psychiatry, I saw patients with schizophrenia experience psychotic episodes after stopping their antipsychotics. Patients who abruptly discontinued their antidepressants often suffered withdrawal symptoms. Later, when I worked in a kidney transplant center, I encountered a surprisingly similar situation when patients stopped taking one or more of their immunosuppressants and developed acute rejection of their new kidneys. Colleagues in cardiology, primary care, and other specialties described similar experiences.
The patients’ initial explanations were often familiar. After longer conversations, however, especially when patients’ guilt and shame lessened, they gave other explanations. I started to realize that “I forgot” was sometimes an easier answer, both for the patient and for the health care professional.
Some people worried that they would become dependent on medication — not necessarily in the pharmacological sense, but because needing treatment every day felt like losing control over their own bodies. Others stopped medication temporarily to prove to themselves that they could still function without it. Research suggests that many factors leading people to discontinue treatment take root before the first dose, when they are still trying to understand what their illness and their medication will mean in their lives.
In mental health care, I encountered people who believed that medication changed who they were. They didn’t mean the common adverse effects, such as sleepiness or weight gain. They described something harder to define: a feeling of being disconnected from themselves, as if an important part of their personality had changed.
One case, in particular, stayed with me. He was a young man who had received a kidney transplant as a teenager. For years, he had taken his immunosuppressants correctly. At 23, he experienced his first episode of acute rejection.
His initial explanation seemed simple. He had traveled for work and said he had forgotten to bring his medications. Later, during an informal conversation as we walked through the hallways of the hospital, a different explanation emerged. His girlfriend was pregnant, and he told me he felt he needed to “become a man.”
At that moment, it became clear that the medication had taken on a meaning beyond its pharmacological function. For him, depending on a daily treatment seemed to conflict with the image of strength, autonomy, and responsibility that he associated with adulthood.
This conversation changed the way I understood adherence. Medication can become entangled with the way people see themselves, and the kind of people they believe they need to be.
Specifically, for men and younger patients, I noticed that needing a treatment could feel like admitting vulnerability, weakness, or limitation. And stopping it could become an attempt to regain a sense of control over the body and over one’s own life.
Only later did I find research that helped explain what I had been seeing in practice. Studies on medication adherence have shown that people’s beliefs about medicines influence whether they take them as prescribed, including how they weigh their perceived need for treatment against their concerns. A 2024 systematic review on illness identity added another layer to this picture, showing that the way people integrate chronic illness into their sense of self was associated with whether they could manage their health problems and how they adapted to treatment. Research on preventing nonadherence likewise suggests that these beliefs need to be recognized early, potentially before the first prescription is written.
These findings helped put words to something I had repeatedly observed in clinical practice. A patient can fully understand that a medication is necessary and still struggle with what taking it means. It can become a daily reminder that they are living with chronic illness, a symbol of dependence on something external to function, or a challenge to deeply held ideas about strength, control, and personal identity.
Perhaps the problem is partly in the questions we ask. When we ask only “Did you have side effects?” or “Did you forget a dose?”, we may receive answers that are true but incomplete. We need to create space for more difficult questions: What does this medication mean to you? How do you feel about needing it every day? Is there a part of you that resists the idea of depending on this treatment?
If we want to improve adherence to long-term treatments, we may need to change not only the answers we provide, but also the questions we ask. Explaining how a medication works will always be essential. But understanding what that medication has come to represent may be just as important.
Sometimes, the biggest barrier between a patient and their treatment is not pharmacology.
It is how they see themselves.
Marcela Gottschald is a Brazilian journalist and pharmacist based in Argentina.

At the EU-WHO Strategic Dialogue on Health between the European Commissioner for Health and Food Safety Stella Kyriakides and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, the European Commission (EC) and WHO agreed to enhance strategic cooperation in global health security and architecture. They will also cooperate on the implementation of major initiatives, such as the new European Union’s Global Health Strategy launched this week, the European Health Union and the WHO priorities for the 2022-2026 period.
The partners will mutually reinforce their work across areas of common interest, as called by the EU Global Health Strategy, to further bolster a strong multilateral system with the WHO at its core, powered by a strong EU.
Addressing together the challenge of global health security
Many significant elements of global health security will be under discussion in the coming two years. These include the currently ongoing negotiations of a future pandemic accord and of amended International Health regulations, shaping a permanent pandemics platform, top leadership engagement in global health issues, and financing global health.
The EC and WHO will coordinate closely throughout these discussions to shape an effective multilateral system that considers the lessons of the COVID-19 pandemic and provides comprehensive health security for citizens across the world.
“Our citizens expect a step change in global health security, and the new EU Global Health Strategy is our contribution to this process. Combatting health threats effectively requires a strong multilateral governance with a more effective, accountable, and sustainably financed WHO at the center and where the EU has a seat at the table. Reinforced strategic cooperation and alignment between the Commission and the WHO will be essential to deliver better health for all in a changing world.”, said Stella Kyriakides, Commissioner for Health and Food Safety.
Other areas of cooperation include cross-border threats to health and digital health. To ensure mutual reinforcement across areas of common interest, both sides will review all current joint projects and actions by May 2023 and identify further areas of collaboration and specific projects to support. Both parties will meet in June 2023 to take stock, define the lines of future joint work, and provide the political impetus as and when necessary.
“A healthier Europe is stronger and more prosperous Europe, and a stronger and more prosperous Europe is a stronger and more prosperous world. We look forward to scaling up our cooperation with the European Union in the years ahead for a healthier, safer and fairer world.”, said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General at the launch of the Strategy in Brussels.
Background
The new EU Global Health Strategy offers a framework for EU health policies leading up to 2030. It sets policy priorities and guiding principles to shape global health, and it identifies concrete lines of action. It outlines what the Commission will do and what it invites the 27 EU Member States to do, each strictly within their respective competences and institutional roles. The strategy builds on contributions received during a wide public consultation with a broad range of key stakeholders in Europe and beyond.

Here's how the Slate truck gets software updates without built-in infotainment
Using your phone to phone home.
The Slate truck doesn't just lack an infotainment system. The base version of the EV also skips a radio, speakers, power windows and even a paint job (hello, vinyl). But without built-in cellular, the truck can still get over-the-air (OTA) software updates. It does so by piggybacking on your device.
Maximum minimalism
Slate Auto's approach to minimalism isn't just a design choice. It's also the core of the company's business model: it reaches its sub-$25,000 entry price by slashing everything unrelated to driving and safety.
Of course, the company will still be happy to sell you a long list of add-ons to fill those missing pieces. These include speakers, an iPad mount (to turn it into something more like a traditional infotainment system), a kit that transforms it into a five-seat SUV and a telematics module that enables in-app door unlocking. All that can add up, with a fully loaded version of the modular vehicle surpassing $45,000. The upsell temptation could be strong.
The EV has an estimated 205 miles of range, a 1,550-pound maximum payload and a 2,000-pound tow rating. It's designed more for short-run hauling and errands than long road trips, so it isn't an apples-to-apples comparison with other electric trucks. Still, the company is betting that a surprisingly affordable vehicle that cuts corners on luxuries will find its niche.
How updates work
Typically, OTA software updates use cellular or Wi-Fi. But the Slate truck's lack of tech means it needs a workaround.
The process happens through the Slate app on your phone. When an update is available, the app downloads it onto your device. Plug your phone into the truck's USB port on the dash, and wait for the initial file transfer (the part where your phone needs to be connected). That takes about a minute. Then the truck finishes installing on its own, a step that can take around 45 minutes.
The company says the updates will stick to bug fixes and small improvements, so don't expect big, flashy new features to arrive after installation. And the same app you use for updates also helps with other common tasks, like displaying range, helping you find chargers and passing those directions to Google Maps, Apple Maps or Waze.
Privacy
A truck that doesn't phone home could attract buyers tired of the techification of all things. So it probably helps Slate's case that it says it won't sell app data and only collects what it needs for things like diagnostics, service and update status. Those familiar with the recent GM data selling debacle could see the allure here.
Whether enough buyers want an electric pickup that scales back on so much is an open question. But at least the software will still stay up-to-date for those who do.

BJP wary as Jagan Mohan Reddy hints at shift towards INDIA bloc
Senior BJP party leaders who spoke on condition of anonymity said the YSRCP joining the INDIA bloc will pave the way for a political shift not just in the state, but also in the neighbouring Telangana.
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is closely watching developments in Andhra Pradesh where former chief minister and YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) chief Jagan Mohan Reddy’s statement expressing support for the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and seeking electoral reforms is being perceived as an indication that the once “friendly party” could be moving towards the opposition bloc.
Reddy on Sunday said the appointment of election commissioners should be independent of the government in power. He also expressed regret over his party’s support for the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, which governs the appointment of Election Commissioners in 2023.
“Approving that, I am regretting it now,” Jagan said, while addressing the media.
The former CM also expressed concerns over the SIR and said 4.6 million fake voters had been identified across the country, and the government had decided to proceed with the elections using an unrevised electoral roll. He alleged that the delimitation of divisions and wards had been carried out to favour the ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA) coalition.
Earlier this week, Jagan, in a post on X, said, “A proactive approach always yields better results than a reactive stance. The system has a flaw that needs to be corrected. Trust in the electoral process must be restored. The arrests of Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka do not solve anything; it only aggravates the situation. I empathise with @SauravDassss and @AshutoshRanka.”
The tweet was seen as an endorsement of the CJP, which is part of the ongoing demonstrations in the Capital against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, for what they allege are irregularities in the conduct of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
Senior BJP party leaders who spoke on condition of anonymity said the YSRCP joining the INDIA bloc will pave the way for a political shift not just in the state, but also in the neighbouring Telangana.
The possible realignment also comes at a time when the BJP is scouting for support for the passage of the Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty First Amendment) Bill, 2026 and the Delimitation Bill, which seeks to redraw boundaries based on the 2011 census and is necessary for implementing the 33% quotas for women in legislatures.
The YSRCP has 8 MPs—four each in Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha. Even as it was not part of the ruling NDA, it was counted as a friendly party that supported the government on several key issues including the Citizenship Amendment Act; the abrogation of Article 370 and the farm laws.
The BJP was counting on it to support the delimitation bill as well as the Constitutional Amendment bill that requires two-third majority, even though Reddy had asked the Union government to ensure that the southern states do not lose out on seats owing to better population control measures. The party had also demanded that the government’s assurance of proportionate increase in seats for southern states should be inserted in the text of the delimitation bill.
The delimitation bill needs a simple majority for passage, which the NDA, with its numbers in both the Houses, can achieve—in the Lok Sabha, it has over 300 while the simple majority mark is 272 of 543 members; in the Rajya Sabha it has 153 of 245. But the ruling coalition falls short of 360 votes, required for the two-third majority in the Lower House and 164 required in the Upper House for the passage of the Constitutional Amendment Bill.
On the political impact of the realignment, BJP leaders said the coming together of Reddy and the Congress in Andhra Pradesh will pose a challenge to the ruling Telugu Desam Party (TDP), a key ally of the BJP-led NDA. And in Telangana too, the BJP, will have to contest against a formidable opponent.
“Of late, there have been indications that the YSRCP will join the INDIA bloc. If that were to happen then the opposition will gain support from the larger coalition of Christian and Muslim voters in AP. The percentage of Christian voters is high in AP and they support Jagan, they also have a significant presence in Telangana, which the Congress will benefit from,” said a BJP leader.
In AP, Christians are 1.37% of the electorate while Muslims are a little over 9%; in Telangana Christians are 1.27%, and Muslims are a little over 12%. “However, estimates put the percentage of Christians at 10-15% in both the states, as many practising Christians who are originally Dalits continue to identify as Hindus for reservation benefits,” said the leader.
Explaining the shift in votes, he said that if the YSRCP aligns with the Congress, the Reddys in Telangana too will shift alliance to CM Revanth Reddy. “There is a significant settler vote (voters who shifted from Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema but are registered voters in Telangana) that is crucial in 20-30 constituencies in Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) region, in places such as Gachibowli, Khammam, and Suryapet, which the Congress will gain if the realignment occurs,” the leader said.
However, a second party leader said Reddy’s statements came close on the heels of the CBI and the Enforcement Directorate (ED), which are probing cases against the former CM, moving the court to seek a daily trial.
“This is a fight for survival. The issue of vote chori that the opposition has raised has no traction on the ground here…” the second leader said.
