The national telemedicine consultation helpline e-Sanjeevani has integrated an AI-enabled clinical decision support system for healthcare providers. This is just the latest example of AI’s increasing integration into medicine and medical care worldwide, and in India. As AI begins to influence clinical decisions, such as reassurance, referrals, or investigations, its regulation has now become an urgent patient-safety question. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation’s (CDSCO) July 2026 guidance on software in medical devices becomes important in this context. The document brings software (including AI-enabled) used for a medical purpose into a clearer approval pathway. However, it explicitly says that it reflects existing practice and is not a new regulatory control.
What is MedTech?
Medtech refers to instruments, apparatus, implants, software, or related devices used for diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, or treatment, whose primary action is not achieved through pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic means. A thermometer, glucometer, blood pressure apparatus, pacemaker, dialysis machine, and CT scanner are considered MedTech. Software is the set of instructions that makes a digital device work. A digital blood-pressure monitor, for example, uses embedded software to control cuff inflation, read pressure sensors and calculate the final BP value. Within software are algorithms, which are step-by-step rules that convert inputs into outputs.
AI (built on advanced algorithms such as machine learning and deep learning models) learns patterns from large amounts of data and uses them to make inferences. All AI depends on algorithms, but not every algorithm is AI. Netflix and YouTube recommendations are familiar examples of algorithms. But a medical algorithm is not a film recommendation. AI may reduce workload, improve consistency and extend specialist support to places where it is scarce. But a false positive can send a healthy person through anxiety and unnecessary tests, while a false negative can do the opposite. A model trained on one population, or one hospital network, may behave differently elsewhere. So, a model that works in Boston is not automatically ready for Bihar.
Risk before labels
India currently regulates medical devices by stretching the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which was intended mainly to penalise spurious drugs. In 1982, an amendment allowed the government to classify devices as ‘drugs’. The Medical Devices Rules, 2017, established the first dedicated rulebook. The rules introduced four classes - Class A for low risk, B for low-to-moderate risk, C for moderate-to-high risk, and D for high risk. The manufacture of devices under classes A and B is generally handled by State licensing authorities, while the central authority regulates manufacture of devices under classes C and D as well as the import of all classes. In 2020, all devices meant for medical use, including software, came under the law. While AI does not create a fifth class, the risk it poses depends on its intended use and the consequences of incorrect output.
The July guidance translates this risk-based approach classification specifically to software as Software in a Medical Device (SiMD - embedded in or controlling hardware), or Software as a Medical Device (SaMD -where the software itself performs the medical function). Software that only stores or transfers patient information is treated differently from one that influences diagnosis or treatment. Standalone medical software is assessed according to both the severity of the clinical situation and the extent to which its output guides medical decisions. Software intended solely for general wellness or routine tracking of body parameters may remain outside the medical-device framework.
Proof followed by surveillance
Validation for AI-enabled devices is sought uniquely. The CDSCO seeks evidence of a sound clinical association between the output and the condition; whether the software technically produces the intended result, and whether it performs clinically in the population and setting (deployment) where it will be used.
Developers are expected to describe training, validation and test datasets, including demographic, geographic and clinical diversity when using AI. Models developed outside India may require justification and validation in representative Indian populations. Bias, generalisability and subgroup performance matter because even ‘95% accurate’ means little without asking — accurate at what, in whom, and against which reference standard? Approval is also a continuous process as algorithms can be retrained, software can be upgraded, while performance can drift. The CDSCO discusses change in management, retraining, rollback, version control and post-market surveillance of the system.
Guidelines, not law
India’s AI regulation is outlined in policy papers of NITI Aayog, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. In 2018, NITI Aayog released the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, which named health care a priority. ICMR then, in 2023, issued ethical guidelines for AI in health care, stressing the need for accountability, fairness and patient autonomy. In November 2025, the Electronics & IT Ministry’s AI Governance Guidelines chose not to propose a separate AI law, leaving each sector’s regulator to act.
In February 2026, the Health Ministry launched the Strategy for Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare for India (SAHI), which addresses governance, data, validation, deployment and monitoring of AI across healthcare. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has developed AI-specific lifecycle approaches, including predetermined change-control plans for defined future modifications. Europe combines medical-device regulation with the EU AI Act, which adds requirements for high-risk AI such as risk management, data quality and human oversight.
Way forward
The new guidance raises a larger question: can a technology that decides who is sick and who is sent home be governed by guidelines alone? India’s guideline-led approach has enabled regulators to move quickly without waiting for Parliamentary legislation. While its insistence on Indian data is ahead of many similar guidelines elsewhere, a dedicated statute for AI-enabled medical devices could make Indian validation mandatory for high-risk tools, clarify liability, and create a public registry of approved AI devices.
The question is whether technologies that can influence life-and-death decisions should continue to rely on guidance built on an 80-year-old law or be governed by a clear statutory framework that patients and clinicians can trust.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

The French government was in crisis talks on Sunday after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted, and more than 2000 people arrested in cities across the country.
Politicians on the left and right called for the resignation of the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, after the government appeared to have been caught by surprise by the scale of violence as state buildings were stormed and torched, bus stops smashed, roads barricaded and shops broken into and destroyed.
The president, Emmanuel Macron, who is standing down next spring, was preparing to address the nation on Sunday night. He wrote on social media there was “no place for violence” in France.
Police and officials faced challenges of different types on Saturday. First, tens of thousands of peaceful protesters attended calm marches through major cities including Paris, supporting schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools. Those marches, which came after four weeks of street marches and barricades of schools, were attended by parents, teachers and grandparents as well as students and workers protesting over the high cost of living. The demonstrators carried banners saying the government was not listening to them and calling for more money for public services.
But separately to those peaceful demonstrations, different groups caught police and officials by surprise with moving gatherings, sporadic burning, the barricading of streets and clashing with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.
Finally, masked looters took advantage of what French media called the “chaos” on the streets to smash shopfronts and grab goods. In Paris, groups of looters, some of whom appeared to be children, were seen running through the night with clothes and shoeboxes after masked adult men smashed shopfronts.
In Paris, where police said a record 855 people had been arrested, the burnt-out remains of barricades built using bikes, bins and other materials littered streets on Sunday. Several streets had smashed shop windows and the remains of torched cars. The capital had experienced “a level of violence that we have never seen before, I believe”, said the Socialist deputy mayor, Lamia El Aaraje.
In Limoges in central France, where the 19th-century town hall was burned down, the mayor, Guillaume Guérin, said the people who stormed his building “were not demonstrators that defend causes” but “people organised for war”. He said those who stormed and torched the town hall had told a building caretaker he would be killed, and told elected officials they would “burn”. He said there had been a failure of the state to deal with the crisis.
“Around 3:30pm our municipal police, although present in number, found themselves no longer able to fight against the violence of rioters because they had run out of munition,” Guérin said. He called this “a colossal failure of the state”.
In Marseille, where masked groups stormed the city hall and a police station, the Socialist mayor, Benoît Payan, told BFMTV: “I have no words … I never thought I’d ever live through something like this. Hordes of rioters and looters attacked our common [state] buildings … with no real demands, but with the sole aim to wreck the demands of those who had demonstrated legitimately.”
Payan said questions must be asked about policing tactics, as other town hall buildings, for example in Lille, were also targeted.
Grégory Doucet, the Green mayor of Lyon, said he had never seen such violence in his city, including the torching of the historic tourist office. He told Le Monde: “I’m stunned by the violence against public and state property. I saw and heard fear and anger. Shop-owners felt abandoned.”
Doucet said the government must find a “sense of nuance” in properly examining what happened and “avoiding stereotypes”. He said the government needed to give a political response to long-running societal demands from peaceful demonstrators on one hand, and also examine roots of violence.
Traders’ unions said over 1,500 shops and businesses had been ransacked with a cost running into tens of millions of euros. “This had nothing to do with the peaceful protesters,” said one shoe-shop owner in Paris. “These were organised groups who were breaking things and looting. We’d never seen anything like it.”
Opposition politicians questioned the government’s policing tactics, saying there had been a lack of state intelligence.
The interior ministry said there had been more than 2,000 arrests and about 600 police, firefighters and paramedics had been hurt. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Étienne.
Macron’s centrist government and the far-right frontrunner for the presidential election, Marine Le Pen, both blamed what they called “ultra-left” groups for the violence. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would not be “intimidated” by violence, and blamed the unrest on the “ultra-left” and criminals.
The radical-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who attended the peaceful street demonstration in Paris on Saturday, accused the government of organisational failings that had “opened the door to chaos”.
Lecornu replied on social media: “Laying the responsibility for violence on heads of police is a dangerous and cynical reversal of responsibilities.”

Desperate to clear toxic haze, Indonesia to douse its skies with dry ice
- Published
As toxic smog continues to billow from wildfires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands, authorities are looking at an experimental way to disperse the haze.
A trial on Thursday will see an aircraft scatter pellets of dry ice - solid carbon dioxide - in the air above South Sumatra province, one of the regions worst hit by the haze.
Indonesia is battling its most dire wildfire season in a decade, as an unusually strong El Niño has exacerbated drought conditions and made flames harder to put out.
Amid increasingly urgent efforts to clear the hazardous air, authorities in Indonesia and neighbouring Malaysia have turned to various weather modification methods.
These include cloud seeding, a technique that speeds up the natural process of water vapour condensing inside of clouds by dispersing compounds such as silver iodide to form ice crystals.
Authorities have been carrying out such operations for weeks.
But Thursday's dry ice trial is different.
Rather than interacting with clouds to trigger rain, the dry ice is meant to "break down" haze in the lower atmosphere "so that it can rise upward", said Dudung Abdurachman, the coordinating minister for political and security affairs.
"If this trial is successful, we will continue with other areas that are central to the haze, such as Central Kalimantan and its surroundings."
The trial will involve 1.5 tons of dry ice, according to authorities.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for agencies to step up efforts to extinguish the wildfires and mitigate the impact of toxic smog billowing from the hotspots.
New cloud seeding operations are also set to take place in Central Kalimantan - another haze-stricken area - on Thursday and Friday.
Meanwhile, firefighters on the ground are continuing to tackle out-of-control blazes and authorities have deployed dozens of helicopters to extinguish the wildfires - though these operations have at times been disrupted by poor visibility in the haze.
Residents across Kalimantan and South Sumatra are bearing the brunt of the toxic smog, with air in many cities turning a dusty amber.
Pollutants have also drifted across borders to neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia, raising public health concern as air quality scores soar to unhealthy levels.
In parts of Malaysia with particularly hazy air - including its capital Kuala Lumpur and the city of Johor Bahru, near Singapore - local authorities have conducted their own cloud seeding operations.
Last month, Indonesia granted permission for Malaysian agencies to enter its airspace for cloud seeding operations along the countries' shared border.
More than one million wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia this year, burning almost 900,000 hectares of land, according to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas.
Much of the public frustration is directed at agricultural companies that burn vegetation as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.
Indonesian police have named more than 200 individuals and nine companies as suspects in connection with the fires.

Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India’s election chief on Sunday, as a court ordered the release of the “cockroach” movement founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and two other senior leaders.
Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday, as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi.
Indian authorities on Saturday deployed a sweeping crackdown across Delhi and detained thousands of protesters as the youth “cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fuelled anger at the prime minister, Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Reuters reported police detained more than 2,000 people to thwart Saturday’s protest. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.
Most detained on the first day of protests were released on Saturday night, police said.
Opposition parties and critics of Modi’s government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters.
The UN human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said: “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled.” He urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
India’s foreign ministry said the UN’s approach was “selective” and its statement constituted “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
The protests are calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years.
Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party.
Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
The BJP and the commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The “cockroach” movement, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi’s education minister.
The CJP has called its protests against Kumar “Season 2” on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India’s election system was reformed.

The rapid rise of a former art dealer to Europe's hottest young manager
- Published
When Brighton lost at home to Crystal Palace in February, Fabian Hurzeler was booed by his own supporters and subjected to chants of "you're getting sacked in the morning".
"There are only two options," said the German after the 1-0 defeat by their fierce rivals left his team floundering 14th in the table with one win in 12 Premier League matches.
"Give up or keep pushing harder, and that's always the option I choose in my life."
Eight months on, Brighton are reaping the benefits of keeping faith with the man who became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in June 2024 at the age of 31.
Palace return to Amex Stadium on Sunday (14:00 BST kick-off) to face opponents who are third in the table after statement wins over defending champions Arsenal and Europa League winners Aston Villa.
Hurzeler's stock has rocketed after 11 wins in 18 top-flight games, a run that has propelled the Seagulls back into Europe and left fans - who shouted "you don't know what you're doing" at him just a few months ago - worried that he could be lured away.
Following last Saturday's win at Sunderland, there was chat on the post-match phone-ins that Hurzeler, rewarded with a new long-term contract before the end of last season and given £150m to spend on signings in the summer, could be a prime target for a big club looking for a manager.
"You learn more about yourself and the people around you when you are losing games," former Brighton striker Glenn Murray told BBC Sport in reference to last season's poor run.
"Hurzeler has come out the other side and the way he has got this group of players performing is exceptional."
Scott McCarthy, from the We Are Brighton fan site, said Hurzeler appeared to have lost the crowd to such a degree at one stage last season than even a few wins would not be enough to turn it around.
"He looked like a manager who was out of ideas," McCarthy told BBC Sport.
"Leaving the stadium after losing at home to Palace, the only conversation fans were having was: 'he has got to go'.
"It's totally different now. It's worked out phenomenally."
Will Brighton manage to keep hold of Hurzeler, who has gone from managing in Germany's fifth tier to reported interest, external from Manchester United?
- Hurzeler signs to 2029 as Brighton rival elite clubs 
  - Published7 May
'Wet behind ears' to Champions League?
The determination Hurzeler demonstrated in the face of anger from fans following last season's defeat by Palace has been evident throughout his 10-year coaching career.
In 2016, after one injury too many following spells in the reserves at Bayern Munich, Hoffenheim and 1860 Munich, the former midfielder gave up playing professionally to accept a player-manager role at German fifth-tier side Pipinsried at the age of 23.
It was the start of a coaching journey that has led to the Premier League.
To make ends meet at village club Pipinsried, which is about 30 miles from Munich, football-obsessed Hurzeler worked for an art dealer selling paintings to wealthy Bavarians.
In an interview with the Guardian, external in 2024, he revealed he was fired from that job because he was spending too much time watching games.
"If you want to sell something to a person, you have to try to convince them by doing something," he said when comparing selling pictures to managing Premier League players.
"And you can't go there and say: 'Look at this picture, it's an amazing picture'. You have to understand the needs and the wishes from the clients.
"That's a little bit similar to being a coach.
"The most important thing is to understand the person behind the player. What are his needs? What are his values? How is he educated? How was his past? Where does he get education?"
Hurzeler's obsession to succeed runs deep.
While managing St Pauli - who he left in 2024 to join Brighton after guiding the Hamburg club back to the Bundesliga following a 13-year absence, external - he was invited to Tottenham's training ground to watch Ange Postecoglou's side train.
Hurzeler - who was born in Houston, Texas, before moving to Germany at the age of two - asked so many questions that Postecoglou had to ask another member of his coaching staff to step in and take over.
He also picked up tips from Roberto de Zerbi at Brighton, a few months before replacing him after Kieran McKenna,, external who had been heavily linked with the job, opted to stay at newly promoted Ipswich.
Despite respectable back-to-back eighth-placed finishes, Hurzeler's time at Brighton has not been without its difficult moments.
In addition to fans calling for his dismissal last season, the Seagulls were thrashed 7-0 at Nottingham Forest in his first season in charge, while former Arsenal and England defender Martin Keown labelled Hurzeler "wet behind the ears", external on the BBC's Final Score following Brighton's 4-2 defeat at Chelsea in September 2024.
So what is the reason for the shift in fortunes since his own fans called for his dismissal?
"It's partly because Hurzeler went back to basics," adds McCarthy.
"He relied on an experienced core in the side to get out of the hole, which is testament to him because it shows his pragmatic side. You get managers who are wedded to their philosophy and won't change.
"Hurzeler realised what he was doing was not working and that it could cost him his job, so tried something else. You can now see this is a team more in his image, because they press insanely."
Will Hurzeler leave Brighton if another club comes for him, or stay and attempt to write his name in club folklore by qualifying for the Champions League?
"I personally don't think he will go," says McCarthy.
"The money would obviously be tempting but he is a very intelligent guy. He didn't become a Premier League manager at the age of 31 without having his head screwed on.
"Does he want to go to another club where he isn't going to get time? What has happened at Brighton has shown he needs two-and-a-half-years to build a squad."
Back in Pipinsried, Hurzeler's name is still revered - and he has not forgotten where his coaching journey began.
"Yes, he does enjoy coming back every now and then - to see if everything's in order," Sepp Ankner, their chief finance officer, told The Athletic, external in 2024.
"When he does, he talks to everybody. He's really retained that connection with Pipinsried."
But his rapid ascent means gilded surroundings might not be far away for Europe's hottest managerial property.

Here's why some people say the 2-day weekend is due for a makeover
Henry Ford widely credited, but labour movement fought for it in Canada and U.S.
As the two-day weekend turns 100 years old, some say it's high time for a calendar shakeup.
"Almost nobody alive remembers the time before we had a five-day week and a two-day weekend," said Grace Tallon, co-founder of Work Time Revolution, a Toronto-based consultancy group that helps employers adopt shorter work hours.
Labour historians and advocates for workweek reform point out that much has changed since the two-day weekend became standard about a century ago, depending on where you are in the world.
Tallon notes that only 20 per cent of women were in the workforce at that time. "Now we have mostly dual-income households, yet we still have a situation where we have a five-day workweek that doesn't serve really any family."
Experts also point out that the weekend is a human-made concept that has evolved before and can evolve again.
Grace Tallon, co-founder of Work Time Revolution, a Toronto-based consultancy group that helps employers adopt shorter work hours, says the way we live and work has changed a lot since we last revisited the length of the workweek. (Submitted by Grace Tallon)
How the two-day weekend came about
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, a long workweek was the norm.
"Basically, if you were working for wages, the regular work week was six days of 10 hours a day," said labour historian Craig Heron, a professor emeritus at York University in Toronto.
"The beginning of the weekend was the Sunday that everyone got off for religious reasons," Heron told Cost of Living host Paul Haavardsrud.
Though Henry Ford is widely credited with instituting a two-day weekend, there's quite a bit more to the story, including decades of work by the labour movement.
Prior to Ford's five-day-week, small groups of workers had achieved similar reforms.
"The most famous group were the printers," Heron said. "They managed to get an eight-hour day by about 1910."
An illustration published in the Canadian Illustrated News shows workers taking part in a Nine-Hour Movement march in Hamilton, Ont., in 1872. The movement pushed for shorter working days and helped spur major changes to Canadian labour law. (Canadian Illustrated News/Library and Archives Canada)
When Ford announced in October 1926 that his factories would move to a five-day week, the company became the first major U.S. employer to do so.
That same month, the American Federation of Labor passed a resolution at its annual congress calling for a five-day week, Heron says.
But it would be a while until the two-day weekend was broadly adopted, including in Canada, he says.
Many workplaces in North America and elsewhere first reduced Saturday work to half a day.
The labour movement grew stronger in the 1940s as the Second World War drove demand for workers, giving unions greater leverage to win shorter workdays through major strikes, he says.
Governments began to take note and legislate accordingly.
In workplaces that adopted policies that reduce hours while maintaining pay through pilots run by the non-profit 4-Day Week Global, participants reported an improvement in their ability to combine paid work with their social lives. (Tint Media/Shutterstock)
Work has changed
Since then, the nature of work has changed significantly, in ways that can affect whether a two-day weekend feels adequate.
"We have a much more fluid kind of work schedule for a lot of people who work electronically, who work at all hours, all times of the day or week, and can be on call anytime," said Heron. "Their cell phone could ring whenever their employer wants them."
While working hours steadily decreased from the late 19th century to the middle of the 20th, they began to increase again after that, says David Henkin, a historian at the University of California, Berkeley and author of The Week: A History of the Unnatural Rhythms That Made Us Who We Are.
The erosion of boundaries between work and personal time has not only increased the amount of work that people do, he says, it has also "decreased the amount of insulation, psychic insulation, that people have from work."
When every weekend is a long weekend
A desire to address that erosion is part of what's fuelling momentum for a four-day workweek.
Tallon is also a former executive director of the non-profit 4-Day Week Global, which conducted four-day-week pilots starting in 2022, in which hours were reduced while pay remained the same. She says all 41 participating companies in Canada and the U.S. kept the four-day week after the six-month trials ended.
One of them was Praxis, a public relations firm in Toronto.
Meredith Nebel, an account director for public relations firm Praxis, says that since the company moved to a four-day week she's been able to keep her weekends more free for family time because she can get errands, chores and appointments out of the way on Fridays. (Submitted by Meredith Nebel)
Meredith Nebel, an account director for Praxis, says days off are staggered. Colleagues cover her work while she's off on Fridays, "and then I take on their Monday work just to make sure that there's no pause in the workflow."
- These Canadian companies switched to a 4-day work week. Here's why
- Why experts say it's time to adopt a 4-day work week
Nebel says she doesn't think she could go back to a five-day week.
"I have more time with my kids. I have time within my own community. I have more time for my own life and my own desires and just building myself as a human," she said.
Nebel says she uses Fridays to get appointments, household errands and chores out of the way so weekends are free for family time and kids' activities.
Charles Latimer, who works for Greenpeace, says having Fridays off since the organization adopted a four-day week has given him time to volunteer.
"I just started a little kids' basketball program after daycare on Tuesdays," said Latimer, who works remotely from Lund, B.C., about 200 kilometres north of Vancouver.
On Fridays Latimer takes care of administrative tasks for the program and also keeps his four-year-old home from daycare, he says.
Charles Latimer, seen here with his four-year-old daughter and their dog, works as head of strategic integration for Greenpeace, which reduced hours to a four-day schedule. (Submitted by Charles Latimer)
Consultant Grace Tallon says switching to a four-day schedule takes considerable planning. "That could mean that you need to restructure your meetings; that could mean that you need to ensure that everybody has heads-down time, when that previously wasn't respected."
At Praxis, Nebel says it hasn't been a struggle to get the work done in less time.
"Work just seems to expand to fill the time that you give it," she said, "but with the four days there's a natural urgency so we plan more deliberately and we're sharper about what actually needs to get done."
'The week is unnatural'
We tend to think of the week — with its five days of work and two of rest — as set in stone.
But Henkin says the very idea of the week as a whole, let alone the way we divide it, is considerably more arbitrary than the other units humans use to measure time.
"The week is unnatural because it is not actually rooted in any of either the astronomical phenomena that produce things like days or … hours or years, nor are they rooted in the biological rhythms that produce patterns of day and night."
Tallon says that whether a workplace is looking to adopt a four-day week or just rein in long hours, it's about "how you start to respect your own time and how the company starts to respect your time."
"And many of these people then feel, 'I can turn off my notifications in the evening. I'm not gonna look [because] I feel I have to. Because nothing's going to blow up or burn down.'"

National Award-winning singer, composer and actor GV Prakash Kumar has opened up about lending his voice to Yash’s character Raavan in Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana. In an exclusive statement, the musician spoke about how he came on board, the scale of the composition and his experience of recording a song for the mythological epic. Prakash Kumar revealed that his association with the film began after a call from composer AR Rahman. He had recently returned from Ayodhya following the promotions of Nayyi Naveli when he received the opportunity.
GV Prakash Kumar says Ramayana’s Raavan composition has “a certain scale” and “intensity”
“To be a part of a film like Ramayana, which brings this timeless epic to the big screen on such an extraordinary scale, is an absolute privilege. My journey with the film began quite unexpectedly. I had just returned from Ayodhya after the promotions of Nayyi Naveli when I received a call from A. R. Rahman sir, asking me to sing the song for Yash’s Raavan,” he said.
GV Prakash Kumar on bringing Raavan’s character into the music
Prakash Kumar also spoke about the complexity of Raavan and the challenge of translating the character's personality into a musical performance.
“Dussehra is a time when we celebrate the triumph of good over evil, but the story of Ramayana also reminds us that its characters are far more layered than a single interpretation. Raavan, in particular, is one of the most fascinating characters in our mythology, immensely powerful, exceptionally knowledgeable,” he said.
According to the singer, the composition required an approach that went beyond simply performing the song.
“Raavan is a character of extraordinary complexity, power, intelligence and intensity, and I believe the music has to capture something far beyond what words alone can express. There is a certain scale, and an almost elemental energy to this composition that makes it unlike anything I have sung before,” he said.
Praising Rahman's work on the project, Prakash Kumar added, “With Rahman sir’s extraordinary musical vision, the soundscape of Ramayana is being imagined on a truly magnificent canvas. As a singer, the challenge is not merely to sing the notes, but to become a part of that world and contribute something that makes the character feel larger than life.”
GV Prakash Kumar wants audiences to experience the song in theatres
The musician also expressed his excitement about the film and its ensemble cast, which includes Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi and Yash in key roles.
“I feel incredibly fortunate to have received this opportunity from Nitesh Tiwari sir’s Ramayana, with Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi, Yash and such an exceptional ensemble bringing this epic to life,” he said.
Prakash Kumar particularly hopes audiences experience the song on the big screen.
“I am particularly excited for audiences to experience this song on the big screen. There is a scale, a sound and an intensity to it that deserves that cinematic setting,” he added.
He concluded by asking listeners to approach the song without expectations and experience it in the context of Raavan's character.
“I would love for listeners to discover the song without any preconceived notions and let the music take them into Raavan’s world. This Dussehra, as we celebrate the eternal significance of the Ramayana, I feel honoured to have contributed my voice to a cinematic journey that promises to be truly memorable,” he said.

Filipino authorities say they have fined six companies 1.76 billion pesos ($27.9m; £21m) for forming an "onion cartel" that caused the price of the vegetable to skyrocket.
In 2022 the price of onions, a staple of Philippine kitchens, surged to a record 800 pesos per 1kg, surpassing the country's daily minimum wage and overtaking the price of meat.
The crisis put pressure on then newly-elected President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, who had promised to bring down surging food prices.
The Philippine Competition Commission (PCC) said Wednesday the fine against the companies, comprised of onion importers and storage and shipping firms, was the largest since its formation in 2016.
For months between late 2022 to early 2023, onions disappeared from restaurant menus and became the object of smuggling attempts.
The bulbous vegetable even became something of a status symbol, having been used on at least one occasion as a wedding bouquet.
Authorities approved the emergency import of onions and Marcos vowed to go after those behind the shortage, saying there were "Filipinos dying from starvation and poverty because of what they are doing".
The crisis ended as local bumper harvests entered the market later in 2023 and prices stabilised.
A parliamentary committee tasked to investigate the price crisis said a cartel was behind the "artificial" surge in onion prices.
The PCC said evidence retrieved during raids on the companies showed that the six firms had collectively controlled nearly 50% of all approved import clearances for onions in 2020 and 2021.
The companies were involved in an "illegal market allocation scheme in the importation, cold storage, and whole sale distribution", the commission said.
The hefty fine shows a "commitment to holding cartels accountable across all sectors of the economy and protecting consumers from the harmful effects of anti-competitive conduct", the PCC said.
The commission also said that offenders may also be criminally prosecuted by the Department of Justice.

Sopore, Oct 17: Bazm-e-Sher-o-Adab North Kashmir organised a one-day literary conference and Naatia Mushaira at Government Boys Higher Secondary School, Sopore, bringing together prominent literary figures, poets, writers and admirers of Urdu literature to celebrate the region’s rich literary and cultural heritage.
The event provided a platform for intellectual exchange, literary discussion and poetic expression, highlighting the enduring significance of literature in preserving cultural identity, promoting linguistic heritage and strengthening social and moral values.
During the conference, speakers emphasised the need to promote literary and cultural activities across North Kashmir, particularly among the younger generation. They stressed that languages and literature are vital components of a society’s identity and called for collective efforts to preserve the region’s rich linguistic traditions, encourage creative expression and cultivate a lasting interest in reading, writing and poetry among young people.
The speakers also underlined the importance of organising literary gatherings, Mushairas and conferences to provide emerging poets and writers with opportunities to showcase their talent, interact with established literary personalities and contribute to the growth of Urdu and other regional languages.
A special felicitation ceremony was also held during the programme in honour of Yousuf Samim, President of Bazm-e-Sher-o-Adab North Kashmir, in recognition of his association with the literary organisation and his contribution to promoting literary and cultural activities in the region. The ceremony reflected the gathering’s appreciation for individuals dedicated to preserving and advancing the literary traditions of North Kashmir.
The Naatia Mushaira added a spiritual dimension to the programme, with the gathering reflecting the reverence, devotion and literary beauty associated with Naatia poetry. The proceedings created an atmosphere of literary appreciation, cultural pride and spiritual reflection.
At the conclusion of the event, Mohammad Saeed Masoodi delivered the vote of thanks, expressing gratitude to the distinguished guests, poets, writers, organisers and all participants for their presence, cooperation and contribution to the successful conduct of the programme.
The one-day literary conference and Naatia Mushaira concluded in a warm and spiritually enriching atmosphere, reaffirming Bazm-e-Sher-o-Adab North Kashmir’s commitment to nurturing literary talent, preserving linguistic heritage and keeping the region’s rich traditions of poetry and literature alive for future generations.

Kochi Mini Cooper crash: Driver’s mother appeals for privacy, extends condolences to victims’ families
Suhail Sajeev’s mother said the investigation into the Mini Cooper crash must proceed in the right direction and that the truth must prevail
A week after a 19-year-old rammed a Mini Cooper into a scooter, killing three people near Kochi, his mother appealed to the public to give her family some privacy as they navigate the aftermath of the horrific crash.
Nooha Sajeev, who runs apparel stores in Kochi and Alappuzha under the brand ‘Iha Designs’, is the mother of Suhail Sajeev, who was arrested on October 11 in connection with the car accident that claimed three lives. In a video posted on Facebook, Nooha expressed her condolences to the families of the three victims.
"We have lost three valuable lives. I convey my condolences to their families. I can understand the pain they must be feeling. We raise our children with a lot of hopes and dreams, and when they suddenly leave us, it is unthinkable. My words can never compensate for their grief," Nooha said in the video.
Also Read | Mini Cooper driver who killed 3 in Kochi car crash had 5 times legal blood alcohol limit, say police
She said that the investigation must proceed in the right direction and that only truth must prevail. Nooha also requested the public to desist from spreading half-truths and give her family some privacy.
"This issue is being discussed a lot on social media. Many people are angry at us. But I want to appeal for privacy for me and my family. There are a lot of half-truths going around. Please understand that I am also a woman and a mother hailing from an ordinary family. I am concerned about my son's future just as I am deeply sad about the three people who lost their lives," she said.
The 19-year-old’s mother said she felt utterly “helpless” and had been unable to even sit up over the past few days.
"Please remember that I have a family of four. We also have lives to go about," she said.
This is the first time Nooha Sajeev has spoken publicly about the fallout of the October 11 car crash that led to her younger son, Suhail, being jailed. Nooha had gifted him the Mini Cooper on his birthday this year and shared the moment on Facebook. She had said then that both her sons were car enthusiasts and that she was “happy” to gift the luxury car to her younger son.
Around 1:45 am on October 11, Suhail’s Mini Cooper rammed into the rear of a scooter on the road leading to Cochin International Airport near Nedumbassery. Devika, Gopika and Iyas, all in their early 20s, were riding the scooter at the time. They worked at a crafts retail shop and succumbed to their injuries.
Suhail was charged with culpable homicide not amounting to murder, while three of his friends, who were in the car at the time of the accident, were booked for abetment.
Police found that Suhail and his friends were heavily intoxicated at the time of the crash. Suhail’s blood alcohol concentration was found to be five times the legal limit for driving in India.

An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.
Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5%, respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.
Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in ChatGPT owner OpenAI.
The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, logging its worst performance since July.
The sell-off comes after US data showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher than expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.
The figure has rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.
“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid, said.
Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”
The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said earlier this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk.
“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.
The latest jitters hit China, where Shanghai’s CSI 300 slipped as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.
European stocks were skewing lower at the start of trading, with the Europe Stoxx 600 down by 0.4%, the UK’s FTSE 100 down 0.06%, France’s CAC 40 down 0.19%, and Spain’s Ibex falling 0.17%. Germany’s DAX fell by 0.53%.
In the US, stock futures pointed to losses for tech stocks, with the Nasdaq 100 futures dropping 1%.

A new bill proposed by Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) aims to establish new regulations that would ensure that “buying a video game would give the consumer ownership of the game rather than a license to play it,” including assurances that they can continue to access the games for years after they are released.
The announcement names NBA 2K25 as an example of the problem the bill aims to solve; that game launched on September 6, 2025, but is scheduled to become unplayable on December 31 due to server shutdowns. The bill, which is called the Power to Players Act, directs the FTC to take action to prevent outcomes like that in the future.
Torres published the following statement on the bill:
When you pay for a game, you should own it. Consumers must have the right to own, the right to play, and the right to transfer the games they buy. A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale. Families in the Bronx and across the country save up to buy these games, and they deserve better than a license that can vanish at any time. The Power To The Players Act ensures consumers own what they buy and can keep playing long after a company moves on.
“I think there should be a simple rule: if you pay for it, you own it,” Torres told Kotaku. He called the new status quo the bill proposes a “restoration to the historical norm,” referencing how most games were experienced by players back in the ’90s.
A wider movement
The bill comes at a time when game ownership and preservation is a hot-button issue. Some consumers have been protesting Sony’s announcement that it plans to discontinue releases of PlayStation games on physical media.
In its most recent financial earnings report, Sony revealed that digital downloads account for 82 percent of full-game unit sales across PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5 for the covered fiscal year, suggesting that less than 20 percent of games are still purchased in physical media form. But the argument is that continuing to offer physical discs is not just about satisfying a minority of players’ habits. Players hope it would aid with long-term preservation of games, which are sometimes delisted from digital marketplaces and then become inaccessible.

Israeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land.
Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground on Saturday.
The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.
The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.
Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her seventies and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury.
Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armoured car belonging to the Belgian mission.
Maxime Prévot, Belgium’s deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, condemned the violence against Palestinians, foreign diplomats and journalists, and said his country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers.
“Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack,” he said. “This violence cannot be separated from Israel’s illegal settlement policy … The occupation of the Palestinian territory must end.”
Palestinian residents of Taybeh have lived with years of escalating attacks from Israeli militants, but settlers had never targeted foreign diplomats there, said Father Bashar Fawadleh, the town’s parish priest.
“What happened today is not an isolated incident. It represents a deeply disturbing escalation in settler violence,” Fawadleh said. Since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September, Israeli militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and financially vital to their communities.
Since 27 September, settlers have launched more than 170 attacks, Israeli rights group Yesh Din said. They killed at least four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees, according to Palestinian authorities.
Even the presence of Israeli activists, diplomats, senior clergy and journalists no longer serves as a deterrence to extreme violence.
“If such violence can take place before international witnesses, one must ask what protection remains for local families and farmers when those witnesses are no longer present,” Fawadleh said. “No individual should have to risk physical assault simply to harvest olives from their own land.”
On Friday, Israeli militants attacked and severely injured Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as she reported on the harvest in the town of Abu Falah. She required surgery on Saturday morning and is now in “moderate” condition, according to a spokesperson for Israel’s Beilinson hospital where she is being treated.
Israel had already severely restricted the harvest this year by imposing new rules barring Palestinians from trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.
Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the attacks and said police had opened an investigation. He said foreign diplomats risked attacks from Israeli civilians if they travelled in the occupied West Bank without military coordination.
Demanding diplomats give advance notification of travel violates both diplomatic conventions international law, said one western diplomatic source who asked not to be named. “Israel is in charge of security in Area B and C (the majority of the West Bank), so is obliged to assure safety there for all,” the source said.
A culture of near total impunity for Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has prompted former prime minister Ehud Barak to call for the international criminal court to intervene.
Gadi Eisenkot, an opposition politician and former general hoping to unseat prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu in elections held later this month described the attack as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the Israeli government”.
Eisenkot backs Jewish Israeli expansion in occupied Palestine but wants militant violence brought under control because the attackers are “harming the settlement enterprise in [the West Bank] and national security”.

Sachin Baby stepped into his familiar role as crisis man with aplomb, scoring his 16th first class century to rescue Kerala on the opening day of the Ranji Trophy match against Odisha at the Sports Hub, Greenfield Stadium here on Sunday.
After being put in, Kerala was staring down the barrel after a disastrous start (18 for three) but Baby turned the savior with a masterful knock (112, 235b, 11x4, 1x6). Mohammed Azharuddeen made a timely return to form (72 batting 135b, 6x4) and his alliance with Baby for the sixth wicket (141 runs) helped Kerala recover from 101 for five to end the first day at 245 for six.
Earlier, Odisha medium pacers Rajesh Mohanty and Lalit Yadav made optimum use of the seamer friendly conditions and had Kerala on the mat at the end of the first hour. Abhishek P. Nair, the centurion from the first match, drove loosely at a delivery from Rajesh and was caught at point by Soumya Lenka for a duck.

The promoted Jalaj Saxena lasted only six balls as Lalit squared him up and had him caught in the slips. Abhishek J. Nair (11) was caught behind by Sandeep Dhuper off Lalit to leave Kerala tottering at 18 for three.
The recovery began when Baby added 40 runs for the fourth wicket with captain Vishnu Vinod (21) who was caught behind off Lenka. Salman Nizar and Baby defied the Odisha attack to add 43 runs for the fifth wicket. Salman (21) was dismissed playing back to Badal Biswal soon after the lunch break.
Azharuddeen had an early stroke of fortune when Shantanu Mishra dropped him in the slips when he was on five, but he made Odisha pay dearly for the miss with a watchful knock. However, the new ball gave Odisha the much needed breakthrough as Baby was caught down the legside off Lenka.

If you like restaurants where the evening can stretch from dinner into drinks, music and long conversations, Supa San Bandra is built for that kind of outing. The Japanese izakaya is less about rushing through a meal and more about ordering several small plates, trying a few drinks and settling in for a while. After trying its food, cocktails and desserts, some dishes stood out more than others — but the experience begins with a setting designed to make you stay a little longer.
A space that puts music in limelight  
Located on the 14th floor of Mansionz One on Linking Road, Supa San is the latest Bandra outpost, following its BKC location. The 110-seater restaurant takes inspiration from Japanese izakayas, listening bars, vinyl cafés, neighbourhood eateries and karaoke culture.
As soon as you step inside, the first thing you notice is the music-led atmosphere. There is a communal dining area along with more intimate seating, while the open-to-sky alfresco section has a retractable roof. Neon lights add to the mood, live DJ sets the tone and there is also a private karaoke room for those looking to make the night a little louder.
One of the more interesting elements for me is The Culture Shelf, which features interesting vinyl records, Japanese-inspired objects, artwork and memorabilia. And if you're a music freak, you should definitely look around this corner. It feels more like part of the restaurant’s personality than a decorative afterthought.
Overall, the space has an easygoing, social vibe. It is the sort of place where you can imagine spending a few hours with friends, ordering drinks, listening to music and grazing through the menu rather than sitting down for a formal meal. 
And grazing is exactly what the food menu encourages.
Small plates with some hit & miss 
With more than 100 dishes and almost half the menu offering vegetarian options, Supa San has deliberately kept the food approachable. The menu is divided across The Counter, The Grill and The Pot, with sushi, sashimi, gyoza and smaller plates filling out the experience. 
Chef Kripasha Miniya says the idea was to make the Bandra menu easier to navigate and suitable for different preferences, including Jain diners. “You should never reach main course,” she explains, describing a menu designed around smaller plates that allow guests to keep trying different dishes with a drink in hand.
The experience started with an otōshi, a complimentary welcome dish of creamy cabbage finished with Parmesan and miso dust, served with their signature spicy miso chilli sauce (which you can use throughout the dishes).
Midori No Mori |
Then came Midori No Mori, a green apple and avocado tartare served with edamame, cucumber, spicy onion dressing, jalapeño, and a lot other ingredients, alongside crispy nori chips. This was one of the stronger starters. The green apple brought sweetness and tang, while the avocado gave the dish a creamy texture. The fried seaweed chips added the crunch it needed, making every bite a mix of different textures. It was fresh, flavourful and light enough to work as a first order.
Tori Wasabi Sarada |
The Tori Wasabi Sarada, however, was more divisive for me. The salad combines romaine, iceberg and radicchio with grilled chicken, pecans and a wasabi dressing. The chicken was well cooked, and the dressing was not overwhelmingly sharp or spicy. But as I continued eating, a bitterness started lingering in the mouth. The first few bites were enjoyable, but the flavour became less pleasant towards the end, making it something that would not call for again.
Tori Teba and Tori Tsukune |
The grill section fared better. The Tori Teba, or stuffed chicken wings, takes deboned chicken wings and fills them with minced chicken before finishing them with chilli, roasted garlic and green onions. The chicken was juicy inside with a smoky exterior, and I squeezed lemon over it which lifted the flavours. I would suggest pairing it with the signature spicy miso chilli sauce for spicy kick and made the dish more interesting.
Another good grill was Tori Tsukune, chicken meatballs covered with honey butter and served with a creamy egg sauce made with soy sauce and egg yolk. The kebab-like meatballs were juicy, well-cooked and smoky on the outside. The honey butter added sweetness, while the egg and soy sauce brought creaminess, savouriness and a mild kick.
Tori Gyoza and Renkon Chizu Gyoza |
For gyoza, I preferred the Tori Gyoza over the vegetarian Renkon Chizu Gyoza. The chicken version, made with minced chicken, cabbage and shiitake mushroom, was juicy and umami-rich while still feeling like a classic gyoza. The signature sauce on the table adds spice and is worth using. The Renkon Chizu Gyoza, made with lotus root, corn, edamame and cheese, had a crisp shell and creamy filling, but the flavours felt relatively mild. If you like vegetarian gyoza and prefer something subtle, it works, but it did not leave as strong an impression on me as the chicken version.
Tori Karaage |
Then came the Tori Karaage, and this was another easy win. The Japanese fried chicken had the right contrast — crisp and crunchy on the outside, moist and juicy inside. The spicy, tangy sesame sauce worked well against the fried chicken, giving it enough heat and kick.
Sake Sashimi |
The Sake Sashimi was also worth mentioning. The thinly sliced raw salmon was fresh, soft and umami-rich, with a melt-in-the-mouth texture. Served with wasabi and pickled ginger, it stayed close to the simplicity expected from good sashimi.
For something more filling, the Tori Kamameshi was the comfort-food option. The chicken rice pot combines grilled chicken, carrot and mushroom with rice and a thick chicken-based sauce. The rice gets its flavour from a broth-style sauce made with chicken stock, soy, sake and mirin, which is reduced until it reaches a thicker consistency. The chicken was cooked well, and the rice absorbed the sauce nicely. It is not the most exciting dish on the menu, but it is comforting and satisfying when you want something substantial.
Cokctail menu that dances with tunes 
The cocktails are where Supa San leans heavily into its music identity. The beverage menu, titled NOW PLAYING, is designed like a record collection, with 22 drinks spread across five sections — Low Volume, The Hits, Covers, Deep Cuts and Full Volume. The progression moves from lighter, flavour-forward drinks to more spirit-driven options.
The cocktail names are inspired by Japanese music, anime and some of the best artists, so the music reference is built into the drinks rather than simply being part of the restaurant’s décor. As mixologist Rohan Vengurlekar puts it, “The idea was to match the energy, emotion and personality of a song with the character of a drink."
From the Low Volume section, Shinunoga E Wa, inspired by Fujii Kaze’s popular song, is made with crème de banana, hazelnut liqueur, milky oolong tea and Japanese melon. It is silky, light and not particularly alcohol-forward. The sweetness builds gradually, followed by nutty notes, making it a comfortable choice if you prefer softer cocktails without a strong spirit hit. According to Rohan, the drink draws on the song’s “romantic, slightly obsessive and playful energy."
Shinunoga E Wa and Unravel |
Unravel, from The Hits, takes inspiration from TK’s song associated with Tokyo Ghoul. Made with tequila, green apple, sage, wasabi and bubbles, it is refreshing and easygoing. I could pick up the green apple and a little tequila, followed by a peppery finish, but the wasabi was barely noticeable. It is decent rather than particularly memorable.
Summertime |
For a zero-proof option, Summertime combines zero-proof gin with shiso, lychee, cucumber, lemon and bubbles. It is sweet, refreshing and dominated by cucumber, making it a straightforward choice if you want something light without alcohol. Inspired by the song by cinnamons and evening cinema, Rohan says the drink is intended to capture “that carefree feeling of a warm evening, good music and an izakaya table full of friends”.
Gurenge |
The prettiest of the lot was Gurenge, the tequila sour inspired by LiSA’s Demon Slayer song. The purple drink combines tequila, beetroot cordial, toasted sesame, raspberry, honey and foam. It has a silky texture with sweet raspberry and honey notes, followed by nuttiness from the sesame and a gentle tequila finish. It is rich but still easy to drink.
Kick Back |
If you want something considerably bolder, Kick Back from Full Volume is the one. Inspired by Kenshi Yonezu’s Chainsaw Man track, it is made with tequila, roasted bell pepper, Japanese spices, hickory smoke and agave. It is spicy, savoury and sour, with a serious kick from the spice coating around the glass. If you like a Picante-style cocktail, this is likely to work for you.
Definitely keep room for the desserts  
Don't miss their desserts. The Chokorēto Sumomo Gatō, a chocolate and plum gateau, combines flourless almond cake, plum compote and São Tomé chocolate mousse. The mousse is dense and rich, almost cake-like, but the plum brings enough tanginess to cut through the chocolate. It is indulgent without becoming overly sweet, and this was easily my favourite dessert of the meal.
Chokorēto Sumomo Gatō |
The Ube Basque Chīzukēki is a burnt ube Basque cheesecake served with kinako crumble, semifreddo and berries. The cheesecake has the familiar baked Basque texture but with the earthy, slightly umami flavours of ube. It is not excessively sweet, and the berries bring freshness. However, ube is an acquired taste, and between the two desserts, I would still go for the chocolate and plum gateau.
Ube Basque Chīzukēki |
Final Verdict  
Overall, Supa San Bandra works best when approached as a long evening rather than a quick dinner. The menu is broad enough to encourage sharing, with some dishes clearly stronger than others. Meanwhile, the cocktail menu is playful without making every drink aggressively experimental, and there are enough styles to suit different preferences.  
My biggest takeaway? Come for the drinks, stay for the music and order several small plates rather than trying to build a traditional starter-main-dessert meal. And if you have room at the end, don't skip the Chokorēto Sumomo Gatō.
Location: 14th Floor, Mansionz One, Linking Rd, Bandra West, Mumbai
Cost for two: ₹4000 (including alcohol)

The health ministry has drawn up guidelines outlining points to consider when creating advertisements in collaboration with movies and television dramas to raise awareness of government policies.
The move came after a poster promoting support for cancer patients that the ministry created in a tie-up with a film drew criticism on social media, informed sources said.
To raise awareness of the support system for cancer patients, the ministry partnered with a film about a woman who was diagnosed with cancer.
It sent the poster to hospitals and other institutions, but faced repeated criticism, with some questioning what patients would think of the poster given the film deals with the death of a woman.
The ministry eventually called on institutions to take it down.
The guidelines call for confirming “whether such policy ads would be accepted by the people concerned” and “whether they pose a risk of fostering misunderstanding or prejudice.”
The guidelines state that the public relations office first checks the relevance of the policy, whether the content is sound and whether there are any social risks for people appearing in the ads.
Next, staff in the section in charge watch a preview to familiarize themselves with the content before presenting the advertising plan to the parties concerned, as well as patients and their families.
For example, the guidelines say that opinions should be sought from cancer survivors, patients’ families and medical professionals when planning awareness campaigns promoting cancer screening.
Finally, any tie-up would be confirmed by the director of the bureau in charge.
Among government agencies, the Justice Ministry had partnered with an internet program featuring a former motorcycle gang member, but later canceled the tie-up following criticism of a remark made by one of the cast members.
The issue is a common challenge for all government ministries and agencies, and the health ministry has received inquiries about its guidelines, sources familiar with the matter said.

Nursery owner in China jailed for life after hundreds of children poisoned
- Published
A nursery owner and five members of her staff have been jailed after they were found to have poisoned more than 200 children with lead-tainted food.
Li Huifang, who operated the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui, in the Gansu province, was sentenced to life in prison for producing and selling toxic and harmful food, according to Chinese state media.
In July 2025, 247 pupils and staff at the nursery were found to have abnormally high blood lead levels after children began falling ill.
A report into the incident found that chefs at Heshi Peixin had used inedible paint to "enhance the look" of its meals to attract more students - despite the paint being being clearly marked as such.
In addition to the sentence, the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court also ordered the confiscation of 500,000 yuan (£56,200; $74,700) of Li's personal assets, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
Nursery executive principal Zhi Jinglin was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,00 yuan.
Four other members of staff who worked in the nursery's kitchen received sentences of between six to eight years, according to state media.
The court found the four had been instructed by Li and Zhi to add toxic and harmful ingredients to food served to children and staff.
Food samples were later found to contain lead 2,000 times in excess of China's national safety limit.
The investigation into the poisoning began after 235 children from Heshi Peixin nursery had to be treated for lead poisoning after eating steamed red date cakes and sausage corn buns.
Investigators found that the red date cake and the corn sausage rolls had lead levels of 1052mg/kg and 1340mg/kg respectively, both of which far exceed the national food safety standard limit of 0.5mg/kg.
Lead poisoning is "particularly harmful to young children" and can "severely damage the brain and central nervous system", according to the World Health Organization.
Officials later found that dozens of provincial officials and hospital staff attempted to cover up the incident by tampering with blood tests and accepting bribes from a nursery investor.
China has since published a set of national guidelines for the provision of meals on campuses. Among the measures is the requirement for every new batch of food to be tested, and for flour, rice and cooking oil to be purchased from centralised procurement points only.

How land power could help US forces counter China in the Indo-Pacific

The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.
The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible sign that the deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed – if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers.
Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.
Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations inside Yemen in January, cutting off its funding supply line.
Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states.
The separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.
Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.
There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.
The UAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen, and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.
UAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, the Houthis are determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen.
On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported.
The missiles landed about 500 metres from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 metres from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani.
The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.
Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia.
In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging more closely with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue.
The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures.
Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter. The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law.
No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups.

The Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to an eighth province in the country’s north, authorities said on Sunday.
