Saskatchewan-born man achieves dream of becoming Jeopardy! Champion
Rian Robertson won a total of $66,101 US from playing on 5 episodes of the show
A Saskatchewan-born man has achieved a longtime dream of appearing on the television show Jeopardy!
Rian Robertson became a returning champion winning four consecutive games. Across his five appearances he won a cumulative total of $66,101 US.
"I mean obviously as someone who loves the game of Jeopardy!, I wish I could keep playing in perpetuity, but I mean you have got to lose at some point, I guess," said Rian.
The Jeopardy! champion was born and raised in Outlook, Sask., a town located about 80 kilometres south of Saskatoon, with a population of just over 2,300.
He now lives in Ottawa with his wife and four kids, where he spends his days as a software developer at a tech startup that he co-founded. Although he hasn't lived in Outlook for many years, that doesn't mean that his hometown wasn't cheering for him.
"Well, I was kind of lucky because I'm in Ottawa now, so I kind of had two pockets of support, here in Ottawa, but also back home my family, my parents and my sister and old friends were rallying behind me and being my biggest cheerleaders," he said.
"It was just awesome to see the support that was happening back there because I'm obviously from a little small town. So, when someone kind of gets on a big stage like that, it is cool to see everyone rally behind you."
From a young age, Rian has been a fan of Jeopardy! He used to watch the show with his father, Ian Robertson, as part of their after school ritual.
While Rian's parents Ian and Susan Robertson were "thrilled" by their son's casting on the show, health issues prevented them from being able to travel to Los Angeles where the show is filmed.
Not being able to attend the show's tapings did not stop the proud parents from celebrating their son's achievements. The couple hosted a viewing party for around 15 people when Rian's first episode of Jeopardy! was aired about a month after it was filmed. Rian tried to convince his mom that he had lost the first episode, but she knew better.
"To be honest, I had my suspicions because I'm quite sure when we told him that we were having friends over to watch, if he hadn't done well, he probably would have said, 'oh, no, no, don't do that.' But he didn't. So I suspected that he won at least one game, but, you know, I wasn't sure," said Susan.
His parents now live a few kilometers down the road from Outlook in Broderick, Sask. They say that the community has been overjoyed by Rian's success.
"I mean, Outlook's not that big, but there are still people I don't know, but they would stop me on the street and congratulate me, to pass it on to him," said Susan.
A big step toward a lifelong dream
For Rian, making it on the show was a dream years in the making. He says that he's been trying to get on the show seriously for about 15 years, but his interest in facts and general knowledge questions can be traced further back to childhood.
His father remembers when he started curating his own collection of fascinating facts.
"When he was younger, whenever he found out a fact that he kind of liked or was interested in, he would write it in this loose leaf paper and stick it in a binder. And he called it his book of knowledge," said Ian.
Rian's wife Kristina Robertson also knew from their first meeting that Rian was a whiz with general knowledge. The couple met at a trivia night, although Kristina says that trivia is very much Rian's domain in their marriage.
Kristina was able to watch the filming of two of her husband's Jeopardy! episodes, including his nail-biting second episode where he came from behind to win. She knows that for her husband being on Jeopardy! is a stepping stone to achieving his bigger dream.
"Rian's goal, yes, it was to get on Jeopardy!, but ultimately his goal is to win that Tournament of Champions," said Kristina.
"You know half of his dream has come true, put it that way."
Jeopardy! champion Rian Robertson stands smiling behind his podium. (Submitted by Rian Robertson)
But back in Broderick, Rian's quest to achieve his dreams has already changed at least one life.
"I am just so thrilled, because I mean to see anyone achieve a lifelong dream is amazing, and in fact, he's inspired me to get back on the bandwagon because my dream is to be fluently bilingual in French before I die," said Susan.
"Maybe that's not the best way to put it, but since he was on Jeopardy!, I've taken back up on my lessons in French. So he's an inspiration to his mother."

‘Nowadays, you need a lot fewer people’: Laid-off Stelco workers not alone as steel jobs disappear
Number of jobs in Canada's primary steel manufacturing industry have roughly halved since 2003
Stelco Holdings laid off 85 employees at the end of last week, according to union leader Ron Wells. The week before, he says the company issued 90 layoff notices.
While the U.S.-owned steelmaker insists its plan to lay off up to 500 workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., is only a temporary consequence of the Canada-U.S. trade war, new technologies and demand dynamics are working in concert with tariff-related headwinds to compress the industry’s once-robust workforce.
According to Statistics Canada, direct employment in Canada's primary steel manufacturing industry has slipped from nearly 29,000 workers in 2003 to about 14,000 workers as of July.
Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, and a 47-year veteran of Stelco, says the workforce at Stelco alone was about 14,000 strong when he started working for the company.
"To make a ton of steel nowadays, you need a lot fewer people," Wells told CBC News. "Now, it’s a lot more streamlined."
According to U.S. regulatory filings, the total workforce of Cleveland-Cliffs — the Ohio-based owner of Stelco and North America’s largest producer of flat-rolled steel — shrank from about 30,000 employees to roughly 25,000 between Dec. 31, 2024, and Dec. 31, 2025.
This year of job cuts included about 600 layoffs in Dearborn, Mich., as Cleveland-Cliffs idled a massive blast furnace. CEO Lourenco Goncalves blamed soft demand from North American automakers.
The move prompted another 600 cuts in Minnesota to align the company’s raw ore output with reduced blast furnace demand.
An aerial image of Stelco's facility in Nanticoke, Ont. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)
In late September, three months after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order applying up to 50 per cent tariffs on certain steel and aluminum imports from Canada, Stelco announced up to 500 layoffs at its two Ontario operations.
That provoked the current clash between the company and the federal government over Stelco’s obligations under the Investment Canada Act to maintain a certain number of workers in Canada.
- Laid-off Stelco steelworkers stressed about company's future — and their own: 'We're being sold out'
But Stelco’s workforce isn’t the only cohort of Ontario steel workers facing job uncertainty.
Last December, Algoma Steel issued layoff notices to about 1,000 workers, nearly a third of its workforce. While the Sault Ste. Marie, Ont.-based company blamed U.S. tariffs for crushing its export competitiveness, the announcement coincided with plans to fast-track its transition to greener and less labour-intensive electric-arc furnace production.
That came after ArcelorMittal Long Products Canada announced the permanent shutdown of its Parkdale wire-drawing facility in Hamilton in June 2025. The company is a subsidiary of ArcelorMittal S.A., the world’s second-largest steel and mining company.
"Despite our best efforts, the ongoing economic challenges, increased steel imports in Canada and market conditions made it clear that we needed to reduce our operating footprint," company spokesperson Jean-Philippe Grou told CBC News at the time.
Calls to address cheaper foreign steel imports
In a letter to Industry Minister Mélanie Joly obtained by The Canadian Press, Stelco president Paul Simon complained that imports of cold-rolled and coated steel accounted for 45 per cent of market share for those products.
Wells says Ottawa is not doing enough to shield Canadian producers from cheaper foreign imports. He wants tariff-rate quotas increased to impede the flow of foreign steel competing with Canadian supply.
"There’s too much capacity coming from offshore," he said. "It dilutes the price in Canada."
A new forecast from research firm Wood Mackenzie shows the contrast between the steel industry in the U.S. versus Canada. It predicts U.S. steel production will rise about 4.5 per cent this year, even as demand in America shrinks. Senior research analyst Tiago Vespoli sees a different reality in store for Canada.
"The increase in U.S. steel tariffs to 50 per cent has significantly disrupted … established trade flows, creating a situation in which U.S. steelmakers can increase production and market share, while Canadian producers face growing pressure on export volumes and capacity utilisation," he wrote on Thursday.
Wells says he’s encouraged by a recent uptick in spot prices for galvanized steel — a product Stelco is pivoting away from in Hamilton.
"Galvanized steel is now at $1,800 a ton in Canada, which is a vast improvement from six months ago. That’s why we find these layoffs and the idling of the cold mill and coated [steel] quite puzzling. It seemed like [prices for] coated products were starting to rebound. That’s why we believe this layoff is partially to get Carney to act and get a trade agreement," he said.
"We think it’s to get Trump to look good in the midterms, that his tariffs are working, Canadian steel workers are getting laid off."
Goncalves has openly supported Trump’s tariff agenda, a fact that has prompted blunt criticism from Joly and Prime Minister Mark Carney.
With a courtroom clash between Cliffs and Ottawa looking increasingly likely, Wells says he continues to hold onto hope that Stelco will recall the workers being laid off.
"It's hard to take them at their word anymore, to be honest with you," he said.
"I strongly believe these layoffs are temporary. I think this trade situation will get sorted out soon and our members will get back to work."

Flat Ethernet cables probably aren't the answer to your home networking problem
For the most reliable performance, round cables are generally superior.
Unless you're relying entirely on Wi-Fi, chances are you've had to wrangle an unsightly mess of Ethernet cables at some point in your life. One way to make your home internet setup a little easier on the eyes is to use flat Ethernet cables, which have become much more popular in recent years. Flat Ethernet cables can be easily bent and hidden from sight, making it possible to wire a home for internet without causing an eyesore.
But before you trade out all your chunky old Ethernet cables for aesthetic flat ones, there are a few tradeoffs you should be aware of that might not be obvious at first. While round and flat Ethernet cables rated for the same speed will have nearly identical performance under perfect conditions, the real world is full of complications that often make round cables a better choice even if they don't look quite as good. It all comes down to why Ethernet cables are round in the first place and what it takes to turn them into that more pleasing flat shape.
Does a flat Ethernet cable affect speed?
Standard Ethernet cables consist of multiple sets of wires twisted into pairs, with each pair then twisted around each other. The twisting actually serves an important purpose, preventing the signal running through one pair of wires from interfering with the others, which could cause slow internet speeds and unstable connections. Flat Ethernet cables still contain twisted pairs of wires, but those pairs are laid out in a line, which makes them more susceptible to interference from each other. Some round Ethernet cables include additional shielding to prevent interference from outside devices, which typically isn't available in flat cables.
Another potential problem comes from the gauge, or thickness, of the wires inside Ethernet cables. To ensure that flat cables are as thin as possible, manufacturers typically use a thinner gauge wire than is used in round cables. The thinner a wire is, the more resistance the electricity traveling through it faces, meaning flat Ethernet cables can actually degrade signals over a long enough distance.
While the technical specifications of Ethernet make flat cables a dicey choice, the real problem comes from how they tend to be used. Flat Ethernet cables are easy to bend around corners, run under doors, and hide beneath rugs, but all of these applications make them much more likely to fail. Bending any cable or repeatedly compressing it under a door can end up damaging the wires within, no matter what shape it's in. The thinner wires in flat Ethernet cables make them more fragile, and since they're laid out in a row, they lack even the slight cushioning that the shape of round cables can offer.
Are flat Ethernet cables any good?
While there are real drawbacks to using flat Ethernet cables, that doesn't necessarily mean that they should be avoided at all costs, and there are some circumstances where using them makes a lot of sense in a home setup. If you absolutely need to run a cable under a door or through another space too narrow to fit a round cable, using a flat cable may be your only option, especially if you're renting and can't make big changes to your living space. It may also be worth the risk to use flat cables you can hide under rugs if the alternative is turning your office into a rat's nest of visible wires.
If you absolutely need the fastest, most reliable connection, round Ethernet cables are almost always going to be the best choice. Where that's not necessary or possible, though, flat cables can work fine as long as you know their limitations. The increased risk of interference and signal degradation introduced by flat cables only really comes into play when you're using cables of considerable length, so it's best to opt for round cables there, too. But over short distances where you don't need to bend a cable to get it into place, flat Ethernet cables will still do the job.

US senator accuses Turkey of ‘thuggish behavior’ toward Greece and Cyprus
Republican U.S. Sen. Rick Scott accused Turkey of “thuggish behavior” toward Greece and Cyprus and questioned Ankara’s commitment to NATO amid longstanding disputes over Aegean airspace, maritime boundaries and the divided island of Cyprus
ATHENS, Greece -- Republican U.S. Sen. Rick Scott on Saturday accused Turkey of “thuggish behavior” toward Greece and Cyprus, delivering unusually blunt criticism of a NATO ally during visits to both countries.
The Florida senator told The Associated Press that Turkey was “not acting like a NATO ally,” citing its airspace and maritime disputes with Greece and its continued military presence in northern Cyprus. The island has been divided since 1974.
Scott’s comments come amid renewed tensions over a planned undersea electricity link between Greece and Cyprus, with a possible extension to Israel. Turkey says it should be consulted before seabed surveys proceed.
Scott, a member of the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, held talks with Greek officials on defense and energy following a visit to Athens last week by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
“You’re not acting like a NATO ally when you take F-16s and fly over somebody else’s country. You’re not much of an ally when you occupy a portion of another country’s land. And that’s what they’re doing,” Scott said of Turkey.
“So, I’m hopeful that it will change, but if you look at it, it’s thuggish behavior,” he added.
Greece and Turkey, both NATO members, have been embroiled for decades in disputes over maritime boundaries in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean, as well as the divided island of Cyprus.
The electricity project has become the latest source of friction between Ankara and Athens.
“I think what Greece, Cyprus and Israel are doing is going to be good. It’s good for them, good for us,” Scott said. “We’re going to do everything we can to be helpful. We’re going to do everything we can to make sure Turkey does not cause problems with it.”
Scott also said the U.S.-Greek relationship would not be affected by the recent departure of Kimberly Guilfoyle as U.S. ambassador to Greece. The White House publicly called for her resignation over allegations of improper and possibly illegal conduct, which she denies.

A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
- Published
Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide
The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above; a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood.
"This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.
The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars.
"You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.
He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat; he could be humming a tune.
We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.
Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.
Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.
We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States.
At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over.
It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl.
The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added.
When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce."
Medetomidine, is what he means. Like Xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me.
They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat.
Recovery group offering hope
At the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma.
They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty.
One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life.
As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid.
"It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement.
Both in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose".
"In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers.
Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so.
"The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it."
Overdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds.
His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina.
That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine.
"The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements."
And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois.
I meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity.
Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means.
He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever.
When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico.
"If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability."
And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear.
"Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me.
A novel approach
Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening.
"In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel."
The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures.
Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens.
It was indeed, as Sheriff Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters.
"Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained.
Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures.
In August, I joined Sheriff Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search.
As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of.
As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates.
The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells; it's here where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper.
Now every piece of mail that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected.
Outside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them.
In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell.
Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs.
She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing."
Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants.
The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous".
"Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me.
Tom Dart has been Sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs is progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me.
And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics.
"The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it."
Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail.
"You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way."
'A lot of people are struggling'
Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track.
It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb.
As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed."
A pregnancy test changed her mind. She then spent time in Cook County jail for theft. Her parents, sensing an opportunity for her to get clean, refused to pay her bail money. So Karen got clean, and Abby was born inside the jail.
When I ask Abby, who wants to become a tattoo artist, if she's ever been tempted to experiment with drugs, she says: "Nah, I've seen it mess with my family too much, with my dad, my mom, killing my aunt, my uncles. You know, it's not worth it to get high for like a couple of hours."
She continues: "There's a lot of people are struggling, especially that our country is raising our prices, raising the prices on food and it's causing it. A lot of mental health now is very expensive so people can't get help, and one way they can turn to that is by drugs."
Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis, but it is never the same crisis. It has shifted from heroin, to prescription opioids to fentanyl and now to a whole new range of synthetics.
Successive administrations have fought - and lost - the war against drugs. The dealers, the suppliers, the cartels and users all adapt, always a few steps ahead of efforts to stop them.

A 7-year-old girl is recovering from surgery after being shot in the face during Thursday’s deadly shooting at an elementary school in Oregon, which left three children and a teacher dead.
Little Saylor Graham, who uses a wheelchair for a disability, survived the shooting and underwent surgical treatment following the attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend on October 15, according to a family friend who spoke to NBC News. She was stabilized in serious condition.
The youngest known survivor of the rampage, Saylor — who is well known in the community through a local youth program — has drawn an outpouring of support as she faces a long recovery.
A GoFundMe campaign has so far raised over $380,000 for the schoolgirl and her family as they travel to Portland for her ongoing medical care. In addition to the injuries sustained in the shooting, she has further medical needs due to living with a rare genetic condition called CASK.
The fundraiser, launched by a family friend, described Saylor as a “feisty, loving child” with a “fierce determination to thrive.”
“On October 15, 2026, Saylor survived a tragedy no child should ever have to endure,” the page reads. “This unimaginable trauma has brought medical expenses and uncertainty to her family during an already difficult time.”
The campaign noted that both of Saylor’s parents are self-employed and currently unable to work while staying at her bedside.
“This fundraiser is to help ease the family’s urgent financial burdens, including time away from work, hospital bills, lodging, and transportation,” the page states.
Saylor is known in the local community through her involvement with Bend High School as a designated “Sparrow.” Under the Sparrow Clubs program, local schools adopt children with medical needs to inspire student fundraising and community service.
Matt Sampson, the executive director of Sparrow Clubs, told Central Oregon Daily News that Saylor was adopted into the Bend High Lava Bear Sparrow program in 2025.
“Saylor is the definition of light and joy,” Sampson told the outlet. “And one of those kids that, you know, when she’s in the room. You can't think of anything else other than what Saylor’s doing, ‘I need to get to know her.’
“She's just very inspirational, very joyful, very courageous, and inspirational.”
Sampson added that her presence left a lasting impression on the student body.
“Saylor was the Sparrow catalyst for Bend High School when she was a Sparrow, and the little girl was used to teach kids things that many of us probably couldn’t have taught them without her,” Sampson said. “She opened their eyes to new perspectives, and she really just unified that school.”
High school seniors who participated in her fundraising campaign reflected on the experience in written statements.
One student wrote that helping Saylor “made me feel empowered to create positive change in the community. It was wonderful to be part of something larger than myself, and I am so proud to have contributed.”
Another student added: “Helping Saylor made me feel that there is still hope and humanity in this world. It taught me how much I love to help people in need as it makes me feel like I'm worth more.”
As Saylor continues her medical treatment, community leaders expressed confidence in her recovery.
“She's a fighter, and we’re praying that she fights through this and her family,” Sampson said. “I want to express to her family how much we love them and how valuable they are to us. We’re here for them in whatever way we can be.”

Cloudstreet, Tim Winton’s sprawling Australian family epic, has been voted Australia’s favourite book in a poll run by ABC Radio National.
The broadcaster announced over the weekend the results of a nationwide poll to determine a list of readers’ top 100 Australian books.
Markus Zusak’s 2005 novel The Book Thief took second place, while Trent Dalton’s Boy Swallows Universe came in third.
First published in 1991, Cloudstreet follows two working-class Australian families, the Lambs and the Pickles, over their 20 years living together in an old rambling house called Cloudstreet, in postwar Perth.
The story – Winton’s fifth novel and ninth book – won a swathe of awards upon publication, including the Miles Franklin in 1992, and has been a staple of Australian English literature classes for decades. It’s sold hundreds of thousands of copies in Australia alone.
Cloudstreet has topped previous polls on Australian books, including one by the Australian Society of Authors surveying writers on their favourites in 2003, and a subsequent poll run by the ABC the same year, surveying the public. Winton’s novel appeared in a 2019 BBC list of “100 novels that shaped our world”.
The final top 100 in this year’s ABC Radio National poll included adult fiction, nonfiction, young adult fiction, children’s picture books, history and cookbooks.
The Australian Women’s Weekly Children’s Birthday Cake Book made it into the top 50 (at No 22), while Stephanie Alexander’s The Cook’s Companion came in at number 56. RecipeTin Eats: Dinner by Nagi Maehashi made the cut at 96.
Authors Helen Garner, Melissa Lucashenko, Geraldine Brooks, Anna Funder, Peter Carey and Hannah Kent all had multiple books in Sunday’s top 100. Books by children’s authors Alison Lester, Paul Jennings, Mem Fox, Jeannie Baker and Ruth Park appeared in the final 100.
The earliest published work was For the Term of His Natural Life by Marcus Clarke from 1874 (No 80). The most recent were Sally Hepworth’s Mad Mabel and Charlotte McConaghy’s Wild Dark Shore, both published in 2025.
Kate Evans, the host of ABC Radio National’s literary show The Bookshelf, said the list included “audacious literary fiction to historical accounts of who we’ve been and how we might understand all that complicated past, to joyful children’s books, Indigenous stories of both pain and humour, and many, many family stories”.
“This list defies any glib conclusions about how we read – and surely that’s the point,” Evans said.

At least 17 people have been killed and many more injured in a crush at an event in the Indian city of Kolkata to mark the Hindu festival of Durga Puja, officials say.
The incident occurred during sudden rainfall, which witnesses say prompted a surge of people to try to seek shelter.
West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari said a seven-year-old girl was among the dead, and that 25 people were being treated for injuries.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi described it as a "tragic" incident and said the regional government was providing help to affected families.

Two years ago, 121 people were killed in Uttar Pradesh during a Hindu religious gathering.

Making an emotional appeal for someone to “put an arm around” West Indies cricket financially, head coach Daren Sammy hoped that a closely fought series against India would put it in a place to have more meaningful conversations with sponsors to swell the money flow into the struggling Caribbean cricket.
After pushing India hard in a 1-2 ODI series defeat, the Windies held the two-time defending T20I world champion to a 2-2 draw in the five-match series.
Sammy wanted to use the series as a pivot to change the financial fortunes of his nation. West Indies has been finding it hard to survive under the current revenue-sharing model of the ICC, which was adopted in 1997.
“My mom always said, you must have a care factor. No matter what you do in life, you should never lose that care factor. I think we’re in a position where we need somebody to put a shoulder around West Indies cricket — financially, that is,” Sammy said after the washed-out fifth and final T20I in Bengaluru on Saturday night.
“Series like this, here in India against the best team in the world, puts us in a conversation closer to that,” he added.
Sammy then drew a comparison between the Indian and West Indian cricketing landscapes, underlining the benefits of financial strength and structured growth.
“India will win the World Cup every time they go somewhere in an ICC event. They expect to win. It is because of all the things they’ve put in place. When the West Indies goes somewhere, we’ve got to perform in spite of. Because and in spite…there are two different words,” Sammy noted.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on autonomous vehicles, policy, and road rules, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
How it started
The first state to pass a law legalizing self-driving cars operating on public roads was Nevada in June 2011 — long before such vehicles were operating on public roads. This was three years before the introduction of Tesla’s Autopilot, five years before Waymo spun out of the Google self-driving car project, and seven years before the first commercial robotaxi service got underway (in Arizona, not Nevada). Nevada was ahead of the curve primarily due to lobbying: Google saw Nevada as prime testing ground for its prototypes, so it urged lawmakers to pass the law that allowed it to do so. The legislation even included a provision exempting drivers from text-messaging bans while the automated system was engaged.
Back then, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars with open arms, eager to be seen as future-forward and pro-innovation. They had no inkling that over a decade later, they would be back at the drafting table crafting legislation to rein in these same self-driving cars.
While federal regulators scramble to establish safety standards, legislation that would establish rules for autonomous vehicles remains stalled in Congress — and has been for years. Washington’s paralysis has left local lawmakers to create their own playbooks to ensure robot cars at least follow some rules of the road.
The result is a patchwork of rules and regulations for robotaxi operators to follow — an outcome that many industry leaders were desperate to avoid. And as robotaxis continue to spread to new cities, local officials are discovering more unintended consequences of their new robot residents, leading to even more rules and an ever-growing patchwork of complexity for operators.
How it’s going
Municipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, but they hold broad authority over street operations. As such, they’ve been using that authority to pass their own laws governing the rollout of robotaxis. There’s not an exact count of the number of local regulations and ordinances that have been passed since robotaxis have gone mainstream. But in the absence of any federal rules, cities and states have been flexing their authority in an effort to bring order to some of the chaos.
Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies direct control over AVs in emergencies. And Austin firefighters have expressed concern over the Tesla Cybercab’s lack of steering wheel or pedals, which they argue could lead to issues if first responders need to move a stalled vehicle. They want to require AV developers to establish dedicated, rapid-response towing protocols and direct human operator communications for emergency situations.
It’s not just cities or blue states taking a harder line, either — the pushback is blurring traditional political lines. It used to be the case that Republicans were seen as more welcoming of autonomous vehicles, while Democrats were seen as more skeptical. This has certainly borne out in a handful of Democrat-led cities — New York City, Chicago, Washington, DC — that still haven’t legalized driverless cars. But now even some red states are considering tightening the leash, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Iowa.
Even in tech-friendly California, state lawmakers are mulling ways to bring robotaxis to heel. Several bills have been introduced to give cities direct authority to limit AV fleet sizes, restrict operating hours, or enact local permit bans within municipal limits. Additionally, emergency protocols were drafted to require AV companies to give local police and fire departments physical override access or emergency remote shut-off mechanisms.
Some municipalities are flexing their land-use and zoning powers to crack down on robot cars. Culver City explored emergency moratoriums on building permits for AV fleet facilities, while Santa Monica used local noise and traffic ordinances to restrict 24-hour charging hubs. It would seem that even robotaxis aren’t immune to NIMBY complaints.
What happens next
As the local debate over autonomous vehicles intensifies, AV developers are increasingly looking overseas as a potential hedge to more obstacles in cropping up in the US. Waymo is planning to expand its service in London, Tokyo, and Munich. Uber is teeing up vehicles for Manchester, Madrid, and Dubai. If the US is getting too complex and over-regulated, perhaps they can find friendlier reception elsewhere.
Still, the US presents the industry’s best chances of turning a profit, especially as costs for developers continue to grow. Rather than fighting strict local regulations head-on, companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Aurora are prioritizing states with explicit legislative preemption that prevents individual cities from banning the technology. And at the national level, industry trade groups like the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association are aggressively pushing for more preemption powers in an attempt to create more unified standards.
Congress may eventually get around to passing high-level safety legislation, but it’s highly unlikely that any bill passed at the federal level would seek to strip cities of their core police, zoning, and emergency response powers. States will also have a say, and sometimes that may complement or conflict with their own cities. Even airport authorities are getting in on the action, proposing their own slate of rules for robotaxis. AV companies would be well advised to get used to the patchwork — it’s not going anywhere.
By the way
- Even if the feds pass a sweeping national framework, like the proposed SELF DRIVE Act, cities and states would still keep their authority over local road usage. In other words, cities are going to be the main arbiters of robotaxi permission for the foreseeable future.
- Texas may be the Wild West, with fewer rules governing self-driving cars than most states, but California is still the gold standard. Securing a deployment permit from the California Public Utilities Commission, for example, is viewed by the industry as a definitive safety validation.

Government doctor among 3 arrested as Rajasthan ANTF seizes 3.764 kg of raw MD
Rajasthan’s Anti-Narcotics Task Force arrested a government doctor and two others after busting an alleged mephedrone manufacturing unit in Balotra.
A government doctor was among three people arrested after Rajasthan’s Anti-Narcotics Task Force (ANTF) busted an alleged mephedrone (MD) manufacturing unit at a house in Balotra district on Saturday. Police seized 3.764 kg of raw MD, chemicals and equipment, ₹3.41 lakh in cash and a car.
The ANTF team, with assistance from local police, raided the premises in the Siwana police station area after receiving information about an alleged MD manufacturing unit, deputy inspector general of police Abhijeet Singh said.
Police identified the three arrested men as prime suspect Suresh Kumar Vishnoi (27), a resident of Mithora; Dr Mukesh Vishnoi (29), and Utkarsh Vishnoi (19), a resident of Modran village in Jalore district.
From failed government job aspirant to alleged MD manufacturer
Suresh completed his graduation and attempted several government recruitment examinations, including those for patwari, gram sevak, Rajasthan Police, forest guard and police sub-inspector posts, but failed to secure a government job, an ANTF officer said.
In 2022, he moved to Bengaluru with a friend and began working in pharmaceutical sales as a medical representative. After working in the field for around two years, he allegedly found the earnings insufficient.
Police said Suresh returned to his village in 2024 and came into contact with people involved in drug trafficking. He allegedly began purchasing, selling and supplying MD before deciding to manufacture it himself in pursuit of higher profits.
Investigators suspect that he learnt the process of manufacturing MD by watching videos on YouTube and other social media platforms. He allegedly used chemicals and equipment to prepare the drug at his house in Mithora.
According to the ANTF, Suresh had called Dr Mukesh Vishnoi and Utkarsh Vishnoi to his house to sell a consignment of MD. The two allegedly arrived in a car.
Police suspect that Suresh used Dr Mukesh’s contacts to supply the drug in and around Jalore and Siwana. During questioning, Suresh allegedly disclosed details about supplying MD through his associates and other people involved in drug trafficking.
Raw MD, chemicals and equipment seized
The ANTF team had received information that Suresh was operating an MD manufacturing unit at his house and in the adjoining premises. After verifying the information, the team conducted a raid with local police.
Officers said that the three men were found sitting in a shed outside the house. A search of the house and surrounding premises led to the recovery of raw MD, chemicals and equipment allegedly used to manufacture and dry the drug. All three were arrested, and the seized material was taken into custody.
The seized material included 3.764 kg of raw MD, including its packaging, and two packets of powder allegedly used in manufacturing the drug, weighing 888 grams including the plastic bags.
Police also seized 800 grams of methylene dichloride (MDC) and 514 grams of a chemical described in the seizure details as isopropyl acid.
The equipment recovered from the premises included an electric churning machine, an induction cooktop, a large glass jar, a thermometer and a piece of cloth bearing a substance allegedly used in drying MD.
In addition, the team seized ₹3,41,700 in cash and a Kia Seltos bearing registration number RJ-19-CT-10351.

The uncertain future of Canada's 30 rescued belugas
- Published
Tofino approached each of his handlers in turn as they knelt in shallow water and stroked his sides.
Shortly after, a crane hoisted the more than 1,500kg beluga whale into a lorry to be shipped out of Canada to his new home, SeaWorld San Antonio - the last of 30 belugas and four dolphins to leave Marineland, a shuttered sea park near Niagara Falls.
Marineland needed to find a new home for its whales. But when the Canadian government rejected its plan to sell them to China over concerns about animal welfare, the park's operations said they would have to be euthanised.
That spurred an international rescue operation by several aquariums, leading to the largest ever transfer of captive whales this summer. But hopes that the animals were headed to a better life have been dampened by a number of deaths in the group.
Photographer Carlos Osorio documented the move, which involved whales being flown to Chicago, Atlanta, San Diego, San Antonio, and even Valencia, Spain.
Osorio recalls watching footage from a drone overhead as Tofino appeared to say his own goodbyes.
Tofino was the last captive whale in Canada. The country banned cetacean captivity and breeding seven years ago, and Osorio felt the weight of the moment.
"This is the last one to happen, and it's never going to happen again," he says.
Despite the rescue operation, tragically, five of the belugas have since died, as well as one dolphin.
Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has seen the most deaths. Peekachu, 23, Rain, 20, Orisis, 26, and Caspian, 27, were all transferred from Marineland, while longtime Shedd resident Beethoven, 34, also died after eight Marineland belugas were brought there over the summer.
Necropsies found chronic inflammatory disease in the gastrointestinal systems in Peekachu and Rain.
Foreign objects were also discovered in their stomachs, including feathers, large rocks and flecks that appear to be paint – objects Shedd believes were ingested before they were moved to Chicago.
Osiris's preliminary examination identified chronic liver disease.
Europe's largest aquarium, Oceanogràfic València in Spain, recorded the death of one beluga, Jelly Bean, and one dolphin, Echo. The dolphin arrived with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, it said, and "began having difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems" in the hours before she died.
Experts say it is too early to judge the outcome of the transfers, especially considering the whales were facing euthanasia and had been living in an ageing facility. According to a tally by the Canadian Press, about 20 whales died at Marineland between 2019 and September 2025.
Once the country's most popular amusement park, Marineland closed in 2024 after years of animal welfare concerns and financial woes, and following the death of its longtime owner.
Public attitudes towards keeping whales in captivity have also changed drastically since Marineland opened in 1961. Like Canada, more countries are moving to ban or restrict the practice, including France and Mexico.
Melissa Matlow, a spokeswoman for World Animal Protection Canada, says that worldwide there are about 3,600 captive cetaceans – a group of marine mammals which includes whales, dolphins and porpoises.
But there are few alternatives for whales raised in captivity without the skills to survive in the wild.
Matlow says that leaves a "growing animal welfare crisis on our hands".
Still, her organisation had concerns about the relocation of the Marineland whales.
"If an animal was not healthy enough to withstand the stress of transport, it should not have been transported," she said in a statement.
In early October, Shedd said it knew some of the Marineland belugas "could have substantial, longstanding medical needs".
Assessments before the move "informed our planning but could not reveal every underlying condition or predict how each whale would respond to the transition. The rescue offered a path to continued, specialised care".
They said the remaining rescued belugas show positive signs, including eating well.
World Animal Protection Canada had suggested two alternatives: repurpose Marineland into a hospice-style facility for the remaining captive whales and dolphins, or fast-track development of a proposed seaside sanctuary in Nova Scotia, the Whale Sanctuary Project.
As they can't be released, "the next best thing we could do is provide sanctuary for them, where they can at least live in the ocean, and they can have back their autonomy", says Lori Marino, a neuroscientist behind the Whale Sanctuary Project, which she hopes could eventually house about 12 to 15 whales.
"I look at it as an exit ramp," she adds.
The project was initiated a decade ago, she said, but construction only began in the last two months. Fundraising is continuing and needs an additional C$6m ($4.2m; £3.1m).
But offshore sanctuaries have yet to be proven a successful solution for retiring performing whales.
One offshore facility for belugas is being created in Iceland, but in July organisers determined that more work was needed, and delayed the introduction of two whales until next summer.
"They are kind of more theoretical and aspirational at this point," says Michael Weiss, research director at the Center for Whale Research in Washington state, who adds that they would definitely "improve the welfare of the animals" compared to concrete tanks.
"It's a very old idea," he says, noting that net pens have been used to rehabilitate injured wild whales, or temporarily used while re-introducing captured orcas back into the wild.
Many critics note that Canada's law banning captivity also banned the breeding of whales - but the places where they were sent do not have the same laws, and some are likely to breed them, perpetuating whale captivity.
Jason Jones, senior curator of animal well-being at Georgia Aquarium, says "breeding is a natural part of an animal's life".
"Breeding is part of good animal welfare, and so we want to make sure that they get the opportunity to do so."
Georgia Aquarium recently took in two male Marineland belugas, named Balor, 10, and Zephyr, 7. They joined the four females already in their care.
They arrived "bright, alert and responsive" and quickly began "vocalising to the females on the other side of the gate", he says.
"There was a little bit of a meeting and greeting period, but afterwards they were all kind of swimming together in a big group."
"They were exploring their new habitat, coming over and participating in sessions, eating and interacting with enrichment. So those were all really positive signs from the get-go, and we've just seen progress since then."
Phil Demers, a former Marineland handler, like many people who the BBC spoke to, said the end of Marineland is "bittersweet".
He's grateful to see the facility shut down, and hopes that Canada's ban will inspire changes in other countries. But for now, the ban won't mean the end of captivity for the Marineland whales, only a change of habitat.
He says for people curious about whales, they should join a whale-watching tour, or watch a nature documentary on TV.
"I'd rather see a whale fart in the wild than do a triple backflip in a tank," he says.

With an ad aimed at Trump, this Republican exposed GOP angst about Latino voters
MIAMI – At the heart of Little Havana neighborhood here, is Máximo Gómez Park, also known as Domino Park. Cuban Americans play games of dominos here to escape the pressures of daily life.
But what started as a typical day at the park last week took a turn: Miami police arrested a player in the middle of a game after a dispute with a city worker. It spurred other players to worry about deportations, setting off a broader political debate over whether President Trump or former President Biden was responsible for a higher cost of living.
"It's Biden," said Alejandro Torres, a Republican voter.
"It's Trump," responded Ricardo Carracedo, who plans to vote for Democrats in the midterm elections.
This same divide is playing out across Florida's 27th Congressional District, a Miami-Dade County seat that is more than 70% Latino. It is a warning for Republicans, whose 2024 wins relied heavily on this crucial electorate.
That year, Trump cut Democrats' margin with Latino voters nationally to just three points – down from 25 points four years earlier, according to Pew Research Center. Cuban Americans, the district's largest Latino group, have been reliable Trump supporters. But many of their friends and relatives have been swept up by the administration's deportation agenda. A crack among them could signal broader trouble for Latino support for Republican candidates.
Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Cuban-American Republican in her third term, has been sounding the alarm. Last month, Salazar filmed a television ad in front of the White House warning President Trump that he's "gone too far" on immigration.
"The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," she said.
Trump hit back at Salazar after the ad. On his TruthSocial account, he shared a post in which another user called her a "back stabber."
Salazar told NPR she didn't see the comments as attacks, saying she later spoke to the president.
"I told him, 'You know, what I'm telling you is what my people are feeling,'" she said. "This is Democracy where we tell the boss, 'hey, this is what's happening in my neck of the woods.' And that's exactly what I did."
Salazar's read of the effect of Trump's policies may be right. Polling firm Equis Research found in a recent survey of registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino that if the election for Congress were held today, voters would pick the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a margin of 57 to 31.
At a Salazar campaign event this past Thursday, friends Mirla Loredo and Ramona Tunon were divided on whether they sided with her take or Trump's.
"Him, I tell you," Loredo said in Spanish.
"I like her position," Tunon said.
Salazar has pushed against aggressive immigration policies in the past. For several years, she has proposed legislation she called the Dignity Act to block deportations of immigrants considered pillars of their community – such as hospitality, construction and farm workers.
Still, Carracedo, the Democratic voter from Domino Park, said he'll vote a straight blue ticket. He said Salazar's recent push against Trump's aggressive deportations is too little, too late.
"I'm not going to vote for her, because at the last hour she's defending Hispanics. But the entire time she supported Trump and the money Trump wanted for ICE," or Immigration and Customs Enforcement, he said in his native Spanish.
Trump, he said, reminds him of the communist leaders he left behind in Cuba.
In the past, Republicans' messaging on socialism had a powerful impact on this district. But now that message has lost some of its potency, eclipsed by worries about a higher cost of living and deportations.
Eduardo Gamarra, a politics professor at Florida International University, says the local economy's malaise has eclipsed all other issues.
"It's probably the number one thing. And that cuts across all of the electorate," he said.
He said the second top issue is deportations, which have devastated some Miami businesses that have lost workers and customers.
An opening for Democrats
Salazar's Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, is a former broadcast journalist with Cuban roots like Salazar. He says he wants to revamp the immigration judge system, and restore federal food assistance after cuts that have hurt constituents.
Still, he concedes his party has a lot of ground to make up after largely walking away from Florida.
"One of the biggest mistakes that Democrats have made in Florida is to think that Florida is unwinnable. But I beg to differ."
Polls in the district have shifted more towards Democrats' direction in recent weeks, but Republicans are still favored. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated the race "lean Republican."
Gamarra, the politics professor, says the GOP will need to rely on its political infrastructure to pull out a win
"They're not going to win on the issues ... They're going to win on turnout … the enthusiasm is on the Democrat side. But Republicans have a machinery."

Pandemic preparedness, support for Ukraine, and the fight against superbugs topped the agenda Tuesday as WHO and UK health leaders met in London to discuss their shared global health priorities.
In their first one-on-one meeting, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and UK Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Steve Barclay MP spoke at length about their shared commitment to delivering a pandemic instrument – a new international agreement being negotiated by WHO Member States – to strengthen global collaboration to help protect the world from another pandemic.
Mr Barclay outlined the UK government’s priorities for a pandemic instrument, which include faster and more efficient data sharing between WHO Member States; quicker, more equitable access to affordable vaccines, tests and treatments; and stronger collaboration on scientific research and development.
“The World Health Organization has reached a significant milestone this year in the marking of its 75th anniversary, and I’m proud of the UK’s longstanding relationship with WHO to improve public health,” Mr Barclay said. “The UK is playing a leading role in tackling some of the world’s greatest health threats, including antimicrobial resistance for which we recently announced £39 million for research into new drugs to combat infections.”
In 2022 and in the previous biennium, the UK was the largest contributor to WHO’s Core Voluntary Contributions Account. The account provides flexible funds that WHO can use and allocate as needed within its approved programme budgets. 
Earlier in the day, Dr Tedros joined International Development Minister Andrew Mitchell and Health Minister Will Quince for the annual UK-WHO Strategic Dialogue to discuss how to tackle global health challenges together and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. 
They spoke about effectively responding to health emergencies, preventing the next pandemic and confronting threats to health posed by climate change.
Ministers Mitchell and Quince emphasized the importance of building strong health systems in countries and protecting the health and rights of women and girls. Ministers also cited the importance of reform to strengthen WHO as an organization, expressing support for WHO’s extensive efforts to prevent and respond to sexual misconduct.  
“WHO highly values its strong and impactful collaboration with the UK Government to promote and protect the health of people worldwide,” Dr Tedros said as the meetings concluded. “Today’s strategic dialogue with Ministers Mitchell and Quince, and my productive discussions with Secretary of State Barclay, demonstrated the UK’s commitment to global public health, its support of the World Health Organization, and the great potential and impact of our partnership. I look forward to continuing our joint work to make the world healthier and safer on many fronts, from combatting antimicrobial resistance to supporting the UK and countries around the world to develop a generational accord to prevent and respond to future pandemics.”

Could this 93-year-old sprinter's muscles hold clues to healthy aging? Scientists think so
Emma Mazzenga got back into running in her 50s. Forty years later, she's as fit as when she started
At 93, Emma Maria Mazzenga still gets the jitters before a race.
"On race day, I'm very tense," she said. "People ask to interview me, and I tell them: Don't come near me until I've run."
Over the last four decades, Mazzenga has won 11 world titles, 31 European championships and 115 Italian races. She currently holds the 200-metre world record in the women's over-90 category: 50.33 seconds, set in 2024, when she was 91.
Now she is giving scientists a rare look at just how much of the physical decline we associate with aging may not actually be inevitable.
Mazzenga ran as a university student in Padua, in northern Italy. She then stopped for three decades while she taught high school biology and raised two children, largely on her own after her husband died.
In 1986, when she was 53, the president of her old university running club rounded up former athletes for the growing field of masters competitions, for those over age 35.
"One by one, my friends quit," she said. "I kept going."
In this 2024 file photo, a then-90-year-old Mazzenga shows her membership card for the Italian Athletics Federation, ahead of a race in San Biagio di Callalta, Italy. It shows her birthdate: Aug. 1, 1933. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)
She still trains three times a week, mostly short repeats of 50 to 200 metres. Slow jogging bores her.
What drives her isn't winning, Mazzenga said. In Italy, she has no rivals in her age category. "I come first because I have to. I'm the only one," she said. "I can't get any emotion out of that."
So she races the clock instead. "If I win with a mediocre time, it gives me no satisfaction."
Her proudest moment is still her first world title, the 400-metre W75 race at the World Masters Athletics Championships in Sacramento, Calif., won in 2011.
"There were just a handful of us Italians. I found myself alone on the podium," Mazzenga recalled.
From VO2 to muscle fibres
But eventually, her performances drew a different audience: Scientists.
Two years ago, Antonio La Torre, a scientist at the University of Milan and technical director of Italy’s athletic federation, tipped off two researchers who were studying how the body ages.
"We were told there was this woman who was able to run 200 metres in a very short time," said Martino Franchi, an associate professor of human physiology at the University of Padua. "But it was her age that we were really interested in."
Mazzegna became the most extreme case in a broader, two-year project called Trajector-Age, which tracked how muscles, nerves, heart and metabolism change in people over 50 to see whether exercise can slow decline.
Researchers from several Italian universities and the University of Wisconsin-Madison put Mazzenga through a gruelling cycling test and took biopsies from her thigh.
Mazzenga, then 90, competes in the 100-metre W90 category race in San Biagio di Callalta, Italy, on May 4, 2024. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)
Franchi says Mazzenga's maximal oxygen consumption is comparable to that of someone in their 50s. Also known as a VO2 max, it represents the greatest amount of oxygen a body can take in and use — a key measure of cardiovascular fitness.
"And she's 90," he said. "This is fantastic."
The bigger surprise was inside her muscles, said Franchi. Mazzenga has lost some of the fast-twitch fibres used for explosive movement, although fewer than expected. But her slow-twitch fibres — the ones that resist fatigue — are extraordinary.
"They are as big as a girl in her 20s," he said. "That's unique."
Martino Franchi gestures toward a screen showing a microscopic view of muscle fibres at his lab at the University of Padua, in Italy. (CBC)
Researchers think those unusually large fibres may help her hold her pace and compensate, at least partly, for the fast fibres lost with age.
Aging has happened, Franchi said, "but in a slower way." And so many years of training means that her body runs almost on auto-pilot when her feet hit the track.
The research was published earlier this year as two cases in the Journal of Applied Physiology, with a rendition of a Mazzenga landing on the cover. Lead scientist Marta Colosio received an award for the work at the American Physiology summit.
The team is now analyzing a second round of biopsies, along with genetic and molecular data, trying to tease apart what Mazzenga inherited versus what decades of training may have preserved.
Mazzenga walks with Martino Franchi, one of the researchers who has studied the 93-year-old's muscles and athletic performance to glean new insights into human aging. (CBC)
'A bit of a rarity'
Mazzenga has her own theory. "I always say that if I had been sitting on the sofa, I would have aged differently."
With the running came fame — eventually. "No one paid much attention to me in my 80s, but after 90, yes," she jokes. "They look at me as a bit of a rarity."
She now speaks regularly at public events, most recently at la Repubblica's Festival di Salute, an annual health festival that draws Nobel laureates, scientists and sports champions.
As friends die and family members get busy with their own lives, Mazzenga says those connections — along with her masters teammates — matter almost as much as the training.
Mazzenga shows off her first pair of track shoes, when she first took to racing in her early 50s, at her home in Padua, Italy. (Megan Williams/CBC)
Franchi has his own reason for pushing exercise.
During the COVID-19 lockdowns, he noticed his father, then in his 70s, struggling to get up from the sofa. So Franchi printed out graphs linking inactivity to mortality.
"I said, 'Dad, I study sarcopenia. This is it,'" said Franchi, referring to the loss of muscle mass, strength and function with age. "He got scared, so he went back to the gym."
Today, Franchi's father can pull off full lunges and hikes several times a week.

- Alberta woman, 61, breaks her own world record by planking for 5 hours
Franchi likes to tell the story to his students, telling them that physical activity is important — but be sure to keep doing it when you're older.
Asked what she'd tell someone 80, or even 90, thinking about taking up a sport, Mazzenga laughs. "You'd want to start a little earlier."
For those still able, she says, see a doctor, find a coach and match your body to the effort.
She herself has no plans to slow down. At a recent club final, she ran faster than she had two years earlier. "I was very pleased."
Mazzenga, centre, is seen in a photo with two fellow racers when she won the European Championship in 1998. (Megan Williams/CBC)

Firefighters have rescued a teenager from the "maze" of stormwater drains under Brisbane.

Outstanding quality. Great noise control at lower volumes. Autofocus improvements are noticeable, if short of life-changing.
TIRED
The massive case desperately needs a redesign. Still very expensive. Poor streaming quality.
This fall, hearing-aid manufacturers have been busily rolling out new and improved devices en masse, including Jabra, a leading maker of direct-to-consumer, over-the-counter devices. The brand has replaced its entire product lineup with all-new gear, swiftly retiring the Jabra Enhance Select 700, 500, 300, and 50R, all of which were only a year or two old. Three new models replace them: Enhance Select M3, M2, and M1. Each of the M-series hearing aids looks and works about the same as the models from last year and the year before that. Most of the updates here happen under the hood—but even those changes are hardly extreme, as I learned with the M3 pair I tested.
Historically, a more expensive device has meant a slightly smaller chassis—not so with Jabra's new hearing aids. Each of the three new models weighs the same: 2.12 grams, give or take a few hundredths of a gram, depending on the ear tip you choose. While the M2 and M1 share an identical form factor, the M3 is a bit squatter in design, measuring a few millimeters shorter than its siblings. Even so, all three are virtually indistinguishable unless you look at the fine print. That is, unless you select the red model; it's an M3 giveaway, as the M1 and M2 aren't available in that color.
Jabra M1 on left, M3 on right
Photograph: Christopher Null
Taking the traditional form of behind-the-ear teardrops, the M3 aids feature a single button on the back. Various presses and holds let you use these buttons for power, volume adjustments, and environmental mode changes that work to varying degrees of usefulness. Even so, the device is among the best available right now.
Within Earshot
Photograph: Christopher Null
Jabra calls its audio enhancement system SoundScape, which launched last year and claims to reduce noise and improve overall speech clarity. SoundScape features are variably available across the three devices in the M line, and two new capabilities are exclusive to the M3. These include a revamped autofocus tool that “locks onto” speech in complex, noisy environments, like restaurants, which I found to be moderately effective. I experienced clean dialog, even when a conversation partner walked fully around me in a circle.
INSERT GROUP ASSET: IMG_3735 and IMG_3734
ScreenshotSoundScape app via Christopher Null
ScreenshotSoundScape app via Christopher Null
The other new SoundScape feature for the M3 is an advanced adaptive listening mode that's responsive to a given environment (whether a restaurant, outdoors, or several other options) in real time to optimize noise reduction. The environmental modes weren’t very useful; keeping the hearing aids in “all around” mode, then tweaking levels manually (especially noise reduction) was the best way to improve the hearing experience.
I tested the M3 hearing aids in a variety of settings and am pleased to report that they work just as well as previous Jabra generations. Clarity in quiet environments (like having a one-on-one conversation or watching television) was just about perfect. Keeping the volume at 30 percent maximized hearing improvement while minimizing hiss, which grows geometrically louder with each upward tick of volume level.
Bluetooth streaming quality has never been Jabra’s strong suit, and while these new devices support Auracast—which lets various audio sources broadcast directly to the hearing aid—I don't expect I’d use any of the streaming modes much. Overall streaming audio quality on the M3 offers a slight improvement from previous generations, but music and movie audio are both too washed out at any level below the highest volume. And any amount of ambient noise still kills the experience completely.
Programming on Demand
Photograph: Christopher Null
The app and other features in the new lineup remain remarkably similar to previous Jabra models. Jabra has a history of offering great customer service: All purchases include three years of access to on-staff audiologists who can make tuning adjustments live over video chat and train new users on their hearing aids. Jabra’s built-in self-test system also remains top-notch, allowing you to create an audiogram from scratch in just a few minutes.
Its massive case unfortunately hasn’t changed, providing three recharges of your spent hearing aids before it also needs to be plugged in. A fully charged pair of hearing aids still lasts for 24 hours, as specified. In fact, I got closer to 26 hours in my testing before I needed to power up.
Notably, pricing also remains consistent, with the M3 starting at $1,995—the same launch price as the Jabra 700 last year. If history is any guide, a few months of patience are likely to reward you with a $200 price cut, and Jabra coupons are available fairly regularly. It's still a big ask for a nonprescription product. But to be fair, you’d likely pay twice as much for a prescription aid that can match the quality of these latest M3s.
My bottom-line recommendation? If you can afford the two grand for the Jabra M3 hearing aids, you'll get the most advanced over-the-counter devices available. That said, those with more modest means will do nearly as well with the $1,695 M2 or $1,195 M1 hearing aids—or one of the even more affordable options featured in my Best Hearing Aids buying guide.
