Have you ever taken months off training – maybe due to an injury, a new baby or crushing work deadlines – and come back convinced you were starting from zero?
Research from our team has some good news: At the cellular level, you probably weren’t.
We found that muscle and liver cells store memories fromevery training session in ways that may help improve endurance, control blood sugar levels and even slow weight regain after inactivity.
Use it or lose it? Maybe not
For most of the past century, long before fad diets and fancy workout trends took off, exercise was considered one of the most effective lifestyle changes to lower the risk of heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, several cancers and early death for people of all ages. But people typically understood exercise as something whose beneficial effects fade away over time: You use it or lose it.
When you stop training, your maximum oxygen uptake, muscle gains and insulin sensitivity drift back to where they started, often within weeks. Physical activity guidelines are built on this fact, which is why they emphasise consistency above all else.
Consistency, however, is a luxury that roughly 3 in 4 American adults aren’t able to enjoy. People can experience injuries, illness, pregnancy or jobs that limit their time for or ability to exercise. If adaptation really resets, every time you step into the gym would be as if you’ve never been there before. But that scenario doesn’t match what coaches and returning athletes typically describe: In practice, people who have trained before can get fit again faster than those who haven’t undergone similar training.
In recent years, however, scientists have started challenging the concept of “use it or lose it.” New research hints that your cells might keep a record of your training history so all of your gains are not completely lost.
More than muscle
We areexercise physiologists who study how cells remember exercise. Our lab and others have shown that the body is able to store a form of exercise memory across different organs.
To study how this exercise memory works, our team of researchers use an ON-OFF-ON exercise training protocol in mice, which involves an initial four- to eight-week training period, followed by detraining – a period of no exercise – and a second training bout. This method allows us to examine how cells form a memory of exercise, maintain a record of exercise through detraining, and recall memories of prior training when exposed again to exercise.
Using this strategy, our team found that skeletal muscle memory accelerates muscle growth. Compared to mice with no training history, mice who retrained grew bigger muscles, and the individual muscle fibers inside those muscles grew too. Larger muscle fibers meant that the working cells were themselves getting bigger, rather than the surrounding tissue.
Looking more closely at these muscle cells, we found that retrained muscle is better at matching energy production to demand – meaning, the muscles were better at drawing from energy stores when it’s needed most – and this ability persists without further exercise. This memory held even when the mice ate a high-fat diet, suggesting that prior training can still offer benefits even when diet is working against those gains.
Muscle isn’t the only body part that learns from exercise. Working muscle needs fuel, and the liver supplies it during and after training sessions.
My colleagues and I found that liver cells also store exercise memory and uses it to feed muscle more efficiently. In both mice and people who trained, stopped, then trained again, their livers released higher levels of a family of enzymes called carboxylesterases. These enzymes chop up lipids circulating in the blood, delivering fat in a form that muscle can take up and burn as it grows.
A record that outlives you
Recorded cellular memories of exercise may even be passed down to future generations.
In mice, we found that three to four weeks of maternal and paternal endurance exercise can have a lasting effect on their offspring. Compared to offspring born to sedentary parents, parental exercise granted protection against poor blood sugar levels and excess weight gain for an entire year after birth.
Researchers have hypothesized numerous ways that prenatal exercise may affect offspring. For example, maternal exercise might allow offspring to spend more time developing in the womb or lead parents to producer higher quality milk.
But there remains much to be discovered on how parents influence the health of their children and whether their lifestyle could provide a fitness advantage across generations.
Every cell remembers
Biology has traditionally granted memory to a short list of cells. Neurons store memory in the connections between them. Immune cells store memory so they can recognize pathogens faster and more strongly the next time they encounter them.
Researchers previously considered all other cells to be memoryless; a cell responds to a signal, then returns to baseline without keeping a record of that interaction. But that assumption is now coming apart.
Skin stem cells can keep a record of inflammation, allowing them to heal a new wound faster months later. Human fat cells keep a record of obesity that persists even after substantial weight loss, which may account for why you gain weight faster when switching back to a high-calorie diet – the so-called yo-yo effect.
We propose that every cell in the body remembers exercise, regardless of how little or how much someone trains. The question is how long these records are stored and whether researchers could prolong or expand each cell’s storage capacity. Better understanding of how cells learn and remember exercise, where they store memories and how those memories are preserved could help improve exercise guidelines for those who cannot exercise for prolonged or consistent periods of time.
To be clear, none of these findings are evidence for skipping the gym; nothing in our data suggests the effects of past training can substitute for present training. But there is hope that the work you put into getting in shape isn’t completely lost over time.
Somewhere, deep in your cells, there is a record waiting to be replayed the next time you lace up your running shoes, pick up a pair of dumbbells or want to fulfill a New Year’s resolution.
Diego Hernandez-Saavedra, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Yi-Heng (Hank) Huang, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

France shaken by fiery street protests uniting students, workers and 'yellow vests'
What began over under-funded high schools has converged with a fierce anti-austerity movement
France is about to wake up to an uneasy morning after.
On Saturday, the country saw massive — and unusually violent — cross-generational protests that brought together high schoolers, trade unions and "yellow vest" demonstrators, all choking the streets of Paris, Lille and other French cities.
While many aspects of this day of protests were peaceful, there were also fierce confrontations between brick-throwing protesters dressed in black and police armed with water cannons and tear gas.
The confrontations left parts of Paris looking like a war zone.
One minister estimated 400 people had been arrested, with 110,000 demonstrators in Paris alone. French TV aired video of businesses and retail stores that had been looted and the city's mayor said entire streets had been vandalized.
While the tear gas and smoke from burning vehicles cleared relatively quickly, the violence will no doubt leave a deep scar on the city.
Saturday's events also speak to a deeper, more ideological cleavage over values, spending priorities and crucially, whether the French state should protect its economic standing, or its most vulnerable first.
'Turning point'
What began weeks ago as high schoolers demanding repaired classroom boilers has transformed into an existential battle over the very definition of the French Republic.
"France is coming to a major turning point," Bally Bagayoko, the left-wing mayor of the working-class Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, told CBC News.
"Today, unfortunately, this France is in sadness. It is unable to provide concrete answers to the legitimate demands of high schoolers ... and the only concrete answer it can provide is a heavy handed police response.”
Over the last three weeks of the teenagers' protest, supporters have harshly criticized police tactics. One young person lost part of an arm during an especially violent confrontation and there were reports Saturday in Paris of other people enduring similar injuries.
A view of the momument in La Place de la République after police fired tear gas at protesters to try to disperse the crowd. (Chris Brown/CBC News)
The involvement of the yellow vest movement amplifies the stakes for France's government. Initially formed by disillusionsed working class voters a decade ago to battle high fuel prices, the movement petered out during COVID lockdown. Its reconstitution now could help potentially transform the student's school-focussed protests into a cause with much longer staying power.
In the aftermath of Saturday's violence, France's key political leaders were unanimous in their condemnation of the violence on the streets, and attempted to separate the instigators from those who were there peacefully.
"We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who seek only to bring down our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so," posted French President Emmanuel Macron.
The country's centrist Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu took a similar approach.
"Today, ultra-left groups have orchestrated violence in several French cities; delinquents have joined in to pillage and destroy," he wrote.
France's far-right party, the Rassemblement National (RN), rejected the protesters and their message, and instead praised the conduct of the security forces.
Mayor Bally Bagayoko represents the Paris subburb of Saint-Denis. He put himself between protesters and police at a student demonstration earlier this month. (Adrian Di Virgilio/CBC News)
Toxic convergence
On the surface, the current crisis looks like a familiar French budget dispute.
But on the ground, the view from inside the student movement reveals a toxic convergence of fiscal collapse, class warfare, systemic racism and a worrying escalation of state force.
In the days leading up to this weekend's mass protests, CBC News went inside the student movement in the northern city of Lille to better understand the issues driving it.
Many of the organizers are very young — some just 14 years old. CBC News required their parents' permission to speak to them.
At the fences of Lycée Faidherbe, amidst the thick black smoke of smouldering plastic bins that some students had set ablaze, the teenagers' demands sounded immediate and concrete.
"We hope the school will be closed," Lille organizer Soan Rauch, 16, told CBC News, standing near the barricades.
Soan Rauch, 16, has taken a lead role organizing high schoolers in the city of Lille, France. (Jason Ho/CBC News)
When asked why shutting down their own education is a victory, his fellow classmate, 15-year-old James Caron, didn't hesitate.
"It helps put pressure on the government," Caron said. "Because if everything is burning, the government can't ignore us."
While conservative critics have attempted to dismiss the movement as the political manipulation of minors by populist left-wing politicians, independent analysts say the teenagers' grievances are grounded in real, physical decline.
"Actually, they do understand what they're doing, and they're not manipulated," Blanche Leridon, a political analyst with the Paris-based think-tank Institut Montaigne, told CBC News.
"There is a huge topic about the deterioration of the condition of education, and deterioration of their buildings. [Teachers] are missing and it's really hard for them to learn in good conditions."
Rauch took CBC News to Lycée Fénelon, his shuttered school, pointing out student-painted banners demanding "respect" written in multiple languages.
Beyond the political slogans, he said that the daily reality inside French public classrooms has become untenable.
"We ask for classrooms that are much less crowded — we are 35 students per class," said Rauch. "More particularly, we have problems with hallways and thermal boilers. It means that it's very hot in summer and very, very cold in winter."
French riot police stand in position amid clashes with protesters during a demonstration at La Place de la République in Paris. (Abdul Saboor/Reuters)
As the student disruptions have rippled across the nation, the Macron government attempted to quell the anger by offering a temporary package consisting of thousands of new substitute teachers. The student unions swiftly dismissed the proposal, calling it an empty gesture.
The race factor
Mayor Bagayoko argues that this structural neglect is concentrated heavily in diverse, working-class communities plagued by high unemployment, like Saint-Denis, which sits at a staggering 35 per cent jobless rate.
"When you grow up in the working-class neighbourhoods, you are treated less well than in the beautiful Parisian neighbourhoods," said Bagayoko.
"All the children of France must be treated equally."
The Macron administration continues to claim its hands are tied, pointing to a crushing sovereign debt crisis and severe warnings from global credit rating agencies.
But inside the student strategy meetings that CBC News sat in on, that economic narrative is rejected as a corporate myth.
"I don't think the government should reduce its social spending, but they should rather try to increase [it]," argued 14-year-old Lille student Bastien Duprez. "And probably decrease budgets to, for example, budgets to the army and, for instance, subsidies to big corporations.”
"We know that a lot of money from the government goes to rich people," added Alice Note, 17. "So we also think that the money that the rich people have will go to us, to education."
Leridon, the French political analyst, sees France as a country stuck in an economic vice.
"We are really aware of the specific difficulties we have regarding our debt or deficits ... but [people] are not prepared to make any sacrifices. They don't want higher taxes, they don't want to work longer," she said.
Masked protesters walk past burning barricades amid clashes in Paris. (Jack Taylor/Reuters)
Clashing priorities
This clash of priorities has translated into an exceptionally aggressive law-and-order response.
Prior to the weekend, more than 8,000 high school students had been arrested nationwide, the vast majority of them minors. Mayor Bagayoko claims hospital rooms continue to fill up with teenagers suffering from broken jaws, fractured limbs, and severe chemical gas inhalation.
The protest line violence became so intense that on Oct. 6 in Paris, he physically placed his own body between charging riot police and fleeing high schoolers during a protest at Place de la Nation.
"I made the choice to intervene by trying as much as possible to protect the high schoolers first, because I remember that they were minors," Bagayoko said.
The video of his intervention flashed around the country, transforming him into a central figure in the ongoing crisis.
France is less than six months away from a pivotal presidential election.
With the centrist government entirely paralyzed and unable to pass a budget through a deeply fractured Parliament, the political void is rapidly being filled by the far right.
Marine Le Pen, who will be the Rassemblement National's candidate in the upcoming presidential election this spring, appears to be in a commanding position. She has called for strengthened anti-riot legislation and largely ignored the issues at the centre of the student's complaints, instead focusing on the need to restore order on the streets.
For the teenagers holding the barricades, a right-wing takeover isn't just a political shift, it's a direct threat to their safety.
"We're afraid. We have a lot of fear," Rauch admitted. "We don't know what's going to happen tomorrow.

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
- Published
"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.
Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.
The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.
Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.
At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”
Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.
When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.
Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.
“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.
The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.
In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

Sidewalk sleepers: They have nowhere else to stay while a loved one is in the hospital
DELHI, India — At 2 a.m. on the sidewalk outside one of Delhi's best-known public hospitals, Shabana Kumar gently wakes her husband. They sleep in shifts of about an hour at a time because their 6-year-old son is a patient in the oncology ward, being treated for leukemia, a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. They are afraid that if they are both asleep, an urgent call could come about their son's condition and they might miss it.
The Kumar family lives more than 600 miles from Delhi in the state of Bihar. Arun, 32, works as a farmer. Shabana, 30, is a homemaker caring for their only son.
They made the trip to Delhi because they could not afford the cost of their child's cancer treatment in Bihar. The All India Institute of Medical Sciences, or AIIMS, subsidizes expenses for families in need.
But for many families, there is one challenge they must bear on their own — finding a place to live in Delhi during the days, weeks, even months of treatment. Like the Kumars, families who can't afford to rent lodging often set up a temporary dwelling on the sidewalk.
On a night in August, dozens of families were sleeping on blankets or sheets spread directly on the sidewalk. Some tie mosquito nets to railings to protect themselves and their kids. They keep their bags and other belongings beside them as they sleep.
During the day, families move between the sidewalk and the hospital for appointments, tests, medicines and consultations. They carry their most important belongings with them while leaving less valuable items at their sleeping spot. One family member often stays behind to keep an eye on their things.
Like the family from Bihar, people who've accompanied a patient may sleep outside while the patient is housed in the hospital. In other cases, the person receiving care is seen during the day but does not have a bed, so they sleep on the sidewalk as well.
At night, the sidewalk dwellers return to the pavement, where a small ecosystem has grown around the families. Women cook rice over makeshift brick stoves. Volunteers distribute food. Nearby shops sell medicines and other necessities. Nearby tea stalls not only serve beverages but let families charge their phones.
Once strangers, they exchange information about doctors, tests and where to find a free meal or, when none is available, an affordable one they can pay for.
Vishnu Singh, 38, runs a tea stall outside AIIMS.
"I see poor people sleeping here every day, so many that I cannot even count them," he said.
At AIIMS and Safdarjung Hospital, which is associated with Vardhman Mahavir Medical College, we interviewed families who had traveled from across India, often hundreds of miles from home, to seek medical care. The two hospitals stand opposite each other, treating patients with illnesses ranging from cancer and heart conditions to intestinal disorders and other serious ailments.
Some families had been there for a week, others for a month or longer. For many, returning home between hospital visits was impractical, so patients and the relatives accompanying them stayed in Delhi for the duration of their care.
The families we spoke with described their experiences spending days or weeks in Delhi while navigating appointments, tests, consultations and treatment.
When treatment means living outside
It is a startling contrast — a hospital that provides critical care, that, according to its annual report, gives subsidies to thousands of poor families for treatment — and that is ringed by folks who traveled great distances to find care for a loved one and who cannot afford a place to stay.
NPR reached out to the hospital by email to ask about the issue of accommodations and the community of sidewalk dwellers. The hospital did not respond.
AIIMS' website notes that its Medical Social Service Unit provides financial assistance for medical treatment and travel costs for some patients coming from outside Delhi. It also states that the unit helps arrange accommodation for out-of-town patients and their family members and caregivers at dharamshalas, traditional charitable lodging facilities affiliated with AIIMS, or other low-cost accommodation.
The website does not say whether AIIMS pays for those accommodations or provides financial assistance specifically for the lodging costs. Shalini Yadav is one of the patients who sleeps on the sidewalk with her parents.
Yadav is a second-year college student from Piprat village in Tikamgarh district, Madhya Pradesh, in central India. She had been preparing for the state civil service examination. Her plan was to become a government officer.
Now she is spending her days reading Gunahon Ka Devta (The God of Sins), a famous 1949 Hindi tragic romance novel written by Dharamvir Bharati, on the pavement outside AIIMS, waiting to find out when her treatment will begin and when she can go home.
Yadav says she has been dealing with an intestinal illness for five or six years and has already undergone two operations. Her family had sought treatment elsewhere before relatives and neighbors advised them to travel to Delhi in search of better treatment at AIIMS — a trip of roughly 370 miles. "We thought AIIMS was the best hospital in India," she said. The cost of staying in Delhi was also a burden: Her family could not afford a room and had already spent thousands of rupees on travel and other expenses.
When we interviewed her on Aug. 3, she had been there for about three weeks with her parents, Surendra Singh Yadav, 47, a farmer, and Kalpana Yadav, 45.
"We thought the facilities would be good, the doctors would be good, and everything would happen quickly. We never imagined that we would have to sleep on the road," she said.
For her, the pavement is not just uncomfortable, it is also frightening. During the day, she says, she can manage. At night, she worries about the people around her.
"There are all kinds of people here," she says. "Some are good, but some drink or use drugs. There is shouting and fighting. As a girl, I feel very uncomfortable here at night."
But the family has little choice. They cannot afford a room in Delhi, she says. "We have decided that we have to sleep on the road because there is no other option."
During the day, Yadav goes into the hospital for appointments, tests and checkups, then returns to the pavement while waiting for the next step in her treatment. Everything is on hold — her college education, her hopes of qualifying for a government job, her father's farming work.
"It feels like we are being forced to live like this," she says.
"I just pray that I can meet a doctor"
Lakhi Bai, 62, from Ramnagar in Maihar district, Madhya Pradesh, in central India, about 500 miles away, came to Delhi seeking treatment for diabetes and a condition that she says causes numbness and a loss of sensation in parts of her body.
She says she could sometimes sustain an injury without feeling pain. When we met her, she had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about 20 days. During that time, she says, she had been going to different doctors and departments for consultations and tests but had not yet received a treatment plan.
Bai is a farmer and describes herself as a homemaker. She said she has three sons but is no longer in contact with them. She came to Delhi alone.
"I cannot afford to bring someone with me," she says. "If I bring someone, I have to pay for their food and accommodation, too."
It's been a difficult period. "Sometimes I don't even get food," she says. "I sleep with an empty stomach."
Sleeping outside is also stressful. The heat is hard to endure, she said, as is rainwater.
"When it rains, water comes here," she said. "There is nowhere to go."
AIIMS did not respond to requests for comment about her account or the experiences described by other families interviewed for this story.
Bai did not know how much longer she would have to remain in Delhi. "I have no place to stay," she says. "I just pray that I can get the treatment I need and something can be done."
A month outside awaiting a child's heart treatment
In August, Balraam Singh, 35, a brick-kiln worker from Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about a month with his wife and their 7-year-old son, Munna Singh.
Munna has a heart condition that his father describes as a "hole in the heart."
They had come from about 50 miles away seeking further medical evaluation and treatment at Safdarjung Hospital.
"We came with a lot of hope that we would find a doctor and my son would be treated," he says. "But now it feels like we may have to go back without knowing what will happen next.
For Singh, who can earn $5 to $7 a day at the kiln where he works, staying in Delhi means not only a loss of income but the need to spend money on food and other daily needs.
Six months of saving for another hospital visit
Gulshan Bano, 38, had come to Delhi from Bihar with her 60-year-old mother, Asma Khatoon, and her 6-year-old daughter, Fiza. They had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about a week when we met them in August.
Bano says her mother has had a heart condition for several years and was receiving treatment in Bihar. Her mother had undergone checkups and tests there, but the family felt she needed further evaluation and care.
Relatives also advised them to seek treatment in Delhi, and the family decided to travel for further consultations and tests.
Bano said doctors have told them that her mother has a heart problem and have prescribed medication rather than recommending surgery.
The family returns to Delhi for checkups about every six months. To pay for the trips, Bano works in domestic jobs in Bihar.
"I work for months and save whatever I can, and then I come here," she says. "Whatever little money remains has to be used here."
Bano said her husband does not contribute to her mother's medical expenses and she has little choice but to keep making the journey to Delhi.
A visit can last about a month, Bano said, as the family waits for scheduled consultations, tests and follow-up care. Because they cannot afford other accommodation, they sleep outside the hospital between appointments and tests rather than return home and make another journey to Delhi.
"Where should I go?" she said. "I have to come here because my mother needs treatment."
For families like Bano's, charities and volunteers can provide some of the practical support they need while they wait outside the hospitals.
Rajiv Ranjan, who works with the Delhi-based Donate A Meal Trust, said his organization regularly helps patients and their attendants staying outside AIIMS and Safdarjung Hospital by distributing food, clothes and rations.
He said the organization has seen many families remain outside the hospitals while seeking treatment or caring for relatives inside.
"We come here for people who sleep outside while they or their family members are receiving treatment inside the hospital," he says. "They have nowhere else to stay, so we try to help with whatever we can." The group distributes about 100 meals a day, Ranjan says.
Food, however, is only one of the needs.
"People need shade from the sun, and during the rainy season they need somewhere to stay dry," Ranjan said. "Some of them take shelter under the Delhi Metro, the city's rapid-transit rail system, when it rains."
For Shalini Yadav, the 20-year-old college student from Madhya Pradesh who traveled to Delhi for treatment, the food distributions and other help have become part of life outside the hospital. She said people arrive to help in whatever way they can, but the assistance does not reach everyone.
"Sometimes we get food. When we don't, we buy it nearby. But there are many people here who don't get anything to eat."
For families, treatment means returning to Delhi again and again
Suhana Bano, 47, from Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh, has been bringing her 18-year-old son, Mohammad Sameer, to Delhi for treatment for about two years.
Sameer has irritable bowel syndrome. He was in seventh grade when this digestive ailment forced him to leave school. The family first sought treatment at several hospitals in Bareilly, about 155 miles from Delhi, before traveling to Safdarjung Hospital.
Suhana Bano said the family turned to Delhi after seeking treatment locally, hoping to find the specialized care Sameer needed.
The family travels to Delhi whenever Sameer is due for a consultation or tests. Typically, they stay one to two months, Bano says. While in Delhi, the family sleeps outside Safdarjung because they cannot afford a room.
Aamar Singh, 60, a farmer from Hathras, Uttar Pradesh, had been sleeping outside AIIMS for about a week when we met him in April.
His 35-year-old daughter, Neelam, was admitted to the AIIMS intensive care unit with a respiratory problem, he said. His 40-year-old sister, Rashima, stayed outside with him. At night, they sleep alongside stray dogs that also gather on the pavement.
Singh does not know how long his daughter will remain in the ICU after being admitted for treatment and therefore does not know how long he will have to remain outside.
Food is not always available, he said, and some days they go hungry.
"Sometimes you eat, sometimes you don't," he said. "My daughter is inside, so I have to stay here. What else can I do? This is our situation."
So Aamar Singh waits on the pavement for news about his daughter until he can take her home.

US officials visit Palestinian village after settler attacks on diplomats
UN bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law, but Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
TAYBEH, West Bank/JERUSALEM: US diplomats visited a Christian Palestinian village in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Sunday (Oct 18) following attacks by militant Israeli settlers on European diplomats and an American photojournalist in the previous two days.
Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labor, Brian Burch, US ambassador to the Holy See, and a number of other diplomats visited the Latin Convent church and were expected to meet with members of the Christian community in Taybeh.
Belgian, French and Polish diplomats, along with a French mayor and Palestinian civilians, had been attacked near Taybeh on Saturday by masked Israeli settlers.
The previous day, Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was taken to hospital after being assaulted while covering a Palestinian olive harvest near another West Bank village.
The diplomats' visit coincided with US President Donald Trump endorsing his ally, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, for Israel's parliamentary election on Oct 27.
Meanwhile, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee attended a settler conference in the West Bank on Sunday.
Huckabee, an evangelical Christian and longtime supporter of Israel, earlier wrote on X calling for "those who attacked" the Washington Post photojournalist, a US citizen, to be jailed.
NETANYAHU CIRCUMSPECT ON SETTLER VIOLENCE
Trump has expressed his opposition to Israeli annexation of the West Bank, but his administration has put little pressure on Netanyahu's right-wing, pro-settler government to change its policy.
UN bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law, but Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
While Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the Israeli military both blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats, Netanyahu, whose coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, has been more circumspect.
He has said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination" with the Israeli military, and that the facts of the attack on Levine are "unclear".
France urged Israeli authorities to arrest Saturday's attackers and to end criminal violence in the West Bank, but by Sunday there was no announcement from Israeli authorities of any arrests in either of the two latest incidents.
The West Bank is home to some 500,000 settlers and at least 3 million Palestinians.
Settler attacks on the Palestinians are surging, with at least 170 since Sep 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.
Yet prosecutions of Israeli settlers are rare.
On Sunday, Reuters saw a group of at least 10 settlers, masked and dressed in black, hurling rocks at Palestinians and activists harvesting olives near the Palestinian West Bank town of Salfit, prompting the farmers to flee.
Israeli border police were in the area and shot tear gas towards the hills.

After public school teacher Gary Keblish was diagnosed with melanoma in 2019, a surgeon cut out the tumor. But he wasn’t out of the woods. In some patients, melanoma aggressively recurs after surgery, so his doctors referred him to a new trial: for Merck and Moderna’s personalized mRNA cancer vaccine.
Speaking by video at the STAT Summit on Thursday, Keblish compared the journey — in all its physical and emotional turbulence — to a trip on Ms. Frizzle’s Magic School Bus. “Seatbelts, everyone!” he said, quoting the iconic line.
He’s glad he went. Today, he is still teaching, and Merck and Moderna are preparing to file the vaccine for approval, after announcing in August that it significantly delayed both cancer recurrence and the development of metastatic disease in melanoma patients like Keblish, in a large Phase 3 trial.
It’s a landmark moment for a cancer vaccine field that has long struggled to live up to its hype. But the two companies’ work is far from complete. They are now looking to prove the vaccine isn’t just a powerful tool for certain melanoma patients but that it can also transform a sea of other tumors, as an early generation of immunotherapies did.
It is careful and costly work.
“We have a lot of exploring to do and need to prioritize where we explore,” Moderna President Stephen Hoge said on stage at the summit.
Beside Hoge, Merck R&D chief Dean Li outlined an exploration strategy. The vaccine, known chemically as intismeran autogene, works in combination with Merck’s blockbuster immunotherapy Keytruda, which has been tested in thousands of trials over the last 15 years. Keytruda works better in some tumors — so-called hot tumors, which often have lots of mutations — than other so-called cold tumors.
“We know exactly where I-O [immuno-oncology] works, where a checkpoint inhibitor works, where it doesn’t, where it almost worked and didn’t make it,” said Li.
The pair has largely focused to date on settings where Keytruda has worked best, such as an adjuvant — add-on — therapy for melanoma patients whose visible tumors have already been removed by a surgeon. They are already running trials in adjuvant lung, kidney, and bladder cancer.
Li and Hoge suggested other settings they may explore or where trials are just beginning, including in tumors where Keytruda failed but another kind of immunotherapy worked, or as a standalone therapy in very early-stage tumors. “There’s an incredible opportunity to think about how we bring immunotherapy into earlier interventions and really intercept cancer so that we don’t present with stage 3, stage 4 disease later,” said Hoge.
Li contrasted their approach with “other people” who “may not have the advantage” of their expertise and have chosen to go after cold or metastatic tumors — an apparent nod at Moderna’s mRNA rival BioNTech, which has some early promising early data but also notable failures.
“We have chosen not to do this,” Li said. “But I can tell you: Anyone has positive data and it’s out there, you will never see Moderna and Merck pivot [so] fast.”
Small tests in adjuvant pancreatic and gastric cancer are underway, to test the possibility. Li also floated the possibility of using the vaccine in patients whose metastatic tumors have already been shrunk by other treatments.
In the meantime, they continue to try to improve the technology. The vaccine is made by looking at individual tumors and using an algorithm to select up to 34 mutant proteins, in hope that you can then flash those as a “wanted sign” to the immune system.
The algorithm is imperfect. But by closely analyzing the immune systems of patients in their trials, Moderna and Merck could in theory build even better software.
“It’s a real privilege to have all that information across the now several thousand people in our Phase 3 program,” Hoge said. “I’m looking forward to digging into it.”

Lucknow/Mirzapur, October 18: Religious tourism in Vindhyachal is expanding beyond Maa Vindhyavasini Mandir to encompass the entire 'Vindhya Trikon'. Around 1.84 crore devotees visited the Maa Vindhyavasini, Maa Kali Khoh, and Maa Ashtabhuja temples in 2025. In 2023, this number was approximately 1.15 crore.
Thus, devotees visiting the three temples increased by around 60% in two years. The centuries-old 'Vindhya Trikon Parikrama' is now emerging as a new identity for religious tourism. Yogi government is also working to expand this sacred pilgrimage route by developing a Shaktipeeth circuit.
The number of devotees visiting Maa Vindhyavasini Dham, part of Vindhya Trikon, continues to rise. While around 73 lakh devotees visited the shrine in 2023, the figure rose to 78.15 lakh in 2024 and reached approximately 1.20 crore in 2025. This represents an increase of around 64% in the number of devotees over two years. This surge in faith is continuing at a rapid pace in 2026 as well. From January to August alone, around 90 lakh devotees had visited Maa Vindhyavasini. This figure is about 75% of the total number of visitors recorded in the previous year. Notably, these figures are from before Sharadiya Navratri. With the influx of devotees increasing during Navratri, number of visitors to the Dham could set a new record.
Along with Maa Vindhyavasini Dham, devotees visiting Maa Kali Khoh and Maa Ashtabhuja temples have also increased rapidly. The expansion of religious tourism in Vindhyachal is reflected in the growing number of visitors to these two temples as well. In 2023, around 42.36 lakh devotees visited Maa Kali Khoh and Maa Ashtabhuja temples combined. In 2025, this figure rose to about 64 lakh, a more than 51% increase in two years. The figures indicate that devotees visiting Vindhyachal are now offering prayers not only at Maa Vindhyavasini's shrine but also at the shrines of Maa Kali Khoh and Maa Ashtabhuja. As a result, Vindhya Trikon Parikrama is emerging as a major religious tourism attraction.
Tourism and Culture Minister Jaiveer Singh stated, "The growing number of devotees in Vindhyachal reflects the positive impact of development works. Under CM Yogi Adityanath's leadership, Vindhyachal Dham is being developed as a comprehensive Shakti tourism destination. Vindhyachal will become a key center of the state's expanded Shaktipeeth circuit. This will help connect devotees from India and abroad with UP's rich tradition of Shakti worship and promote religious tourism."
The state is spending around ₹208.09 crore to improve devotee facilities and revamp religious sites in Vindhyachal. Under this initiative, facilities are being expanded at Maa Ki Paidi, along connecting roads, the Parikrama route, nearby roads and within the main temple complex. Alongside development around the Vindhyavasini Swaroop Devi Temple, basic facilities are also being strengthened in the Ashtabhuja and Kali Khoh areas. The ropeway has played an important role in making access to hilltop temples easier. This has been particularly convenient for elderly devotees and families.
Meanwhile, under the Trikon Parikrama Yojana, a ₹35.50 crore project to develop the Maa Kali Khoh area reached the tendering stage in October. These efforts make it clear that government's focus is no longer limited to the main temple, but is on developing the entire Vindhya Trikon into a well-equipped religious tourism destination.
Along with expanding facilities in Vindhyachal, efforts to organize religious tourism have also gained momentum. Under the 'Visit My State' initiative, Uttar Pradesh State Tourism Development Corporation (UPSTDC) has launched two special travel packages. The first package, covering two days and one night, connects Varanasi and Vindhyachal. Under this package, tourists can visit the temples and ghats of Kashi as well as all three goddess temples of the 'Vindhya Trikon'. The second package, covering two nights and three days, links Lucknow, Varanasi, Vindhyachal, and Prayagraj into a single religious travel circuit. This will allow devotees to experience the tradition of Shakti worship at Maa's Dham while also visiting major pilgrimage sites in Kashi and the Sangam region.
Amrit Abhijat, ACS, Tourism, Culture and Religious Affairs Department, said the growing number of devotees in Vindhyachal is strengthening the state's circuit-based tourism strategy. State government is focusing on making travel easier for devotees through better connectivity, improved facilities, convenient darshan arrangements, and well-organized travel packages. This will increase tourists' stay duration and enable local businesses and communities to benefit from tourism-generated income.
Promoting the Vindhya Trikon Parikrama is expected to strengthen the local economy. Increased movement of devotees can expand businesses related to hotels, transport, guides, and food services, as well as the sale of flowers, garlands, and prasad. This will not only boost religious tourism but also create new local employment opportunities.

Pakistan’s imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on October 11 has placed the province under direct federal control, effectively suspending the regional administration led by imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).
The move, which invokes Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, comes amid a worsening security situation and a crackdown on opposition leaders and protesters. It has also renewed questions over Pakistan’s decades-long policy of using militant groups for strategic gains, which critics say has fuelled the violence now threatening its own territory.
The emergency has extended federal control across 12 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, further weakening elected authority in a province that has long borne the consequences of Pakistan’s security policies. The move follows years of political turmoil, including Khan’s imprisonment, constitutional amendments that have weakened judicial independence, and the removal of the PTI-led provincial government.
The concentration of power in unelected authorities, alongside the military’s expanding role in civilian affairs, has raised concerns over the state of democracy in Pakistan, according to a report by news agency ANI.
Decades of militant policy and blowback
Pakistan’s security crisis has deep roots in its long-standing use of militant groups as instruments of state policy. For more than five decades, the country has pursued strategic depth through its relationship with armed groups, while distinguishing between factions considered useful and those viewed as threats.
This approach has contributed to a cycle of violence that has increasingly turned inward. The state has repeatedly shifted its position towards militant organisations, including groups hostile to its own security forces. During former army chief General Qamar Javed Bajwa’s tenure, cadres of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were relocated to parts of the erstwhile Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
The consequences have proved difficult to contain. Pakistan’s struggle with militancy has exposed the risks of treating armed groups as strategic assets while assuming their violence can be directed towards selected targets.
Former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton captured this danger in a widely cited remark: “one cannot rear snakes in a backyard and expect them to bite only neighbours, as they will eventually turn on their keepers”.
Rather than confronting the broader implications of this policy, Pakistan has continued to differentiate between militant factions it considers acceptable and those it seeks to eliminate. The resulting security failures have placed civilians, particularly in the tribal areas, at the centre of a prolonged conflict.
Emergency rule and the erosion of elected authority
The imposition of emergency rule marks another stage in the concentration of power within Pakistan’s security establishment. The federal intervention has effectively displaced the PTI-led provincial administration, depriving the opposition of its remaining provincial government.
The move follows Khan’s incarceration and constitutional changes that have curtailed judicial independence and shielded military leadership from accountability. Critics argue that these developments have weakened the institutions meant to limit executive and military power.
The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers. In the affected districts, the constitutional distinction between judicial and executive authority has reportedly been set aside, concentrating control in unelected hands.
Instead of addressing the failures behind the province’s deteriorating security situation, authorities have expanded federal and military involvement in civilian administration. The move has intensified concerns that emergency powers are being used not only to manage the security crisis but also to consolidate political control.
Opposition crackdown deepens rights concerns
The intervention has been accompanied by a wider crackdown on the opposition. Leaders and legislators have been detained, residences raided and political demonstrations suppressed. Protesters have faced police firing, tear gas and mass arrests.
The treatment of political opponents has fuelled concerns that dissent is increasingly being treated as a security threat. The use of force against protesters has also raised questions about the government’s claim that extraordinary measures are needed to restore law and order.
The crackdown comes amid concerns over restrictions on reporting from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, following earlier developments in Khyber before a blanket media ban was imposed on events in the province. Such restrictions risk limiting public scrutiny of security operations and their impact on civilians.
The growing concentration of authority has therefore created a parallel crisis. While the state faces a persistent militant threat, its response has further narrowed the space for political opposition and public dissent.
Tribal communities face renewed uncertainty
The latest intervention has also placed additional pressure on communities that have endured years of displacement and insecurity. Past military operations, including Zarb-e-Azb and Radd-ul-Fasad, remain associated with civilian hardship and human rights concerns.
Thousands of displaced families are still awaiting return and rehabilitation. For these communities, the emergency raises fears of another period of disruption, particularly as the authorities expand their control and military involvement in civilian affairs.
The consequences of Pakistan’s security policies have thus extended beyond the fight against armed groups. Tribal populations have faced displacement, civilian casualties and prolonged instability, while the failure to resolve the underlying conflict has left many vulnerable to further intervention.
The emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa brings these tensions into sharper focus. A state that has long relied on militant groups to pursue strategic objectives now faces the consequences of violence within its own borders. Its response, however, has centred on expanding federal control, weakening elected authority and restricting opposition activity.
Rather than resolving the crisis, the latest measures risk deepening the divide between the state and the communities it claims to protect. The removal of an elected provincial government, the concentration of power in unelected institutions and the crackdown on dissent point to a broader struggle over Pakistan’s democratic future, even as the country confronts the long-term fallout of its militant policies.

The Best Automatic Cat Feeders
Featured in this article
An automatic cat feeder just may change your life. No more screeching at 4 am. Plus, it can give some peace of mind while you're away from your fur baby. As seen with the rise of automatic litter boxes and pet tracking, technology has made it so we can closely monitor our pets without having to do a lot of the manual labor normally involved.
Gravity-fed automatic dry-food dispensers were invented nearly a century ago, but today most automatic cat feeders utilize Wi-Fi and are connected to an app on your phone that allows you to make a schedule or feed on demand from afar, all while monitoring your pet’s eating habits. Newer models have taken this tech further, like the Petkit YumShare Dual-Hopper 2 Automatic Feeder With Camera ($170) which has a built-in, AI-enabled camera to analyze the remaining food in the bowl and will stop dispensing to prevent overfeeding. Automatic wet-food dispensers—our top pick in this category is the Petlibro Polar Smart Wet Feeder ($170)—are relatively new, often using ice packs or mini-refrigeration cooling systems to ensure the food stays as fresh as possible.
Automatic feeders are also helpful for pet parents who want to monitor their pets’ health, have specialized schedules, or want to foster healthier eating habits. (A customizable automatic cat feeder can help with the endless gorging-vomiting cycle many cats struggle with.) Nearly all of the automatic cat feeders on this list are marketed toward cats, but some can be used with smaller dogs, and I’ve noted these below.

Others Tested
Oneisall 2-in-1 Automatic Cat Feeder and Water Dispenser for $54: Generally, I'm a fan of all the Oneisall pet products I've tested. While they aren't the most technologically advanced, they are always reliable and cheap. This model is relatively simple. To set up, you'll need to hook up the bowl supports and dishwasher-safe stainless steel bowls, fill the water and kibble compartments, and plug in. This model runs on corded electricity but has an optional 4 AA batteries in case of power outage. There is no connected app. You'll just set the clock and adjust meal settings, and you can schedule one to six meals per day with adjustable portions, from one to 10 portion sizes. I don't love having food and water so close, since cats prefer them to be separate to prevent cross-contamination in the wild. I always recommend automatic pet fountains instead for a fresh source of water, but if you don't have a lot of space, are on a budget, and need a temporary solution for getting fresh water to your kitty while you're out of town, the gravity-fed water system ensures water stays relatively fresh (plus, the translucent tank makes it easier to check water levels). I'd recommend this basic option if you're on a budget and need a temporary solution for when you're out of the house (and don't mind not having a connected app).
Closer Pets C200 2-Meal Automatic Pet Feeder for $50: This automatic feeder is super simple, which is both its weakness and its strength. It’s essentially two shallow plastic containers with stainless steel inserts (both dishwasher safe) and tamper-resistant lids that are locked and automatically open using an old-school egg-style timer that runs on a AA battery rather than electricity. Although the container has an ice pack to keep the wet food cool, after one night it lost virtually all of its coolness. There’s a lid-link clip attachment, a small piece of plastic that links the lids to ensure they will open at the same time, which is super helpful for owners of two cats like me. I wish the timer were electric so I could program it to the exact time I want it open, rather than guesstimating the timing on the little marks. However, this is a simple solution to help make sure both my cats are given wet food without me having to wake up at the crack of dawn.
Oneisall Cordless WiFi Automatic Cat Feeder for $70: I had high hopes for this cordless feeder that boasts a rechargeable battery with a 100-day life and an integrated app, but it's just too unreliable. Through the app, you can program up to 10 daily meals (in 1-12 portions each), monitor pets' eating habits, and customize meal calls. Unlike other apps, you're not able to choose portion size, but instead have to multiply the number of servings. The app gave me constant problems, and would often disconnect from the feeder and be unable to reconnect to WiFi. Luckily, I was able to program meals via the screen and buttons, but it would've been a whole lot nicer if the app had worked reliably.
Do Not Recommend
Catit Pixi Smart 6-Meal Feeder for $100: Like others on this list, the Catit Pixi wet and dry feeder uses ice packs to keep wet food fresh and rotates the meals in six compartments on a set schedule. The schedule can be programmed via the app or changed on the body of the feeder. At this price point, the app shouldn’t be this limited and glitchy. The schedule is available in military time only, and the app is extremely limited—you can only set the meal schedule for the same day, and when I wanted to do only two to three meals a day spread over two days, I had to reschedule the meals for every new day. The feeder didn't keep it cold enough to spread the meals out and the wet food was not at a safe eating temperature. At this price point, just get the Petlibro Polar wet feeder for a few bucks more.
Catit Pixi Smart Cat Feeder for $140: Kibble is stored in the body of this dry feeder, but it doesn’t have a window to visually check food levels. The calendar to plan meals shows only a week at a time, and although it should repeat daily based on the schedule, I found that some days there would be no schedule despite setting one up. The Pixi also doesn’t tell you how much food was dispensed; it just refers to it as a “portion”—I manually measured and found the portion was less than a tablespoon of kibble. After using it continuously for more than a month, I found it was extremely glitchy and almost never reliably stuck to the programmed schedule, sometimes skipping meals altogether. This feeder is potentially dangerous, and I'd caution pet parents against relying on it.
Closer Pets C500 for $75: This automatic wet and dry feeder can schedule up to four pre-portioned meals (and one meal given manually) that are opened on a timer system using three AA batteries (sold separately). The user presets the four times they want the bowls, which have ice packs underneath, to rotate. The bowls are quite deep and narrow and aren’t super easy for cats to reach, which could cause whisker fatigue. And although there are two relatively large ice packs, when I checked on the feeder after a night’s sleep, the packs weren’t very cold. This may be OK for kibble, but wet food was kept at unsafe temperatures, and my cats couldn't reach all of the food.
Why Use an Automatic Feeder?
Automatic feeders are great for pet owners who want to help manage their pets’ weight and monitor eating patterns. Plus, they allow for a lot more control and precision for owners to learn exactly how much their cat is eating and when. Because cats are naturally more nocturnal, many have the annoying habit of waking you up in the early hours, demanding food, and these allow you to set up a schedule that fits more to their schedule without inconveniencing yours.
Of course, it’s never recommended to leave pets alone for long periods, but these automatic feeders give more peace of mind and are a whole lot healthier for your pet than leaving a huge amount of food for free-feeding while you're away for the night. Simply put, it’s an easier way to feed and monitor your cat’s health with less work for you, the human.
How I Tested
I have two rescue cats, ages 4 and 5, and they eat two wet-food meals a day and small amounts of dry kibble throughout the day. Vets (and TikTokkers) have successfully persuaded me to move toward a primarily wet-food diet, however, which has a higher water content. This provides more moisture in their diet, which helps with potentially life-threatening problems like UTIs, which are especially prevalent in male cats. I still like to give smaller dry-food meals throughout the day for them to satisfy their need for crunch.
For dry food, I use Hill’s Science Diet, and for wet food, I use Friskies' Shreds variety. (Yes, only Shreds. Fellow cat owners will understand.)
I set up the feeders, noting ease of setup, potential problems, and app navigation. I also tested various schedules and manual feedings through the app, noting any issues. I used each of the feeders for at least a week, if not more.
How Long Can I Leave My Cat Alone?
Although cats are generally thought of as less high-maintenance than dogs, it’s still not good to leave your cat for prolonged periods. Under dire circumstances, you can leave a cat alone for 24 to 48 hours with scheduled feedings and a clean water source, but it’s not ideal—especially for cats with health issues, kittens younger than a year, or very elderly cats. Although these feeders are automatic, and meals can be scheduled in advance and over multiple days, our pets still need their human pals around for enrichment, care, and well, love.

As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice.
Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday.
“This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman, was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.
“We will first observe the results, and if effective, there is a possibility that this method could be implemented in other regions.”
Since January, almost 900,000 hectares have been burned Indonesia-wide in the worst fire season in more than a decade, exacerbated by this year’s “godzilla” El-Nino and as the practice of “slash and burn” to clear land for crops such as palm oil persists.
For months, millions of Indonesians have been subject to thick smoke and an apocalyptic tangerine haze, with criticism mounting of the government’s response, including a class action lawsuit filed last week accusing it of “gross negligence”. Tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to the haze.
Air quality has also plummeted in neighbouring countries, shuttering schools, grounding flights and driving a spike in respiratory illness.
The haze has drifted into neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and as far afield as the Philippines. Timor-Leste has said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday and urged families to keep children indoors or to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment starting on Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes occurred. The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents.
In the past week, the financial hub of Singapore was listed among the most polluted cities globally. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected, was at number two.
On Thursday, a Cessna aircraft will reportedly disperse 1.5 tons of dry ice over the South Sumatran city of Palembang, a move the government hopes will ease the smoke and improve air quality and visibility.
The technique was first deployed in the 1940s to promote ice formation in clouds, Bloomberg reported.
But experts say the use of dry ice, or solid carbon dioxide, might only offer local, and limited relief.
“It’s got some potential for local relief that might work for a while,” says Rick McRae, an adjunct professor from the University of New South Wales’ (UNSW) bushfire research group.
“Weather systems are all moving from east to west. So if you’re in a town under that and you clear the smoke, there’s gonna be more blowing all the time,” he says, “So it’s a constant … It’s not going to be simple and it’s not going to be a permanent fix in any way.”
In the Indonesian province of central Kalimantan on Wednesday, the ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200 – or four times the “hazardous” level of 300 – environment ministry data showed.
Local news footage showed thick haze blanketing the provincial city of Palangka Raya, cutting visibility for motorists to a minimum.
Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto has ordered firefighting efforts to be stepped up, and called for a crackdown on those suspected of starting fires.
But the government has struggled to combat the fires, the worst of occur in peatland areas, which can burn for weeks underground and are difficult to extinguish.
“As time goes by and climate change kicks in, I think it could become a global problem, not just the fix that one country needs to find,” said McRae, of the widening regional issue. “There’s a lot of interconnectedness on a global scale.”

Thieves reportedly stole around 30,000 premium wine bottles from Italy’s Marchesi Antinori in Tuscany. The shipment was valued at around $5.8 million (over ₹55 crore). The theft targeted a logistics facility near Cortona during the night of 3-4 October. Employees discovered the missing bottles on 5 October. Investigators are examining the gang’s planning and possible knowledge of the shipment. At least seven masked men reportedly entered the premises and disabled security systems. They allegedly used the winery’s own forklifts to load bottles onto two trucks. The operation reportedly lasted around three hours before the gang escaped. The company subsequently worked with investigators before details became public several days later. The stolen bottles were reportedly ready for export. Investigators are considering whether the thieves knew which stock would be available. However, reports have not established that any employee helped the gang. They also have not confirmed whether a particular buyer ordered the theft. The shipment reportedly included the 2023 vintages of Solaia, Tignanello and Guado al Tasso. Reports suggested roughly 10,000 bottles of each label were taken. However, estimates differ, and the exact breakdown remains uncertain. Solaia comes from Antinori’s Tignanello estate and blends three grape varieties. These include Cabernet Sauvignon, Sangiovese and Cabernet Franc. Tignanello combines Sangiovese with international grape varieties. It helped establish the Super Tuscan movement, which challenged traditional Italian winemaking rules. Guado al Tasso comes from Antinori’s Bolgheri estate on the Tuscan coast. Its grape varieties include Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc. Super Tuscans gained recognition for their quality, distinctive styles and ability to age. The stolen labels are among Antinori’s recognised premium offerings. Investigators are examining surveillance footage along possible escape routes. They are also checking possible connections with other recent wine thefts in Italy. No link between those incidents has been publicly established. Recovering the shipment could be difficult if bottles pass through middlemen in smaller quantities. Transport records, packaging details and information from legitimate distributors could help trace them. Recognisable labels and vintages might alert merchants and collectors to suspicious offers. However, individual bottles could be harder to identify without unique tracking details. As of now, no arrests or recovery of the shipment had been confirmed. Finding where the trucks travelled remains particularly important to the investigation. Marchesi Antinori traces its winemaking history to 1385. The family business is now in its 26th generation.
