Congress gets Delhi Police nod for Ramlila Maidan rally amid SIR protests
A No Objection Certificate (NOC) has been issued to the Congress for a rally at Ramlila Maidan, said Delhi Police on Saturday.
Speaking to ANI, Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP) Central Rohit Rajbir Singh said the ground will be booked from October 25 to November 3.
This follows Jantar Mantar being de-notified as a designated venue for organising protests and demonstrations in Delhi. The Delhi Police has designated three alternative locations for holding such activities. The three new designated protest venues are Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi.
Deep Dive
The DCP said that the Congress first asked the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) about availability, which said the ground would be free from October 25 to November 3. "The MCD stated that the venue would be available from October 25 to November 3. After receiving the venue availability certificate, the Congress party approached us," he said.
"After interacting with them and understanding the security arrangements required, we decided to grant them the No Objection Certificate (NOC). We issued it today. They will now take the certificate back to the MCD, which is the owning agency responsible for the land, and then begin their preparations. The ground will be booked from October 25 to November 3," he added.
DCP Singh further said that any other stakeholder or organiser wanting to book the ground may also follow the same process.
The Congress's proposed rally comes amid a broader row over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which has escalated over the weeks as multiple protests erupted in the national capital led by INDIA Bloc and activists. The opposition camp has been demanding the roll-back of SIR and resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The protests also witnessed a police crackdown as over a hundred of demonstrators were detained amid heightened security in central Delhi. Congress has been staging continuous protests against the CEC, with INDIA Bloc allies joining the chorus.

Authorities invoked Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), imposing strict prohibitory orders against public assemblies in Central Delhi. Dipke has been granted bail in Delhi, subject to certain conditions, Delhi Police said.

NEW DELHI: Unknown gunmen opened fire at actor Tiger Shroff on Sunday, injuring his driver and another person, an autorickshaw driver. The incident took place near Mumbai's Pushpa Park, within the limits of Juhu police station in the western suburb.According to police, the actor escaped unhurt, while his driver, identified as Firdaus, sustained an injury to his left hand."The chain of events leading to the incident is being pieced together," a police official said."Shroff is safe and has not sustained any injuries in the firing incident. His driver, identified as Firdaus, and another driver of the autorickshaw, identified only as Chauhan, were injured in the shooting and were rushed for medical treatment," the official added.Shroff and his driver were taken to Nanavati Hospital in Vile Parle. Doctors said the actor had sustained a few abrasions but no bullet wounds.The third person was taken to Cooper Hospital after sustaining bullet injuries to his chest.
Lawrence Bishnoi gang claims responsibility
Meanwhile, Anil Pandit and Harman Sandhu, purportedly associated with the Lawrence Bishnoi gang, claimed responsibility for the attack."Ram Ram to all the brothers. Anil Pandit and Harman Sandhu take responsibility for what happened to Tiger Shroff today.
We had called him and tried to explain things to him, but he did not understand. So today, we made him understand properly," Anil Pandit said in a Facebook post."Anyone in the Mumbai film industry who does not listen to us or works with Salman Khan will be next. Wait and watch."Note: And those dogs from other groups who think they can gain fame by using our name - we will soon kill them and make them famous."Salute to the martyrs," he added.The authenticity of the claims and their alleged link to the firing had yet to be independently established. Police are investigating the incident and examining the available evidence to determine the motive behind the shooting.
Police launch massive manhunt
Meanwhile, Mumbai Police has launched a manhunt to nab those involved in the incident. Specialised teams are examining CCTV footage from the area for leads."The incident occurred while Tiger Shroff was returning in his car. He was not hit by any bullets and is completely safe. Mumbai Police has formed multiple teams and initiated further action. The forensic team has begun its preliminary analysis, with approximately 15 teams currently working on the case," DCP Mohit Garg said."Further information will be shared as it becomes available. As I mentioned, the forensic team is carrying out its investigation. At this stage, it would not be appropriate to disclose specific details regarding the number of rounds fired," he added.
Fadnavis directs Mumbai Police to expedite probe
Meanwhile, Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis called the Mumbai Police commissioner to seek details about the firing incident.He directed the commissioner to expedite the investigation and take strict action against those responsible.Fadnavis also called Tiger Shroff and spoke with him.He assured him, saying, “We are all with you. We will trace and apprehend the accused at the earliest.”Maharashtra deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde also condemned the incident and said Mumbai Police has formed several teams to track down those who opened fire. He added that the accused will be given a response in their own language."Tiger Shroff’s vehicle was targeted. This incident is deeply concerning and condemnable; I condemn it in the strongest possible terms. I have spoken with the Police Commissioner, and I have also spoken with Tiger Shroff. The Mumbai Police Commissioner has formed several teams to track down those who opened fire—they will be apprehended and given a response in their own language. Our current priority is to keep Mumbai and its citizens safe. Whether it is a celebrity or an ordinary citizen, ensuring their safety is the responsibility of the police and the government, and there will be no negligence in this regard," Shinde said."No gang will be spared; we will not let them get away with this. We have seen large-scale gang wars like this before, back in the 1990s. Even then, the Mumbai Police effectively handled the situation—they dealt with the perpetrators in their own language, ensuring that law and order were maintained. So, any gang attempting to spread terror here should think twice. This is Mumbai; this is Maharashtra," he added.
Rohit Shetty, Salman Khan among film personalities targeted
Several personalities from the film industry have been targeted in shooting incidents in recent years.In February this year, five rounds were fired outside filmmaker Rohit Shetty's residence in Juhu. The Lawrence Bishnoi gang claimed responsibility for the firing.
In April 2024, two men on a motorcycle fired five rounds outside actor Salman Khan's Galaxy Apartments in Mumbai's Bandra area.Mumbai Police arrested several suspects linked to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang. The trial against five accused - Vicky Gupta, Sagar Pal, Harpal Singh, Sonukumar Bishnoi and Mohammad Rafiq Choudhari - is underway. The sixth accused, Anuj Kumar Thapan, died in police custody in May 2024.

Meet the Democrats breaking through in the country’s most pro-Trump town: ‘Tough nut’
Democratic voters in the country’s most MAGA county could all fit together in an Uber — but with Trump’s popularity slipping, organizers aren’t giving up, Brendan Rascius learns

Political outreach can be an uphill battle. But for Democrats trying to make inroads in Roberts County, Texas, it can feel more like a full-bore sprint into a brick wall.
This rural patch of the Texas Panhandle has long been described as America’s most pro-Trump county with more than 94 percent of its voters backing Donald Trump in each of the past three presidential elections.
By contrast, the county’s Kamala Harris voters could all fit comfortably on a school bus. This year’s Democratic primary voters could share an Uber.
“We just haven't been able to get any traction there,” Sean Birkenfeld, president of Panhandle Democrats, a regional political action committee, told The Independent.
In interviews, Democrats described the Sisyphean task of gaining a foothold in Roberts County where Fox News plays in local businesses, Trump signs dot lawns and the party of Franklin Roosevelt has spent decades in hibernation. Some suspect there are actually more Democrats than election returns suggest but that they remain “closeted,” reluctant to advertise their politics for fear of backlash.
How Roberts County became Trump country
Roberts County, located about 80 miles northwest of Amarillo, is home to roughly 870 people. Its economy revolves around agribusiness and oil, and it is one of just three Texas counties that still prohibits alcohol sales. Its only city is Miami, pronounced “My-am-uh.”
The county earned its reputation as Trump’s most loyal in 2016, when he won 94.58 percent of its votes — the highest Republican vote share of any county in that election. Its support has remained remarkably consistent: Trump took 96.18 percent of the vote in 2020 and 95.63 percent in 2024.
For some residents, Trump represented a promise that people like them would not be overlooked. “I feel like Trump has my back, I hope he doesn't prove me wrong,” local resident John Faith told a news outlet in 2016.
Another resident, Steve Porter, emphasized strength, immigration and jobs in an interview with ABC News in 2018. “I realized that we needed a president who believed America was great. Greater than all other countries,” he said.
Trying to gain a foothold
Democrats hoping to establish a presence in the county have had their work cut out for them. This year’s Democratic primary drew just three voters, while the GOP’s drew 306.
Mark Nair, the Democratic nominee for Texas’ 13th congressional district, which encompasses the county, said he has visited Roberts County several times. Drawing a crowd has proved difficult.
“Seriously, it's like two people that would come,” he told The Independent.
Birkenfeld’s attempt to organize an event in Roberts County, meanwhile, never reached the point of counting attendees. He contacted people about setting something up, he said, but the plans fell through. “I haven't actually been able to get any engagement,” the political organizer said.
There is currently no Democratic county chair to help make the introductions or rally potential volunteers. The position is vacant, Birkenfeld said, leaving the party without local leadership.
For Nair, the difficulty is not a lack of warmth from the people he meets.
“They're very, very nice people who believe in their community and their family. They really do,” Nair said. “But when it turns to politics, it's almost like you're trying to crack this tough nut.”
He added: “And I can make arguments all day long, but it's difficult because they're kind of stuck into this way of thinking that Trump might do something great for them. It's confusing to me because I don't see the evidence of that.”
For now, some of the work of building a Democratic presence is considerably less ambitious than changing anyone’s mind.
The Roberts County Texas Democrats Facebook group is administered by Bonny Krahn, who lives hundreds of miles away in rural Hays County. She created county-specific groups across Texas to provide a starting point where Democratic organizations were absent or struggling, with the intention of handing them over as local chairs emerged.
Posts in the group cover the essentials. “This is your next election. Date, time, and place. This is who's on your ballot,” she said, describing the information she shares.
The Roberts County group currently has 19 members.
The cost of standing apart
Organizers suspect the election returns do not tell the whole story of Democratic life in the rural Panhandle. Some supporters, Birkenfeld says, would rather keep their politics to themselves.
“There's not really a better terminology, but they're in the closet,” he said.
A tale, from a few years back, illustrates what publicly breaking with the majority in Miami, the county seat, can mean.
In a 2020 interview with The Mirror, museum curator Susan Bowers said she had grown up in a Republican household but changed her allegiance after studying in Amarillo and training in social work. Her opposition to Trump, she said, had cost her.
“I feel like the black sheep of Miami,” she told the newspaper. “It’s a lost cause trying to convince people Trump should not be in power. Passions here runs so deep. The sad thing is I have lost friends over this.”
The concern about making one’s politics public is familiar to Birkenfeld, who says people across the wider region have reported stolen or defaced yard signs and hostile reactions to Democratic shirts and bumper stickers.
Birkenfeld, said he has experienced hostility in the region first-hand. At an arts event in Potter County, a stranger spotted his shirt emblazoned with the name of a Democratic candidate and approached him.
“Oh, so you're one of those libtards,” he recalled them saying.
But political isolation cuts both ways. Trump supporters in liberal bastions such as New York City have also described feeling stigmatized and keeping their views to themselves.
Signs of movement
Despite the difficulty of getting people to turn out Nair believes some residents in Roberts County are questioning what their loyalty to Trump has delivered.
The concerns he hears from people center largely on farming and water rights — the county sits above the largest freshwater aquifer in North America. But he acknowledges the limits of those conversations.
“Now, I know it's not everyone in the county speaking, because when I show up, like I said, most of the people won't come to an event,” Nair said. “But the people that do, they really are very upset that they voted several times for Trump, and they're feeling that… betrayal is a good word.”
Krahn said she’s seen movement in the business of rebuilding local Democratic organizations. She estimated that Texas had about 64 counties without Democratic chairs when she began her work; now, she said, there are about 46.
“So we're slowly going the right direction,” she said.
Beyond the Panhandle, Democrats see an opening to loosen the Republican Party’s iron grip on Texas. The most closely-watched opportunity is the U.S. Senate race, where Democratic state Representative James Talarico is challenging Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton for the seat held by outgoing GOP Senator John Cornyn.
Recent polling suggests a competitive contest. A UMass Lowell/YouGov survey, released October 8, put Talarico and Paxton at 45 percent each, with 7 percent of voters undecided. A separate Fox News poll recently gave Talarico a narrow advantage, 51 percent to 49 percent, within its margin of error.
In Roberts County, though, the work described by organizers is less about an election night transformation than building something that can last beyond November: finding a county chair, reaching people reluctant to speak up and getting a few more residents to turn out.
In a place where this year’s Democratic primary drew three voters, even modest gains would mark a start.

CJI Surya Kant calls on graduates to ‘defend liberty, uphold Constitution’ at Bengaluru law college
Addressing students at NLSIU, the CJI said legal education must go beyond academic learning and prepare students to engage with diverse perspectives.
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Saturday urged graduating law students to uphold justice, defend liberty and remain committed to constitutional values, saying the legal profession demands courage, integrity and the ability to listen to voices that often go unheard.
Addressing the 34th annual convocation of the National Law School of India University (NLSIU) here, he said legal education must go beyond academic learning and prepare students to engage with diverse perspectives and serve society.
"The purpose of legal education extends beyond learning the principles of criminal or constitutional law; it rests in the invigorating experience of encountering those who see the world differently than we do," he said.
Emphasising the responsibilities of the legal profession, Surya Kant said it required not only knowledge of statutes and precedents but also the courage to stand up for justice and the humility to hear the concerns of those whose voices are often overlooked.
"The legal profession is not for the faint of heart. It demands not only the mastery of statutes and precedent but also the courage to defend what is just, and the humility to listen to voices that are often unheard," he said.
He also stressed the importance of intellectual independence and fairness, urging graduates to hear different viewpoints before forming judgments and to respect the dignity of those with whom they disagree.
"This intellectual independence also calls for fairness: hearing before judging, distinguishing a person from a position and disagreeing without denying another person's dignity," he said.
The CJI said the law was not static but evolved through the minds and actions of those who practised it, with every case argued, contract drafted, advice given and judgment written contributing to the larger architecture of justice in the country.
He said the years spent at law school had prepared graduates to navigate the complexities of the profession, combining intellectual agility with ethical responsibility and the resilience to withstand pressure.
The CJI cautioned the graduates against compromising their principles for convenience or taking shortcuts in their professional lives. He urged them to remain guided by the values they had imbibed at the institution.
"It is this relentless pursuit of honesty which will cement your professional reputation. There will come times when compromise tempts, when expediency entices, and when others take breezy shortcuts. And it is in those moments that you must let the wisdom imparted here, be your compass and stay true to the values you have imbibed in this eminent institution," he said.

Highlighting the rewards of serving through the legal profession, he said lawyers could derive satisfaction from correcting injustices, defending individual liberty and upholding the Constitution.
"As you leave this campus, you step not only into a profession but into a calling- to be guardians of autonomy and servants of the people," he said, adding that the law would test their patience and ethics but also offer the satisfaction of righting a wrong, defending liberty and upholding the Constitution.
Surya Kant also paid tribute to Urvashi Krishnatra, a graduate of the university's LLB programme who was no longer alive to receive her degree at the convocation.
"She should have been here today, receiving her well-deserved degree and sharing this milestone with her classmates," he said, offering condolences to her family and friends.
The CJI acknowledged the contribution of parents, faculty and staff in shaping the graduates, saying the students' achievements reflected the sacrifices and support of their families and the guidance of their teachers.
Appealing to the graduates to recognise their wider responsibility to the country, Surya Kant said the nation expected them to contribute to society beyond their roles as legal practitioners.
"As you step out into the world, know that the nation looks to you- not just as practitioners of law but as heralds of hope. May your careers be distinguished, your endeavours impactful and your contributions everlasting," he said.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday (October 18) blamed immigration for the unrest sweeping France and urged the country to tighten its border controls, as violent protests left at least 1,800 people arrested, damaged hundreds of businesses and caused losses estimated at several hundred million euros.
“France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform. “Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!”
Trump's remarks came a day after US Vice President JD Vance also blamed immigration and diversity policies for the violence. French authorities, however, have not linked immigrants to the rioting, attributing some of the violence to radical far-left groups and others who joined demonstrations to loot shops.
Quick answers to key questions
The protests began in September as students demonstrated over staff shortages, under-resourced schools and deteriorating school conditions. They widened to include anger over rising living costs, inequality and declining public services.
French authorities said at least 1,800 people were arrested nationwide. Paris police reported 855 arrests in the capital region.
Damage to French retailers was estimated at several hundred million euros, with around 1,500 retail establishments directly affected. Fires, looting and damage were also reported at public buildings and other sites.
French authorities estimated that around 550,000 people demonstrated across the country. Organisers put the turnout at approximately 800,000.
No. Trump blamed immigration for the unrest, but French authorities had not linked immigrants to the rioting. They attributed some violence to radical far-left groups and others who joined demonstrations to loot shops.
Vance wrote in a social media post: "Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn't listen. I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn. And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country."
The unrest has piled pressure on French President Emmanuel Macron, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets to protest rising living costs, inequality, deteriorating public services and poor conditions in schools.
According to French authorities, around 550,000 people participated in demonstrations across the country, while organisers put the figure at approximately 800,000. More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.
The demonstrations descended into violence in several cities on Saturday, with masked groups setting fires, attacking public buildings, clashing with police and looting businesses.
Alexandre Bompard, CEO of Carrefour and president of the Trade and Distribution Federation, estimated that around 1,500 retail establishments had been directly affected, according to Ukrinform. The damage to French retailers was estimated at several hundred million euros.
Businesses affected included supermarkets, clothing stores, sports retailers, luxury boutiques and mobile phone shops. Looting and damage were reported in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Nantes and Nice, among other cities.
In Bordeaux, Mayor Thomas Cazenave said up to 100 stores had been looted. Marseille Mayor Benoit Payan announced emergency financial assistance for businesses affected by the violence.
Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire announced the creation of an emergency unit to help businesses assess the damage.
“The scale of the damage is considerable and unprecedented,” Grégoire wrote in an open letter, adding that the French capital must remain a place where people can demonstrate freely while ensuring that businesses can operate safely.
The damage extended beyond commercial establishments. In Limoges, a city in central France, a fire engulfed the 19th-century city hall, causing its roof to collapse.
The protests began in September, when students at a high school in Créteil, southeast of Paris, demonstrated against staff shortages and deteriorating conditions in their schools.
The movement subsequently spread to other Paris suburbs and cities across France, with students organising class strikes, blockades and demonstrations. Hundreds of schools were forced to close because of damage or attacks on staff, according to reports.
Students have complained about under-resourced schools, dilapidated buildings and insufficient teachers, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. French media reports have highlighted problems including leaking roofs, damaged furniture, collapsed ceilings and rodent infestations.
Some students have also raised concerns about classrooms becoming unbearably hot during summer heatwaves and cold in winter because of inadequate facilities. Long school days and what students consider an unfair or complicated university admission system have added to their grievances.
The demonstrations have since expanded beyond education, drawing support from people angry about rising living costs, inequality, public spending cuts and the deterioration of public services.
The General Confederation of Labour (CGT), one of France's largest trade unions, backed the protests and called for lower prices and higher wages and pensions.
This convergence of student anger and wider economic discontent helped turn a movement initially focused on school conditions into nationwide demonstrations involving hundreds of thousands of people.
Although many demonstrations remained peaceful, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted shops and attacked police officers and vehicles.
Police used tear gas and water cannon in Paris, where demonstrators threw stones and fireworks. Violent incidents were also reported in Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse, Angers and other cities.
In Marseille, protesters stormed the town hall and painted an anarchist symbol on a wall. In Lyon, demonstrators set fire to the city's tourism office.
French authorities said at least 1,800 people had been arrested nationwide. Paris police reported 855 arrests in the capital region alone, while the Paris prosecutors' office said 557 people had been kept in police custody.
On Sunday morning, damaged storefronts, shattered glass, dislodged cobblestones and burnt-out bicycles marked the aftermath around Paris' Place de la République and other commercial and tourist areas.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez defended the right to peaceful demonstrations while condemning the violence.
“The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not,” he wrote on X, pointing to the looting of businesses across several major cities.
Macron was scheduled to hold an emergency meeting with senior government officials on Sunday afternoon before addressing the nation at 8 pm, according to his office.
The unrest has put the French government under pressure to respond to both the immediate violence and the underlying grievances over education, living costs and public services.

Ukraine sets Saint Petersburg refinery ablaze in large-scale drone attack
SAINT PETERSBURG: Ukraine hit Saint Petersburg with a large-scale drone attack, causing fires at an oil refinery and depot, Moscow said on Sunday (Oct 18), as Kyiv accused Russia of violating United States President Donald Trump's "energy ceasefire" dozens of times and leaving tens of thousands without power.
Trump last week announced an "energy ceasefire" - which neither side said they agreed to beforehand - that quickly collapsed, with Moscow continuing strikes on Ukraine's power grid and Kyiv eventually resuming hits on Russian oil refineries.
Trump has been angered by Kyiv's strikes on Russian refineries - which he says are contributing to a surge in global fuel prices.
On Sunday, Ukraine hit Russia's second city as its ties with Washington strained in recent days.
Kyiv says its retaliatory strikes are fair retribution for years of Russia's offensive and destruction of its energy infrastructure.
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia on Sunday of hitting Kyiv's energy, oil and gas facilities 76 times since Trump announced his ceasefire.
Saint Petersburg governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city - President Vladimir Putin's hometown - in the night-time strikes.
Authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.
Flights were restricted at the city's Pulkovo airport, Beglov said, adding that 12 housing blocks were also damaged.
Russia's VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit in the city and Ozon - Russia's second largest retailer - also reported a hit on its logistics centre.
The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the 2022 war.
Ukraine has attacked Moscow and Saint Petersburg throughout the Kremlin's dragging offensive but large-scale hits on Russia's main cities are rare.
US-led peace talks have not led to a breakthrough. In a fifth year of war, few see a way out.
"There's a general feeling: they're attacking, we're attacking - it's become the dreadful routine of war," 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
Sergei, another resident of the city who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
"I don't know if I was scared, what must be will be," he told AFP.
"My main thought was that petrol would run out at the petrol stations and I'd better fill up."
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier this year.
"GETTING ON MY NERVES"
Leningrad governor Drozdenko said 20,000 people were without power in the town of Yanino, where a substation was hit.
He said a woman and three children were hospitalised "with symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning" in the region after drone debris fell on a house, causing a fire.
Smoke rose above Saint Petersburg's shipyards and was visible from the historic city centre, on the banks of the Neva River.
"I woke up at night, heard bangs, looked out of the window and there was a fire," 40-year-old Saint Petersburg resident Igor told AFP.
"They're getting on my nerves already," he added, referring to Ukraine.
Putin this week appeared in military uniform and said Moscow intended to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine by force.
"THEIR BET ON WAR IS PAYING OFF"
The attack came a day after Zelenskyy called on allies to keep up pressure on Moscow to end the war and as he denounced Trump's move to block new sanctions on Russia.
On Sunday, he said Russian strikes hit substations in four Ukrainian regions, leaving "tens of thousands of families without power".
He has warned Moscow is trying to leave Ukrainians without heat and power ahead of winter.
Russian strikes also killed two people in an "agricultural enterprise" in the western Volyn region - bordering NATO member Poland - on Sunday, the wartime leader said.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements," Zelenskyy said, adding:
"On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting."
Trump this week blocked a package of new sanctions on Russia which was meant to target Putin, as well as Russia's energy and defence sectors.
The US leader also signed an agreement with Moscow this month to buy diesel, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of elections.
Kyiv and its European allies worry the White House is taking Russia's side in Europe's worst conflict since WWII.
"It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance," Zelenskyy said on Sunday.

In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.
Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.
Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.
So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.
Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.
Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.
Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.
Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.
Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.
Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?
What else we’re reading about
Flydubai incident | Indian pilot Smit Machchar is being hailed as a hero for helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.
Datacentres | Protests against water-guzzling datacentres erupting from the US to Australia are gathering momentum in India. South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a $15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.
Art and design | Designer Vikram Goyal, celebrated for his signature repoussé brass work, brings his installation Wings and Tales to a Georgian townhouse in London’s Mayfair from 12 to 16 October. The exhibition includes furniture designs inspired by landscapes from the Indian epic Ramayana.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
13,626
This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.
Vibe check
Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.
The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

For years, NASA hoped to bring humans back to the moon’s surface, and Artemis III was going to be the mission to accomplish this feat. That will no longer be the case.
Following the successful Artemis II flyby last April, the program’s schedule was revised. According to the most recent announcements, the next mission will have to wait until 2028, and while the new plans are admittedly less spectacular than a lunar landing, they’re hardly dispensable.
In 2027, NASA plans to test in Earth orbit whether the Orion capsule can safely rendezvous and operate with commercial lunar landing systems from SpaceX and Blue Origin before attempting those same maneuvers around the moon. WIRED en Español spoke with Barbara Cohen, a scientist on the Artemis III project, to better understand this upcoming mission—the conversation ranging from the role humans still play in the face of increasingly capable robots and sensors to what we can learn about the solar system’s violent past from traces preserved on the moon.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
JORGE GARAY: What should people expect from Artemis III, and why does this mission matter even if it won’t land astronauts on the moon?
BARBARA COHEN: Artemis III is an Earth-orbiting mission. That’s the one that’s coming up next. We will send the Orion capsule to Earth’s orbit with the people in it. Blue Origin and SpaceX are the companies that are making the lunar landers, so each one of those companies will make a test article. It won’t be the full lunar lander, but those companies will send their version of the test article into Earth’s orbit to meet up with Orion. This is to make sure that Orion can meet with the lunar landers, so that when they do go to lunar orbit, they can do that safely.
Where does science fit into the Artemis program, and what have you learned so far about how astronauts can contribute scientifically?
The Artemis missions, just to be clear, are not science missions. They’re exploration for a lot of different reasons. We do that for technology development. We do that for inspiration. And we try to get the science that we can from the opportunity. And so we still work really hard to identify unique science opportunities that exist because the mission exists.
One of the things on Artemis III we’re doing is like a dress rehearsal for bringing samples back from the moon. When we land on the moon and start to bring samples back, those samples change as soon as you take them out of their natural environment. We try to make sure that they change as little as possible, but they are going to change.
You have to bring them back and put them into curation so that scientists can study them. We want to understand every step along the way: What could be changing the samples, how the samples could be reacting, especially to the environment around them. So we’ll have our crew deploy these witness materials—pieces of aluminum foil, pieces of Teflon, maybe pieces of ceramic. They’re very clean surfaces, very small pieces, maybe the size of a quarter or a nickel. And the team will be opening those up and exposing them to the crew cabin throughout their flight. That’ll give us a feel for how the humans change the environment around them.
With the capabilities of probes and other robotic tools today, what is the purpose of sending human astronauts into space?
If you just want to take pictures, you do that with robotic assets. Robots can take pictures. They do that all the time. We have lots of pictures in the area. We also have, on the International Space Station, a way for us to ask, “Please take a picture of this. Please take a picture of that.” That’s not what we did with Artemis II, and that’s not what we’re trying to do with Artemis III or Artemis IV, V, VI. With the Artemis missions, we’re trying to use the humans to their best capability, and what the humans are really good at is seeing a wide scene, zooming in on details very naturally, and then trying to interpret what they’re seeing and take the next step.
We don’t know everything about the moon. To learn more, we need to literally go on the surface and figure out what’s there and where to go next. So some of this is trying to train—not just the crew onboard—but the flight directors and the science team and the engineers. We all need to work together to enable humans to do what they do best.
We also give the crew science prompts. We say, “What do you think is happening in this scene? There’s something like a storm or an algal bloom or a fire. What do you see? How do you see the scene changing? What do you think that means? What do you think is causing that change? What do you think is going to happen next? If you could do anything, what would you do next?” That helps us understand what they’re looking at, which is not just taking pictures. It’s making observations, making understanding, making inferences with their brains. That’s what humans are really good at. That’s what we’ll be asking them to do.
From a science point of view, we learned a lot about how crew really wants to use their powers of observation, and how we should participate in the observations and train them in the science that we want them to do. We also had the ability to include science directly in flight. On Artemis II, we had our science officer talk directly to crew. That was a new thing that we’ll be carrying forward to Artemis III and beyond.
When humans return to the lunar surface, what scientific questions would you most like Artemis to help answer?
I have a personal opinion. My personal scientific interest is how old craters on the moon are. If you look at the moon—with binoculars or a small telescope, or even in pictures—you see that it is covered in craters. In fact, we call it saturated, because every crater that forms does so on another crater. The whole surface is covered in craters. The Earth is not, but I promise you that for every crater that formed on the moon, there was a crater that formed on Earth.
The moon doesn’t get hit more than the Earth, but we have a lot of water. We have erosion on our continents. Our continents move around. They get subducted. We get new land that forms. All of those processes on the Earth erase craters. And so, if we want to know what was hitting the Earth in the past—and I promise you that things were hitting the Earth—we can’t find that evidence on the Earth anymore. We’ve erased it. So we have to go to the moon to figure that out.
There was a period in time when the solar system was forming—4.5 billion years ago, 4 billion years ago. Humans weren’t around. Life hadn’t arisen on Earth yet. We think that the solar system was very dynamic, and there were a lot of impacts happening, a lot of material being exchanged. So there were a lot of craters—big, big craters, basin-size craters, craters the size of continents. They really disrupted the moon, and they would have disrupted the Earth as well. Like I said, we don’t have any evidence of that because we don’t have any rocks from that time anymore. But it’s really worth knowing. Did we disrupt the Earth several times? How did life get going? How did we get nutrients? How did material move around the solar system? That evidence is preserved on the moon.
There is a big crater called the South Pole-Aitken Basin. It’s on the lunar far side, but it intersects the South Pole of the moon, where we expect humans to be going. It would be my personal desire that humans could collect pieces of that big crater, and we could understand when it formed and what it did to the moon and what was happening in the solar system at that time.
Artemis III won’t do that just yet. Lunar touchdown is currently expected as part of Artemis IV, which is expected to take off in early 2028. Before then, the upcoming third mission will have to demonstrate something far less spectacular, but crucial for the program’s future: That the spacecraft, procedures, and the people who will one day carry out these missions can work together safely.

Trump waives several Russia sanctions as new US law takes effect
- Published
US President Donald Trump has used his presidential authority to block numerous sanctions on Russia that were recently passed by the US Congress in an effort to punish the country for its war on Ukraine.
In an executive order on Friday night, Trump said that it is in the US "national interests" to withhold some of the sanctions. Trump signed the sanctions bill into law in September, and it was due to take effect on Sunday.
It comes days after Trump said the US would import Russian diesel in an effort to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections in November, which will decide which party controls Congress.
The plan shocked lawmakers, and has triggered a bipartisan backlash.
The US sanctions law is named for the late Republican South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, who was one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.
The law took aim at Russia's economy, and gave Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.
Additionally, the law includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.
On Thursday, a bipartisan group of 20 US lawmakers issued a letter calling on Trump to respect the new law, which is due to take effect on 18 October.
The lawmakers thanked Trump for signing the sanctions bill, and urged his "full and faithful implementation" of the law.
The lawmakers said it would be "decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously" and called on the Trump administration "to apply the Graham law's sanctions to their fullest extent and without delay".
Democrats such as the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer have already criticised Trump's sanctions move, accusing him of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X.
On 9 October, Trump announced that he had held a phone call with Putin, and had agreed to purchase diesel from Moscow. Since the war with Iran started in February, US fuel and especially diesel prices have skyrocketed, adding to the financial pressure faced by American voters already worried about the cost of living. Trump hopes to bring fuel costs down before next month's mid-term elections.
US allies criticised the diesel deal, anxious that it could help Russia in its war effort.
Next month hundreds of troops from Britain, France and Germany - key European allies of Ukraine - will take part in a major military exercise in Poland.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the drill was "to ensure we are ready to support the military training and post-war rebuilding that Ukraine will need".
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called Trump's diesel deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".
On Sunday, 11 October, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire", insisting that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.
Zelensky expressed surprise at the announcement, but said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same, but Moscow said it had never agreed to the deal and continued its attacks. After three days, Kyiv resumed its strikes.
This prompted scathing criticism from Trump, with the president calling Kyiv's strikes on Russian oil refineries a "disgrace". Zelensky responded, saying he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests".
Tensions were further heightened earlier in the week, when restrictions were placed on the US-owned Starlink internet network, which is critical for Kyiv's military abilities to defend itself.
During a slowdown on Tuesday night, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying there was no prior warning.
On Friday, Zelensky called the slowdown a "very dangerous and unpleasant surprise", adding that Starlink speeds were still not fully restored.
The Trump administration had previously warned that it could withhold intelligence-sharing - crucial for Ukraine's defences - if Kyiv does not stop hitting Russia's oil refineries.

As polls indicate Democrats could take back the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the Trump administration. But that may prove to be a difficult task, even with a majority in both chambers of Congress.
In late September, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a report on Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency titled “DOGE: Congress and the Public Lack Assurance That Systems and Data Were Protected at Multiple Agencies.” In it, the GAO revealed that multiple executive branch agencies had refused to fully cooperate with investigators about the extent and nature of DOGE’s access to sensitive systems and information. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), which DOGE and the Trump administration gutted in the early months of the president’s second term, sent GAO a letter accusing investigators of bias and alleging the report was “misleading.”
The report, just the latest example of the Trump administration seeking to dodge congressional oversight, raises questions about what—if any—avenues the legislature has to enforce accountability, or even access basic information about what the government has been doing.
“In a world where there is no shame, it's hard to think of what Congress can do that doesn't involve some coercion of some kind,” says Emily Berman, a law professor at the University of Houston. “Like withholding money or going to court.”
The GAO serves as Congress’ primary investigative body; its work is most often initiated by requests from Congress, but it is independent and nonpartisan. It does not, however, have the ability to enforce laws or take on prosecution. Federal agencies don’t necessarily have to enact the agency’s suggestions, but they are legally required to cooperate with GAO’s requests for information and auditing.
The GAO and a Democratic congressional aide who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity, though, say that the agencies investigated by the GAO for the DOGE report—the CFPB, the Department of Veterans’ Affairs (VA), the Department of Education, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and the Small Business Administration (SBA)—all, in one way or another, refused to cooperate with the investigation.
“We have experienced increased challenges in obtaining information from agencies over the past year and a half,” GAO spokesperson Sarah Kaczmarek says. “As this report demonstrates, when agencies do not provide requested information, it can limit GAO’s ability to provide Congress and the public with assurance that federal programs, systems, and information are appropriately managed and protected.”
As an example, every agency included in the report refused to do so much as name which DOGE operatives they’d played host to—even when that information had already been publicly reported. The CFPB refused to name all six of the DOGE operatives who were detailed to the agency even though, in February 2025, WIRED identified three of them: Nikhil Rajpal, Chris Young, and Gavin Kliger. DOGE members Jeremy Lewin and Jordan Wick were also part of the team at the agency.

According to the report, both the SBA and the VA “did not respond to requests for information needed to determine the access DOGE team members had to their systems.” Previous reporting from WIRED found that the DOGE affiliate at the VA, Sahil Lavingia, sought to use AI to write code for the agency’s systems, and at the SBA, DOGE affiliates Edward “Big Balls” Coristine and Donald Park were granted broad access to the agency’s financial and loan systems.
VA and SBA did not respond to a request for comment.
The Democratic aide says that in addition to the VA and SBA refusing to provide information, several agencies slow-walked their responses to the GAO. The aide says that meeting some resistance within an agency to a GAO investigation is not unheard of, but that responses to the DOGE inquiry represented a “surprising” level of obstruction.
“We did see a little bit of a range in terms of cooperation,” they say. “Normally, an agency might be reluctant to provide as much information as the GAO requests, but then they try to find accommodations. If they can't provide X, they provide Y. If they can't provide Y maybe they could walk investigators through something, or show different things. But there's just a complete lack of willingness to kind of get to yes.”
And it’s not just the agencies named in the DOGE report that have been resistant to congressional efforts to investigate. In a statement to WIRED, Senator Ron Wyden, the Oregon Democrat, says that his office was notified by the GAO that the Commerce Department “is refusing to cooperate with my request with Sen. Welch to investigate the effectiveness of U.S. export controls to address AI-fueled national security risks.”
The Department of Commerce did not respond to a request for comment.
“There is no good reason to deny GAO investigators the access they need to root out corruption and waste in federal programs,” says Wyden.
While the current Republican-led Congress appears to have little interest in using them, there are tools to enforce cooperation with a GAO investigation. The most obvious–and likely–is using their subpoena power, which the Democratic aide says members of Congress are preparing to do. “We are expecting that the administration is gearing up for the [the next Congress] to be hostile,” they say.
If someone refuses to cooperate with a subpoena, Congress can hold them in contempt. “It used to be that if Congress threatened to hold an executive official in contempt of Congress, that was like a huge embarrassment,” says Berman. “And that imposed a lot of pressure on the executive branch to reach some agreement with Congress.” But in recent years this has changed. Since 2012, three different attorneys general have been held in contempt of Congress, with seemingly few repercussions.
This is because without the cooperation of executive branch agencies like the Department of Justice, Congress has little power to enforce a subpoena or hold those who don’t comply in contempt.
Last month, Congress held billionaire Leon Black in contempt for refusing to answer subpoenas to return and testify under oath regarding his connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Whether Black will face any consequences, however, is now out of Congress’ hands—the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia will ultimately decide whether or not to prosecute him.
Without being able to count on the support of agencies nested under the executive branch and staffed by presidential picks, Berman says, today’s Congress now has fewer options than in the past. It could impose fines on those held in contempt; it “can arrest them and put them in their little jail cell in the basement of the Capitol;” or it could file a lawsuit, potentially winding all the way up to the Supreme Court. But any legal case could easily stretch beyond the House’s two-year term, creating “a real problem” for using the courts to enforce accountability, says Berman.
“This is part of a broader shift of power from Congress to the executive branch,” she says. “Over time, the way the law has moved is to give the executive branch more and more power and discretion over decisions within its own branch. So it's had the effect of essentially broadening the scope of what the executive branch can argue they're entitled to keep secret.”
With its own oversight powers limited, Congress is going to have to think of other ways to force the executive branch to cooperate. Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat who serves as the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, told reporters in September that Congress has “the power of the purse” as a way to pressure the executive branch to comply with investigations.
But in order for this power to be effective, Congress would need to change the way it legislates. As it stands, Berman says, the budget is a “blunt tool” because Congress often passes legislation in large omnibus bills. This means that critical funding for regular government operations, or initiatives that have broad bipartisan support, is often bundled along with other allocations for the administration’s priorities. For instance, following the killing of Alex Pretti by two Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents during the Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota, Senate Democrats refused to pass an appropriations bill that included funding for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees CBP. What followed was a months-long partial government shutdown. But DHS is also home to the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), meaning that TSA workers went without pay for weeks, and led to massive delays at airports around the country.
Berman says that if Democrats take control of the Senate, they could also put pressure on the administration through refusing to confirm appointments unless the executive branch cooperates with investigations.
But in reality, she says, “there are no good options.”

Ethnic wear brand Libas is opening nine exclusive brand outlets (EBOs) across five Indian cities during Navratri, expanding its retail footprint during a key festive shopping period. The rollout spans high-street locations and shopping malls in Bengaluru, Jaipur, Kanpur, Noida, and Jabalpur. With these nine new openings, Libas now operates 55+ stores across India. Flash floods have swept through Nepal’s central Gorkha district after a pre-dawn landslide on 11 October blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, triggering severe downstream flooding. Two villages in the worst-affected Chumanubri rural municipality were reportedly destroyed, with homes, roads and bridges washed away. Part of a hydropower station was also damaged.
After river levels surged from 2 metres to nearly 8.5 metres within hours, the national disaster risk reduction and management authority reported that 204 homes were damaged, and more than 650 people had been affected. More than 100 foreign trekkers were stranded in the popular hiking region. The floods come just two months after catastrophic flooding and landslides devastated parts of the country on the border with Tibet, leaving thousands dead or missing.
An exceptionally deep area of low pressure barrelled towards Iceland this week. The central pressure was measured at 931mb on 14 October. The pressure plummeted by 49mb in 24 hours, meeting the thresholds for explosive cyclogenesis, or a weather bomb. The system brought sustained winds of 55–60mph to the southern shores of the island before moving north-east through the North Atlantic towards Norway.
However, Iceland was spared the strongest winds as the track of the storm meant they remained out at sea. The system also affected areas beyond Iceland: a 108mph gust was recorded at Bealach Na Bà, in the Scottish Highlands, in association with a trailing 1,000-mile cold front that stretched from Norway to the mid-Atlantic.
Summer-like conditions have extended even further into meteorological autumn in Portugal. After temperatures of 40C at the end of September, on 14 October a maximum of 35.6C was recorded in the southern town of Mora, representing a climatological anomaly of more than 10C.
The heat was not localised, with numerous stations recording temperatures well into the mid-30s celsius. The latest forecasts show that the high pressure and unseasonably warm upper air temperatures will remain in place for the next few days. Looking further ahead, however, temperatures are expected to slowly return towards the average around the middle of next week.

Does Scott's Disney+ exit unmask wider issue in coverage of women's game?
- Published
On Thursday, former England footballer Alex Scott stepped away from Disney+'s coverage of the Women's Champions League after two rounds of matches.
The streaming giant is in the second season of a five-year deal to cover European football's flagship competition and this year introduced new formats, including a watchalong show with Scott alternating presenting duties with Shebahn Aherne.
However, it has had some technical issues and been criticised for a difficult opening night that included an unscheduled advert break during Arsenal's game against HB Koge.
Scott has not said why she left this role but told BBC Sport she was "grateful" for the opportunities she had at Disney+ and hoped to "continue working together" in the future.
But does her sudden departure highlight the challenges broadcasters face covering the women's game in an ever-changing media landscape?
- Ad break in Women's Champions League was unscheduled 
  - Published23 September
Broadcasters 'not sure who the audience is'
The explosion in interest in women's football during the past five years has been spearheaded by two of the biggest broadcasters in the UK – Sky Sports and the BBC.
In snapping up the Champions League before the 2025-26 season, Disney added its heft into the game, recognising its potential for capturing new audiences.
Indeed, Scott herself has launched her own YouTube show this season, One More Word WSL, which she presents on a Sunday night alongside ex-England internationals Anita Asante and Fara Williams.
Broadcasters have ramped up experiments with format, style and tone - Disney+ even had a dog on set during their coverage - but perhaps unsurprisingly, not every idea proves to be successful.
Journalist Carrie Dunn, who has covered women's sport for more than two decades, says opinions about coverage reflect a tension at the heart of the game.
"The challenge broadcasters are finding is that they are not sure who the audience is," she says. "A lot of it is targeted at a new generation and it's clearly not for people who have watched women's football for longer.
"Often it's a resourcing issue. Budgets are being cut and you're finding the same presenters and the same pundits trying to be all things to all people. It just doesn't work."
In the summer, the BBC announced its Women's Super League highlights show would not return for the 2026-27 season, but insisted it remained "fully committed to women's football".
To illustrate, it cited a bespoke new YouTube channel, the introduction of a debate show entitled The Women's Football Fallout, exclusively on BBC iPlayer, and the availability of clips and analysis on the BBC Sport website as evidence.
The decisions are part of a move away from linear television that the BBC says reflects changing audience habits.
It is a shift in emphasis that comes with difficulties.
"It's a tough balance where you've got to explain some context to the new fans without patronising your older fans," Dunn adds. "That's something the major broadcasters have not found a solution to yet.
"If people are willing to take risks on different kinds of women's sports coverage, that's fantastic.
"But start by choosing one thing and doing it really well – and that's got to be decent match coverage."
What do WSL managers think?
Aston Villa interim boss Brian Sorensen started as a coach in Denmark in 2009 and believes the innovations in women's football coverage are a good thing, even if some do not always work.
"A lot of positive things are happening, but there are a lot of new areas that we haven't tried before," he said. "Sometimes it's trial and error and finding the right way for us.
"From when I started - with the worst live stream you've ever seen - to where we are now, is a very big improvement."
Andree Jeglertz, manager of champions Manchester City, agrees, acknowledging that the fact women's football has a much bigger audience now is a huge positive.
"I think the most important thing is that it is available and that people can see the best players on TV or live," he said. "The more, the better, no matter what."
Tottenham counterpart Martin Ho says the onus is on clubs and players to ensure the product on the field is worth watching.
"Whatever a broadcast partner decides to do, they have their reasons for it," he said. "All we can control is that we put on a good advert for women's football."
Finally, Chelsea's Sonia Bompastor suggested she was open to new expressions in covering the game provided they were properly analysed.
"Anytime you try to do something new, you will please some people and upset others," she told BBC Sport. "Sometimes you need to be patient and analyse as it is too soon to say if something is right or not."

US President Donald Trump built his political identity around a simple promise: he could strike “deals” that traditional politicians could not. From repeatedly claiming he could end wars to attempting to reshape global trade through tariff threats, Trump has presented himself as a negotiator capable of turning pressure into results. But his record in the White House is raising questions about the limits of that approach. Trump’s reputation as a dealmaker predates his political career. In 1982, shortly after Trump Tower opened in New York, the then 38-year-old developer suggested he could negotiate arms-control agreements with the Soviet Union better than President Ronald Reagan. His 1987 book, The Art of the Deal, later cemented that image. Four decades on, the same persona remains central to his presidency. Yet the conflicts involving Iran and Russia, alongside trade disputes triggered by his tariff policies, have highlighted the challenges of translating ambitious promises into lasting outcomes. “He’s not as good at this as he thinks he is,” Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center, an international security think tank, told the Associated Press. Trump promised to end Russia’s war in Ukraine within a day, but the conflict continues. His handling of Iran has also drawn scrutiny. After projecting confidence in a swift outcome, he announced what he called a “great” ceasefire, which quickly faltered. His repeated assertions that Tehran was eager to negotiate have not consistently produced the outcomes he had described. Trade policy has presented another test. Trump argued that tariffs would give Washington leverage to secure favourable agreements. However, unilateral duties have fuelled trade tensions, including with Canada, while raising costs for American businesses and consumers. Trump’s negotiating style took shape during decades in real estate, where aggressive bargaining and high-risk ventures helped build his public profile. His business career, however, also featured financial setbacks, bankruptcies and legal disputes involving contractors, business partners and creditors. Marty Latz, a negotiation expert and author of The Real Trump Deal, told AP that Trump had secured some successful agreements but had also experienced major failures. Barbara Res, a former Trump Organization executive responsible for construction, argued that Trump's personal pride could complicate negotiations. “He could be a better negotiator if his ego didn’t get in the way,” Res said, according to AP. Trump’s preference for presenting negotiations as contests with winners and losers can project resolve. But diplomacy often requires compromise, sustained engagement and confidence that commitments will be honoured — conditions that can be difficult to establish through threats alone. The 2004 debut of The Apprentice gave Trump's business persona a fresh platform. The reality television show portrayed him as a decisive executive who evaluated contestants and controlled the boardroom, reinforcing an image that later became central to his presidential campaigns. Tim O’Brien, author of TrumpNation: The Art of Being The Donald, told AP that unpredictability was central to Trump's negotiating style. “If he’s the one causing the chaos, he’s often the only one who can end it,” O’Brien said. Trump outlined his approach in The Art of the Deal: “I aim very high, and then I just keep pushing and pushing and pushing to get what I’m after.” Such tactics can create leverage, but they can also harden opposition when counterparts refuse to yield. The White House has defended Trump's record, citing trade agreements and investment commitments as evidence of his negotiating abilities. Trump’s supporters also point to the Abraham Accords, negotiated during his first term, as a significant diplomatic achievement. His business career, meanwhile, involved extensive litigation. Latz has argued that legal disputes could serve as bargaining tools to pressure counterparties or reduce financial liabilities, according to AP. With inputs from AP. During four decades of studying the effects of interaction with computers, Sherry Turkle has developed a reputation as a careful if critical social scientist who approaches her work with academic rigor and distance.
Her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, breaks this mold. It is a polemic warning that we have reached a state of emergency where our humanity is at risk from overreliance on soulless machines who pose as our tutors, mentors, friends, colleagues, and lovers. Turkle is aiming for the high bar of books —Silent Spring, The Jungle, Unsafe at Any Speed—that awaken the public to impending crises.
Essentially, this diminutive MIT professor is taking on a multitrillion-dollar industry backed by a government eager to accelerate AI into every corner of our personal and professional lives.
STEVEN LEVY: Your previous books reported results of your research as a social scientist, often leading to troubling conclusions about how people, especially children, interact with computers. But this book reads like you’re breaking the glass and pulling the fire alarm. Why the shift?
SHERRY TURKLE: Like I do with all my books, I went in curious. But after 10 or so interviews, conducted during the pandemic, neutral-curious was no longer my state of mind. This was terrible! Here are these people during the pandemic, their families are suffering, reaching out to them, and they're talking to me about how they really want to just hang with their chatbot. When I was able to interview people face to face, I was not happy. People don't want to do anything in politics because they just want to live in chatbot-land. So the arc of the book ended up as—reality needs you. It couldn't be a worse time to give up on reality.
You write that social media set us up for this.
Social media softened us up by getting us used to the idea that if you're feeling sad or blue, open up your computer. Then it made you mad and kept you with your own kind. But now we have this new technology that has no reason to be first-person.
Do you think that we should ban chatbots from using the first person?
Yes! After a career of having credibility as not being Luddite-crazy, I'm not in the mood to give all that away and say all chatbots are toxic all the time. But this is very dangerous, a slippery slope. This is being used to basically say we don't need to pay for psychotherapy, we can use chatbots. In every serious interview I do, people invoke this myth about practice—that you use chatbots to practice for talking to your boss, your lover, your teacher. But when you’re bathing in the warm soup of total acceptance [from LLMs], talking to chatbots becomes the endgame.
You also have a problem with reliance on chatbots in the workplace, and a particular loathing for the term “human in the loop.”
When they use that term, it means the human has been taken out of the productive process and is there to do some sort of cleanup work, to catch the hallucinations or things the AI doesn’t see. That doesn't work, because employers only have a couple of humans in the loop. Those people basically can't change anything. They are there partly to make it sound good when they're litigated, and partly to give people a false sense that the process hasn't been delegated to an AI. But it has been delegated to an AI.
Maybe powerful chatbots are a new form of interaction that isn’t necessarily worse than human conversation, but different, as people report feeling encouraged and empowered by the positive feedback they provide.
An AI won't ever replace human conversation. It’s really not afraid of death, it’s not afraid of illness, it's not afraid of pain, it doesn't love its children, and it doesn't care if you kill yourself or make dinner. So if we raise our kids with it, or have our most intimate conversations with it, we're going to lose contact.
Still, a lot of people have nobody to talk to. They feel that talking to chatbots helps them.
If there's a crisis of loneliness, it's because we're abandoning each other. Give me one data center, and I will turn it into resources for the elderly.
Studies show that most people are skeptical about AI, and there has been considerable pushback. Yet hundreds of millions of people use them. Even people who push back against data centers are using chatbots.
The goal of this book is to expand the terms of the pushback to include this more intimate connection.
Do you really feel that our growing intimacy with AI can be stopped?
I have more hope now than I did six months ago, because of all of this talk about extinction events and Hugging Face and getting into the Australian civil service by mistake. I feel that people will be willing to look at the intimate as well as the non-intimate costs.
