The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed prohibiting the addition of sucrose and fructose in food products intended for infants up to six months of age.
The draft Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Amendment Regulations, 2026, published in the Gazette of India on Friday (October 16, 2026) proposes to amend the existing regulations governing the nutritional composition, quality and safety of infant nutrition products.
The proposed amendment states that “sucrose and fructose shall not be added in the products intended for infants up to the age of 6 months”.
Under the existing Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, lactose and glucose polymers are the preferred sources of carbohydrates in infant nutrition products. Sucrose and/or fructose may be added when required as a carbohydrate source, subject to prescribed limits.
The draft amendment seeks to introduce a specific restriction on their addition in products intended for infants in the first six months of life.
Critical period
“The first six months are a critical period for infant growth and development, making appropriate nutrition particularly important. The proposed restriction aims to ensure that products intended for this age group meet their nutritional requirements without the addition of sucrose and fructose,” the government maintained in a release issued on Saturday (October 16).
It added that early exposure to added sugars is a public health concern because of its potential implications for the development of dietary preferences and long-term dietary habits. Unhealthy dietary patterns are among the risk factors associated with childhood obesity and related health problems.
“The proposal also complements public health recommendations advocating exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life. The World Health Organization recommends exclusive breastfeeding during this period, followed by the introduction of nutritionally adequate complementary foods alongside continued breastfeeding,” said the release.
For public consultation
The notification has been issued for public consultation. Stakeholders have been invited to submit objections and suggestions within 60 days from the date on which copies of the official gazette containing the notification are made available to the public.
FSSAI will consider the representations received within the stipulated period before finalising the amendment. The proposed restriction will become part of the regulatory framework only after the amendment is finalised and notified.

Kenya confirms second Ebola case - a relative of the first victim
- Published
Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The new patient, a 39-year-old man, is a close relative of the first case and was already in quarantine when he fell ill on Tuesday, Kenya's health ministry says.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Detecting his illness early had improved his chances of recovery and limited the chance of him passing the virus on to others, the ministry said, as it urged the public to "stay calm but vigilant".
"Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," the ministry said.
"Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings", it added.
The 40-year-old Kenyan man who died on 5 October was diagnosed with Ebola shortly after being admitted to hospital in the capital, Nairobi.
A relative had taken him there shortly after picking him up at the airport. He had travelled from DR Congo, through Uganda to Kenya without his illness being detected.
Since his death, officials had determined that he had been in contact with 128 people - and since Tuesday 113 of them had been found, the health ministry said.
Of these, 108 were in quarantine in Kenya and tracing of the remaining 15 continued, it said.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
"Anyone with fever, unusual tiredness, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding should seek care promptly at the nearest health facility," Kenya's health ministry said.
The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.
However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the continent's leading public health agency, has reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements for the six weeks leading up to his death.
It revealed that he first started feeling unwell in DR Congo on 15 September - and showed how several opportunities to detect the infection were missed, including during several visits to Congolese medical facilities.
He then managed to travel through Uganda to Kenya - and was again not detected at airports screenings.
Health experts say it highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.

Why it's important to avoid plugging in a damaged external hard drive
Resist the urge to plug in the drive you just dropped to see if it's OK.
On the surface, your external hard drive might look like a sturdy device. But beneath that enclosure are a number of moving parts (sometimes including glass) working together to store your data and retrieve it when requested. In other words, your external hard drive is more fragile than you think; that's why it's important to avoid immediately plugging it back in after a fall or other damage.
Unlike speedier external SSDs, external hard drives are more susceptible to damage. It's thus even more important to handle HDDs with care and know what to do after they take a hit. To give some perspective, the read/write heads and platters in a typical external hard drive usually operate just nanometers away from each other — even a small drop can close that gap. After the impact, your data is likely still intact. But if you plug it in thinking it was no big deal, you significantly increase the risk of permanent data loss.
What happens when you plug in a damaged hard drive?
External hard drives work by spinning very fast (5,400 or 7,200 RPM), and that speed is one of the reasons why plugging in a damaged hard drive is risky: it makes damage spread quickly. For example, suppose the read/write heads were misaligned by the fall. The moment you plug the drive back in, it forces the heads back over the platters (where your data is stored). This can scratch the magnetic surface, and scratched platters equal permanent data loss. So the longer it's plugged in, the more data you're likely to lose.
Also, debris from the first scratch can get caught up in the spin and cause further damage as it collides with and contaminates other parts of the drive's platter surface. And the risks of this happening become more likely if the drive was running when it fell.
Plugging in a damaged hard drive not only complicates repair, but it also makes data recovery much harder. Technicians usually perform data recovery by replacing damaged parts with donor parts, then they copy the data off the platters bit by bit. But if the drive is plugged in after it absorbs damage, each spin-up will further scratch the platters, resulting in more lost and unrecoverable data.
What to do with a damaged external hard drive
If your external hard drive takes a fall or is otherwise seriously hit, it's best to treat it as damaged until you know otherwise, especially if it was running at the time. The tricky part is safely confirming the drive's health after the fall. Most importantly, don't plug it into your computer, and unplug it immediately if it's still connected. Resist the urge to try tapping it, shaking it, opening it up or freezing it. Any of those actions can worsen the hard drive's condition if it was damaged.
The only true way to safely assess the drive's condition after a fall is through professional evaluation. If the data inside the drive matters to you and isn't backed up, get it to an established data recovery service before taking any risks. If the data is not that important or you're willing to take the risk, then do a careful single test. Plug in the drive and listen closely as it spins up. If you hear any abnormal noises like clicking, beeping or grinding, or the drive repeatedly restarts, unplug it immediately.
If it mounts and operates normally, immediately copy your most important files off the drive before running diagnostic tools. After you've saved your important files, check the hard drive's health through its SMART data (the drive's built-in health monitoring) using tools like CrystalDiskInfo. If the tool returns warnings like reallocated or pending sectors, treat the drive as unreliable and move the rest of your data to another safe location.
Keep in mind that some USB enclosures can't report SMART data and passing tests isn't a guarantee of a drive's ongoing health, although it is a good sign. Going forward, practicing habits like not moving a drive while it's running and remembering to eject external drives properly can reduce the risk of damaging your drive. And if you plan to retire one, store the old drive properly so it stays safe in the archives.

Two teenage boys have been arrested following an alleged fight at Mosely Square in Glenelg, after reports of a disturbance involving a large group of youths.

The reason why your drive shows less storage than you paid for
Understanding the difference between decimal and binary.
Device storage is extremely valuable these days. The rabid appetite of AI datacenters is inflating drive pricing so badly that companies like Apple and Valve have jacked up the prices of some products by hundreds of dollars. Even if that wasn't happening, though, the size of apps, media and operating systems is continually growing, filling up the storage we do have. Some PC and console games can top 100GB, especially if they're live service titles with a lot of downloadable content.
All this is to say that if there's a gap between the amount of storage you're promised for an internal or external drive versus what's actually usable, the disappointment may be palpable now more than ever. Recently, for example, we discovered that a 512GB drive only registered as offering 477GB accessible to Windows. On paper, that 35GB difference might be enough to fit someone's entire photo library, or maybe a converted 4K HDR movie.
In most instances, the root of these discrepancies boils down to how different companies calculate data, rather than a naked attempt to rip you off. At other times, it may be a matter of a device being unusable without some of that space going to pre-installed software.
The harsh impacts of math
Frequently, storage makers calculate storage capacity using a base-10 (decimal) system. In that arrangement, a kilobyte is 1,000 bytes, a gigabyte is 1 billion bytes, and so forth. And that probably makes sense to you, given how measurements work in most other areas of life, especially if you live in a country using the metric system for weights and distances. It's a lot easier to market to the average consumer.
The thing is, software platforms like Windows often gauge capacity in binary terms. That transforms a kilobyte into 1,024 bytes, and a gigabyte into 1,073,741,824 bytes. As figures get larger, the gap between binary and decimal calculations becomes vast. A 1TB drive may show as holding just 931GB in Windows, despite nothing actually being lost. You will see the full 1TB available on a Mac, where decimal reigns supreme.
This is obviously problematic if you're expecting storage marketed in binary terms versus the way hardware makers label it. To our knowledge, Microsoft doesn't have any intention of switching Windows from binary to decimal, and Apple isn't planning to revert the Mac, iPad, iPhone or other products back to binary. You can expect this inconsistency to exist in the market for a while longer.
There have been attempts to make the situation clearer by using binary-specific terms such as "kibibyte" (KiB) and "gibibyte" (GiB). As you've probably noticed, though, these haven't caught on, even within binary-based platforms. If you check the file size of something in Windows 11, you'll see KB or GB instead.
The operating system complication
A complaint you'll run into occasionally is that the new phone, tablet, laptop or console they bought doesn't have as much usable space as they expected. This can potentially be linked to the binary-decimal split we just talked about, but the bigger culprit tends to be the device OS, which has to be pre-installed for anything to work. iOS 27 consumes over 22GB (decimal) on a 128GB iPhone 16 Pro, and on one of our gaming laptops, Windows 11 occupies over 81GB (binary). It's no wonder that 64GB devices are effectively extinct, and that even 128GB is becoming impractical.
As if things weren't complicated enough, operating systems tend to grow every year as new features are added. And to run smoothly, most devices need additional cache and swap space for temporary files. This space isn't necessarily marked off-limits. If it isn't, though, you can accidentally harm performance by downloading too many files or installing too many apps. Vanishing swap space bogs down performance, and can lead to apps crashing or freezing.
To cope with this unfortunate scenario, all you can really do is be conservative with your usage and shopping habits. If you avoid waste and overestimate the amount of storage you need, even a few dozen gigabytes can be an acceptable sacrifice. Don't panic if you notice this when planning your next electronics haul.

The Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection) Bill, 2026, that will be tabled in the Assembly on Tuesday aims at promoting healthy and active ageing, registration and regulation of senior citizen care centres, capacity-building for family and caregivers, and protection of rights, dignity, and social security of the elderly.
The Bill underscores the principles of right to dignity, ageing in place and home-based care, safety and social care ecosystem, and senior citizens’ participation in policy making. Thrust is also given to rights such as access care, safe public spaces, digital inclusion, legal aid, reporting of abuse, and access to dignity-preserving products.
The Bill points out that the population of the elderly has been increasing in Keralam. However, modernisation and globalisation had paved the way for nuclear families, adversely affecting the living conditions of the elderly. In order to accommodate their needs, various systems need to be put in place and long-term forward planning is required.
It calls for urgent policy intervention to integrate and standardise home-based health-care services and create a legal framework for their operation.
The government also aims at ensuring that older persons are not marginalised or left unprotected, advocating for their financial security, health care, shelter, and protection of rights.
Protection unit
According to the Bill, the government will set up a State Senior Citizen Protection Unit, besides a District Senior Citizen Protection Forum in each district. A District Senior Citizen Protection Unit will also be formed in each district to assist the District Senior Citizen Protection Forum.
The forum will monitor the policies and schemes of the government implemented through the District Senior Citizen Protection Unit, activities of care centres, mobilise local organisations to carry out activities related to care and protection of the elderly, and take suo motu action on complaints.
The Bill deals with registration of senior citizen care centres in detail.
It requires every home-care service agency that operates or engages caregivers through a digital platform, mobile application, website or other online intermediary to maintain an accurate and updated list of caregivers deployed through it.
Training to caregivers, with phased certification compliance, is another aspect. It proposes that the government establish a ‘Keralam Geriatric Care Certification Framework’ providing progressive certification pathways for caregivers. A ‘State Register of Caregivers’ is also mooted in the Bill.
Other mechanisms proposed include Senior Citizen Cyber Fraud Cell in all cyber police stations and a State reserve fund for protection, care, welfare and social security of the senior citizens.
The Bill also lays down punishment for violation of provisions of the Act and rules and guidelines issued under it.

A powerful new genetic toolkit that could make it easier to study the bacteria responsible for Tuberculosis (TB), one of the world’s deadliest infectious diseases, has been developed by Vinay Kumar Nandicoori, Director of the CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB).
Investigate how different proteins work together
Designed for use in mycobacteria, the new system could accelerate efforts to understand how the TB bacterium survives, grows and causes disease. It gives scientists tools to switch genes on, track proteins inside bacterial cells, and investigate how different proteins work together.
Despite decades of research, many genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the bacterium that causes TB, remain poorly understood. Scientists typically rely on specially designed DNA molecules known as ‘shuttle vectors’ to introduce genes into bacterial cells and study their functions. However, the complex protein interactions within a cell are difficult to monitor.
New shuttle vectors with fluorescent markers
To address this challenge, Mr. Nandicoori’s research student Asis Kumar used existing knowledge to create a collection of 40 new shuttle vectors. These molecular delivery vehicles carry selected genes into bacterial cells, enabling researchers to study them in different ways.
The new genetic toolkit offers greater flexibility because the shuttle vectors can be equipped with fluorescent markers such as Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) and ‘mCherry’, which make proteins glow under a microscope. This allows researchers to observe where specific proteins are located inside bacterial cells and how they move during growth and division, explained Mr. Nandicoori, in an exclusive interaction.
The team tested the new tools in Mycobacterium smegmatis, a harmless relative of the TB bacterium that is commonly used in laboratories. The fluorescent tags successfully highlighted the locations of key proteins involved in cell growth and division, confirming that the system worked as intended.
The toolkit also enables scientists to study several proteins simultaneously. The research team examined how four different regulatory proteins from the TB bacterium functioned within a single bacterial cell, providing insight into how proteins interact and coordinate critical cellular processes.
Another significant feature is a new purification method that reduces background contamination and improves the identification of proteins that naturally interact inside the cell. This is important because many biological processes are carried out not by individual proteins, but by groups of proteins working together, said the Director.
Mr. Nandicoori said the genetic toolkit could be expanded in the future with new genetic switches, protein tags and regulatory elements, making it adaptable to a wide range of experiments. The study was published in ‘Journal of Bacteriology’.

How Can I Tell Which AirPods I Have?
How do you know which case to buy? Apple has several generations of its AirPods, whether you have the standard AirPods or the AirPods Pro, so be sure the case you select works with your model. (Some cases are interchangeable, particularly the first- and second-generation AirPods and the first- and second-generation AirPods Pro.) If your AirPods aren't connected to an Apple device, you can find the model number on the device itself. It's on the underside of each earbud—you may need to use your smartphone's zoom feature to read it.
Once you have the model number, you can cross-reference it with this tool to identify the generation. You can also just check the receipt in your order history if you purchased them online.
You probably know if you bought a different case for your AirPods, but it's worth checking the case's model number, too, as Apple has released stand-alone models with wireless charging and MagSafe support. You can find those details here.
How We Test AirPods Cases
I make sure these cases provide adequate protection in day-to-day life. I keep my AirPods in most of the time and always tote them around, so these cases get a lot of field testing. I also make sure they allow the full use of AirPods' features, like hearing the Find My tone or allowing wireless charging. A Reform UK mayor is under police investigation for allegedly showing “naked and sexualised” images of himself to a female member of staff.
Luke Campbell, a former Olympic boxing champion and the mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire, is understood to have been questioned under caution by Humberside police earlier this month.

The woman said she had felt “shocked, embarrassed and humiliated” and claimed she had been forced out of her job soon after, according to documents submitted as part of an internal grievance procedure at Hull and East Yorkshire combined authority (Heyca).
Campbell, who was elected last May, has not responded to requests to comment. It is understood that he has not been arrested in relation to the allegations, which Reform UK has said he “firmly denies”.
A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Luke firmly denies the allegations. They come from a disgruntled employee attempting to leverage a settlement in a meritless workplace dispute.”
The allegations against Campbell came to light after a year-long ITV investigation uncovered racist comments from a number of Reform UK councillors and a prospective MP.
An aspiring Reform UK MP was suspended after telling an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers crossing the English channel should be put in “concentration camps”, in footage due to be broadcast on Sunday night.
Nigel Farage’s party said it had opened investigations where activists or members had “clearly behaved inappropriately”, adding that there was “no room for racism” in the party.

In one document, corroborated by the Guardian, a senior female colleague said Campbell had called her over to a computer screen, where she was shown “several naked and sexualised images” of the mayor.

If you got a DM from an unverified Jon Bon Jovi account after commenting on one of his official Instagram posts, what would it take to make you believe it was really the rock star hoping to connect? And at what point when he starts asking you to send money—like lose-your-house kind of money—would you snap out of the fantasy and stop draining your bank account?
In a documentary premiering Saturday—Super Scam Me—investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller goes deep into this toxic love-bombing terrain. In a clip that Ars is exclusively debuting below, you can see how van Zeller worked with an ethical hacker, Arman the Cyber, to use a fake bitcoin receipt and bait the fake Bon Jovi, giving the victim some much-needed closure.
Scamming a romance scammer
Broadcasting on National Geographic at 9 pm ET and available to stream on Disney+ and Hulu, the documentary takes viewers on an empathetic quest to understand how the line between “lover” and “fraud victim” gets blurred in romance scams that the Federal Trade Commission says cost Americans nearly $1.5 billion in losses each year.
Often targeting older women with resources who lack community and seek out connections online, such as widows or divorcées, these scams are now a leading form of financial fraud in the US, the FTC has warned. Most victims never get their money back, and overseas scammers are only getting more sophisticated, thanks to AI, Experian forecasted in January.
In Super Scam Me, viewers get a chance to go beyond a single victim’s story and see how romance scams operate so effectively to squeeze funds out of the people they target on social media apps like Instagram or dating apps like Match and Tinder. Van Zeller has spent years reporting on the scam industry, and when she saw how many victims were broken and stranded by romance scams, she devised a social experiment in which she became the target. Her plan worked quickly, hooking a scammer in Ghana who began posing as a handsome overseas four-star military general named “Mark Turner.”
Relying on a wig, big glasses, and a prosthetic nose to cover her true identity as a journalist (should the scammer try to reverse-image search her profile), van Zeller posed as a middle-age antiques dealer named “Mary Zelle.” She staged her pictures to show she was a fun-time gal living her best single life. Once she hooked the scammer, she used the same tactics that outed the fake Bon Jovi in a scheme to meet her scammer face to face. To track him down, she partly relied on distributing flyers in his neighborhood that included a mashup photo of the supposedly loving couple that “Mark Turner” made to woo “Mary Zelle.”

Pune Police has booked Rapido parent Roppen Transportation Services Pvt Ltd for allegedly running bike-taxi services without the required licence and regulatory approvals, according to an FIR registered at Vishrantwadi police station yesterday. The FIR alleges that the company used its app to facilitate paid passenger rides on two-wheelers registered as non-transport vehicles. The development was first reported by Times of India. Inc42 has reached out to Rapido for comment. The story will be updated on receiving a response. The alleged violation came to light when Pune RTO motor vehicle inspector Prasad Govardhan Surwase booked a ride through the Rapido app during an enforcement drive against unauthorised bike-taxi operations. The action came a day after Pune District Collector and Regional Transport Authority (RTA) chairman Jitendra Dudi directed Rapido to immediately suspend bike-taxi operations across Pune district until it obtained an ebike taxi aggregator licence. The FIR also states that the RTO issued the company a notice on Thursday (October 15). The directive followed a meeting with representatives of auto-rickshaw and cab driver unions and aggregators. Dudi warned that continued operations would invite legal action and said the service would not be allowed to resume without a licence. At the same meeting, Dudi directed cab aggregators to submit monthly fare data to the district administration and display RTA-approved fares separately on their apps. The directions followed complaints from auto-rickshaw and cab drivers that aggregators were violating prescribed fare norms. According to Dudi, the existing norms require drivers to receive 80% of the RTA base fare, while passenger fares can range from 50% below the base fare to 1.5 times that amount. He said the administration had received complaints about drivers being underpaid and passengers being charged beyond the permitted range, prompting the monthly reporting requirement. FIR Cites Previous Regulatory Proceedings The complaint also recounts Rapido’s earlier attempts to secure permission to operate in Pune, including the rejection of its licence application in December 2022 and subsequent proceedings before the Bombay High Court and Supreme Court. The complaint also refers to a notice issued by the Transport Commissioner’s Office on April 29, 2025, over alleged unauthorised passenger transport through Rapido’s app. According to the FIR, Rapido applied for an aggregator licence with the Transport Commissioner’s Office in Mumbai on August 11, 2026, but had not received approval at the time of the incident. Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a new framework for thinking through your ethical dilemmas and philosophical questions. This unconventional column is based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Here is a Vox reader’s question, condensed and edited for clarity.
I give to charity — but never to people on the street. Is that wrong?
The quest to give effectively feels like it’s turning me into an cold-hearted jerk.
I think I have a duty to help people much poorer than me, and I give 10 percent of my salary to charities that I think are effective at preventing early death due to poverty. I also live in a city with a lot of visible homelessness, and am often solicited for money. My brain says that this is not an effective way to help people; the people asking might not be the neediest among the homeless in my city, and the people I’m sending malaria bednets and pills to are even needier. At the same time, I feel callous simply ignoring all these requests. What should I do?
Dear Would-Be Optimizer,
Nine times out of ten, when someone’s got an ethical dilemma, I think it’s because a couple of their core values are conflicting with each other. But you’re that tenth case. I say that because I don’t actually believe your question represents a battle royale between two different values. I think there’s one core value here — helping people — and one strategy that’s masquerading as a value.
That strategy is optimization. I can tell from your phrasing that you’re really into it. You don’t just want to help people — you want to help people as effectively as possible. Since extreme poverty is concentrated in developing countries, and since your dollar goes much further there than it would in your home country, your optimizing impulse is telling you to send your charity money abroad.
Optimization started as a technique for solving certain math problems, but our society has elevated it to the status of a value — arguably one of the dominant values in the Western world. It’s been on the rise since the 1700s, when utilitarian thinkers seeded the idea that both economics and ethics should focus on maximizing utility (meaning, happiness or satisfaction): Just calculate how much utility each action would produce, and choose the one that produces the most.
You can see this logic everywhere in modern life — from work culture, with its emphasis on productivity hacks and agile workflows, to wellness culture, with its emphasis on achieving perfect health and optimal sleep. The mandate to “Live your best life!” is turbocharged by Silicon Valley, which urges us to quantify every aspect of ourselves with Fitbits, Apple Watches, and Oura Rings, because the more data you have on your body’s mechanical functions, the more you can optimize the machine that is you.
Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column?
Fill out this anonymous form! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here!
Optimization definitely has its place, including in the world of charity. Some charitable organizations are much more effective than others trying to achieve the same goal. All things being equal, we don’t want to blow all our money on the wildly ineffective ones. Effective altruists, members of the utilitarian-flavored social movement that aims to do the most good possible, are fond of noting that the most effective charities out there actually produce 100 times more benefit than the average ones. Why not get the biggest bang for your buck?
The problem is that we’ve stretched optimization beyond its optimal limits. We try to apply it to everything. But not every domain in life can be optimized, at least not without compromising on some of our values.
In your case, you’re trying to optimize how much you help others, and you believe that means focusing on the neediest. But “neediest” according to what definition of needy? You could assume that financial need is the only type that counts, so you should focus first on lifting everyone out of extreme poverty, and only then help people in less dire straits. But are you sure that only the brute poverty level matters?
Consider an insight from the Jewish tradition. The ancient rabbis were exquisitely sensitive to the psychological needs of poor people, and they argued that these needs should also be taken into account. So they decreed that you shouldn’t only give poor people enough money to survive on — they need to have more than that so they themselves can give charity to others. As Rabbi Jonathan Sacks writes, “On the face of it, the rule is absurd. Why give X enough money so that he can give to Y? Giving to Y directly is more logical and efficient. What the rabbis understood, however, is that giving is an essential part of human dignity.”
The rabbis also figured that those who used to be well-off but who fell into poverty might feel an especially acute sense of shame. So they suggested helping these people save face by offering them not just bare necessities, but also — when possible — some of the nicer things that graced their former lifestyles. In the Talmud, we hear about one rabbi who gave a newly poor person a fancy meal, and another who acted as the person’s servant for a day! Clearly, the ancient rabbis weren’t only aiming to alleviate poverty. They were also alleviating the shame that can accompany it.
The point is that there are many ways to help people and, because they’re so different, they don’t submit to direct comparison. Comparing poverty and shame is comparing apples to oranges; one can be measured in dollars, but the other can’t. Likewise, how can you ever hope to compare preventing malaria with alleviating depression? Saving lives versus improving them? Or saving the life of a kid versus saving the life of an adult?
Yet if you want to optimize, you need to be able to run an apples-to-apples comparison — to calculate how much good different things do in a single currency, so you can pick the best option. But because helping people isn’t reducible to one thing — it’s lots of incommensurable things, and how to rank them depends on each person’s subjective philosophical assumptions — trying to optimize in this domain will mean you have to artificially simplify the problem. You have to pretend there’s no such thing as oranges, only apples.
And when you try to do that, an unfortunate thing happens. You end up rushing past all the unhoused people in your city and, as you put it, you “feel callous simply ignoring all these requests.” Ignoring these human beings comes at a cost, not only to them, but to you. It has a damaging effect on your moral conscience, which feels moved to help but is being told not to.
Sign up here to explore the big, complicated problems the world faces and the most efficient ways to solve them.
Even some leaders in effective altruism and the adjacent rationalist community recognize this as a problem and advise people not to shut up that part of themselves. Rationalist Eliezer Yudkowsky, for example, says it’s okay to donate some money to causes that make us feel warm and fuzzy but that aren’t producing maximum utility. His advice is to “purchase fuzzies and utilons separately” — meaning, devote one pot of money to pet causes and another (much bigger) pot of money to the most cost-effective charities. You can, he says, get your warm fuzzies by volunteering at a soup kitchen and “let that be validated by your other efforts to purchase utilons.”
I would also suggest diversifying your giving portfolio, but it’s not because I think you need to “validate” the warm fuzzies. Instead, it’s because of another value: integrity.
When 20th-century British philosopher and critic of utilitarianism Bernard Williams talked about integrity, he meant it in the literal sense of the word, which has to do with a person’s wholeness (think of related words like “integration”). He argued that moral agency does not sit in a contextless vacuum — it is always some specific person’s agency, and as specific people we have specific commitments.
For example, a mother has a commitment to ensuring her kid’s well-being, over and above her general wish for all kids everywhere to be well. Utilitarianism says she has to consider everyone’s well-being equally, with no special treatment for her own kid — but Williams says that’s an absurd demand. It alienates her from a core part of herself, ripping her into pieces, wrecking her wholeness — her integrity.
It sounds like that’s what you’re feeling when you pass a person experiencing homelessness and ignore them. Ignoring them makes you feel bad because it alienates you from the part of you that is moved by this person’s suffering — that sees the orange but is being told there are only apples. That core part of you is no less valuable than the optimizing part, which you liken to your “brain.” It’s not dumber or more irrational. It’s the part that cares deeply about helping people, and without it, the optimizing part would have nothing to optimize!
So rather than trying to override it, I would encourage you to honor your wish to help in all its fullness. You won’t be able to run a direct apples-to-apples comparison, but that’s okay. Different types of help are useful in their own way and you can divvy up your budget between them, even though there’s no perfect formula to spit out the “optimal” allocations.
Diversifying your giving portfolio might look something like this. You keep a small amount of cash or gift cards on you, which you hand out to unhoused people you encounter directly. You put aside a larger amount to donate to a local or national charity with a strong track record. And you devote another amount to a highly effective charity abroad.
You might feel annoyed that there’s no universal mathematical formula that can tell you the best thing to do. If so, I get it. I want the magic formula too! But I know that desire is distinct from the core value here. Don’t let optimization eat the real value you hold dear.
Bonus: What I’m reading
- I recently read Optimal Illusions, a book by mathematician Coco Krumme that traces the roots of optimization’s overreach. As she puts it, “Over the past century, optimization has made an impressive epistemic land grab.”
- When torn between competing moral theories, does it make sense to diversify your donations in proportion to how much you believe in each theory? Some philosophers argue against that view, but Michael Plant and coauthors defend it in this new paper.
- This gorgeously written essay by anthropologist Manvir Singh introduced me to the term “cooperating without looking” (or, because it’s a New Yorker essay, “coöperating without looking”). This “tendency to willfully ignore costs and benefits when helping others” — to help without calculating what you’ll gain from the altruistic act — is “a key feature of both romantic love and principled behavior.” When we help this way, people trust us more.

Why does one person develop memory problems while another experiences seizures or changes in behaviour? And how do doctors find out whether these symptoms are caused by Alzheimer’s disease, an immune disorder or something else?
Sometimes, the answers may lie in tiny changes in the body’s chemistry. Diseases can cause certain proteins and other molecules to appear in different amounts or behave differently. By measuring these changes, doctors can find clues as to what is happening inside the body, even when the cause is not immediately obvious.
These clues, called chemical signatures or biomarkers, are being studied to improve the diagnosis of several diseases, particularly those affecting the brain and nervous system. The challenge is to establish what these changes mean, how reliably they point to a particular disease and whether patients can access the tests.
According to the World Health Organization, 57 million people worldwide were living with dementia in 2021, with Alzheimer’s disease accounting for an estimated 60% to 70% of cases. The WHO also estimates that nearly 10 million new cases of dementia occur each year.
What are chemical signatures?
A chemical signature is a unique pattern of molecules, elements, isotopes, or by-products identified in a sample by analytical instruments such as spectrometers or chromatographs. “Chemical signatures are like the body’s fingerprints,” says Sreenivas U.M., consultant neurologist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai. When a disease develops, the balance of certain chemicals or proteins may change, providing clues to the problem, he adds.
In Alzheimer’s disease, for instance, doctors and researchers look for changes in proteins called amyloid-beta and tau. Certain forms of these proteins can be measured in blood and cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Tests measuring phosphorylated tau, particularly p-tau217, can help identify changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease.
Sruthi Degapudi, consultant neurologist, Prashanth Hospitals, Chennai, says these tests help doctors look beyond a patient’s symptoms and investigate the underlying cause. However, finding a disease-associated change does not necessarily mean that a person will develop dementia.
Researchers are also studying alpha-synuclein, a protein associated with Parkinson’s disease. In another condition, autoimmune encephalitis, tests that detect antibodies directed against particular brain proteins can help identify an immune response affecting the brain. This condition can cause seizures, memory problems and changes in behaviour.
The type of sample needed depends on the disease. Blood is relatively easy to collect, while cerebrospinal fluid can provide information about processes affecting the brain and spinal cord. Skin samples are also being studied for certain neurological conditions.
Detecting symptoms
Some diseases begin changing the body long before a person notices anything unusual. Detecting these changes may help doctors identify the underlying disease earlier, although it does not always mean that symptoms can be prevented. Finding these changes also does not always mean an individual has, or is going to have a particular disease.
The distinction is important: a test may identify changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease, but doctors still need to consider the person’s symptoms and overall health before deciding what those results mean.
Chemical signatures can also help distinguish conditions that appear similar. Autoimmune encephalitis, for example, may initially be mistaken for a psychiatric illness because it can cause behavioural changes and problems with memory. Identifying specific antibodies can help doctors recognise the condition and begin appropriate treatment.
“In neurosurgery, examining the molecular characteristics of a brain tumour can help doctors classify it and decide on treatment,” says Aqib M., senior consultant neurosurgeon, Dr. Mehta’s Hospitals, Chennai. Selected molecular tests are already used in specialist practice. Researchers are also studying markers such as neurofilament light, a protein that can indicate damage to nerve cells, he adds.
However, not every promising test is ready for routine use. Some markers indicate damage that can occur in several diseases rather than identifying one specific condition.
Testing and diagnosis
A chemical signature cannot always give the full picture. Age, kidney function, medication and other illnesses can affect the levels of certain molecules. The stage of a disease and the way a sample is collected and tested can also influence the results.
This is why doctors do not rely on a blood test alone. They consider the patient’s symptoms, medical history and examination findings, along with brain scans and other investigations when necessary. In some cases, several biomarkers may be needed to distinguish between diseases that produce similar symptoms.
Cost and availability pose further challenges in India. Specialised tests may not be offered at every hospital, and patients may have to travel to larger centres to access them. Differences in laboratory methods can also affect how consistently results are interpreted.
So, for patients, chemical signatures could mean clearer answers and shorter waits for a diagnosis. But their importance lies not just in detecting changes in the body, but in understanding what those changes mean.

Zelenskyy speaks to US envoys amid Trump spat
Zelenskyy spoke to the American officials as he accused Moscow of breaking Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warning Moscow planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.
KYIV: Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the midst of his spat with Donald Trump Sunday (Oct 18), saying "a lot depends on America" as he earlier warned Washington not to side with Moscow in Europe's worst conflict since WWII.
The wartime leader spoke to the US officials as both Russia and Ukraine hit each other's energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on Saint Petersburg since the start of the 2022 war.
Trump and Zelenskyy have clashed as the US leader blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow, fuelling fears in Kyiv and Europe that the White House was steering towards Moscow.
After speaking to Trump's business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner, Zelenskyy said "a lot depends" on the US position in the war but that "it is clear that there are many things that matter to all of us and that this war must be brought to an end."
Ukraine, he said, was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly" and that: "We expect exactly this approach from all our partners, both from the Europeans and, of course, from the American side."
He said he discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defence systems, as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.
Zelenskyy earlier told US media NBC it would be a "historic mistake" if Washington formally supported Russia and that he hoped Trump would "change his decisions."
But he also said he was "thankful" the US resumed intelligence sharing after a pause that left his country vulnerable to Russian missile strikes.
A US-led push to end the Ukraine-Russia war has so far not led to a breakthrough and Trump has in the past grown frustrated with both Zelenskyy and Russia's Vladimir Putin because of their lack of progress.
Zelenskyy spoke to the American officials as he accused Moscow of breaking Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warning Moscow planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.
Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power in several regions, he said, with Ukrainian officials reporting three people had been killed.
Ukraine's army launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg on Sunday night, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.
'Dreadful routine of war'
Rising smoke was visible from Saint Petersburg's historic city centre on the banks of the Neva River, with Russia saying Ukraine struck an oil refinery and depot in night-time strikes that killed one person.
Saint Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city.
Authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.
Russia's VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit and Ozon, Russia's second largest retailer, also reported a hit on its logistics centre.
The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the 2022 war.
The Kremlin, however, said Ukrainian attacks on its cities will not change its war aims.
"The Kyiv regime is putting up a fight, but that cannot change the course of events," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media.
Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine and, in a fifth year of war, few see a way out of the conflict.
"There's a general feeling: they're attacking, we're attacking, it's become the dreadful routine of war," 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
'Getting on my nerves'
Moscow has rained drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities daily and Kyiv says its strikes are fair retribution.
Sergei, another Saint Petersburg resident who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
"I don't know if I was scared, what must be will be," he told AFP.
"My main thought was that petrol would run out at the petrol stations and I'd better fill up."
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier this year.
Leningrad governor Drozdenko said 20,000 people were without power in the town of Yanino, where a substation was hit.
He said a woman and three children were hospitalised "with symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning" in the region after drone debris fell on a house, causing a fire.
"I woke up at night, heard bangs, looked out of the window and there was a fire," 40-year-old Saint Petersburg resident Igor told AFP.
"They're getting on my nerves already," he added, referring to Ukraine.

In October 2026, social media users spread an image that claimed to show a woman being punched in the face at one of U.S. President Donald Trump's rallies.
The person in the picture was wearing a shirt that said "RELEASE THE EPSTEIN FILES." (The Justice Department has released millions of files related to its investigation of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, but critics allege the agency made redactions to obscure information.)
The image circulated on platforms such as X and Facebook. Many users sharing the image appeared to believe it was authentic.
"If there's one photo to sum up the Trump era, this is it," one X post aid.
While a protester wearing a similar shirt was, in fact, attacked at an Oct. 12 Trump rally in Youngstown, Ohio, the image above was created using generative artificial intelligence, according to OpenAI's detection software. As such, we have rated this image as fake.
OpenAI's verification tool detected an invisible watermark on the image called SynthID, which the company's AI tools, like ChatGPT, embed in generated images. (As such, the service can only detect images generated with OpenAI's software and does not detect AI generation via other large-language models, such as Google's Gemini.)
(OpenAI)
SynthID detectors are largely accurate but can still be fallible. However, a review of credible footage taken from the Trump rally indicated that the actual protester was wearing slightly different clothing, including an open flannel layered on top of the T-shirt. The T-shirt the real person wore also had variations in the lettering style and coloring, unlike the more uniform version in the AI-generated image.
A reverse-image search could not determine the original creator behind the AI-generated picture.
Numerous reputable news organizations, including NBC News and an ABC affiliate, have published legitimate footage of the event.
NBC News' video shows rally attendees chanting, "USA, USA, USA" as a man in a gray shirt and a baseball cap appears to push down the protester. Another man in a dark blue or black shirt appears to tackle the protester, hit her and put her in a headlock. Security officials then escort the protester away. 
Another clip posted by WKBN, a Youngstown television news station, shows that the same man pulled on the protester's hair:
Images of the incident are also available via credible photo repositories, including Getty Images and Reuters.
NBC News reported that there were no arrests "because deputies didn't see the beating and the woman elected not to file a report, Sheriff Jerry Greene said."
Trump, meanwhile, mocked the protester's weight while watching the attack unfold. "You know they're paid protesters," Trump said, without evidence. "That's a very low-class protester."
The protester has not publicly shared their identity with the media as of this writing.

October 2022 - Geneva, WHO signed new agreements with a variety of civil society, political and community stakeholders in October at the World Health Summit in Berlin, a three-day hybrid event that reached some 60 000 participants worldwide.
For the first time, WHO co-hosted the Summit, which drew 4,100 in-person participants from 141 countries to more than to more 60 sessions with a common goal: improving health for everyone, everywhere. At the event, WHO expanded partnerships with civil society and advocates, and formalized strategic engagements with non-traditional stakeholders - relationships critical to reaching global health goals.
Read on for highlights from the Summit:
International Association of National Public Health Institutes (IANPHI)
IANPHI and WHO signed a memorandum of understanding outlining ways the two agencies intend to work together to strengthen public health functions and health emergency preparedness.
WHO and IANPHI share the vision that essential public health functions are a comprehensive and cost-effective approach to advance universal health coverage, health security and healthier populations. The strengthened alliance between WHO and IANPHI is critical to ensure that global and regional structures are designed to support national and local capacities and provide the right avenues for collaboration and coordination.
Read more: International Association of National Public Health Institutes partners with WHO
UNITE, Parliamentarians Network for Global Health
Showing the diversity and wide reach of the Summit, WHO also signed a memorandum of understanding with UNITE at an event attended in person by more than 40 parliamentarians from 30 countries.
The agreement represents a new step in strengthening WHO engagement with parliaments; UNITE committed to support WHO in raising awareness and building capacity of parliamentarians in three strategic areas of global public health:
- equitable access to health, with a focus on universal health coverage;
- health system strengthening, with a focus on supporting sustainable financing for global health; and
- efficient global health architecture and security and the promotion of the pandemic treaty.
Read more: Parliamentarians commit to support global health (18 October 2022)
Dr Ricardo Baptista Leita, President and Founder of UNITE and Dr Tedros, Director-General, WHO
King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief)
WHO and UNICEF signed US$ 10 million in funding agreements with KSRelief to bolster polio and measles programmes in eight countries.
The new funding - providing US$ 5 million each to WHO and UNICEF - comes in response to an emergency call to action by the two agencies to avert major polio and measles epidemics. Both Organizations have urged countries to prioritize childhood vaccination following global disruptions to immunization programmes caused by COVID-19.
WHO plans to co-organize the 2025 World Health Summit.
Read more: UNICEF and WHO welcome KSRelief funding for measles and polio epidemics prevention
From left to right: Catherine Russel, Executive Director, UNICEF; Dr Abdullah Al Rabeeah, Supervisor General of King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief); Dr Tedros, Director-General, WHO
A global consortium to help smokers quit
WHO also launched a business coalition to support the Organization’s work on tobacco cessation and bring more smokers the tools and medications they need to quit. The Tobacco Cessation Consortium is a public-private partnership fighting tobacco dependence.
An estimated 1.3 billion people use tobacco products, 80% of whom live in low- and middle-income countries. In Germany, where the Consortium was launched, 23% of the adult population smokes.
Latest numbers show that 60% of tobacco users worldwide have expressed a desire to quit, but only 30% have access to comprehensive tobacco cessation services.
The Consortium will focus on solving challenges in collaboration with partners, across five pillars: pharmacotherapies and steady delivery of products and medicines that help people quit tobacco; strengthening health systems; speaking to people in power and advocating for increased investment in cessation; identifying innovations and research ideas, reaching more people through digital channels, and promoting the tools developed by partners.
Pledging to end polio worldwide
ermany co-hosted a global polio eradication fundraising drive at the Summit that yielded pledges of US$ 2.6 billion.
The money will help the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) carry out its 2022-2026 strategy to overcome the final hurdles to eradicating polio, including vaccinating 370 million children over the next five years and continuing disease surveillance across 50 countries.
GPEI is seeking US$ 4.8 million to end polio, which would become the second disease after smallpox to be eradicated by human intervention.
Pledges came from Australia, France, Germany, Japan, Republic of Korea, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Spain, Turkey, United States, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Bloomberg Philanthropies, the Islamic Food and Nutrition Council of America, Latter-day Saint Charities, Rotary International and UNICEF.

Actor Imran Khan ordered to leave India after participating in protest
- Published
Authorities in India have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by 28 October after he participated in a protest, seeking electoral reforms.
An American citizen, Khan holds an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which allows people of Indian origin to visit and stay in the country. But an OCI cannot vote or contest elections.
"Imran Khan participated in the agitation at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar," police said in a statement on Thursday.
Khan's lawyer has said the actor will challenge the order in the Bombay High Court.
Police said the Foreigners' Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had served Khan a notice for violating laws by protesting.
But the actor's lawyer said that no provision of the law or any rule for OCI cardholders prohibit him from participating in a protest.
The Press Trust of India reports that the actor's petition against the Mumbai police notice termed it as "drastic".
Khan is known for the 2008 hit romantic comedy Jaane Tu... Ya Jaane Na.
He first appeared as a child actor in popular films such as Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak in 1988 and Jo Jeeta Wohi Sikandar in 1992.
Since his debut as a lead actor in 2008, he has starred in a number of films like I Hate Luv Storys, Mere Brother Ki Dulhan and Delhi Belly.
The notice to leave the country comes as Khan returns to acting this year with the Netflix film Adhure Hum Adhure Tum after a hiatus of over a decade.
On 10 October, the actor participated in the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a wider GenZ-led movement that has been holding demonstrations for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud. India's poll panel denies these charges.
"Imran Khan had participated in the agitation despite not being an Indian citizen," police said in their statement.
The complaint against Khan was lodged by Kirit Somaiya, a leader of India's and the state's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who accused the actor of being "involved in a conspiracy to spread anarchy in India".
Khan did not address Somaiya's allegation directly, but had spoken to reporters about his participation in the protest.
"I don't have demands. I'm here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I'm here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted, why people's voices are being suppressed," he'd said.
He added that he was not at the protest as the representative of any organisation.
Following the protest, Khan was briefly detained by the police along with other protesters.
He posted a photo of himself inside the police detention van on Instagram with the caption, "Apparently I'm going for a drive." The post received more than two million likes on the social media platform.
Over the weekend, thousands of protesters had marched in Delhi, Mumbai and other parts of India, demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar ahead of crucial state elections in response to the CJP's call.
On Monday, leaders of many of India's main opposition parties, including Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, led thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place to the Supreme Court in Delhi.
On Wednesday, two top CJP leaders were sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi.
The CJP has called for another protest on Friday evening in the capital.

The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has undertaken trade margin rationalisation (TMR) of 137 identified non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs.
“The move is aimed at making cancer treatment more affordable, and improve access to anti-cancer medicines,” said a senior Union government official.
The move is expected to bring down the maximum retail price (MRP) of the identified non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs by up to 70%, depending on their existing price structures.
The revised prices will be effective from November 9.
“This intervention builds upon the success of NPPA’s 2019 pilot TMR exercise, under which trade margins for 42 anti-cancer drugs were capped at 30%. Following that exercise, MRP of 526 brands of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was reduced by up to 90%. The present exercise extends this approach to a larger set of anti-cancer drugs, based on the list recommended by the Expert Committee under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS),” notes a release issued by the Centre.
It added that an expert committee comprising leading oncologists, medical specialists, experts from hospitals across the country, and government officers recommended 137 drugs for inclusion under TMR. “This list would be updated periodically,” said the release.
Considering the drugs recommended by the committee, NPPA has capped the trade margin at 30% of the MRP in accordance with paragraph 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013.
“Price of these medicines even after margin cap will remain out of reach of many people. The move alone will not bring down the cost of treatment because hospitals may find ways to charge high prices on other items, consumables, diagnostics, consultation charges, etc,” said K.M. Gopakumar, co-convenor of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments.

Paris police report 855 arrests after violent clashes and looting during protests
Paris police have arrested 855 people after violent clashes during a protest against rising living costs
PARIS -- Paris police said Sunday that 855 people were arrested in the French capital region after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during a protest march that drew about 110,000 people who denounced rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.
Violent clashes, fires and looting on Saturday marred demonstrations across France. Authorities said groups of masked protesters targeted public buildings, including city halls and local government offices.
Authorities said about 550,000 people took part in protests across France, while organizers counted about 800,000.
One person died of a heart attack, Paris police said in a statement, without providing further details. French media reported a protester suffered a medical emergency in the street during the march.
Thirteen police and gendarmerie officers and two firefighters were injured, the statement said.
Around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday morning, dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass marked the aftermath of the events. Looting and damage were reported around the square and in some other tourist and shopping areas in the city center.
Police said groups numbering from several hundred to more than 1,000 people formed unauthorized marches across central Paris on Saturday. “By late afternoon, a new phase began with the arrival of large numbers of people whose sole aim was to steal and loot, taking advantage of the unrest,” police said.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez attributed some of the violence to “radical far-left groups” and said others later joined to loot.
“Peaceful demonstrations have every place in our Republic. Arson, looting and attacks do not,” Lecornu said in a message posted on X.
The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon, the country's three largest cities, requested a meeting with the prime minister in the coming days “given the extent of the damage and the seriousness of the situation.”
In the southern port city of Marseille, some protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall and a police station was damaged. In Lyon, a fire broke out inside a tourist office.
In the central town of Limoges, the City Hall was set on fire, gutting the 19th-century building and collapsing the roof. Haute-Vienne prefect Maurice Barate told LCI television that the blaze, which was under control Sunday, was deliberate.

France has released its Global Health Strategy for 2023-2027, in Lyon today, in the presence of three French Ministers, the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, the Minister of Health and Prevention, the Minister of Higher Education and Research, and WHO’s Director-General.
As a lead player for shaping global health policies, France has called on national and international stakeholders to support building a new global health architecture towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and in particular SDG3, focused on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all, at all ages.
The new Health Strategy aims to help reduce health inequalities and strengthen the One Health approach to better prevent and prepare for future global health emergencies. It urges the global community to address the health consequences of climate change and the environmental impact on health systems.
To underscore WHO’s and France strong collaboration and in recognition of France’s pivotal global health role, Dr Tedros travelled to France to join the launch event.
“France was a founding member of WHO in 1948 and has been a strong friend to WHO throughout the 75 years since then,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health, and the new Global Health Strategy will enhance that role. It aligns well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, empower and perform for health.”
France shares key health priorities with WHO, adopting a crosscutting approach and prioritizing universal health coverage (UHC) as part of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. France also provides support for transformative initiatives at WHO such as the WHO Academy and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) which the Ministers visited today.
Dr Tedros addressed the audiences at the Academy and IARC together with Ms Catherine Colonna, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention, and Ms Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research.
"The World Health Organization, whose 74th anniversary we are celebrating today, must continue to play a central and driving role,” said Ms Catherine Colonna, the French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “France will continue to support the WHO and its ambitious governance and financing reforms."
"France is also committed alongside the WHO Academy through several partnership with universities, research institutes, and public health institutions," remarked Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research. "Our goal is to enrich the learners' experience through a diversified training portfolio within the Academy."
"The launch of this Global Health Strategy is the perfect opportunity to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the WHO. The Organization plays a central role in global health, and we must continue to support it," said Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention. "This is why, I am announcing today, France is keen to host, in the first quarter of 2024, in partnership with the WHO, the first international financing conference for the fight against meningitis."
The 2023-2027 French Strategy for Global Health is the fruit of collaboration involving a wide range of French actors: public agencies, civil society organizations, higher education and research organizations, scientific institutions, foundations, organizations of human, animal and environmental health specialists, local government bodies and the private sector. They will all be represented within a monitoring committee to track the Strategy’s implementation and progress.
From left to right: Minister of Health and Prevention H.E. Aurélien Rousseau, WHO’s Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs H.E. Catherine Colonna, and Minister of Higher Education and Research, H.E. Sylvie Retailleau.

Blue Origin announced a major expansion of its already considerable Florida launch facilities on Friday morning with the intent of eventually flying 150 rockets a year from there.
The company said it would add two additional launch pads for the New Glenn rocket, in addition to two already under construction at Cape Canaveral. The company is also investing heavily in a new manufacturing facility that will produce up to 150 upper stages for a larger variant of the New Glenn rocket.
Additionally, the company plans to procure two additional landing ships to catch and return the first stage of the New Glenn rocket (it currently has one, named Jacklyn). Finally, Blue Origin said it would add a new customer integration facility, built in conjunction with the US Space Force, that will feature four payload bays to process multiple missions at the same time.
“These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently,” wrote Ian Richardson, senior vice president of operations at Blue Origin, in an update on the company’s website this morning. “As we look ahead, this infrastructure is designed to support multiple flights per week by the end of the decade.
$3 billion and counting
To date, Blue Origin has invested about $3 billion in facilities and infrastructure in Florida, largely to support the construction and launch of the heavy-lift New Glenn rocket. The company now has more than 5,000 employees working in Florida and 500 suppliers in the state.
“Our manufacturing and operations footprint has more than doubled in the last couple of years, now spanning more than 20 sites across Brevard and Orange Counties,” Richardson wrote. “Blue Origin is the only company—and the largest employer—to manufacture, launch, and refurbish rockets on the Space Coast.”
That would seem to be a reference to superseding the 800-pound gorilla on the Florida Space Coast, SpaceX, which has launched hundreds of rockets into orbit over the years from Florida. Blue Origin has launched to orbit twice.

I worked on death row for 18 years. This is why the livestream execution was cancelled
The idea to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan was all about the US administration wanting to show power and test what is acceptable, death row lawyer Dr Asim Qureshi tells Suha Kidwai

Since the US Supreme Court reinstated capital punishment in 1976, state and federal authorities have executed 1,684 individuals.
For half a century, this violence has been conducted with clinical distance – shrouded in quiet, standardised procedure.
When defence secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan would be broadcast live to the world, that bureaucratic veneer dissolved.
Labeled by the United Nations as “tantamount to a public execution” – a spectacle unseen in American justice for nearly a century – the Pentagon’s proposal transformed state-sanctioned killing into primetime political theatre.
Donald Trump has since backtracked, reversing the decision to stream the execution following international condemnation and internal political friction.
But for Dr Asim Qureshi, director of CAGE International, who has spent two decades navigating the legal mechanics of America’s death row, viewing this retreat as a victory for human decency is to misunderstand how the Trump administration operates. ‘
The policy balloon has been floated, the precedent logged, and the public appetite tested.
“Mine was quite a reaction of horror,” Dr Qureshi says, reflecting on the initial announcement of the live streaming. “It’s presented as accountability, transparency, justice – but at the heart of it, it is this fascination with wanting to show power. This administration is built on the optics of projecting power.”
When a government seeks to broadcast a state killing, it relies on a specific, fragile logic: that absolute dominance can be demonstrated through controlled violence.
The White House’s sudden U-turn exposes the inherent risk of that calculation. Unfiltered spectacle is a political “wild card”, which, once broadcast, cannot be controlled.
“I think one of the main reasons it was cancelled is that the Trump administration has discovered that livestreaming horror doesn’t really work,” Dr Qureshi explains, pointing to the shift in global consciousness over recent years.
“For the past three years, we’ve watched a livestreamed genocide. And because of it, opinions toward Israel – across both the Democrat and Republican parties – are at an all-time low.”
In criminal defence, “mitigation” is the methodical reconstruction of a defendant’s life to understand the factors that brought them to the moment of their crime. In bringing a camera into the execution chamber, the state unwittingly invites the public to conduct its own act of mitigation.
“To livestream an execution would force people to mitigate and reassess the case of Nidal Hasan,” Dr Qureshi states.
“When it comes to it, Nidal Hasan’s issue was with American malfeasance across the world – his reasons were rooted in American foreign policy in Afghanistan and Iraq. And I don’t think Trump, or anyone in his administration, wants people asking those questions.”
This creates “a bizarre duality” for the White House: where the desire to punish Hasan for his actions must be reconciled with the possibility that Americans may interrogate what led to them.
But even in the cancellation of the livestream, the proposal has already changed the course of American justice. By floating the idea of a televised execution, the state has expanded the boundaries of what violence can be considered “just”.
“If you want to shift public opinion, you need to bring the most egregious act to the table,” Dr Qureshi explains. “And bit by bit, the mainstream narrative will move toward the next, slightly less egregious thing.
“It’s worked, because everybody is talking about whether Nidal Hasan’s execution should be livestreamed, but nobody’s talking about why he is being executed in the first place.
“And in doing so, it has made a future livestreamed execution a much more realistic possibility.”
But this baseline has never been a just one.
“We are looking at a country where 98 per cent of criminal defendants are coerced into plea deals, where one third of Black men face the shadow of incarceration, and where children lose years of their lives to wrongful convictions,” explains Dr Qureshi.
“This is not a system suffering from administrative flaws. It is an unjust system.
“This livestreamed execution is not indicative of anything other than the direction that American justice is barreling toward.
“And there will be no justice without a fundamental rethink.”
