But, 2015 global milestones and measles elimination goals are off track
The number of measles-related deaths has decreased 79% from 546 800 at the beginning of the century to 114 900 in 2014. New data released by WHO for the Measles & Rubella Initiative, estimates that 17.1 million lives have been saved since 2000, largely due to increased vaccination coverage against this highly contagious viral disease. Measles vaccination has played a key role in reducing child mortality and in progress towards Millennium Development Goal 4.
However, the new data published in this week’s edition of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC), "Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report" and WHO’s "Weekly Epidemiological Record", shows that overall progress towards increasing global immunization coverage has recently stagnated. While coverage with the first dose of the measles vaccine increased globally from 72% to 85% between 2000 and 2010, it has remained unchanged the past 4 years.
“We cannot afford to drop our guard,” says Dr Jean-Marie Okwo-Bele, Director of WHO’s Department of Immunization, Vaccines and Biologicals. “If children miss routine vaccination and are not reached by national immunization campaigns, we will not close the immunization gap.”
Based on current trends of measles vaccination coverage and incidence, the 2015 global milestones and measles elimination goals set by WHO’s Member States will not be achieved on time.
Although all countries include at least 1 dose of measles-containing vaccine in their routine vaccination schedule, only 122 (63%) have met the target of at least 90% of children vaccinated with a first dose. Additionally, only half of the world’s children are receiving the recommended second dose of the vaccine.
Success of immunization campaigns
In 2014, mass vaccination campaigns led by country governments with support from the Measles & Rubella Initiative and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, reached approximately 221 million children. Twenty-nine countries supplemented their routine vaccination programmes with mass immunization campaigns, helping to reduce measles incidence in 4 out of 6 WHO regions last year. Overall, since 2000, these campaigns have enabled 2 billion children to receive a supplemental dose of measles vaccine.
In the African Region, cases dropped from over 171 000 in 2013 to under 74 000 in 2014, likely due to campaigns in Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Nigeria. WHO’s Eastern Mediterranean, European and the South-East Asia regions also saw decreases in measles incidence in 2014.
Large-scale campaigns in 2014 included:
- Bangladesh – more than 53.6 million children vaccinated
- DRC – more than 18.5 million children vaccinated
- Pakistan - more than 25 million children vaccinated
- United Republic of Tanzania – more than 20.5 million children vaccinated
- Yemen – more than 11.3 million children vaccinated
- Viet Nam – more than 15.1 children vaccinated
“Last year, the Measles and Rubella Initiative supported campaigns in 29 high-risk countries to stop measles, including in Liberia where a serious outbreak occurred following the Ebola epidemic. Funding for many of the largest campaigns came from Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. Gavi’s support for measles campaigns in large countries like DRC and Pakistan, and measles-rubella vaccine introduction through campaigns targeting children under 15 years of age, is providing a strong boost to measles control and elimination in those countries, ” says Dr Robert Linkins, Chief, Accelerated Disease Control and Surveillance Branch at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
“Despite our success in these countries, globally over 100 000 children needlessly died from measles last year. That’s a tragedy which can be easily prevented if we intensify our measles surveillance and vaccination efforts,” Linkins concluded.
Measles outbreaks remain an issue
Measles outbreaks, which happen when there are gaps in vaccination programmes, continue to pose a serious challenge to meeting global targets. The Americas and Western Pacific regions saw increased numbers of cases in 2014, mostly due to large outbreaks in China, the Philippines, and Viet Nam. In other regions, although the overall number of cases fell, some individual countries still had large outbreaks, including Angola, Ethiopia, India, the Russian Federation and Somalia.
Accelerating progress
Measles is highly infectious and strong, sustained efforts are needed to maintain the current level of control. Together with changes in policies and practices in high-burden countries, vaccination and surveillance efforts need to be funded, maintained and strengthened, WHO and its partners say.
“Despite the welcome reduction in measles deaths, this highly-infectious disease continues to take a terrible toll on the lives of children around the world,” said Dr Seth Berkley, CEO of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. “A coordinated approach that puts stronger routine immunization at its core will be central to getting measles under control and securing further reductions in mortality from this vaccine-preventable disease.”
Note to editors
Please note these figures are from 2014 and do not include numbers from outbreaks in early 2015.
Measles
Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, which affects mostly children. It is transmitted via droplets from the nose, mouth or throat of infected persons. Initial symptoms, which usually appear 10–12 days after infection, include high fever, runny nose, bloodshot eyes, and tiny white spots on the inside of the mouth. Several days later, a rash develops, starting on the face and upper neck and gradually spreading downwards.
There is no specific treatment for measles and most people recover within 2–3 weeks. However, particularly in malnourished children and people with reduced immunity, measles can cause serious complications, including blindness, encephalitis, severe diarrhoea, ear infection, pneumonia and death.
About WHO
WHO is the directing and coordinating authority for health within the United Nations system. It is responsible for providing leadership on global health matters, shaping the health research agenda, setting norms and standards, articulating evidence-based policy options, providing technical support to countries, and monitoring and assessing health trends and improving global health security.
About the Measles & Rubella Initiative
Launched in 2001, the Measles & Rubella Initiative is a global partnership led by the American Red Cross, United Nations Foundation, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), UNICEF and WHO. The Measles & Rubella Initiative is committed to ensuring that no child dies from measles or is born with congenital rubella syndrome; reducing measles deaths by 95% by 2015; and achieving measles and rubella elimination in at least five WHO regions by 2020.
The latest data is published in this week’s WHO’s Weekly Epidemiological Report and in CDC’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.
About Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance
Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance is a public-private partnership committed to saving children’s lives and protecting people’s health by increasing access to immunisation in poor countries. The Vaccine Alliance brings together developing country and donor governments, the World Health Organization, UNICEF, the World Bank, the vaccine industry, technical agencies, civil society, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and other private sector partners. Gavi uses innovative finance mechanisms, including co-financing by recipient countries, to secure sustainable funding and adequate supply of quality vaccines. Since 2000, Gavi has contributed to the immunisation of an additional 500 million children and the prevention of approximately 7 million future deaths.
World Health Assembly agreed milestones
In 2010, the World Health Assembly established 3 milestones towards the future eradication of measles to be achieved by 2015:
- increase routine coverage with the first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) for children aged 1 year to ≥90% nationally and ≥80% in every district or equivalent administrative unit;
- reduce and maintain annual measles incidence to <5 cases per million; and
- reduce estimated measles mortality by >95% from the 2000 estimate.

Urban Company’s board today approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr, alongside approving its financial performance for the September quarter. The proposed funding could involve issuance of equity shares, warrants, fully convertible debentures and convertible preference shares. The fundraise will be executed in one or more tranches via preferential allotment, private placement or one or more qualified institutional placements (QIPs), subject to shareholder approval. The final issue pricing and structure is yet to be determined. “The business is materially larger than at listing, growth has stepped up, and we now operate three businesses at scale with proven economics. The proposed raise of up to ₹2,500 Cr is about flexibility: it lets us invest with conviction across each of them, cement leadership in InstaHelp, and pursue inorganic opportunities selectively, without trading off one for another,” Urban Company said in a letter to shareholders. The fundraise proposal comes at a time when Urban Company’s quick home services vertical InstaHelp is facing tough competition from the likes of Snabbit and Pronto, resulting in the prospect of a war for market share fuelled by cash burn. Hefty investments in powering the quick home services vertical is also creating a dent in Urban Company’s bottom line. For the September quarter, Urban Company’s net loss more than tripled YoY to ₹182.5 Cr, while operating revenue jumped 41% YoY to ₹537.29 Cr. Separately, the board also granted in-principle approval to explore residential air conditioners as a new business category under its product brand Native. This would be subject to further evaluations and final board clearances. “This category represents a large market in which the Company already services millions of units annually, providing it with first-hand insights into the existing product gaps and customer needs,” noted UC’s board. Urban Company made its debut on the bourses just around one year ago. Hence, its proposed fundraise puts it among the ranks of several new-age tech companies like Kissht, Swiggy, Ather Energy, and Ola Electric that have sought to return to the public markets for fresh capital soon after their IPOs. 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
- Published
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV."
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia.
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer."
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner.
Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact".
There are many causes of isolation in China. Like when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country.
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives.
Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that.
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs.
"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine."
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added.
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.
The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible.
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows.
There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles.
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile.
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC.
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult.
But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood.
"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him.
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits.
Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic.
"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards."
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves.
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious."
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection.
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee.
"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect."
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province.
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said.
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month.
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said.
"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her."
After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude.
"The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback."
Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity.
Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly.
"It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said.
"I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy.
"I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.
More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.
The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.
The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.
Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”
Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.
Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.
The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.
While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.
Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.
“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”
She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.
The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.
LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.
The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.
The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.
There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.
In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021. In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death.

After Dubois' dominant win, what's next for heavyweight boxing?
- Published
Daniel Dubois' demolition of Fabio Wardley has strengthened his position among the heavyweight elite.
The 29-year-old needed only two rounds to stop his British rival at London's O2 Arena, retaining his title with a performance far more emphatic than their thrilling first encounter in May.
Dubois can now turn his attention towards unification and some of boxing's biggest names.
Meanwhile, Oleksandr Usyk is approaching retirement, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are finally preparing to meet and a new group of world champions are looking to establish themselves.
So what is next for the heavyweight division?
Who is next for Dubois - and where does Wardley go?
IBF champion Filip Hrgovic made his intentions clear, entering the ring after Dubois' victory, with both keen on a rematch.
Dubois stopped the Croatian in June 2024, but Hrgovic has since rebuilt his reputation, claiming the vacant IBF title with victory over British prospect Moses Itauma in August.
But Hrgovic, 34, has Cuba's Frank Sanchez waiting as a mandatory challenger.
Promoter Frank Warren is working towards staging Hrgovic's first defence in Croatia early next year, potentially delaying a reunion with Dubois.
The biggest financial prize for Dubois could be a meeting with the winner of Fury and Joshua's December showdown.
"All those names are there to do a unification fight next year and that's what we'll be working on," Warren said.
Wardley, meanwhile, has shown he can compete at world level, but the manner of Saturday's defeat exposed a gulf in technical ability.
A return against a lower-ranked opponent could help restore confidence, but questions remain over whether Wardley can make the adjustments needed to challenge the division's elite again.
Fury v Joshua - finally, but what happens afterwards?
After years of negotiations and false starts, Fury and Joshua are finally scheduled to meet at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on a card that begins on 11 December, with the main event expected in the early hours of 12 December.
The Netflix-streamed contest has demonstrated its extraordinary commercial appeal, with about 80,000 tickets selling out within an hour.
Warren says the vacant WBA 'super' title will be at stake, potentially opening the door to unification fights in 2027.
However, WBA 'regular' champion Murat Gassiev has questioned the decision and called for the winner to face him.
That appears unlikely to be a priority for either Briton, with both reportedly set to earn close to $100m (£75m) in December.
A rematch would offer another enormous payday, particularly if the first encounter is close or controversial, but a one-sided defeat could push the loser towards retirement.
Is Kabayel the forgotten champion?
Germany's Agit Kabayel has built one of the strongest records in the division.
The unbeaten 34-year-old has stopped Arslanbek Makhmudov, Sanchez and Zhilei Zhang, but remains a relatively unfamiliar name to casual boxing fans.
Kabayel, elevated to WBC champion when Usyk vacated, makes his first defence against Albania's Nelson Hysa on 28 November.
A unification fight against Dubois in 2027 could provide the opportunity to become a much bigger name in the sport.
Usyk's final fight - and what about Verhoeven and Wilder?
Usyk's decision to vacate the WBA, WBC and IBF titles in June means the unbeaten Ukrainian can call the shots over the final chapter of his career.
The pound-for-pound star, who defeated former kickboxing world champion Rico Verhoeven in May, has indicated he wants one final contest before retirement.
Dutchman Verhoeven exceeded expectations before suffering a controversial 11th-round stoppage defeat, and wants a rematch.
Verhoeven says he has accepted an offer to face Deontay Wilder on the Fury-Joshua undercard, although the American has yet to agree and has also been linked with cruiserweight Jai Opetaia.
Wilder previously emerged as a contender for Usyk's farewell, but negotiations appear to have stalled.
A third meeting between Usyk and Fury has also been mooted.
But having already beaten Fury, Joshua and Dubois twice apiece, how much more does Usyk have to prove?
How does Itauma rebuild?
Itauma's charge towards a world title was halted when he suffered his first professional defeat against Hrgovic.
Itauma, 21, is expected to return in January, with Warren promising credible opposition rather than a straightforward confidence-building contest.
The priority will be developing the stamina, pacing and tactical patience required over 12 rounds before pursuing another world title opportunity.
A rematch with Hrgovic remains a longer-term possibility, but there is little need to rush with time firmly on Itauma's side.
What else is happening on the global and domestic scene?
American Jarrell Miller remains highly ranked, while compatriots Jared Anderson and Richard Torrez Jr, an Olympic silver medallist, are rebuilding.
New Zealand's former world champion Joseph Parker is seeking a return after his provisional doping suspension was lifted in August.
Australia's Teremoana Teremoana has stopped all 12 professional opponents within two rounds, while Uzbekistan's two-time Olympic champion Bakhodir Jalolov extended his unbeaten record by beating Solomon Dacres on Saturday.
In Britain, Derek Chisora, 42, is considering another comeback and says he expects to face WBA 'regular' champion Gassiev in December.
British champion Richard Riakporhe is pursuing world honours after moving up from cruiserweight, while former cruiserweight world champion Lawrence Okolie is targeting a return after reaching an agreement with the WBC over an adverse drugs test finding.
David Adeleye, Dave Allen, Johnny Fisher and Frazer Clarke remain on the domestic scene, while Leo Atang, 19, and Ireland's Adam Olaniyan, 20, are emerging talents.
With Usyk, Fury and Joshua approaching the ends of their careers, the heavyweight division is entering a new era.
There is no shortage of potential big fights, but bringing the champions together before mandatory obligations, rematches and boxing politics get in the way could prove the greatest challenge.

Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, fifteen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Cost of Living
They don't make instant coffee like they used to. It's getting gourmet now
Instant coffee sales have increased across Canada in recent years
In a world of fancy espresso machines, gourmet blends and cold brews, instant coffee has often been considered to be at the bottom of the proverbial coffee barrel. But the powder is getting a glow-up, thanks to better quality, social media trends and advancements in instant coffee technology.
"It's having a moment," said Joey Pittoello, general manager of the coffee roaster Just Us! in Halifax. "I think people have discovered that instant coffee can be of much better quality now."
More brewers are choosing to highlight instant coffee, from big brands such as Starbucks, to smaller roasters like Just Us!, in part because they are seeing an increased demand for it.
At Just Us!, which has been selling instant coffee for over 15 years, instant coffee sales have grown around 15 per cent in the last two years, says Pittoello, with other coffee companies such as Eight Ounce Coffee and Canadian Heritage Coffee Roasters in Calgary reporting similar increases in recent years.
According to a 2025 Agricultural Canada report, instant coffee sales totalled $330 million in Canada in 2024, up 10 per cent from the previous year.
"Instant coffee is undergoing the same transformation as a lot of coffee drinks," said Robert Carter, a food industry analyst and the president of the Coffee Association of Canada.
"There's more premiumization that's taking place. And I think that's resulting in an increase in consumption."
Social media trends are also improving instant coffee's rep. There's the Dalgona coffee trend, popularized during the pandemic, which is a whipped drink made by whisking instant coffee, sugar and hot water, then putting it over milk.
People are also using instant coffee to make lattes or iced coffees at home. Additionally, Pittoello says people use it in baking, or in seasoning when barbecuing.
"It's easy to make interesting sweet milky drinks with instant coffee. You just have to add it, right?" said Pittoello.
A change in quality and technology
Instant coffee isn't anything new though. Big brands like Nescafé and Maxwell House have been selling instant coffee for decades.
"I don't think it ever really went anywhere," said Pittoello.
What has changed, though, is the quality of instant coffee. Pittoello says the robusta bean, which has a simple flavour profile compared to arabica, had commonly been used to make instant coffee.
"You're enhancing the level of low quality by turning it into instant coffee and that's really what defined instant coffee for decades," said Pittoello.
Joey Pittoello is the general manager of the coffee roaster Just Us! in Halifax. (Harrison Newman Jardine)
Now more specialty roasters are using better beans to make their instant coffee. Just Us! uses arabica, as does Starbucks.
But that's not the only reason you're seeing specialty coffee shops selling their own instant coffee. Josh Hockin, head of coffee at Eight Ounce Coffee in Calgary, says it's easier than ever to manufacture it, thanks to advancements in technology.
Mainstream brands like Nescafé and Maxwell House make large amounts of instant coffee through a process called spray drying, which involves brewing coffee as strong as possible, then spraying that coffee into a heated chamber, creating the instant coffee powder.
But Hockin says a better quality coffee can be made by brewing the coffee then freeze-drying it instead. Years ago, the machine to do so would cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, and was as big as a shipping container.
Now, he says the machines cost about $3,000 to $4,000 Cdn, and can plug into the wall.
"It's not cheap to do, but it's certainly way less expensive than it would have been in the past," said Hockin.
Instant coffee jars sit on display in a Tesco supermarket on July 6, 2022 in Northwich, England. More specialty roasters are now offering their own take on instant coffee. (Getty Images)
Paying a premium
According to Robert Carter, it's not that people are replacing their at-home set up with instant coffee. Rather, Carter says, instant coffee is giving people another option to enjoy one of the most consumed drinks in Canada.
"We're not seeing a cannibalization taking place. We're seeing an expansion of the types of coffee products being consumed that are different than just your traditional brewed coffee.”
Starbucks VIA Ready Brew instant coffee is offered for sale at Starbucks coffee shop back in 2009. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
And people are willing to pay a premium for that, says Hockin. He says it's the equivalent of buying a cup at a coffee shop, with some packets of four selling for $11, while some varieties sell for $42 for a six-pack.
But, he says, the quality is just as good, and it's as convenient as it gets.
"It's not their everyday cup of coffee, obviously. But they are very willing, very very willing to pay that money.”

3 men sentenced to 158 years for the killings of Australian, US surfers in Mexico
The sentencing marked the end of a lengthy legal process over the killings.
ENSENADA, Mexico -- A judge on Friday sentenced three Mexican men to more than 158 years in prison each for the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, a case that tarnished Mexico’s image by exposing the risks foreigners face when visiting the tourism-dependent country.
The sentencing, which came a week after the men were found guilty, marked the end of a lengthy legal process over the killings of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, and American Carter Redd Rhoad. Their bodies were found in May 2024, and at least four people were arrested for their alleged involvement in the crime.
A judge in the coastal city of Ensenada, in Baja California state, ruled that Jesús Gerardo García, known as “el Kekas,” Irineo Francisco “N” and Ángel Jesús “N” would each serve 158 years and nine months in prison for murder, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
Antonio Otañez, president of the Baja California surfers’ association, welcomed the outcome, saying “justice has been served.” But he acknowledged that the killings had caused a “major drop” in tourist visits, particularly by surfers, to the region known for its beautiful beaches.
Here is a look at the key facts and events in the case:
The Robinson brothers — Callum and Jake — and their American friend decided to travel to Mexico in late April 2024 to pursue one of their passions, surfing, at a beach in Punta San José, about 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the city of Ensenada in Baja California state.
Unaware of the risks they faced, the three friends decided to camp on the beach on the night of April 27, 2024.
Their attackers confronted them there, shot them dead in the early morning hours and then dumped their bodies into a well more than 15 meters (50 feet) deep. The bodies were found on May 3 after several days of searching.
The Baja California prosecutor’s office announced on May 5, 2024, that it had arrested García, known as “el Kekas,” identifying him as the suspected gunman in the killings of the three foreigners.
State authorities said García had a criminal history in Ensenada involving alleged drug dealing, unlawful entry into a home, domestic violence and vehicle theft.
García’s former partner, Ary Gisell Silva Raya, and two of his alleged accomplices, Irineo Francisco “N” and Ángel Jesús “N,” were also arrested in the case.
Silva Raya, whom authorities found in possession of a cellphone belonging to one of the victims, agreed to an abbreviated trial and in November was sentenced to 20 years in prison for aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
State prosecutor María Elena Andrade alleged that the attackers wanted to steal the tires from the foreigners’ pickup truck and that the victims resisted.
“The attackers pull out a gun they were carrying and kill the person who initially resisted the robbery, then turn on the other two,” she added.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.

Loneliness among parents whose adult children have migrated abroad is associated with higher psychological distress, difficulties in regulating emotions and problematic series watching, an exploratory study by researchers from NIMHANS has found.
The findings assume relevance on World Mental Health Day, observed on October 10, which draws attention to mental health and the need to address psychological well-being. The study highlights the emotional challenges that parents may experience when their children settle abroad and everyday family interactions become less frequent.
64 ‘empty-nest’ parents
Published in BMC Research Notes, the study examined 64 ‘empty-nest’ parents aged between 45 and 65, whose adult children had emigrated and lived away from home for at least two years. The sample comprised 30 fathers and 34 mothers from different families in Karnataka, Haryana and Punjab. Most belonged to middle socioeconomic backgrounds and nuclear families, and more than half had been in the empty-nest phase for over five years.
Rajesh Kumar, associate professor in the department of clinical psychology at NIMHANS and the corresponding author of the study, said the findings highlighted the relationship between loneliness and emotional well-being among parents adjusting to life without their children at home.
“We found a significant association between loneliness and psychological distress. Loneliness was also associated with difficulties in emotion regulation and problematic series watching, which refers to excessive or difficult-to-control viewing that interferes with everyday functioning. This also resulted in the risk of developing non-communicable diseases (NCDs),” he said.
Loneliness significantly predicted psychological distress even after accounting for age and gender. Of the 64 participants, 22 (34.3%) were classified as having higher levels of loneliness, while 42 (65.7%) fell into the lower-loneliness group. Those reporting higher loneliness also reported greater psychological distress, more difficulties in regulating emotions and higher levels of problematic series watching, Mr. Kumar said.
Social changes
Manoj Kumar Sharma, professor in the department of clinical psychology at NIMHANS and head of its SHUT Clinic, said the findings needed to be understood in the context of the emotional and social changes that parents may experience when their children settle abroad.
Dr. Sharma, who is one of the authors, cautioned that the study did not establish that loneliness causes psychological distress or excessive series watching. As it was cross-sectional, it could identify associations but not determine the direction of the relationships, he said.
Mothers reported greater loneliness
Women in the study reported significantly higher levels of loneliness and psychological distress than men.
The researchers said that this was consistent with earlier research suggesting that mothers may experience greater emotional difficulties during the empty-nest phase, potentially reflecting their involvement in caregiving and emotional relationships with their children.
Possible coping mechanism
The researchers said digital media and streaming services could provide an easily accessible form of solitary leisure for parents experiencing less day-to-day interaction with their children.
However, the study did not examine why participants watched series or whether they used viewing deliberately to cope with loneliness or negative emotions. The researchers cautioned against assuming that excessive viewing was necessarily a coping response.
Other factors that could influence media use include social support, physical mobility, retirement, living arrangements, marital relationships, the frequency and quality of communication with adult children, and access to technology.
Social and psychological support
The findings underline the need to pay greater attention to the emotional well-being of parents whose children migrate abroad, as changing family structures and international migration can reduce opportunities for regular face-to-face interaction, Dr. Sharma said.
The authors said interventions to strengthen social connectedness, promote adaptive emotion-regulation strategies and encourage healthier technology use could potentially help parents navigate the empty-nest transition.

Matos on tactics, Klopp's influence, and taking Swans to top of the league
- Published
When Vitor Matos took charge of Swansea in November 2025, concerns around a potential relegation were on people's lips. Yet almost one year on, the Swans sit top of the Championship 10 games into the season.
In retrospect, the hire appears to have been a masterstroke considering the fact that Matos had only managed 12 senior games before moving to Swansea - those coming in the Portuguese second division.
Behind those 12 games, however, lives a coaching journey spanning 23 years across many continents and a variety of roles.
Prior to his spell in charge of Maritimo, the 38-year-old spent five years working under Jurgen Klopp as an elite development coach at Liverpool, before joining Red Bull Salzburg as Pep Lijnders' number two.
I called the Portuguese manager to explore his influences, principles and the ever-changing tactical landscape.
'Liverpool influenced me a lot'
Building a squad on a foundation of counter-pressing feels apt for Matos when you consider the time he spent working under Klopp.
"Liverpool influenced me a lot in terms of counter-pressing, pressing, intensity, and what makes you grow as a team," he said.
"The most important thing is how much you believe in your idea and this style is how I see football. That's why I wanted this to be the foundation for our team."
Although the influence is clear, it would be unfair to paint Vitor with a Klopp-shaped brush entirely.
"I started at a really young age wanting to be a coach and was influenced by many different styles," he added.
Evidence of these many influences are clear to see in Swansea's game-model this season, with Vitor pulling together ideas from his time at FC Porto, Shandong Taishan and Liverpool.
Matos detailed his list of priorities when he replaced Alan Sheehan at Swansea.
"The most important thing was to make the team feel confident again, to make the players fall in love with playing with each other," he explained.
"For that, we wanted to take steps first on making the team much more aggressive without the ball.
"Giving them that boost of confidence by demanding a more aggressive game, creating a good feeling after a high regain or a wonderful tackle – it creates a better mood inside the group."
He also opted to play a back four.
"Before I arrived there was also some change between a back four and a back five. I thought the squad was built for a back four at that time and to give consistency to the players, sticking with that was another priority.
"So, in our 4-3-3, we had a clear idea - to become a pressing and counter-pressing team, brave enough to take that risk.
"But then it's about, trying to find out the ways to be more aggressive."
In that sentence, Matos subtly revealed a key thread to his managerial approach and one that came up time and time again throughout our conversation.
He spoke about his many fixed footballing principles but believes the route to accomplishing those ideas must be shaped by the players at his disposal.
As a result, he takes a holistic approach to each player, seeking to understand them deeply, as footballers and human beings. Only then does he know how best they can work within his system.
"We want to press but where will we set up in terms of starting positions?" he continued.
"Who should start the press? Which are the triggers? Who are the players who buy in more or are more ready for this type of style in a short period of time?
"When you start from the players you have in front of you, you start from a position of comfort for them. This allows the players to be more confident which helps you to build your idea over time."
'When we go, we really go'
"When I spent time with the youth of FC Porto, I developed my understanding of positional play," Matos explained.
"We used a very positional 4-3-3, understanding the spaces, the timings, waiting for the ball to arrive to you at the right time. Players moved the ball until gaps started opening."
This season, we have seen those principles, honed at Porto, become the basis of an impressive Swansea side.
"How we solve problems depends on if we play against a man-marking team or a complete zonal team," said Matos.
"When you play against a complete zonal team, the most important thing is that you understand that you need to move them. By moving the opposition, you create spaces, you create a free player."
Much of the historic success of positional play has been underpinned by that same idea – finding the free player.
Against zonal defences, an attacker can occupy a gap between opponents and become a free, unmarked player. If a defender comes across to mark him, they risk leaving another attacker unmarked elsewhere.
But the rise in man-to-man pressure in recent years presents a different challenge. With defenders following individual opponents, the free player can cease to exist altogether.
To solve this problem, Matos has drawn on his time in China for answers.
"In China, I understood that to arrive at a more positional game, you could have different steps beforehand," he said.
"There is a benefit to having more players close to each other, rather than spreading them over space.
"If you spread them over space, you are demanding that, technically, they can solve many situations one-v-one. If they come closer to the ball, you can generate more possibilities. You can create a tempo that allows other players to be better in the big spaces."
It is unique style of play but these overloads have given Swansea extra solutions around the ball, helping disorganise both zonal and man-marking systems.
Matos added: "Especially if you play with a midfielder outside, you can overload one side a little bit more. Let's exchange the ball here five times, eight times and then when we go, we really go."
1 of 4
'With our two full-backs, we can tweak a lot of things'
Knowing that good positioning, overloads around the ball, and relentless off-the-ball running help Swansea disorganise defences, it is likely the dynamic and roaming full-backs that embody these qualities best.
Both full-backs have been used as tactical tools to undo a team's defensive strategy too:
"With our two full-backs, we can tweak a lot of things because these are normally positions where, especially if the opposition defend zonally, it's harder to press," Matos said, shedding light on why many top coaches have experimented in this position.
"Opponents need to make a decision on how they're going to press those spaces. And by pressing those spaces, there is the potential to create a lot of unbalance in the structure."
1 of 3
'Only when you are yourself can you really add value to something'
Successful young coaches are often praised for their tactical acumen, but management is as much about the moments away from the tactics board.
Matos, only 38, feels like a bridge between coaching generations.
"In the end, what I try to do is to value everyone in the right way. I try to make the best of everyone and try to allow everyone to be themselves. Only when you are yourself can you really add value to something," he said.
"The time with Jurgen was massive regarding that. How he was as a leader, how he took care of the club, how he took care of the players - that moulded a lot of me."
Now Matos draws on that experience for his own player-focused approach.
"I come from Portugal, but someone will come from Argentina, Brazil, Germany or the UK. And all of us have different ways to arrive at this specific moment," he said.
"Maybe I had a good house to live in and maybe one of them didn't, so he might be more emotional than me. Trying to understand them, trying to have sensitivity to that, is important.
"Knowing all of that, in the end we all are here for one thing: to win the next game."

The Netherlands reaffirmed its position as a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO and a leading donor of flexible and predictable resources to WHO. In picture: WHO Director-General Dr Tedros and Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport Ernst Kuipers. ©WHO
The Netherlands strengthened its longstanding engagement with WHO on Monday with the renewal of the multiannual contribution of the Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to WHO for €13.34 million for 2024–2028 and for €6 million to the technical partnership with Dutch WHO collaborating centres.
With the new contribution, the Netherlands reaffirmed its position as a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO and a leading donor of flexible and predictable resources to WHO.
"Amid increasingly complex and connected threats, from pandemics and climate change to conflicts, the Netherlands remains an essential supporter of WHO and global public health," said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus during the agreement signing.
"The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport's new contribution reflects the Netherland's commitment to its long partnership with WHO, and its support of the sustainable financing for WHO that Member States have agreed. This will enable WHO to respond quickly to global health challenges, and strengthen public health worldwide, including in the Netherlands."
Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport Ernst Kuipers added that “the Netherlands values our strong and long-standing relationship with WHO. Given the global challenges we collectively face, and the added value the Netherlands can deliver, we believe this renewed arrangement with long-term flexible funds well represents our commitment to advancing health worldwide. These funds will be used to achieve our shared priorities in the WHO’s General Programme of Work, facilitate the secondment of Dutch experts, and to support the Dutch WHO collaborating centres.”
The Netherlands recently recommitted to its role as a leading voice for global health through its Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030. The strategy aims to strengthen health systems at home and worldwide, better prepare for pandemics and address the impact of climate change on public health.
The Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport has provided for many years critical financial and technical support to WHO’s efforts to strengthen health security, improve the capacities of countries to address health emergencies, fight antimicrobial resistance, promote access to medicines, and support food safety, tobacco control and mental health.
The renewed partnership expands the joint work of the Netherlands and WHO into new global health challenges, such as those posed by climate change.
The interconnection between the health of the Earth and human health makes climate change a fundamental threat to decades of progress on health. The joint work of the Netherlands and WHO aims to make healthcare more climate resilient and sustainable while mainstreaming health into internal climate policies.
***
The Netherlands also funds crucial activities in sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care and antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.
Between 2022 and 2023, the Netherlands provided US$ 80 million to WHO, including over US$ 66 million in voluntary contributions.
The Netherlands also contributed over US$ 20 million in flexible and thematic funding to WHO, making it the third-largest flexible contributor to the Organization. Such support allows WHO to be agile and strategic in its efforts to help countries improve the health and well-being of their populations.

How Alberta separatism went from fringe cause to referendum
For decades, Alberta separatism was a fringe cause
EDMONTON, Alberta -- For decades, Alberta separatism was a fringe cause. On Monday, voters in Canada’s oil heartland will decide whether to take the first step toward a referendum on leaving the country.
Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is not voting to leave Canada on Oct. 19. Instead, voters will decide whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, has said that support for starting the separation process, which was around 23% in a recent poll, is “still too high for my liking.”
Alberta has long feuded with the federal government over oil and federal power. Liberal prime ministers Pierre Trudeau and, decades later, his son Justin became deeply unpopular in the province over energy policy.
Justin Trudeau’s government imposed a national carbon tax and other climate measures that Alberta leaders said hurt its oil industry. Yet separatist parties typically drew only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney said.
Then came the pandemic and the Freedom Convoy, which paralyzed parts of Ottawa, the Canadian capital, and blocked major Canada-U.S. border crossings.
“They needed a new cause,” Kenney told The Associated Press. “And it naturally morphed into separatism.”
Jeff Rath, a leader of the independence movement, said federal vaccine rules preventing unvaccinated Canadians from flying were his breaking point.
“If Trudeau won’t let me leave Alberta, I’m just going to pick up my whole province and go,” Rath recalled telling a friend. “COVID was really the straw that broke the camel’s back.”
“A lot of people were radicalized by the convoy,” he said.
The 2022 Freedom Convoy began over vaccine requirements for cross-border truckers but grew into a broader revolt against pandemic restrictions.
Kenney said people mobilized over anger at globalization, vaccines and pandemic restrictions, while social media allowed previously isolated activists to find one another and organize.
“They found each other and they found a cause,” Kenney said.
Kenney said the movement also became more professional, building organizations, raising money and drawing in political operatives with campaign and fundraising experience.
He also sees substantial overlap between separatist activists and people who support Russian President Vladimir Putin or believe conspiracy theories about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Kenney stressed he was describing activists, not typical separation voters, whom he characterized as frustrated Albertans sending Ottawa a message.
Kenney said the MAGA movement has been “inspirational” for some separatist activists. He said they “tried to infiltrate with at least some success” the United Conservative Party he founded. Smith replaced Kenney in 2022 after appealing to United Conservative Party members angry over COVID-19 restrictions.
“Literally, you can look at the players,” Kenney said of the convoy and separatist movements. “It’s the same people.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney has made getting Alberta oil to new markets a national priority and backs a proposed pipeline to the West Coast. His more business- and energy-friendly policies, along with his opposition to U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and 51st-state rhetoric, have made the federal Liberal leader unusually popular in conservative Alberta.
Kenney, one of the most prominent conservative critics of Trudeau's approach to Alberta, said Carney “speaks as an Albertan,” understands the province’s grievances and aspirations, and is moving in the right direction on energy.
Rath called Carney a “formidable opponent,” saying “every major politician” in Alberta and Canada is against the separatists and acknowledged an uphill battle. He said he would be “thrilled” with more than 30% of the vote — well short of a majority.
“Canada is facing real threats to our economy, to our security, to our way of life,” Carney said. “We have to be strong and we are stronger together.”
Alberta sends roughly 90% of its crude oil exports to the United States, and separatists have taken their campaign directly to Washington.
Rath confirmed he and other independence advocates met with U.S. State Department officials three times and presented a document outlining what an independent Alberta could offer the United States.
Rath claimed people involved in the meetings were going directly to the White House and that a possible oil pipeline through the U.S. to the Pacific was “literally a topic of our last meeting with the U.S. State Department.”
The State Department said that “The Department regularly meets with a wide range of representatives. The vote is a decision for the people of Alberta.”
Kenney called the outreach “bonkers,” saying people with “zero democratic mandate” were discussing with a foreign government “the status of a separate state that does not exist.”
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta “a natural partner.”
Keith Wilson, another Alberta independence leader who was lead counsel for the 2022 convoy organizers, said separatists see the vote as a way to give Alberta more leverage in dealing with Ottawa, even short of independence.
“That’s right, because it’s called leverage. It’s called negotiation,” Wilson said. He said he would accept substantial structural changes to Alberta’s relationship with Ottawa short of independence.
“I don’t think it will recede,” Kenney said of the separatist movement in Alberta. Even 10% to 20% support, he noted, would far exceed separatists’ historic vote share. If low turnout pushed them toward 30%, “they’re going to be even more emboldened.”
“That’s not a threat to Canada,” Kenney said. “But it is a threat to the conservative movement.”
Alberta is not Canada’s only national-unity challenge. Quebec voters returned the separatist Parti Quebecois to power Oct. 5, although support for independence remains around 30% and its leader has said he will not hold a referendum while Trump is U.S. president.
Quebec voters have twice rejected independence, most recently by a razor-thin margin in a 1995 referendum.

Britain's Kartal misses out on biggest title of her career
- Published
Britain's Sonay Kartal missed out on what would have been the biggest title of her career as she faded in a gripping Wuhan Open final against French Open runner-up Maja Chwalinska.
Kartal, 24, was bidding to lift the trophy in only her third event since returning from a six-month absence caused by a back injury.
But an extraordinary week seemed to catch up with Kartal as she ran out of steam - physically and mentally - in a 2-6 6-4 6-2 defeat.
Kartal was playing in just the 10th match of her impressive comeback and was attempting to become the first Briton to win a WTA 1,000 title since Johanna Konta in 2017.
Ranked 170th in the world at the start of the event, Kartal reached Sunday's final by seeing off a host of notable opponents, including current top-10 players and former major champions.
However, Poland's Chwalinska, who made a shock run to this year's Roland Garros final, dragged Kartal into a brutal battle and ultimately got the better of it.
Kartal dominated the first set and led by a break in the second before Chwalinska turned momentum in her favour.
Chwalinska, 25, felt a few nerves as she closed in on her first WTA 1,000 title, but took her third championship point when Kartal hammered a forehand long.
Despite losing the final, Kartal has enjoyed a transformational week which even she did not see coming.
On Monday, Kartal will climb to 50th in the world rankings - just below her career high - and become the British number one for the first time.

Eight workers died and 12 others were injured after a car ran over them on Lehragaga-Jakhal road in the Sangrur district of Punjab on Sunday, PTI reported citing police authorities.
A group of more than 20 workers enrolled under the Viksit Bharat Guarantee Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission Gramin (VB-G RAM G) were engaged in some work in the area when the incident occurred. Some of them were also reportedly sitting on the road.
This is when the speeding car coming from the direction of Jakhal mowed down the group.
The driver then went on to abandon the vehicle and flee from the spot, PTI reported citing Superintendent of Police Palwinder Singh.
Five workers died at the spoy while the injured were taken to a hospital nearby. Some are said to be in critical condition.
The car, which was a sedan as per a report by NDTV, lost control and slammed into the group of workers. The car's model has been identified as a Chevrolet Optra Magnum. The driver has been identified as Raidhrana village's Pargat Singh Kala, as per the report.
Among the victims, six were women - Karmjeet Kaur, Niki, Sarbjeet Kaur, Ranjeet Kaur, Karmjeet, and Rani Kaur, and two were men - Jivan Singh and Des Raj.
Punjab Cabinet Minister Barinder Kumar Goyal, the local MLA, expressed grief over the incident, PTI reported.
He said the injured are being provided medical treatment, and assured all possible help from the government for the victims. Ambulances have been deployed to shift bodies, he said.
Finance Minister Harpal Singh Cheema, too, condoled the death of workers. "The tragic incident that occurred with women labourers working under MGNREGA near the village of Alisher in Lehra is extremely sad. In this hour of grief, heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families. May the Almighty grant eternal peace to the departed souls and give strength to the families to bear this loss," Cheema was quoted as saying by PTI.
Congress MP Amrinder Singh Raja Warring expressed grief over the deaths. "Deeply saddened by the tragic incident in Lehra where eight MGNREGA workers were mowed down by a speeding car, leaving several injured. This is heartbreaking.
"These are the poorest workers who toil hard to earn a living. I urge the administration to ensure immediate medical aid for the injured, sternest action against those responsible and adequate compensation for the families of the deceased. May the departed souls rest in peace," the Ludhiana MP said in a post on X.
Leader of Opposition in Punjab Assembly, Partap Singh Bajwa, also expressed grief over the tragic incident. "The tragic loss of eight MGNREGA workers in Lehra after being struck by a speeding vehicle is deeply distressing. Several others have also sustained injuries in this horrific incident.
My heartfelt condolences to the families who have lost their loved ones. May the departed souls rest in eternal peace, and may the injured recover soon," he said.

Markets regulator SEBI has given its go-ahead to gym chain Cult.fit’s ₹950 Cr IPO about three months after it filed draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with the regulator. As per SEBI’s latest processing status, the regulator issued its final observation on the offer documents of Cult.fit on October 12. In SEBI parlance, the issuance of final observations signals the regulator’s go-ahead for a company to proceed with its public issue. Cult.fit filed its DRHP in July this year. The company’s IPO will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹950 Cr and an offer for sale of up to 17.86 Cr shares. As per sources, The total IPO size is likely to be around ₹4,000 Cr. Early investors like Temasek Holdings, via MacRitchie Investments, Schroders Capital, German fitness operator LifeFit Group, Accel, Tata Digital and cofounder Mukesh Bansal are among the shareholders who plan to offload shares via the OFS. Cult.fit plans to utilise the funds raised through the fresh issue towards setting up new gym centres, expenditure toward leasing, renting and licensing of existing identified fitness centres, repayment and prepayment of certain borrowings, setting up new exclusive brand outlets, marketing and promotional activities and general corporate purposes. Axis Capital, Goldman Sachs, Jefferies India, JM Financial and Morgan Stanley India are the book running lead managers (BRLMs) to the issue. Founded in 2016, Cult.fit operates a chain of gyms and fitness centres and offers online classes for physical and mental wellbeing. It operated 708 fitness centres across 77 cities in India and had more than 9.87 Lakh paid members as of March 31, 2026. Out of these, 218 centres are owned and operated by the company. The rest are owned or operated by franchises (288 centres) or by independent owners (202 centres). Cult.fit managed to narrow its net loss for the fiscal year FY26 to ₹251.8 Cr from ₹480.8 Cr in FY25. It posted an operating revenue of ₹1,720.6 Cr, up 41.5% from ₹1,215.5 Cr in FY25. The business benefits from a diversified revenue profile, with fitness services contributing roughly 70% of revenues and the fitness products business accounting for the remaining 30%. Cult.fit has raised over $800 Mn to date from investors like Zomato, Accel, Kalaari Capital, Chiratae Ventures, South Park Commons, among others.
