Noah Adams, longtime host of NPR's All Things Considered, has died
Noah Adams, a writer, broadcaster, and storyteller who hosted All Things Considered for 18 years, has died.
Adams died Friday at his home in Yellow Springs, Ohio, according to his wife, Neenah Ellis. He was 84.
He guided listeners through major events like Ronald Reagan's landslide electoral victories, the fall of the Berlin Wall, and the September 11 terrorist attacks. But to the people who worked alongside him in the newsroom, Adams' journalism shone through in the softer features he reported.
Adams would ride trains across the country, or spend days in small towns talking to whoever he came across. He'd ask questions. He'd listen. He'd write down notes and observations. And then he'd produce long, thoughtful radio pieces that helped listeners understand and appreciate the world a little bit better.
"He was always observing," recalled Melissa Block, who produced pieces alongside Adams for years before hosting All Things Considered herself. "He would have a little reporter's notebook and he would be taking notes in shorthand. His writing is almost illegible – it would just be the vaguest sketches of things. But somehow, when we came back, he would capture the character of a place or a person or a town in the most vivid, rich, simple language. It was a complete picture based on his unbelievable powers of observation."
Adams, who was born in Kentucky, came to NPR in the mid-1970s, when the network was still new, and still figuring things out.
He was private - intensely private - but told people he'd bopped around a series of jobs before falling into radio. He worked construction. He sold cars, as he recounted once in an on-air essay. In 1972, he started working at the public radio station at the University of Kentucky. Three years later, he applied for a job as a production assistant on All Things Considered.
For years, the show's staff has begun each morning with a long meeting about the day's news, and what should and should not be included in the two-hour broadcast. Like all meetings, it can be rote or boring, and many staffers can, at times, view it with some cynicism.
Adams never saw it that way. "You would pay attention to all the mysteries out in the world," he once recalled in an NPR essay looking back at his career. "You'd have a deep curiosity about the yearning. You'd notice who was in trouble, why? What does Washington mean?"
Listening carefully, and caring
Like most reporters, Adams yearned to get out of the newsroom and into the world. He tried to steer his reporting away from officials and politicians in Washington.
"He never liked talking to people who he knew had pre-programmed things to say," said Block. "He wanted people who were genuinely speaking from their heart and with conviction and sincerity. And that's how he was. That's how he approached things."
He'd also try to write and talk about dogs as much as possible, working them into scenes, and into interviews.
It's how Adams began one memorable interview in 1987. He was talking to an 8-year-old girl named Betsy Walter, whose parents had gotten divorced. To get her comfortable, he started chatting about dogs.
The approach stood out to the producer Adams was working with that night: a young Ira Glass. "It's the fastest, most efficient warm up of a child," Glass remembered years later. "He's not talking down to her. And then he just launches into the interview."
Adams was so good that day — at getting Betsy comfortable, at getting the quotes they wanted from the interview — that Glass took the tape of the full interview home with him, to save.
As Glass listened to the taping and studied Adams' approach, he realized how well and quickly Adams connected with the girl. How he framed his questions in just the right way, so the interview became a conversation that produced memorable quotes about the pain and confusion of divorce.
Over the years Glass would repeatedly cite Adams and his interviewing style as an inspiration for the feel and tone of the public radio program he'd go on to create: This American Life.
Glass admitted that as a young producer, he was intimidated by Adams and his quiet confidence. "You know, he was paired with [co-host] Susan Stamberg," Glass recalled. "And Susan Stamberg's character on the air, as the host of All Things Considered, was this warm, mensch-y, chatty New York lady. And he was this sort of cool, traditional broadcaster next to her."
A voice for rural America
In 1987, Adams left All Things Considered. Another public radio icon, Garrison Keillor, had walked away from A Prairie Home Companion, and Adams went to Minnesota to launch a new variety show to replace it. "I remember [thinking] wow, the nerve!" said Glass.
The variety show didn't work out, and two years later, Adams was back at All Things Considered, where he was paired alongside Robert Siegel and Linda Wertheimer.
The two men brought different experiences and views of the world to the show. "Noah was a voice for our going to rural America, doing stories about what was happening in small towns far from the Interstate 95 corridor," said Siegel.
"He was a productive writer," said Siegel. "He admired good writing and good writers. And he tried to be as good as he could be."
Adams wrote five books, including Piano Lessons (1996) a memoir about a year he spent learning to play the piano at age 51, Far Appalachia, Following the New River North (2001), and The Flyers: In Search of Wilbur & Orville Wright, (2003).
Adams' writing for the radio reached its peak, according to Siegel and many others, in an extraordinary 1981 radio documentary called "Father Cares: The Last of Jonestown."
Jim Jones, the head of the cult that eventually committed mass suicide in the jungle of Guyana, had recorded hundreds of hours of audio. NPR got its hands on it, and Adams, producer Deb Amos, and author James Reston, Jr. made it into an experimental documentary.
One aspect of it was controversial: Adams narrated it not as a journalist, but as a fictional composite character presented as a survivor of the cult. His delivery was purposely flat, and filled with trauma.
To Siegel, the documentary was NPR as Noah Adams wanted it to be: "Experimental use of sound. Interesting writing. I think he aspired to our not just having tomorrow's front page on tonight, but to have the rich back-page [features]" he said.
Adams helped shape NPR at a moment when the network's identity was still malleable. At a time when it wasn't quite a fully professionalized and institutionalized news gathering operation, Adams wanted the network to live up to the ideals formed during that era, says Melissa Block.
"To really capture the character of the country and the voices of everyone in their own style, in their own perspective, from their own perspective," she explained, "and to pay attention to things that were outside of the centers of power."
Quietly, purposefully, with his notebook and his typewriter, that's what Noah Adams did.

Tim Winton's Cloudstreet named number one in ABC Radio National's Top 100 Australian Books
When Tim Winton wrote the last lines of Cloudstreet, he had no notion of how successful the book would be.
He was on the Greek island of Hydra, on the tail end of a European residency that had taken him and his growing family to Paris and rural Ireland.
When, in 1988, his wife, Denise, became pregnant with their second child, they decided to return home to Western Australia, where Winton grew veggies, fished and knuckled down to edit his manuscript.
By the time it was due to go to print in 1991, the outlook was not great.
"We were publishing it into a hideous recession," Winton tells ABC Radio National's The Book Show.
"Interest rates were at 17.5 per cent. The economy was just really struggling. People were doing it hard. We were broke ourselves.
"By the time the book came out, we had no money."
The dire economic circumstances prompted his publishers, Hilary McPhee and Diana Gribble, to release the book as a more affordable paperback rather than as a pricier hardcover.
But despite their concerns, it was immediately clear they had a hit on their hands.
"Within a week, it was just doing mad things," Winton says.
"That was the book that saved us."
Thirty-five years on, Cloudstreet has been adapted for radio, theatre, opera and television and has never been out of print.
"It's been translated into so many languages," Winton says.
"I still get mail. It's an odd phenomenon that I just can't account for."
His readers are in no doubt as to the book's appeal, however.
With more than 280,000 votes counted, Cloudstreet has placed first in Radio National's Top 100 Australian Books.
Three other Winton novels made the list, with Breath (2008) coming in at 33, Dirt Music (2001) at 41 and Juice (2024) at 88.
'A bravura performance'
Winton was just 21 when he won the 1981 Australian/Vogel Literary Award for his first novel, An Open Swimmer.
His next novel, Shallows, published three years later, won his first Miles Franklin Literary Award.
He published two more novels, That Eye, the Sky and In the Winter Dark, by the time he started work on Cloudstreet in the late 80s.
"[Cloudstreet] was a book that I was thinking about all of that time," Winton says.
"I needed to build up to it because it was a bravura sort of performance in a way. It took a lot of nerve, and I didn't have that nerve for a long time. I needed to work on my chops during my 20s."
Cloudstreet follows the fortunes of two families — the Lambs and the Pickles — over two decades in mid-20th-century Perth.
It won Winton his second Miles Franklin, an award he has now won four times (Dirt Music took it out in 2002 and Breath in 2009).
Dedicated to his grandparents, Cloudstreet draws on the tall tales Winton heard as a child, hiding under the table during family lunches.
He remembers being transfixed by his grandparents' voices, so different to his own.
"They sounded like they were from a different world," he says.
"I was a child of the space age, and my grandparents were people from the horse and cart era. They sounded like people in a Chips Rafferty movie."
The stories took on a sacred cast with each retelling, bringing long-dead family members back to life.
Growing up in a family of storytellers and larger-than-life characters shaped Winton as a writer.
"All that tale-spinning around the table … embedded itself in my memory," he writes in That Book, the final essay in his new collection, Songs from the Firefront.
In Cloudstreet, Winton sought to honour that lost world.
"It was hitching a ride on that oral storytelling tradition which was fading in white working-class culture in the 60s and 70s, and which I clung to and tried to reinvigorate in the 80s."
A metaphor for society
Cloudstreet's industrious matriarch, Oriel Lamb, is modelled on Winton's paternal grandmother, Olive.
Like Oriel, Olive Winton lived in a tent under the mulberry bush in the backyard for 30 years.
"I just thought it was normal," Winton says. "I thought everybody's nana lived in a tent."
His grandmother was diminutive but "mighty" in character.
"She was tiny, but a very impressive person," Winton says. "She'd had a really tough life."
Born into a poor family in Albany at the turn of the century, Olive left school to care for her siblings before working as a scullery maid for a wealthy family in Subiaco.
Despite her limited education, she loved poetry.
"Language was precious to her," Winton says.
"She'd reel off hundreds and hundreds of lines of [19th-century poets] Longfellow and Browning … That was a big influence on me as a kid."
The Wintons, like the Lambs, were hardworking, driven by a Protestant work ethic.
In contrast, the Mifflins — Winton's mother's family — were, like the Pickles, reliant on luck: "More carefree, more feckless, not religious at all," Winton says. "[They] lived it up."
While the two branches of Winton's family never resided under one roof, the Lambs and the Pickles live side-by-side in Cloudstreet, the source of much of the novel's tension.
Winton came to see this juxtaposition as a metaphor for society more broadly.
"That's what a culture is, that's what a village is, that's what a neighbourhood is," he says.
"People of all sorts and different inspirations and possessed by different impulses trying to get along, trying to make peace with their differences and trying to find each other interesting."
A new appreciation for history
Cloudstreet may be an Australian classic, but Winton wrote much of the manuscript abroad.
He had never travelled overseas before, and the homesickness he felt imbued his writing.
"It's a kind of physical affliction. I felt like my skin had been peeled," he says.
The geographic distance provided Winton with the perspective he needed to see his home anew.
"It clarified my thinking, and it was helpful to me," he says.
At the time, the Perth of Winton's childhood was being demolished in the name of progress, replaced by modern, characterless buildings and freeways.
"Perth had a provincial shame about old houses and buildings, and a misplaced pride in the shiny stuff it could erect in their stead," Winton writes in That Book.
In Europe, Winton encountered a different way of life, one that honoured the past and preserved the built environment.
In Ireland, Winton lived in the shadow of a medieval castle; his son went to kindy in Paris over the road from where Balzac lived more than a century before; while the drama of the Odyssey unfolded across the water from where he lived in Greece.
In white working-class Perth, where connections did not extend "back beyond a generation or two", history was not valued in the same way.
The energy he felt in centuries-old European buildings — "storied places" where "you could feel the joys and woes of long-dead humans" — found expression in his novel.
Cloudstreet, the ramshackle Victorian-era house that gives the book its title, is a character in its own right, heaving and sighing, growing and shifting.
"The house in my book was alive," Winton writes.
An ancient culture
Much of Cloudstreet unfolds around Derbal Yerrigan, as it is known by its Noongar custodians, or the Swan River.
Winton hoped the river — "the abiding metaphor of the book" — might also serve as a metaphor to help drive reconciliation, an idea that was gaining momentum at the time.
For millennia, Noongar people have gathered on the river's banks.
It was a waterway also valued by Winton and his forebears. "We played there, hunted there, feasted there, danced and celebrated there," he writes.
But by the 80s, the river was ailing after decades of mismanagement under colonisation.
The characters of Cloudstreet, products of the world around them, embody the disconnect between White Australia and the land's traditional owners.
"The sad thing is that the people in Cloudstreet don't always understand what's right in front of them," Winton says.
"I was keen to write about these white working-class people and to honour their lives and their hardships and their aspirations.
"But I couldn't make them any more enlightened than they were … They could see the river, but they didn't really understand what the river was, how sacred and how ancient it is in the same way that they couldn't really appreciate how sacred and ancient the land is.
"I couldn't give them contemporary opinions or attitudes because they didn't have them. They couldn't have them."

The F1 pit stop that helped save lives

When the McLaren pit crew refuelled a car, changed its tyres and relayed information to their driver in less than seven seconds at the Spanish Grand Prix in 2001, they were just doing their jobs.
But 700 miles away in the break room at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), Dr Martin Elliott and his colleagues were watching after completing a life-saving operation on a young child.
The brief glimpse would change how the doctors approached patient care. From surgery-to-ICU handovers and neonatal care to air-ambulance response times, F1's innovations have made an impact far beyond the track.
At Ferrari's factory in Maranello, the medical team studied how pit crews organised roles, communication and handovers.
Doctors and nurses started each procedure with a checklist, setting out specific roles and tasks. This reduced human error and helped ensure key tasks were completed. All patient data was also shared from the operating theatre to the care unit.
Gaps in performance were identified and addressed, while repeated rehearsals helped refine the process.
As a result, the process from surgery to intensive care became more organised, and a 2007 study by researchers at GOSH and the University of Oxford found the F1-inspired handover process reduced technical errors, information omissions and handover time.
Reflecting on the project, Dr Elliott, then a consultant paediatric cardiothoracic surgeon at GOSH, said: "The environment we were working in then and in many ways still do is fundamentally potentially dangerous at every step.
"And of course, fundamentally, that's how F1 doesn't make mistakes. They have created an environment of complete precision, not only in engineering, but also in process, because they simply can't afford financially or from a race perspective to slip up.
"It's the same, you know, the precious parcel on the trolley is the same as the precious parcel in the car. You have to get all of those steps right."
The model was later adopted by other healthcare teams.
From trackside to bedside
Fifteen years ago, Williams worked with the University Hospital of Wales to improve neonatal resuscitation.
Former Williams human performance specialist Gemma Fisher recognised that the organisation of pit-crew equipment to prevent delay could also be applied in a hospital setting.
Video analysis unveiled the chaotic reality of medical emergencies with overlapping voices and misplaced equipment.
Standardising roles - deciding who stood where, who needed to be heard at what moment and where equipment was stationed - allowed for a faster, more efficient response.
Debriefings allowed medical staff to review what had happened and identify what could be improved for future emergencies.
The changes also encouraged junior doctors to raise concerns without fear of blame.
The collaboration extended beyond working practices and into engineering. Advanced Healthcare Technology and Williams have since developed the Babypod: a carbon fibre carrier designed to withstand a 20G crash, which can help prevent injury in the transportation of babies from ambulance to hospital.
Every second counts
F1 continues to find new ways to apply its expertise in emergency medicine.
At this year's race at Silverstone, a collaboration with Air Ambulance Cornwall showed how response times could be improved, with take-off time reduced from five minutes to three and a half.
This was achieved using many of the same methods, including quick and organised starts, having equipment ready for use and clear communication across the team.
David Richards, chairman of Motorsport UK and former team principal of BAR and Benetton, said: "You might not see one and a half minutes in the overall scheme of things, but one and a half minutes when you're lying by the side of the road or you've fallen off a horse or you've fallen down a cliff and you've hurt yourself, those minutes must seem like years for the person who's injured."
Richards said the partnership would continue to look for ways to reduce response times further.
Twenty-five years after Dr Elliott first saw a pit stop that inspired a new way of thinking, lessons from the sport continue to influence healthcare, from neonatal treatment to emergency response.

SIT headed by sitting judge to probe Kolkata pandal stampede; CM announces ₹25 lakh aid, government job
At least 19 people died in a Kolkata Durga Puja pandal stampede. The state has announced a judicially headed SIT probe and compensation for victims.
West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari has announced that a Special Investigation Team (SIT), headed by a sitting Calcutta High Court judge, will investigate the stampede at a Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata that killed at least 19 people and injured 25 others.
The stampede took place at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal on Saturday evening, October 17, amid heavy crowds and rain on Maha Saptami. Adhikari said the state government would write to the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court to nominate a sitting judge to head the probe.
The SIT will include officials from the Special Task Force (STF), the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and other departments.
Deep Dive
Track the Kolkata stampede LIVE
CM announces compensation, government jobs
Adhikari announced ₹25 lakh in compensation and a Group D government job for the family of each person who died in the stampede. Those injured will receive ₹5 lakh each, and the state government will cover their full treatment costs at a hospital of their choice.
The chief minister said authorities were examining CCTV footage to establish what happened and identify those responsible for any crowd-management failures.
"We will check the footage and take appropriate measures against those who failed to manage the crowd. That could be a member of the puja committee, a homeguard, a temporary worker, a policeman, or a private company security guard. Nobody will be spared," Adhikari said.
According to the chief minister, officials had detained some puja committee members, private security guards and personnel on duty. Their detention does not establish responsibility for the incident.

Police examine stampede CCTV footage
A police officer said people waiting outside the pandal rushed forward when rain began, causing some to fall on the road and triggering the stampede. Adhikari also said an announcement made by the organisers led to a sudden surge in the crowd.
The exact sequence of events and responsibility for the incident are yet to be established. Kolkata Police's Anti-Rowdy Section has collected CCTV footage as part of the investigation.
Following the incident, authorities advised popular theme-based pandals to temporarily close to prevent further crowding. Kolkata has around 3,500 Durga Puja pandals.
PM Modi, Mamata Banerjee, Amit Shah express grief
Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced financial assistance of ₹2 lakh from the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund (PMNRF) for the next of kin of each deceased person. Those injured will receive ₹50,000.
"The stampede in Kolkata is extremely distressing. My thoughts are with those who have lost their loved ones. May the injured recover at the earliest," Modi said.

Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee also expressed grief over the incident, offering prayers for the recovery of the injured and strength for their families. President Droupadi Murmu and Governor RN Ravi also conveyed their condolences.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah postponed his scheduled programmes and said he would visit the injured.
Helpline for affected families
The state government has issued a toll-free helpline for information related to the stampede. Kolkata Police also provided a control room number for assistance.

The shortage of doctors in India, particularly in rural areas, is well documented. This shortage compounds the suffering of rural communities, where people must suffer not only with disease but also with the struggle to access care. Illness in rural India is therefore not merely a departure from good health. It can push entire families into generational poverty and, in some cases, drive people to take their own lives. It is no coincidence that illness is among the leading causes of suicide in India.
To address this disparity, doctors are routinely called upon to move to rural areas and serve those most in need. Instead of fixing an underfunded healthcare system, the responsibility is placed on individual doctors to be “good” and fill the void left by governments that have consistently failed to prioritise people’s health.
I define a good doctor as someone who is compassionate, competent, and courageous. However, I am increasingly realising how risky it is to be such a doctor in India.
Being a good doctor
A good doctor is not merely empathetic. Compassion goes beyond feeling another person’s pain; it demands action to alleviate it. Over time, doctors who take this responsibility seriously begin to recognise that a prescription or surgery may address a symptom without touching the larger suffering that produced it. They begin asking why a person fell sick in the first place. And that is what makes them risky.
In Indian medical colleges, disease is often taught as the consequence of an infection, a genetic predisposition, or an unhealthy lifestyle. But step outside these institutions and into the communities where disease takes root, and you begin to understand how inadequate this framework can be. The people living with illness often understand its causes very differently from the institutions tasked with treating it.
“What is your biggest problem in the village?” I asked 25 villagers in rural Assam who had gathered for a cancer screening camp.
“We don’t have a road here, which makes it difficult to travel to and from the village,” said the eldest man in the group. The others nodded. “Because of the poor road, it is difficult to bring water into the village. When somebody falls sick, we cannot take them to the hospital on time,” he continued.
The connections were obvious. The absence of a road restricted access to water and healthcare. Inadequate access to water exposed people to illness, while poor connectivity delayed treatment. These were not separate problems. They were interconnected consequences of deprivation.
Last year, in a village in rural Tamil Nadu, I learnt how health was tied to land rights. “The government took our land away and gave us land 20 km away. We cannot grow anything on that land. We do not have money to buy food every day. Whatever we grow is what we eat,” a group of Adivasis living in the hamlet told me.
When people cannot access adequate food, clean water, or timely healthcare, can the solution to their illness really end with a prescription?
Why a good doctor is risky
A good doctor begins to understand that a prescription cannot compensate for the denial of land rights, that surgery cannot undo displacement, and that no medicine can substitute for the basic infrastructure a government has failed to provide. They recognise that confronting corruption and demanding accountability for broken promises may do more to protect a community’s health than any individual clinical intervention.
Dr. Binayak Sen understood this. A paediatrician and public health specialist, he served rural communities in Chhattisgarh while questioning the structural conditions that shaped their health. “At present, the greatest violence is structural violence. Violence is not restricted to a few groups; it pervades the structure of our society. We need to break out of this structure of violence through a process of dialogue,” he said in an interview with The Hindu.
Anyone who has travelled through rural Chhattisgarh, or indeed much of rural India, will recognise the realities underlying this argument. People do not fall sick simply because of individual choices or personal failures. Poverty, malnutrition, displacement, hunger and illiteracy all shape health outcomes. So does a government that fails to address these conditions. To treat the resulting illnesses without confronting their causes is to leave the machinery of suffering intact.
In 2010, Dr. Sen was convicted on charges relating to his alleged links with Naxalites and sentenced to life imprisonment. His case became symbolic of the risks faced by those who challenge the political and economic structures governing people’s lives. In his acceptance speech for the Paul Harrison Award for Meritorious Service in Rural Areas in 2004, Sen had argued: “The first point that I would like to make is about the primacy of politics in any relevant programme for health and health care. By politics I do not mean the farcical electoral charades of political parties, but the matrix of power that determines control over resources at entry level of community.”
Nearly two decades later, the question of what happens to doctors who challenge these structures remains painfully relevant.
Randall Sequeira, a general medicine specialist and rural practitioner, was arrested on October 16 and, according to reports, remains in judicial custody. His work with Adivasi communities in Odisha has involved addressing health concerns linked to mining activities. He has also stood in solidarity with these communities in their resistance to mining projects.
The implications are chilling. When a doctor connects illness to the consequences of mining, displacement and the denial of rights, healthcare ceases to be a politically neutral exercise. It becomes a challenge to the interests that benefit from these conditions remaining unchanged; conditions that ideally the state should be preventing. A doctor working with marginalised communities should not have to fear incarceration for asking why those communities are being made sick.
What will it take to keep India healthy?
What, then, does India need to keep its people healthy? More evidence on the health consequences of mining? Or do we need yet another explanation of how dispossession, exploitation and crony capitalism devastate Adivasi communities?
Evidence matters, but evidence alone cannot protect people when the political will to act on it is absent, or when those who demand accountability are treated as threats.
India needs good doctors more than ever. Not merely competent clinicians who are up to date with the latest evidence, write appropriate prescriptions and perform complex surgeries, but doctors who have the courage to question the systems that repeatedly make their patients sick. Doctors who understand that health is inseparable from the distribution of land, wealth, power and public resources. Doctors who refuse to accept preventable suffering as an inevitable feature of life for the poor.
Healthcare workers have a moral responsibility that extends beyond the consulting room. They must challenge the forces that expose people to disease, deny them care and then blame them for their suffering. This does not mean that every doctor must become an activist or that clinical care is unimportant. It means recognising the limits of medicine when the conditions producing illness are left untouched.
But a doctor who speaks about these conditions risks being labelled a troublemaker, an agitator or a threat to the state. The experiences of Dr. Sen and Dr. Sequeira raise an urgent question: what kind of society punishes those who seek to protect the health of its most marginalised people?
If being a good doctor means treating the patient while remaining silent about the forces making that patient sick, then perhaps we need to reconsider what goodness in medicine means. And if questioning those forces is enough to put a doctor’s freedom at risk, the problem is not with the doctor.
It is time for healthcare workers to speak up, collectively and without fear. Silence is not neutrality when the suffering is preventable, and the forces responsible are identifiable. The longer we remain silent, the easier it becomes for those in power to keep the tap of suffering open.
(Dr. Parth Sharma is a community medicine physician and a public health palliative care researcher. parth.sharma25@gmail.com)

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

The Union Health Ministry has asked all States and Union Territories to ensure the prominent display of rates charged for services and facilities offered by clinical establishments.
In a move aimed at strengthening transparency, accountability and patient-centric healthcare delivery, Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava, in a letter to the Chief Secretaries of all States and Union Territories, called for compliance with regulatory provisions, and ensuring information on service charges was clearly visible to patients and their attendants.
“Display of rates would help patients and their families understand the likely cost of treatment, make informed healthcare decisions, and plan their medical expenditure,’’ Ms. Srivastava said, adding that greater transparency would also help minimise avoidable confusion and billing-related disputes.
The letter refers to the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 and the Clinical Establishments (Central Government) Rules, 2012.
Under the Rules, clinical establishments in States and Union Territories where the Act is applicable are required to display the rates charged for each type of service provided, along with facilities available, at a conspicuous place, in the local language as well as in English.
Since health is a State subject, in States and Union Territories where clinical establishments are regulated by their own respective frameworks, several of which also contain provisions relating to the display of rates, the Health Secretary has called upon Chief Secretaries to ensure effective compliance.
The letter also places particular emphasis on transparency in healthcare pricing for international patients.
States and UTs have been requested to encourage the prominent display, wherever applicable, of package rates offered to foreign patients travelling to India on medical or Ayush visas.
“This would enable international patients to make informed choices, help minimise pricing and billing-related grievances and further strengthen India’s position as a trusted destination for medical and Ayush care,’’ the Ministry said.

An executive of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party on Sunday denied that scandal-hit former agriculture minister Kazuo Yana had influenced budget cuts for municipalities whose mayors did not support him in a general election.
Commenting on Yana’s remark that road budgets had been significantly reduced for the municipalities, LDP Executive Acting Secretary-General Koichi Hagiuda said on a television debate program that “we have not been able to confirm that the results of the (budget) allocations to individual projects were changed as a result of Yana’s words or actions.”
“It is not a system that allows one lawmaker to raise or lower the budget of a local government,” Hagiuda said.
He apologized for the fact that Yana’s remark about budget cuts had led to his replacement as agriculture minister and called on Yana to properly explain what he did.
“Budget allocations must not be arbitrarily influenced,” Hagiuda said. He added that any suspicions about budget allocations must be thoroughly investigated, leaving open the possibility of examining whether funds are being allocated appropriately.

People have been killed and injured in a fire at a military base in the Canadian province of Alberta, the country's defence minister has said, with officials yet to clarify what caused the incident.
Defence minister David McGuinty said a “serious” incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright had caused a major fire, though he provided few details and no precise figures for how many people had died or been hurt.
"I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base," McGuinty said at a news conference in Ottawa.
McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in the investigation and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate".
He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information, but suggested it was a major and unprecedented event.
"I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," he said.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4pm local time (10pm GMT) on Saturday after reports of a fire in a training area at the base, which lies about 180km (120 miles) south-east of the provincial capital, Edmonton.
The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire crossed the base's fence and was spreading rapidly because of high winds, and that firefighters from several areas were responding. No evacuation order was in effect, but residents were asked to avoid the area, keep roads clear and stay away from the Wainwright Health Centre unless they needed critical care. Gusts of up to 100kmph hit large parts of the province during the day.
Patients were taken to hospitals across Edmonton because health facilities in Wainwright were overwhelmed, according to Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency physician at the city's Royal Alexandra Hospital.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr Thirsk told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."
Prime minister Mark Carney said in a social media post: "Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected."
Alberta premier Danielle Smith said in a post on X that the province was "learning of a significant and tragic fire that is affecting many of our brave military personnel".
Opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said in a social media post: "Pray for Wainwright, everyone."
General Jennie Carignan, the chief of the defence staff, said in a post on X: "We are dealing with a serious incident at CFB Wainwright, and are fully engaged with federal, provincial and local authorities."
The base is one of Canada's busiest military training sites, where soldiers prepare for combat operations, and it is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre.
The fire disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday's referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early on Saturday and that the ballots were transported securely.

Leap seconds have driven a raging debate in the metrological community for three decades. Now, that argument has been put to rest: The leap second is officially dead.
Doing away with an obscure metric the average person has been blissfully unaware of may seem like a novelty, but killing the leap second has major ramifications for technology you rely on every day. It also helps stave off what could’ve been a dangerous moment in time: The possibility of the world’s first negative leap second.
The International Bureau of Weights and Measurements (known by its French acronym BIPM) on Thursday said that in May 2027, it would stop issuing leap seconds to adjust what’s known as Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), 32 of which have been added since 1972.
The world implemented the leap second in 1972 due to a growing gap between time measured with atomic clocks and time based on the Earth’s rotation. The reason for the discrepancy? The latter is slowing down due in large part to tidal friction caused by the moon and Earth’s rotation not lining up. The molten core of the Earth as well as oceans and the atmosphere also affect the spin rate.
Leap seconds are a way to keep atomic-clock-driven UTC in line with astronomically kept Universal Time (UT1). Think of it like adding a little extra track for a train to keep running exactly parallel with another one. Rather than happening on a set interval—like a leap year—BIPM uses the average of hundreds of atomic clocks around the world and compares their time calculations to astronomical time to determine when a leap second is necessary. The most recent one was added in 2016.
Of course, adding track is no small effort, and it may seem like a lot of hassle for a measly second. But UTC is vital for all sorts of technology given the number of APIs and databases that rely on it. Introducing a leap second helped keep UTC and UT1 aligned, but it also wrought havoc on various systems running on UTC and forced companies to figure out how to deal with them when they were added every few years.
A number of tech companies like Google and Meta use “a ‘smear’ method of dealing with leap seconds,” Judah Levine, a fellow at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, writes in an email. In essence, they spread a leap second out over the course of a day or so in tiny increments. But leap seconds have thrown off other systems; the airline Qantas, for example, saw its booking system borked by a leap second in 2012.
Adding a leap second is hard enough as it is. But the odds of having to add a negative leap second have been rising in part because the Earth has picked up rotational speed in recent years due to climate change. (There’s always a climate angle.) Melting ice has caused a shift in the planet’s gravity so extreme that a negative leap second may have been required as soon as 2029, according to a 2024 Nature study. Part of the calculus of ditching the leap second altogether was that going negative isn’t worth the risk.
“There are continuing problems with positive leap seconds even after 50 years, and the concern was that the negative leap second would be much more serious because its effects had never been tested,” Levine says.
BIPM time department director Patrizia Tavella confirmed those concerns in an email to WIRED. “The probability of a negative leap second convinced us [to] set the application date in 2027,” she wrote, adding that there was added urgency following tests by an industry standards group that “showed several failures with a negative leap.”
Tavella says the group is waiting until May 20, 2027 to implement it because it's the anniversary of 1875 signing of the Metre Convention, creating BIPM, as well as Metrology Day. In other words, it’s the perfect time to mark the passing of time—or more accurately, the lack thereof.
The death of the leap second makes life easier for everyone now. “The nice fact is that we have nothing to do!” Tavella says. “Just continue to accumulate second[s] and ‘normal’ minutes of 60 seconds.”
Levine concurs, writing that “life will have one less hassle.”
But kicking the can on adding leap seconds doesn’t mean atomic time and astronomical time won’t continue to drift apart. That’s why BIPM also agreed to create a leap hour. Given how long it takes leap seconds to add up, a leap hour is millennia away. (There are, after all, 3,600 seconds in an hour.)
“We do not speak of leap hour yet,” Tavella says. “If systems rely on UTC, they have nothing to do. If they rely on UT1, they have to be able to use the information UT1-UTC which, in [the] future, will be larger than 1 second.”
In other words, not our problem, and good luck to future generations!

Eugenio Chacarra won the DP World India Championship by two strokes to move top of the Race to Dubai standings ahead of Patrick Reed and Rory McIlroy.
Spain's Chacarra finished on 21 under, with American Reed and world number two McIlroy well off the pace by the final round of this event.
After opening with successive scores of 67 in his first two rounds at Delhi Golf Club, bad light halted play with Chacarra still on the 11th hole of his third round on Saturday.
That left the 26-year-old with extra work on Sunday and he concluded his third round with a five-shot lead after a nine-under 63.
A two-under 70 in his final round was then enough to see off the challenge of New Zealand's Daniel Hillier who birdied the last to put the pressure on the victor.
The win was Chacarra's third of the season as he looks to emulate Jon Rahm and Seve Ballesteros to become the third Spaniard to top the season-long standings on the DP World Tour.

Polls and pundits alike are widely — if sometimes cautiously — predicting a blue wave in the midterm elections on November 3. But there’s an important caveat to predictions of a Democratic triumph: Republicans have far more cash at their disposal.
Republicans have a huge fundraising advantage. Will it matter?
Astead Herndon speaks with Shane Goldmacher about the way the GOP’s big money midterm strategy.
President Donald Trump’s super PAC alone had around $400 million on hand earlier this fall, and Elon Musk has personally pumped hundreds of millions into critical races, including $158 million for Texas alone.
Democrats, by contrast, have lagged far behind, especially relative to their performance in past cycles, with the party’s candidates propped up more by small-money donors than deep-pocketed institutional players.
Shane Goldmacher, a national political reporter for the New York Times, has extensively covered the role of money in American electoral politics. He spoke with America, Actually host Astead Herndon about where that money is coming from, how the GOP is spending it, and the effect that it might have on the coming elections.
They also discuss the races that aren’t getting funded — and what current fundraising patterns might tell us about the candidates who could be in the mix in the next presidential campaign cycle.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
A couple of weeks ago we asked, “What is the GOP strategy to try to win?” And one of the answers we got is they simply have more dollars than Democrats. Everyone’s talking about this GOP money advantage, but how big is it really, and where is it coming from?
It’s bigger than I’ve basically seen in the last 20 years, and it’s almost entirely coming from big donors. President Trump has a super PAC. It had about $400 million in it at the beginning of September, and there was no Democratic counterpart.
And then the Republican National Committee, which is functionally controlled by Trump, had another $130 million. More than Democrats, because the DNC has literally more debts than cash. That’s a half a billion dollars.
You’re saying this is a historic edge.
In 2024, Kamala Harris outspent Donald Trump significantly in the general election. In 2020, Joe Biden significantly outspent Donald Trump in the general. In 2016, Hillary Clinton. And in the midterms along the way, same story.
This is a switch, and when you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances.
Do we know anything specific about the people putting in money to the Trump super PAC and the RNC to give them such a lead?
Most of these folks are disclosed. And Trump has been pretty open about raising money from the very moment that he won. He’s been pretty clear that he is in business to help people who are helping him. And so there are big crypto industries that are giving money that are expecting or hoping for favorable regulation from the administration.
So it’s a lot of big businesses. It’s a lot of wealthy Republicans who generally support him anyway, and there are industry groups that see benefit to being in favor.
I will never forget, obviously, the scene from Trump’s second inauguration when he had the Zuckerbergs and the Bezoses and Elon Musk behind him. Is that how I should think about the people funding this donor advantage? Is it tech oligarchs? Is it tech forward?
There’s a lot of tech. I wouldn’t say it’s exclusively [tech]. And Musk, by the way, is like an extra pot of money. Musk, the world’s richest person, is said to be spending at least $200 million. So that’s a bigger chunk. He has given some money directly to the Trump super PAC. He’s given some money to these congressional super PACs.
Is this just quid pro quo? Is this just a group of businesses who think, “Hey, no matter how unpopular this guy is, it is worth investing in him and his party because they’re gonna, regulate or not regulate in a way that’s favorable for us”?
It’s not quite just that. He raised a ton of this money when he was not so unpopular. If you want to say something smart that he did, it was that. Throughout 2025 he was raising all of this money.
And I don’t want to overstate the Republican advantage. A lot of these Democratic candidates are raising a ton of money. James Talarico stands out as maybe the peak example of this.
The Texas Senate race is the most expensive race in the country right now, and Republicans are pouring $200 million to save the nominee there. So a big chunk of that advantage is going to Texas. And the Democrats have put very little money from outside groups into Texas.
Talarico has captured the imagination of these small Democratic donors, and he’s raised tens and tens of millions of dollars. I would be shocked if he doesn’t hit $100 million by the end of the cycle.
You reported that the GOP’s pulling back in North Carolina. What should we take from that in terms of how the GOP sees its own landscape when it comes to the federal races?
Where have Republicans put that money? They put it into South Carolina right next door to protect a seat that was once thought, on the Senate front, to be safe for Republicans. This is the former Lindsey Graham seat that his sister is now running in. And then even more of it has gone to Kansas. This is a state that has not elected a [Democrat] to the Senate for nearly 100 years.
If you’re the Republican Party and you’re pulling money out of a state like North Carolina that hasn’t elected a Democrat since 2008, and then putting it into a place that hasn’t elected one since 1932, that tells you where the, the bar is moving.
I think the concern for Democrats right now is there might be a wave, but Kansas has a big red wall. It’s hard to beat that kind of institutional advantage for the Republican Party.
Considering how close we are to Election Day, like, what are they actually spending this money on? Is it just more ads? Is it just more mailers?
I was in Pennsylvania this month, and I was trying to watch political ads on YouTube for various races. And I was getting pre-roll of three political ads before I watched the political ad I was trying to watch. So much about our elections is being decided now by people who are actively trying not to consume political news. It costs more money to reach people who are avoiding it on purpose.
There are some organizing things that happen, but most of the money is various versions of advertising.
On the Democratic side, considering this GOP edge, what are the races that you currently describe as underfunded? Where do the Democrats wish they had more money?
Number one is governors’ races, actually. When you look at where Democratic donors swoon, it’s Senate races. There are no candidates for governor who have made people swoon like this in recent years.
[James] Talarico is raising all this money, but in Texas also, Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, does not have that kind of money, and she’s running against Greg Abbott, who had $100 million.
What should we ascribe that to?
I think there’s actually a pretty simple answer, which is, if you don’t live in the state, it doesn’t impact you. If you’re a small donor and you live in California, you can be excited about a Senate candidate because you want Democrats to control the Senate. Are you as excited about a Democratic governor of Georgia?
It’s hard to argue that the governors of these key presidential battlegrounds aren’t some of the most important races on the ballot this year.
By the way, a problem with both parties. Republican national donors and these super PACs also don’t fund these governor’s races at the same level. So it’s not just a Democratic issue, but it’s more acute [for them] because Democrats are so well-funded at the small-donor level.
Fundraising is a huge part of what sets the presidential candidates apart from one another. The money game among those candidates has already started. Is there anyone who’s quietly built some donor network that’s worth thinking about? Is there someone who stood out as a particularly effective fundraiser when we think about the 2028 crowd?
Let me give you my favorite stat from the last Democratic primary, which is that Mike Bloomberg spent twice as much as Tom Steyer, who spent twice as much as Bernie Sanders, who spent twice as much as Joe Biden, who became the Democratic nominee. And so money isn’t gonna determine who wins the next Democratic presidential primary.
One person who has unlimited money, functionally, is JB Pritzker. He’s a billionaire, the governor of Illinois, and he is spending his money now to help other Democrats, which is a good way to make friends.
My last question is an open one. What’s an underexplored story that we should be following going forward when it comes to campaign cash or both parties’ relationship with money?
One of my big questions is what happens to Republican small-dollar fundraising in that post-Trump era. Because there have basically not been any other Republicans who have excited donors for a decade.
Not JD Vance?
I have not seen evidence. JD Vance was not a good fundraiser before he [joined] the ticket with Donald Trump. When he ran for Senate, his primary run was funded chiefly by Peter Thiel through a super PAC.
There are candidates who’ve raised some money, but nothing on the scale of what these Democratic candidates have been able to raise online. When you talk about that Trump era [ending] at some point, are there others who are going to get Republican small donors excited? We don’t know. We haven’t seen it yet.

A female elephant died of anthrax in Periyanaickenpalayam forest range of the Coimbatore Forest Division, forcing the Forest and the Animal Husbandry Departments to step up vigil against the disease.
Forest Department staff spotted the carcass during a routine patrol within the Gopanari reserve forest of the Periyanaickenpalayam range around 4 p.m. on October 13.
According to the department, the carcass appeared to be about a day old. After reviewing the photographs of the carcass, veterinarians raised suspicion of a possible anthrax infection.
Blood smear sample collected from the carcass was sent to the Animal Husbandry Department on Wednesday. The department examined the sample and confirmed the presence of Bacillus anthracis, the bacterium that causes anthrax.
A senior official from the Forest Department said that the carcass was burnt on Thursday, without opening it, as per the protocol based on instructions from the Animal Husbandry Department.
Persons who handled the carcass wore personal protective equipment while carrying out the task.

Dozens arrested in Paris as tens of thousands expected to protest across France
Violent clashes are ongoing between police and protesters over high prices and weak public spending

Around 40 people have been arrested ahead of widespread demonstrations expected across France on Saturday against high prices and inequality.
Police said the arrests were "primarily for carrying weapons or prohibited protective gear" and said that “enhanced checks” are being carried out.
The protests began last month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
A large police presence was visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as the Avenue des Champs-Elysees and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of the two official demonstrations.
Hundreds of other protests were planned across France, with tens of thousands set to participate.
Protesters in hi-vis vests blocked streets, an echo of the unrest that dogged President Emmanuel Macron's previous term, while in Marseille, trash cans were set alight.
"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said a 19-year-old protester in Paris who gave her name as Lola.
The police have drawn criticism for their response due to a grisly list of injuries among demonstrators, including one teenager who had his hand blown off after picking up a stun grenade.
Prime minister Sebastien Lecornu said more than 900 police had also been injured.
The internal police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen cases of alleged police violence.
France suspended the use of stun grenades for the student demonstrations, but Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said they could be used on Saturday.
"If there were to be clashes, all types of intermediate weapons can be used," he told Telematin TV on Friday.
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, leaving behind a polarised electorate and a badly fragmented political landscape.
A long struggle to reduce rising public debt has not impressed investors, who are ditching French bonds, driving borrowing costs to their highest levels in more than two decades.
Mr Lecornu said on Thursday that authorities fear unrest during the protests. The government accused the hard-left France Unbowed of inflaming the protests, an accusation it denies.
Calls on social media for members of past protest movements to join the fray appear to have worked, suggesting the protests could grow significantly.
The Yellow Vest movement started in 2018 as a protest against taxes on diesel before expanding into an outpouring of anger at high living costs and income inequality.
However, things have been largely quiet since Macron agreed to billions of euros in tax cuts.Yannick Maillou, a teacher from La Crèche in western France, joined the Yellow Vests in 2018 and remains involved in the movement.
He said there were several nearby meeting points for protesters on Saturday, with unions also calling for participation.

No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme.
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”.
 
“We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
 
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
 
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
 
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
 
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed Israeli Prime Minister 
Benjamin Netanyahu
 for re-election, backing his long-time ally nine days before Israel’s parliamentary election. The vote will be the country’s first national election since the 2023 Hamas attack.
Ahead of the October 27 polls, Trump praised Netanyahu’s leadership and partnership with Washington, particularly in confronting Iran, as the Israeli leader seeks to retain power after years of regional conflict.
In a lengthy post on Truth Social addressed to the people of Israel, Trump described Netanyahu as a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” and “an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran”.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump wrote.
He added, “This is the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much.”
Making his support explicit, Trump wrote, “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”
Trump also warned that a change in leadership could affect Washington’s role in confronting Tehran.
“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” he wrote, adding: “BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”
The endorsement comes after Trump had earlier indicated that he would prefer to stay out of Israel’s election. In August, he said, “I think it’s most appropriate for me to stay out of Israeli elections, but I may endorse somebody."
Israelis will vote on October 27 to elect the 120-member Knesset. According to the Times of Israel, the party system means that the leader who can assemble a coalition with sufficient parliamentary support is positioned to become prime minister; a majority generally requires 61 seats.
Around 7.33 million Israelis are eligible to vote in the election, accounting for 71.15 per cent of the country’s population of 10.3 million. In the 2022 election, 70.63 per cent of eligible voters cast their ballots.
Netanyahu, who leads the Likud party, faces a challenge from opposition parties, with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party among the key contenders, according to recent polling. Apart from Bruno Fernandes, who scored a hat-trick against Ipswich in August, no-one else in Michael Carrick's squad has scored more than one.
But it's meagre fare. It is true to say Manchester United did reasonably well in their 1-1 draw at Leeds United, just as they did at Atletico Madrid on Tuesday after conceding inside the first minute.
Carrick told BBC Radio 5 Live afterwards he "had the headphones on" this week so he hasn't heard the external noise created by Lisandro Martinez's rant.
However, he knows his side have to win matches at some point.
That is six without a victory now, the worst run since 2018-19, when form nosedived after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was confirmed as permanent manager.
"Because they haven't lost at Leeds, we're thinking United have done all right," said former Liverpool and England defender Jamie Carragher on Sky Sports.
"But in some ways that is a negative. We are dropping the standards. We shouldn't really be talking about Manchester United like that."
A fresh start for Man Utd?
After the corresponding fixture last season, Ruben Amorim gave the explosive press conference that triggered his dismissal within 24 hours.
This time, it was Lisandro Martinez who lit the touchpaper before the game, criticising sporting director Jason Wilcox and the United hierarchy for failing, in his view, to recruit effectively during the summer.
Wilcox was in the stands at Elland Road, while Martinez started the game following his apology for the timing and forum of his attack rather than the words themselves.
To highlight the general view that United failed Carrick by not bringing in competition for Luke Shaw at left-back, Diogo Dalot became the fifth different player to start in that position this season.
It remains to be seen if Shaw will be fit enough for Wednesday's Champions League trip to Serie A outfit Como, but the repeated changes cannot be helping Carrick.
Martinez went off at half-time with a thigh injury, and such is the delicate nature of Matthijs de Ligt's fitness after almost 11 months out with a back complaint, Carrick preferred to bring on full-back Noussair Mazraoui rather than the Netherlands international.
Carrick's side ended the game 13th in the Premier League table, with the possibility they might drop further before the match round is complete.
Unlike Amorim, Carrick found it easy to come up with a positive spin on the present situation.
"It felt like a bit of a fresh start today, to be honest, with where we're at - accepting it and doing something about it," Carrick said.
"I'm not accepting it as everything's great by any stretch. I'm realistic with that.
"But sometimes you do struggle. Sometimes there's a bit where you have to find a way through.
"There has been a cycle at times here over a period of time when it can go in different directions. We've got to be stable enough to keep doing the right things. We're more than capable of winning football matches.
"I understand the situation doesn't look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I've got no doubts that we can go on a good run."
Mbeumo's sacrifice
Mbeumo's performance wasn't flawless by any means.

But in a campaign when so many of Carrick's attacking players are struggling – skipper Fernandes has been a shadow of the player who broke the Premier League assists record last season even though the United boss said the Portuguese was 'absolutely fine' – Mbeumo's performances have been vital.
Their importance has been heightened by the continued absence of striker Benjamin Sesko with a shin injury.
Mbeumo spent the first few games on the right of United's attack when Amad Diallo was ruled out by injury. When Amad returned, Mbeumo moved into the number nine role.
At Elland Road he was shifted again, to the left as Fernandes played more through the middle.

"When you are the kind of player who can be very good in a lot of positions, managers will always say: 'Can you do this? Can you do that?'" former Red Devils striker Dion Dublin told BBC Sport.

Carrick was even more effusive in his praise.

People with longCOVID, where symptoms persist after recovery from an acute Covid-19 infection, may have distinct differences in the mix of bacteria living in their mouths and lungs, research has shown.
The differences in the lung microbiome are linked to respiratory symptoms, as well as the cognitive and digestive problems known to occur in longCOVID, researchers said.
The findings, published in the European Respiratory Journal, may contribute towards understanding why some people develop long COVID and point to new ways to treat the condition, they said.
"Prior studies have shown some changes in the gut microbiome with long COVID, but Covid is a lung disease and so it makes sense to look to see if the lung microbiome is changed in long COVID," lead author Daniela Alferes de Lima Headley from the University of Dundee, UK, said.
"We know that millions of people worldwide are still affected by long COVID and its cause is still unknown. Long Covid affects multiple organs. The microbiome is important to maintain health throughout the body, so it is a strong candidate for something that may contribute to long COVID," she said.
The study examined 771 people treated for Covid-19 at one of 38 UK hospitals between February 2020 and March 2021.
The participants were divided into four groups based on how bad their symptoms were five months after being discharged from hospital, ranging from 'very severe' with serious physical, mental, and cognitive impairments to 'mild', with few symptoms and good recovery.
Six months after hospital discharge, samples were collected from patients' mouths through saliva and from their lungs through sputum. DNA sequencing was used to identify the microbes present.
By analysing the variety and quantities of microbes and comparing them with patients' symptoms, researchers found that people with very severe long COVID had marked differences in their oral and lung microbiomes compared with those who did not have severe long COVID.
The results also revealed differences linked to specific symptoms, including reduced lung function, in which the lungs cannot hold as much air as normal or air cannot flow in and out as easily.
The researchers also found differences in the mouth and lungs microbiome between people with varying neurocognitive symptoms -- including 'brain fog', difficulties with memory, attention and concentration -- and gut symptoms, including pain, nausea, diarrhoea and loss of appetite.
Among the changes associated with long-COVID symptoms, was an over-abundance of bacteria that produce lactic acid, which was also linked to signs of inflammation found in samples of patients' blood.
Lead researcher James Chalmers, chair of respiratory research at the University of Dundee, UK, said, "People who had the worst symptoms five to six months after COVID infection had big changes in the microbiome in their mouth and lungs."
"We also found that changes in the airway microbiome were linked not just to lung problems, but also to symptoms like brain fog and gut symptoms, suggesting the lung microbiome could have effects on health more broadly," he said.

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for “heinous” crimes from 18 to 16, reversing a longstanding policy in what is widely seen as a desperate electoral gambit.
The U-turn, which Lula announced during a Thursday night interview with TV Globo, comes with the presidential runoff in just over a week. The incumbent faces an uphill battle to overturn the first-round victory of his opponent, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who remains slightly ahead at the polls.
Both the senator and his father, the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, have long supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility – they want it reduced to 14 rather than 16 – but Lula and his party have always opposed the change.
After repeated opinion polls, the latest of them this week, showed that 80% of the population supports lowering the age, Lula said: “My view, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any and every heinous crime, I am in favour of lowering the age.”
He answered “yes” when the reporter asked whether he meant lowering it to 16.
The list of crimes classified as “heinous” under Brazilian law is extensive, ranging from murder and rape to the falsification of medicines and drug trafficking – the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving prison sentences in Brazil were incarcerated.
Human rights organisations and security experts have long criticised proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, arguing that they do little to tackle violence while increasing recruitment into organised crime in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons.
On Thursday, before Lula’s interview, the proposal had been discussed in the senate. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation, had criticised it for “not addressing the causes of violence”, adding that placing young people “prematurely in the prison system tends to deepen cycles of violence and exclusion, undermining their rehabilitation”.
The columnist Josias de Souza wrote in his UOL column that, by reversing his longstanding position, Lula “decided to change himself. It was no ordinary transformation. On public security, Lula turned himself inside out. He began defending what he had always rejected.”
The incumbent has doubled down in recent days in an effort to overturn Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead by appealing to independents and undecided voters. He has secured congressional approval for a shorter working week – a proposal on which Bolsonaro himself U-turned and decided to support at the last minute, when it appeared ready to pass – and debt relief for microentrepreneurs, as well as promising free public transport on weekends.
