A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?
- Published
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.
Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.
But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.
Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.
That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.
Morocco never found the requisite finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.
For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.
The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.
At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.
"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".
"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.
"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."

  - Published8 hours ago
From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.
He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.
And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.
Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.
The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.
President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.
Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.
"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."
Why is Rwanda a controversial choice?
Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.
Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.
The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.
But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.
The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.
Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.
Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.
F1 is not blind to such issues. Its own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders to address any issues that arise.
It also says it focuses its efforts "in relation to those areas which are within our own direct influence".
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."

Bolt comparisons a 'privilege' - Dambile
- Published
Commonwealth 200m champion Sinesipho Dambile says it is a "privilege" to be compared with Jamaican great Usain Bolt as he looks to establish himself among the world's leading sprinters.
The South African has enjoyed a breakthrough season, producing a string of impressive performances and underlining his credentials as one of Africa's emerging track stars.
Speaking to the Warm Up Track podcast, the 24-year-old revealed that he "enjoys the pressure" that comes with being mentioned alongside the fastest man in history.
"Pressure is a privilege," he said. "I love it because that's where I excel."
Dambile recalls meeting the eight-time Olympic champion at the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, where the Jamaican offered him some advice.
"For Bolt, charisma naturally goes to him. Being able to meet him in person last year in Tokyo, he said: 'Please make sure you enjoy this thing'.
"That, until this day, still stuck with me."
Victory at last year's South African national championships secured Dambile's place in Tokyo, where he finished eighth in the 200m final, having set a new personal best of 19.97 seconds in the semi-finals.
That time was broken this season as Dambile accelerated his development.
June's Diamond League meeting in Doha saw him clock 19.74 seconds - the fourth-fastest time recorded by any athlete in 2026.
He went on to finish second behind the USA's Kenny Bednarek, but ahead of Botswana's 2024 Olympic champion Letsile Tebogo, in last month's Diamond League final in Brussels, while he was fourth in the inaugural Ultimate Championships.
However, the year's high point was undoubtedly the Commonwealth gold medal won in Birmingham in July, a result which made him the first South African to win the event.
While it is clear the 200m remains Dambile's principal event, he is "mentally willing to put in the work" to mimic Bolt, who likewise began his career specialising in the longer distance before going on to also dominate the 100m.
"He (Bolt) paved the way," Dambile said.
"I spoke to my team a couple of times and I was like, 'I want you guys to count me in on the 100m'.
"I want to do both. I know I'm going to be successful."
Akani Simbine's mentor role
A relaxed character, Dambile insists he will follow Bolt's advice to enjoy his time on the track, promising that fans will "get more of my personality" in future.
"I've never been a loud person, trying to bring attention to me," he said, contrasting his approach to the brash showmanship of Olympic 100m champion Noah Lyles.
"I'm always smiling out there, I'm always looking at the crowd, looking at the kids, and that's just me.
"I just want to go out there and do my thing, to make sure that everybody enjoys the show."
Dambile's success has coincided with a growing sense of belief within South African sprinting.
He was part of the quartet that won 4x100m gold at the World Relays in Guangzhou last year, running alongside team-mates Bayanda Walaza, Bradley Nkoana and Akani Simbine.
"We go as a squad, so we have that little bit of energy," Dambile said when explaining how the group's camaraderie has played an important role in their success.
"We pump each other up because we're going for the one thing - doing it for our country.
"The biggest sport in our country is rugby, so you get the Springboks going there winning the World Cup and we wanted to have the same feeling."
The influence of the experienced Simbine has been crucial.
The 2018 Commonwealth 100m champion finally landed an Olympic medal at Paris 2024, picking up silver in the 4x100m relay, having agonisingly finished fourth in the individual 100m finals in both the French capital and at the 2020 Games in Tokyo.
"He's made all the finals. He's been there. He's been the guy. He's been one of the best sprinters in the world," said Dambile.
"So when someone like that from home can do it, we also start to believe that it's actually possible to do it."

"It was so much relief because what I did was not just a small thing," he explained.
"It was huge, especially for myself [and] the country of South Africa. My emotions were all over the place.
"I just pushed through everything and when I was in that moment, I knew I deserved it because of the amount of work I've put in."
A double medallist at the 2021 Under-20 World Championships in Nairobi, Dambile's progression from promising junior to established senior athlete has not, however, been straightforward, with injury curtailing much of his 2024 season.
This year's success has changed things.
"It's easier to recognise me in the country now with me winning the Commonwealth," he explained.
"A bit of fame now - you can see people when they talk about you. It's like I've been experiencing beautiful things happening."
Things could get even better with plans already being made for next year's World Championships in Beijing and the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.
"We've already set up a map towards that," he said.
"We definitely know how important it's going to be over the next two years.
"I want to be the best 200m athlete the sport has ever seen.
"I need to make sure that I have the World Championship [and] Olympic title. I want to do things that have never been done in my country."

Plex, which made a name for itself by letting users share movies they own, is now helping sell movie theater tickets. The company is looking to monetize its content-discovery capabilities and expand its business beyond its media server software.
Plex partnered with Fandango, which has sold movie tickets since 2000, to drive ticket sales from people searching for movies to stream. Per the announcement:
Starting today, Plex users in the US will see a Fandango ticketing option on title pages for movies currently playing in theaters, allowing them to click through to Fandango to find showtimes and purchase tickets. The integration also enables direct attribution through Kochava, giving studios and advertisers greater visibility into how campaigns and audience engagement translate into ticket sales.
Fandango says it sells tickets for 31,000 movie theater screens in the US. The Plex deal allows it to leverage data from Plex’s streaming service (Plex claims users of the service “make more than 100 million streaming decisions each month”), including “ratings and cross-platform viewing” to gain “insight into audience intent,” the announcement said.
“Plex has a unique view into what movie fans are actively considering, from what they’re searching for to what they’re watching across services,” Jerramy Hainline, executive vice president at Fandango, said in a statement. “By connecting those discovery signals with Fandango ticketing, we’re making it easier for fans to turn that interest into a trip to the theater, while giving studios and advertisers a more direct, measurable path to ticket sales.”

Nagoya – Toyota plans to make all of its roughly 50 vehicle models software-defined vehicles by 2030, company officials have said.
The move will allow all Toyota vehicles to have their functionality enhanced through software updates. The decision is aimed at establishing a business model under which its software platform is installed in about 10 million new vehicles produced worldwide each year, generating revenue through software update fees after delivery.
The Japanese automaker first adopted its Arene in-vehicle software platform in the RAV4 SUV launched in 2025. It plans to expand the number of models equipped with Arene by 2030 and provide the platform to partner automakers afterward, the officials said Friday.
The development of software-defined vehicles is currently led by Tesla and Chinese automakers. Competition is also intensifying in Japan, with Honda and Nissan agreeing to jointly develop in-vehicle software.

Pope Leo XIV leaves hospital days after lung cancer surgery
Pope Leo XIV left Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican after doctors said he was well enough to be discharged following surgery that removed part of his right lung.
The Vatican press office released a statement outlining details from Dr. Luigi Carbone,the Pope's personal physician, and Professor Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli's chief of thoracic surgery who led the team that operated on Leo. The two doctors said the pope had undergone blood tests and a chest X-ray that morning, with the results confirming his clinical condition meant he could leave hospital.
They said he was expected to lead the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment on Sunday.Video showed Leo waving to well-wishers outside the hospital as he walked out without physical support, flanked by officials and security guards in dark suits.
Before leaving, the pope had celebrated Mass in a room set aside for that purpose on the hospital's 10th floor, according to the press office.
Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said "the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week." Leo's discharge came on his fifth day in hospital and was sooner than had been expected at the time of the operation's announcement.
A diagnosis made public
Leo, 71, had told crowds in St. Peter's Square last Sunday that doctors had discovered a "localized nodule" in his lung at a "very early stage."
"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," he said.
The surgery on Tuesday went further than the nodule, however, with surgeons using a video-assisted technique to remove the lower lobe of the pope's right lung in an operation that lasted about 90 minutes. His doctors said lung tissue examined afterward confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma. With adenocarcinoma making up about 40% of all lung cancers in the U.S., it is the nation's most common form of lung cancer, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.
That is true among nonsmokers too, according to Dr. Otis Brawley, an oncologist at Johns Hopkins University and former chief medical and scientific officer of the American Cancer Society.
Leo is not known to have smoked, but cancer does run in his family. His mother, Mildred, died of cancer in 1990, and on Tuesday the Vatican announced that his older brother Louis, who lives in Florida, has been hospitalized with a form of cancer.
Encouraging signs
Doctors not involved in the pope's care say the treatment so far points to a cancer that has been caught early.
"The fact that surgery was the first tool that they utilized is a really good sign," Dr. Vin Gupta, a pulmonologist and board member of the American Lung Association, told NPR. "It suggests that they think this is early stage."
Gupta said the fact that doctors removed a larger portion of the lung than first announced is not in itself a bad sign. "People have parts of their lungs removed all the time for all sorts of reasons, and they recover just fine," he said. "And in his case, he's pretty robust at baseline from a health standpoint."
Leo still exercises regularly, playing tennis each week with his personal secretary and riding horses at Castel Gandolfo, the papal retreat to the south of Rome.
The Vatican has not announced any further treatment.
Travels ahead
Leo's office has cleared his public schedule until at least Oct. 20. His next major international trip, set for early November, includes Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he lived on and off for two decades and holds citizenship.
"He had a minimally invasive surgery," said Dr. Jonathan Villena Vargas, a cardiothoracic surgeon at Weill Cornell Medical Center in New York City. "Because we do this all the time, most patients are allowed to travel about two weeks after the surgery."
Brawley from Johns Hopkins agreed. "I think he can do it," he said, adding that patients in good physical shape who have this type of procedure "very frequently are back to normal in seven to 10 days."

SUNDAY AM Writethru after Saturday update: Refresh for more updates… It’s a healthy third weekend at the October box office even with a bellyflop in 20th Century Studio’s $60M Whalefall in the mix which is only swallowing a $8M opening. Paramount/Legendary/Capcom’s Street Fighter is doing what it’s supposed to do with a $31M start, largely pulling in an older dude demo over 35 at 45% (that’s what’s walloping Whalefall‘s business, the overlap in male demos).
But the scene stealer again this year after Backrooms (and even Primetime) is A24 with their 3 hour Elizabeth Holmes non-fiction title You Can See Everything which is now coming in with a $15M opening at 855 screens (and potentially higher by tomorrow), easily the second best opening ever for a documentary at the box office after 2004’s Fahrenheit 9/11 ($23.9M). Eight years after the tech blood analysis company Theranos cratered due to controversy, and four years after Hulu’s Emmy winning Amanda Seyfried starring limited series, The Dropout, who knew there was still this much interest in Holmes? Well, A24, you certainly seduced everyone with your sneaky secret world premiere mic drop at Telluride.
Meanwhile, the HBO hatched Canadian reality comedy wisenheimer Nathan Fielder was the belle of the ball last night at the Academy Museum Gala last night (forget about the Kardashians and Jacob Elordi) surrounding by Gen Z cool kids Curry Barker, Inde Navarette, and Kane Parsons (the YouTube sketch born Barker is a massive Fielder fan). In regards to big box office to limited theatrical play, the success here with Fielder and You Can See Everything is reminiscent to that of Sacha Baron Cohen when he shot out of a cannon in early November 2006 with Borat which bowed to $26.4M on 837 theaters for a $31,6K theater average. You Can See Everything‘s per theater average is $17,5K. In fact, the opening here for You Can See Everything is the biggest for a title under 1,000 engagements since Borat.
Watch on Deadline
We understand that there’s been over 2,000 sellouts so far this weekend with lines around the block for You Can See Everything at the Village East in NYC as well as the Belcourt in Nashville, Tenn. See below The constant chorus heard here in LA is “you can’t get a ticket.”
There is no CinemaScore on You Can See Everything because it’s under 1,000 screens. The plan here for A24 was to keep this nice, tight and limited to get into the cultural ether before ripping the band-aid off wider next weekend. “Who knows where this will go,” says one box office source this AM.
A 4.8 on Letterboxd is the highest ever recorded for the platform. Definite recommend is an unprecedented on Screen Engine/Rentrak’s PostTrak with 91% for a documentary — that’s the type of scores successful Marvel movies like Black Panther would put up back in the day. Where is my flying car? The enduring question sort of, kind of, might have an answer: In McGregor, Texas.
On Thursday, Tesla showed off a version of its new Roadster 2 sports car in a demonstration at SpaceX’s rocket development testing facility. And in its own way, with an awkward jerking maneuver, the Roadster flew a few dozen feet. The vehicle, which doesn’t yet have a price but is likely to be very expensive, is slated to go into production in 2028. The vehicle didn’t have a human occupant during the demo “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Tesla CEO Elon Musk said at the event.
Tesla’s Roadster “sort of, kind of, might” be an actual flying car because aviation experts say legally catching air in the vehicle will likely involve plenty of government permissions and red tape.
“The [Federal Aviation Administration] has jurisdiction over any machine that leaves the surface of the earth,” says Scott Miller, an airline pilot and a lecturer in the Aviation and Technology program at San José State University. The vehicle “is going to introduce a whole set of regulatory issues.”
At the event Thursday, Musk acknowledged as much. “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions," he said. “This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car.”
The FAA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Any flying vehicle that weighs more than 250 or so pounds would need to go through an FAA approval process and require clearance to operate in the national airspace, says Michael McCormick, a former FAA official who now heads the Air Traffic Management program at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Getting that certification, he predicts, could take “at least a year.” Your standard drivers license, meanwhile, wouldn’t cut it. Any Tesla owner piloting such a vehicle would likely have to obtain a recreational aviation license.
Actually taking off and landing the Roadster 2 would likely present its own set of issues. Most states require aircraft to take off from airports or designated helipads. Launching from the road to the air would fall under state or local rules, says Miller, and many places do not look kindly on the concept of sudden aircraft intrusions on their streets and highways. That’s the reason “it’s pretty rare to be able to jump in a helicopter and land at your favorite steakhouse to have a steak,” he says. Drivers might only be able to truly operate the vehicle on a large, private piece of land.
The FAA today is working on rules, regulations, and pilot projects around another sort of “flying car,” or what’s more commonly known as an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) vehicle. These aircraft use several smaller electric motors and propellers to carry up to four passengers between 20 and 150 miles, sometimes autonomously. The companies building the technology envision them taking off from small, local “vertipads,” allowing riders to skip urban traffic by floating above the fray.
The Trump administration this year launched a limited, three-year pilot project using the aircraft, where companies are able to test the tech in several states. It has taken years for the companies to receive certifications from the federal government.
When it comes to the Roadster 2, there are practical questions, too. True flying cars have struggled to take off because of the physics-led contradiction at the heart of the idea. What makes a car safe and durable enough to operate on roads is weight. But “weight is the enemy of an airplane,” says Miller. “Flying cars haven’t been able to find that balance of power versus weight.”
Still, Miller found himself impressed by Thursday’s demo. “If this does make it into production, that is a truly impressive engineering and production feat,” he says.

From Delhi to Dehradun, Congress intensifies protests seeking fair probe in Ankita Bhandari murder case
Appointment of BJP's Dushyant Gautam as Sikkim governor amid the ongoing CBI probe into the alleged 'VIP' angle Ankita Bhandari murder case has stirred a row.
Several people were reportedly detained outside Delhi's Patiala House Court on Sunday after a crowd, including Congress leaders, held a protest demanding a transparent and monitored investigation in the 2022 murder of Ankita Bhandari.
The protesters were later detained by Delhi Police, news agency ANI reported.
Fresh row in Ankita Bhandari murder case
Ankita, a 19-year-old receptionist at a resort in Uttarakhand was found dead near Rishikesh in September 2022. Protests demanding justice reignited following the appointment of BJP leader Dushyant Gautam as Sikkim governor amid the ongoing CBI investigation into the alleged 'VIP' angle in the murder case.
Gautam's appointment has triggered fresh row, with opposition parties alleging that he was the 'VIP' whose role is under scrutiny in the case, though allegations have not been established.
The Congress also held a candle march in Dehradun, Uttarakhand on Saturday to protest the appointment of BJP's Gautam as Sikkim governor, alleging that it raises questions amid a CBI investigation into the alleged 'VIP' angle in the 2022 murder of Ankita Bhandari.
The march, led by Congress general secretary and state in-charge Kumari Selja and state unit president Ganesh Godiyal, began at the state party headquarters on Rajpur Road, passed through Ghantaghar and returned to the starting point, news agency PTI reported.
Former chief minister Harish Rawat, Leader of the Opposition in the state assembly Yashpal Arya, and other leaders of the Uttarakhand Congress, including Mahila Congress president Jyoti Rautela, and several legislators and former MLAs participated in the march.
Congress' student wing National Students' Union of India (NSUI) also organised a candle march in Delhi demanding justice for Ankita Bhandari and questioned the appointment of a person with a pending investigation as Sikkim Governor.
The protest march was led by NSUI national president Vinod Jakhar amid heavy security presence. He questioned the BJP's claims of women's empowerment and its commitment to women's safety and dignity, the organisation's statement said.
Raising concerns over the appointment of a person -- against whom an investigation is still underway -- as Governor of Sikkim, Jakhar said, "The way the BJP speaks about 'Nari Vandan', the daughters of this country are watching, and the entire country is witnessing how you are appointing someone as a Governor when an investigation against him is still underway."
Ongoing CBI probe and ‘VIP’ role
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has registered a case against unknown persons to investigate the alleged role of a 'VIP' in the murder.The CBI probe was ordered by Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami in January this year on the demand of Ankita's parents after audio and video clips purportedly indicating the involvement of a 'VIP' circulated on social media.
The clips were circulated by actress Urmila Sanawar, who has claimed to be the wife of former BJP MLA Suresh Rathore.
On Sunday, a team of CBI officials arrived at the residence of Urmila Sanawar in connection with the Ankita Bhandari case, news agency ANI reported. Ankita was murdered by resort owner Pulkit Arya and two of his employees, all of whom have been sentenced to life imprisonment.

The year 2026 has been disappointing for Pan-India films, but Jailer 2 has emerged as a major exception. The Rajinikanth starrer opened with a bang and the extraordinary response has ensured that it continues to hold strongly across the country. In the North, the Tamil version has performed particularly well, with encouraging occupancy in single screens and non-national multiplexes despite the film not releasing in national multiplex chains in any language.
Jailer 2 becomes the FIRST South film to get midnight shows in North India in its original language; cinemas replace Nayyi Navelli, Prahaar with Rajinikanth starrer’s Hindi version
The response has been so overwhelming that MovieMax organised midnight shows of Jailer 2 at two of its properties – MovieMax Huma in Kanjurmarg, Mumbai, and MovieMax Gold in Kalyani Nagar, Pune. While shows after midnight have become increasingly common in the post-pandemic era, exhibition sources claim that Jailer 2 is the first South film to achieve this distinction in the North Indian market after its release, that too in its original language. Interestingly, midnight shows are usually held in weekends but MovieMax Gold will also play the 1:45 am show of Jailer 2 on Monday, October 19.
Meanwhile, the Hindi version, Rajini: The Jailer 2, is also enjoying an impressive run. The film collected Rs. 2.56 crores on Thursday, October 15, followed by Rs. 2.41 crores on Friday. Collections jumped to Rs. 3.63 crores on Saturday, while Sunday's earnings are expected to touch the Rs. 4 crore mark. Though the numbers may appear modest, they are significant considering that the film hasn't been released in national multiplex chains like PVR INOX, Cinepolis and Miraj. This is due to its four-week OTT window, as national chains generally insist on an eight-week gap between theatrical and streaming releases.
A trade source told Bollywood Hungama, “Initially, Rajini: The Jailer 2 had limited showcasing because of its absence from national chains. Moreover, it had to share screens with new releases like Prahaar and Nayyi Navelli, as well as the successful holdover release, Drishyam The Conclusion. However, the response to Jailer 2 has been superb, while Nayyi Navelli has failed to impress. Prahaar has excellent word of mouth, but unfortunately, it's attracting the elite multiplex audience largely.”
The source continued, “The demand for Rajini: The Jailer 2 is huge. With Nayyi Navelli and Prahaar underperforming, several cinemas have started replacing their shows with those of the Rajinikanth starrer.”
Mumbai's Citylight cinema, for instance, has dropped Nayyi Navelli, the Marathi film Sohla and even Drishyam The Conclusion from Monday, October 19. Instead, it will play two shows each of Prahaar and Rajini: The Jailer 2. The source explained, “Prahaar is a local story and has found an audience in Mumbai. Hence, it has managed to retain shows in certain theatres where its performance has been encouraging. However, in several centres, especially in North India, even Prahaar has lost shows to Jailer 2.”
The growing demand for Rajini: The Jailer 2 is also reflected in its rapidly expanding show count. On Thursday, the Hindi version had 1,730 shows across the country. This number nearly doubled to 3,266 on Friday before rising further to 3,690 on Saturday.
Interestingly, several cinemas have decided to devote almost their entire showcasing to Jailer 2. For instance, Maratha Mandir cinema will play three shows daily of the Hindi version, while Kasturba in Malad will also screen three Hindi shows along with one show of the Tamil version.
The source added, “Rajini: The Jailer 2 can now comfortably continue its theatrical run until Diwali. Rajinikanth's previous release, Coolie (2025), collected Rs. 34 crores in its Hindi lifetime (it had a release in national chains). Jailer 2 should aim to surpass this figure, which will be a feat, especially considering that it will achieve these numbers without any support from national multiplexes.”
An industry insider commented, “Monday, October 19, will be almost like a holiday, while Dussehra will be celebrated on Tuesday, October 20. Rajini: The Jailer 2 can perform exceptionally well on both days. Dubbed action films have traditionally found a strong audience in Gujarat, but the territory is yet to come on board fully as patrons are currently occupied with Navratri celebrations. Expect collections to zoom in Gujarat from October 20 or 21.”

Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian and US surfers in Mexico
- Published
A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each.
The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial.
The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.
The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".
The convicted killers' full names were not given for legal reasons, meaning they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús.
In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.
The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.
At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.
Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.
The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them.
Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

The Rejinagar and Nandigram by-elections in West Bengal concluded on October 9, Friday, with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) clinching victory in both seats. BJP’s Shankharavh Sarkar won in Rejinagar and Hasirani Rath won the Nandigram seat.
Polling in both the assemblies were, however, marred by allegations of electoral malpractices, with the Congress demanding repolling.
Amid these allegations, digital censorship emerged as another flashpoint, with social media content documenting alleged electoral malpractice and vote rigging being restricted in India. The restrictions also added to concerns over the growing suppression of online criticism of the ruling party. For the past couple of months, Alt News has reported extensively on this social media censorship frenzy in India.
On October 7, the Facebook page of the Murshidabad district wing of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress (@DCCMurshidabad) was restricted under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules. The page remains unavailable at the tome of this article being written.

On the same day, prominent local news outlet NBTV Bangla’s (@nbtvbngla) Facebook page was also restricted in India for seven days following the same notification. With over five lakh followers, the outlet reported critically on issues of the government or law enforcement in the context of the Nandigram and Rejinagar bypolls.
Alt News learnt that the two videos uploaded by the Facebook page of NBTV which were restricted in India directly addressed allegations of voting malpractices in the Rejinagar by-election.
The first of the two videos — both of which are still accessible on Instagram — shows a woman claiming that voters in Rejinagar were being intimidated away from the polling booths. A man also appears in this video, alleging that not even 10 voters had been able to cast their votes.
View this post on Instagram
Another video shows allegations being levelled by voters of the Mirzapur Gram Panchayat area in Rejinagar. “Who I choose to vote for is entirely my own decision. They marked our fingers with ink and sent us home, even though we had not yet cast our votes,” a man appearing in the video claims.
View this post on Instagram
“It is not the first time this has happened. Several of our social media posts have been restricted in the past,” Zeba Noshin, a reporter at NBTV, told Alt News.
Notably, the notices received by Congress’ Murshidabad district page and NBTV Bangla state that the account had been restricted pursuant to legal requirements. This indicates that the restrictions followed a legal request or official complaint concerning the content on these pages, rather than being flagged by Meta’s own content-moderation process.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
A video uploaded on Facebook by Bengali digital media outlet Inscript.me was restricted in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000 on the day of the polls, October 6. A representative of the platform told Alt News that the banned video was regarding allegations of rigging in Rejinagar.
The title of the video visible on the notice sent by Meta reads, “People of Rejinagar allege rigging in byelection”.
On October 9, another Facebook post by Inscript.me, a report on Rahul Gandhi’s detainment by Delhi Police during the protests demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, was also restricted.
A Facebook user named Diya Maity also alleged that her page with close to 2.5 lakh followers had been restricted for seven days. She was also posting content on the alleged election rigging in the Rejinagar constituency.
Rigging, Malpractices & Intimidation: Opposition
The October 6 bypolls were necessitated in Murshidabad’s Rejinagar and East Medinipur’s Nandigram, after AJUP chief Humayun Kabir and Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari chose to vacate these two seats respectively, having secured victory in two constituencies apiece.
Suvendu Adhikari’s home constituency, Nandigram has a Muslim population of around 27 per cent. He vacated this seat, and retained Bhabanipur, where he defeated former chief minister Mamata Banerjee.
The demography is entirely different in Rejinagar, with Muslims accounting for around 69 per cent of its electorate. Kabir won both Nowda and Rejinagar and subsequently vacated the latter, where his victory margin was more than 58,000 votes. His son, Golam Nabi Azad, was contesting the seat vacated by him.
Opposition leaders repeatedly alleged that the BJP was manipulating votes and applying pressure tactics in the lead up to the polls. On the day of polling, the AJUP chief was taken into custody by the police after a heated altercation. He was released from the Rejinagar police station after spending 12 hours in custody.

Works well in a dark room or in daylight. Provides a brilliantly colorful video image. The projector itself packs amazing sound quality. Plenty of settings are available to tweak to get the perfect picture.
TIRED
Slight issues with auto-keystoning and height channel audio.
It takes a special home theater projector to get me to stick through a movie like Supergirl. Critics panned it for dark themes, and its visually dark tones make it literally tough to see. But when I used the AWOL Vision Aetherion Max to project it onto a 120-inch screen with Dolby Atmos sound blasting from every corner of my basement, the film looked stunning.
The Aetherion Max, with its precise picture-quality settings and sharp 4K clarity, provides an experience rivaling that of a movie theater. Supergirl might suffer from bad CGI and even worse dialog, but the projector's features, like Dark Detail and Enhanced Black Level, brought the film to life, making reds and blues pop with amazing vividness.
Priced at $4,499, this ultrashort throw model sits right next to the wall or projector screen. In some ways, it reminds me of the LG Micro RGB Evo television with highly adjustable picture-quality settings. Ultimately, though, I'm a fan of the Aetherion Max because it projects a breathtakingly colorful image.
An Engineering Marvel, Except for the Remote
Photograph: John Brandon
Photograph: John Brandon
Before taking stock of its powerhouse specs, I noticed the Aetherion Max's design. Shaped a bit like a Tesla Cybertruck, the silver projector has sharp edges that lend a modern look. The front of the machine (the side that faces you) has no buttons except a single white line that animates when you power it on—a detail I found to be distracting and then powered off. The other side (which faces the screen) is where you'll find three HDMI 2.1 ports (including one for eARC passthrough audio), a USB-A port for a local storage device, optical and 3.5mm audio-out ports, and a 1 GBps Ethernet port for wired streaming.
This model runs on Google TV, and that’s a relief because it meant setup only took a few minutes. Auto-keystoning with manual screen-size options worked just fine. There’s also a QR code you can use to automate keystone correction from your phone, but my room was too dark, and it didn't work for me. (AWOL Vision reps told me it should have worked fine even in a dark room like mine.)
The portable projector weighs 19.3 pounds—notably less than its 23-pound competitor Hisense XR10 Smart Projector (8/10, WIRED Recommends)—and I found it both easy to grip and move around between rooms. For wireless streaming, the Aetherion Max supports Wi-Fi 7, offering nice compatibility and speed. It also runs quite fast thanks to 8 GB of internal RAM and offers 128 GB of internal storage for storing content, though I relied mostly on streaming.
Unlike the highly rated Xgimi Titan Noir Max, the Aetherion Max's iris does not adjust dynamically as you watch content. But similar to the Hisense XR10, you can adjust picture-quality settings to match the room. For example, Dolby Vision Bright works best in a bright room, allowing the iris to let in more light.
For color accuracy, the projector hits 110 percent of the Rec. 2020 spec. That means if you watch a movie that meets that color spec, like Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 or Inside Out, you will see the entire color palette. AWOL Vision also lists the contrast ratio as 6,000:1 and lumens at 3,300 ISO, but—as I've learned from personal experience—those specs are not the final arbiter of picture quality. Many other factors come into play, including the darkness level of a room.
Photograph: John Brandon
The weak spot here is the remote, which is functional if not impressive. I like its large Home button that’s centered and easy to find in the dark without looking. There’s also a button for Google Gemini and convenient shortcuts for apps like Netflix. My main issue is with the volume buttons, placed just above the shortcuts, but small and hard to find. Only the upper half of the remote is backlit, which uselessly doesn't extend to all of the buttons, including volume.
Don’t Fear the Bright Sunshine
The Aetherion Max's ability to work in a brightly lit room blew me away throughout testing. I watched the movie Mayday on Apple TV+ from start to finish in broad daylight, projecting the image on a wall that measures nearly 16 feet diagonally. I didn't notice any contrast problems and could see nighttime scenes just fine. The slight warping on my wall distorted the image a bit, but that's to be expected of ultrashort throw models.
In my windowless testing room, with a full surround-sound system that even includes height channel speakers in the ceiling, the Aetherion Max performed even better. To test a projector's contrast ratio and brightness, I typically play dark scenes in the movies Awake and The Creator, and I've never seen the scenes look as great as they did when rendered by the Aetherion Max. I didn’t even have to tweak the picture-quality settings (and generally when I test these specs, such is not the case).
Dark scenes in House of the Dragon, which I streamed using the HBO Max app, did require some user intervention, though. A beach scene in the moonlight involving a mysterious dragon would be hard to render even on high-end home cinema projectors, but once I enabled Dark Detail and Enhanced Black Level, I could suddenly see everything clearly, just as the TV show creators intended.
Indeed, every time I ran into a slight issue with picture quality, I found a matching setting that solved the problem. In a dark hallway scene during the movie The Batman, gun flashes looked bright red and clear, but some amber tones on Batman looked a shade too dark. Once I switched to Dolby Vision Bright, I could easily make out the grimaces and muscle flexes. Some projectors look a bit out of focus on the edges, but that's not true with the Aetherion Max; in Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu on Disney+, a snowy scene showcased the extreme pixel clarity all the way to the ends of the screen.
Photograph: John Brandon
Photograph: John Brandon
For games, I tested NBA 2K27 with the new Nvidia GeForce driver on an Alienware Aurora gaming laptop. The jaw-dropping graphics, which use realistic lighting and details, made a convincing case for Anthony Edwards of the Minnesota Timberwolves being in my testing room. When I tried Onimusha: Way of the Sword on PC, I was equally blown away by the crisp graphics. At this larger size, with ultra-clear pixel depth across the entire screen, every samurai slash seemed more realistic. Great for gaming, the projector uses extremely low latency—just 1 millisecond—for no lag, graphical stuttering, or delays, allowing for quick controller responses.
Sound is strong on the projector itself. When I watched the movies Civil War and Unbroken via an Onkyo TX-RZ50 AV receiver, I felt I was in a movie theater. A slight glitch was that the audio cut out when I used height channel speakers for 7.1.2 sound (AWOL Vision is investigating why).
The Aetherion Max also passed demo-reel benchmarks with flying colors—for the most part. While scenes with flowers, white mist over a snowy mountain, water in the deep blue ocean, and two horses in a field looked mesmerizing and realistic, it was tough to make out dark trees on a dark background. The skin-tone test also yielded unimpressive results. I’m not sure why, but two faces looked way too similar in a group shot, and a few other tests showed a lack of tonal variety. Adjusting settings didn’t help. However, this detail didn’t heavily factor into my overall takeaway of the projector, since it's a subtle color benchmark.
The AWOL Vision Aetherion Max is ultimately an amazing projector: a rock star of color accuracy, with crisp pixel clarity across the entire image and superior contrast. While the price is in line with other high-end models, this is one seriously capable home cinema model.

For Czech developer David Konecny, Dreadline Express brings together a lifelong fascination with trains, psychological horror, and stories shaped by difficult choices. His debut game takes players aboard a train at the end of the world, where a distinctive card-based system lets them explore the lives of its varied passengers and see how their stories and fates unfold. Drawing inspiration from games like Duke Nukem 3D and SOMA, as well as films made by Ari Aster, Konecny has created an unsettling world that challenges players to trust their instincts and confront morally complicated decisions.
Below, Konecy spoke to Deadline about his journey into game development, childhood influences, and the challenge of giving players the freedom to discover its secrets.
DEADLINE: You’re a solo game developer in the Czech Republic; this is the first game that you’re putting out, right?
Watch on Deadline
DAVID KONECNY: The situation is a little more complicated. It’s a solo project, but I have some coworkers who help me with art and audio because those are areas where I’m not as fluent as I’d like to be. I’m still developing the art direction, giving them concepts, drawing level layouts, and providing inspiration. Then we discuss the results. Everything comes from my head, but they help me bring it to life.
It’s my first commercial game. I’ve made some free titles, participated in game jams, and worked on a lot of projects that never saw the light of day because something always went terribly wrong and I couldn’t finish them. But, yeah, this is the first one.
DEADLINE: You’ve also been working in software development as your main job. But how long have you been making games, and how did you get started?
KONECNY: When I was little, we didn’t have computers, and I kept begging my parents to buy me magazines about games. I read about them without having any way to play them. I would look at the images and imagine how the games worked. I begged my parents to get me a computer or a game console.
I was also a tech-savvy child and interested in anything technological, so I asked them to sign me up for a children’s programming group. That’s where I gradually started to understand how things worked. I made my first little games, including text adventures in HTML. Later, I went to university to study programming and software development. That’s my career now. Thanks to games, I’m a software developer, and I think I’m a good one [laughs].
There weren’t any universities for game development at the time, so there wasn’t a way to learn it as a main career. The two big centers of game development in the Czech Republic were studios such as Altar and Bohemia Interactive, which made games like Operation Flashpoint. They were nowhere near my city, so there was no way for me to learn anything there. That’s why I started working in software development as my main career. But I always wanted to make games, and making games is different from making regular software. I kept learning about games in my free time, always creating and writing something.
DEADLINE: What games did you play growing up that influenced how you think about game development?
KONECNY: The good thing was that every computer lab had a bunch of games installed on the computers. When the teacher wasn’t looking, we were all playing. I remember Warcraft II being a regular choice, but probably the most influential game for me was Duke Nukem 3D.
I really loved the world and all the little details that made the experience feel real. When you killed a monster, and it was under those doors that opened and closed, the door would crush the monster. When it opened again, you could see its innards stretched across the door. It was an immersive experience for me. I thought, “This is the best we can get. The game cannot be more realistic than this. This is it, guys. This is the stuff.”
I also loved how some levels changed. There was a level where you had to start a demolition, and the whole building collapsed, opening a new way forward. That was so innovative to me. Those experiences stayed with me, and I want to create a world that feels alive and real. That was huge for me.
DEADLINE: Let’s talk about Dreadline Express. It’s a train at the end of the world. When we spoke at Gamescom, you mentioned that people had compared it to Snowpiercer, although that wasn’t necessarily an inspiration you had in mind. Where did the idea originate, and how long had you been thinking about it?
KONECNY: There are a lot of inspirations, but I like trains. I think it all began when my great-grandmother used to take me to watch trains while she was looking after me. We’d go to an overpass and watch them from above. That’s one of my core memories.
The game itself came about during a period when I was having a crisis in game development. I stopped making games for two or three years and started writing short stories and novels. Nothing was ever published, but I was developing these stories, and eventually I came up with one about this train. I love trains, and I love Lovecraft. I also wanted to incorporate a totalitarian regime because it’s something that’s in our DNA as Czechs.
I put all these elements together and realized I wasn’t sure how I wanted the story to unfold, because everything seemed interesting and there were so many possible directions. The only logical decision was to make it a game so players could decide which path to take and which character’s story interested them most. That was the beginning of Dreadline Express. The card mechanics came later, and that’s a completely different story.
DEADLINE: Talk about the card mechanics. Players have a lot of control over what they discover, and this system is a distinctive way to approach storytelling. Why did you decide to use cards?
KONECNY: Originally, it came from Steam Trading Cards, the cards you get for playing games that you can sell or combine. It’s a dopamine mechanism that Steam has built in. I always found it a little strange. I wondered, “Why is it there? I’m playing games, and I don’t need another reward for playing because the game itself is a reward.” It’s not like you’re doing your taxes and get a card. That would be cool, actually. If you filled out your taxes and got something, that would be nice [laughs]. I started thinking about how to take these cards, which people obviously love collecting, and turn them into a proper game mechanic. Completing a full set feels good, but I wanted the cards to give players more than the satisfaction of unlocking something. I wanted them to provide options. That’s how the idea was born.
I wanted to create a gameplay loop where you get a card, discover something, and immediately start thinking: “OK, I have this new item, this new thing. How can I use it? What can I combine it with? What possibilities will it open up for me?”That’s why I chose cards. They’re cool; they let us create really nice illustrations, and a lot of love goes into them.
DEADLINE: Let’s talk about the art design, both the cards and the game itself. The characters have these angular pixelated features that give them an unsettling quality. What look were you and the art team going for, and why?
KONECNY: One consideration was that we’re not a huge team with a huge budget, so we need to make things quickly and work within our limitations. This PS1-style, low-resolution, pixelated graphics approach is great for horror because it leaves something to the player’s imagination. It suits these stories much better than photorealistic graphics do because players can fill in the gaps, making the experience more immersive.
I also really wanted the characters to be distinctive, so we went a little over the top with their designs. We gave them really sharp features, which become even more pronounced with that low-resolution style. You really see those edges, and that makes them more memorable. I wanted the characters to be a little horrifying. The idea was to show how the train had taken something from them, a part of their humanity. They’re sitting there, and you can see how crumbled they are and how they don’t blink.
DEADLINE: They look a little gothic and spooky. What did you want players to feel when they first encountered these characters?
KONECNY: I wanted players to feel a little afraid of the characters when they first meet them, when they stare at you with those dead eyes. Then, as you start talking to them and gradually understand their stories, I wanted you to find your way toward them. You might initially feel repulsed by them or genuinely afraid, but eventually you might feel sorry for them or find some connection with them.
DEADLINE: What other games, films or filmmakers influenced the horror in Dreadline Express?
KONECNY: I really love good psychological horror. Off the top of my head, I can think of Ari Aster’s Hereditary and Midsommar. The Menu is also great horror. I like it when it’s about the story rather than jump scares or a monster that’s simply bad because it’s bad. I love it when everything has layers.
We have antagonists on the train, of course, but even they have their own stories. I love the ambiguity of it, where nothing is entirely good or bad, and you have to decide for yourself. Another example is Hellraiser, because I really love the Cenobites. They’re not bad guys. They want to show you something incredible from their perspective, but it might not be so incredible for humans. It’s really interesting to look at something from different points of view. The psychological aspect is even more interesting than the body horror. If you look at something from different perspectives, it becomes really compelling. That’s what I wanted to put into this game.
In terms of games, Frictional Games is probably my favorite horror studio, especially because of SOMA. It’s psychological horror, and it connects to some of your internal fears. It makes you think about your life in different contexts. For me, it was a life-changing experience. I always wanted to make something that could stick in people’s minds and make them think about the game or the story after they finish it. That’s really important to me.
DEADLINE: What was the biggest challenge in developing the game, whether narratively, in terms of level design or otherwise?
KONECNY: The first thing is that I’m making a horror game in which you cannot die. That’s unusual compared with games like Resident Evil, Silent Hill and Dead Space. The biggest challenge, though, is that I’m putting a lot of trust in the player. I let them discover clues and figure out how to play for themselves. That’s a big part of the experience. Players need to feel clever, like, “I did this. I figured it out. The developer didn’t tell me anything, and I managed to find a way.”
It’s hard to strike the right balance. You want to provide just enough clues without making things too obvious. That was a huge challenge. I traveled with the game to different conventions and game development events for a year and a half, collecting data and asking people questions to find the right balance. That was a huge part of development. I hope I nailed it, but we’ll see.
DEADLINE: What do you hope players take away from Dreadline Express?
KONECNY: I hope they find a game that values their time, doesn’t overstay its welcome, and gives them exactly the experience they want to have. I’m especially looking forward to seeing players talk to each other about their different experiences with the game. I hope it creates conversations and discoveries, maybe even brings some people together. I’m excited about that sense of discovery.
Maybe someone will learn something about themselves based on the choices they make, who they sacrifice, or how they approach different situations. I think we have something quite big prepared for the ending, and I hope as many people as possible will really appreciate it. Maybe if it makes someone cry, I’ll be happy [laughs].
Dreadline Express is now available on Steam.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.
